articles.text: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that the rainstorm on Tuesday, March 21 downed at least 13 trees and left about 1,100 Piedmonters without power. “Most of the damage that occurred involved privately owned trees,” said Gonzales. While much of this damage happened in the eastern side of the city – on streets including La Salle, Huntleigh, Indian, Lexford, and Estates – trees were also down on Monte, Lower Grand, Sunnyside, Hazel Lane, and in Dracena Park. Public Works Maintenance Supervisor Nick Milosevich and his crew worked through the night on Tuesday, as reports kept coming in about trees that had fallen, many onto power lines. “We’re a small crew of four,” explained said Gonzales. “Almost everyone had been out since the storm, but on the initial day on Tuesday they all were out and remained working late. Two went home around midnight, and the other two worked all night.” On Grand Avenue a mammoth deodar cedar fell onto the roof of a house on the 1600 block, puncturing the roof, destroying a fence, and leaving a crater where the stump was unearthed. To make things worse, the couple who lived in the damaged home had recently purchased it and moved in the previous day. articles.text: After a three-year absence due to COVID, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. With the theme of “Maskarade,” guests are encouraged to show their creativity and wear bird-themed masks. Created in 1963, by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, the Bird Calling Contest grew into an annual event that over the decades has attracted national and international attention. The winners appeared for many years on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, and then on Late Night with David Letterman. A panel of judges has been selected to consider the merits of the contestants based upon authenticity of call, poise and delivery, and content of contestants’ introduction of their bird. The judges include: • Rosemary Orozco, Weather forecaster KTVU • Michael Poryes, Television Producer • Joe Fendel, 1991 Bird Calling Contest winner • Jamie Mockel, PHS English teacher • Irma Munoz, PHS Vice Principal Serving as celebrity judges will be Rosemary Orozco, a meteorologist at KTVU, and Michael Poryes, a 1982 PHS grad who created the popular television series “Hannah Montana.” Orozco taught at San Francisco State University and has worked as a meteorologist, journalist and news anchor for several stations. She also has worked as a model and has her own fashion line in San Francisco. Poryes is a three-time Emmy nominee who was an original member of the creative team that developed and launched “Saved by the Bell.” Joe Fendel was a four-time bird caller 1988-91. First-year PHS English Teacher Jamieson Mockel comes from a family of bird callers, including his brother. His mother, Peggy, helped Leonard Waxdeck with the show for many years. articles.text: There are threads that appear and reappear in our lives. Some we recognize and some may even give us pause. For me, newspapers have always been such a I was a paperboy during the early 1950s, and as I reflect on those days, I realize that my route took me out of my narrow world of school and friends to a world beyond the familiar, a neighborhood of large and small bungalows, most with one-car garages, listing wooden fences and squares of patchy lawns. I knew the people on my route, meaning those who subscribed to the paper. As for those who didn’t, after finishing my Sunday delivery, I’d work up the courage to knock on their screen doors. If they answered, well, we’d stand there, peering at one another through a scrim of wire mesh, and I’d ask if they might want to take the paper. Had they asked me, I would have been hard pressed to explain why they should subscribe. What I knew about the Oakland Tribune was that it consisted of sheets of white paper, blocked headlines, columns of words, the inside peppered with small and large ads for appliances, clothes and cars. As for all the stories above and below the fold, I never read a word. The paper was a huge part of my life and yet it wasn’t. I often rode my bike through Brookdale Park and I’d see older men sitting on benches, newspapers held open in front of them, reading I recall not long after I became a paperboy, passing by what must have been a union hall. Glancing through a large plate glass window I saw men, dressed in rough clothes, most wearing hats, seated on wooden benches, not unlike church pews, waiting for what I assume now was work. What caught my attention as I gazed through the window was that almost to a man they were reading newspapers, held like white sails, all lost in that day’s news, a haze of smoke from cigars, pipes and cigarettes drifting above them. I glanced at their faces, partly obscured by the papers, wondering who they were and I felt a momentary connection to them. Perhaps two or three were reading a paper I had delivered the day before. I glanced down at my hands and saw the familiar ink embedded in the crevices of my palms, a reminder of the 60 papers I folded earlier that afternoon. As years passed, the memories of my route and newspapers dimmed. I knew that they were referred to as “the press.” But I had no idea what that really meant: I had never seen massive rolls of newsprint, drums of ink, linotype machines, all resulting in the papers that sat upright on racks or on the counters of corner kiosks. As I grew older, I came to realize that their bold headlines marked moments, some greater than others. I will always remember the blocked black words, “PRESIDENT KENNEDY KILLED IN DALLAS,” seeming so breathtakingly final, conveying the wrenching grief that rippled across our country. It was the same with MLK and Bobby. I still recall when my awareness of newspapers shifted. I was in the Peace Corps stationed in Cartagena, Colombia. articles.text: Earlier this month the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD) voted to end the sale of new gas furnaces and gas water heaters as early as 2027. The rules are meant to reduce air pollution and target nitrogen oxides (NOx) from gas heating appliances, which can cause respiratory issues and smog. According to BAAQMD, up to 85 premature deaths caused by air pollution will be avoided each year due to the new rules. The appliance standard will also reduce greenhouse gas emissions. In Piedmont, residential buildings account for 49% of greenhouse gas emissions, with the overwhelming share of these emissions coming from natural gas used for heating and cooling. What does this mean for Piedmonters? After 2027, if your gas water heater breaks and cannot be repaired, you’ll need to replace it with an electric one. The same goes for gas furnaces starting in 2029. While heat pumps and heat pump water heaters can be costly upfront, many rebates are available to offset the price. Earlier this year, the City of Piedmont launched an electrification rebate program, which offers an $800 rebate for heat pump water heaters, a $750- $1,500 rebate for heat pumps, and a $500 rebate for panel upgrades. To learn more, visit the Rebates and Incentives page on the City’s Planning and Building Department website at bit.ly/3JSLwxQ. Rebates available from other organizations such as BayREN and California Energy Smart Homes can be stacked on top of the City’s rebates for maximum savings. Visit SwitchIsOn.org to see what rebates you qualify for. At the federal level, the High-Efficiency Electric Home Rebate Program, created by the Inflation Reduction Act, will provide an upfront rebate of up to $8,000 for heat pumps, a $1,750 rebate for heat pump water heaters, and a $4,000 rebate for electrical system upgrades. The program is anticipated to launch next year. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions. articles.text: As excavation work continues at the Piedmont Community Pool construction site, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that recent storms have delayed the original schedule by an estimated four weeks, mainly due to PG&E delays. He was optimistic that the contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, could work with the city to “mitigate the delay and gain time back.” With 335 working days (including adjustments for weather) assigned to Wickman when the project began on January 19, the project was originally estimated to finish in late spring or early summer in 2024. Excavation work is expected to continue into late spring and has been more difficult due to rainstorms as water accumulates in the holes cut in bedrock for the foundation of a new main and medium-sized pool. To prevent flooding, Gonzales said the contractors have been busy pumping the water out “through tanks, or to filter it through a series of what [the EPA] calls Best Management Practices. They don’t pump directly into storm drains.” However, the biggest storm-related challenge has been PG&E. As of March 10, pool work was Photos by Jay Russell Excavation work at the Piedmont Community Pool site, during a break in the recent rains already delayed until PG&E workers — who have themselves been delayed by rain damage response — pull meters and disconnect the power from the sites of former pool facility buildings. Gonzales said that as of Monday, March 27, PG&E still hadn’t arrived. “We expect a delay because PG&E workers have been so busy dealing with power shutoffs,” he said, Once they arrive after the storms, “I believe it’ll only take Soil removed and piled by an excavator at the pool site Excavation work continues between rainstorms on the Piedmont Community Pool. a day or two total. There’s one electric meter that went to the old Carriage House, and gas and electric meters at the old Pool House location.” On Thursday, March 23, the Public Works Department invited neighbors of approximately 48 homes to meet at the Recreation Department for a onemonth check-in of noise impacts. Although only three residents attended “it was a good opportunity to hear their concerns,” said Gonzales. Most of their concerns were minor and involved noise, traffic impacts, and contractor arrival and departure times. “We’ll certainly address them with the contractor,” Gonzales said, “and we have emphasized to residents that backup alarms [on contractor vehicles] have to be loud, as a safety measure to those nearby.” Community members can stay informed about pool construction and get direct updates about traffic, noise, and other impacts by subscribing to the City’s Community Pool Construction Updates email list at bit.ly/3SAmveF. In late June, 2021, the city chose the construction management firm Griffin Structures to serve as project manager for pool construction. Those with questions or comments about the pool project can contact Construction Manager George Sanen of Griffin Structures by email at gsanen@ griffinstructures.com, or by phone at 415-858-8582. Those with questions or comments about parking and traffic changes presented by the project can contact Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont. ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, March 30, in the Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Tickets are $55, with a reception at 6 p.m. and dinner and awards beginning at 7 p.m. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now, such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impacts also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver Award, the highest recognition a council can give a volunteer, will be presented to longtime Scout volunteer Chris Lee. He was chosen for outstanding leadership as council youth protection champion, as well as decades of volunteer service as a den leader, committee chair, board member (three terms) and service on the tree lot committee. “Scouting provides leadership opportunities for young people and teaches them a wide range of values including responsibility and giving back to the community,” said Lee. “It’s one of the best youth programs in the country.” When asked why he served as the council’s Youth Protection Champion, Lee answered, “Youth Protection Training is critical for protecting our youth. It’s also important for building credibility. pages.text: Wednesday, March 29, 2023 3 Storms delay excavation for new pool By Selen Ozturk As excavation work continues at the Piedmont Community Pool construction site, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that recent storms have delayed the original schedule by an estimated four weeks, mainly due to PG&E delays. He was optimistic that the contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, could work with the city to “mitigate the delay and gain time back.” With 335 working days (including adjustments for weather) assigned to Wickman when the project began on January 19, the project was originally estimated to finish in late spring or early summer in 2024. Excavation work is expected to continue into late spring and has been more difficult due to rainstorms as water accumulates in the holes cut in bedrock for the foundation of a new main and medium-sized pool. To prevent flooding, Gonzales said the contractors have been busy pumping the water out “through tanks, or to filter it through a series of what [the EPA] calls Best Management Practices. They don’t pump directly into storm drains.” However, the biggest storm-related challenge has been PG&E. articles.text: The Piedmont High Affinity Mentorship class, in collaboration with the Piedmont Education Foundation, held a student speaker and panel discussion, “Creating a Culture of Belonging,” in the Alan Harvey theater, Monday, March 20. Students shared their experiences of “othering” within Piedmont and the school district with an audience of nearly 200 community members. Three student speakers and a panel of 10 students of various religious, ethnic, and racial backgrounds, gender identities, and nationalities explained the ways in which microaggressions, slurs and social hierarchies within Piedmont have left them feeling unsafe and uncomfortable within their own skin. The speakers included seniors Morgan Hunt, Sohrab Ford and Stephanie Tsung, alongside panelist Danny Allen, Meher Bachher, Sofia Prieto Black, Adelina Mbise, Cole Nash, Dahlia Saffouri, and Elena Stevens. English teacher and teacher union president Dr. Elise Marke commended the success of the event during a school board meeting on Wednesday March 22. “The words said on that stage really need to be heard by every parent, teacher and staff member, administrator and community member in this city,” said Marks. Student presenters shared stories and experiences about facing alienation from classmates, and the negative impact it had on their sense of self. “Although it may not be the blunt racism such as saying the n-word to my face, but the subtleties of simply leaving me out, or making sure that I knew what set me apart from everyone else was heartbreaking,” Morgan Hunt said in her speech Monday night, “It completely ruined the way that I saw myself, it made me grow to become ashamed of my Blackness, I didn’t want to be the exception, I just wanted to be me.” Hunt has given multiple speeches about her experiences in Piedmont, and is upset by the lack of change, even as these topics continue to be brought to light by students. “It’s frustrating that we have to keep on talking about this topic and the culture hasn’t changed. A lot of people that go to Piedmont might never have to interact with minorities….and that’s a big problem,” Hunt added. Stephanie Tsung’s speech portrayed unique perspective, moving from somewhere she was the majority and fit in, to being othered in Piedmont. “I moved from Hong Kong, where the majority is Asian, and so I fit in pretty well. But after moving to Piedmont, I was able to experience certain things that I hadn’t before,” said Tsung. “The little things people said, made me feel like I’m not one of them, or that I’m different or I didn’t belong here.” Tsung believes these racist statements often come from ignorance, rather than an intent to be harmful. “Intent and impact aren’t always aligned, but people need to be more aware of their words. I think a lot of the time it’s just ignorance,” said Tsung. Panelist Meher Bachher, a freshman, believes that more administrative accountability would encourage students to understand the impact of their words and actions. “A lot of the problems are perpetuated by lack of administrative accountability, and lack of action. When a student does something wrong, instead of helping them understand the consequences of their actions, the incident as a whole is just brushed under the rug,” said Bachher. Bachher has been in the Piedmont Unified School District since the 1st grade and has seen Students in the Affinity Mentorship class hosted a pivotal discussion called “Creating a Culture of Belonging: Student Perspectives on Inclusion/Exclusion & Raising Kids who are Allies.”

articles.text: Lake Merritt, the beloved jewel in the center of Oakland, is in jeopardy. Recent events do not bode well for the future of the city’s home to waterfowl, joggers, and dog lovers. For decades, the Lake Merritt Institute, a community oriented nonprofit sponsored by a contract with the City of Oakland and with donations from supporters, has worked to keep the downtown estuary clean by empowering volunteers to remove trash. But now, problems are threatening to overwhelm the lake, and the needs are many. Last summer (2022) a red toxic algae bloom triggered water oxygen levels to drop to zero. A fish kill resulted in 10,000 fish dying and washing up on the shoreline. Even if the two city contracts proposed for 2023-2024 are approved, that funding would not meet requirements to keep Lake Merritt clean. To combat Lake Merritt’s problems, the Lake Merritt Institute has established a gofundme campaign at: Gofundme.com/f/help-save-lakemerritt-and-lake-merritt-institute. So far, $14,533 has been raised toward a goal of $150,000. The Funds will be used for: • A fourth water quality monitoring buoy to be deployed in the channel through which tidal water enters and exits the lake. This buoy would be deployed for a year to measure nutrients and other data necessary to design a system to prevent future fish kills. Goal: $20,000. • An electric quad utility vehicle to replace an old truck, and to be used to haul bags of trash removed from the lake. Goal: $22,000 • Accounting and tax preparation services, and updated accounting software. Goal: $5,000. • Staff assistance to maintain social media accounts, help prepare the newsletter, maintain bulletin boards, and monitor water quality. Goal: $73,000. • New nets, trash bags, barrels, as well as protective gear such as gloves and boots. Goal: $4,000. • Three shallow water aerators to replace fountains where depth is now too shallow to operate, and which will create islands of oxygenated water where fish can find refuge during fish kills. Goal: $18,000. In addition, major funding is needed for a lake-wide aeration and oxygenation system that would prevent future fish kills. This system will be designed in 2023, and costs could be as high as $2,000,000. For further information, contact LMI Executive Director James Robinson at 238-2290, or see Lakemerrittinstitute.org. Since December 1996 the institute has been removing between 1,000 and 6,000 pounds of trash from the lake each month under a contract with the City of Oakland. Much of the work is done by volunteers. An Oakland Public Works crew removes dead fish from Lake Merritt during the summer of 2022. Lic. No. 702138

articles.text: The Appreciating Diversity Film Series will present an evening of Short Films on April 20 at 7:00 p.m. at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on the Havens School campus at 325 Highland Avenue. Help the Appreciating Diversity Film Series enrich the Piedmont Food Fest’s celebration of Bay Area diversity with five family friendly films that will explore the many flavors of families. Bring your family and friends and experience the range of family diversity through themes such as adoption, homelessness, women’s issues, education, and gender identity. The films are appropriate for children ages 10 and up. As always, Diversity films are free. A list of films that will be screened starting at 7:00 p.m. are listed below in the order in which they will be shown. The total running time for all five films is about one hour. • Absolutely No Spitting A Jewish mother and her multiracial 4-year-old adopted daughter explore their DNA profiles and what it means to have many identities and cultures in your genetic heritage. • A Concerto Is a Conversation A virtuoso jazz pianist and film composer traces his family’s lineage through his 91-year-old grandfather from Jim Crow laws in Florida to the Walt Disney Concert Hall in Los Angeles. The grandfather describes the development of his love for music as well as his ingenious methods of getting ahead that made it possible for his family to thrive then and for coming generations. • Almost Famous: The Silent Pulse of the Universe In 1967, a young astronomer, Jocelyn Bell, made a breakthrough discovery in astronomy, but as a woman in the sciences her role was overlooked and unfairly ignored. While Jocelyn was belittled and sexually harassed by the media, the Nobel Prize was awarded to her professor and his boss. • What You’ll Remember The story of young Bay Area parents determined to give their four children a good life despite moving in and out of homelessness over a period of fifteen years. While the family waited for stable, affordable housing, they nurtured and educated their children in resourceful, inspiring ways, creating a feeling of “home” even when there was no house. • Texas Strong Kai Shappley, a 6-year-old trans child in Texas, fights to be recognized and accepted by her devout Christian family. Kai’s mother, Shirley, must deal with her church, while Kai navigates life at school, where she is banned from the girls’ bathroom. Winner of the 2018 Emmy for Outstanding Short Documentary. The Appreciating Diversity Film Series is co-sponsored by Piedmont School District, the City of Piedmont, the Oakland and Piedmont Leagues of Women Voters, and the Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Committee. articles.text: Three local high school seniors have recently been awarded DAR Good Citizen scholarships from the Piedmont Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution. Piedmont winners were Aryana Fisher from Piedmont High, and Xiaowei Elias from Millennium High. Hannah John from Redwood Christian High School in San Lorenzo, also received the DAR award. Outstanding Community Service was part of the basis of the awards. Xiaowei is active in his community raising funds for the Alameda Food Bank, cooking and delivering food for Youth Homeless Shelters; volunteering as a Junior Tennis Coach for Piedmont Rec Department; participating in Rebuild Together Oakland; and volunteering at Blue Water Sailing Foundation, an organization that brings sailing to under privileged and underserved youth. Aryana is active in her community volunteering as an intern and translator for the Social-Justice Collaborative; volunteering as a teacher and coach for the ENGin Program, an organization that helps international students learn English and prepare for college entrance exams; and volunteering at Piedmont Gardens as an assistant Activities director for the memory-care unit. pages.text: 6 Wednesday, March 29, 2023 SchOOLs Title IX Committee donates 66 books to school libraries 3 high school seniors receive annual DAR Good Citizen Award Three local high school seniors have recently been awarded DAR Good Citizen scholarships from the Piedmont Chapter of the Daughters of the American Revolution. Piedmont winners were Aryana Fisher from Piedmont High, and Xiaowei Elias from Millennium High. Hannah John from Redwood Christian High School in San Lorenzo, also received the DAR award. Outstanding Community Service was part of the basis of the awards. Xiaowei is active in his community raising funds for the Alameda Food Bank, cooking and delivering food for Youth Homeless Shelters; volunteering as a Junior Tennis Coach for Piedmont Rec Department; participating in Rebuild Together Oakland; and volunteering at Blue Water Sailing Foundation, an organization that brings sailing to under privileged and underserved youth. Aryana is active in her community volunteering as an intern and translator for the Social-Justice Collaborative; volunteering as a teacher and coach for the ENGin Program, an organization that helps international students learn English and prepare for college entrance exams; and volunteering at Piedmont Gardens as an assistant Activities director for the memory-care unit. articles.text: Twenty-one Piedmont High School journalism students attended Columbia Scholastic Press Association’s Spring Convention fro March 15-17 at Columbia University in New York City. After lectures, workshops, and discussions, the students returned home with new ideas for improvements for the school news magazine, The Piedmont Highlander (TPH). The PHS students were chaperoned by newspaper advisor and English Department Chair Beth Black, and former PHS science teacher Tom Huffaker. Black has brought students to the convention since 2002, interrupted only by the pandemic. “I take kids on the trip because I want students to recognize the amount of press freedom they have in California. The only way to do that is to meet other journalists from across the country,” Black said. “I [also] want them to celebrate what they do well and recognize how much they already know,” she said. During the three-day convention, TPH staff attended seminars taught by professional journalists, each focused on a specific aspect of journalism. articles.text: Full-Time Savings Classification Equivalent (FTE) Annual Salary The Piedmont School Board adopted a resolution on March 8 to help balance the school district budget after the 2nd Interim Financial Report was issued. It outlines a reduction of $1,200,000 based upon plans to decrease the number of employees next year due to a lack of work and/or lack of funds. These initial notices were sent out to individual employees by March 15 to comply with Education Code and final determinations are made by May 15. articles.text: If you research speech and language development, you will find many references to “word count”. “Word count”, although not the entire speech/language developmental picture, is often used as a quick and easy measure of a child’s developing communication profile. Beginning as early as the 12- or 18- month pediatrician visit, you will likely be asked about your child’s current “word count”. Developmental norms suggest 3–5 words at age 12 months, and 20–50 words at 18 months. How do those first words magically appear? And what can we do if they do not? We can look earlier and deeper than the “word count” for the answers. Learning to talk starts long before a child says their first words. First words are built upon four layers: understanding, interacting, gesturing and making sounds. The foundation for speaking words is understanding words. You cannot use a word correctly if you do not completely understand it. There is a gap between how many words children understand and how many they can produce, with the words understood outnumbering the words used. A suggestion is to hold up items as you talk about them or point to pictures in books as you say the word, so the child can focus on learning the meaning of words. Next, participation in back and forth interaction is layered upon the foundation of understanding. Effective communication requires sustained reciprocal interaction. But before the turn taking is verbal, it is nonverbal. Beginning as early as the 12- or 18- month pediatrician visit, you will likely be asked about your child’s current “word count”. Developmental norms suggest 3–5 words at age 12 months, and 20–50 words at 18 months. How do those first words magically appear? And what can we do if they do not? We can look earlier and deeper than the “word count” for the answers. Learning to talk starts long before a child says their first words. First words are built upon four layers: understanding, interacting, gesturing and making sounds. The foundation for speaking words is understanding words. You cannot use a word correctly if you do not completely understand it. There is a gap between how many words children understand and how many they can produce, with the words understood outnumbering the words used. A suggestion is to hold up items as you talk about them or point to pictures in books as you say the word, so the child can focus on learning the meaning of words. Next, participation in back and forth interaction is layered upon the foundation of understanding. Effective communication requires sustained reciprocal interaction. For example, “moo” may precede the word “cow”, and blowing may precede the word “hot” Tip: Model sounds in daily activities such as “sshhh”/quiet or raise arms/up. And finally, we add the element of speech sound production to the layers of understanding, interacting and gesturing. articles.text: Over the three-day weekend of March 11-13, Girl Scouts in Troop 33587 camped for two nights in San Simeon State Park on the central California coast. On Saturday, they set up camp in the fog and drizzle and cooked a delicious stew for dinner. The girls went straight to bed as they had a busy day planned for Sunday. pages.text: Wednesday, March 29, 2023 11 Girl Scouts Continued from page 10 The beach is filled with weaned elephant seal pups. Elephant seal mothers give birth to one 70-pound pup in January and spend the month nursing their pups. While nursing, elephant seal pups gain an astounding 10 pounds per day, weighing an estimated 300 pounds at the end of weaning. After weaning, mothers abandon their pups forever, and return to the ocean to feed. The pups spend one month on the beach and learn how to swim before leaving the beach to feed in the ocean. The first pup born on this beach was in 1992. Since then, the San Simeon elephant seal colony has grown to an estimated 25,000 sea lions. After the tour, the Girl Scouts ate lunch and went up the hill to Hearst Castle, now a state park, for a tour. The Roman Pool was a favorite stop on the tour, along with the dining room and movie theater. In the evening, the girls returned to their campsite and cooked a spaghetti dinner. It was dry enough to have a fire, so everyone enjoyed s’mores and singing around the campfire before heading to bed. articles.text: Photos by Todd Marshburn The Highlander girls’ lacrosse team beat Berkeley 13-8 on Friday, March 24 at Witter Field. Piedmont lost 13-12 in double overtime loss to the Yellowjackets in last year’s Western Alameda County Conference playoff semifinals. “We just asked the girls to focus, keep really good communication, trusting each other, and playing as a team. We have a pretty young team, and we found it’s taking a little bit of time for everyone to come together. So far this season, we’ve seen some really good halves, but tonight I thought we played a full game,” said assistant coach Greg Tschider, who was filling in for coach Carlton Chan on Friday. It was a strong offensive performance for Ruby Guzdar and Molly Ashton, who combined for seven goals. “On offense, Ruby is really quick. There are certain players who know how to get to goal and put it in the back of the net, and Ruby is one of those players. We really look to Molly and Eleanor [Lavin] to provide leadership on offense, keep us controlled, and focused. It was an aggressive game by both teams, this game was ultimately won by the team that got more ground balls and who had fewer turnovers,” said Tschider. Ruby Guzdar (3) scored four goals against Berkeley. Game Recap Piedmont jumped out quickly to hold a commanding 5-1 advantage by halftime. They added seven more goals and conceded seven after intermission. The Highlanders led 3-0 before Berkeley scored its first goal. Guzdar opened scoring eight minutes into play, then Friedie Schickendanz scored a minute and a half later with 15:55 remaining. Guzdar scored again nearly 30 seconds later. Berkeley made it 3-1 with 10:51 left in the half, but it was the only time they’d get on the scoreboard in the opening 25 minutes. From there, Ashton scored her first goal with 7:19 to go and then Eleanor Lavin netted one with 3:23 left. Piedmont’s win over Berkeley puts them in second-place of the Western Alameda County Conference. Molly Ashton had a hat trick against the Yellowjacktes. In the second half, the two sides traded goals all the way until the end—scoring seven apiece. Berkeley scored 30 seconds into the action, but 18 answered a minute later and Guzdar got her hat trick after another 40 seconds. 2 made it 8-3 with 19:36 to go, and then Piedmont went up 10-3 with a pair of goals by Ashton. Berkeley then scored three consecutive times to make it 10-6 with 9:38 left in the game. After back-and-forth possessions, PHS’ Guzdar scored her fourth goal with 5:52 left and 14 added one with 5:05 remaining. The Jackets netted one with three minutes to go, but 18 scored Piedmont’s 13th goal with 2:18 remaining. Berkeley scored the game’s final goal with 1:19 on the clock. Final stats: Guzdar scored four goals, recovered three loose balls, and won five draws. Ashton had three goals. Lavin had one goal, two ground balls, and won two draws. Watson scored twice and won two draws. Bentley scored once and had two ground balls. Schickendanz scored once and had two assists. Graham had a goal and assist. Tuesday vs. Las Lomas Piedmont traveled to Walnut Creek yesterday tp play Las Lomas . See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-3 overall, 1-1 league) hosts North Coast Section opponent San Marin this Saturday, April 1 at Witter Field 11:30 a.m. They will also host Moreau on Monday evening, April 3 at 5:30 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team swept past North Coast Section foe Lick-Wilmerding 7-0 at home on Wednesday, March 22, setting the stage for a closer margin of victory two days later against Bishop O’Dowd, 4-3, in a match March 24 at Merritt College. “We had a victorious week. We are just about at full strength with Ben [Breber] back in action. I think our quality dipped a bit after the win over Lick-Wilmerding, but we still won a close match against O’Dowd,” said coach Jim Landes. Wednesday’s win over Lick featured No. 2 singles starter Ben Breber, a junior, returning to the lineup after missing all but one match this season due to illness. He won both his matches, defeating Lick’s Este Ciu 6-4, 7-5, and O’Dowd’s Colin Sweeney 6-3, 6-4. “It feels so good to be back out here – especially for the team. It hasn’t been just me missing time; people have been in and out of the lineup. It felt really good to come out at full strength against a good team,” said Breber after winning the clinching fourth match against Lick. Breber showed his usual array of thunderous forehands and serves to overpower his opponents. No. 1 singles starter Lucas Smolko, a freshman, continued his impressive debut season with a pair of wins, beating Soahil Mishra of Lick 6-4, 6-3, O’Dowd’s Neo Chai, 6-2, 6-3. Smolko is a 3-star nationally ranked recruit who is competing on a team environment for the first time in his tennis career. “It’s a little more pressure, Staff Photos Freshman Lucas Smolko talks about the nuances of tournament tennis compared to high school team play. but it’s a really cool environment where I get to have teammates and we can support each other. Tennis is a really solitary sport, so it’s nice to have that difference. With high school matches, you’re feeling pressure to win for your team as opposed to just yourself,” Smolko explained. 7-0 shutout vs. Lick-Wilmerding In singles, Smolko won 6-4, 6-3 at the No. 1 spot while Breber won 6-4, 7-5 at No. 2. Ethan Pham won handily at No. 3 with scores of 6-0, 6-1, and Brady Colbert won 6-4, 6-2 at No. 4. At No,1 doubles, Nate Welch and Monte Imburg went to three sets before winning, 6-3, 5-7, 10-7. Playing No.2, Arun Brahma and Nick King also won in three sets, 6-4, 5-7, 10-3. Will Tenney and Graham Alban at No, 3 closed out the match in two sets, winning 6-4, 6-4. Ben Breber made his return to Piedmont High after missing several matches this season due to an illness. He won both matches last week at No. 2 singles. Monte Imburg and Nate Welch won their matches in three sets against Lick Wilmerding and Bishop O’Dowd.

Piedmont’s track and field team traveled to Castro Valley for two separate meets last week. They competed in a 4-school league meet on Thursday, March 23 with Castro Valley, Hayward, and Encinal. Two days later, Saturday, March 25, they participated in the Castro Valley Relays, where they had five athletes in the top three. They won 11 events at the league meet. Stanford Invitational This weekend, March 30-April 1, PHS will send its largest squad of athletes to the prestigious Stanford Invitational. It will have athletes competing in 10 different events, including the boys’ 4x100 and 4x400 relay teams, and girls’ 4x100 relay team. In individual events, Parker Long will run the 800, Christian Taylor both the 800 and 1600 meters, Matthew Riordan in the 400 meter hurdles, and Spencer Sorenson in the pole vault and 400 hurdles. “The Stanford Invitational track meet is the most prestigious mid-season invitational in Northern California. I submit my kids’ marks and cross my fingers to see if they get in. This is the team’s largest batch of acceptances in school history. This is about as exciting as it gets,” said coach Pouyan Assadi. The boys’ 4x400 relay team of Christian Taylor, Spencer Sorensen-Wald, Sam Shelby, and Parker Long placed third of 12 teams with a time of 3:30.30. For the girls’ team, freshman Skylar Best finished third of 12 runners in the 1600 with a time of 5:53.65. In the shot put, Brie Sotelo was fifth of 20 with a distance of 27 feet, 2 inches. articles.text: 3-2 victory over Berkeley at Binks Rawlings Gym on Friday, March 24. The Yellowjackets shared last year’s league title with O’Dowd. March 24 marked the school’s first win over Berkeley in school history. “I didn’t know that Piedmont’s boys’ team had never beat Berkeley, so that’s a bit of a statement for our players,” said PHS coach said coach Mariah Cardenas. “We’ve always been considered the underdogs.” Defeating Berkeley was a preseason goal for the squad to plant itself as a top-three team in the WACC. “We had some friends on Berkeley last year who graduated, so we were keeping an eye on them to slip,” said senior leader Wilson Wong following their victory over the Yellowjackets. Against Berkeley, Piedmont dropped the first game 25-22, but followed up with wins of 25-23 and 25-16. The Yellowjackets fought to a 26-24 victory in the fourth game, but the Highlanders closed out the fifth-set strongly with a 15-6 victory. Friday’s win over Berkeley marked a breakout performance for freshman Albert Bellingrath. The tall freshman entered as a middle blocker, and recorded five kills while getting his most playing time this season. “I put in our freshman to play middle blocker and shifted our usual middle blocker to the outside. I felt that making that shift worked great. Albert has never played volleyball at this level and had a good game. He’s pretty good for a freshman, for sure,” confirmed Cardenas. “Coming into this match, we had a few injuries, including our outside hitter John Champion aggravating an ankle injury. But we’ve been able to fill his role pretty well with Owen [Kelly] and James [MaNguyen], who is an athletic monster and can play anywhere. And our freshman, Albert [Bellingrath] has been shocking everybody. We’re loving how good this guy is,” added Wong. Wilson Wong had 14 kills on Berkeley and five against Bishop O’Dowd. 3-1 over Berkeley In the first game, Piedmont held an early 10-8 lead but the Jackets eventually went ahead 14-13 and never relinquished the lead on its way to a close 25-22 victory. In the second game, Piedmont responded well and led 24-19 with game-point, but conceded four straight points to make it 24-23 before Wong’s winning spike. Piedmont’s third game was a mighty 25-16 win where Berkeley led earlier 5-4. The Highlanders had nine kills in the game, including four from Kraft and three from Bellingrath. Berkeley won the fourth game in extra points, 26-24. Piedmont held match-point at 24-20, but the Yellowjackets tacked on six straight points to win. articles.text: The Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame (PSHOF) will host its 12th ceremony on April 8 at the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. Doors open at 1:30 p.m. with the ceremony taking place from 2:00-4:00 p.m. A beer and wine reception will be held from 4:00 to 6:00 p.m. across the street at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. This year’s ceremony will honor six athletes: • Lauren Barbieri Track & Cross Country, Class of 2001 • Devin Brown Football and Basketball, Class of 2009 • James Danielson Football, Track and Soccer, Class of 1981 • Georgia Hill Softball, Class of 2013 • Jon Minor Basketball, Class of 1983 • Kerri Roemer Tennis, Basketball, Track & Softball, Class of 1999 The program will be expanded to recognize all past Piedmont Sports Hall of Fame Inductees who can attend and allow for a current student athlete representative for each varsity team to be recognized. Two levels of tickets are available at www.pshof.org. General admission tickets are $25, or $40 to include the reception. For more Information, contact Scott Hill at scotthillhomes@ gmail.com (510-435-6667). Lauren Barbieri • Lauren Barbieri Class of 2001, Track, Crosscountry Lauren was the recipient of the Track MVP award all four years at PHS, a 4-year qualifier for NCS (North Coast Section), broke PHS records in the Triple Jump, 4x400 relay and 100 Hurdles, and qualified for the California State Meet. At Cal, Lauren competed in both Cross Country (two years) and Track (four years) where she was named Academic All-Pac-10 for Track and Field. Jon Minor Devin Brown
articles.title: Sports Hall of Fame slated for April 8

articles.text: James Danielson • James Danielson Class of 1981, Football, Soccer, Track In Soccer, after his MVP year, James led the Piedmont team to its first North Coast Section Championship appearance, while earning Piedmont’s first North Coast Section Individual Player honor in 1981. He broke the school record for the Triple Jump and was the 1981 track Optimo winner. James was distinguished as team captain and a 1st Team All-League recipient in each sport. He received 10 total varsity letters at Piedmont High. • Jon Minor Class of 1983, Basketball Jon was a dominant 6’6” starting center his junior and senior years, earning 1st Team All-League honors and Alameda County Athletic Conference (ACAL) Player of the Year both seasons. He also received the Optimo Award his senior season as the team’s Most Valuable Player. Jon continued his basketball career at UC Davis. Kerri Roemer • Kerri Roemer Class of 1989, Tennis Kerri led the tennis team to North Coast Section all four years, highlighted by winning the team championship in 1998. Kerri played doubles with Meghan Wardlaw and reached the semi-finals one year and finals another year. As PHS team captain (‘98) she won the CIF sportsmanship/ citizenship award. Kerri was ranked in the top 20 USTA NorCal during her junior year and was nationally ranked her senior year. At UC Davis, she was named the Western Conference D-II Rookie of the Year for 1999-2000.

articles.text: Piedmont High School and Middle School jazz bands will perform two shows at Yoshi’s jazz club in Jack London Square on Monday evening, April 3. articles.text: Brass and vocal teacher Dorothy Moskowitz Falarski retired from Piedmont School District in 2015. Since then, she has collaborated remotely with writers and composers from all over the country as well as abroad from her Piedmont home studio. She’s written songs for several plays, released a soundtrack album and done vocal tracks for fellow composers. Her most recent work with Italian composer Francesco Paladino and his partner, writer Luca Ferrari, attracted the attention of Josh Rosenthal, founder of Tompkins Square Records in San Francisco. The album is called “Under an Endless Sky” by Dorothy Moskowitz and the United States of Alchemy. Rosenthal and his associates are hosting a “meet-and-greet” to celebrate the new release at Mars Records in Oakland on April 8. The public is invited to meet Dorothy and hear some of the details about the new album.

articles.text: Filoli Historic House and Garden in Woodside will host botanical bouquet workshops from April 4 through 7 to celebrate its spring blooms. Filoli’s ‘Flora Party” begins on Tuesday, April 4, The garden’s veteran staff will guide you through a bouquet-making session featuring the estate’s well-prized flowers. Filoli is home to 16 acres of formal gardening grounds and a vast collection of native and exotic flowers. The most fertile and popular flowers during March are Camellias, Magnolias, Irises, and Wisteria. In April, the historic gardens will welcome a bloom of roses and Lavender. The workshop is from 2 p.m. to 4 p.m. Light refreshments and wine are provided with registration purchase. Visit https://filoli.org/events/ flora-party/ or call (650) 364- 8300 to purchase tickets. Filoli is located at 86 Canada Road in Woodside. The Garden House on a spring morning
articles.title: Botanist-guided classes April 4 - 7

articles.text: The Asian Art Museum currently is exhibiting Color Trip: Yoshida Hodaka’s Modern Prints, the first ever solo exhibition of the artist in the United States. His exhibit showcases the Japanese printmaker’s influential craft. Hodaka, a native of Tokyo, was an influential figure of postWorld War II Japanese printmaking. Born in 1926, he is known for his abstract and colorful prints. Hodaka included surreal landscapes and abstract forms in his art, which is inspired by photography, poetry, and ancient art. “Hodaka was a rebel in the best sense – someone who imagined a new way of seeing the world,” explained the exhibition organizer Yuki Morishima, associate curator of Japanese art at the Asian Art Museum. “By combining the centuries-old woodblock printing with the modern methods of photo etching and collage and contemporary influences like Pop art and foreign travel, Hodaka opened up a new frontier in Japanese printmaking that was completely original to him.” Hodaka’s collection of a dozen poster-size prints, Zodiac Landscape (1973), is on view, as well as his sketchbooks and a collection of artwork made by his family members. “Hodaka playfully assembled and juxtaposed ordinary objects out of context, creating his surreal scenes with dreamlike atmospheres. Every time you look at these prints, you find something new and exciting hiding in the landscape,” Morishima said. The exhibition will be on view through May 1. For tickets and more information, see https:// exhibitions.asianart.org/exhibitions/color-trip-yoshida-hodakas-modern-prints/ Originally designed in 1909, this Oakland Historical Landmark Building has long been considered one of the most beautiful historic buildings in all of California with designs from noted architects Julia Morgan and Aaron Green. -a an nd d- -e ev ve en nt ts s/ /e ev ve en nt t- -

articles.text: The Oakland Museum of California will celebrate Earth Day on Friday, April 7. The free family-friendly event begins at 5 p.m. at OMCA’s courtyard and garden. Guests will discover the unique flora and foliage of the Foothill Oak Woodland, Chaparral, and Redwood Forest regions of California. Young museum goers can create art inspired by California’s native plants, and learn about Earth Day events offered in the Bay Area this month. A special guest, Stomper, the mascot of the Oakland A’s baseball team will be in attendance. From 6 to 7 p.m., educator Bowen Lyam Lee will read Stories for a Healthy Planet in the garden. Lee is a fifth generation Chinese American born and raised in Oakland, and has been a teacher for 36 years, incorporating storytelling into all aspects of teaching. Music will be provided in the Amphitheater from 6 to 8 p.m. This event is part of the museum’s Friday Nights series, where food trucks, live music and art-inspired activities are available. For more information, visit https://museumca.org/event/friday-nights-at-omca-with-off-thegrid-earth-day/.
articles.title: Oakland Museum celebrates Earth Day on April 7

articles.text: All Quiet on the Western Front won the 2023 Academy Award for Best International film. All Quiet on the Western Front is extraordinary, beautifully photographed and acted, nominated for nine Oscars at the recent 95th Academy Awards and the winner of the Best International film. It is based on Eric Remarque’s 1929 classic anti-war novel of the same name, and it could be argued that its contemporary context is today’s war in Ukraine. The narrative opens with Paul Baumer (Frank Krammer) marching in a long line of new recruits. They are headed toward the front, filled with patriotic eagerness, singing a song, filled with German patriotism, unaware of the carnage that awaits them. Each is wearing a uniform salvaged from a dead soldier, freshly laundered, the bullet holes patched. But soon, for these young men, and countless others, the agony and finality of war will become a reality. The camera follows Paul, running through the icy water of the trenches, claustrophobic warrens filled with pools of blood and shattered bodies. Before long his spirit is crushed and the look in his eyes is now vacant, his face twisted with fear, the optimistic rationale for the war lost to him, replaced only with his will to survive. In one chilling scene Paul stabs a French soldier and then sits next to him as he slowly dies. Sitting in a bomb crater, his face in his hands, he is overwhelmed by what he has done, grieving for his lost humanity. Meanwhile, far from the front, the French and German powers sit across from one another, attempting to negotiate a cease-fire, fully aware that while the hours pass hundreds are maimed or killed by withering gunfire and explosives. The world watched then as the casualties mounted, much as it does today, and the futility of it all, the frightful unyielding tragedy of war continues as history repeats itself. Peter Jackson’s much acclaimed documentary, They Shall Not Grow Old, also a profound and detailed look at the horrors of World War I from an English perspective.
articles.title: All Quiet on the Western Front - profound, unforgettable

articles.text: What Peter Jackson has accomplished in They Shall Not Grow Old is extraordinary, bordering on the magical. Given access to hundreds of hours of World War I archival news footage from Britain’s Imperial War Museum, he began what was to be a 30-minute short. It ultimately morphed into an astonishing, years-long restorative achievement. Using computer-generated, state-of-the-art technology Jackson undertook what was a meticulous cleaning of the dusty, scratched, grainy film. Realizing that the footage was hand cranked and had been shot at various speeds, he synched it up to a standard 24-frames-per-second. Then he and his talented cohort began the painstaking process of colorization in which the restorers went to astonishing lengths to achieve accuracy. They included trips to actual locations where they shot countless reference photos. Then they created a soundtrack that is spot-on, In images where soldiers are speaking, they hired lip readers to determine what was said and hired local actors to get the accents just right. No narration was used; rather they listened to some 600 hours of BBC recordings of WWI veterans and used 100 voices. We hear them reflecting on their experiences, offering their memories absent even a hint of cynicism. The result is almost surreal. It’s as if we are literally stepping back in time and observing from the camera’s point of view what is taking place. The story is told chronologically, beginning with contextual images shot in black and white of enlistees (some as young as 14 years-old) arriving at boot camp as civilians and then gradually turned into disciplined soldiers. We learn through voice-overs that to a man they believed they were embarking on an unrivaled adventure, one not to be missed, wrapped in patriotism and heroism and a promise that the war would end within months. England vibrated with war fever. Train stations were filled with cheering, f lag waving crowds saying goodbye. Men on the streets of London not yet in uniform, were often approached by young women who handed them white feathers, symbols of cowardice, urging them to join their comrades. On walls and buildings were posters, appealing to men (and boys) to enlist and do their part. It’s at this point in the narrative that the screen fills with color and we, the audience, begin in earnest to comprehend that what Jackson has done is create a work of art. We are there. All but shoulder to shoulder with these young men who soon came to realize that the much-anticipated adventure proves to be an unimaginable ordeal, harsh, stark, all but unendurable. The young Brits found that this was a war fought from the warrens of crooked trenches, often filled with the stench of death, filled with water and partially buried bodies, blackened hands and arms sticking out of layers of mud. To confront the enemy meant climbing up and over the top, onto the field of battle, often into withering machine gun fire and exploding shells, later spending nights trying to sleep in shallow hollowed out caves while an unrelenting bombardment from Germans shook the ground. For many this adventure became life maiming or life ending. And those who stopped and looked into the box-like cameras, gave stoic smiles or long gazes of brittle confidence; in truth they knew what was ahead. World War I (1914-1918) was referred to as “The War to End All Wars.” After watching They Shall Not Grow Old, it is clear why it was unimaginable that such carnage would ever be repeated. The toll was staggering, 5,500,000 men were killed, and an additional 12 million wounded. Poison gas was used, inflicting 1.3 million casualties. Civilian deaths totaled over 4 million. And 1 million British boys were killed. The loss for a small island nation was incomprehensible. At no time during They Shall Not Grow Old is there any commentary by Jackson or others about the nature of war. And yet, after the last frame fades from the screen, it is all but impossible not to conclude that what was created is an anti-war film. To see WWI as it was, while knowing that the horror was far worse (the archival footage was meant for audiences back in England), is revelatory. And, of course, embedded in the 99-minute film is the haunting question: why does war seem to be ever with us? They Shall Not Grow Old. WWI Documentary. A Centenary Restoration by Peter Jackson. 1 hr., 39 min. Rated R. Released in 2019. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/HBO MAX/Apple tv An example of how original World War I footage was restored and colorized for Peter Jackson’s documentary, They Shall Not Grow Old.
articles.title: They Shall Not Grow Old a monumental film

articles.text: Ghost in the Shell is a live action remake of the classic Japanese anime film created by Mamoru Oshii in 1995. When it was made it was considered visionary, even revolutionary and explored the nexus between robotics/computers and sentient beings. Embedded in its narrative was the question that if we begin to merge with sophisticated machines, how will that merger ultimately affect our essential humanity? articles.text: Reese Witherspoon and Pico Alexander star in Home Again If you enjoy romantic comedies (rom-coms), then it’s likely you’ve seen one of Nancy Meyers’ films dating back as far as Baby Boom or Something’s Gotta Give. Or perhaps you saw It’s Complicated or The Holiday. Meyers was and still remains a filmmaker who found a niche and perfected it. Her world in film is as light as a wedding shower balloon, so enticingly surreal that it qualifies as pure warm-hearted escapism. And now here is Meyers’ daughter, Hallie Meyers-Shyer, debuting with Home Again, written and directed by Hallie and in almost all ways a mirror of the genre staked out by her mom. This film stars Reese Witherspoon as Alice, a separated mom, a recent New York transplant to L.A., living with her two daughters in her departed father’s Hollywood Spanish villa cum guesthouse. All is soft California sunshine, blue skies, with a room in the house dedicated to her once famous filmmaker father. Her mom, Lillian, ex-actress, played wonderfully by Candace Bergen, oversees her daughter’s, and granddaughters’ transition. What mom did not plan on was abruptly having three twenty-something aspiring filmmakers win her heart and temporarily living in her guesthouse. One, Harry, portrayed by Pico Alexander, is totally captivated with Alice, no matter the age difference (Alice is 40). As you can imagine, it’s complicated, especially when Alice’s husband, Austen (Michael Sheen), arrives unannounced from New York, hoping to make his case for a second chance in the marriage. The film has its comedic moments as well as a bit of drama for a diversion. It’s also the stuff that makes critics cranky. But if you’re looking for an escape and wishing to spend 97 minutes with some decent, attractive and mannerly people who will make you smile, then this fantasy rom-com is just the answer. Home Again. Starring Reese Witherspoon, Pico Alexander and Candace Bergen. Directed by Hallie Meyers-Shyer. 1 hr., 37 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Home Again a film that will make you smile

articles.text: The mission of Mended Hearts is twofold. 1. The group provides peer-to-peer support to cardiac patients, their caregivers and their families. 2. It seeks to educate on all aspects of cardiac healthcare. Part of the educational goals include hosting monthly meetings via Zoom on the first Saturday of each month. This month’s webinar will be on Saturday, April 1, from 10:00 to 11:30 a.m. Knowledge of Alzheimer’s disease, like any form of health care, is always evolving. From the different therapies used to treat patients, to different ways of measuring symptoms, it’s important to know what options and resources are available now, and in the future to ensure that you are making informed decisions. Information about the causes of cognitive decline and dementia seems to revolve around several concepts and studies. Learn with the college nursing students, what the current wisdom is about plaques and Tau tangles, the three risk factors for dementia, and the tests to discover your vascular risk exposure. articles.text: the wine loving world knows about Ridge Vineyards. Instead of hailing from Napa or Sonoma Valley, they are perched up on a…well, ridge in Cupertino overlooking Silicon Valley. They also have an outpost in Sonoma County on Lytton Springs Road that gives birth to their iconic old vine Zinfandels. Since the 1960’s when the winery was started by some vino loving Stanford professors, it has been the quintessential American winery – down to the use of American oak barrels rather than French. When I go to France for a home exchange or a special winery visit, I always slip a bottle of Ridge Zinfandel into my suitcase as a gift. “Here,” I proudly say to my French friend, “This is the best we Yanks can do.” One of the things I marvel about is the sheer amount of wines they make. On their website are page after page of different wines available for sale. Many are tiny little lots from a small vineyard they found somewhere and available only through one of their wine clubs. Others are large production wines available all over the country. And the list is always changing. I look forward to the annual new release of wines to see what they will come up with next. This year’s releases include some old stalwarts and some newcomers – all worth checking out. • 2021 Ridge Mancini Ranch This is a new one to me. A blend of 73% Carignane and 27% Zinfandel from the Russian River Valley. Both in France and in America, Carignane is the overlooked step-sister of grapes. Rarely does it play a starring role and is usually considered a backup blending grape. This bottling shows what a charming performer the grape can be. It is elegant and lithe with bright cherry and plum notes. It has great acid and structure and a clean satisfying finish. A perfect wine for grilled burgers. • 2020 Ridge Syrah Grenache Mataro This blend is heavy on Syrah (79%) which makes for a dark, brooding, beefy wine. The Grenache lends bright fruit and the Mataro (Mourvedre) an interesting earthy complexity. It is bursting with blackberry, cassis and leather aromas with tons of luscious dark berry fruit in the mouth. This big, structured wine should last a decade in the cellar. • 2022 Ridge Rose Lytton Estate Wow. My first Ridge Rose. They have made tiny quantities for their wine club in the past, but this is the first national release. Made from Grenache, Zinfandel, Cinsault and Counoise, this light salmon colored wine is bursting with fresh strawberry and fig aromas. Lots of lucious juicy stone fruit on the palate and a clean, refreshing finish. A perfect spring and summer picnic wine. • 2021 Ridge Zinfandel East Bench From a high-altitude vineyard overlooking Dry Creek Valley, this 100% Zinfandel has a bright berry nose, medium body with good acid to give it balance. A very food-friendly type of Zinfandel/ Try it with grilled steaks or chops. • 2021 Ridge Zinfandel Paso Robles From one of Paso’a best vineyards, the Benito Dusi Ranch, this is a huge, brooding wine that floods your mouth with blueberry and blackberry fruit. It has good concentration which leads to a long finish. This Zin should improve in the cellar for 5 years. • 2021 Ridge Chardonnay Ridge is so strongly associated with red wines that its lovely Chardonnay often gets overlooked. Grown up on Montebello ridge next to their esteemed Cabernet grapes, this wine shows perfect acidity and structure. It has an attractive nose of peaches and apples with a touch of baking spices. It finishes long with lingering oak and toast notes. • 2021 Ridge Geyserville Along with Lytton Springs this is Ridge’s flagship Zinfandel blend. It includes 16% Carignane, 6% Petite Sirah and 2% Alicante Bouchet. The wine boasts a dense ruby/purple color in addition to deep chewy blue-

articles.text: Thomas D. Clark, a 50-year Piedmont resident with his wife Judie who died in their home May 2022, has entered into an endowment gift agreement with the University of California Berkeley that will provide more than $3 million for UC Berkeley Law School. UC Chancellor Carol T. Christ thanked Clark for his gifts as “remarkable commitments establishing the Thomas David and Judith Swope Clark Current Use Chair in Constitutional Law and the Thomas David and Judith Swope Clark Symposium on Constitutional Interpretation Fund. “We are truly grateful for this extraordinary act of generosity, which will broaden our ability to educate, research, and host engaging and groundbreaking symposia around constitutional law topics,” Chris said. Thomas and Judie grew up in Willits and both graduated from UC Berkeley, Thomas in 1967 and Judie in 1966. In 1972 Thomas graduated from Berkeley Law and in 1975 Judie graduated from Golden Gate Law School. Thomas’s first trial during his initial year of legal practice was in Federal District Court where he successfully defended Oakland Airport regulations that he wrote on expressive activities at the Airport which were challenged by the American Civil Liberty Union. The ACLU did not appeal. Thomas has been a lifelong member of the ACLU and deeply admires the US Constitution and its protection of civil rights and liberties. As his gift Agreement with UC states, “Tom’s purpose in making an endowment to Berkeley Law is especially to support scholarship in US Constitutional law, particularly interpretation of the law as a counterweight to the US Supreme Court’s fatally-flawed, mean and narrow ‘originalism’ policy-driven interpretation.”
articles.title: Thomas Clark creates $30 million Endowment for Berkeley Law School

Christ thanked Clark for his gifts as “remarkable commitments establishing the Thomas David and Judith Swope Clark Current Use Chair in Constitutional Law and the Thomas David and Judith Swope Clark Symposium on Constitutional Interpretation Fund. “We are truly grateful for this extraordinary act of generosity, which will broaden our ability to educate, research, and host engaging and groundbreaking symposia around constitutional law topics,” Chris said. articles.text: Ford Roosevelt, son of Elliott Roosevelt and grandson of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt and Eleanor Roosevelt, recently paid a visit with the Piedmont Seniors about his famous grandparents and the USS Potomac, known as the floating White House when FDR was in office (1933-1945). Ford never got to meet FDR, who died before he was born; however, he did get to know his grandmother, Eleanor During his talk with the Seniors on February 22, he mentioned that his father and brothers and sisters had 19 marriages among the five children. His father, Elliott, was married five times and adopted Ford when he was about nine years old. Elliott’s siblings were Anna, James, Franklin Jr, and John. An older brother, Franklin, died as an infant. Ford encouraged the Piedmont Seniors to read some of his father’s works, including the “Eleanor Mysteries”, which include Murder in the Executive Mansion, Murder in the Chateau, Murder in the Map Room, Murder in the Blue Room, and Murder and the First Lady. This event was the largest audience the Piedmont Seniors has ever had, in large part due to the prominence and popularity of the Roosevelt name. Though Ford was pleased to talk about his family, he was even more eager to speak about the USS Potomac, the Presidential Yacht. Ford relocated from Southern California one year ago to serve as Executive Director of the Potomac, now permanently berthed at Clay Street in Oakland. Previously, Ford was involved in K-16 education for over 40 years. He also served as a manager of College Relations and Recruitment at several California Businesses. The USS Potomac has a unique history. It was used as FDR’s personal yacht from 1936 until his death in 1945. Because he lived with polio and was confined to a wheelchair, he disliked flying and preferred conducting meetings on the Potomac. The ship was owned by Elvis Presley for a short time and has quite a colorful past. It began its decline and was seized in San Francisco in 1980 as a front for drug smugglers, and was impounded at Treasure Island, where it unceremoniously sank. Ford encourages people from Ford Roosevelt, grandson of President Franklin Delano Roosevelt, is Executive Director of the USS Potomac formerly known as the floating White House and now berthed at Clay Street in Oakland. the Bay Area to visit this historic yacht located at Jack London Square. articles.text: The Piedmont Adult School is hosting a three-day Expo on April 21-23 at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia. The Adult School has dozens of affordable class options during its spring session, portions and aspects of the course offerings which will be on display during the Expo for the first time. articles.text: Dr. Elizabeth MacDonald, a Piedmonter who has co-owned and run the Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital since 2018, spoke with the Post about growing up in Piedmont (Head-Royce Class of 1991), her lifelong love of animals, and her experiences in running the independent veterinary clinic. As one of five MacDonald kids, she said, “I am what one might call a lifer. I have wanted to be a vet my entire life. I think half of Piedmont’s outdoor pets that lived on Wildwood Avenue conveniently ‘followed me home’ when I was a child. I also owned snakes, birds, cats, dogs, chinchillas, rats and hamsters while I was growing up. I am sure if Piedmont had allowed it, there would have been chickens, ducks or goats in there as well.” Her father, Ward, served on the Piedmont School Board. Her mother, Mimi, created the Boosters Club for Piedmont Middle School sports families, and was instrumental in encouraging the editor of this paper to start the Piedmont Post 25 years ago. MacDonald herself majored in biology at Davidson College in North Carolina and graduated from the UC Davis School of Veterinary Medicine in 2000. After completing a one-year internship in New York City at The Animal Medical Centre, she returned to California to practice. At Grand Lake, she and co-owner Dr. Eleanor Dunn manage both an out-patient and in-patient hospital, a pharmacy and a surgical center, and have 45 employees. “There is a reason I spent 20 years trying to find my way back home. Piedmont is a unique community because, despite being in the middle of a huge metropolitan area, it has managed to maintain small community values. As a community, Piedmont is committed to supporting neighbors, friends and families, and in general looking out for one another,” she said. Grand Lake opened in 2013, Piedmont native Elizabeth MacDonald is now a veterinarian and co-owner of Grand Lake Veterinary Hospital on Grand Avenue. and while it has always centered on the care of animals, the staff was especially strained during the pandemic, when pet ownership surged and many veterinary ERs were so overloaded that they had to turn away new patients. “There was a national shortage of vets already due to a shortage of schools and the fact that they’re so expensive,” said MacDonald. “Once the pandemic hit, we never closed, and we did everything we could to see our patients the same day or next day.” “Our staff were tasked with being their best selves at a time when clients were anxious and stressed. We are grateful that Piedmonters were so patient and kind.” Her clinic was further strained when nearby and corporate-owned Montclair Veterinary Hospital closed its doors last April, leaving an estimated patient load of 5,000 without medical care overnight. “That doesn’t happen with individual, privately owned hospitals very often,” MacDonald said. “Vets are part of and serve the communities they live in. I know how deeply these community values are respected in Piedmont. “Since returning home, I get to help pets live better, happier, healthier lives, and help their owners do the same. I’m optimistic that more vets will get back into privately owned, community-centric hospitals,” she added. At the end of the day, said MacDonald, “I do have the best job in the world. Every day, I still get unconditional love and licks from furry patients. My father always used to say, ‘You will spend more time at work than you will with your family, so you must love what you do.’” “I would add to that ‘You must love who you do it with,’” she said.
articles.title: Elizabeth MacDonald returns to her hometown as co-owner of Grand Lake Vet

articles.text: Are you dreaming of taking a trip to Italy, speaking Italian with the locals and savoring “La Dolce Vita?” Piedmont Adult School is offering Italian for Travelers starting on April 19. The class will be Wednesdays, April 19 to May 31, from 7-9 p.m. The class will be taught by Piedmont resident Rosalie Marshall, who has lived and studied in Italy and France, and holds degrees in Italian, French and Spanish. In this class, students will learn how to communicate in social and travel settings, as well as important information about the country’s culture, cuisine, and its unique lifestyle. The class is designed for travelers, foreign business professionals and those who simply enjoy a new academic adventure. To register for this or other classes, call Piedmont Adult School at 594-2717 or visit piedmontadultschool.org.

articles.text: Fifteen lucky Piedmont Seniors took a trip to San Francisco on Wednesday, February 8, to visit the deYoung Museum in Golden Gate Park and see the unique, extraordinary collection of Egyptian artifacts, including mummies, jewelry and so much more, with 181 ancient relics on display. This exhibition represented the largest collection of Ramses II objects and jewelry to travel to the United States. The exhibit, “Ramses the Great and the Gold of the Pharaohs”, is a once-in-a-lifetime opportunity to recapture the time of Ramses II, also known as Ramses the Great. Ramses, the most powerful pharaoh, was believed to be a god on earth. He ruled for 67 years, and during his reign, he oversaw the erection of enormous temples, statues and monuments. He even made an idealized statue as a tribute to his mother. There were also newly discovered mummies of animals and treasures from the royal tombs of Dahshur and Tanis. Egyptians believed in an afterlife, and their tombs were filled with valuable artifacts and jewelry that they could use on their next journey. The Seniors walked among the towering statues that re-created moments from Ramses’s life, including his triumph at Kadesh, the largest chariot battle ever fought. The group was provided with personal audio tapes to help them decipher the individual exhibits. Though the hall was crowded, entry to the hall was timed to minimize crowding around the exhibits. One was reminded of a Disney ride where, Ramses the Great gets rock star treatment at SF’s de Young Museum. upon exiting the galleries, visitors came upon the museum’s gift shop, In this case, it was the museum gift shop selling Egyptian souvenirs. In addition, the deYoung has a wonderful selection of books, stationery, jewelry and unusual goods for purchase, comprising two floors of shopping. The exhibition also has a 10-minute optional opportunity to participate in a Virtual Reality show. The more adventurous Seniors who chose to participate in this immersion experience saw Ramses and his wife, Nefertari on the ‘Journey to Osiris’. None of the Seniors had ever experienced this type of show, which could be compared to a Hollywood movie set, only with an Egyptian theme where Nefertari made a loving tribute to her husband, Ramses, with most unusual visual effects. Due to its popularity, both the exhibit and the virtual reality sold out early, and the exhibition closed on February 12. The Seniors worked up a hearty appetite after visiting the exhibits and had boxed unches from the De Young Café waiting for them, avoiding long lines at the café. After leaving the De Young Museum, the group wasn’t quite ready to go home so their accommodating bus driver was willing to serve as a tour guide, pointing out popular spots in the city, including Diamond Heights, the Painted Ladies Victorian houses at Alamo Square, the Castro District, and Mission Bay including Chase Stadium and the UCSF hospital. The Piedmont Seniors hold monthly meetings at the Piedmont Community Hall, typically on fourth Wednesday of each month from 10 a.m. to 12 noon. Monthly excursions travel to a variety of destinations throughout the greater Bay Area. If you would like more information about this active group, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. You do not have to be a Piedmont resident to join in the activities. Piedmont Seniors in front of the deYoung Museum in San Francisco, Pictured are (front) Larry Hu, Tanya Hu, Gloria Wilmer, Merilee Hoffman, Mona Jamieson, Sue Getreuer; (back) Jim Ayotte, Ann Morales, Janet Epstein, Nancy Hinsch, Jan Yager, Susan McCreary, Irene Westler, Penny Robb, and Yorkman Lowe.

By Cookie Segelstein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just got a new iMac, and I was wondering if I can still use my old external drive to back it up with Time Machine? The older drive is the same age as my old Mac, about eight-years-old. Also, I seem to remember that when you set it up, you had to format that external drive. If I get a new one, will I have to do the same thing? –Janice D, Oakland Dear Janice: I remember that we ordered you a new iMac, because (besides the fact that the newer operating system would not run on it) your old one was starting to make a lot of noise, clicking, coming from the internal hard drive. This means that the internal hard drive was starting to fail and was probably damaged. So, if you imagine that external hard drives and internal hard drives are the same types of devices, using an eight-year-old external drive with a new machine is probably not a good idea. External hard drives, as well as internal ones, don’t last forever, and there is a saying in the tech world, “it’s not a matter of whether your hard drive will fail, it’s a matter of when.” So, my general rule of thumb, is that when you get a new machine, also get a new back up drive. This doesn’t mean you have to throw your old one away. I suggest that you put the date of the most current backup, and the word “archive” on a label, and store it away until you are sure that you have everything transferred to the new machine. Currently, there are two kinds of hard drives commonly used, Hard Disk Drives (HDD) and Solid-State Drives (SSD). Solid-state drives are much faster, but also much more expensive. Hard disk drives are very reasonable. You can get a 2 TB one for under $70. It’s a small investment to make sure that your data is backed up. And if you are using the external drive to back up your machine, you don’t particularly need a fast hard drive. An SSD is useful if you are accessing files from the external drive to use on your machine, for example, photos, videos, or music. The data transfer rate is much faster, but in your case not necessary. To use one of these hard drives for Time Machine on your Mac, they must be formatted to make them compatible with Mac. Occasionally, you can find some that are already formatted for Mac, but in many cases, you must do it yourself. It’s much easier than it sounds and usually takes less than five minutes. Your computer comes with an application, called Disk Utility. Apple provides instructions for how to do this. When you reformat a hard drive, you are actually erasing it, and then choosing a file format that works best for Mac. If you have OSX 10.13 or later, the format that works best for Time Machine is APFS (Apple File System), and for systems before OSX 10.13, Mac OS Extended (Journaled) is the one to use. Don’t forget, that since your Mac is new, whether or not you bought Apple Care, you can call Apple Support (800-275- 2273) and they can either talk you through it, or log onto your machine, and visually show you the way. Whether you do it yourself, or with Apple’s help or with a tech professional’s help, getting the backup set up and running is as important as plugging in your machine.
