articles.text: David Moody Brown, a former resident of Piedmont, passed away at home in San Diego on February 5, 2023. He was 89. Born in Oakland on October 13, 1933, he was the son of Beulah Borden Moody and Earle William Brown. He was raised in the Bay Area and lived in Oakland, Berkeley, San Francisco and Piedmont. David graduated from University of California, Berkeley in 1956, and served as a Lieutenant in the U.S. Coast Guard until 1959. He devoted 30 years to the growth and success of the College of Engineering at UC Berkeley. David was a big Cal Bears supporter, attending many Cal football and rugby games, and following their seasons throughout his adult life. In 1963 David married Patricia Mae DeWitt and began a life together in Berkeley, and then moved to Piedmont where they raised their two daughters. David shared his love of boating with his family. He was found either water skiing or snow skiing throughout his life. He enjoyed jazz music. His joy of traveling took him all over the world, including Clear Lake and Maui, two of his favorite places to visit with Patty and his family. David is survived by Patricia David Moody Brown, a former Piedmont resident, died on February 5, 2023 at age 89. DeWitt Brown, his loving wife of 59 years, and by two daughters, Victoria Moats (Thomas) and Elizabeth Brown (Samisoni). He is also survived by five grandchildren, Jessica Moats, Kenneth Moats, Ryan Moats, Noah Molimoli and Olivia Molimoli. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests memorial contributions to the Alameda County Food Bank (https://www.accfb.org/) or UC Berkeley Engineering Fund. (https://give.berkeley.edu/fund/ FN3200000)

articles.text: Piedmont High School student Bruno Banuelos (right) helps Piedmont Seniors with computer questions. The Piedmont Seniors group received their second tutoring session on technology from Piedmont High AP Computer Science students Wednesday, March 22. The 30-minute session allowed Seniors to get answers for their questions primarily about the use of cell phones and computers. Organized with Seniors Coordinator Janet Epstein, the monthly help sessions are called “Juniors Helping Seniors” and take place on the 4th Wednesday of the month at the Community Hall from 12:45-1:15 p.m. Students Bruno Banuelos and Ishaia Goldberg-Berman have become teachers during their lunch hours to answer tech questions, and PHS junior Laurel Bentley, has signed on to help at the next session on April 26. “Getting the opportunity to assist elderly people with their technology has been super meaningful. I’ve worked with people on numerous issues including managing notifications, printing from iPhones, wifi connection, and more. Technology is an amazing resource and I’m so glad that we are able to help everyone utilize it to the full extent they want,” said Banuelos. One couple even learned how to better program their Tesla using their iPhone, and another person received instructions on using a cell phone for voicemail. “The kids are fantastic. Ishaia helped with Google Maps and knew more than the guy at the Verizon store,” said Epstein. The next session will be on Wednesday, April 26. Student volunteers are welcome to sign up. articles.text: Becoming a grandparent doesn’t happen to everyone. When it does, it can come at the most unexpected time of life, or it can come after years of readiness and anticipation. Nothing we do can hurry it up or postpone it. Although we know that every family is unique, there is something universal about becoming a grandparent. Grandparents in cultures all over the world share similar hopes and dreams for the health and happiness of their grandchildren. Many work hard to help their adult children tackle all the tasks associated with raising a young family. Grandparents pass on family lore and wisdom every chance they get. And elders try every day to make the world just a little bit better so that their grandchildren inherit a safe and sustainable planet. Since the life stage called Grandparent is one that hits some of us, but not all of us, and may strike anywhere from age 35 to 100, it’s not unusual for a new grandparent to have no close friends or acquaintances that are going through the grandparent stages at the same time. New parents have lots of options such as parent groups, neighborhood get-togethers, and social media, but grandparents may not know where to turn for advice and support. Enter the Grandparent Group. Grandparents can gather together and learn from each other. Similar to a support group, but not necessarily therapeutic, grandparent groups (or meet-ups) offer grandparents a safe and confidential place to share their experiences. It can be wonderful to be able to talk about your grandchildren without fear of boring the listener. And if you’re going through a tough time communicating with your adult children about an issue regarding the little ones, it’s likely that another grandparent in the group can offer strategies that worked for them. In return, you no doubt have a few helpful ideas that you can share with others. Once you’ve stepped into the role of grandparent, no matter when it happens to you, you might want to explore the benefits of a grandparent group in your area. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com and on Facebook.
articles.title: Grandparents helping grandparents

articles.text: On Friday, January 20, at 11:30 pm, Piedmont police officers and fire fighters were dispatched to a home on Greenbank Avenue for a person suffering a possible drug overdose. The individual was transported to an area hospital for treatment. Mushrooms were confiscated at the home and sent to the county crime lab for analysis to identify the complete narcotic makeup. There was concern that the mushrooms had been mixed with fentanyl and the individual suffered an overdose because of the fentanyl exposure. The police department recently received the lab analysis results and have been informed there was no fentanyl detected in the submission. As our nation continues to struggle with the tragic results of the fentanyl epidemic, we ask the community to discuss the danger of fentanyl and the risks with ingesting substances which may be laced with fentanyl. For consideration, the websites below contain valuable information on the effects of narcotics and what parents can do to prevent narcotic consumption. The Department is committed to continued work on this critical issue with the Piedmont Fire Department, Piedmont Unified School District and our health organization partners. On Friday, January 20, at 11:30 pm, Piedmont police officers and fire fighters were dispatched to a home on Greenbank Avenue for a person suffering a possible drug overdose. The individual was transported to an area hospital for treatment. Mushrooms were confiscated at the home and sent to the county crime lab for analysis to identify the complete narcotic makeup. There was concern that the mushrooms had been mixed with fentanyl and the individual suffered an overdose because of the fentanyl exposure. The police department recently received the lab analysis results and have been informed there was no fentanyl detected in the submission. As our nation continues to struggle with the tragic results of the fentanyl epidemic, we ask the community to discuss the danger of fentanyl and the risks with ingesting substances which may be laced with fentanyl. For consideration, the websites below contain valuable information on the effects of narcotics and what parents can do to prevent narcotic consumption. The Department is committed to continued work on this critical issue with the Piedmont Fire Department, Piedmont Unified School District and our health organization partners. For more information, contact Captain Chris Monahan at CMonahan@piedmont.ca.gov. The Paperboy Continued from page 2 sons that now escape me I was in Bogota. It was late in the summer of 1968. Pope Paul VI was visiting Colombia, part of a Latin America tour, and the city vibrated with anticipation. I was having breakfast in a hotel dining room, seated at a table covered in white cloth. Colombia was a very Catholic country and I knew the coming days would be momentous. Looking around the large room, I noticed men and women seated at tables leafing through notebooks and talking animatedly. At their feet were portable typewriters in black cases. They were clearly journalists, there to write about the man from Rome. In that moment I wanted to be one of them, to cover this story, to be part of that headline that would soon emerge. I wanted to write stories, help keep the nation’s record and I thought about those days so long ago that I had delivered the newspaper. Chris Honore’ is a staff writer with the Piedmont Post, and for more than 20 years has been the paper’s principal movie reviewer. READ IT IN THE POST

Among those on hand were: Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Charlene Louie, Lisa Euphrat, Mike Nachtwey with K-9 best friend Clooney, Nancy Henn, John Lenahan, Phil Witte, Priscilla Wanerus, Vincent Fisher, Bill Ahern, Joyce Ahern, Sherry Jacobs, Quincy Dong, Rob Smith, Will Adams, Gloria DaSilva, Harriette Louie, Woody Bailey, Karen Palmer, Fangfang Lai, Mike Henn, Kat Lang, Joanne Larson, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, Brenda Ferrero, Pat Keller, Garrett Clifford, Melba Yee, Albert Chen, Christine Calliste, Laura Goldman with K-9 best friend Vivie, Jim Kuo, Helen Dong, and Dick Carter. Less than 12 hours after a major rain and windstorm battered Piedmont, the Walking on Wednesdays group was back in action exploring Piedmont streets on Wednesday morning, March 22. The weather was cloudy, but with no rain in sight. The prior Wednesday the walkers had discussed the history of Walter Blair, the first European settler in the hills that would become Piedmont. They walked the streets below Highland Avenue and discussed Blair’s history, but not gone to the area above Highland to Coaches Field on Moraga Avenue. Blair came to California in 1852 during the Gold Rush at the age of 22 and purchased 600 acres in the Piedmont hills for $750. It was most of the land between today’s Moraga, Scenic, Magnolia, and Grand Avenues on which he had grain fields, a dairy, and a quarry. He also constructed the Piedmont 35. The Duke of ___, "Rigoletto" role Springs Hotel in 1872 where the Exedra is today and built a horsecar trolley line which ran from film with Kevin Costner Mountain View Cemetery to Vernal (now Highland) Avenue and his hotel. To increase his riders in 1884, Blair developed 40 acres between the cemetery and Moraga Avenue as a picnic park with many attractions. He named it Blair Park. This Blair Park is not the current Blair Park further up Moraga. The walkers headed off to Coaches Field going on Highland Avenue, and passed the site of Blair’s original cabin at 111 Highland Avenue. At Highland and Moraga Avenues, the group crossed Moraga to where the park’s entrance once was. Blair’s park had financial difficulties almost immediately. After he died in 1888, it continued to be operated, but appears to have closed in 1905. Parts of the park’s land were sold to the cemetery and developers. The City of Piedmont bought the eastern portion in the 1920s for its Corporation Yard. In the next decades the nearby canyon was partially filled and eventually provided the land for today’s Coaches Field. The walkers crossed Moraga and walked over the boardwalk along Moraga that spans the edge of the canyon below. A creek in the canyon was more of a river, and a pond was more of a lake. Up Moraga a sign said the road was closed for tree work. Coaches Field was first dedicated in 1994, and in 2001 the sports field was created with the support of Piedmonter Ken (Bebe) Rawlings. Past Recreation Commissioner Vincent Fisher pointed out the newly constructed tall cell phone tower that will someday improve reception in the area. The group went along the backside of the field to a gate that is the entry to Kennelly Skate Park, a flight of steps above the sports field. The park was opened in 2001 and was named after the Kennelly family whose donation helped pay for it. At the top of the stairs they admired the concrete ramps and deep bowls that much younger people fearlessly skate up and down. As the walkers began making their way back to the middle of town, most of them took a side trip a half block above Highland to visit Hardwick Avenue and Langdon Court. Once back at the Exedra a few walkers made another side trip to the top of Piedmont Park to see the rushing waters of Bushy Dell Creek. In all, it had been a little over a two mile walk full of Piedmont history, parks, streets, and friends on a once again clear, no-rain Wednesday morning. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 AM. Everyone is invited to join the group. There is no charge. The Piedmont Police Department said that it answered 230 storm-related calls of Tuesday. Likewise, firefighters went from site to site to assess damage, call PG&E when power liens were involved, and clear as many streets as possible. Initial street closures included Lincoln from Crocker to Seaview, La Salle from Crest to Hampton, and Moraga from Maxwelton to Harbord. Gonzales said that a tree that fell on Moraga Avenue near Harbord, just over the Oakland border, was “responsible for most of the power outages we had in town.” A PG&E map showed that, as of Friday afternoon, March 24, power was still out for some Piedmont residents, including those living near Moraga Avenue. Approximately 50-100 homes experienced longer outages lasting into Friday afternoon. The Corporation Yard was among the buildings in Piedmont subject to power outages. “Our power didn’t come back on until Thursday or Friday,” said Gonzales. The building remained fully operational through the storm due to portable backup generators which the city received from Alameda County on Tuesday. “When you get high winds like and the ground is so saturated, chaos can occur,” said Gonzales. “We always recommend that residents hire an arborist to inspect and prune their trees, but sometimes it’s just impossible to predict which trees will fall, and where. Once the power’s out, everyone gets a bit cranky and everything gets very challenging. It’s definitely been keeping us busy.” contest. No Stopping Us Now feels like a particularly timely book for [this year’s] Readmont [community reading project], given the tremendous success of the 2023 girls high schools basketball team.” From March 20 to April 19, PHS athletes are taking time from their schedules to join each 5th grade library session at each of the three elementary schools. Fifth graders will hear high school athletes read one of the newly donated books, engage in a discussion about the importance of Title IX, and then view a short video of Title IX champion Congresswoman Patsy Mink. “I am thrilled that Piedmont has stepped up to have a conversation about Title IX this year. Last fall the Speaker Series and the Diversity Film Series covered this topic for adult audiences,” said mayor Jen Cavenaugh. “Activities this spring help a younger generation become informed about the impact of Title IX and the opportunities available to them. No Stopping Us Now, the selected Readmont book this year, is based on the author’s high school years, the book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her Oregon high school. It is a book about the love of sports and finding one’s own voice. The Recreation Department encourages all kids to try sports through Try It Out Mondays and its annual Play Like a Girl+ event, this year at Witter Field on April 23 from 10:00 a.m - 1:00 p.m. PHS in New York Continued from page 7 extended beyond journalism. It taught us how to be better leaders in all aspects of our lives. [It was] a lot about the importance of confidence when you’re in charge of a large group, but also stressed that respect is needed for a functioning relationship, and for a strong newspaper,” said senior Ava Adarkar, the Campus Editor. Each session cultivated a space for students to meet other journalism students from across the country, allowing them to learn from like-minded individuals. “It was inspiring to see newspapers from other schools and meet advisors from around the country because everyone genuinely cares so much,” Adarkar said. “The sessions and conversations made the class find a better understanding. Everyone expanded their knowledge on the subject, but it felt especially formative in finding your own niche,” said junior Phoenix Nwokedi, a staff writer. This year, students also had the opportunity to meet individuals in the journalism industry. Gady Epstein, The Economist’s China Affairs Editor, shared his story with the class and answered questions about pursuing a career in journalism. “[Epstein] shared about his experiences writing at his high school newspaper and how that contributes to his work today,” said junior Hana Thomas, the TPH web editor. On the Columbia University campus, Anusha Shrivastava, the Associate Dean of Career Development at the Columbia Journalism School, led TPH staff on a tour of the Journalism School. “[The tour] gave me a lens into what pursuing a career in journalism would even look like. Hearing about all the [alumni] and how they’ve used their degrees is inspiring,” Adarkar said. At the end of each day, the staff met to debrief what they learned and discuss how to incorporate new ideas into The Piedmont Highlander. “We all had many new ideas that we were so excited to implement into TPH once we got home,” Thomas said. “Sharing our ideas with each other inspired our staff and got us excited for the remainder of the school year.” Black said that this is one of her main goals in taking students on the trip. “I love that they come back with so many new ideas that they bring from across the country to Piedmont High School,” Black said. Students also had time to explore the city. As a staff they saw the musical comedy Some Like it Hot on Broadway and walked throgh Central Park and Times Square. “Our class was able to bond a lot throughout the trip and understand each other better as both people and journalists. I feel like we were all reminded of why we took the class in the first place, and why our job is so important,” Adarkar said. Sage Gilbert is a member of the Journalism Class and a junior at Piedmont High School. PHS students on a tour of Columbia’s School of Journalism in front of a stained glass window that was originally in the office of Joseph Pulitzer. The Piedmont Police Department said that it answered 230 storm-related calls of Tuesday. Likewise, firefighters went from site to site to assess damage, call PG&E when power liens were involved, and clear as many streets as possible. Initial street closures included Lincoln from Crocker to Seaview, La Salle from Crest to Hampton, and Moraga from Maxwelton to Harbord. Gonzales said that a tree that fell on Moraga Avenue near Harbord, just over the Oakland border, was “responsible for most of the power outages we had in town.” A PG&E map showed that, as of Friday afternoon, March 24, power was still out for some Piedmont residents, including those living near Moraga Avenue. Approximately 50-100 homes experienced longer outages lasting into Friday afternoon. The Corporation Yard was among the buildings in Piedmont subject to power outages. “Our power didn’t come back on until Thursday or Friday,” said Gonzales. The building remained fully operational through the storm due to portable backup generators which the city received from Alameda County on Tuesday. “When you get high winds like and the ground is so saturated, chaos can occur,” said Gonzales. “We always recommend that residents hire an arborist to inspect and prune their trees, but sometimes it’s just impossible to predict which trees will fall, and where. pages.text: 32 Wednesday, March 29, 2023 Sara Lillevand Continued from page 1 happy to say that’s changed completely for Piedmont High after forty-something years.” She transferred from Stanford to UC Davis in her second year of college, was a star on the Aggies basketball team, and graduated as a physical therapy major in 1991. After one year as a physical therapist at Stanford Children’s Hospital, she worked for 18 years at California State University in Hayward as kinesiology instructor, head women’s basketball coach, and Athletic Director. She was named Coach of the Year in the Cal Pac Conference in 2000- 2001. Lillevand was lured to city government by longtime Piedmont Recreation Director Mark Delventhal and was hired as his replacement in 2014. During this time, she led the Hampton Park renovation project. On her transition to local government from intercollegiate sports, she said, “It was a unique opportunity to be close to home and give back to a city that’s given so much to me, and in particular the Rec. Department,” she said. Five years later, on June 17, 2019, she became the city’s top employee as its City Administrator when Paul Benoit retired. On August 8, 2022, Lillevand announced her intent to retire on her birthday, April 5, 2023. In recent weeks she has been in conversations with her replacement, Rosanna Bayon Moore, who was hired by the City on February 16. “I’m not surprised she’s been so deeply involved in advance of her start date,” said Lillevand. “I think the city’s really lucky to have her and it won’t take long for the community to recognize that.” Reflecting on the difference between athletics and municipal government, Lillevand said, “The coaching role translates well to local government – it’s just a different kind of team. I see everything through the eyes of a coach.” Of her time as City Administrator, Lillevand said that she was “proudest of having navigated the COVID pandemic. It’s been fairly dominant during my time here, and I think the response by city staff in rising to that unprecedented challenge showed what an exceptional team we have, individually and collectively. articles.text: After a two-hour discussion on Monday, March 20, the Piedmont City Council voted to adopt Piedmont’s 6th Cycle 2023-2031 Housing Element and Initial Study-Negative Declaration (IS-ND). As par t of Piedmont’s state-mandated General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 — a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. This drafting cycle is repeated every eight years. The IS-ND is a document accompanying the Element which fulfills a California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requirement that public agencies disclose potential impacts of proposed projects before adopting them. Kathryn Slama from Lisa Wise Consulting, the project manager of Piedmont’s Housing Element update provided the council with a report and recommendation. Describing the update process since Piedmont submitted its draft Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for a 90-day review on November 18, 2022, Slama said, “The Planning Commission recommended adoption of the [Element and IS-ND] earlier this year” on January 12. The 90-day review for the Element was completed on February 16, when the city received HCD comments. articles.text: The Piedmont School Board will present the Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award to the 2023 recipient at tonight’s board meeting. The meeting will be held in City Hall starting at 7:00 p.m. The main discussion at the March 22 meeting will be a presentation on the possibility of making changes to grading at Piedmont High and Piedmont Middle School. It will occur in the open session at approximately 7:20 p.m. PHS Principal Sukanya Goswami and PMS Principal Karyn Shipp will lead the discussion with the help of PMS English teacher Jamie Van Kleeck, and math teacher Kate Waldron The is the first public discussion of the studies of the work of Education Consultant Joe Feldman and his book, “Grading for Equity.” One topic is the elimination of zeros in grading practices, making a grade of an “F” 50-60% and under 50% an Incomplete. The board background document says: “San Leandro Unified administration shared the changes their high school teachers were making in their grading practices after engaging in action research around the essential question: Which grading practices are most accurate, bias-resistant, and motivate continued learning?” Equitable Grading is a possibility to aid in the district’s LCAP Goal 2 states which state: All students will engage in relevant learning experiences that foster life-long curiosity, creativity, collaboration, critical thinking, communication, and responsible citizenship. A new student representative to the board, junior Siddharth Bhatia, will have a seat at his first school board meeting. Bhatia, follows Gianna Yan and Cleo Tahawi, each representative has around three months to sit on the board as student representatives, in the first year of the position. articles.text: When the Silicon Valley Bank failed it sent shock waves through financial markets. Perhaps it shouldn’t have been a surprise that when discussing causation many Republicans attributed its collapse to the fact that it was a “woke” bank. What gave me pause was their use of the word “woke.” The word, initially regarded as slang, was added to the Oxford English Dictionary in 2017, and is now a part of the mainstream language. It is derived from African-American vernacular, and was meant to describe one who is alert to and aware of the presence in society of prejudice and discrimination as well as systemic oppression and injustice. The term has since become contemporized. Beginning in 2014 it became identified with the Black Lives Matter movement and was often used during protests or when debating the role the police should play in society. But ultimately what does “woke” mean? Prior to its being appropriated by other activist groups, Perry Bacon, Jr., a columnist for the Washington Post, gave the term a comprehensive definition (one not necessarily shared by many centrist Democrats). He asserted that to be “woke” meant a rejection of American exceptionalism; incorporated the belief that America has never been a true democracy; that people of color suffer from systemic, institutional discrimination; that women suffer from inherent sexism; that individuals should be able to identify with any gender or even none; and that Donald Trump’s election was not an aberration, but a reflection of the prejudices regarding people of color held by a large part of the American population. “Woke” however, has recently been co-opted by conservatives and is often used as a single-word pejorative rallying cry when referring to progressives (or Democrats in general) and the issues they advocate. It is generally said with an insulting, denigrating sneer and is likely followed by the words “political correctness.” For example, Florida governor, Ron DeSantis – who will, presumably, soon announce his candidacy for president – in a recent speech characterized his state as “the place where ’woke’ goes to die”. Additionally he signed a law named “Stop the Woke Act.” We reject ‘woke’ ideology, he said, and “we will never surrender to the ‘woke’ agenda, or the ‘woke’ mob,” thus reminding his audience of his adherence to “anti-wokeness.” He has advocated the erasure of race-related content, the 1619 Project, African-American history courses in Florida’s high schools, and the Critical Race Theory. the definition of which is as elusive as the term “woke”. He has also supported barring transgender athletes from competing, and supported enhancing criminal penalties for people arrested for protesting during demonstrations (recall those that took place in reaction to the death of George Floyd). Our language is dynamic, ever changing, some words evolving into internet memes. Nouns (even proper nouns) can become verbs. An example would be the phrase, “I just bricked my phone,” meaning rendering it useless. Or. my sister “Houdinied her way out of a locked closet.” While some words seem to spontaneously appear in usage such as “woke”, others simply vanish. But for as long as they last, they are convenient shortcuts. Just ask any conservative whom you’ve “friended”. 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Selen Ozturk Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Sohrab “Seb” Ford (intern) Micah Temple (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: Vandalism, racial slurs at PMS (2022) Piedmont Middle School staff found anti-Asian slurs inside vandalized classrooms over the weekend of Dec. 17, according to a letter sent to PMS parents and students from the PMS administration. (Someone] broke into a total of four classrooms and one bathroom. In addition to leaving the slurs, other items were moved and supplies were used. At the time of the letter’s release, on Dec. 19, PMS administration had not yet identified the students responsible for the vandalism. However, according to interim superintendent Dr. Donald Evans, the students have since been identified and staff has taken action to discipline them. Emails detailing the incident were sent to PMS parents and students, as well as PHS parents. The lack of communication from the district to the PHS community prompted some frustration from PHS student groups. When discussing the incident, student groups like Asian Student Union and Piedmont Affinity and Identity Mentors expressed concern that the administration’s lack of response was becoming a pattern. Fantasy Slut League (2012) The “Fantasy Slut League” was a group created by PHS varsity athletes in which male students earned “points” by engaging in sexual activities with female students, according to a notice to parents from then principal Rich Kitchens. According to Kitchens’ notice, the league had been in existence for five to six years at the time. Piedmont received national media attention when the league was discovered. Kitchens and the PHS administration responded by releasing an extensive notice to parents, detailing the information they had and their plan moving forward. According to the notice, staff conducted an investigation which included interviewing students, parents, and staff. The notice was only sent to parents of PHS students, not the students themselves. Swastika in Boys Restroom (2021) In April of 2021, a swastika was found carved into a stall in the boys’ bathroom, according to a letter addressed to PHS families. An investigation was then conducted, but the results of the investigation were not shared with families. The administration’s response letter was sent to parents, students, and staff six days after the swastika was initially found. In the letter, administration briefly reported the incident and briefed families on the investigation and steps to come. A majority of the email focused on reiterating that acts of hatred, bigotry, dehumanization, or division have no place in the community, and thanked students upstanders who actively chose to reject anti-Semitism and other hate. The letter concluded by asking students to follow the school mantra of “see something, say something.” White Support Circle (2021) Dr. Cheryl Wozniak sent out an email on April 21 offering a “white student support circle” in response to the trial, verdict, and experiences related to George Floyd. articles.text: An incident at a high school basketball game at Piedmont High School on February 7 involving an adult male charged with battery on a male student appears to be unresolved by the school a month and a half later. Piedmont resident Yoel Asulin, was issued a 21-day Temporary Restraining Order by the Alameda County District Attorney’s office following the incident, and the order was extended for 21 more days this week. The victim, a high school senior, stated that he was grabbed violently in the bleachers and thrown down. His necklace was ripped and his shirt was torn. The student, who was emotionally distraught, was taken to a hospital and released. PHS Assistant Principal Erin Igoe, Athletic Director Bradley Smet, and Counselor Chris Hartford were on the scene, but did not call the police. The next day the boy, and four classmates who were with him at the game, gave their statements to the Piedmont Police. The incident did not appear on the Piedmont Police Department log. Since it was a late-reported event, the police did not file an emergency protective order. Police Capt. Chris Monahan confirmed that Asulin was charged with battery, which involves the act of physical harm, as opposed to assault, which also involves a threat of physical harm. Responding to a request for comments on March 7, Igoe said “While I was one of the school employees on scene, I don’t feel comfortable providing any comments. I will tell you, though, that choking is not what occurred.” Asulin has a prior arrest record. In 2015 he was arrested at his home for child endangerment under California Criminal Code 273A(A). On Tuesday, March 7, one month after the incident, PHS principal Sukanya Goswami sent an e-mail to PHS families about the incident. At that time she described as “a physical and verbal assault on one of our students at a varsity basketball game by a parent.” Goswami wrote, “A stay away letter has been issued to the adult involved. This stay away order means that this individual will not be allowed on campus for 14 days.” She added, “As a school system, we are re-evaluating the policies and procedures in place for communicating with students, parents and the greater community following any critical incident on campus.” However, neither the school nor the school district have yet specified when the stay-away letter was issued and whether it has been renewed, nor how the TRO will be enforced by the school district. Piedmont resident Yoel Asulin, was issued a 21-day Temporary Restraining Order by the Alameda County District Attorney’s office following the incident, and the order was extended for 21 more days this week. The victim, a high school senior, stated that he was grabbed violently in the bleachers and thrown down. His necklace was ripped and his shirt was torn. The student, who was emotionally distraught, was taken to a hospital and released. PHS Assistant Principal Erin Igoe, Athletic Director Bradley Smet, and Counselor Chris Hartford were on the scene, but did not call the police. The next day the boy, and four classmates who were with him at the game, gave their statements to the Piedmont Police. The incident did not appear on the Piedmont Police Department log. Since it was a late-reported event, the police did not file an emergency protective order. Police Capt. Chris Monahan confirmed that Asulin was charged with battery, which involves the act of physical harm, as opposed to assault, which also involves a threat of physical harm. Responding to a request for comments on March 7, Igoe said “While I was one of the school employees on scene, I don’t feel comfortable providing any comments. I will tell you, though, that choking is not what occurred.” Asulin has a prior arrest record. In 2015 he was arrested at his home for child endangerment under California Criminal Code 273A(A). On Tuesday, March 7, one month after the incident, PHS principal Sukanya Goswami sent an e-mail to PHS families about the incident. At that time she described as “a physical and verbal assault on one of our students at a varsity basketball game by a parent.” Goswami wrote, “A stay away letter has been issued to the adult involved. This stay away order means that this individual will not be allowed on campus for 14 days.” She added, “As a school system, we are re-evaluating the policies and procedures in place for communicating with students, parents and the greater community following any critical incident on campus.” However, neither the school nor the school district have yet specified when the stay-away letter was issued and whether it has been renewed, nor how the TRO will be enforced by the school district. articles.text: Scouting volunteers will be recognized at the Piedmont Council’s Annual Recognition Dinner on Thursday, March 30 in the guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. The selection committee was chaired by former Council President Seth Hilton, and included many longstanding Piedmont leaders. “Our volunteers support our local youth development, and provide service to the greater community as well,” said Scout Executive Kate Benson. “They are guiding these youth through service projects that impact our community right now- such as Scouting for Food, creek clean ups, and more. But their impacts also continue for decades, as today’s Scouts carry the ethic of service throughout their lifetime.” The Silver Beaver Award, the highest recognition a council can give a volunteer will be presented to longtime Scout volunteer Chris Lee. He was chosen for outstanding leadership as council youth protection champion, as well as decades of volunteer service as a den leader, committee chair, board member (three terms!) and service on the tree lot committee. “Scouting provides leadership opportunities for young people, and teaches them a wide range of values including responsibility and giving back to the community,” said Lee. “It’s one of the best youth programs in the country.” When asked why he served as the council’s Youth Protection Champion, Lee answered, “Youth Protection Training is critical for protecting our youth. It’s also important for building credibility. It assures Scouts’ parents and guardians that there is a safe place for their youth to participate in the program.” Volunteers being honored At the dinner, the council will recognize many volunteers, including: • Silver Beaver: Chris Lee • District Award of Merit: Glyn Burge and Bryan Gros • William Peterson Youth Award: Julia Banuelos and Nathan Fredericks • President’s Award: Sara Cumbelich Distinguished Scouter awards will go to volunteers who have contributed strongly to the Scout program in their Packs, Troops and coed units over the past year. Community members are welcome to attend, and tickets are available online at www. piedmontbsa.org. For more information, call the Piedmont Scout office at 547-4493. articles.text: More than 50 Piedmont community members gathered at Havens Library on Wednesday, March 15, to participate in a discussion with members of the Piedmont Police Department about community safety. Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers, Captain Chris Monahan and other members of the police department led the discussion and participated in the event which provided a valuable discussion of the current social climate, preventive actions and community building. Bowers spoke about the diversity, equity, and inclusion training and initiatives by the police department, and highlighted the distinction between a hate crime and hate incident. “I am very appreciative of the opportunity to engage with the people who took the time out of their busy lives to hear from the Photos by Lisa Douglas Police Chief Jeremy Bowers spoke to community members about public safety on March 15 in the Havens library. Chief Jeremy Bowers (left), Mayor Jen Cavenaugh, PUSD’s DEI Director Dr. Vaanden Wyngard, Commander Lisa Douglas, PAAC Co-Presidents Cassindy Chao and Catherine Zhang, Black Youth Family Collective President Nairobi Kim, and Captain Chris Monahan. police department. It is clear that public safety continues to be one of the prime areas of focus for our Piedmont community,” said Bowers. “I look forward to the continued collaboration and conversations, because public safety is everyone’s responsibility,” he added. Monahan detailed some crime statistics, to include a spate of catalytic converter thefts. Monahan implored residents not to interfere with crimes-in-progress for their own safety. Converter thefts have been on the rise in Piedmont and throughout the Bay Area, and thieves at times are armed. Commander Lisa Douglas stressed the importance of not inundating 911 with non-emergency calls, and Sgt. George Tucker shared safety tips regarding property protection and lighting. Cassindy Chao and Catherine Zhang, co-presidents of Piedmont Asian Club, helped promote the meeting due to concerns of antiAsian hate and safety issues. “It is unfortunate in today’s society that people have been encouraged by politicians to be blatant in expressing anti-Asian hate expressions and crimes, anti-Semitism,” said Mary Geong of the Piedmont Asian American Club. The meeting included support by Black Youth Family Collective, Piedmont Jewish families, and the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign. Nairobi Kim, President of the Black Youth Family Collective, said “Wednesday night was a wonderful representation of the community with Chief Bowers and his team at PPD. It warms my heart to see the many faces of our community come together.” For more information on community programs, crime statistics, and public safety tips, visit the Piedmont Police Department website at Piedmont.ca.gov/services___departments/police.
articles.title: Police, residents discuss community safety

articles.text: After a three-year absence due to Covid, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m. in the Alan Harvey Theater. With the theme of “Maskarade,” guests are encouraged to show their creativity and wear bird=themed masks. Created in 1963, by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, the Bird Calling Contest grew into an annual event that over the decades has attracted national and international attention. The winners appeared for many years on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, and then on Late Night with David Letterman. A panel of judges has been invited selected will consider the merits of the contestants based upon authenticity of call, poise and delivery, and content of contestants’ introduction of their bird. The judges include: • Rosemary Orozco, Weather forecaster KTVU • Michael Poryes, Television Producer. • Joe Fendel, 1991 Bird Calling Contest winner. • Jamie Mockel, PHS English teacher • Irma Munoz, PHS Vice Principal. Serving as celebrity judges will be Rosemary Orozco, a meteorologist at KTVU, and Michael Poryes, and 1982 PHS grad who created the popular television series “Hannah Montana.” Orozco taught at San Francisco State University and has worked as a meteorologist, journalist and news anchor for several stations. She also has worked as a model and has her own fashion line in San Francisco. Poryes is a three-time Emmy nominee who was an original member of the creative team that developed and launched “Saved by the Bell.” Joe Fendel was a four-time bird caller in 1987-91. First-year PHS English Teacher Jamieson Mockel comes from a family of bird callers, including his brother. His mother, Peggy, helped Leonard Wadeck with the show for many years. Assistant Principal, Irma Munoz is a former committee member for the Bird Calling Contest The contest will be directed by Piedmont High School Librarian Kathryn Levenson. “We have an able flock of student interns handling the technical aspects of the production. A student choreographed dance number will open the show and the student Jazz Quartet will entertain while the judged make their deliberations,” said Levenson. Tickets are available online at Showtix4u.com/event-details/67041. General admission tickets are $25; student tickets are $15. The Alan Harvey Theater is located at 800 Magnolia Avenue, on the high school campus. For more information contact Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@ piedmont.k12.ca.us, or 594-2781. articles.text: “Speak, Forgive, Forget,” echoed throughout Alan Harvey theater, as Piedmont High’s Advanced Acting class pushed the audience’s limits for forgiveness, with four dramatic performances of Everything is Wonderful the weekend of March 16-18. Written by Chelsea Marcantel, the play was directed by PHS Theater teacher Kimberly Taylor, with a talented rotating cast portraying an unlikely reunion of an Amish family. Junior Miranda Long, who has been acting since elementary school, carried the lead role of Miri in all four shows as the excommunicated daughter of an Amish couple intent on following their faith through forgiveness. “I really enjoyed playing Miri. I didn’t have to do an accent or wear the Amish dress for the whole play, but I appreciated how she was in an environment that was trying to encourage her just to forgive and forget.” When her brothers are killed in an accident, Miri returns to be with her family after being forced to leave five years earlier for not forgiving a man who assaulted her. Long continued, “Even though the high school usually doesn’t do such intense plays, I think it was important to spread awareness about the different struggles that the play highlighted, such Miranda Long (left) as the lead character Miri with Isabella Wire Eden Lorin (left) and Isabella Wire in traditional Amish dress Charles White (left), Miranda Long, Andres Roberts and Isabella Wire have a heated family discussion at a dinner table. as addiction, assault and grief. I appreciate that it brings to light those problems.” Senior Callan Mitchell, in his first performance as an actor, portrayed Jacob, the man who assaulted Miri. “It has been really weird performing such an upsetting character, and promoting the production, knowing that people might not view me the same,” said Mitchell, “It’s interesting to be myself one second in a classroom setting, and then go to rehearsal and play this terrible person.” Jake Hanke, a sophomore, took a major role in three performances as Eric, a young man struggling with alcoholism, who is taken in and forgiven by a couple whose sons he hit in a carand-buggy accident. “The play shows the importance of not having to forgive immediately, and giving yourself time to process your emotions,” said Hanke. Senior Charles White joined the acting class as a freshman. Despite COVID and having no theater on campus, he persisted in his acting pursuits to give his fourth and final Advanced Acting performance in Everything is Wonderful. He was cast as a stoic person with a beard in two performances as Miri’s father, Abram. “It is super unique what the acting class gets to do. We get to challenge ourselves as actors, especially with this play, while also being in a fun environment. Everyone is really good friends and we all had a great time,” said White. While the play encourages forgiveness, White acknowledged it’s not quite that simple. “The play has to do a lot with unconditional forgiveness, but also shows how not forgiving can be okay. People like to have a clean-cut resolution, where everybody is happy, but that doesn’t necessarily happen in this play,” White added.

articles.text: Piedmont’s community reading project, Readmont, now in its 13th year, has selected No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe as this year’s collective read. It was chosen to help celebrate the 50th anniversary of Title IX, the federal legislation requiring equal funding for women’s and men’s sports. It is a book about the love of sports, finding one’s own voice, and activism. Led by Piedmont High School English Department Chair Beth Black, Readmont will host a community discussion with the author on Wednesday, April 26, at 7:00 p.m. in the Piedmont High School library. Based on the author’s true story, it is a compelling examination of standing up for what is right. The book follows the story of Louisa who fought to bring her hometown into compliance with the new Title IX law so she could play basketball at her high school to attend the evening event. English department chairperson Black will also lead discussions during lunchtime on April 25 and 26. Books are available for check out at all Piedmont school libraries. Books are funded through the support of the Title IX celebration committee and the Piedmont League of Women Voters. A Great Good Place for Books in Montclair is offering a 20% discount on this title. Readmont aims to have a common reading experience to forge positive connections among students, staff, parents and community members. For more information, contact Kathryn Levenson, Teacher Librarian at Piedmont High School at klevenson@piedmont. k12.ca.us (594-2781), or Beth Black, PHS English Department chairperson, at bblack@piedmont.k12.ca.us. No Stopping Us Now by Lucy Jane Bledsoe was named a Finalist for both the Golden Poppy Award and the Rainbow Award. in Oregon. Those interested in discussing the book and learning more about the author are encouraged

articles.text: I am a focus coach in Piedmont and work with students and people with ADHD (Attention Deficit and Hyperactivity Disorder), helping them overcome obstacles and achieve their goals. I am certified in Applied Positive Psychology and use my education and my personal experience with ADHD to coach my clients. This week’s topic is Ego Depletion, one of the fundamental concepts I teach to clients who struggle with procrastination and completing tasks. Ego Depletion is the idea that each person only has a certain amount of self-control in a day and it depletes as it is used throughout the day. It’s that feeling of dread when you’re only halfway done with everything you need to do but your tank is empty and you have no energy left. The more willpower we use, the less we have… simple right? Some other things that deplete willpower besides using it are: stress, pain, multi-tasking, sleep deprivation, substances, a weak immune system, premenstrual cycle, and having low blood sugar. Now that we know that willpower is a set amount that depletes as we use it, how does that apply to ADHD and procrastination? People with ADHD often struggle to complete tasks from start to finish and frequently struggle with procrastination. I teach my clients about Ego Depletion as a way to get them to think strategically about how to prioritize their tasks. One exercise you can try is making a list of the things you need to do tomorrow and then ranking them in order of difficulty (make sure each task is broken down into one action item). List the willpower that you think you’ll need to get each one done. Once you have your list, you’re going to want to complete the tasks in order of how difficult they are and complete the most difficult ones first while you have the most willpower left. As you use up your willpower, you’ll have only the easy tasks to complete. Understanding and teaching ego depletion allows me to make effective to-do lists with my clients. Navigating a long to-do list can be very challenging for Strategize your to-do list. anyone, especially people with ADHD. Learning about ego depletion teaches people not only how to prioritize tasks, but also why it is so important to do the difficult tasks first. I use this and other concepts from Positive Psychology to teach and reinforce good habits so they can achieve their goals. What goals could you achieve if you knew the next steps? Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing. She can be reached at 415- 680-6990 or mindsglowing@ gmail.com. articles.text: Hedonists seek to maximize pleasure in life by indulging in anything and everything that elicits good feelings. To a hedonist, life is but a vehicle for happiness. Summer camps are not run by hedonists. If you handed a hedonist a summer camp, they would crumple at the sheer amount of displeasure that comes with the territory. Bugs. Dirt. Homesickness. Shared bathhouses. Surprise frogs in the showers of bathhouses. No amount of zip-lining could outdo the sacrifice of pleasure and comfort a hedonist craves. Yet, an untrained eye may believe Camp Augusta is engaging in this very act of folly: jamming so much unbridled fun into the day to somehow counteract the difficulties of rustic living. But that is not so. Watch and be amazed as we embrace displeasure at every turn. • Peer into the unflinching eyes of a counselor watching a camper notice the spider sharing their bunk. • Observe as the staff do absolutely nothing to install electricity or air conditioning into the cabins. • Be astounded when two campers who don’t get along are kept in the same cabin. Camp Augusta is not run by hedonists, oh no, no, no. Camp Augusta is run by people who understand that terribly arduous trials are in fact very healthy for children’s development. This isn’t to say we at Camp Augusta don’t also love fun and games (after all, we hire three Masters of Fun & Games to ensure maximum fun is to be had every season). We simply believe that a fun time and a challenging time can go hand in hand, and that challenge makes the summer camp experience sweeter (even if it isn’t felt in the moment). Those trials of terribly arduous displeasure mentioned earlier? Listen in for all to be revealed. • The spider lives at camp, too, and isn’t going to hurt us, so let’s figure out what to do together even if we feel a little scared of it. • Electricity and AC are great at home, but we can adapt to new situations even if they are uncomfortable at first. Let’s find a spot for your flashlight so you don’t need to scrounge for it later tonight… • I heard that you’re feeling really frustrated with another camper. I think we can still have a great week together and I’d love to know more about what’s going on and what you’re feeling. Behold! There is wonderful
articles.title: The serious side of being a camper

Camp Augusta is not run by hedonists, oh no, no, no. Camp Augusta is run by people who understand that terribly arduous trials are in fact very healthy for children’s development. This isn’t to say we at Camp Augusta don’t also love fun and games (after all, we hire three Masters of Fun & Games to ensure maximum fun is to be had every season). We simply believe that a fun time and a challenging time can go hand in hand, and that challenge makes the summer camp experience sweeter (even if it isn’t felt in the moment). Those trials of terribly arduous displeasure mentioned earlier? Listen in for all to be revealed. • The spider lives at camp, too, and isn’t going to hurt us, so let’s figure out what to do together even if we feel a little scared of it. • Electricity and AC are great at home, but we can adapt to new situations even if they are uncomfortable at first. Let’s find a spot for your flashlight so you don’t need to scrounge for it later tonight… • I heard that you’re feeling really frustrated with another camper. I think we can still have a great week together and I’d love to know more about what’s going on and what you’re feeling. Behold! There is wonderful Tuolumne Family Camp 2023 Weeklong, weekday, & weekend options Photo by Annie Spratt It’s not all fun and games at Camp Augusta. . . and we don’t plan on changing anytime soon. growth to be had when facing a terribly arduous trial head on. At Camp Augusta fun and games abound. And there are also mosquito bites, hot days, small bunks, and not nearly enough time alone. The staff and many of our returning campers (over 80% return) gladly take it all, a hundred times over. Before long, the pleasure and displeasure blends beyond the point of being able to parse what is what. Our advice? Take it all and trust us when we say it is more than worth it. Randall Grayson has been Camp Augusta’s director for more than 20 years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team continues its strong pace in the Western Alameda County Conference, beating Arroyo 3-1 at home on Wednesday, March 15, and shutting out Encinal 3-0 two days later on March 17, also in Binks Rawlings Gym. The pair of wins brings their record to 6-1 overall, notably including an Arroyo team with a lofty 12-3 record. “We actually had an off-day against Encinal. We had a starting outside hitter [John Champion] suffer an ankle injury right before the game, but we did fine,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. There’s a lot of energy around the team this season, now in its third year since reviving the program prior to the pandemic. With an arsenal of hitters and a vocal crowd in support, there is some swagger on the team that wasn’t present in previous seasons. “I think we’re playing a lot better this season because a lot of guys played club [volleyball] over the offseason,” said senior John MaNguyen, who led the team in kills against Encinal. “Last year we were a little more quiet and we weren’t really accustomed to playing together. This year, most of everyone played club, so we’ve gotten a lot better. We know how to work together because we’ve built close friendships. We try to keep the energy up every game and try to get in our opponents’ heads,” added senior Shunji Higashi, the team’s setter. With hitting options aplenty – MaNguyen, Wilson Wong, John Champion, and Torge Kraft, Higashi is able to send passes to either side comfortably to keep defenses off balance. “It’s really good to have options. When you’re limited to just one hitter, the other team will know and can prepare for it. You want variety,” said Higashi. 3-0 over Encinal It was a 3-0 sweep for the Highlanders against the Jets, winning by scores of 25-21, 25-16, and 25-19. In the first game, Encinal jumped out to a 2-0 lead, but PHS went on to score the next 10 of 11 points and never looked back. The two teams similarly traded points in the second game with Encinal briefly holding an 11-9 lead, but PHS then scored 10 of the next 12 points to lead 18-13, and then finished the second with five of the last six points. In the third game, PHS was able to rotate some bench players in and was still highly productive. Final stats: MaNguyen had 11 kills, Kraft had seven, Kelly had six, Eric Olaru-Hagen had four, Wong had one. Staff Photos John MaNguyen had 11 kills on Encinal and seven on Arroyo. Torge Kraft had seven kills on Encinal and 10 versus Arroyo.

articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team improved its record to 6-2 with a pair of wins in the past week over Division 4 North Coast Section opponents. Playing in Vallejo on March 14, they defeated St. Patrick 9-2. Three days later, Saturday, March 18, they rolled past St. Helena 13-3 in a traditional early season game between the schools. It was an impressive pitching display for Piedmont with a juggled lineup. Infielder Peter Krumins tossed five innings and had 10 strikeouts against St. Helena, while Michael Aikawa,, also an infielder struck out eight in four innings against St. Patrick. “We don’t have a big roster and not a lot of pitchers. We’ll be a by-committee approach this season, but we have a great defense to back up our arms,” said coach Eric Olsen. 13-3 over St. Helena The Highlanders trailed 2-0 following the top of the third, but added runs in the bottom of the third and fourth innings to tie 2-2. The Saints went ahead 3-2 after the top of the fifth, but then Piedmont powered on nine runs in the bottom half to go clear ahead 11-3 and added two more runs in the bottom of the sixth to enact the 10-run rule. In the bottom of the fifth, Michael Aikawa led off with a walk and then sophomore centerfielder Markos Lagios stepped up to crack a two-run homer to centerfield to make it 4-3 Piedmont. With one out, Will Parker reached on a single and advanced to second on an error. Ryan McConathy then brought in Parker on a single, 5-3, followed by Dimitri Papahadjopolous drawing a walk. With John Olsen up, McConathy scored on a wild pitch, 6-3, followed by Papahadjopolous scoring on an error by the catcher, 7-4. From there, Piedmont drew walks from Liam Campbell and Aikawa—which brought in Olsen for another run, 8-3. Lagios then hit a two-run double to score Aikawa and Campbell, and then Peter Krumins hit a double to score Lagios for an 11-3 lead. In the bottom of the sixth, McConathy got things started with a walk followed by a single by Papahadjopolous. Olsen then hit a single to score McConathy, 12-3, then Campbell singled in Papahadjopolous to activate the 10-run rule at 13-3. Final stats: Lagios went 2-for-2 with a home run, double, four RBIs, two runs scored, and two walks. Krumins went 1-for-3 with a double, walk, and two RBIs. McConathy was 2-for-3 with a RBI and two runs scored. Papahadjopolous was 1-for-2 with three runs scored and two walks. articles.text: The girls’ lacrosse team is back in action and has played five games. Piedmont’a girls’ lacrosse team is 2-3 through its first five matches of the season with a building team. They lost to Bishop O’Dowd 14-7 on Friday, March 17, but beat Cardinal Newman 12-6 on Wednesday, March 15. On March 14 they beat College Park 8-5, and lost 15-3 to Acalanes on March 7. Their season opened with a 17-5 loss to Miramonte on February 28. “We don’t have a superstar like in previous years, so they have to play together and for each other. Everything comes together,” said coach Carlton Chan. The Highlanders lost 10 players from the Class of 2022, including former leading scorer Katherine Kinne. Team leaders this year include Molly Ashton, Eleanor Lavin, Hailey Marshburn, and Lindsey Kottle. “Molly is our attack, and she’s been tremendous. She’s patent and she runs the offense. Eleanor is another captain; she is great in transition,” said Chan. Ashton has had a strong start to the season as the squad’s leading scorer with 15 goals including five against Bishop O’Dowd. “We are such underdogs, but we always work together. After the first couple of games, it feels like we’re getting things to work,” said Ashton. In its past two games, Piedmont has done well to stay composed, play good defense, and execute offensively. “When we understand what we need to do, we get it done. We have a team that works really well together,” said Ashton. 14-7 loss to Bishop O’Dowd The Dragons jumped out to an 8-2 lead in the first half, but Piedmont was able to score five second-half goals. articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team competed in the Dublin Distance Fiesta on Friday and Saturday, March 17-18 and at the San Leandro Invitational at Burrell Field on March 18. At the Dublin Distance Fiesta, Parker Long won the 800 meters with a record time of 1:53.25. Pole vaulter Spencer Sorensen-Wald was first at the San Leandro Invitational with a personal record of 13 feet. Piedmont brought a combined 48 athletes to both events, with 41 athletes recording personal records. This year team has 90 athletes – the largest team in recent history. It was also a strong Dublin Distance for Christian Taylor, clocking a time of 4:18.67 in the 1600 meters to finish sixth out of a field of 1,147 runners. Coach Pouyan Assadi is hopeful Long and Taylor’s time will qualify them for the prestigious Stanford Invitational on March 31-April 1, and the Arcadia Invitational on April 7-8. “Parker and Christian take a lot of pride in being our captains,” said Assadi. “They constantly impress the coaching staff and are able to perform in the most intense environments. We’ve submitted their times to the Stanford and Arcadia invitationals and are waiting to hear back.” Long improved his previous best time by 10 seconds, winning his event against a field of 770 in Dublin. It marks the third fastest time in school history behind Gordon Johnson (1:51.10 in 1989), and Reece Proctor (1:52.64 in 2018). His time edged out Cooper Downing’s time of 1:53.40 set last year. “I’m still processing the aftermath of all of it just running that time. I got put in the fastest heat and I didn’t expect that to happen. Parker Long (17) won the prestigious Dublin Distance Fiesta’s 800 meter run in 1:53.25, notching the third fastest time in school history. The guy who got second [Justin Pretre] is committed to Cal and it was super intimidating going against a field like that. With 200 to go, I realized I might have the speed to win,” said Long. Long only competed in the 800 once last season and primarily raced the 1600 and 4x400 relay team. He was a key member of last year’s record-setting 4x400 alongside Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Terrill. “I kind of avoided the 800 for a while, I focused on the mile and two-mile a bit more. After the first race of the season, my coach said I should consider focusing on the 800. In the 800, you have to be good at multiple things. The mile requires a lot of endurance and the 400 you can be good if you’re fast, but you need to have the speed and the endurance in the 800. I think I developed in both of those last year,” said Long. Sorensen-Wald’s height of 13-feet-0 was the best in a field of eight. It’s an impressive 2023 debut for Sorensen-Wald, whose previous best was 11 feet last year. The junior vaulter’s height at the San Leandro invitational ties him for third on the school’s all-time list with Irving Moore (1940), one foot behind No. 2 Marshall Wentworth (2011), and 3 feet, 1 inch behind Terrill’s alltime mark of 16 feet, 1 inch. “I was hoping to go higher in the pole vault, actually, practice has been going really well despite the rain holding us back a little. I didn’t jump in my sophomore year, so it took a bit to get back into it. Pole vaulting has a steep learning curve,” said SorensenWald about his development. It’s a similar start to the season as Piedmont’s record-setting pole vaulter Parker Terrill in 2022, who started his campaign last year with a vault of 13 feet, 1 inch at the Skyline Invitational. Like Terrill, Sorensen-Wald is hoping to develop in the decathlon. He also won the 300 meter hurdles in 42.41 in a field of 15 and tied for third in the 110 meter hurdles in 16.78. “Parker did every event and that’s something I’m trying to emulate. He did decathlon and was a great athlete, I’m trying to learn how to manage everything to not just put my complete focus on the pole vault but improve in other events as well,” said Sorensen-Wald. Spencer Sorensen-Wald cleared 13 feet in the pole vault at the San Leandro Invitational.
articles.title: Long wins 800, Sorensen-Wald wins pole vault

articles.text: Piedmont Swim Team members and parents came together at the Piedmont Center for the Arts to hear from three high school seniors committing to swim in college next year, Simon Lins officially announced he’ll join the University of Virginia, Paige Arnold will swim at Amherst College in Massachusetts, and while Ryan Stokes will head to The College of Wooster in Ohio. “It’s been a pleasure to get to know them and their parents,” head coach Stefan Bill told a large crowd of friends and family members. The three Piedmont swimmers were joined on stage by their parents to share how they encouraged them to attend practice without being pushy. Amy Aubrecht, mother of Kate Aubrecht who started swimming for Amherst College, kicked off the discussion. “If there are any tricks. It was bribing with food, right? Like parents bringing hot chocolate or donuts,” said Aubrecht. Arnold agreed: “Every morning before morning practice, my dad gets up and makes my Ryan Stokes is set to join The College of Wooster in Ohio. Simon Lins officially announced he’ll join the University of Virginia. lunch, which is really nice, and he makes breakfast before early morning practices.” When these swimmers wanted to quit, this is how they pulled out of their slump. “In 6th grade I was fed up and dreading practice, but I had a conversation with my dad. He told me to give it one more year and if I still don’t like it, I can quit,” Lins told his Piedmont teammates. “The next year I fell in love with it.” Stokes added, “To just sit on the couch and miss practice, especially if you have a lot of schoolwork, is really easy. But for me, [it was] just telling myself you’ve gone this far, just one more practice.” Parents and swimmers agreed. The parents’ role in supporting their swimmer is simple. “Coaches coach, parents parent, swimmers swim,” Aubrecht explained. All of this support has given these kids the opportunity to swim in college. Simon is the first from Piedmont Swim Team in at least 10 years to be recruited by a Div. 1 school. “Every single school in the country with a D1 program was talking to me,” Simon admitted. “It was really overwhelming.” Simon was recruited by Cal, Harvard, University of Texas, Yale, Brown and Columbia to name a few but picked UVA. While his swim times were important, that wasn’t the only thing schools cared about. Paige Arnold will head to Amherst College in Massachusetts. “They are making an investment in you, not your times. They make an investment in your character and who you are striving to be,” Lins explained. Arnold committed to swim at Amherst College and Ryan at The College of Wooster. They say the process to swim at a Div. 3 school is different. While D1 schools recruit swimmers, for D3 schools are the ones who initiate it. Amy Aubrecht shared her daughter’s experience getting into Amherst. “You have to have the academics because there are no athletic scholarships,” she explained. College coaches have a certain number of swimmers they can support, which can help you get accepted into the school. Piedmont Swim Team head coach, Stefan Bil talked about his own conversations with college recruiters from around the country. “The Columbia men’s head coach essentially said, I’m going to put him [Lins} at the top of the list.” All the Piedmont swimmers say they sacrificed social events and the opportunity to play other sports. Parents gave up vacations to attend swim meets. “Every time I miss a practice, I think it’s a missed opportunity,” Arnold said. “When things get really hard it’s going to be discipline that will keep you consistent until motivation kicks in,” added Lins. Stokes summed it up: “Trust the process.”
articles.title: Piedmont swimmers Lins, Arnold, Stokes commit to colleges

articles.text: Former Music Director of San Francisco Symphony Michael Tilson Thomas comes out of retirement to conduct on March 30 to April 1. Michael Tilson Thomas returns from retirement to conduct the San Francisco Symphony Thursday through Saturday, March 30-April 1. Tilson Thomas, the revered long-time former music director of the Symphony, received 16 Grammy awards during his tenure; his first recording with the symphony, Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet, won a 1997 Grammy. He serves as Artistic Director Laureate of the New World Symphony, an American orchestral academy based in Miami Beach, Florida. Tilson Thomas will lead the symphony in three evening performances of the music of Gustav Mahler, for which he is well known. In London, Tilson Thomas led the London Symphony Orchestra in major festivals featuring the music of Steve Reich, George Gershwin, Johannes Brahms, and Mahler. Tilson Thomas’ discography includes The Mahler Project, a collection of the complete symphonies and works of Mahler for voice and orchestra performed with the San Francisco Symphony. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfsymphony.org/ Buy-Tickets/2022-23/MTT-Conducts-Mahler-6, or call the box office at (415) 864-6000. All performances begin at 7:30 p.m. ®
articles.title: Michael Tilson Thomas to conduct SF Symphony March 30-April 1

articles.text: Berkeley Repertory’s current production of Cambodian Rock Band continues through April 2. Lauren Yee’s rock-music themed play features songs by Dengue Fever, an American rock band based in Los Angeles that blends traditional Cambodian music with psychedelic rock. Yee’s play borrows tracks from the unique group to tell the story of a young Cambodian-American whose father was a musician persecuted by the Khmer Rouge army. The survivor returns to Cambodia for the first time in three decades, as his daughter prepares to prosecute one of Cambodia’s most infamous war criminals. Directed by Chay Yew, this darkly humorous play is set against a grim chapter of Cambodian history with live music by Dengue Fever. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www. berkeleyrep.org/shows/cambodian-rock-band/. Cambodian Rock Band is playing at Berkeley Repertory Theatre through April 2. Lauren Yee’s rock-music themed play features songs by Dengue Fever, an American rock band based in Los Angeles that blends traditional Cambodian music with psychedelic rock. Yee’s play borrows tracks from the unique group to tell the story of a young Cambodian-American whose father was a musician persecuted by the Khmer Rouge army. The survivor returns to Cambodia for the first time in three decades, as his daughter prepares to prosecute one of Cambodia’s most infamous war criminals. Directed by Chay Yew, this darkly humorous play is set against a grim chapter of Cambodian history with live music by Dengue Fever. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www. berkeleyrep.org/shows/cambodian-rock-band/. By Allyson Aleksey Michael Tilson Thomas returns from retirement to conduct the San Francisco Symphony Thursday through Saturday, March 30-April 1. Tilson Thomas, the revered long-time former music director of the Symphony, received 16 Grammy awards during his tenure; his first recording with the symphony, Prokofiev’s Romeo and Juliet, won a 1997 Grammy. He serves as Artistic Director Laureate of the New World Symphony, an American orchestral academy based in Miami Beach, Florida. Tilson Thomas will lead the symphony in three evening performances of the music of Gustav Mahler, for which he is well known. In London, Tilson Thomas led the London Symphony Orchestra in major festivals featuring the music of Steve Reich, George Gershwin, Johannes Brahms, and Mahler. Tilson Thomas’ discography includes The Mahler Project, a collection of the complete symphonies and works of Mahler for voice and orchestra performed with the San Francisco Symphony. articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum will open a new exhibit, Beyond Bollywood: 2000 Years of Dance in Art, on March 31. The new exhibition features more than 120 artworks borrowed from 20 of the finest museums and private collections in the world, with a focus on the arts of the Indian cultural sphere. Beyond Bollywood includes artwork from India, Pakistan, Nepal, Tibet, Sri Lanka, Myanmar, Thailand, Cambodia, and Indonesia. “We hope visitors will come away with a transformed notion of the importance and power of dance,” said exhibition co-curator Forrest McGill. “[Both] what it has meant in the past, and what it can mean in their own lives today.” Beyond Bollywood will be on display from March 31 to July 10. For more information, and to purchase tickets to the museum, visit https://exhibitions.asianart. org/exhibitions/beyond-bollywood-2000-years-of-dance-inart/. Maharaja Sher Singh and companions watching a dance performance, circa 1850.

articles.text: The de Young Museum is now exhibiting Lhola Amira: Facing the Future, a series of programs in an exhibition available throughout the year. The solo exhibition interprets the museum’s African art collection as a living and evolving practice through the lens of contemporary art. “Lhola Amira: Facing the Future” centers art from Africa as a site of critical exploration for the evolving nature of African culture. Lhola Amira, a South African artist, is offering visitors ways of becoming more open and more sensitized to the pain of others, and the possibilities of the present,” said Natasha Becker, curator of African art for the museum. Artworks from de Young’s permanent collection are placed with Amira’s work, exploring the themes of wounding and healing. Selections include African art pieces from the 19th and 20th century art, including sculptures and ceremonial pieces. On view is Philisa: Zinza Mphefumlo Wami (2022), an art portal considering sacred spaces for the cleansing of wounds, honoring ancestors, and fostering connection. Guests are invited to enter this interactive art portal with healing in mind. Also included in the exhibition is the single-channel video projection IRMANDADE: The Shape of Water in Pindorama (2018–2020), produced by Amira in Bahia, Brazil. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/lhola-amira. Installation of Lhola Amira: Facing the Future at the de Young Museum.
