articles.text: My professor taught a music course for non-majors and posed this very question, playing 3 or 4 recordings from concerts, each one fuzzier and less score-specific than the previous. I finally said no way to the last one, and now realize, years later, I was wrong. The 2022 winner of the Pulitzer Prize in Music, Raven Chacon, was inside the historic Mills College Concert Hall last week playing his own work entailing in part what he calls “noise music,” using an electric guitar. His music formerly would have been excluded because of a Pulitzer requirement that the music be written down and thus potentially replicated by others. There were no clear notes, nor bars nor rhythms nor chords nor tunes in the music, just sound – “noise.” Not even a visible score. This all-Chacon concert was the music of today, gaining great respectability, even better for watching than listening. Outside next to another campus building, a tireless young man with lacrosse stick was bouncing the ball off a wall in irregular patterns, with resonance. Was that also music? I’m not sure. But for Chacon, 45, and his audience, this was a historic time. Last year marked the first time in history that a Navajo Indian of the Indigenous People had ever won the muchsought-after Pulitzer in Music, which every composer-professor alive vies after. Among others. Chacon’s “Round” had six performers around a table activating electronics and a central turntable. There were roars, whooshes, and staticky sounds like shortwave radio still seeking a station. These seemingly semi-improvised sonic explorations reminded one of early electronic concerts in this very hall 50 or more years ago, going from loud to ultra-loud. Happily, free earplugs were there on a stand for the taking. Later, a solo for cello, “Quiver,” with growls, whirlwinds, bow scrapes and spiccato tones. In many ways, Ben Davis’ cello imitated electronic music for over 15 minutes. was the piece with the giant pinecone sliding and rubbing over an electrified kettle drum – just one of some 20 devices employed by percussionist William Winant. This was the soundscape “Duo Improvisation,” where seeing the players became as engrossing as listening. Chacon was on his multi-sound electric guitar, manipulating pedal controls as much as strumming. Meantime percussionist/showman Winant dove into a variety of instruments, working the drums of a stage set and churning about his Composer Raven Chacon won the 2022 Pulitzer Prize in Music. musical arsenal, ranging from shimmers of scrapes over his giant tam-tam to the high-pitched squeaks of a cymbal drawn across an electrified kettle. The pinecone journeyed across the drumskin and reached the far side, all the sounds enharmonic. This must-see duo ended in 20 minutes. The casual informality of the event offered a lot of fiddling – fiddling with the equipment and controls, that is. The conviviality at the break was welcome. This being Mills College, musicians and patrons milled about. When Chacon came over with all his luxurious saltand-pepper hair over the shoulders, people took photos of the celebrity. He is currently composer-in-residence at Mills and a star in an exotic musical medium. Exiting, I hoped that the lacrosse player was still doing his unmetered shots in his competing “concert.” But no, darkness had swept over the campus, and the sycamores untouched by the recent stormy blow stood inordinately quiet, perhaps out of respect. Perhaps because a relative, a pine tree, had provided a vital instrument for an epic concert experience. The Mills Center for Contemporary Music presentors have a distinguished history of bold sonic innovation. A half century ago this same hall had hosted internationally known experimental composers Pauline Oliveros, Lou Harrison, Karlheinz Stockhausen, John Cage, and Robert Ashley via the CCM. COMPOSER-IN-RESIDENCE RAVEN CHACON in his works March 18, Concert Hall, Mills College at Northeastern University, Oakland, CA. For Center for Contemporary Music info: www. performingarts.mills.edu/center-for-contemporary-music. Reviews of Piedmont-based music reviewer Paul Hertelendy are available the classical-music site www.artsSF.com.

articles.text: David Morales conducts the choral group Cantare Con Vivo. Piedmonters know John Malick as an architect. They know Sue Malick as the leader of the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Together they are master chemists – musically speaking. Anyone who attended the Sophie Florence Trio concert at the Center for the Arts on Friday evening observed the results of the Malicks’ musical chemistry. It seems that they were vacationing in Mexico and two of John’s friends were in the area at the same time. Being musicians, they brought their instruments. A young woman heard them jamming and asked to sing a song with them. The results sounded promising. So promising, that Sue Malick offered to sponsor them in a concert in the Piedmont Center for the Arts this spring. The result? The Sophie Florence Trio made its debut in Piedmont on Friday, March 17. Everything looked promising. The audience was far flung – some even came from England. That’s the allure of music. But the chemistry needs to be right, and on Friday it was – from the opening notes. A sentimental ballad, “The House of the Rising Sun“, drew us in immediately. The music was enchanting. And wonder of wonders, the group knew how to add just the right amount of talking to go with the music. Sophie Florence has a gentle voice and she uses intimacy to best advantage. Backing her to perfection were Chuck Jacob on both the harmonica and string bass, and Phil Hirschi on guitar. Whether you call it alchemy or The Sophie Florence Trio performed a debut concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, March 17.
articles.title: Musical alchemy

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, March 22, 2023 What exactly is music on the fringe? The Musical Gourmet Musical alchemy necromancy, the musical chemistry was just right. The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The group led us down the path of affectionate memories. They have since taken their show on the road. Cantare Con Vivo Two days later, another master musician produced alchemy of a different sort. David Morales has an enviable reputation. He is an inspired educator of young people and is Music Director of the well-established Cantare Con Vivo. Their musical vehicle on Sunday at the Scottish Rite Center, Oakland was a slight departure from the usual repertoire. It was Er nest Bloch’s intensely profound Sacred Service. Bloch was born in Switzerland but found success in the Bay Area. He was an instructor at UC Berkeley and also the Director of the San Francisco Conservatory of Music. In many ways Sacred Service is Bloch’s grandest composition. Its position in the Jewish musical liturgy is roughly the same as a high mass to Christians. What Bach did for the Christian liturgy Bloch did for the Jewish liturgy. The similarities are obvious. But the heartbreak is very different. Bach uses his music like a canvas painted by Velasquez. Bloch’s music is more like Picasso at Guernica. The performance of the Sacred Service featured baritone Simon Barrad, who was very convincing as the Cantor. Cantare Con Vivo sang up to their usual high-level. Everything was directed by the inspired leadership of Morales. It is interesting to note that good musicianship embraces all of humanity, and that’s how it was on Sunday. David Morales conducts the choral group Cantare Con Vivo. articles.text: The Secret Lives of Bees, is a family friendly, coming-of-age film based on the best-selling novel by Sue Monk, and is an ideal choice for tweens and newbie teens. It is set in North Carolina, the year is 1964, and has at its center a 14-year-old girl, Lily Owens (Dakota Fanning). Her mother is deceased and she is living with her abusive father, T.Ray (Paul Bettany), and a devoted housekeeper, Rosaleen (Jennifer Hudson). On a beautiful day, Rosaleen tells Lily that she wants to walk into town where she wants to register to vote; instead, she is attacked by a group of thuggish white racists. As a result Lily convinces Rosaleen that they need to escape the cruelty that confronts them daily and so they head for a nearby town call Tiburon. As always, Lily yearns to know the path her mother took just prior to her death. Through a series of serendipitous events, Lily and Rosaleen are taken in by a trio of sisters who live just outside of town where they keep hives of bees and make astonishingly good honey, sold by the local grocers. One owner of a local market tells Lily how to get to the source of the honey. Look for a pinkish two-story house, home of the Boatwrights. And indeed, when the two walk down a long dusty road, they do arrive at a garish home where they first meet August Boatwright (Queen Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson and Alicia Keys in a scene from The Secret Lives of Bees Latifah), the bee-keeping matriarch of the family, as well as the fiercely independent June (Alicia Key), a musician, and May (Sophie Okonedo), a tender-hearted, simple girl. Secret Lives evolves into a warm, generous story where Lily and Rosaleen are embraced by this extraordinary family, and Lily is introduced by August to the hives and comes to understand not only the meaning of family but the magic of making honey. There is also a bit of romance between Lily and a shy black teenager, Zach Taylor (Tristan Wilus), who make the mistake of going to town to see a movie. Innocently, they sit together in the theater. Though it is 1964, racism still survives, which the couple painfully learn is forbidden, and Zach is roughly arrested. The Secret Lives of Bees is never cloying, or overly sentimental. Nor is it a harsh southern documentary about prejudice and discrimination. Rather, it is a tale of strong black women created by a wonderful ensemble cast that will capture the audience from the first scene. The Secret Lives of Bees, Directed by Gina Prince-Bytherwood, Starring Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson, Alicia Keys. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.

By Chris Honoré The Secret Lives of Bees, is a family friendly, coming-of-age film based on the best-selling novel by Sue Monk, and is an ideal choice for tweens and newbie teens. It is set in North Carolina, the year is 1964, and has at its center a 14-year-old girl, Lily Owens (Dakota Fanning). Her mother is deceased and she is living with her abusive father, T.Ray (Paul Bettany), and a devoted housekeeper, Rosaleen (Jennifer Hudson). On a beautiful day, Rosaleen tells Lily that she wants to walk into town where she wants to register to vote; instead, she is attacked by a group of thuggish white racists. As a result Lily convinces Rosaleen that they need to escape the cruelty that confronts them daily and so they head for a nearby town call Tiburon. As always, Lily yearns to know the path her mother took just prior to her death. Through a series of serendipitous events, Lily and Rosaleen are taken in by a trio of sisters who live just outside of town where they keep hives of bees and make astonishingly good honey, sold by the local grocers. One owner of a local market tells Lily how to get to the source of the honey. Look for a pinkish two-story house, home of the Boatwrights. And indeed, when the two walk down a long dusty road, they do arrive at a garish home where they first meet August Boatwright (Queen Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson and Alicia Keys in a scene from The Secret Lives of Bees Latifah), the bee-keeping matriarch of the family, as well as the fiercely independent June (Alicia Key), a musician, and May (Sophie Okonedo), a tender-hearted, simple girl. Secret Lives evolves into a warm, generous story where Lily and Rosaleen are embraced by this extraordinary family, and Lily is introduced by August to the hives and comes to understand not only the meaning of family but the magic of making honey. There is also a bit of romance between Lily and a shy black teenager, Zach Taylor (Tristan Wilus), who make the mistake of going to town to see a movie. Innocently, they sit together in the theater. Though it is 1964, racism still survives, which the couple painfully learn is forbidden, and Zach is roughly arrested. The Secret Lives of Bees is never cloying, or overly sentimental. Nor is it a harsh southern documentary about prejudice and discrimination. Rather, it is a tale of strong black women created by a wonderful ensemble cast that will capture the audience from the first scene. The Secret Lives of Bees, Directed by Gina Prince-Bytherwood, Starring Queen Latifah, Jennifer Hudson, Alicia Keys. 1 hr., 50 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2008. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: At a military ceremony with full flourishes on Wednesday, March 1, the Vandenburg Space Force Base Leadership School was renamed in honor of Chief Master Sergeant Arthur Hicks (1922-2017). His daughter Joyce Hicks, a Piedmont resident since 1987, spoke with the Piedmont Post on Thursday, March 9, about the legacy of her father’s life and career in the Air Force. “My dad felt his upward mobility was stunted because he was so outspoken about civil rights as a young officer,” Joyce said. He retired at Vandenberg after 28 years of military service in bases across the country, from Alaska to Tennessee. Having grown up poor as one of nine children in Atlanta, Georgia, Arthur joined the Army as a mechanic’s assistant in 1940 when he was 19. After seeing an ad in the local Post Office, he applied for and was hired by the Tuskegee Institute in Alabama, now Tuskegee University. As World War II continued, the Army Air Corps, then segregated, needed more pilots so Arthur joined the Civilian Pilot Corps as a Cadet. Soon after, he became a commissioned officer. He became part of the Tuskegee Airmen, the first African-American military airmen in the U.S. Armed Forces, during World War II. “The war ended before he saw time overseas,” said Joyce, “and the Army then had no more need for so many pilots, so he was honorably discharged.” After the war, Arthur married Edith, and they Photo by Airman 1st Class Kadielle Shaw U.S. Space Force Col. Rob Long and Joyce Hicks, daughter of Arthur Hicks, cut the ribbon at the renaming ceremony of the Airman Leadership School at Vandenberg Space Force Base on March 1. had their first son in 1947. He then returned to the army through a program where honorably discharged officers could return as enlisted employees with the rank of Master Sergeant, the highest rank for enlisted men. In his new role as a Maintenance Supervisor for bomber aircraft, Arthur was stationed in Lockbourne, Ohio; then in Smyrna, Tennessee, and then four years at Elmendorf Air Force Base in Anchorage, Alaska, where Joyce was born in 1952. From Anchorage, the Hicks family was transferred to Lincoln, Nebraska, and then to Wichita Falls, Texas. Throughout these moves, Joyce said, her father continually “confronted racism in the military, and always spoke out against it.” In Wichita Falls, the base had Joyce attend a public school far away, instead of a segregated school five blocks from their house. This was in 1963, well after the 1952 Supreme Court case of Brown v. Board of Education which began the desegregation of U.S. public schools. “My father said that if I had to go to the school farther away, they had to send a driver. They did that for a week. After that, the base officials said, ‘Master Sergeant Hicks, your daughter can attend school in the neighborhood’,” Joyce said. From Texas, the family moved in 1963 to Vandenberg Air Force Base in California. But there, too, Arthur encountered trouble: on-base family housing was limited and nearby off-base housing for African-Americans was nonexistent. Through his persistence, he was soon promoted to Senior Master Sergeant, and then to Chief Master Sergeant, the highest enlisted rank in the Air Force and Space Force. After serving for 28 years, Arthur retired in 1970. He earned a Bachelor’s degree that year from the University of Nebraska, and then began a career of 13 years as a history and social studies teacher at Cabrillo High School in Lompoc, California, retiring in 1984. During this period, he also earned a Master’s degree from Cal Poly in San Luis Obispo. “I’m so proud that the [Vandenberg school] was named after him,” said Joyce. “He was a tireless worker, a leader who led by example. He and my mother encouraged me to be the best that I could be, and to exercise my advocacy skills by becoming a lawyer.” Joyce graduated from Berkeley Law School in 1977. She has worked as Chief Assistant to the City Attorney of Oakland, head of the Citizens Police Review Board in Oakland, and Director of the Department of Police Accountability in San Francisco. At the Vandenberg ceremony on March 1, she said: “My father’s advice was, ‘Find it in yourself to contribute to the whole. We can most effectively do that by first making the best possible contribution to our own selves; through education, through questioning, through personal growth and to look toward the goal that is so far out of reach you cannot even imagine what it is at this point in your life.’” GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023 GOOD THROUGH APRIL 2023
articles.title: Leadership School at Vandenberg named after Tuskegee Airman Arthur Hicks

articles.text: Registration for the free, 19th annual Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Features Showcase is now open. There will be two days of online tours on Saturday and Sunday, April 15-16, and two days of in-person tours on Saturday and Sunday, May 6-7. What’s special about California native plants? They are adapted to our soil and climate, naturally water conserving, and easy to care for. California native plants are better than non-native plants when it comes to attracting native birds, butterflies, and other forms of wildlife. As the gardens on the tour show, these lovely gardens display a sense of place that is uniquely Californian. The tours will also showcase green home features. Online tour The online Bringing Back the Natives Garden Tour and Green Home Showcase will take place on April 15-16 from 10 a.m.-3 p.m. This event will be kicked off on April 15 with a keynote presentation by New York Times bestselling nature writer Doug Tallamy. The online tour will feature beautiful native plant gardens that attract birds, bees, and butterflies, as well as visits to homes with solar panels and backup batteries, heat pumps for heating and cooling the house and heating water, and induction ranges. In-person tour The in-person Natives Garden Tour will allow registrants to visit more than 50 beautiful, water-conserving native plant gardens in Alameda and Contra Costa counties on May 6-7 from 10 a.m.-5 p.m. All of the homes have native plant gardens; twenty will be sharing their green home features, such as solar panels and batteries, induction ranges, and heat pumps. Registrants will learn how to design a native plant garden for color and interest throughout the year, garden for wildlife, lower their water bills, protect their family’s health and the environment by gardening without using pesticides, and answering questions about electrification. How to register Register for the tours or learn more at BringingBacktheNatives. net. For more information about the garden tours, contact Kathy Kramer by email at Kathy@ KathyKramerConsulting.net or by phone at 236-9558 during business hours.
articles.title: Annual Natives Garden Tours begin April 15

articles.text: For the past 40 years, Dr. Daniel J Cobb provided innovative, high-quality dental care with friendly and comforting customer service. Dr. Cobb was renowned in the Bay Area for his extensive knowledge in implant dentistry and beloved for his kind demeanor. In June 2022, Piedmont lost a fixture of the community when Dr. Cobb passed suddenly from cancer. His loyal supporters are now witnessing a rebirth of the dental practice at the same location. Dr. Raion “Ryan” Sabo joins the Piedmont community with enthusiasm and passion for providing dental care at the highest quality. He developed his love for Piedmont during his undergraduate studies at UC Berkeley. After receiving his DDS degree from UC San Francisco, Dr. Sabo left the Bay Area to complete a 3-year residency program in Advanced Prosthodontics and became a specialist in complex aesthetic dentistry. When the opportunity to return to the East Bay and carry on Dr. Cobb’s legacy presented itself, a dream became a reality. “Piedmont provides the same tight-knit sense of community and small town vibes of my hometown of South Lake Tahoe, but simultaneously provides access to the amazing amenities Dr. Sabo and his staff occupy the former location of Dr. Daniel Cobb. of a large city. During our office remodel, my family, team, and I have already become frequent visitors of local Piedmont favorites: Ace Hardware, Neecha Thai, and Fenton’s Creamery”. Dr. Sabo is excited to continue exploring the area and start giving back to the community through both dentistry and various community outreach programs. The Piedmont Advanced Dentistry team wholeheartedly believes that despite the rapid rise of large corporate dental offices, there should always be a place to go for exceptional customer service, high-quality dental care, and a personal connection that takes the dental care experience to another level. This bespoke approach to dentistry is what Dr. Sabo strives to bring to Piedmont with his newly remodeled and rejuvenated dental practice. His goal is to make everyone who visits the office realize that dentistry can and should be a pleasant experience. All it takes is a skilled team of people who share a vision for excellence in quality care and kindness. Piedmont Advanced Dentistry is now accepting new patients Monday-Thursday from 8 a.m. to 4 p.m. and available for emergencies by appointment Friday to Sunday. The office accepts most major PPO dental insurance plans and offers their own in-office membership plan to help make high-quality dental care more affordable and accessible to everyone. For more information call (510) 652-1702 or see: piedmontadvanceddentistry.com
articles.title: Advanced Dentistry comes to Piedmont

articles.text: New metal fencing is expected to be installed enclosing the city’s native plant garden next to Piedmont Community Hall by early summer. Piedmont Garden Club president Anne-Marie Lemarche and member Lindsey Meyersieck recently presented a check for $5,000 to Park Commission Chair Patty Dunlap and Parks & Projects manager Nancy Kent. Kent told the Commission that city staff “will be looking at the signage and [refreshing] plant material in the area” after the fencing is completed.” City workers have put the fence posts up. A double swing gate and installing the new fence around the garden will be done next.
articles.title: Improvements coming to Native Garden at Community Hall

articles.text: Dear Jim: I have a sump pump in my basement that has been doing its job fine for the last 10 years. When the big rains started in January, it failed, flooding the entire space and ruining my hardwood floors, rugs, and damaging the baseboards and sheetrock. It was an expensive nightmare. Why did this happen, and how do I keep this from happening again moving forward? Sump pumps can be used in a variety of ways to keep basements from flooding, either as stand-alone units inside a basement or crawlspace, or outside the house as part of a perimeter drainage system for below grade basements. While the pumps themselves are generally reliable and can often run 20-30 years without issues, it is primarily external factors that lead to their failure which can be minimized if the systems are monitored. Common causes of failure You need to check your pump at least twice a year and make sure it is plugged in and running, is in a clean basin not filled with dirt or debris, and with a float that moves up and down freely. The pump should be big enough to do the job, with a ¾ horsepower motor if water needs to go uphill to the street. A check valve needs to be installed next to the pump to keep water from running back into the pit or it may run continuously or way too often. The most common problem is with the GFI outlet that they are normally plugged into. Lack of a proper waterproof cover can allow moisture into the outlet, causing it to fail, especially when it is outside. If the pump is not running for an extended period due to a failed outlet and it remains submerged it can rust out and no longer function. If this sounds like Greek to you, find somebody who will review this information. Lack of attention and simple maintenance can have major consequences for finished basements. Backup systems can be a lifesaver The lesson we learned this year from looking at many of these failures is that things can go wrong in a heartbeat. In an atmospheric river downpour a basement can fill up with sevExamples of smart pumps and water-powered pumps A proper waterproof cover will protect this outlet. eral inches of water in 30 minutes or less, often when you are not around. Given that 100-year floods are something we may be getting every few years now, we are installing mandatory backup systems with our drainage work, such as dual pumps with battery backups, inverters to run main pumps from battery power, and our new favorite, the water-based pump that does not require electricity. We even have backups that tie into the internet and will send you alerts and real-time monitoring to your phone. Given that mother nature has a poor sense of humor and will likely cause this to happen while you are out of the country on winter break. this may be something for you to consider if you have an existing system that may be at risk. Jim Gardner, owner of Jim Gardner Construction, is a longtime Piedmont resident who has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, March 22, 2023 CONVERSATIONS WITH YOUR LOCAL CONTRACTOR Why do sump pumps fail? By Jim Gardner Dear Jim: I have a sump pump in my basement that has been doing its job fine for the last 10 years. When the big rains started in January, it failed, flooding the entire space and ruining my hardwood floors, rugs, and damaging the baseboards and sheetrock. It was an expensive nightmare. Why did this happen, and how do I keep this from happening again moving forward? Sump pumps can be used in a variety of ways to keep basements from flooding, either as stand-alone units inside a basement or crawlspace, or outside the house as part of a perimeter drainage system for below grade basements. While the pumps themselves are generally reliable and can often run 20-30 years without issues, it is primarily external factors that lead to their failure which can be minimized if the systems are monitored. Common causes of failure You need to check your pump at least twice a year and make sure it is plugged in and running, is in a clean basin not filled with dirt or debris, and with a float that moves up and down freely. The pump should be big enough to do the job, with a ¾ horsepower motor if water needs to go uphill to the street. A check valve needs to be installed next to the pump to keep water from running back into the pit or it may run continuously or way too often. The most common problem is with the GFI outlet that they are normally plugged into. Lack of a proper waterproof cover can allow moisture into the outlet, causing it to fail, especially when it is outside. If the pump is not running for an extended period due to a failed outlet and it remains submerged it can rust out and no longer function. If this sounds like Greek to you, find somebody who will review this information. Lack of attention and simple maintenance can have major consequences for finished basements. Backup systems can be a lifesaver The lesson we learned this year from looking at many of these failures is that things can go wrong in a heartbeat. pages.text: Wednesday, March 22, 2023 23 Have you built an emergency fund? Many people make financial New Year’s resolutions, such as reducing their debts or contributing more to their retirement accounts — both of which are certainly worthy goals. But among those who planned to make a financial resolution for 2023, the primary reason was the desire to build an emergency savings fund, according to a December 2022 study by research firm Morning Consult. Factors such as economic concerns and the sharp rise in inflation seem to be driving this greater interest in building an emergency fund. But it’s extremely valuable to maintain this type of fund in any economic environment. An emergency fund can help you prepare for a temporary job loss or early retirement, or pay for large home or auto repairs, sizable medical bills and other needs. So, how much do you need to keep in an emergency fund? The answer depends on your stage of life. If you’re still working, you might want at least three to six months’ worth of living expenses in your emergency fund. If you’re already retired, however, you may need at least three months’ worth of expenses for emergencies, plus another 12 months’ worth of expenses, after accounting for your other sources of income, to cover your everyday spending needs. And if you are retired, it’s especially important to maintain this larger emergency fund so you can avoid dipping into your investment portfolio to pay for any unforeseen costs and daily expenses. As you know, the financial markets can be volatile, so, if it’s possible, you’ll want to avoid having to sell investments when their prices may be down. When building an emergency fund, where should you keep the money? You’ll need it to be accessible, so you’ll want it in a liquid investment vehicle. At the same time, you don’t want to take risks with this fund, so you’ll want to be confident that your principal will likely be preserved. Some possibilities might include short-term certificates of deposit (CDs) or money market accounts. But wherever you put the money, keep it separate from your regular checking or savings account — it’s called an “emergency” fund for a reason, and you don’t want to mingle it with the accounts you use every day. Given the high cost of living, it’s not always easy to sock away money for emergencies — and if you wait until all your bills are paid before addressing an emergency fund, you may only make very slow progress. One possible strategy is to pay yourself first, so to speak, by having some money automatically moved from your checking or savings account each month into your emergency fund. And whenever you get a financial windfall, such as a tax refund or a year-end bonus at work, you might use some of it for this fund. It will take time and discipline to build and maintain an emergency fund. But once you’ve got such a fund in place, you’ll feel more confident in your ability to deal with unexpected costs that could potentially disrupt your progress toward your financial goals. So, make it a priority this year to build or strengthen your emergency fund. It will be worth the effort. articles.text: After years of intense debate, the California Public Utility Commission (“CPUC”) voted unanimously on December 15 to overhaul the rules that govern the way homeowners and businesses are compensated for rooftop solar. The new set of rules, called Net Energy Metering 3.0 (NEM 3.0) will significantly reduce the amount that homeowners will be compensated for energy that is sent back into the power grid from their home solar systems. This change, which will take effect on April 15, 2023, may reduce the benefits of a new solar installation by as much as 75%. The most alarming impact will be the change in the export rate. The export rate is the rate that solar owners can “sell” their excess electricity back to the grid. Currently, solar owners can send energy back to the grid and receive credits EQUAL to the amount that PG&E sells consumers this electricity. Under NEM 3.0, PG&E will charge the consumer approximately 4x what they will credit back to residential solar owners for exporting their electricity (Export rates can vary widely, but studies show it will likely average about a 75% decrease). Clean energy advocates claim that the new rules will devastate the rooftop solar industry and set back progress in the state, while the utilities claim that the new rules do not go far enough to make solar owners pay their fair share for grid maintenance. Under NEM 3.0, the financial benefits of solar will be drastically diminished: • For buyers who pay cash for their Solar, payback “Breakeven” periods will increase. Currently payback periods are approximately 5-6 years and under the new regulation, this will jump closer to 9-10 years. • For buyers financing the systems, their monthly payments for energy will still generally be less than they were without solar. But savings will be 60% lower than current levels. • Complexity will be added to the Solar program by adding new requirements such as a new system design and a requirement to support self-storage. This being said, Consumers will still be able to save money going solar under NEM 3.0. Those who finance their system will still have savings if the system is properly designed and priced. Additionally, by being able to lock in the rate that you pay for electricity by owning solar, you can avoid having rapidly increasing energy bills. What does this mean for you? • Homeowners that DO NOT submit a Solar interconnection application prior to the April 15th deadline will be compensated for energy sent to the grid under the new regulatory rates. HOWEVER, Homeowners that submit prior to the April 15 deadline will be grandfathered into the current rate structure for 20 years, provided that the Solar installation is completed by April 14, 2026. Interconnection applications are prepared by a solar installer and require a signed contract and diagram to be submitted. • As we transition from fossil fuels to clean energy, a larger percentage of the energy we use in our homes and vehicles will be electric. In Piedmont, new Reach Codes will require homeowners making certain renovations to include energy efficiency or electrification measures. The Reach Codes also require some measures to prep homes for electrification, and even require installing solar in some cases. Given the April 15, 2023, deadline, we would encourage people who are considering Solar to reach out to installers to fully understand what solar and storage would look like for you under NEM 2.0 or NEM 3.0. To learn more, or see what these changes may mean to you, feel free to reach out to our team at quotes@bidlist.io. We can also recommend a lot of great solar companies in the area who can assist you. Whatever you do, educate yourself in the near term to potentially earn decades of savings and environmental benefits. .Ian Collins is the Co-Founder of BidList, an application that provides consumers a way to shop for solar and other home improvements without the usual challenges of finding a qualified contractor. articles.text: Here are four ways you can make your finances – including banking, investing, and mortgages – more environmentally sustainable. 1. Don’t let banks invest your money in fossil fuels Are you trying to be sustainable but banking with an institution investing your money into fossil fuels? Find a bank or credit union that isn’t contributing to the climate crisis. The nonprofit organization Rainforest Alliance Network has a list of banks that are the worst financers of the fossil fuel industry. Another nonprofit, JUST Capital, ranks public companies by corporate responsibility and environmental factors. 2. Use a green credit card Check out ClimateAction Center’s Fossil Fuel Free Credit Card Guide to find a card that doesn’t support the fossil fuel industry. Additionally, there are credit cards that can turn your rewards points into carbon offsets, such as the Sustain: Green Mastercard. 3. Try investing sustainably There are more options than ever to put your investment dollars where your values are. Environmental Social & Governance (ESG) investing, also called Socially Responsible Investing (SRI), or Impact Investing, has gained popularity recently. You can invest in individual companies making ESG a priority or in a mutual fund or exchange-traded fund with a pre-packaged group of securities. 4. Look into green mortgages Some financial firms offer mortgages that incentivize buying or owning energy-efficient homes by offering borrowers more favorable terms, usually a lower interest rate or a cashback payment. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions.

articles.text: As we face the daunting, global challenges of climate change, it’s often frustrating to ask what can I do that will make any difference? One answer lies in our kitchens and thinking more carefully about the food we buy, how it’s stored and cooked, and what we throw away. As US food production has streamlined and increased over the years, so, too, has food waste. Food waste and food scraps account for some 35 percent of what we throw away. Consider the financial and environmental losses of wasted food in production, processing, transportation and distribution to markets. Discarding half a fully dressed hamburger, for instance, is equivalent to running shower water for 90 minutes. State Senate Bill 1383 in California has set a 2025 statewide goal of recovering 20 percent of edible food that is likely to be discarded due to its appearance, age, freshness, grade and surplus. Currently, the law requires Starting early — young Piedmonters Ellington and Murray Davis in the kitchen. jurisdictions including Alameda County to recover and redistribute 20 percent of edible food from “food generators” — such as grocery stores, large-scale caterers, and food wholesalers — that would otherwise go to landfills. The recovered edible food may be given or sold to customers, donated to employees, or donated to food recovery organizations and services, such as food banks. As food buyers and consumers, we play a prime role in food recovery. StopWaste.org has easy ways to reduce food waste and increase our food recovery impact: • Eat all of what you buy. Decide what food needs to be used up first, and plan meals around it. • Check the fridge and cupboards to avoid buying food you already have. • Buy fresh foods in smaller quantities more often to waste less and enjoy fresher ingredients. • Choose unwrapped fruit and vegetables over pre-packaged to better control amounts. • Prepare perishable foods soon • • after shopping. Wash, dry, chop, dice, slice and store fresh food items in clear storage containers. Freeze food such as bread, sliced fruit or meat that you don’t plan to eat right away. Cook entire meals ahead of time that can be stored in the fridge or freezer. StillTasty.com has food-specific guides of the shelf life and simple, effective food storage tips: • Separate fruit that is very ripe from fruit that is less ripe. • Store bananas, apples and tomatoes by themselves and store fruits and vegetables in separate bins, to prevent quick overripening. • Use storage bags or containers designed to extend the life of produce. • Wash berries just before eating to prevent mold. “By cooking what’s often called ‘root-to-shoot’—or experimenting with stems, roots, cores, peels, and imperfect parts of fruits and vegetables that might end up in the compost or even the landfill, I often turn a produce-drawer clean-out into a meal,” said Piedmont resident Susan Miller-Davis, Associate Director for the Silicon Valley Food Recovery Initiative. “I like to think of it as a tame, hyper-local version of dumpster diving.” She explained that she is inspired by two ‘roots-to-shoot’ cookbooks: “The edgy manifesto ‘Scraps, Wilts and Weeds: Turning Wasted Food Into Plenty’ by Mads Refslund,” founder of three-Michelin-star Copenhagen restaurant Noma, “and ‘Root-toStalk Cooking: The Art of Using the Whole Vegetable,’ by Bay Area food journalist Tara Duggan.” Marjorie Blackwell is a Board Member of Piedmont Connect, a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. For sustainability and climate action resources, visit Connect’s website: piedmontconnect.org.

articles.text: • 2019 Callaghan Graciano, $35 Virtually unknown in the U.S,, Graciano is one of the backbone grapes of Rioja. A big bold, complex red, it possesses a dense ruby color along with a sweet nose of blueberries, currants and a touch or earth. Some mild tannins are present, but it is not rustic because of the wealth of fruit. In response to this the updated Housing Element involves estimated travel times to schools, parks, and the Civic Center from these areas; emphasizes that unmapped sites like future ADUs and some sites like Moraga Canyon would add units of all income types throughout Piedmont; and demonstrates the fact that walkable access to amenities in a small city like Piedmont does not stop at its borders, but involves amenities in Oakland as well. “These are not isolated [lower-income] units,” said Bergman. “While … some [HCD comments] required significant effort and adjustments,” added City Administrator Sara Lillevand, “the structure and direction of the draft Housing Element remains intact, without changes to the sites inventory.” Karly Kaufman, a planner at Rincon Consultants, the firm which helped the city draft a legally compliant document, told the Council “the [IS-ND]’ determined that the Housing Element as a document will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment.” The IS-ND was published for a 30-day review period between December 9, 2022 and January 8, 2023, Kaufman said, and the two public agencies which provided comments, EBMUD and the California Department of Toxic Substances Control, did not identify impacts requiring revisions. “We’ve been working step by step with Lisa Wise Consulting as well as our staff, and the resolution that you have before you regarding Housing Element adoption … is, in our opinion, legally substantially compliant with state law,” said Piedmont City Attorney Michele Kenyon. Former Piedmont Mayor Teddy Gray King voiced her support of the adoption and shared her experience in developing the Element as a former City Council member. “I started working on the 6th Cycle Housing Element three years ago, back when former mayor Bob McBain was still in office,” King said. “This document is a result of government in action, of democracy in action, of hundreds and hundreds of conversations, communication, meetings, correspondence … and I really just want to cheer you on as you move this project forward.” The complete updated Housing Element and ancillary. Comments are available at bit.ly/3yTa8Sa. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome. org. articles.text: The Bond Oversight Committee reviewed city expenditures on the Community Pool Project at a meeting on Thursday, March 16. The review covered the period of December 5, 2022, when City Council approved a construction budget for Wickman Development & Construction, through February 28, 2023. Based upon a presentation by city Finance Director Michael Sczcech, the contract was awarded to the San Francisco-based Wickman for $21,700,000, with an overall construction budget of $23,870,000. Included in this is a $748,106 electrification fund, as City Council approved an all-electric pool design last April. The total Piedmont Community Pool budget is $28,981,000. The main costs which make this higher than the construction budget are a maximum of $2,550,694 provided to the firm ELS Architecture & Urban Design for engineering and design; $962,700 to Griffin Structures for project management; $36,990 to Isaac Sports Group for operational analysis; $16,956 to Rincon Consultants for a California Environmental Quality Act report; and $14,320 to the firm Forensic Analytical for environmental consulting. The primary source of funding for expenditures is Measure UU, which was approved by voters in November 2020. This measure authorized the city to issue up to $19.5 million in bonds, with revenue funding pool improvements. The revenue from these bonds is currently $24,556,809. The total budget for services covered by Measure UU, including construction, design, engineering, inspection, and management, is $24,718,577. All funding sources — including $3,054,177 in donations; $748,106 in loans and grants; and $460,140 in other funds available for the project — make the total budget $28,981,000. The city has spent $3,058,058 through February 28. A major amount of the donations have been generated by the non-profit Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization (PRFO). As January, it had raised more than $1.25 million of its $2.1 million fundraising goal to bridge the gap presented by inflated construction costs since Measure UU was passed in late 2020. Since January, all donations to PRFO are being matched dollar for dollar up to $500,000 thanks to an anonymous donor. PRFO General Counsel Eric Havian noted that as of March 6, “we’ve received over half of the matching amount. I have a feeling we’re even closer now, and we hope to receive it all by June 1.” The pool project is still on-track to be completed by the summer of 2024. The Bond Oversight Committee has met twice since its creation on October 4, 2021. Its members are John Chiang, Margaret Hiller, Al Lee, Dirk tenGrotenhuis, and Patricia Leicher as committee chair. The Committee is ad hoc and will terminate when the pool project is completed. For more information on the Piedmont Community Pool project, visit piedmont.ca.gov/ newpool. To donate to the project, visit prfo.org/donate. For questions about pool expenditures contact Michael Sczcech by email at msczcech@piedmont. ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3045. drawing a walk. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest 2 is coming to town April 23 and the event continues to grow. Volunteer slots for the day are now available for signup via the website. Guests will want to score prime seating to enjoy this year’s lineup of performers. In the spirit of celebrating the diversity of the Bay Area, groups taking center stage will include: • HiiiWAV Showcase, featuring Meaghan Maples and Tyler Reese. Hiiiwav helps Black musician-entrepreneurs build lasting businesses and uplift their communities. • Emeryville Taiko has entertained audiences throughout the Bay Area for over 25 years • • • with its modern, electrifying “kumi-daiko” style art form, which has its roots in religious and folk festivals of Japan. Renegade Opera’s Jewelz Moyer has brought her operatic arias as a Lyric Soprano to high profile events such as the Edwardian Ball SF and the Lightning in a Bottle festival. LIK H A Pilipino Folk Ensemble helps preserve indigenous Philippine art forms as expressed in music, literature, dance, arts, crafts, and attire through performance, community outreach, and youth development. Oakland Samba Revue returns to the Food Fest stage, bringing its unique blend of “little big band” sounds of Brazilian samba de gafieira which blends together acoustic samba, jazz, and funk. Piedmont Food Fest will include at least 30 food vendors, breweries, and wineries from throughout the Bay Area. To date, the lineup includes Oakland United Beerworks, Buck Wild Brewing, Federation Brewing, Wondrous Brewing Company, Dokkabier, Deer Hill Vineyards, Maker Wines, and Two Broads Ciderworks. Early Bird deals are available at www.piedmontfoodfest.org and include drink packages, KidZone carnival bracelets, collectible water bottles, and a gourmet boba and mochi snack box from Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. The special pricing runs through March 31.

Piedmont Real Estate Update March 2023 How Do Small, Medium, and Large Homes Compare Across Three Cities? For this month’s Calia Homes newsletter, we compared dollar per square foot ($/sqft) values across different-sized single-family homes in Berkeley, Oakland, and Piedmont. Realtors often talk about how $/sqft values decrease as homes get larger. Our research shows that this is the case. In all three cities, smaller houses sold on a higher $/sqft basis than larger homes. When comparing the data across cities, Piedmont has the highest $/sqft prices, on average, for all three size categories of homes. Housing Data Varies by City and by Neighborhood Piedmont is a city with a population of 11,107. Oakland, by comparison, has a population of 433,823—more than 39 times the size of Piedmont. Consequently, we thought it would be interesting to compare Piedmont housing data to housing data for an adjacent Oakland zip code, 94618, with 17,324 people. (2021 US Census Data.) Hawn has over 25 years of experience in education as a teacher, principal, college professor and most recently as Deputy Superintendent for Da Vinci Schools, a charter school system in the Wiseburn School District in El Segundo. Hawn signed a three contract through the 2026 school year, and will be paid $248,000 per year. “I was a teacher for a very long time and I still think like a teacher and really have that lens of teaching and learning,” Dr. Jennifer Hawn has signed a three-year contract to be Piedmont School District’s new Superintendent. articles.text: Despite some rain the weekend of March 11 and 12, more than 500 shoppers attended this year’s Treasures Sale at Piedmont Community Church. The annual sale of thousands of donated goods raised $26,000 for the church’s Youth Mission Trip during Spring Break in which they will build 15 homes outside Tijuana, Mexico. The sale helps pay for building supplies and material plus the food needed for the 195 youth who have signed up to spend the week of April 10-14 building homes for impoverished families in Mexico. Considered a rite of passage for Piedmont teens, the tradition dates back 24 years, during which time more than 350 homes have been built. For most families, it is their first dwelling with a front door and a door lock. The Treasures Sale drew a huge crowd of pickers, deal hunters, antiquers and collectors even before the doors opened at 9:00 a.m. Youth Pastor Scott Kail, who will lead the trip to Mexico this year, estimated that 150 people were lined up waiting to get in and begin bargain hunting. More than 50 volunteers were on hand to help over the weekend, and in the preceding weeks to collect and display all donations. Volunteers put up portable canopies in the courtyard to shelter Youth Pastor Scott Kail thanks volunteers while gathered in the church kitchen for final instructions.
articles.title: Piedmont Community Church Treasures Sale raises $26,000 for youth mission trip to Mexico

articles.text: Demolition of the former Piedmont Pool site has rendered the space unrecognizable with only ghosts of the Carriage House, three pools, and the pool facility remaining. The pool building, which housed the office and changing room, was torn down on Wednesday, March 8. The Carriage house and its 100-year history was turned to rubble in one day last Thursday, March 9. Plans are underway by the City to install a time-lapse camera which will shoot publicly available footage of the construction progress. Demolition of the pools and buildings began on February 7, with construction hours posted as 7 a.m. to 4 p.m., Monday through Friday. The construction site is bounded by Vista, Hillside, Magnolia and Bonita avenues. Excavation work will continue until late spring, said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, after which the general contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, will start grading and doing foundation work. articles.text: The first reference to Eskimo-Intuit peoples having multiple, nuanced words for snow was in the introduction to anthropologist/linguist Franz Boas’ Handbook of American Indian Languages published in 1911. He wrote it after studying the Intuit people of Baffin Island and posited that the structure of language (sound, grammar, vocabulary, etc.) shapes a speaker’s view of the world. But now consider the limitations of our language, the absence of descriptors when we attempt to understand and conceptualize what we refer to as the universe, a word that is understood but also accepted for its expansive vagueness. When an event takes place, astronomers search for language to frame and explain what it is that has been discovered. They need more than 100 words for snow, so to speak. Recently, scientists announced that at last they had captured an image of a stellar phenomenon that up until now had only been theoretical: a black hole. It is something better described as a cosmic abyss, one so deep and dense not even light can escape it. Before now, black holes in space were the stuff of imagination, the geography of writers and artists mining the forgiving realm of science fiction or expressed as computer model algorithms. Now, suddenly, black holes have been revealed as a concrete image of a lopsided ring of red and yellow light, a donut hole of sorts, surrounded by interstellar gas and dust, delineating a redeyed portal into which all matter is pulled, including light. One such eye has been discovered deep in the center of a galaxy known as Messier 87 (M87), some 55 million light-years from earth (in one year, light can travel some 6 trillion miles), meaning the distances in play are beyond extraordinary. To capture the image of M87, 200 astronomers aimed an intercontinental collection of nine mountain top telescopes, called Event Horizon, at the galaxy Virgo, home to M87, a black hole several billion times more massive than our sun. According to Einstein’s theory, it is a place where all matter, space, and time come to an end, a tombstone, and has been referred to as a “behemoth of nothingness.” Its origin is For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. articles.text: Dr. Jonathan C. Augustine is both a pastor in the African Methodist Episcopal Church and a professor of law. In his recent book Called to Reconciliation: How the Church Can Model Justice, Diversity and Inclusion, he notes that it important for us to respect both “the kingdom to come,” the promise of life beyond this life, as well as “the kingdom at hand,” the work God is doing in the here and now. One of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church’s primary commitments to the “kingdom at hand” is our support for, and participation in, the ongoing work of Oakland Ceasefire. I wrote this after spending a day with the leaders of Ceasefire Oakland. On Wednesday, March 8, I was at St. Columba’s Church in North Oakland for the annual Oakland Ceasefire Partnership Retreat. Gathered were service providers, planners, police, clergy, representatives of the elected officials and community members that have made Ceasefire work in Oakland for the last decade. The cover of the notebooks we were given read “Programs don’t change people, relationships do.” At the meeting we recognized that after reducing the number of homicides in Oakland to 67 in 2018 and 75 in 2019, the COVID years have brought a return to annual homicide rates of over 100. We discussed the reasons for this rise while affirming that there is still strong evidence supporting the effectiveness of Ceasefire’s evidence-driven, community-based, relationship building approach to gun violence reduction. At the retreat we reiterated our commitment to keeping people alive and out of jail and reviewed the three central goals of Ceasefire: 1. Reduce shootings 2. Reduce recidivism 3. Build trust between the community and the police During the presentation lifting up the principles of the Ceasefire philosophy I took a picture of a slide titled “Specificity & Intensity.” The slide read. Oakland Ceasefire is a strategy to reduce gun violence in the near term (6, 12, 18 months) and focuses intensive interventions specifically on the largest drivers of violence including: • Retaliatory shootings • Very high risk individuals
articles.title: Ceasefire Oakland strives for reduction in gun violence

articles.text: The Silver Buffalo Award recognizes adult leaders who have provided distinguished service to youth at a national level. It is the highest award that the National Council BSA (Scouts) can present to its volunteers. Bob Coleman, a recipient of the Silver Buffalo this year, will be recognized at the National Annual Meeting in Atlanta on May 31. He is only the second Piedmont Scouter to receive the award. Wes Smith, also a former Piedmont Council president, was given the award in 2019. “The key reason I’m so committed to Scouting,” said Coleman, “is that the Scouting program for youth is the only one organized around teaching the qualities of leadership to young people. You don’t get that with any other organization. What is leadership? Leadership is a 15-year-old patrol leader at 1 p.m. on a campout weekend trying to get a bunch of wild 11 and 12-year olds to clean up the campsite. That’s leadership, and everyone has to do it. America needs more and better leaders.” Bob has deep roots with Scouting. He is one of three generations of Eagles, including himself, his father, James, and his son, Scott. His father’s adventures in Hungary at the 1933 World Jamboree have served as a family marker ever since. James became penpals with an Austrian Jewish Scout named Jacob. After a few years of corresponding, Jacob confided that his parents wanted him to immigrate to the United States but that he would need a work sponsor. Could James help? Well, James and his father searched and searched and were finally able to cable Jacob with the good news. One day later, this chilling cable came back. “Thank you for all your work to find a work sponsor for Jacob, but you are too late by a day!” James never heard from Jacob again. From this experience was born in James and later his entire family an abiding sense of urgency to get things done, something that carries on to this day. Asked about his proudest moment in Scouting, Bob said, “Participating in the vote to allow gay youth into the program. I wondered at the time, why our own Congress couldn’t work things on such a mature basis. We disagreed, we spoke together, we voted and we moved on, together.” After graduating from Wesleyan College and Harvard Business School, and after a decorated The animals cost up to $600, an impossible sum for a poor family. Some years ago Bob instituted an “animal-back guarantee” program whereby if an animal dies, for any reason, while in the care of the Fondouk, the Fondouk will arrange to find a replacement for that animal through discounted prices from animal brokers, favorable loans directly from the Fondouk or outright gifts. Bob visits Fez every year, and says it is rare when he doesn’t accompany the Fondouk’s local director into a souk to find a replacement animal. The hospital is administered by the Massachusetts SPCA. Their new director just finished a three-year surgical internship at Purdue University and is the first U.S. Board certified equine surgeon on the African continent. Bob has always made a connection between his other philanthropic work and Scouts. Bob’s church, Piedmont Community Church, was a chartering organization for Piedmont Scouts more than 100 years ago. Piedmont Language School was brought into the Council as a Learning for Life crew. In the early 2000s, as a member of the Piedmont Council Executive Board, he led a highly successful campaign to increase the council’s Endowment Fund. In only a few years it became one of the largest such funds in Piedmont and helped put Piedmont on the map of the national organization. Bob’s son, Scott, worked for a time in Geneva, Switzerland, with the World Scout Foundation and was part of the first committee to set up the rules for the Messengers of Peace program. Subsequently, Bob became a substantial supporter of Scouting in Morocco. Just last year, a dedication was held in Fez for the completion of an animal stable to be managed by the Fondouk. The half million dollar project was funded by a generous gift from the World Scout Foundation and significant contributions from the mayor of Fez and the local provincial governor. There was active local Scout participation throughout the project and continues today with local Scouts actually mucking our stalls and assisting with the feeding of the animals. The stable also has a dedicated Scout meeting room. “Never being too late by a day” is the driving force behind Bob’s commitment to Scouting. There is much to be accomplished. It must never be too late to get things done. Bob was listed by Barrons as the 8th top broker in America at a time when he and his team managed $3 Billion in assets. A close relationship with his clients afforded him the ability to help assist in their philanthropic efforts. Bob is also an active member of the Messengers of Peace Committee and an enthusiastic promoter of its mission. Bob is most likely the only Moroccan Sharif folks in Piedmont will meet. This honorific stems from the Coleman family’s 96 years of work as founders of the American Fondouk Animal Hospital in Fez, Morocco. The hospital provides free veterinary treatment of any kind to working animals in Fez, a city of two million people. It is the largest and best equipped animal hospital in Africa, and all veterinary treatment is paid for entirely by American donations. At any one time they routinely have up to 45 horses, donkeys or mules hospitalized for periods of up to one month. These hard-working animals rent out for $3 per day – the entire income for that animal’s human family for the day. Without that income, the family’s alternative would be starvation. The mayor of Fez once observed to Bob that the average poor household in Fez may have five to eight people residing in it. Treating 6 or 7,000 animals per year, that means that the presence of the Fondouk in Fez may keep upwards of 30,000 people from starving each year. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland Unified School District students to help keep the lake’s shoreline and creeks clean on a weekly basis. articles.text: Piedmont Food Fest The 2nd annual Piedmont Food Fest is coming to town April 23 and attendees will want to score prime seating to enjoy this year’s lineup of performers. In the spirit of celebrating the diversity of the Bay Area, groups taking center stage will include: • Emeryville Taiko has entertained audiences throughout the Bay Area for over 25 years with its modern, electrifying “kumi-daiko” style art form, which has its roots in religious and folk festivals of Japan. • Renegade Opera’s Jewelz Moyer has brought her operatic arias as a lyric soprano to high profile events such as the Edwardian Ball SF and the Lightning in a Bottle festival. • LIKHA Pilipino Folk Ensemble helps preserve indigenous Philippine art forms as expressed in music, literature, dance, arts, crafts, and attire through performance and youth development. • Oakland Samba Revue returns to the Food Fest, bringing its unique blend of “little big band” sounds of Brazilian samba de gafieira which blends together acoustic samba, jazz, and funk. The Food Fest will feature 26 food vendors, breweries, and wineries from around the Bay, to include Bonito Poke, Pirie’s Swahili Spot, Vegan Mob. and 3 Brothers Kitchen. Early Bird deals are available at www.piedmontfoodfest.org and include drink packages, KidZone carnival bracelets, collectible water bottles, and a gourmet boba and mochi snack box from Bakesum and Tea on Piedmont. Special pricing runs through March 31 so get your tickets this week. Newsstand copies of the Piedmont Post are available at Mulberry’s Market, and Piedmont Shell at Grand & Wildwood Ave. Copies of the paper may be purchased for $1 at all locations during business hours. Weekly delivery to homes in Piedmont and online access is available by subscription. Call 510-652-2051 for information. Or go to piedmont-post.com/subscribe. The Piedmont Post remains available online to all subscribers, no matter where they live. To have access to the online Post, type piedmont-post.com for a Google search. The entire edition is online. You must log in and use your password. Then readers may scroll from top to bottom as if reading the printed version from left to right.

Finally, the painting experience you've been looking for! By Jay Russell QUESTION: Which of the long-take tracking shots you just saw in class, did you find the most effective or well-done? Asked in Mercedes Foster’s new class at Piedmont High School, “Film as Literature,” on Friday, March 10. CHARLIE LUCAS, 12th grade I thought the shot in Baby Driver was the best. It feels like you are just watching the protagonist go about his day, while also showing the credits, and the lyrics to the music playing. It felt energetic and it set the mood for the movie. HENLEY LORIN, 11th grade I really like the movie 1917 in general. I think that opening scene was really effective and powerful. By following the soldiers, it makes the viewer feel like another soldier in the scene. PADEN ANDREWS, 12th grade Using the timer on the bomb in Touch of Evil is so perfect for building suspense; you know what’s going to happen from the first second. I also like how technical it was with the use of cranes in the 1950s. It’s impressive for its time. SAGE GILBERT, 11th grade I really liked the long take done entirely in the car from Children of Men. So much was going on in and out of the car, but it was done so seamlessly you feel like you are in the car with them. GRETA SCHLEUNING, 11th grade I thought the scene in the 1927 film Wings was super interesting since those cameras were so big and heavy. It’s impressive to move the camera through tables to get the shots without it being obvious to the audience. CALLAN MITCHELL, 12th grade Children of Men was probably my favorite example of a long-take tracking shot because of the anxiety that it induced. It was very well done by putting you into the scene which communicates the stress very well. articles.text: Nominations for this year’s Heritage Trees are due at City Hall by this Friday, March 17. The Heritage Tree program, which began in 2018, helps raise awareness of and appreciation for the city’s urban forest. Each year Piedmont designates up to five trees or groups of trees as Heritage Trees. Winners are selected from a pool of community nominations by members of the Park Commission and Public Works staff. This year’s Heritage Trees will be announced at the April 11 Park Commission meeting and highlighted at the City’s Arbor Day celebration on April 27 at Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue.. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized as part of the Arbor Day program and receive a heritage tree lapel pin. To nominate a Heritage Tree, download the nomination form at piedmont.ca.gov/HeritageTreeNomination. Return the completed form to Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager by email at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or by mail at 120 Vista Avenue. Please provide the following information: • the species of the tree or group of trees you’d like to see recognized • address or general location • description of the tree • explanation of the aesthetic, educational, or historical qualities that make this tree noteworthy • photo or link to a map showing the location of the tree, if available Trees selected as this year’s Heritage Trees will join 23 others that have received the designation since 2018. Last year’s winners were the Deodar Cedar at the traffic circle at Alta and Scenic Avenues; the Melaleuca at Beach playground on Linda Avenue; the Northern Catalpa street tree at 46 Nace Avenue; and the Autumn Blaze Maples on the 400 block of Wildwood Avenue. An interactive map of the City’s Heritage Trees, with photos and information on each tree, is available on the City’s Heritage Tree program webpage at piedmont.ca.gov/HeritageTrees. This year’s Arbor Day celebration will take place on April 27 at p.m. at Community Hall (711 Highland Avenue). In addition to recognition of the new Heritage Trees, the event will feature an “Ask an Arborist” booth, food and drink, music from the Piedmont High School jazz band, and a showcase of the trucks and equipment Public Works staff use to keep the city’s trees healthy and thriving. The popular chalk art contest and gratitude trees will return in the week leading up to the festivities. With questions about the Heritage Tree program, please contact Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent by email at nkent@ piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at 420-3064.
articles.title: Winners to be announced at Arbor Day ceremony April 27

articles.text: Compared to the damage from rainstorms in December and January, property damage from mid-March rains has been less widespread. “Although we did have a few maintenance workers on Thursday night, the only thing we’re aware of are two private trees down across roadways,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The trees which fell on Trestle Glen Road and Glen Alpine Road were cleared within hours by Friday. On Tuesday, March 14, police reported in mid-afternoon, “PG&E power lines are down and damaged on Moraga Ave. The power is out in the area and Moraga Ave. is closed between Maxwelton and Highway 13.” As of 6 p.m. last night, PG&E showed that there were power outages in the area at the Piedmont-Oakland border. City Maintenance Supervisor Nick Milosevich confirmed that the outages were due to a tree that had fallen onto a power pole by Moraga Avenue and Harbord Drive. “These storms have been interesting from a public works maintenance perspective,” notes Gonzales. “it’s not a constant drizzle, like you might get in Seattle. The rains are really heavy for just a short duration, and often with high winds.” Listed below are resources for Piedmont residents during these storms.
articles.title: Storm damage update

Stay informed • Check weather.gov for current weather advisories and warnings. • Sign up for safety alerts at acalert.org to learn about flooding or other emergencies.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is now accepting applications to fill upcoming vacancies on several Commissions and Committees. Online applications are due by 5 p.m. on March 29. Many of the programs that Piedmonters enjoy today were initiated and/or first reviewed by Commissions, including Heritage Trees, annual design awards, and the Map Your Neighborhood program. The dozens of residents who serve on one of the City’s 13 volunteer Commissions and Committees act as Piedmont’s eyes and ears, listening to community input, identifying and studying issues, and making recommendations to the City Council for action. Vacancies This year vacancies exist on seven commissions and committees — the Park Commission; the Planning Commission; the Recreation Commission; the Civil Service Commission; the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee; the Community Pool Advisory Committee; and the Public Safety Committee. For most bodies, members are appointed to threeyear terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. How to apply Those interested may apply online at: bit.ly/42bLtpj. When applying, you’ll be asked to provide contact and basic background information (education, occupation), select which body or bodies you would like to apply to serve on, and provide brief written answers to three questions: • What experience do you have related to this appointment? • Why are you seeking this appointment? • What will you bring to this Commission or Committee? The application also asks whether you have previously attended or watched a meeting of the body you’re applying to serve on. Archived meeting videos are available to stream on the city’s website. To be considered for appointment, applicants must attend an interview with City Council members on Tuesday evening, April 4. The interview schedule will be provided to applicants on Friday, March 31. For more information, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at 420- 3040 or by email at CityClerk@ piedmont.ca.gov.

pages.text: Wednesday, March 15, 2023 5 Heritage Tree Nominations due this Friday Winners to be announced at Arbor Day ceremony April 27 Nominations for this year’s Heritage Trees are due at City Hall by this Friday, March 17. The Heritage Tree program, which began in 2018, helps raise awareness of and appreciation for the city’s urban forest. Each year Piedmont designates up to five trees or groups of trees as Heritage Trees. Winners are selected from a pool of community nominations by members of the Park Commission and Public Works staff. This year’s Heritage Trees will be announced at the April 11 Park Commission meeting and highlighted at the City’s Arbor Day celebration on April 27 at Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue.. Nominators of selected trees will be recognized as part of the Arbor Day program and receive a heritage tree lapel pin. To nominate a Heritage Tree, download the nomination form at piedmont.ca.gov/HeritageTreeNomination. Return the completed form to Nancy Kent, Parks & Project Manager by email at nkent@piedmont.ca.gov or by mail at 120 Vista Avenue. Please provide the following information: • the species of the tree or group of trees you’d like to see recognized • address or general location • description of the tree • explanation of the aesthetic, educational, or historical qualities that make this tree noteworthy • photo or link to a map showing the location of the tree, if available Trees selected as this year’s Heritage Trees will join 23 others that have received the designation since 2018. Last year’s winners were the Deodar Cedar at the traffic circle at Alta and Scenic Avenues; the Melaleuca at Beach playground on Linda Avenue; the Northern Catalpa street tree at 46 Nace Avenue; and the Autumn Blaze Maples on the 400 block of Wildwood Avenue. An interactive map of the City’s Heritage Trees, with photos and information on each tree, is available on the City’s Heritage Tree program webpage at piedmont.ca.gov/HeritageTrees. This year’s Arbor Day celebration will take place on April 27 at p.m. at Community Hall (711 Highland Avenue). In addition to recognition of the new Heritage Trees, the event will feature an “Ask an Arborist” booth, food and drink, music from the Piedmont High School jazz band, and a showcase of the trucks and equipment Public Works staff use to keep the city’s trees healthy and thriving. The popular chalk art contest and gratitude trees will return in the week leading up to the festivities. With questions about the Heritage Tree program, please contact Parks & Project Manager Nancy Kent by email at nkent@ piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at 420-3064. Seats on city Commissions, Committees now open The City of Piedmont is now accepting applications to fill upcoming vacancies on several Commissions and Committees. Online applications are due by 5 p.m. on March 29. Many of the programs that Piedmonters enjoy today were initiated and/or first reviewed by Commissions, including Heritage Trees, annual design awards, and the Map Your Neighborhood program. The dozens of residents who serve on one of the City’s 13 volunteer Commissions and Committees act as Piedmont’s eyes and ears, listening to community input, identifying and studying issues, and making recommendations to the City Council for action. Vacancies This year vacancies exist on seven commissions and committees — the Park Commission; the Planning Commission; the Recreation Commission; the Civil Service Commission; the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee; the Community Pool Advisory Committee; and the Public Safety Committee. For most bodies, members are appointed to threeyear terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. How to apply Those interested may apply online at: bit.ly/42bLtpj. When applying, you’ll be asked to provide contact and basic background information (education, occupation), select which body or bodies you would like to apply to serve on, and provide brief written answers to three questions: • What experience do you have related to this appointment? • Why are you seeking this appointment? • What will you bring to this Commission or Committee? The application also asks whether you have previously attended or watched a meeting of the body you’re applying to serve on. Archived meeting videos are available to stream on the city’s website. To be considered for appointment, applicants must attend an interview with City Council members on Tuesday evening, April 4. The interview schedule will be provided to applicants on Friday, March 31. For more information, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at 420- 3040 or by email at CityClerk@ piedmont.ca.gov. READ IT IN THE POST Storm damage update By Selen Ozturk Compared to the damage from rainstorms in December and January, property damage from mid-March rains has been less widespread. “Although we did have a few maintenance workers on Thursday night, the only thing we’re aware of are two private trees down across roadways,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. The trees which fell on Trestle Glen Road and Glen Alpine Road were cleared within hours by Friday. On Tuesday, March 14, police reported in mid-afternoon, “PG&E power lines are down and damaged on Moraga Ave. The power is out in the area and Moraga Ave. is closed between Maxwelton and Highway 13.” As of 6 p.m. last night, PG&E showed that there were power outages in the area at the Piedmont-Oakland border. City Maintenance Supervisor Nick Milosevich confirmed that the outages were due to a tree that had fallen onto a power pole by Moraga Avenue and Harbord Drive. “These storms have been interesting from a public works maintenance perspective,” notes Gonzales. “it’s not a constant drizzle, like you might get in Seattle. The rains are really heavy for just a short duration, and often with high winds.” Listed below are resources for Piedmont residents during these storms. Resources available Sandbags • Sandbags are available at the City’s Corporation Yard (898 Red Rock Road) 7 a.m.-3:30 p.m. Monday through Friday. Reporting downed power lines, trees, clogged drains • If you see damaged power lines or electrical equipment, call 420-3000 to report them to the city, then notify PG&E by calling 1-800-743-5000. Do not touch or drive over a downed power line. If you see a downed power line sparking or smoking, call 911 to report it. • If you see clogged drains, fallen trees blocking roads, or other damage to city infrastructure, call the Public Works Department at 420-3050 during regular business hours (8:30 a.m.-5 p.m.) or the Police Dispatch at 420-3000 after hours. Stay informed • Check weather.gov for current weather advisories and warnings. • Sign up for safety alerts at acalert.org to learn about flooding or other emergencies.
