articles.text: The Piedmont High School Affinity Mentors class invites the Piedmont community, young and old, to an event on Monday, March 20, at the Alan Harvey Theater. The discussion at 7:00 p.m. will provide student perspectives on inclusion versus exclusion and aims to help kids become allies. Students will share their personal experiences with prejudice, discuss the current culture of “othering,” and confront the persistent use of slurs and other forms of microaggression. Student panelists, and speakers along with adult moderators will offer ideas on how the families in our community can be allies to continue to build a culture of belonging in Piedmont. This event welcomes everyone who lives or works in Piedmont and is appropriate for older elementary students and up. The student speakers will be Sohrab Ford, Morgan Hunt, and Stephanie Tsung. Students serving as panelists include Danny Allen, Meher Bachher, Sofia Prieto Black, Adelina Mbise, Cole Nash, Dahlia Saffouri, and Elena Stevens. The moderators will be Jean Takazawa, creator of the Piedmont Affinity Identity MentorPHS students juniors Jessica Lui (left) and Maddy Hill mentoring 1st graders in Piedmont Park in 2022. articles.text: After a three-year absence, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m., at the Alan Harvey Theater. With the theme of “Maskarade,” guests are encouraged to show their creativity and personality using masks. The contest will be under the production of Piedmont High School Librarian Kathryn Levenson. Created in 1963, by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, the Bird Calling Contest grew into an annual event that over the decades has attracted national and international attention. The winners appeared for many years on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, and then on Late Night with David Letterman. A panel of judges will consider the merits of the contestants based upon authenticity of call, poise and delivery, and content of contestants’ introduction of their bird. Tickets are available online at Showtix4u.com/event-details/67041. General admission tickets are $25; student tickets are $15. The Alan Harvey Theater is located at 800 Magnolia Avenue, on the campus of Piedmont High School. Please contact Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or 510-594-2781. PHS senior Macie Gard designed the poster for this year’s Bird Calling Contest.

articles.text: Piedmont High School English teacher Mercedes Foster created and implemented a new elective course this year, Film as Literature. The one-semester course looks deeply into film elements. Judging by student engagement and excitement when this reporter came to visit on Friday, March 10, the class is a blockbuster hit. The day’s lesson focused on a narrative device known as a longtake tracking shot. Students were familiar with the war movie 1917 which attempts to have long-takes and as few cuts as possible. “Does anyone know what a long-take tracking shot is?” Foster queried, to which students comfortably offered answers near and far to the mark. Foster explained the long-take tracking shot as one which uses camera movement and one continuous shot without cuts. Longtake tracking shots can follow or depart from certain characters, objects or tropes, which requires film direction to come from multiple angles at timely intervals. The lights came down in the room and the 1927 silent film directed by William A. Wellman, Wings, served as the first example – a pioneer of the “dolly shot” with a moving camera to create action cinematography. Foster challenged her class to keep in mind how heavy and bulky the cameras were at the time, the timing of the actors, and if moving out of the way of the moving camera was done naturally. The class then jumped through the history of film to 1958 for a famous opening long-take tracking shot in A Touch of Evil, directed by Orson Welles. Other examples included the opening Senior Callan Mitchell (left), junior Jonah Dupree and senior Paden Andrews brainstorm ideas for their shot. Mercedes Foster goes over a few details about long-take tracking shots with senior Teagan Haddawy. scenes of Baby Driver (2017) directed by Edgar Wright and the 1992 film The Player, directed by Robert Altman. Foster described the latter as “half expose and half satire of the inner workings of Hollywood.” Junior Jonah Dupree pointed out the circular movement of the camera in The Player, emphasizing the circular, chaotic conversations that were the subject of the shot. After viewing the examples, small groups of students were tasked with mapping out their own long-take tracking shots with specific criteria: at least three recognizable interactions, an over the shoulder angle, a zoom-in close up, and a pause in movement for at least two seconds. Students eagerly brainstormed their plots and plans for direction then scouted out possible sites on campus. “How do you trigger your actor’s actions on time, during these long scenes without cuts?” Foster asked her class. In 2022, Foster pitched the idea of the course to the school board with a detailed curriculum, the course philosophy and sample course content. If a potential course survives the scrutiny of two readings at school board meetings it can be implemented into the school district curriculum. The class’s first assignment this semester had small groups plot, direct and record a silent film. Their second task built on the first as students recorded sound and music to the silent film, using the “Foley” technique or by recording audio and adding music during post-production. On March 15 the class will be filming long-take tracking shots around campus. This Friday the class will write essays about romantic-comedies, or rom-coms, and Foster will treat the class to popcorn during the assessment. Students are not limited to the obvious fits for that genre and are challenged to pick any movie and find a rom-com element no matter how unconventional or obscure. Later in the semester the class will explore Bildungsroman, or a coming-of-age story, chronicling life events that define characters. Senior Paden Andrews decided to take the semester course twice in a row and now serves as a teacher’s assistant for the class. Discussions get lively as these future Tarentinos and Scorseses exude their love of film, prompting Foster to start a wall for future recommended films in the class. “This is a very sharp group; I’ve been blown away with how much my students already know about film. It’s constantly humbling,” said Foster. Teagan Haddawy (left), Ian Shea, and Eden Lorin plan out their long-take tracking shot which will follow a tray of food through the student center with an “extra” ingredient.
articles.title: Elective course was created by English teacher Mercedes Foster

articles.text: Nominations for Piedmont School District’s annual Arthur Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award are now being accepted and are due to the district office by 4:30 p.m. this Friday, March 17. The award will be presented by the Piedmont School Board at its meeting on May 10. A selection committee will vote on the award recipient, who also will receive the gift of a work of student art. The student will receive a monetary award and commendation from the school board. The award, a de facto Volunteer of the Year Award, is presented annually to individuals who have volunteered over a period of time and have made a difference because of their involvement and commitment to Piedmont’s youth. Mr. Hecht, a member of the Piedmont School Board from 1970 to 1982, was a tireless community volunteer who was dedicated to students in both Piedmont and Oakland. He was very active with the Piedmont Continuation High School (now Millennium High School). In 1998, the Art Hecht Volunteer of the Year Award was established by school board member Dewey Watson in memory of Mr. Hecht. Prior winners include: Hunter McCreary (1998) Ann Chandler (1999) Ruth Cuming (2000) Lisa Lomenzo (2001) Cathie Geddeis and Marion Souyoultzis (2002) Fritz and Mary Wooster (2003) Betsy Gentry (2004) Cynthia Gorman (2005) Grier Graff (2006) Julia Burke (2007) Maude Pervere (2008) Anne-Marie Lamarche and Mark Menke (2009) Janiele Maffei Tovani (2010) Andrea Swenson (2011) June Monach (2012) Bill Drum (posthumously) and Mary Ireland (2013) Ray Perman (2014) Jennifer Fox (2015) Katie Korotzer (2016) Hilary Cooper (2017) Holly Hanke (2018) Cathy Glazier (2019) Sue Smegal (2020) Ken Li (2021) Eileen Ruby (2022) Nomination Forms are available in the District Office at 760 Magnolia Avenue (594-2614) or by downloading at Drive.google. com/file/d/1CS_0eh18kbz0lSmCP-ID_AqcMGKHaZcv, and emailing it to seggert@piedmont. k12.ca.us.

articles.text: For 10 days at the end of June members of the Piedmont Community Service Crew, a co-ed Venturing unit with Piedmont Scouts, will travel to Medford, Oregon to build tiny houses that will be used to start a new village for the houseless in that area. They will take a break in the middle to explore the area and relax a bit. The Crew is now looking for motivated teens who are looking for a hands-on team-oriented summer event. The first few to sign up will help to plan the activities, meals, and transportation. This will be a very inexpensive trip, approximately $500 per person. Community adults who enjoy mentoring teens are invited to join PCSC and the trip. For details, contact Crew Advisor Ken Li at ken.i.li@sbcglobal.net (510-410-4283).
articles.title: Community Service Crew plans summer project in Oregon

articles.text: When the sun sets, the night sky lights up as stars begin to shine above us. Stars range in different sizes and colors, but have you ever looked at a star and wondered how it was formed? Nebulas Star formation begins inside nebulas, which are large clouds of gas and dust. With the help of gravity, the clouds collect and begin to collapse. This collapse creates the core that will become a star. The core is called a protostar and while spinning quickly, heat and pressure goes up. The rising temperature and pressure cause a reaction, which takes us to the next stage of star formation. The Main Sequence The main sequence is the second stage of a star’s lifecycle. At this point, gravity and heat inside the star have balanced. During this phase, stars stop growing or shrinking and begin to shine. What makes stars shine? A reaction takes place inside the star’s core that give it the energy to shine and to stop it from breaking down. The bigger the star, the faster it will use up energy. After using all the energy, the star will move to the next step. The next phase of a star depends on its size. Average Stars When an average sized star runs out of energy it enters the phase called a red giant. During this phase, the star gets bigger and changes in color because of the temperature change. After this stage, the star goes through an explosion called a planetary nebula. As time passes, the outer layers from this explosion will fade away. What is left behind are remains known as white dwarfs. The lifecycle of most average stars will end as white dwarfs. Massive Stars When a massive star runs out of energy, it will first become a super red giant. The size and color changes are more extreme because the star is massive. Next, the super red giant will break down and cause a gigantic explosion, which will lead the star to become a neutron star or a black hole. A regular massive star will end as a neutron star. A neutron star is the core of the star that was left from the explosion. A super massive star will end as a black hole. A black hole is a space that has a strong gravity that can consume other objects. Each star has its own journey, but they all shine above us at some point in time. Stars are different yet in many ways alike. As we continue to explore space, we might get to learn even more about star formation. Isabel Lopez Ramirez is a Marketing and Communication Intern at Chabot Space & Science Center, located at 10000 Skyline Blvd., in Oakland. articles.title: The Life of a Star

Thinking Outside the Classroom By Isabel Lopez Ramirez When the sun sets, the night sky lights up as stars begin to shine above us. Stars range in different sizes and colors, but have you ever looked at a star and wondered how it was formed? Nebulas Star formation begins inside nebulas, which are large clouds of gas and dust. With the help of gravity, the clouds collect and begin to collapse. This collapse creates the core that will become a star. The core is called a protostar and while spinning quickly, heat and pressure goes up. The rising temperature and pressure cause a reaction, which takes us to the next stage of star formation. The Main Sequence The main sequence is the second stage of a star’s lifecycle. At this point, gravity and heat inside the star have balanced. During this phase, stars stop growing or shrinking and begin to shine. What makes stars shine? A reaction takes place inside the star’s core that give it the energy to The Life of a Star shine and to stop it from breaking down. The bigger the star, the faster it will use up energy. After using all the energy, the star will move to the next step. The next phase of a star depends on its size. Average Stars When an average sized star runs out of energy it enters the phase called a red giant. During this phase, the star gets bigger and changes in color because of the temperature change. After this stage, the star goes through an explosion called a planetary nebula. As time passes, the outer layers from this explosion will fade away. What is left behind are remains known as white dwarfs. The lifecycle of most average stars will end as white dwarfs. Massive Stars When a massive star runs out of energy, it will first become a super red giant. The size and color changes are more extreme because the star is massive. Next, the super red giant will break down and cause a gigantic explosion, which will lead the star to become a neutron star or a black hole. A regular massive star will end as a neutron star. A neutron star is the core of the star that was left from the explosion. A super massive star will end as a black hole. A black hole is a space that has a strong gravity that can consume other objects. Each star has its own journey, but they all shine above us at some point in time. Stars are different yet in many ways alike. As we continue to explore space, we might get to learn even more about star formation. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Last weekend 34 members from Highlander Robotics traveled to Fresno with their robot, Paddo the Frog, for the FIRST Robotics Competition Central Valley Regional. After finishing 4th of 38 in qualification rounds with a 10-2 record, they went 4-1 during the double elimination playoffs to challenge the first seed alliance captained by former world champion MadTown Robotics from Madera. They lost two straight in the best of three finals to finish second overall. The FIRST Robotics Competition announces a new game each January to be played by two alliances of three robots, built by high school students. The competition arena is about the size of a basketball court. An entirely new robot must be constructed for each season and competitions begin six weeks after kickoff. In this year’s game, Charged Up, robots up to 125 pounds and 6-feet-6-inches tall score points by collecting and placing 9.5- inch inflatable cubes and 1-foot high rubber cones in a grid of poles and pedestals as well as by balancing robots on a see-sawlike platform called a “charging station.” During regional competitions, teams play up to 12 qualifying rounds with randomly selected partners. The highest ranked eight teams become alliance captains and draft two others to work with throughout the double-elimination playoffs. Draft selections are key to success in the playoffs. All teams at the elite level dedicate significant time and personnel to track every robot’s performance in what can be well over 100 qualifying rounds. The Highlanders, which reached division semi-finals at the World Championships in 2022, substantially improved their scouting system in anticipation of Charged Up. In the fall, Monte Vista freshman Jacob Trentini and Millennium High freshman Colin Cameron wrote an iPhone app while at an off-season competition which simplifies the collection of scouting data. They were later joined by PHS freshman Cassie Colby and senior Barry Balasingham. The four expanded Trentini and Cameron’s proof of concept to a cross platform collection system with score prediction and sophisticated analytic tools. At the end of the first day of qualifications, the Highlanders were in third place after nine Software lead Lewy Seiden makes last minute programming changes. Ambassador Jessica Liu and Pit Lead Helena Young staff the Highlander Robotics pit. Pit Crew members Asha Byers and Chloe Kessinger tune up the robot between matches. rounds. They lost one match due to an alliance partner’s malfunction. In their remaining three qualifiers, they dropped to fourth after an agonizingly close loss to the East Palo Alto Churrobots, 82-80. During the draft, the Highlanders became the third seed alliance captain. Their first pick, the fifth-ranked Buchanan Bird Brains from Clovis, secured a solid scoring partner but their second pick, the 36th ranked Breaker Bots from Pacific Grove, left many scratching their heads. “While they were close to the bottom of the rankings, the scouting data indicated they were ideal for defense,” explained team captain Alex Ware. In their first playoff round, the Highlanders suffered a huge upset by the sixth seed alliance when the Bird Brains robot malfunctioned and became disabled 45-seconds into the match. They fought back, however, and the gamble of their second pick paid off when they won four straight to clinch a finals appearance after edging out the second seed alliance captained by the Churrobots, 124-114. In the best-of-three finals, the Highlanders lost in two world record-setting performances, 162- 117 and 165-95, to a powerhouse alliance formed by captain MadTown Robotics from Madera, the Greybots from Atascadero, and the Arborbots from Visalia. MadTown and the Greybots are both former world champions with four titles between them including one they earned together in 2019. The Highlanders gather at the end of a very exciting weekend.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ lacrosse team is back and in action this spring, currently at 2-1 through three matches. It opened the season with a 13-9 win over Monte Vista at Witter Field on Tuesday, March 7, lost narrowly 15-14 to Marin Academy on Thursday, March 9 in San Rafael, and pummeled Moreau Catholic 18-3 in Hayward last Friday, March 10. The Highlanders return with a wealth of talent from last year’s team and are the favorites to win the Western Alameda County Conference. It would be Piedmont’s seventh consecutive league banner. PHS also returns to North Coast Section’s Division 2 as a team-to-watch after playing in Division 1 since winning the Div. 2 title in 2019. It’s worth mentioning that Marin Academy and Monte Vista are Div. 1 teams. “We have a lot of returners, we’re a strong team that’s senior heavy. We’ve already had some strong performances. We beat Monte Vista and they’re a terrific team; it’s a really good way to start the season. Marin Academy is another strong Division 1 team and that was a back-and-forth game [played] in the pouring rain. It’s exactly the type of game we need; we want to be roadready and play against the best,” said PHS coach Alex Yu. Piedmont returns all four team Nathan Fredericks, last year’s leading scorer, is back as a senior. Staff Photos Piedmont’s boys’ lacrosse team is in pursuit of its seventh consecutive WACC title, with eyes on winning the NCS banner. captains from last season: Nathan Fredericks, Soren Dixon, Henry Brayer and Jack Nelson. Other returners include Oliver Shafroth, Curtis Hohener, Rylan Nelson, Andrew McLaughlin, Keita Clear, Cairo Osman, Logan Huh, Bede Levin, Gus von Metzsch, Bailey Cain, and Axel Saldanha. “We have Henry back and he’s been hungry. Every force is deadly in our attack, we’re running offenses that start from behind the net, up top, and from the sides. It’s difficult for a defense to cover every angle of the field,” said Fredericks. “I definitely think we should compete for the [North Coast] D2 title. After last year, I think the continuity on our roster really makes us a No. 1 contender… We’ve all been playing together for the last three years and it feels like we’re in our prime right now. This is the best this team can be and I think we’re going to capitalize on that,” added Nelson. Nelson and Dixon return after helping lead the boys’ soccer team this winter to its second-consecutive North Coast Section title. Both are four-year varsity players. “Coming off an NCS title definitely helps your mentality. It makes you feel like you have to live up to that and carry the momentum forward,” said Nelson. 18-3 over Moreau Piedmont came hot out of the gates and led 7-0 by the end of the first quarter, extending the gap to 13-0 by halftime. Moreau finally got on the board in the third quarter with PHS leading 15-1 going into the fourth, adding three more in the final going. Final stats: Brayer had six goals and four assists. Dixon had four goals, two assists, and three ground ball recoveries. Reece Beck had two goals, two assists, and six ground balls. Jack Nelson had a goal and two ground balls. Rylan Nelson and Timmy Kalamas scored once. Logan Huh had one goal and two ground balls. 13-9 over Monte Vista Against Monte Vista, Piedmont led 3-1 by the end of the first quarter and extended the gap to 6-1 by halftime with a strong second quarter. Both teams scored three in the third to make it 9-4, while the Highlanders added four goals in the fourth by conceded five. Final stats: Brayer scored five goals with three assists and a ground ball recovery. Fredericks scored three goals and four assists. Rylan Nelson had three goals and an assist. Jack Nelson had a goal and recovered five ground balls. Tuesday vs. Novato Piedmont traveled to Novato last night for a game with its NCS rival. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (2-1) starts its league schedule against arch-rival Bishop O’Dowd at Witter Field this Friday, March 17 at 7:00 p.m. Jack Nelson, a senior leader, is fresh off an NCS title as a member of the soccer team.
articles.title: Boys’ lacrosse team pursues 7th consecutive WACC title

articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team got a break from the rain long enough to compete at the Fighting Knights Relays at Hillsdale HS in San Mateo on Saturday, March 11. Scheduled meets Thursday and Friday, March 9 and 10, were rained out. “We took a handful of varsity sprinters and jumpers to the Fighting Knights Relay meet. This was a highly competitive New Balance sponsored meet with limited qualifying spots per event,” explained OHS head coach Pouyan Assadi. It was a very successful day for Piedmont’s distance medley relay team of Xander Schulte-Sasse, Sam Shelby, Parker Long, and Christian Taylor, who placed first among 13 teams, and beat 2dn place Sequoia by 24 seconds. “Xander battled with Sequoia during his 1200 meters, and handed it off to Sam Shelby, when we were in 2nd place. We took the lead during Sam’s sprint, showing off his endurance and power. From there, Parker Long ran a blazing 1:56 [in the 800], putting the race away. Christian lapped a handful of athletes, finishing the race with another time under 4:30,” said Assadi. Assadi is hopeful that their time will help them qualify for Miguel Long, a sophomore, finished second of nine athletes in the High Jump with a height of 5 feet, 8 inches. the prestigious Arcadia Invitational on April 7-8 at Arcadia HS in southern California. “We’re going to submit this time to Arcadia in hopes to qualify for the Nike sponsored event where athletes across the country fly in to compete against the best of the best,” said Assadi. Shelby, a sophomore, also competed in the 100 meter dash, finishing fifth of 30 runners with Xander Schulte-Sasse (left) was the first leg in Piedmont’s winning Distance Medley Relay team at the Fighting Knights Relays. Breah Bell (middle, right) placed fourth of 24 runners in the 100 meter dash with a time of 13.22.

articles.text: Winter sports has come and gone. Each of Piedmont’s four varsity teams reached the North Coast Section Semifinals for one of the few times in school history. It was an historic time in which the school won three NCS titles (boys’ soccer, girls’ soccer, girls’ basketball), and was the first time in school history when the highlanders won three Section championships in the same season. Here are this year’s AllLeague winners: Girls’ Soccer The girls’ soccer team finished with an 13-1-6 (W-T-L) overall record and won its first Division 4 NCS championship in 20 years of effort. As the No. 3 seed, Piedmont upset No. 1 University 2-1 for the title on February 25. To get there, PHS bashed No. 2 University 3-0 on February 22 in the semifinals, beat No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals on February 18, and shut out No. 15 Sacred Heart 2-0 in the first round on February 15. In the Division 3 CIF NorCal Regional Tournament, No. 8 ranked Piedmont nearly upset No. 1 Sequoia in the first round on February 28, but lost 2-1 in sudden-death overtime. Audrey Lam was named the WACC’s Player of the Year. PHS received seven AllLeague selections: Emily Fitzgerald, Cameron Lorin, and Lam with first-team honors. Ellie DeVan and Hailey Marshburn were second-team selections, while Morgan Hunt and Elle Ruegg earned honorable mentions. Boys’ Basketball The Highlanders went 19-10 and made it to the Division 3 NCS Semifinals as the No. 4 seed before losing No. 1 Branson on February 21. On the way to the title game, PHS beat No. 5 Analy 59-38 in the quarterfinals on February 17, smothered No. 13 Rancho Cotate 65-43 in the opening round on February 14. A.J. Harris was named League Player of the year along with Berkeley’s Samir O’Brien. They received three AllLeague selections: Harris and Brit Burden on first-team, and Declan Linnane as honorable mention. Next week we’ll feature allleague players from the boys’ soccer team and girls’ basketball team. articles.text: spring. Piedmont’s boys’ tennis team will have a new look this spring. After losing eight players to graduation, there will be some new faces in the singles and double lineups. The Highlanders are currently 1-2 after defeating Campolindo 4-3 at home on Wednesday, March 8, and losing to both Berkeley (6-1 on March 2) and Branson (6-0 on March 1). “We lost eight players – about half the team. A good portion of them were starters. We’re a bit stronger at the top and weaker at the bottom,” said coach Jim Landes. PHS has returning starters who earned significant time last season, notably Ethan Pham, Ben Breber, and Monte Imburg. Nick King, Arun Brahma, Brady Colbert, and Graham Alban also saw some action in 2022. “Ethan Pham is playing great. He’s a senior and won his match against Campolindo. Monte is a junior and would probably rather play doubles, but we put him at singles, too,” said Landes. Atop the singles order is a freshman, Lucas Smolko, who Landes considers the best 9th grade varsity member since tennis Mackie McDonald, now playing professionally around the world. Smolko is currently rated as a 3-star recruit by TennisRecruiting.net. “Lucas is our No. 1. He’s been playing since he was very young and is a tournament player. He plays in some national tournaments and is a good No. 1. He’s probably the best freshman I’ve seen on the team in a long time, maybe since McDonald,” said Landes. Despite the loss to Berkeley, Landes thinks his team is capable of competing for the Western Alameda County Conference title. Breber was not available for the opening two matches of the season. “I feel like we have a chance against Berkeley; Ben beat their No. 2 last year. When everybody moves up, it causes a problem. I feel we have a chance to win the league,” said Landes. 4-3 over Campolindo Playing No. 1, Smolko won in singles in straight sets, 7-5, 6-3. articles.text: Piedmont’s baseball team won one three games last week, defeating Redwood Christian 7-1 at Humphries Diamond on Tuesday, March 7. It fell to league opponent San Leandro 9-0 on Wednesday, March 8 on the road, and lost narrowly 4-3 to Berean Christian in Walnut Creek on Saturday, March 11. San Leandro was Piedmont’s first game in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division. It was a strong group of games for Michael Aikawa and Markos Lagios. Aikawa had two doubles against Redwood and Berean Christian, while Lagios smacked the first home run of his high school career against Redwood and also hit a triple on Berean Christian. 7-1 over Redwood Christian The two sides battled through th ree-and-a-half scoreless innings until Piedmont broke out with seven runs in the bottom of the fourth. Redwood Christian didn’t get its first run until the top of the seventh. Piedmont scored all seven runs in the bottom of the fourth with two outs. Ryan McConathy got the rally started with a single, followed by Dimitri Papahadjopoulos hitting a double to center field. With the bases loaded, John Olsen brought in McConathy on a single to break the deadlock. After that, Liam Campbell singled in Papahadjopoulos, 2-0, followed by Aikawa hitting a threeRBI double to center—5-0. With Aikawa on second, Lagios hit a towering two-run home run – his first high school homer – to make it 7-0. Final stats: Aikawa went 2-for-3 with two doubles, three RBIs, one run scored, and a walk. Lagios was 1-for-3 with a homer, two RBIs, a run scored, and a walk. Peter Krumins was 1-for-3 with a double. Olsen and Campbell were 1-for-3 with a run scored and an RBI. Aikawa was the winning pitcher with four innings of work, no runs allowed, and six strikeouts. Lagios went 2.1 innings with two strikeouts. Photo by Mark Aikawa Michael Aikawa makes a throw from shortstop. He hit two doubles against Redwood Christian and Berean Christian. Staff Photo Sophomore Markos Lagios hit his first high school home run against Redwood Christian. Staff Photo Liam Campbell went 2-for-3 with a run scored against Berean Christian. He also scored a run and had an RBI against Redwood Christian.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team is off to a steaming start to its spring season with a 4-1 record. After a pair of 3-0 preseason wins over Bentley School in Lafayette on February 17 and Skyline in Oakland on February 28, Piedmont got its regular season underway with 3-0 shutouts over Hayward (March 1) and De Anza in El Sobrante (March 2). They suffered their only loss against Castro Valley 3-1 on Tuesday, March 7 but followed with a 3-1 win over San Leandro the following day, March 8. On March 9 they won by forfeit against Tennyson. Full stats for the games were not provided. “The boys redeemed themselves after their first loss against Castro Valley. I am noticing that our serve-receive and defense has been really killing it is carrying our team. Our Libero, Brayden Day, and John Champion have really worked hard in the back row and getting the ball to our setter,” said coach Mariah Cardenas. Piedmont takes one of three games By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s baseball team won one three games last week, defeating Redwood Christian 7-1 at Humphries Diamond on Tuesday, March 7. It fell to league opponent San Leandro 9-0 on Wednesday, March 8 on the road, and lost narrowly 4-3 to Berean Christian in Walnut Creek on Saturday, March 11. San Leandro was Piedmont’s first game in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division. It was a strong group of games for Michael Aikawa and Markos Lagios. Redwood Christian didn’t get its first run until the top of the seventh. Piedmont scored all seven runs in the bottom of the fourth with two outs. articles.text: Taylor Rolefson won the 100 butterfly and also helped the 200 individual medley relay team win their event to open the season. Piedmont’s high school swim team opened its season on Friday, March 10 with a dual meet against Bishop O’Dowd and San Leandro at the San Leandro pool. The girls’ team won the 140-76 over O’Dowd and 143-41 over San Leandro, The boys’ team was edged out 109-106 by O’Dowd, but defeated San Leandro 148-49. The Highlander varsity teams won 14 events on the day. The girls’ 200 individual medley relay A-team of Josie Oesterer, Sydney Olson, Taylor Rolefson, and Sonja ten Grotenhuis won their event with a time of 1:57.96, a North Coast Section consideration time. Oesterer, Rolefson, and ten Grotenhuis were joined by freshman Abigail Jacoby for the 200 freestyle relay, winning with time of 1:46.75, also a NCS consideration time. In the 400 freestyle relay, senior Odessa Dando, junior Kate Meyjes, freshman Tai March-Cunningham and junior Anne Reardon won with a time of 4:35.09. Rolefson won two events, the 50 freestyle in 25.94, and the 100 butterfly in 1:01.64. Both were NCS consideration times. Oesterer also won two individual events, claiming the 200 free in 2:02.83 and winning the 100 backstroke in 1:00.57. Jacoby, a freshman, also won a pair of events, the 200 individual medley in 2:27.49 and the 100 freestyle in 59.89. The boys team won the men’s 200 individual medley relay with an NCS consideration time of 1:46.49. The quartet included freshman Nik Costello (backstroke), sophomore Evan Byun (breast), senior Simon Lins (fly), and junior Tom Rolefson (anchor leg - freestyle). Costello, Byun, Lins, and Rolefson also won the 200 Free Simon Lins on the block for the backstroke. He was the Post’s 2022 Honorable Mention for Athlete of the Year. relay in 1:33.33 for another NCS consideration time. Lins is back in the pool after being the first PHS swimmer in over 20 years to qualify for the CIF State Championship meet, where he finished 2nd of 43 swimmers in the prelims and seventh of 18 in the finals. In Friday’s meet, Lins won the 100 Free in 49.2 and also placed first in the 100 Back in 57.29. Both times earn NCS qualification consideration. Senior Ryan Stokes won the 100 Breast with a time of 1:06, while he also finished third in the 100 fly, 1:03.14. Rolefson placed second in the 50 Free with a time of 22.91 for an NCS consideration time,, and was third in the 100 Free in 50.97. NEXT UP Piedmont will host Arroyo in a dual meet at Laney College this Friday, March 17 at 3:30 p.m. Nik Costello helped the 200 IM and 200 freestyle relay teams win their events.

articles.text: And so the 2022 Academy Awards began at the Hollywood Dolby Theater, hosted by Jimmy Kimmel, looking more like the ceremonies of the past. The twotiered venue was filled with the glitterati, with masks and social distancing a thing of the past, as if declaring the pandemic was finally behind us. This year the celebrities entered not on the traditional red carpet, but one the color of champagne, where they paused for brief, sometimes awkward interviews. What struck me almost immediately was the diversity of the Oscars, and clearly the Academy had heard the voiced critique of its homogeneity. As one member of the Oscars stated, the ceremony broke another glass ceiling. This year it pertained to Asian actors who were newly represented and took home seven statues. try celebrating itself, reminding us that films can be an art form, and are testimony to the power of the imagination, collaboration, and storytelling. Unlike in years past, we were reminded that there is an ongoing debate regarding where movies should be viewed – in darkened theaters filled with strangers with a movie on an enormous screen, or in living rooms using streaming platforms such as Netflix, Prime or HBO MAX. articles.text: The ongoing Berkeley Symphony & Friends chamber music concert series, now in its 10th year at Piedmont Center for the Arts, continues this Sunday, March 19, at 4 p.m. with a concert entitled Spring Fever. Following Berkeley Symphony’s sold-out chamber performance in February, Spring Fever will feature Astor Piazzolla’s tango classic, The Four Seasons of Buenos Aires. With its echoes of jazz and its intriguing rhythmic meters, it will serve as a prelude to the Symphony’s Symphonic concert at Zellerbach Hall on April 2. “Spring Fever provides audiences with the opportunity to experience Berkeley Symphony in an intimate venue,” said René Mandel, Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director. “This performance will feature a range of delightful, rich music as we celebrate the changing seasons. March 19th also celebrates our 10th anniversary presenting chamber concerts at Piedmont Center for the Arts.” The program includes Lili Boulanger’s enchanting D’un matin de printemps (Of a Spring Morning) and Antonin Dvořák’s “Dumky” Piano Trio in A Minor, a richly passionate masterpiece based on Eastern European folk music. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony. org or by calling the symphony box office at (510) 841-2800.

articles.text: The Sophie Florence Trio will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, March 17, at 7:30 p.m. Sink back into the mid-20th century, to a night of nostalgia as the Sophie Florence Trio revisits the songs of Ella Fitzgerald, Dina Washington and Patsy Cline. Relive the diverse array of songs that stamped themselves into American culture, like White Rabbit, Summertime, Love Potion Number 9, I Shall be Released, All of Me, House of the Rising Sun, Tennessee Waltz, and many more. The Sophie Florence Trio is headed by vocalist Sophie Florence Prestwich, a young British woman who met Yalies Chuck Jacob ’73, of Brooklyn, NY, and Phil Hirschi ’73, of Seattle, while all were in Queretaro, Mexico. Prestwich is lead singer and plays flute; Phil Hirschi is on guitar and vocals; and Jacob is on upright bass and mandolin. Sophie, from Colchester, England, started playing flute when she was seven and had classical training as a vocalist starting at age 12. She has a fascination with music from the 1950s and ‘60s, and a particular fondness for Patsy Cline, Dinah Washington and Ella Fitzgerald. After studying French and Film at university and spending a year in Paris, she taught English in South America, and then moved to Queretaro, Mexico, where she met her bandmates, Phil and Chuck. A feast of music from the Great American Songbook awaits the audience, especially music from the 1940s to 1960s, Sophie has had classical training, as have both men, who are seasoned musicians who’ve performed in bands since high school. Phil has toured internationally with John McLaughlin and has recorded. All three play a variety of instruments from flute to piano, to bass, to cello, guitar, and mandolin, and will make use of all in this sure-to-be-stunning Piedmont concert. Don’t miss this one-night-only performance at Piedmont Center for the Arts as the trio kicks off their West Coast Tour. Advance tickets are $23 at www.bpt. me/5741445, and $25 tickets will be available at the door. Doors open at 7 pm. articles.text: Photo by Erik Tomasson COLORFORMS is San Francisco Ballet’s first film-to-stage adaptation in the company’s 90-year history. San Francisco Ballet will show Myles Thatcher’s COLORFORMS, the company’s first film-to-stage adaptation, now through Sunday, March 19. Thatcher’s creation first debuted as a dance film in San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season, when arts venues were shuttered due to the COVID pandemic. Vibrant in staging and hue, COLORFORMS will open with Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight (2004) and closes with William Forsythe’s Blake Works I (2016), set to seven songs from James Blake’s album The Colour in Anything. “I’m so grateful to have the opportunity to work with these dancers who are not only physically talented, but also intelligent and capable and generous with their spirit, movement, and time,” said Thatcher. “It’s incredible to work with people who you know and trust, and who know you. Making COLORFORMS is the dream.” The production is staged by Ayman Harper, with costume design by Dorothee Merg and choreographer William Forsythe. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling the box office at 415-865- 2000. Showtimes vary and all performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco.

Following Berkeley Symphony’s sold-out chamber performance in February, Spring Fever will feature Astor Piazzolla’s tango classic, The Four Seasons of Buenos Aires. With its echoes of jazz and its intriguing rhythmic meters, it will serve as a prelude to the Symphony’s Symphonic concert at Zellerbach Hall on April 2. “Spring Fever provides audiences with the opportunity to experience Berkeley Symphony in an intimate venue,” said René Mandel, Berkeley Symphony Artistic Director. “This performance will feature a range of delightful, rich music as we celebrate the changing seasons. March 19th also celebrates our 10th anniversary presenting chamber concerts at Piedmont Center for the Arts.” The program includes Lili Boulanger’s enchanting D’un matin de printemps (Of a Spring Morning) and Antonin Dvořák’s “Dumky” Piano Trio in A Minor, a richly passionate masterpiece based on Eastern European folk music. Tickets are $35 and are available online at berkeleysymphony. org or by calling the symphony box office at (510) 841-2800. SF Ballet’s Colorforms in performance through March 19 Photo by Erik Tomasson COLORFORMS is San Francisco Ballet’s first film-to-stage adaptation in the company’s 90-year history. By Allyson Aleksey San Francisco Ballet will show Myles Thatcher’s COLORFORMS, the company’s first film-to-stage adaptation, now through Sunday, March 19. Thatcher’s creation first debuted as a dance film in San Francisco Ballet’s 2021 digital season, when arts venues were shuttered due to the COVID pandemic. Vibrant in staging and hue, COLORFORMS will open with Helgi Tomasson’s 7 for Eight (2004) and closes with William Forsythe’s Blake Works I (2016), set to seven songs from James Blake’s album The Colour in Anything. “I’m so grateful to have the opportunity to work with these dancers who are not only physically talented, but also intelligent and capable and generous with their spirit, movement, and time,” said Thatcher. “It’s incredible to work with people who you know and trust, and who know you. Making COLORFORMS is the dream.” The production is staged by Ayman Harper, with costume design by Dorothee Merg and choreographer William Forsythe. Tickets may be purchased online at www.sfballet.org or by calling the box office at 415-865- 2000. Showtimes vary and all performances take place at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. Build Your Dream Kitchen Choose an Award-Winning Bay Area Design + Build Firm hdrremodeling.com 510-845-6100 Sophie Florence Trio at Center for the Arts on Friday The Sophie Florence Trio will perform a concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, March 17, at 7:30 p.m. Sink back into the mid-20th century, to a night of nostalgia as the Sophie Florence Trio revisits the songs of Ella Fitzgerald, Dina Washington and Patsy Cline. Relive the diverse array of songs that stamped themselves into American culture, like White Rabbit, Summertime, Love Potion Number 9, I Shall be Released, All of Me, House of the Rising Sun, Tennessee Waltz, and many more. The Sophie Florence Trio is headed by vocalist Sophie Florence Prestwich, a young British woman who met Yalies Chuck Jacob ’73, of Brooklyn, NY, and Phil Hirschi ’73, of Seattle, while all were in Queretaro, Mexico. Prestwich is lead singer and plays flute; Phil Hirschi is on guitar and vocals; and Jacob is on upright bass and mandolin. Sophie, from Colchester, England, started playing flute when she was seven and had classical training as a vocalist starting at age 12. She has a fascination with music from the 1950s and ‘60s, and a particular fondness for Patsy Cline, Dinah Washington and Ella Fitzgerald. After studying French and Film at university and spending a year in Paris, she taught English in South America, and then moved to Queretaro, Mexico, where she met her bandmates, Phil and Chuck. A feast of music from the Great American Songbook awaits the audience, especially music from the 1940s to 1960s, Sophie has had classical training, as have both men, who are seasoned musicians who’ve performed in bands since high school. Phil has toured internationally with John McLaughlin and has recorded. All three play a variety of instruments from flute to piano, to bass, to cello, guitar, and mandolin, and will make use of all in this sure-to-be-stunning Piedmont concert. Don’t miss this one-night-only performance at Piedmont Center for the Arts as the trio kicks off their West Coast Tour. Advance tickets are $23 at www.bpt. me/5741445, and $25 tickets will be available at the door. Doors open at 7 pm. The concert will be followed by a reception to meet the musicians. articles.text: Cal Performances presents the U.S. premiere of South African visual artist William Kentridge’s newest production, SIBYL, this weekend, Friday through Sunday, March 17-19, at Zellerbach Auditorium on the UC Berkeley campus. Kentridge is well-known for his animation artwork and films, as well as design of theatrical productions. Kentridge’s latest opera SIBYL is told in two parts and is inspired by the Greek myth of the Cumaean Sibyl, a prophetess of Cumae, a Greek colony located near Naples, Italy. In Greek mythology, a “sibyl” refers to a woman, usually of prodigious old age, who is reputed to possess powers of prophecy or divination. The first part of the opera, entitled The Moment Has Gone, will feature the U.S premiere of a film by Kentridge, accompanied by live music. Part one features a piano score by composer and music director Kyle Shepherd and an all-male vocal chorus led by choral composer Nhlanhla Mahlangu. The second part of the opera, entitled Waiting for the Sibyl, features nine vocalists and dancers – as well as Kentridge’s famous medium of animation. Music for SIBYL is composed and conceived by Nhlanhla Mahlangu and Kyle Shepherd. Run time for this performance is 85 minutes including intermission. A post-performance discussion with the artists and Cal Performances artistic director Jeremy Geffen will take place on Sunday, March 19. For tickets and showtimes, visit https://calperformances.org/ events/2022-23/illuminations-human-and-machine/william-kentridges-sibyl/.
articles.title: Production by South African artist William Kentridge

articles.text: Cambodian Rock Band is currently being performed at Berkeley Rep through April 2. Lauren Yee’s rock-music themed play, Cambodian Rock Band, features songs by Dengue Fever, an American rock band based in Los Angeles that blends traditional Cambodian music with psychedelic rock. Yee’s play borrows tracks from the unique group to tell the story of a young Cambodian-American whose father was a musician persecuted by the Khmer Rouge army. As a survivor, he returns to Cambodia for the first time in three decades, as his daughter prepares to prosecute one of Cambodia’s most infamous war criminals. Directed by Chay Yew, this darkly humorous play is set against a grim chapter of Cambodian history. Live music is performed by Dengue Fever. For showtimes and to purchase tickets, visit https://www. berkeleyrep.org/shows/cambodian-rock-band/. Photo by Lynn Lane Cambodian Rock Band is playing at Berkeley Repertory Theatre now through April 2.

articles.text: Photo by Randy Dodson An exhibition of the works of American artist John Singer Sargent is currently on view at San Francisco’s deYoung Museum. Artwork by John Singer Sargent will be on view at the de Young Museum in San Francisco through May 14. Sargent (1856-1925), celebrated as the premiere portraitist of his era, is also known for his paintings of churches, coastlines, gardens and royal venues. This exhibition highlights his love of Spain and Spanish culture. Artwork is displayed in the museum’s Rosekrans Court. See Sargent’s oils, watercolors, and drawings, as well as never-before-exhibited photographs showcasing the people, architecture, and urban and rural landscapes of Spain. Visit https://www.famsf.org to learn more. The DeYoung Museum is located at 50 Hagiwara Tea Garden Drive in San Francisco’s Golden Gate Park. Performing worldwide and throughout the United States since 1998, Sierra Ensemble’s mission seeks to build community and add to the unique violin, horn, and piano trio repertoire via composer commissions, education projects and accessible performances.

It might Beethoven’s Theme and Variations from his Trio opened the show. Here was Beethoven at his most gregarious. The composer literally encourages the players to play brilliantly… And they did. In the Beethoven, flautist (and conductor), Martha Stoddard, and pianist Lixi Wang performed admirably. Both the bassoonists are beautiful players – Jeff Robinson and Adam Williams. The second piece was out of the ordinary. It was the Octet for Winds by Franz Lachner. In some ways, Beethoven was the psychological inspiration, and the Piedmont wind players produced an orchestral sound with only eight players. Their ensemble was wellnigh perfect, and they played without a conductor. Tchaikovsky’s Serenade for Strings concluded the program with Stoddard conducting. The small string section played with brilliance and elan. It is a pleasure to be part of this program, and to see the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra’s continued success, both artistically and with the public. And now for some levity I’d like to conclude this article with a bit of humor. Sometimes when you go to a restaurant everything goes wrong. Can you imagine the Three Stooges running a restaurant? Here is a true story. Five of us enter a restaurant in Italy. There is no maître d’ to greet us. After a while I look around and ask to be seated. We wait for a very long time so I ask someone for menus. Another long wait. The waiter comes to take our order and I tell him we didn’t get any menus. Another long wait. The waiter brings the menus. When he comes to take the order, he doesn’t have any paper. He returns with the paper but doesn’t have a pencil. Another long wait. The waiter brings the second course. He realized his mistake, and said he’ll take the second course away and bring the first course. I asked him to leave the second course and bring the first course. A comedy of errors like this would make an excellent Three Stooges movie. This is the script…so who will make the movie? articles.text: A scene from Disney’s 1993 live action remake of Homeward Bound: The Incredible Journey left home alone. Shadow decides that he is not going to stay at the ranch, but will make his way to San Francisco. Chance and Sassy, at first reluctant, agree to go with him on what will be an epic journey into the mountain wilderness of the Sierra Nevada. And so, their adventure begins as these three, who are not prepared for what awaits them, set out on their trek. They will encounter one crisis after another (Shadow and Chance get separated from Sassy, while crossing a swift-moving river). But of course Sassy survives, and is rescued by an old-timer, Quentin (William Edward Phipps). She is later reunited with Chance and Shadow. The three will encounter mountain lions, bears, and a little girl named Molly who is lost in the woods, so of course they help in her rescue. But the rescue party takes the trio to an animal shelter – not where they want to go. They eventually escape and hit the road, their sights still set on San Francisco, where hopefully they will rejoin their owners, the Seavers family. Remember, this is Disney. articles.text: Trellises & Gazebos are part of the landscape concept. Part two in a series Previously printed in the Piedmont Post on September 9, 2020. No matter how dense or “urban” a place is, it can be unified, softened, and made more inviting by thoughtful landscape treatment as an integral part of the design, coordinated with the architecture. With this in mind, walking through the city, it is clear that one of the key components that makes Piedmont such a beautiful place, is the successful landscaping. Many people think of landscape architecture as limited to planting. But it also of course includes everything outside of buildings: roads, parks, pools, fountains, plazas, walkways, benches, fences, retaining walls, play fields, tennis courts, monuments, and even lighting and signage. From manicured and formal to natural and informal— there are many “right” ways to select or design these various landscape components, but they really must be considered all together along with the architecture to form a clear design concept. Planting, the most obvious of the landscape elements, creates a wonderful soft, organic visual counterpoint to the necessarily hard straight lines of the surrounding building(s). It is often successful if there are complementary different scales or sizes of planting involved. This starts with large trees. In addition to providing shade, thoughtfully placed trees can visually frame and anchor the adjacent buildings. And street trees also have the wonderful effect of visually unifying the sometimes very different architectural building styles seen on a single street in a city like Piedmont. Smaller shrubbery can provide screening between uses, a soft background to open space, or a foreground and transition to yet smaller plantings. The small scale of potted plants, window boxes or hanging planters is also a way to introduce flowers and color to the garden or street scene. articles.text: Dr. Stephen Main, the talented Music Director of Piedmont Community Church for 30 years, sat down for a recent conversation with the Piedmont Post about his background as an organist, pianist, choral director, composer of liturgical music, and as a film score composer. “Having been born and raised in New York City,” said Main, “my father, Tom Main, was always very supportive of my path. He played trombone professionally with Si Zentner’s jazz band in the 1960s, so music has been in my blood from the start.” Main attended Choate Rosemary Hall, a boarding school in Connecticut, where choir students sang at St. Thomas Church in Midtown Manhattan. “I discovered then how much I love choral music,” he said, “and I also got introduced to the pipe organ. It was my first great love. One of my degrees is in organ performance.” Main went on to study in college at Oberlin Conservatory in Ohio, with a double major in music and Religious Philosophy. “My father’s emphasis on liberal arts was wise — I got an M.A. and Ph.D. in Religious Philosophy at the University of Chicago,” he said. I met a man at the law school there who worked summers in San Francisco, and I did a year of doctoral research at Stanford. I got my job at Piedmont Community Church around this time, as well.” In 2004, wanting to expand his music career, Main started composing film scores. He has done work for films like “Mr. Marceau” (2010), “All Alone” (2011), “After the Wizard” (2011), “A Family of Clowns” (2013), and for the TV sitcom “Husbands” (2011-2013). “All church musicians work situationally,” Main explained. “You have three oboe players and a soprano who sings slightly flat available on a Sunday, so you write on the fly for them. Film music is a lot like church music. It’s not a concert; the music is only there to service some larger production, but the whole doesn’t work as well without the music.” Main still travels back and forth from the Bay to Los Angeles every two to three months. Ten years ago he would stay for a week every month. “At first, I couldn’t afford to say no to anything — an ad jingle, or something someone else could have done better, like writing for a rock ‘n’ roll band. Now I’m lucky I can explore my specialty: orchestral, choral, keyboard sounds.” Main intends to continue his work at Piedmont Community Church for the foreseeable future. Dr. Stephen Main is Music Director of Piedmont Community Church. He emphasized that the connection offered by composing and conducting for live performance, usually absent in film work, drew him to music to begin with. “One day I might get hit by a beer truck and some dynamic new musician will turn the place around, but for now people assume that that’s how the music has to sound. I’ve been really lucky,” he said. “Piedmonters not only love music deeply, but understand that orchestras and choirs need a scale of funding that writing and painting don’t. After 30 years, there’s a lot of gut-trust with it – the willingness to say, ‘Yes, let’s try this new cockamamie thing that Steve’s come up with.” For example, the church’s annual Christmas concert started in 2011 with a cantata that Main wrote, inspired by a woman’s reaction to a choir and organ piece of his. “She asked: ‘If you knew you had the orchestra and choir from the get-go, rather than starting with a piano piece, how would you write differently?’ I knew I’d write cinematically, shaping more of a story atmosphere with the music.” Although Main is somewhat relieved to currently have the least-busy work docket he’s had in four years, he is still “writing frantically” for a choir and orchestra project in the works for the church called “The Image,” which will premier on June 4. Instead of a standard sermon that day, the concert will take over. “The piece is a narrative, a cinematic, almost operatic history of Western religion,” he said. “The commissioner is keeping a very low profile about it,” said Main, “but he gave me a tall order. Initially I was to pick the words from American poets like Emerson and Whitman, but I didn’t want to twist them out of context — so we agreed I’d write the verses too. It’s an incredibly ambitious project; I hope everyone can mark their calendars.”

articles.text: Imagine you’re an ordinary soul minding your own business, when a couple of thugs snatch you, drive you to an isolated house, accuse you of being a spy and then try to finish you off by pouring liquor down your throat and stuffing you behind the wheel of a sports car they send off down a perilously winding mountain road. Whew! Now imagine this is all great fun, which it is, because it’s the opening gambit of the classic Alfred Hitchcock thriller, North by Northwest, which entertained an enthusiastic crowd at the third gathering of the Piedmont’s new movie group, the Second Thursday Flix Fest. At the end of the showing last week, one audience member shouted out, “That was great!” The film group meets at the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with the film beginning at 10:30 a.m. The event is free and open to those 18 and older. Participants are invited on a drop-in basis. Registration with the PRD is required at https://bit. ly/3PJyxkP. Audience members may bring snacks or lunch. Bob Hall introduced the 1959 film, noting that Hitchcock made it after Vertigo, which was recently voted the best movie of all time by a panel of international critics. Vertigo, however, was a “dark” film, with an unhappy ending, and Hitchcock wanted to follow it with something light, just for fun, so he and his screenwriter, Ernest Lehmann (who also wrote Psycho) concocted this enjoyably preposterous chase film. Cary Grant, in his fourth collaboration with the director, dashes all over the U.S. pursued both by bad guys, headed by actor James Mason, and by the police, who think he’s a murderer. Any upside? Grant gets to meet and romance Eva Marie Saint. Not bad. There’s also Bernard Hermann’s stirring musical score. And then there’s the experience of two classic movie sequences: (1) when a crop duster tries to machine-gun our hero in a corn field, and (2) when Grant and Saint, pursued by armed spies, scramble across the four giant presidential faces carved into the Mount Rushmore monument. The Second Thursday Flix Fest meets again at the Center for the Arts on April 13. The movie will be an award-winning drama dealing with social issues that will be announced to the group in April. Theater reviewer and published author Robert Hall leads a discussion on March 9 with the Piedmont movie group Second Thursday Flix Fest. Please join us for our upcoming seminar

articles.text: To kick off Earth Month on April 1, a Bay Area event called the Regenerative Gala will promote the concepts of ethical consumerism and fashion and art as a vehicle for change. The event’s fashion show rejects so-called “fast fashion” which produces clothes in sweatshops, often made from petroleum-based synthetic fabrics. Joelle Provost, a low-impact painter whose works will be featured, said the focus is on natural fabrics produced on farms avoiding pesticides, rejuvenating the soil, and paying a living wage. “A lot of small brands are saying, let’s source our textiles from the farmers so that we know that the ecosystems are being supported on those small farms,” Provost explained. “It’s all about small-batch fabrics.” The gala takes place on Saturday, April 1, at 6:00 p.m. at Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue, in Piedmont. Julian Adon Alexander, The Regenerative Gala will feature a runway with models wearing fashions made of natural fabrics produced on farms. another featured artist, will offer paintings raising awareness about the lack of green space in urban neighborhoods of color. “I just think exposure to new ideas is really the point of art,” Alexander noted. “I don’t think it necessarily solves problems, it just introduces something into somebody’s mind.” Food & wine The Gala will feature a chef that works closely with local USDA organic farmers and is committed to minimal packaging. articles.text: • Make sure your recyclables are empty, clean, dry The City of Piedmont has “single stream” recycling where all recyclable materials are put into one bin and eventually separated at a facility in Richmond. If recyclable materials haven’t been rinsed or cleaned out ahead of time, it can cause a mess. Paper is especially vulnerable to grease and moisture. One half-full soda can or greasy takeout container can contaminate the other recyclables in the bin, turning them into trash. • Don’t be an “aspirational” recycler Have you ever put an item in the recycling bin because you thought it should be recyclable? This phenomenon is known as aspirational recycling or “wishcycling.” Such materials include single-use utensils and straws, plastic bags, chip bags, and waxed cartons. Often, wishcycling contaminates recyclables and causes whole batches of recyclable loads to be thrown away. Remember: When in doubt, throw it out. • Don’t include e-waste E-waste can be recycled, but it doesn’t belong in the blue bin. Batteries can be dropped off at the Fire Department or can be placed in a sealed zip-lock plastic bag on top of your blue recycling cart on your regular collection day. For other e-waste items, call Republic Services at 800-320-8077 to schedule a curbside pickup. • If it’s smaller than a credit card, it belongs in the trash Small items like clothing tags, bottle caps, straws, and scraps of paper can clog machinery and are unlikely to be recycled. Recycling loads are delivered to Richmond where they are unloaded and put on conveyor belts for mechanical removal of aluminum cans, plastics and glass. The remaining materials are hand-sorted to recover cardboard and other reusable material as possible. • Don’t bag your recyclables Plastic bags can clog recycling equipment, which may lead sorting facilities to throw away your bagged recyclables. By omitting the bag, you’re creating less waste. • Reduce and reuse before you recycle Did you know that the three R’s are in that order for a reason? Recycling should be a last resort, after reducing and reusing. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Dr. Daniel Sperling, the Distinguished Blue Planet Prize Professor of Civil Engineering and Environmental Science and Policy and founding Director of the Institute of Transportation Studies at the University of California in Davis, was the guest speaker on March 1 in Piedmont. His discussion was sponsored by the Piedmont League of Women Voters. Dr. Sperling described renewable electricity generation and EV usage as the #1 and #2 solutions to climate damage. The shift to EVs is already underway with EVs representing 13% of passenger car sales worldwide in 2022. China and the E.U. lead EV passenger sales with approximately 54% and 29% of global unit sales respectively. The U.S. is a distant 3rd place with less than 12% of passenger EV unit sales. Among U.S. states, California is a front-runner in the transition to EVs. Currently, 20% of California’s passenger car sales are EVs – good news for local air quality and public health. Dr. Sperling has kept California in the vanguard of climate leadership in the transportation sector. For the past 16 years, he has held the Transportation seat on the California Air Resources Board (CARB), which adopted its first EV rules in 1990. EV adoption is scheduled to accelerate in California with CARB regulations mandating that EVs reach 33% of passenger car sales by 2026, 66% by 2030 and 100% by 2035. New buses will have to be 100% ZEV (Zero-Emission Vehicles) by 2029 and even new long-haul trucks will be ZEV by 2035. Enabling this rapid transition has been the precipitous decline in battery prices which have decreased 90% in real dollars, from approximately $1,200/ kWh in 2010 to roughly $100/ kWh today. Dr. Sperling shared some mild uncertainties about the pace of EV adoption including fluctuations in battery costs, lags in domestic battery materials supplies, processing, and manufacturing, and slower development of public charging infrastructure, especially to support long-haul road transportation. He is convinced by historical precedents that public and private investment will generate market solutions to surmount these hurdles. In addition to EVs, Dr. Sperling discussed the benefits of, and use-case scenarios for, hydrogen fuel-cell vehicles. He said that hydrogen fuel cells are likely to be important for larger vehicles such as buses and long-haul transportation needs, or for people living in very cold climates who have very long daily commutes. Dr. Sperling closed the session by taking questions from the audience. When asked about housing policy and public transit as means of reducing vehicle-miles-traveled, Dr. Sperling emphasized that reducing vehicle use is a winning strategy that is worthy of public investment. To illustrate this point, he cited the example of his home city of Davis where urban planners and city leaders gradually built a network of safe bike paths widely used by riders of all ages. He said that bikes now account for 30-40% of work trips in Davis. In addition to developing safe biking infrastructure, especially to connect the “last mile” of homes and businesses to public transit, he sees shared, autonomous transportation-on-demand as a promising solution for reducing vehicle-use and for providing convenient and affordable public transportation using larger cars or vans. He notes 3 companies who are currently testing this technology on a limited basis in the Bay Area. Additional question topics included energy and material sources for EVs, using EVs as storage for the electric grid, and EV recommendations. To learn more, watch a recording of this event on the League of Women Voters of Piedmont’s YouTube channel: https://www.lwvpiedmont.org/. The final event in the Series will be on Wednesday, April 5 at 4 p.m. when Stanford University professor, Dr. Mark Jacobson, will discuss renewable energy and storage. This presentation was the penultimate in the six-part 2022-23 Climate Speaker Series by Piedmont Connect and the League of Women Voters of Piedmont. This event was cosponsored by the Leagues of Women Voters of Solano County and Portland, Oregon.

articles.text: Participating with Walking on Wednesdays on March 8 were Bill Ahern, Laura Goldman and best K-9 friend Vivie, Elizabeth Richter, Dave DeRoche, Alan Goldhammer, FangFang Lai, Albert Chen, Karin Fetherston, Jim Kuo, Lisa Euphrat, Pat Keller, Alicia Rivera, Helene Farber, Priscilla Wanerus, Phil Witt, Jim Kellogg, Harriette Louie, Elene Manolis, Mary Hedley, Melba Yee, Cheryl Coleman Jones, Bob Wong, Adriene Hamlin, Tina Shum, Garrett Clifford, Stella Houston, Kathy Rolefson, Noemi Alvarado, Joanne Larson, Joyce Ahern, Joanne Bailey, Swee Ling Chen, Matt Gerhardt, Tyler Johnson, Vincent Fisher, Helen Dong, Brenda Ferrero, Rob Smith, Christine Calliste, Sherry Jacobs, Edith Lee, Nancy DeRoche with K-9 best friend Chili, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Elane Rehr, and Dick Carter. The group was pleased to welcome Alissa Quan, Ken Moy, Leonore Deaton, Dale Breen, and Steve Canine with K-9 best friend Mochie who were with the group for the first time. The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group had another big crowd of 50 walkers and a kennel of K-9 best friends last week. Besides the good weather there was another reason for the large turnout. A special destination was planned. Some of the walkers remembered in 2021 when they visited a home on Littlewood Drive with a truly unique yard, the site of of a historical former Silk Farm. They went down the cul-de-sac to its end where there is a private driveway that continues to a red London phone booth in front of a home’s gates. owner Laura Plitkins was coming out and invited the walkers to come see the “tropical oasis” she and her husband, Michael, had created. Walkers Swee Ling and Albert Chen are her neighbors and told her how much the group had enjoyed their first visit The house is going on the market in April, so the group knew it needed to schedule a visit before then. The walkers made the first climb up Mountain Avenue. They passed the stately former home of U.S. Senator William Knowland on Sea View Avenue and continued on to Dudley Avenue, passing beautiful tulip magnolias in full bloom, to the top of Littlewood. They regrouped there to hear Piedmont Historical Society President Gail Lombardi’s surprising history of Piedmont’s Silk Farm. In the early 1880s the Ladies’ Silk Culture Society purchased 15 acres of land at the top and eastern side of Mountain Avenue, where Dudley and Littlewood Avenues are today. They planted mulberry trees, whose leaves are food for silk worms. Unfortunately, the Silk Farm didn’t prosper. The canyon was not warm enough for the worms and the women would not work for less than a dollar a day, while Chinese silk workers were only paid six cents a day. In 1895 the farm closed. The group descended Littlewood’s canyon where the Silk Farm’s mulberry trees were once planted. At the end of the street Laura Plitkins was there to greet the walkers, and led them down their long, steep driveway to the side of their house and pool, guarded by a large statue of a dinosaur. Michael was waiting for the group and told them the house is one of six homes built on land that was once owned by the daughter of Domingo Ghirardelli, founder of the Ghirardelli Chocolate Company. The Plitkins bought the house in 2014. Michael has a company that creates unique structures and virtual soundscapes. Over five and a half years the Plitkins transformed the area at the house’s front into an incredible tropical garden with a pool, water slide, and pool house. Jungle sound effects enhance the other-world imaginary. Michael encouraged the group to walk below the pool on a stone path where they found replica Mayan tablets, bamboo and palm trees, and a natural creek running alongside. The walkers emerged near the pool house where Laura had coffee and pastries waiting for them. The group talked with Michael and Laura for some time before taking a group photo by the pool. All too soon it was time to retrace their steps back to the Exedra. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Pardee Home Museum has announced that the Carriage House Salon series of events will continue on Sunday, March 26, at 4 p.m. with a lecture on quilt making in America. It is part of celebrating Women’s History Month. Pardee Family Museum board member Gloria Taylor will talk about her family quilts, and audience members will learn about the quilts in the museum that belonged to the Pardee family. Taylor will introduce Marsha Carter, a renowned artist, poet and quilt maker, who will display a modernized method of quilting, using the fusion of fabric. Carter will bring a quilt depicting Delilah Beasley, and provide her history. Audience members are encouraged to bring photos or quilts for a sharing time. After the lecture there will be a champagne reception with sweets and savories. Depending on the weather the event may be held outdoors or in the Carriage House with social distancing. Tickets are $25 per person. The Pardee Home Museum Carriage house is located at 672 11th Street in Oakland. For more information call Richelle Lieberman at 510-381-1973.

articles.text: During its meeting on Monday, March 13 the Piedmont Planning Commission received an update on the city’s response to the state on its Housing Element. Planning staff will bring the Element and its Initial Study-Negative Declaration (ISND) to City Council, to be considered for adoption, next Monday, March 20. On the whole, Jackson emphasized, the comments by California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) reviewers don’t “requir[e] a structural change to the Element, such as a change in the sites identified in the inventory.” The Element and HCD review are available at PiedmontIsHome.org. On Friday, March 17, the revised Element will be posted on piedmont.ca.gov and PiedmontIsHome.org, as part of the agenda packet for the Monday, March 20 City Council meeting. After the Element is posted, said Jackson, “there will be seven days where the public can submit comments before we can send [the Element] off to HCD for a second review, and that generally lasts 60 days, which would put us at the end of May.” Among the additions requested in the HCD comments were a discussion of the “effectiveness of the previous Housing Element’s programs to address the housing needs of special needs populations”; “how the city proactively complies with fair housing laws and regulations”; and how the Element sites are expected to “improve and/or exacerbate fair housing conditions.” Much of the additional analysis requested regarded the needs of lower-income and special needs populations. For example, the city’s definition of a family as applied to zoning use “appears to have potential constraints on persons with disabilities such as requiring families to be ‘traditional,’ ‘sharing household activities’ and requiring a ‘single written lease.’” “While the Element identifies the total number of households overpaying for housing,” reviewers requested that the city quantify “the number of lower-income households overpaying for housing,” he added. Reviewers also asked that the Element demonstrate that the city’s existing and planned water and sewer infrastructure can accommodate planned housing without any overload. The city’s presentation included research showing Piedmont’s compliance with fair housing laws; proof of water and sewer capacity to accommodate new housing; how Piedmont’s housing programs impact economic and housing mobility for low-income and special needs populations; and recent rental and sale prices in Piedmont. Many comments referenced the fact that Piedmont’s Housing Element relies on non-vacant sites to accommodate over 50% of its lower-income housing, and the fact that “a large portion” of these “lower-income [sites] is isolated in three remote areas on the boundaries of the city yet a significant portion of the moderate and above moderate [sites] is located throughout the city.” The city’s approach is to show the travel times to schools, parks, and Civic Center from these areas, and demonstrate the fact that “Piedmont is a neighborhood-size small city … that access to amenities does not stop at the City boundary, that amenities in Oakland are generally [accessible] within a reasonable walking distance.” Furthermore, Jackson emphasized that unmapped sites like future ADUs and some sites like Moraga Canyon would “add units of all income types” throughout Piedmont. As part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. Completing this requirement, the IS-ND determined that the Housing Element as a document will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For questions about the plan, contact Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at 420-3039, or Pierce Macdonald Powell by email at pmacdonald@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone 420-3063. publicize positions and attract educators,” explained Hawn. Hawn will also need to be prepared for the high level of parent expectations for student achievement and plenty parent involvement. “I have a lot of experience in districts that are similar to Piedmont with parent involvement, a high level of it, including high expectations, academic expectations. I thrive in that environment, I really see parent involvement as an asset to the district. Sure, people have different opinions and they have every right to express them,” said Hawn Hawn earned a B.S. in Communication from Arizona State University, then attained a Master of Arts in Teaching English from Loyola Marymount University, and ultimately obtained a Doctorate in Education from the University of Southern California.
