pages.text: 30 Wednesday, March 15, 2023 City responds to state comments on Housing Element By Selen Ozturk During its meeting on Monday, March 13 the Piedmont Planning Commission received an update on the city’s response to the state on its Housing Element. Planning staff will bring the Element and its Initial Study-Negative Declaration (ISND) to City Council, to be considered for adoption, next Monday, March 20. On the whole, Jackson emphasized, the comments by California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) reviewers don’t “requir[e] a structural change to the Element, such as a change in the sites identified in the inventory.” The Element and HCD review are available at PiedmontIsHome.org. On Friday, March 17, the revised Element will be posted on piedmont.ca.gov and PiedmontIsHome.org, as part of the agenda packet for the Monday, March 20 City Council meeting. After the Element is posted, said Jackson, “there will be seven days where the public can submit comments before we can send [the Element] off to HCD for a second review, and that generally lasts 60 days, which would put us at the end of May.” Among the additions requested in the HCD comments were a discussion of the “effectiveness of the previous Housing Element’s programs to address the housing needs of special needs populations”; “how the city proactively complies with fair housing laws and regulations”; and how the Element sites are expected to “improve and/or exacerbate fair housing conditions.” Much of the additional analysis requested regarded the needs of lower-income and special needs populations. For example, the city’s definition of a family as applied to zoning use “appears to have potential constraints on persons with disabilities such as requiring families to be ‘traditional,’ ‘sharing household activities’ and requiring a ‘single written lease.’” “While the Element identifies the total number of households overpaying for housing,” reviewers requested that the city quantify “the number of lower-income households overpaying for housing,” he added. Reviewers also asked that the Element demonstrate that the city’s existing and planned water and sewer infrastructure can accommodate planned housing without any overload. The city’s presentation included research showing Piedmont’s compliance with fair housing laws; proof of water and sewer capacity to accommodate new housing; how Piedmont’s housing programs impact economic and housing mobility for low-income and special needs populations; and recent rental and sale prices in Piedmont. Many comments referenced the fact that Piedmont’s Housing Element relies on non-vacant sites to accommodate over 50% of its lower-income housing, and the fact that “a large portion” of these “lower-income [sites] is isolated in three remote areas on the boundaries of the city yet a significant portion of the moderate and above moderate [sites] is located throughout the city.” The city’s approach is to show the travel times to schools, parks, and Civic Center from these areas, and demonstrate the fact that “Piedmont is a neighborhood-size small city … that access to amenities does not stop at the City boundary, that amenities in Oakland are generally [accessible] within a reasonable walking distance.” Furthermore, Jackson emphasized that unmapped sites like future ADUs and some sites like Moraga Canyon would “add units of all income types” throughout Piedmont. As part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. Completing this requirement, the IS-ND determined that the Housing Element as a document will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. More information about the Housing Element and IS-ND is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For questions about the plan, contact Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone at 420-3039, or Pierce Macdonald Powell by email at pmacdonald@piedmont.ca.gov or by phone 420-3063. articles.text: Tonight, Wednesday, March 8, the Piedmont School Board will reveal the identity of the next Superintendent of Piedmont School District at the 7:00 p.m. board meeting. The new superintendent will attend the meeting at City Hall. Although the school board made its selection sometime prior to February 13, no details about the individual or terms of employment have been revealed. The agenda for tonight’s meeting specifies the contract for the Superintendent is for three years. “I will give a detailed update on the selection process. And once the announcement is made at the meeting, board members will have a chance to comment,” said Board President Veronica Anderson-Thigpen. People in attendance and on Zoom will have the option to speak during public comment after the announcement. The search firm Leadership Associates received 22 applications for the position which was vacated by Randy Booker at the end the 2021-22 school year. Current PUSD Superintendent Dr. Donald Evans, came out of retirement from Berkeley Unified to serve in a one-year interim capacity for this school year. “The board is grateful for the partnership with Leadership Associates. They led us through a solid search process and we are tremendously excited about the person we’ve selected,” said Anderson-Thigpen. The new superintendent will begin work on July 1. articles.text: Editor: I read with interest articles in the Piedmont Post on February 15th and 22nd about electrification. There are some roadblocks regarding electrification in Piedmont. First off, my wife and I are in favor of electrification. When we moved here from the Oakland Hills a little over a year ago, we put in solar panels and a battery backup as quickly as the Piedmont permit process would allow. We added a 240-volt outlet to charge our Leaf EV. We also replaced the 25-yearold gas cooktop with a new induction one and replaced the old energy hog refrigerator with a new efficient one. We plan some other improvements but found out that we have to upgrade our electrical service from 100 amp to 200 amp to be able to add any additional electrical load. This is where the problems come in and may impact the city’s goals for reducing their carbon footprint. We are in a neighborhood that was undergrounded, and when the city did that, they put in conduits that can only accommodate a 100 amp power cable. We contacted PG&E to find out what we needed to do, and because our power comes from under the street and not an overhead cable, we have to dig a trench to fit the larger conduit and cable. We also have to add a new electrical panel for the power to come into the house, even though we put in a new one when we added the solar panels. Our electrical contractor showed us where the new panel should go, and we contacted PG&E to contract with them to trench and put in the new cable. This is going to cost $400 per linear foot, which could cost us over $20,000. However, when PG&E came to look at the site, they said they could not trench as planned because it would go under two retaining walls, and the panel would need to go in a different location. The contractor said the city of Piedmont Design Review might not approve that because the panel might be visible from the street. We are now waiting for another site visit to determine where the trench can go. At this point, with the cost of the trenching to run the power cable, the fee for the electrical contractor to connect everything, the cost of the panel and other equipment the job will need, as well as the city permit, we’re looking at over $30,000. And we still don’t know if the city will approve the location of the electrical panel. The people we’ve dealt with in the building and design review departments, as well as our contact at PG&E, have all been very responsive and easy to work with; however, we still don’t know how long it will take to get this resolved. We also want to put in a heat pump and remove our gas furnace and water heater, to reduce our (and the city’s) carbon footprint, but we can’t do anything until all this is resolved, and the location of the electrical panel is approved by the city. I don’t know how many other residents will be willing to go through this to help reduce the carbon the city emits. articles.text: Comments made on the subject of pickleball by resident Rick Schiller at a recent Recreation Commission meeting were misinterpreted by the Piedmont Post. We apologize for the error and for the insufficiency of a correction printed in the Post on March 1. The full text of comments by Mr. Schiller on February 21 are: Good evening, I know how thorough this commission is and I read all the correspondence that you had received while we were all waiting, and there’s two themes that seem to come up I just wanted to flesh out from those that perhaps oppose this program. One has been that the Recreation Department has not acted properly, there’s been a bad process and there’s been a biased process. The other is that all venues have not been looked at. Now, fortunately, by the report that I’ve heard tonight from Ms. Putzer, Chelle, it was objective thorough and data driven, and even went far beyond I had imagined. And I think that answers all those questions, I will no longer have to write letters in Exedra, or PCA, or Post, and have people come back at me. And I’m quite serious about that. I mean, there’s been some really irrational comments, I get it that people are afraid of change. Sometimes it’s very difficult. But I’ve lived in the neighborhood a very long time, since 1980, on Fairview Avenue. And I remember when there were hard, hard surface basketball, there’s been a lot of different changes there. This is a big change for people. I understand that. But pickleball has grown phenomenally. It is a phenomenal success that most represents Piedmont in the most favorable possible light. Diane Santos and Art came in today from other cities, just about everybody that comes in says, we’re the friendliest program in town. And when they read the bad press in the Chronicle, every other week about Piedmont, that we’re doing some horrible thing, that our Piedmont police are bad or housing’s bad, all of a sudden, here’s pickleball. And they even say that, like when people come because I’ve volunteered quite a bit to work with staff to do scheduling. When there’s a problem people go, “I’m not gonna go talk to Rick.” So they send people to me, and those people have to deal with me and they still say, this is the friendliest program. This is the friendliest program. And it truly is. Finally, I mean, being involved in pickleball has changed my life. And I hope you put the trial through. articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved on March 6 a total design budget of $510,285, including a $471,471 agreement with Roseville-based Bennett Engineering Services and a $38,813 contingency, for Phase 6 of the city’s Sanitary Sewer Rehabilitation Project. This phase includes rehabilitation of about 14,200 feet of the city’s sewer system. The project is in accordance with an Environmental Protection Agency consent decree that Piedmont and several other Alameda County cities reduce sanitary sewer overflows and reduce the infiltration of groundwater into their sewer system. To comply with this decree Piedmont must replace a rolling average of linear feet of sewer per year; currently the requirement is around 3,300 feet. Piedmont has approximately 48 miles of sewer pipeline, and about 75% has been upgraded. The completion of Phase 6, which the city put out to bid on August 26, 2022, will leave the city with about 49,000 linear feet left to upgrade, confirmed Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales. All past phases of the sewer system rehabilitation have been financed through the State Revolving Loan Fund (SRF) program offered by State Water Quality. The city anticipates that, once approvals are received from the State for the SRF loan, costs for Phase 6 preliminary work – including preliminary engineering, environmental document preparation and grant application preparation – will be repaid. Because the sewer project is a matter of both public and private work, Gonzales said that coordination strategies with private property owners who need to upgrade their sewer lateral – the underground part of the pipe that connects a building’s plumbing from the foundation to the public sewer main – will be ongoing. “We have quarterly meetings with EBMUD, about where their future projects will be and where we should adjust our own resurfacing of roadways. We do the same thing with our sewer; we want to make sure that our utility projects are not going to be occurring on a street that we paved last summer,” Gonzales added. Sewer repair methods are less invasive than excavating and removing old pipe. Pipe lining can be installed remotely in existing pipes without having to excavate. Those with questions about the Sanitary Sewer Rehabilitation Project can contact Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061.
articles.title: City Council approves $510,000 sewer project

articles.text: During its meeting on Wednesday, March 1, the Park Commission received an update by Parks and Project Manager Nancy Kent and Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales on city park projects including Piedmont Park, new water stations, and the Linda Park off-leash dog area. Piedmont Park Speaking on the steps under construction in Piedmont Park, by Highland Avenue and Guilford Road, Kent said that “the ultimate plan is to have a small entry plaza at the sidewalk level…[with] three memorial benches and at least two memorial trees.” Despite muddiness on the site through the ongoing rains and a three-week delay due to weather, Kent said that Bay Construction “is still making really good progress.” Gonzales confirmed that the project may be pushed back one month. Plans are underway to add metal fencing around the native plant garden in Piedmont Park. Water stations Kent said that the city has purchased three water bottle filling stations courtesy of a $20,000 donation from the Piedmont Beautification Foundation and a $5,000 grant from CalRecycle. The city hopes to have the fountains installed by July 4. One water station will be installed near the pathway that goes to Community Hall in Piedmont Park, and another installed in the quarry area in Dracena Park. A third will be installed at Coaches Field to replace an existing fountain. Linda Park dog area The off-leash dog area at Linda Park was reopened on February 20, but was closed again on February 24 due to additional rain. Gonzales said “Our hope is to keep this park open for as much as we can, but the reality seems to be pushing us in the other direction … I believe we have rain forecast until mid-month, which means that we are not going to be reopening it … probably for most of this month.” A corner of the Linda Park off-leash dog area after the February rains “Don’t worry. None of their hearing aids work.”

articles.text: The Piedmont City Council approved a final design this week for bulb-outs at the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections of Oakland Avenue on March 6, and authorized city staff to put the project out for bid. The plan calls for four permanent “bulb-outs” at each intersection, extending the sidewalk to make the pedestrian crossing shorter and safer. In addition to the bulb-outs, the plan provides for pedestrian-activated rectangular rapid flashing beacons across Oakland Avenue at both intersections, similar to those installed on Highland Avenue by Havens School, on Linda Avenue in front of Beach School, and on Grand Avenue in front of Ace Hardware. Due to AC Transit requirements for bus stop relocations on Oakland Avenue, the plan will result in a net loss of six parking spaces by El Cerrito Avenue, and one parking space by Jerome Avenue. The plan is based upon the Piedmont Safer Streets Plan, which lists the Jerome and El Cerrito intersections as two of the 10 highest-priority crossings for pedestrian safety improvements. “This plan has been in the works for ... more than a decade, I believe. When I joined the city as the Recreation Director in 2014, this was being talked about,” said City Administrator Sara Lillevand. The Safer Streets Plan itself was based upon the city’s Bike Pedestrian Master Plan, which was adopted in 2014. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that this plan identified the two intersections as high-enough priority that, in 2018, Council approved a contract with the Santa Rosa-based firm Coastline Civil Engineering to start design work. The work began that year and continued until spring 2019, when progress was stalled by discussions of design alternatives. In 2021 the city received a $19,000 Safe Route to Schools grant from the Alameda County Transportation Commission to continue design development. Furthermore, as Piedmont Beautification Foundation president Karen Sullivan attested at last Monday’s Council meeting, “Piedmont Beautification Foundation fundraised for this … [and] made a donation to total $50,000 towards this project, because we felt it was important to support the Piedmont Safe Routes to School,” said PBF president Karen Sullivan. Design deliberations continued until November 2022, when a public meeting was held. Gonzales said that in the four months since that meeting, in which much of the concerns were related to parking, the Public Works Department has been in constant communication with AC Transit to develop a plan with minimal parking changes. The original bulb-out plan at that time involved a net loss of 10 parking spaces. Some crosswalks at the affected intersections already emptied onto private driveways, and many residents contended that the bulb-out plan would create more, not less pedestrian traffic on a busy street. To the rescue came Oakland Avenue resident, Charles Oraftik, and architect. “Without the talent, effort and persistence of Chuck Oraftik, this design for the Oakland/Jerome [intersection] could have turned out very, very differently,” said neighbor Kathy Moody. Oraftik personally measured driveways affected by the bulbout plan and compared them for city staff with official construction diagrams. Those with questions about the new bulb-out plan may contact Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales by email at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: The City of Piedmont is now accepting applications to fill upcoming vacancies on several Commissions and Committees. Online applications are due by 5 p.m. on March 29. Many of the programs that Piedmonters enjoy today were initiated and/or first reviewed by Commissions, including Heritage Trees, annual design awards, and the Map Your Neighborhood program. The dozens of residents who serve on one of the City’s 13 volunteer Commissions and Committees act as Piedmont’s eyes and ears, listening to community input, identifying and studying issues, and making recommendations to the City Council for action. Vacancies This year vacancies exist on seven commissions and committees — the Park Commission; the Planning Commission; the Recreation Commission; the Civil Service Commission; the Budget Advisory and Financial Planning Committee; the Community Pool Advisory Committee; and the Public Safety Committee. For most bodies, members are appointed to three-year terms, with a limit of two consecutive terms. How to apply Those interested may apply online at: bit.ly/41QhGSS. When applying, you’ll be asked to provide contact and basic background information (education, occupation), select which body or bodies you would like to apply to serve on, and provide brief written answers to three questions: • What experience do you have related to this appointment? • Why are you seeking this appointment? • What will you bring to this Commission or Committee? The application also asks whether you have previously attended or watched a meeting of the body you’re applying to serve on. Archived meeting videos are available to stream on the city’s website. To be considered for appointment, applicants must attend an interview with City Council members on Tuesday evening, April 4. The interview schedule will be provided to applicants on Friday, March 31. For more information, contact City Clerk John Tulloch at 420- 3040 or by email at CityClerk@ piedmont.ca.gov. For 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. The Post invites families to send photos with the Post from near and far for publication in Where in the World Are We on the back page of the paper. With people able to travel once again, there is no better time to have your photo in the Post. Send photos as jpg. files to: news@piedmont-post.com, and be sure to include a brief description of the location where the photo was taken.

articles.text: Back in uniform again, George Tucker a veteran member of the Piedmont Police Department since 2013, has shed his detective street clothes and now wears his dress blues but with a new title: Sergeant. On March 1, after learning the ropes by shadowing Sgt. Willie Wright for two weeks, Tucker officially became a Sergeant. Born in Southern California, he grew up in San Ramon. He attended Diablo Valley College in 2002 before transferring to Whitworth University in Spokane, Washington, where he played college basketball. – Sergeant George Tucker Piedmont Police Department “I grew up playing sports. I played high school baseball and basketball and played college basketball. Being in that team environment, and having that camaraderie was pretty important to me,” Tucker said. After college Tucker worked for a company selling police, fire and postal uniforms, which gave him his first look into a police station while delivering uniforms and gear. “It’s funny. A lot of guys [I delivered uniforms to] said, ‘Why don’t you just step over the counter and be a peace officer?’ I thought they were crazy, but sure enough, two years later that was the career path I chose,” Tucker said with a smile. Tucker took a basic course in 2010, where he learned penal codes and had his first experience firing a gun. “After that course I knew this was a profession I wanted to be in and that I would love to be a peace officer,” he said. Tucker graduated from the Contra Costa Police Academy in 2011 and started his career in George Tucker (left) receives his sergeant’s badge from Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers on February 22. Piedmont as a traffic officer and motorcycle cop, a role he held for five years. His career advanced to become a field training officer, training recruits new to the department. Tucker became a detective and then embarked on the six month process of studying to become a Sergeant. “It was a tough, grueling process. The (Sergeant) test is about policy and current events and required a lot of reading about leadership. I was lucky enough to be selected as the next sergeant, and I’m honored because I’ve worked pretty hard to get to this point,” Tucker said. Tucker joins current Piedmont Sergeants Robert Jaime, Willie Wright, and Nicole Casalnuovo. “Sergeant George Tucker earned his promotion by consistently demonstrating a high-level of competence and investment in the vision of the Piedmont Police Department by contributing to community safety and equity by continually exemplifying the best of policing,” said Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers. “Being a police officer every day, nothing’s really the same. That’s part of the good and bad of being a police officer. Every day and with each call, something can change. That makes it somewhat exciting, but it also can be dangerous,” Tucker explained. Tucker lives in Dublin with wife Jackie and their 10-year-old son Chase. A badge- pinning ceremony will be held in Piedmont City Hall on March 20.
articles.title: George Tucker promoted to Police Sergeant

articles.text: If you’ve been eager to check out what’s coming to Piedmont Food Fest on April 23, the wait is over. Early Bird packages are now available at www.piedmontfoodfest.org and include drink packages. Packages contain KidZone carnival bracelets, a collectible water bottle, and a premium snack box featuring gourmet mochi bites from Bakesum and a bottle of tea of Piedmont’s top-selling honey chrysanthemum boba. Early bird deals run through March or while supplies last. Festival attendees are in for a treat, as the Food Fest has now confirmed 26 food vendors, breweries, and wineries coming in from all around the Bay (and as far as San Luis Obispo). Recent food additions include Abaraya Japanese Fried Chicken, Vegan Mob, and Arthur Mac’s Tap & Shack. Buck Wild Brewing, Wondrous Brewing Company, and Maker Wines have also joined this year’s beer & wine lineup. Piedmont Food Fest’s focus on celebrating the diversity of the Bay will be on full display with live performances onstage by Emeryville Taiko, the Filipino folk dance troupe LIKHA, Jewelz Moya of Renegade Opera, and Oakland Samba Revue. The Food Fest team recommends showing up early to secure a good spot to enjoy the continuous entertainment running throughout the day. The Food Fest team encourages attendees to invite friends and family to join one another for a memorable day in the park. For Early Bird packages, a mailing list, and volunteer signups, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org.

articles.text: Sixteen current and former Piedmonters contributed recently to a Women’s Health Quilt Project that was created to honor those who defended the rights of American women to safe abortions and reproductive health care that was terminated on June 24, 2022 by the U.S. Supreme Court. In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Court decided that the right to privacy guaranteed in the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution did not apply to women seeking a pre-viability abortion. Jackson Women’s Health, known as the Pink House, was the only abortion clinic in the state of Mississippi prior to the Dobbs decision. Following Dobbs, the Pink House relocated to New Mexico, where state law still allows women access to abortion care. On August 5, six weeks after leaving Mississippi, The Pink House West began providing abortions and reproductive health services in Las Cruces across the border from El Paso, Texas. On March 1st, Piedmont resident Karen Joffe delivered two quilts featuring designs and messages to Shannon Brewer, the director of as Cruces Women’s Health Organization. Messages were written by 25 contributors from across the US, including Piedmont, and from as far away as Spain. In the clinic waiting room is the Emmy Award that Shannon received for her role in the documentary Jackson (now on HBO Max). Joffe created the quilt project to honor front line abortion clinic caregivers and their clients. The quilt is an homage to the long tradition of American women quilting as an art form to tell their stories and raise their spirits. HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY
articles.title: Piedmonters show support for Jackson Women’s Health in Las Cruces

Recent food additions include Abaraya Japanese Fried Chicken, Vegan Mob, and Arthur Mac’s Tap & Shack. Buck Wild Brewing, Wondrous Brewing Company, and Maker Wines have also joined this year’s beer & wine lineup. Piedmont Food Fest’s focus on celebrating the diversity of the Bay will be on full display with live performances onstage by Emeryville Taiko, the Filipino folk dance troupe LIKHA, Jewelz Moya of Renegade Opera, and Oakland Samba Revue. The Food Fest team recommends showing up early to secure a good spot to enjoy the continuous entertainment running throughout the day. The Food Fest team encourages attendees to invite friends and family to join one another for a memorable day in the park. For Early Bird packages, a mailing list, and volunteer signups, please visit www.piedmontfoodfest.org. “I grew up playing sports. I played high school baseball and basketball and played college basketball. Being in that team environment, and having that camaraderie was pretty important to me,” Tucker said. After college Tucker worked for a company selling police, fire and postal uniforms, which gave him his first look into a police station while delivering uniforms and gear. “It’s funny. A lot of guys [I delivered uniforms to] said, ‘Why don’t you just step over the counter and be a peace officer?’ I thought they were crazy, but sure enough, two years later that was the career path I chose,” Tucker said with a smile. Tucker took a basic course in 2010, where he learned penal codes and had his first experience firing a gun. “After that course I knew this was a profession I wanted to be in and that I would love to be a peace officer,” he said. Tucker graduated from the Contra Costa Police Academy in 2011 and started his career in George Tucker (left) receives his sergeant’s badge from Piedmont Police Chief Jeremy Bowers on February 22. Piedmont as a traffic officer and motorcycle cop, a role he held for five years. His career advanced to become a field training officer, training recruits new to the department. Tucker became a detective and then embarked on the six month process of studying to become a Sergeant. “It was a tough, grueling process. The (Sergeant) test is about policy and current events and required a lot of reading about leadership. I was lucky enough to be selected as the next sergeant, and I’m honored because I’ve worked pretty hard to get to this point,” Tucker said. Tucker joins current Piedmont Sergeants Robert Jaime, Willie Wright, and Nicole Casalnuovo. “Sergeant George Tucker earned his promotion by consistently demonstrating a high-level of competence and investment in the vision of the Piedmont Police Department by contributing to community safety and equity by continually exemplifying the best of policing,” said Chief of Police Jeremy Bowers. “Being a police officer every day, nothing’s really the same. That’s part of the good and bad of being a police officer. Every day and with each call, something can change. That makes it somewhat exciting, but it also can be dangerous,” Tucker explained. Tucker lives in Dublin with wife Jackie and their 10-year-old son Chase. A badge- pinning ceremony will be held in Piedmont City Hall on March 20. Piedmonters show support for Jackson Women’s Health in Las Cruces Sixteen current and former Piedmonters contributed recently to a Women’s Health Quilt Project that was created to honor those who defended the rights of American women to safe abortions and reproductive health care that was terminated on June 24, 2022 by the U.S. Supreme Court. In Dobbs v. Jackson Women’s Health Organization, the Court decided that the right to privacy guaranteed in the 14th Amendment of the U.S. Constitution did not apply to women seeking a pre-viability abortion. Jackson Women’s Health, known as the Pink House, was the only abortion clinic in the state of Mississippi prior to the Dobbs decision. Following Dobbs, the Pink House relocated to New Mexico, where state law still allows women access to abortion care. On August 5, six weeks after leaving Mississippi, The Pink House West began providing abortions and reproductive health services in Las Cruces across the border from El Paso, Texas. On March 1st, Piedmont resident Karen Joffe delivered two quilts featuring designs and messages to Shannon Brewer, the director of as Cruces Women’s Health Organization. Messages were written by 25 contributors from across the US, including Piedmont, and from as far away as Spain. In the clinic waiting room is the Emmy Award that Shannon received for her role in the documentary Jackson (now on HBO Max). Joffe created the quilt project to honor front line abortion clinic caregivers and their clients. The quilt is an homage to the long tradition of American women quilting as an art form to tell their stories and raise their spirits. articles.text: After a three-year absence, the famed Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest will return to Piedmont High School on Thursday, March 30, at 7:00 p.m., at the Alan Harvey Theater. With the theme of “Maskarade,” guests are encouraged to show their creativity and personality using masks. The contest will be under the production of Piedmont High School Librarian Kathryn Levenson. Created in 1963, by PHS science teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck, the Bird Calling Contest grew into an annual event that over the decades has attracted national and international attention. The winners appeared for many years on The Tonight Show with Johnny Carson, and then on Late Night with David Letterman. Students spend time perfecting their bird calls and will be judged based on three criteria: • Authenticity of Call • Poise and Delivery • Content of Introduction (Contestants write and deliver their own sketches.) Tickets went on sale March 2 at Showtix4u.com/event-details/67041. General admission tickets are $25. And student tickets are $15. The Alan Harvey Theater is located at 800 Magnolia Avenue, on the campus of Piedmont High School. Please contact Kathryn Levenson at klevenson@piedmont.k12.ca.us, or 510-594-2781. Students have until March 14 to sign up to be a contestant. PHS senior Macie Gard designed the poster for this year’s Bird Calling Contest.
articles.title: Annual Bird Calling Show returns on March 30

articles.text: On Tuesday, March 7, Piedmont High School Principal Sukanya Goswami sent a letter to families of high school students regarding an assault that happened during a basketball game in the high school gym on Tuesday, February 7. The text of the letter follows: Hello PHS Community: As we prepare for our Spring activities and events, I want to remind parents that safety is important to all of us. As administrators, we are experiencing a lot of excitement as our teams have performed well at NCS and CIF Regional over the past few weeks. But I want to address an issue that happened last month where there was an altercation between adults and students. There was a physical and verbal assault on one of our students at a varsity basketball game by a parent. This is unacceptable and we have a zero policy for this type of behavior. We want to make sure our students and all spectators feel safe at our sporting events and other activities. As such, the following actions have been taken: • A stay-away letter has been issued to the adult involved. This stay-away order means that this individual will not be allowed on campus for 14 days. • As a school system, we are re-evaluating the policies and procedures in place for communicating with students, parents and the greater community following any critical incident on campus. It goes without saying that we expect all members of our community, adults, and students to conduct themselves in a way befitting the values of the Piedmont Unified School District. Please contact my office with any questions. Sincerely, Sukanya Goswami Principal Piedmont High School
articles.title: Letter from PHS principal concerning Feb. 7 incident

articles.text: The 50th annual Oakland-Fukuoka High School Student Exchange Program will be hosted June 29 to July 10 in Fukuoka, Japan, Oakland’s sister city. The Oakland Fukuoka Sister City Association (OFSCA) is accepting applications for six students until this Friday, March 10. The estimated program cost is $2,500, which includes airfare, room & board (homestays), organized activities in Fukuoka, and travel insurance. Students currently attending high school are eligible. A representative or representatives from the Oakland Fukuoka Sister City Association will chaperone the students during the trip. The City of Fukuoka will partner with the Fukuoka–Oakland Friendship Association, a volunteer group based in Fukuoka to organize home accommodations and daily activities for the group during their stay in the Japanese city. During the program, each student will stay with a host family to experience Japanese family life. Organized activities will introduce students to the culture of Japan; potential activities include a Japanese high school experience, a visit to the US Consulate, Japanese language classes, Japanese cooking classes, and an excursion to the city of Nagasaki, including the Peace Park. To apply and for more details, visit oakland-fukuoka.org/home/ programs/youth-exchange, or contact program coordinator Jason Lambert at 709-9367 (e-mail: ofsca1962@gmail.com).
articles.title: Application deadline is this Friday, March 10

articles.text: What does a focus coach do? I get this question a lot when I tell people what I do for a living – and for good reason. Though ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is well known, focus coaching for ADHD is still a relatively new concept. I am a former student of Piedmont schools (Havens, PMS and PHS) and I recently started an ADHD focus coaching business called MindsGlowing. I decided to leave my career in tech sales and become a focus coach when I came to realize the unique set of challenges that people with ADHD face when tackling the world around them. I understand these challenges and have faced them in my own life. Before I was diagnosed, I struggled with procrastination, lack of organization, and other ADHD symptoms, It wasn’t until after college when I was diagnosed with ADHD that I began to find relief through medicine and developing systems for myself. After I was diagnosed, I decided to complete a program in Positive Psychology to better understand how the mind works. I now use my certification in Applied Positive Psychology to help people with ADHD achieve their goals. One of my clients is a pre-medical student at Columbia University who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD. We meet Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch a show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. a few times a week for targeted focus sessions where we work on goal setting, craft her to-do lists, and tackling her more difficult projects. My coaching takes many different forms depending on the client, the. day, and a multitude of factors. I customize each session based on my client’s unique goals and challenges because there is no one size that fits the way to coach people with ADHD. I want to introduce one concept called intentional relaxation which I work on with my clients who struggle with procrastination. The idea behind intentional relaxation is: when you’re watching TV or scrolling through Tik Tok when you’re supposed to be doing something else, it doesn’t feel very good. It becomes hard to enjoy the thing you’re doing when you’re worried about the things that need to get done. To try intentional relaxation you want to set aside time where you are aware that you’re relaxing and can enjoy it more fully. The best time for this would be when you don’t have too much to do. You can also use it as a break between two tough tasks or in between school and doing homework. Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch the show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. Then once it’s over, you’ll have more energy to complete the task at hand. Thinking Outside the Classroom Focus coaching helps people with ADHD thrive By Erica Monical What does a focus coach do? I get this question a lot when I tell people what I do for a living – and for good reason. Though ADHD (Attention-Deficit/Hyperactivity Disorder) is well known, focus coaching for ADHD is still a relatively new concept. I am a former student of Piedmont schools (Havens, PMS and PHS) and I recently started an ADHD focus coaching business called MindsGlowing. I decided to leave my career in tech sales and become a focus coach when I came to realize the unique set of challenges that people with ADHD face when tackling the world around them. I understand these challenges and have faced them in my own life. Before I was diagnosed, I struggled with procrastination, lack of organization, and other ADHD symptoms, It wasn’t until after college when I was diagnosed with ADHD that I began to find relief through medicine and developing systems for myself. After I was diagnosed, I decided to complete a program in Positive Psychology to better understand how the mind works. I now use my certification in Applied Positive Psychology to help people with ADHD achieve their goals. One of my clients is a pre-medical student at Columbia University who has recently been diagnosed with ADHD. We meet Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch a show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. a few times a week for targeted focus sessions where we work on goal setting, craft her to-do lists, and tackling her more difficult projects. My coaching takes many different forms depending on the client, the. day, and a multitude of factors. I customize each session based on my client’s unique goals and challenges because there is no one size that fits the way to coach people with ADHD. I want to introduce one concept called intentional relaxation which I work on with my clients who struggle with procrastination. The idea behind intentional relaxation is: when you’re watching TV or scrolling through Tik Tok when you’re supposed to be doing something else, it doesn’t feel very good. It becomes hard to enjoy the thing you’re doing when you’re worried about the things that need to get done. To try intentional relaxation you want to set aside time where you are aware that you’re relaxing and can enjoy it more fully. The best time for this would be when you don’t have too much to do. You can also use it as a break between two tough tasks or in between school and doing homework. Set a timer for 30 minutes and let yourself watch the show or go on Instagram and really enjoy the time. Then once it’s over, you’ll have more energy to complete the task at hand. Check back next month for more on ADHD, focus coaching, and positive psychology tips. Erica Monical is the founder and focus coach at MindsGlowing and a monthly columnist in the Piedmont Post. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Micah Temple An astronomer peers up at the cosmos through the lens of a telescope; a Navy researcher pours over blueprints below deck; and an engineer sketches the future hull of a ground-breaking rocket. Though each of these feats is remarkable, the three female minds who performed them have been largely unsung. However, an anonymous Piedmont donor is working to change that. At a Makers fundraiser, a donor purchased naming rights being offered for the three workspaces in the high school’s new STEAM building. Piedmont Makers plans to host a Grand Opening for the new areas on Saturday, April 29. The first of the three spaces is one of the building’s most defining features; the cage-covered engineering patio. The patio is set to be named after Annie Jump Cannon, one of the first women to contribute to the field Engineer Raye Montague frequently briefed the Joint Chiefs of Staff and taught at the U.S. Naval Academy in Annapolis, MD. Annie Jump Cannon, was not only a pioneer for women in astronomy, she did so after becoming deaf at the age of 30. Mary Golda Ross was depicted on the 2019 Native American $1 coin by the U.S. Mint for her contributions to the U.S. space program. of astronomy. Cannon developed an instrumental classification system for stellar bodies, known as the “Harvard Classification Scheme.” The second space set to be renamed is the Engineering Lab, used for everything from crafting electric guitars to building complex robots. The lab will be named after the first known female Native American engineer, Mary Golda Ross. Ross’ fame derives primarily from being one of the founding engineers for an elite and highly secretive aerospace project, as well as her immense contributions to the Agena Rocket. The last of the three spaces is the PHS computer lab, to be named after Raye Montague, one of the first Black female naval engineers in history. She’s known for her work modeling a digital rendering of a navy ship as well as being the first female program manager in the U.S. Navy. Three plaques created by students of the Piedmont Makers organization will be unveiled at the grand opening, celebrating the three women’s lives and accomplishments. Will Becker and Micah Temple are Piedmont High School students and interns with the Piedmont Post.
articles.title: High School STEAM lab honors women of STEM

articles.text: This year’s Spring Fling will be co-chaired by Piedmont elementary school parents Catie Osborn and Anne Wheeler. Osborn and Wheeler will work with the Piedmont Education Foundation to plan the annual event. “When I learned about the possible reductions in the school budget for next year, I wanted to do something to help,” said Osborn, “I have a background in fundraising and saw Spring Fling as an opportunity to really make a difference.” Spring Fling is scheduled for May 6, but the months leading up to it are packed with events that contribute significantly to elementary school fundraising. Parent sponsorships are a popular way to support the elementary schools, with three sponsorship levels. This year’s sponsors will enjoy a magical evening on April 6 at the elegant King Avenue home of Melissa and Ali Partovi. Guests will be fêted with cocktails and a feast of savories by noted cook- 2023 Spring Fling Co-Chairs Catie Osborn (left) and Anne Wheeler book author and Chez Panisse Chef Anthony Tassinello. Sponsorship information is available at PiedmontSpringFling.org. “My oldest just started at Wildwood last year, so we haven’t yet experienced the Spring Fling tradition. I want to help with the relaunch by creating some unforgettable events that bring us together as Piedmonters,” said Wheeler. Funds raised through Spring Fling sponsorships, auctions and events directly support Beach, Havens, and Wildwood elementary schools. PEF works with the three school principals and parent club presidents to determine the greatest need.
articles.title: Catie Osborn, Anne Wheeler to lead this year’s Spring Fling

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team’s magic winter season came to a close on Saturday, March 5 at Binks Rawlings Gym, where the No. 1 seeded Highlanders suffered a surprising 48-45 loss to No. 5 Salesian in the CIF Open Division Regional Semifinals. It was a night when the ball just wouldn’t go in, and seemingly every bounce fell the way of Salesian. “It was a very interesting game. We didn’t shoot it well and we turned the ball over much more than usual. The stars were just lined up the wrong way, and we just couldn’t get it going,” said coach Bryan Gardere. It was a strong defensive game for both sides, Piedmont led 10-7 to end the first quarter and went into halftime holding a razor-thin 22-21 lead. Salesian inched ahead with a 34-33 lead heading into the fourth quarter, but the Highlanders couldn’t find their way back to the front. There were 10 lead changes in the first three quarters. Natalia Martinez led Piedmont with 20 points, but fouled out near the end of the game. Eva Levingston had 11 points, Trinity Zamora and Maddie Hill had six, Adrienne Blackwell had two. “You have to give Salesian credit. It wasn’t a high scoring game, and a lot of things didn’t go our way. I don’t want to take anything away from our year, and that’s the hardest part,” said Gardere. Regardless of Saturday’s result, this was an historic season for Piedmont. They captured their first Western Alameda County Conference championship, won their first North Coast Section banner since 2006, and closed the season with a stellar 27-1 overall record. “We won 27 games, so it doesn’t feel very good now,” said Gardere, “Overall, the girls did a great job; it was an amazing year. It was so much fun, and we had great support throughout the community.” Saturday’s game in the Rawlings Gym was a rocking environment, with more than a capacity crowd. The game had to be halted for a short while in the second quarter due to too many people standing along the baseline Staff Photos Natalia Martinez led Piedmont with 20 points but fouled out in the final minutes against Salesian. Trinity Zamora takes the ball up court in her final appearance at Binks Rawlings Gym. searching for a seat. It was a special time for girls’ basketball and a scene rarely seen since the days of the famous Paris twins. “When you think about it, this senior class had the pandemic hit their freshman year later that spring. This team missed out on having those camp appearances with kids and making an impression on them. It was awesome for them to finally get that connection now that fans were back,” said Gardere. “We had an amazing group of young ladies who hopefully inspired the next group of girls,” said Gardere, recalling young kids lining up for autographs of his players. Departing from this year’s team will be a massive group of Zamora, Hill, Levingston, Perseas Gioukaris, and Blackwell. But continuing is Western Alameda County Conference 2023 Player of the Year, Martinez. “She’ll be the main focus for sure next season. Nat is one of those rare players and deserves all the accolades coming her way. She’s going to see a lot of different defenses next season, and I’m sure she’ll rise to the challenge.” Martinez is set to be named Cal Hi Sports’ Scholar Athlete of the Year, and is an in-demand prospects who has yet to announce her collegiate plans prior to finishing high school in one year. In addition to Zamora, Gardere also expects Levingston, Hill, Gioukaris, and Blackwell to announce collegiate basketball plans in the near future. Eva Levingston in front of a packed Binks Rawlings Gym.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s Cinderella season in sports came to a close on Thursday, March 2 at Marin Academy, when the Highlander boys’ soccer team, seeded no. 4, lost 4-0 to the eventual CIF Division 4 NorCal champions, the No. 1 seed, in the Regional Semifinals. To get there, PHS defeated No. 5 Kimball 2-0 at Witter Field on Tuesday, February 28 with goals by William Daniel and Enzo Bernales. For Marin Academy, it was a bit of a surprise to see them put in Div. 4 after losing the Division 3 final in penalty kicks with No. 2 Terra Linda. The Wildcats have now won three CIF NorCal titles, winning the D2 crown in 2022 and 2019. All four goals on March 2 were scored by League MVP Malcolm Zalayet, a junior. “It was tough to take. We were in it for the first 20 and gave them some problems, but Marin Academy’s class showed, said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. “They were able to move it around and find some gaps, and that’s what a proper team does. It was great exposure for our guys to play a top team and see what I aspire our program to be.” Piedmont’s Regional Semifinals appearance was the furthest Piedmont High has gone in post-season playoffs since the new CIF tournament started in 2018. PHS lost in 2022 to No. 3 Sacred Heart. “It’s hard to put into words just how great this season was,” said captain T.J. O’Neil, a senior.” It was such a great group of players who came together as a team. At Junior striker Aiden Woolwine will lead a potentially potent attack next year. Sophomore Enzo Bernales scored a penalty kick against No. 5 Kimball. He finished his season as Piedmont’s leading scorer. the beginning of the season, we set our long-term goal to get to the NCS Final. We have full confidence in our coaching and our players. Being able to win NCS and take it a few steps farther makes me so proud.” “This season was about building off of what we did last year. To win it in 2022 and then come back to win it again was such an amazing feeling,” added junior striker Aiden Woolwine. The loss closes Piedmont’s season with a 13-6-5 (W-T-L) record and a second consecutive North Coast Section championship after upsetting No. 1 Cardinal Newman, and then No. 5 Healdsburg and No. 2 University on their way to the banner with the No. 8 seed. Looking ahead to next year, Piedmont will have to replace 14 seniors on this year’s roster and will be in their second season in the Foothill (upper) division of the Western Alameda County Conferencel. But returning to the roster will be routine starters like Woolwine, Bernales, and Sam Shelby, while Gianluca Bini, Bosco Lorin, Rylan Nelson, and Riley Stratman all progressively earned larger roles. “I’m excited to play alongside those guys. They are going to be scary, especially with our other seniors coming up. We’ve built a strong connection and it’s just continuing to build and connecting to find that fluidity on the field,” said Woolwine.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer teams’ magic season came to a close last Tuesday, February 28 a in a 2-1 overtime loss to No. 1 Sequoia HS in Redwood City in the first round of the Division 3 CIF NorCal Regional Tournament. The match closes PHS’ year with a 13-1-6 (W-T-L) overall record and its first Division 4 North Coast Section title in 20 years. “It was a really special team. I told the girls this was the best team I’ve ever had. Anything after winning the NCS title is a bonus, I’m so proud of this team,” said PHS coach Dan Chubbock. Seqouia struck first in the 13th minute when Nina Mills jumped on a ball in a passing lane to play a ball over Piedmont’s back line. Emily Fitzgerald (right) scored Piedmont’s only goal against Sequoia. Audrey Lam (left) finishes her distinguished career at Piedmont as the 2023 WACC Player of the Year. Photos by Todd Marshburn Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team ended its season with an overtime loss to No. 1 Sequoia in the first round of the D3 CIF NorCal tournament. On the volley, Mills sent a shot over goalkeeper Morgan Hunt. But with just eight minutes left in the game, Emily Fitzgerald continued her playoff form and scored on a beautiful right-footed rocket over the keeper’s head. In the buildup, Audrey Lam used a slide tackle to push the ball to Hailey Marshburn, the player who scored the game-winner in the NCS Final. Marshburn sent a long ball from deep in Piedmont’s defensive third to freshman Miranda Liu. Liu, using her speed, accelerated in front of the defender and sent a back heel pass to Fitzgerald while in between three defenders. Fitzgerald pounced on the ball, taking a touch with her left foot and followed through with the right, flying through the keeper’s hands and into net for a 1-1 tie. Piedmont couldn’t find any looks at net in regulation time, but drew several corners and free kicks. In overtime, Marshburn had a shot on target to the bottom left corner five minutes into the first overtime period, forcing a diving save. Piedmont looked like the better side in overtime, pressing forward and winning possession in good areas. However, Sequoia scored on a swift counterattack for the game-winner with three minutes left. Fitzgerald departs as one of Piedmont’s most successful NCS postseason players in school history with 10 goals in nine North Coast Section appearances, “She’s always been one of those players who turns up for big games. She loves to compete and play against the best teams,” said Chubbock. Lam was also a two-year starter for Piedmont and joined the program after spending time with the U.S. Women’s Youth National Team. She is one of the most accomplished soccer players in PHS history and her impact as a maestro in the midfield was easy to see—bringing a flair on the field rarely seen at the high school level. “It was a joy to watch Audrey. She’s already such an accomplished player and has played at really high levels, but you can tell how much winning NCS meant to her. She was ecstatic alongside her teammates,” said Chubbock. When looking ahead to next season, Piedmont will have to replace 10 seniors, but will return some key starters including Liu at striker, midfielders Arden Sorensen-Wald and Louisa Symkowick, and defender Elle Ruegg.

articles.text: Piedmont’s track and field team is off and running in its first year under new head coach Pouyan Assadi. They began their season on Saturday, February 18 at the Grizzly Invitational at San Lorenzo HS, then competing in the Sunset Invitational at Kezar Stadium in San Francisco on Friday, March 3. The final event was the Dan Gabor Invitational at Amador Valley HS in Pleasanton the following day, March 4. “The sprinters, jumpers, and throwers seemed to pick up right where they left off from the 2022 season,” said Assadi. Referring to the Sunset Invitational at Kezar, he said, “It was an impressive outing by a young but confident group under the bright lights at the historic San Francisco venue. The Sunset Invitational has over 500 athletes competing from 30 schools.” Saturday’s event at Amador Valley focused more on distance runners. Returners like senior Christian Taylor finished 2nd of 241 runners in the 800 with a time of 1:59.40. He was also 6th out of nearly 400 runners in the 1600 with a strong early-season time of 4:23.44, a personal record. “A very impressive outing by our distance crew on Saturday night at the Dan Gabor Invitational. Christian Taylor led the way with a silver medal in the 800. And new PRs were made by Christian, Parker Long, Xander Schulte-Sasse, and Alex Aubrecht,” said Assadi. Dan Gabor Invitational results Aside from Taylor’s impressive display at the invitational, Xander Schulte-Sasse placed 8th of 241 in the 3200 with a time of 9:40.02 for a personal record of seven seconds. Also in the 3200 was Parker Long in 9th, 9:45.89. Julien Lee was 27th in 10:29.4, Alex Ware was 60th in 11:13.03, Thomas Worthington placed 69th in 11:26.6, Oliver Horsley was 77th in 11:37.4, Henry Horsley was 79th, 11:41.6. In the 1600, Schulte-Sasse was 17th of 395 in 4:31.50 while Lee was 59th in 4:44.53. In the 800, Alex Aubrecht finished 45th of 241 in 2:14.38. Jamie Schwarz led the girls’ team, She placed 12th in a field of 136 runners in the 800, clocking a 2:28.83. Schwarz also placed 32nd of 173 milers in the 1600 in 5:44.88. Freshman Skylar Best was 48th in 5:53.16. Sunset Invitational results Sam Shelby made his varsity track debut, placing 12th in the 100 meter dash with a time of 11.82 seconds. Marcis Filho was Photos by Steve Zirkelbach Christian Taylor is a senior leader on the track team. Parker Long is another senior runner on the track team. 17th in 11.90, and Isaac Saxonov was 35th in 12.36 seconds. Tommy Ashton placed 5th of in the shot put with a distance of 37.5 feet, and Charles White was 4th with a heave if 106.9 feet In the discus. Sprinter Leah Bell was 3rd in a field of 90 speedsters in the 100 meters in 13.53 seconds. Teresa McKay, a Piedmont Junior Olympic fencer, placed 39th in 14.93. Ella Yasar was 6th in the 200 meters in 28.46 seconds, and was 7th in the 400 with a time of 1:06.83. NEXT UP Piedmont hosts Hayward, San Leandro, and San Lorenzo for a WACC Center Meet at Witter Field tomorrow, March 9, at 3:30 p.m. Breah Bell is a sprinter competing in the 100-meter dash.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont’s softball team is 2-0-1 and has a potent batting order this season. Piedmont’s softball team has started its season with a 2-0-1 record after bashing St. Mary’s 17-3 on February 17 at Witter Field, blasting NCS rival Miramonte 18-2 on Thursday, March 2 in Orinda, and tying Moreau Catholic 10-10 at Witter Field on Friday, March 3. The strength of Piedmont’s batting order will the hallmark of this year’s team with returning starters Leah Bell, Morgan Hunt, Angelina Wu, Miya Fujimoto, Gretchen Gerhardy, Hailey Ronen, and Ginger Gardner. “We have a roster of 14, but have a core group who can push us forward. We’ll have to lean heavily on seniors like Leah, Morgan, Gretchen, Hailey, and Ginger,” said coach Gene Denard following the game with Moreau. However, Piedmont will be searching for an answer on its pitching rotation following the graduation of Izzy Epstein. Also, last year’s No. 2 pitcher, Annabelle Castronovo, is no longer on the team. Through three games, Denard has used Fujimoto, Wu, and Gardner as his pitching rotation, all infielders. “Miya is our No. 1 but I don’t like using her on the mound because it weakens our defense. With Ginger pitching, we’re probably at our strongest point,” said Denard. The Highlanders once again, been bumped up to the WACC Foothill (upper) Division after winning last year’s Shoreline Division. Denard, speaking frankly with the Post, says the league never considered PHS’ roster of just 14 routine players and no junior varsity team. He said the call to be moved up was pushed by San Leandro coach Kelsi Thomas. “I thought it was a horrible ordeal. We had two COVID seasons [2020-2021], and lost our star pitcher [Izzy Epstein] and catcher [Chiara Lundin]. We’ve Leah Bell has hit two home runs in her first three games of the softball season. had one successful season in three years and we got moved up,” said Denard. Their move to the Foothill Division with teams like Alameda, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, and Arroyo makes the competition more difficult. All schools have larger enrollments than Piedmont. 10-10 tie with Moreau Piedmont led 7-0 until Moreau scored seven runs in the top of the third and went ahead 8-7 in the top of the fourth. The Highlanders scored once in the bottom of the fifth but the Mariners scored two more in the top of the seventh to go ahead 10-8 with the sun setting on the Witter Softball Diamond. In the bottom of the seventh, Moreau struck out the first two batters, but Wu followed up with a single to center field. Bell then drew a four-pitch walk. Gerhardy then hit a fly ball to right field, but it was dropped by the outfielder and badly overthrown into the infield, allowing Wu and Bell to come all the way around to score—tying it at 10-10 with Gerhardy sliding in to third base. Hunt and Ronen then drew walks to load the bases, but with the sun completely set into dusk, the game was called with Gardner stepping to the plate. Angelina Wu, an infielder, also will see some time on the mound as a pitcher.

articles.text: It’s been a strong start to the season for Piedmont’s baseball team, winning their first three games of the season by outscoring their opponents 40-18. They opened the season beating Lick-Wilmerding 14-6 on February 25 in San Francisco, won 12-8 over Justin-Siena on Thursday, March 2 in Napa, and won their home opener 14-4 over Albany the following day on Friday, March 3. Evident by the scoring output through the first three games, the team is going to be carried by its cast of returning players, Michael Aikawa, Ryan McConathy, Markos Lagios, Peter Krumins, Dimitri Papahadjopoulos, and Liam Campbell. “We definitely have some returning talent and some players who are playing varsity baseball for the first time. We have a blend of an influx of talent and players who have been here for four years like Mike [Aikawa],” said coach Eric Olsen. This is all despite having just 11 varsity members on the roster, requiring Olsen to frequently pull from his junior varsity roster. However, the lack of numbers means Olsen will mix-and-match the pitching rotation. Six players have appeared on the mound with junior Seve Sanchez leading the way with seven innings pitched and four strikeouts. Piedmont was bumped up to the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division after winning last year’s Shoreline title over Encinal. The Highlanders will face larger enrollment schools like Arroyo, Alameda, Berkeley, Bishop O’Dowd, Castro Valley, and San Leandro. “As a coach, having a smaller roster is great because you can give individual attention and really coach each kid. Obviously we wish we’d have a little more depth, especially in the pitching department, but the kids are doing great and are playing roles they weren’t accustomed to,” said Olsen. A hallmark of an Olsen led ball club is patience in the batters’ box and an ability to get players on the base. Piedmont drew 11 walks on Lick-Wilmerding, 10 on Justin-Siena, and 13 against Albany. “Having a smaller team, our chemistry is going to just be better. Our defense is stellar, we don’t make many errors and just play together… We always want a better walk-to-strikeout ratio. Being patient is very important, especially when going up against pitchers who may not have the best arm. We just have to be on our toes and be ready,” said Aikawa. McConathy, a senior, is eager to get back on the field after undergoing elbow surgery. “Going so long without playing, I missed this feeling so much. Now that I’m hitting bombs, it feels like I’ve never left. I’m just grateful to be finally be healthy and playing baseball with my friends,” said McConathy. 14-4 over Albany Piedmont opened the game in a 4-0 deficit after the first 2.5 innings until a bottom of the third inning rally by PHS. Liam Campbell started things with a single, while Lagios reached first on an error with one out. Then Krumins hit a fly ball off of the leftfield wall to bring in Campbell. With the bases loaded, McConathy hit a single to left field to bring in Krumins and Lagios, 4-3. Papahadjopoulos then hit a double to tie it at 4-4, followed by PHS scoring five straight runs by drawing walks to go ahead 9-4. Batting around, McConathy then smacked a double off of the left field wall to make it 11-4. Piedmont added three more in the bottom of the fifth to activate the 10-run rule. They drew four straight walks to start the inning, bringing in Lagios, then Papahadjopoulos singled in Krumins. Junior John Olsen, coach Olsen’s nephew, hit a sacrifice fly to score Ryan McConathy has six RBIs through the first three games. Seve Sanchez on the mound pitched seven innings in his last two starts. Staff Photos Michael Aikawa, a four-year starter, hit a home run in the season-opening win over LickWilmerding. Will Parker, 14-4. Final stats: McConathy went 2-for-2 with a double, five RBIs, and one run scored. Papahadjopoulos went 2-for-3 with two RBIs and one run. Lagios had three runs scored and an RBI. Sanchez was the winning pitcher with four innings of work. 12-8 win over Justin Siena Piedmont opened with a 6-0 lead after the first two innings, but the Braves powered back to a 6-4 deficit in the bottom of the third. The two teams traded runs in the fourth inning, 7-5, then PHS scored twice in the top of the sixth, 9-5, leading off with a homer by Aikawa. Justin Siena then narrowed the gap to 9-8 in the bottom of the sixth, but PHS scored three in the top of the seventh thanks to a three-run home run by Krumins. Final stats: Lagios went 3-for-3 with a double, two RBIs, two walks, and four runs. Krumins was 3-for-5 with a homer and five RBIs. Aikawa went 1-for-3 with a homer, one RBI, three runs scored, and two walks. Krumins was the winning pitcher with three innings, one strikeout, and five hits allowed. Lagios pitched two innings, Aikawa three two innings and struck out two. 14-6 victory over LickWilmerding Piedmont trailed 5-2 going into the top of the fourth and jumped ahead with 11 runs, scoring one more in the top of the sixth. Final stats: Lagios was 2-for-4 with a double, triple, three RBIs, two runs scored, and a walk. Krumins was 1-for-4 with one run scored and three RBIs. McConathy was 1-for-3 with a double and two walks. Ellis Moss went 2-for-4 with two runs scored and an RBI. Moss was the winning pitcher with two innings, three strikeouts, and one hit allowed. Sanchez threw three innings and struck out four. Aikawa had an inning pitched and allowed no hits. Tuesday vs. Redwood Christian Piedmont hosted Redwood Christian on Tuesday, March 7. details. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-0) travels to San Leandro today, March 8, for a 3:30 p.m. game with Redwood Christian. They will play Berean Christian in Walnut Creek on Saturday, March 11 at 3:00 p.m.

articles.text: Piedmont’s Jasper Schuetz (middle) won the freshman boys category. The Piedmont Mountain Bike Team raced in La Grange’s Exchequer Mountain Bike Park on Saturday, March 4 on a 5.8- mile course with 700 feet in elevation. Piedmont freshman Jasper Schuetz won his event with a time of 51:30 minutes in a two-lap race in a field of 40. Zoe Wolfers finished the JV girls’ race in 24th of 45. He logged times of 25:19 and 26:10 in his event, beating second-place Salinas rider Alexander Tudor by 1:09. In the varsity boys’ category, PHS senior Andres Roberts placed 15th of 34 with a time of 1:19:34 in a three-lap race, clocking times of 25:51, 26:50, and 26:53. Also in the varsity race, Aleksi Valkonen placed 23rd in 1:24:56. with lap times of 27:40, 28:06, and 29:09. In the junior varsity girls’ two-lap race, senior Zoe Wolfers finished 24th of 45 riders with a time of 1:17:31. Heather Stoneman placed 30th in 1:21:22, and Anne Marie Gibbs had a time of 1:49:51. Cary Ward finished the sophomore boys’ D1 category in 9th with a time of 1:00:29 in a two lap race, clocking lap-times of 29:41 and 30:48. For the JV boys, Schuyler Sawicki finished 8th of 78 riders with a time of 55:53 in a two-lap race, with times of 27:02 and 28:51. Mark Hsia was 12th in 56:22, Matteo Scanu was 15th in 56:32, and Max Rivera was 19th in 57:22. Freshman Olive Reining finished her event in 1:52:41. but faced difficulties with her shoes and managed to complete the race in her sopping-wet socks.

articles.text: One wouldn’t expect a small town of just over 11,000 to produce a growing group of talent in the sport of fencing. During the week of February 17-20, the Piedmont Fencing Team sent four PHS student-athletes to the 2023 Junior Olympics in Denver, Colorado. The group included freshmen Niko Kalamas and Jonah Kim, and sophomores Oliver Greenebaum and Teresa McKay. It’s one of the most prestigious events for junior fencers. Piedmont Fencing Team coach David Sinkkonen has watched the program build from just six members 10 years ago to nearly 70 in multiple skill levels today, The fencer train in the Piedmont Community Church gym. “Fencing is a very difficult sport; it takes a really long time to build a successful program because it takes a long time for students to develop. Last year, we didn’t have anybody that made it [[to Junior Nationals]. What’s great is that fur of them (Kalamas, Kim, Greenebaum, McKay) all qualified for National Championships in July. These kids have been working hard, and this sport takes a lot of patience,” said Sinkkonen. The re-introduction and resurgence of fencing in Piedmont is quite a surprise to some/ Recently Piedmont’s best known fencer Oliver Greenebaum (left), Niko Kalamas, and Teresa McKay of the Piedmont Fencing Team. was Rafaella Gomes, PHS Class of 2021, who trains at the prestigious Massialas Foundation in San Francisco, and is a member of the Brazilian National Team. “It’s pretty unusual. It’s not a mainstream sport, although there are a lot of people who compete at events like the Junior Olympics. Everyone is probably very aware of the track team, basketball, football, and baseball, but there’s this little fencing program that we’ve built from basically nothing,” said Sinkkonen. In the Junior Olympics in Denver, Kim competed in the Junior Men’s Foil category on February Piedmont Fencing Team coach David Sinkkonen with Oliver Greenebaum, Lorenz Finney, and Niko Kalamas.
articles.title: Piedmont fencing team sends 4 to Junior Olympics

During the week of February 17-20, the Piedmont Fencing Team sent four PHS student-athletes to the 2023 Junior Olympics in Denver, Colorado. articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art (SF MOMA) is currently exhibiting the work of Bay Area-based artist Joan Brown, comprising 80 colorful paintings and sculptures from the celebrated artist. The exhibit ends on Sunday, March 12. Brown (1938-1990) is considered one of San Francisco’s most important local artists. She was once dismissed by critics as ‘unserious,’ but was recognized for her influential artistry after her untimely death in 1990. Works on display include The Dancers in a City #2 and Gordon, Joan and Rufus in Front of S.F. Opera House, which both show how much influence the city of San Francisco had on Brown’s art. Her work was included in SFMOMA’s annual exhibits in both 1957 and 1958. She was the youngest artist exhibited as part of Young America 1960 (Thirty American Painters Under Thirty-Six) at the Whitney Museum of American Art. “We are thrilled to present Joan Brown, a reassessment of the unabashedly personal, defiantly independent and enduringly relevant career of one of San Francisco’s most important local heroes,” said Janet Bishop, Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/exhibition/joan-brown/ to learn more. Museum hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays through Tuesdays and 1 to 8 p.m. on Thursdays. The museum is closed Wednesdays. The Joan Brown exhibition at the San Francisco Museum of Art remains on view through this Sunday, March 12.
articles.title: Joan Brown exhibit at SF MOMA ends on Sunday

articles.text: Photo by Stella Olivier Vocalist S’busiso Shozi in William Kentridge’s Sibyl Cal Performances will present the U.S. premiere of South African visual artist William Kentridge’s newest production, Sibyl, from Friday to Sunday, March 17-19. Kentridge is well-known for his animation artwork and films, as well as design of theatrical productions. His latest opera, Sibyl, is told in two parts and is inspired by the Greek myth of the Cumaean Sibyl, a prophetess of Cumae, a Greek colony located near Naples, Italy. In Greek mythology, a “sibyl” refers to a woman, usually of prodigious age, who is reputed to possess powers of prophecy or divination. The first part of the opera, entitled The Moment Has Gone, will feature the U.S premiere of a film by Kentridge, accompanied by live music, with a piano score by composer and music director Kyle Shepherd and an all-male vocal chorus led by choral composer Nhlanhla Mahlangu. The second part of the opera, Waiting for the Sibyl, features nine vocalists and dancers – as well as Kentridge’s famous medium of animation. Music for Sibyl is composed and conceived by Nhlanhla Mahlangu and Kyle Shepherd. A post-performance discussion with the artists and Cal Performances artistic director Jeremy Geffen will take place on Sunday, March 19. For tickets and times of performances, visit https://calperformances.org/events/2022-23/illuminations-human-and-machine/ william-kentridges-sibyl/.
articles.title: Cal Performances presents the U.S. premiere of William Kentridge’s Sibyl

articles.text: The annual Making History concert by Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir will take place on April 22. It will feature the world premiere of Robin Estrada’s Nag Iibang Hangin (Changing Winds) and the premiere of Artistic Director Eric Tuan’s In the Desert. Featuring premieres of new works, past commissions, and up and coming exciting new voices in the choral landscape, the concert – an annual celebration of new music – features all four of the choirs’ advanced performing ensembles. The world premiere of Berkeley composer Robin Estrada’s Nag Iibang Hangin was commissioned by the choir. It describes the two seasonal winds in the composer’s native Philippines and juxtaposes western composition with traditional Filipino vocal and musical forms and practices. Continuing the choir’s commitment to uplifting women composers and BIPOC voices, the program also includes works by Stacy Garrop, Meredith Monk, Rhiannon Randle, and Eric Tuan’s Taloowa Chipota (Children’s Songs), a two-movement work evoking traditional stomp dancing by Jerod Impichchaachaaha Tate, the Composer-in-Residence of the Chickasaw Nation. The Making History Concert will be performed on Saturday, April 22, at 7:30 p.m. at First Congregational Church of Berkeley, 2330 Durant Avenue, Berkeley. Tickets are $30 for adults and $20 for students and seniors. Purchase tickets at: https://event.auctria.com/6dda65c5-78da-4539-a7fa-cef7f- 903f5ab/ Please note: All tickets will be picked up at will call. There will be NO SALES AT THE DOOR, but the ticketing link will be live until the start of the event. PEBCC requires our patrons to be masked indoors during performances and respectfully requests that, if symptomatic/ ill, patrons forego attending the performance. PEBCC is happy to honor unused tickets as a donation to the Choirs.

articles.text: Roy Eaton Roy Eaton. You probably recognize his name because he is often featured on our local music station. In an atmosphere often overpopulated by negativity, Roy Eaton is a breath of fresh air… An inspiration. Let’s see why. The first time I heard Roy Eaton on the airways, I was somewhat confused by what I heard. The sound quality of the recording told me that it was a modern recording, but the piano playing harkened back more than 100 years. There was a gentle resonance in the touch which reminded me of the great Polish pianist-statesman Paderewski. The phrasing was noble and the rhythm was slightly wayward, but in a way that made perfect sense. His Chopin was classic and his performances of Scott Joplin Rags sounded as if the composer were playing them. I asked myself: “who is this guy?” What I discovered is the essence of this article. Eaton was born in Harlem way back in 1930, the son of Jamaican immigrants. His talent was recognized early and he was playing concerts and winning prizes almost from the beginning. Running parallel to his achievements were the prejudices he suffered as a black man. How he overcame them is an inspiration. I was very interested to see a video interview. One of the things that Roy Eaton said was that black kids need to have good role models in life and also in classical music. Even at his advanced age he continues to go to schools to motivate kids. How about that for an inspiration! In many ways, Roy Eaton reminds me of my high school music teacher, Samuel Rodney Browne (1908-1991). There is a very good interview of Mr. Browne where he tells about overcoming the same prejudices. The coincidences are startling. We are never too old to have good role models – nor too young. Usually we think of a role model as an adult influencing a young person, but sometimes the influence is the other way around. I think of this every time I hear the concerts of the Kensington symphony. The Kensington symphony has Geoffrey Gallegos as its conductor and Music Director. The results are musically gratifying because he is a real maestro. I recognized his talent when he was in the eighth grade. If you haven’t guessed, Geoffrey was a student of mine. A music critic must make every effort to be free from prejudice. Those are my watch words. Generally speaking, I write about
