articles.text: The Piedmont High School shield was designed in 1922. Piedmont is a small town with deep traditions. Here are three traditions that are over 50 years old. One of the long-standing traditions dates to the construction of the first Piedmont High School in 1921. The High School opened with an expected enrollment of 250 students. At the end of the first week, there were 360 students and 400 students by the end of the first semester. These students came from 14 secondary schools. In order to create a cohesive student body, the 1922 Clan-OLog – the year of the school’s first graduation class, tells us that the Rob Roy, as the school’s mascot, began in 1959. He appeared at each football game with the cheerleaders and pom-pom girls. This Scottish theme is still strong in many aspects of the school. The school’s athletic teams are called the Highlanders, sometimes Scots. T he 1924 Clan- O -Log describes the students’ thoughts on naming the first yearbook in 1922. “From the Scotch [sic], we have coined the word Clan-OThe Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling during halftime at a 1961 Piedmont football game. student body officers selected the school colors and the school motto. They also designed the school shield and created the Clan-O-Log that first year. They chose purple and white as the school colors. As noted on the High School’s website, “Royal purple symbolizes regality and suggests to all Piedmont students, the necessity of learning to rule their lives and ambitions by the mastery of their own thoughts and actions. White represents purity and suggests that true PHS students will strive to be pure in thought, speech, and act.” The student body officers then chose the school’s motto, “Achieve the Honorable,” meaning that all students demonstrate academic and personal integrity in their work. Students worked together to design the school shield with classic symbols of a winged sandal (athletic ambitions), torch (scholastic achievement), the helmet of knighthood (bravery, courtesy, honor), Minerva (patron goddess of wisdom) and the open book that shows knowledge is open to those who will learn. These were intended to address all aspects of student life. Log, Clan standing for the students and Log meaning history.” The yearbook was to be a record of all the students. The Piedmont Highlander is the student newspaper. Sweatshirts and T-shirts are printed with “Highlanders.” The Highland Fling Spring Carnival dates to 1922, and the Alpha Clan honor society began in 1924. The school’s fight song was adapted from “On, Wisconsin” with Scottish references: A Scottish Theme The students also chose a Scottish theme. Piedmont is a highland, like Scotland. The Scots were never conquered, hence the Piedmont spirit to never give up. We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Bold and bonny bunch! We eat thistles for our breakfast, Granite for our lunch, Munch, munch, munch … We are Piedmont’s fighting Scotsmen, Come from Highlands brown … So fight, Piedmont, Fight till every foe is down! In the 1960s, the Scottish Highland theme was at the High School football games. Rob Roy became the official school mascot in 1959 and was on the field during all the games. At halftime, the Kiltie Band played, and the Highland Lassies danced the Highland Fling. Today, the words to the fight song have been changed from “fighting Clansmen” to “fighting Scotsmen.” The yearbook name was changed from “Clan-O-Log” to “The Pride” in May 2018. Bird Calling Contest The Leonard J. Waxdeck Bird Calling Contest has been a beloved tradition since 1963 when a student approached biology teacher Leonard Waxdeck and asked, “Can we do something to liven things up around here?” Waxdeck gave the students an assignment to select a bird, give a report on that bird and give its authentic bird call. The raucous bird calls drew the attention of students in nearby classrooms who came to see what the noise was. What began as an exercise quickly outgrew his classroom and moved to the home economics classroom, a larger space. One year later it was moved to the school auditorium. The contest evolved into a highly competitive contest with elaborate skits and (sometimes) costumes. The top winners were flown to the Johnny Carson Show in Burbank, and later the Late Night Show with David Letterman in New York to perform their bird calls. This television exposure brought international attention to the Bird Calling Contest and to the community of Piedmont. Television performances ended when Letterman retired in 2015. Today, after 55 years, the Bird Calling Contest continues to fill the Alan Harvey Theater at the High School each spring. Fourth of July Parade Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade officially began in 1965 when Recreation Commissioner Dick (Pear) Johnson decided to start a city-wide parade. Years before, his El Cerrito Avenue neighborhood had been celebrating the 4th of July with their own bicycle parade, watermelon eating contest and water balloon toss. Johnson thought it was too quiet in Piedmont in the summer and expanded his neighborhood parade to a city-wide event on Highland Avenue, the main thoroughfare. Over the years the parade has grown to include bands, antique cars, floats, horse patrols, unique groups including the Balloon Platoon of tubby sailors, and the all-important neighborhood entries. The post-parade music program in the park fills the lawn with picnickers, and many residents end their day at block parPiedmont biology teacher Leonard J. Waxdeck arranged each year to have a friend, a commercial artist, create a fanciful, distinctly original poster to promote that year’s Bird Calling Contest.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont students took time to get all gussied up for 2023 Winter Ball on Saturday, February 11, at the cavernous Scottish Rite Center on the shores of Lake Merritt. An estimated 400 students showed up for the fun. Winter Ball is open to all juniors and seniors, but students are allowed to invite one other student from another grade or school. Richmond Country Club catered the event with pasta, steak, chicken and garlic bread “to die for.” Three different dessert cakes were available as well. Table settings included a deck of cards for games of go-fish, poker and blackjack. Students danced with music from a DJ. PHS senior Seb Ford, an intern with the Piedmont Post, took charge of the photo booth, while Piedmont dad Todd Marshburn perused the crowd getting candid photos of students dressed to the nines. Photos by Todd Marshburn Laurel Bentley (left), Soren Dixon, Charlotte Davies, Peter Krumins, Lola Biehn, Matthew Riordan, Kate Meyjes, Elle Ruegg, and Jack Nelson Jonas Kra-Caskey (left), Charles Ethan White, and Andres Roberts pose in the photo booth. Isaac Guan (left), Kevin Blodget, Owen Kelly, Holden Canty-Hilchey, Cole Knapp, Harry Passion, and Aleksi Valkonen Brady Hinsch (left) and James Manguyen sit in barber chairs while Andrew Szerdy declares their haircuts to be perfect. Piedmont Post intern Will Becker takes a break from his newspaper duties to have fun with his classmates. Laurel Langager (left), Cleo Tahawi, Kat Melian, Lindsey Wirgler, Molly Wagner, Rina Higashi, and Lucy Wheeler PUSD’s 2023 Winter Ball was held in the first floor and grand lobby of the Scottish Rite Center.

articles.text: The No. 8 seed Piedmont boys’ soccer team proved that the Division 4 North Coast Section title will belong to someone else this year. The Highlanders pulled off the biggest upset of the soccer playoffs, beating No. 1 ranked Cardinal Newman 1-0 in Santa Rosa on Saturday night, February 18. With a Golden Goal by Miles Corcoran in the 94th minute in the second overtime period, the Highlanders have advanced to the North Coast Section semifinals. “We drew a corner [kick] and were getting ready for penalties [penalty kicks to decide the winner]. We had our mind on that. And then the corner came in and Miles attacked it so well. He rose above everybody, and it was sort of slow motion. It was like he froze in time when he headed it to the top corner,” said an elated Piedmont coach Todd Sullivan. Entering the postseason with just four losses but with a nondescript record at 8-6-4, the Highlanders were given a low ranking (#8 seed) and had only one home playoff game, a 2-0 win over No. 9 St. Helena on February 15. So far, four lower seeded teams have defeated higher ranked opponents, suggesting that the North Coast Section seriously botched this year’s seedings. In other notable upsets, No. 14 Salesian beat No. 3 Roseland 1-0 in the first round, and No. 5 Healdsburg shut out No. 4 St. Photos by Scott Stratman Miles Corcoran (center) lands a perfectly struck header for the gamewinning goal against top-ranked Cardinal Newman. It was mayhem on the field in Santa Rosa after Miles Corcoran (5) scored the only goal of the game to stun No.1 Cardinal Newman.

articles.text: Staff Photos Freshman Miranda Liu scored a hat trick against No. 6 Sonoma Academy. Piedmont’s No. 3 seeded girls’ soccer team has punched its ticket to the Division 4 North Coast Section semifinals and is set to face No. 2 Urban in San Francisco tonight, February 22. The Highlanders have looked strong this postseason, beating No. 14 Sacred Heart 2-0 in the first round on February 15 and handling No. 6 Sonoma Academy 4-1 in the quarterfinals on February 18. PHS senior and UC San Diegobound forward Emily Fitzgerald continued her impressive season, scoring both goals against Sacred Heart and adding one more against Sonoma Academy. Fitzgerald, a four-year starter, has scored eight NCS goals in seven appearances, including four in the 2022 first round against College Prep. “I honestly think I play better against good competition. NCS just brings out the competitive side of everybody and the most competitive side of me,” said Fitzgerald. A multi-goal performance when the playoff lights are bright is proving to be a habit for Piedmont forwards. Freshman Miranda Liu scored a 3-goal hat trick against Sonoma Academy, two of which came in the second half to put the game away. The speedy freshman often uses her pace to stretch defenses. “My sister and parents are here and it was great to score in front of them… I feel like I’m pretty fast and that’s one of the things in my game,” said Liu. The Highlanders will now travel to No. 2 Urban in San Francisco for the NCS Semifinals tonight. With a win, they’ll face No. 1 University or No. 4 Marin Catholic for the NCS championship. 4-1 win vs. No. 6 Sonoma Academy Piedmont’s first goal came in the 19th minute after Ellie DeVan drew a corner. On the ensuing play, Cameron Lorin connected with a perfect cross to Fitzgerald on a well-timed near-post run, finishing with a first-touch shot into the bottom corner. Liu scored her first goal 10 minutes later on a well-timed run to create a 1-on-1 situation. In the buildup, Lorin sent a long ball out of the back to Liu starting her run. The ball was placed well enough to skim just over the leaping defenders’ head and then successfully corralled by Liu. Sonoma Academy got one goal back in the 35th minutes on a counterattack, making it 2-1 at the half. But in the second half, it didn’t take long for Piedmont to extend the lead with Liu’s next goal in the 45th. In the buildup, Audrey Lam sent a pass through the defense to the freshman attacker, Emily Fitzgerald scored twice against Sacred Heart and once against Sonoma Academy. She has scored eight NCS goals in seven appearances.

articles.text: No. 4 seeded Piedmont walked out of its Division 3 North Coast Section quarterfinals game with a 59-38 win over No. 5 Analy of Sebastopol on Friday, February 17. History was made in the game when senior forward A.J. Harris finished with 37 points. It marked 1,552 points in his high school career, and set a school record for Harris passed Sean Rodriguez, PHS Class of 2016, for the all-time lead when he hit the 28-point mark with a 3-pointer with five minutes left in the game. “It’s still surreal. It means a ton to me. There have been a lot of great players to come through Piedmont. Luke Barrett was here tonight. My brother, Luke Harris, was a great player here. The list goes on; JoJo Murphy, Sean Rodriguez, Eric Flato – a lot of people who have gone on to play at higher levels. It’s an honor to be mentioned with them and feels great to cement myself in the Piedmont history books,” said Harris after the game. Harris earning a starting role as a sophomore and had the 2021 season shortened due to COVID. It seemed a fitting way for Harris to end his final game in Binks Rawlings Gym as a Highlander. “The record speaks for itself. He didn’t play varsity as a freshman and got a 16-game season as a sophomore with the pandemic, so half a year. The fact he put up over 1,500 points in two-and-ahalf seasons is mind blowing. He put up 26 points per game this season being face-guarded, boxed in one, double-teamed, and trapped,” said coach Ben Spencer. Harris shot the lights out on Friday night, in the zone with every shot he took. After converting a 3-pointer, Harris was smiling knowing he had set a new school record for most career points. “I felt good in warm-ups In the beginning, I was a little shaky. We held them to 12 points in the first half, so I knew if we kept up our defense, the shots were going to fall,” said Harris. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ volleyball team is getting its spring season underway with a 3-0 season-opening win against Bentley School in Lafayette on Thursday, February 16. The scores were 25-17, 25-8, and 25-22. “Our first non-league game went great,” said Piedmont coach Mariah Cardenas. “The varsity group did fairly well. We lost some players last year, but I have confidence that we will thrive this year.” “We only had one real practice before the game because it’s difficult to get gym time with basketball still going on. We had a rough start, and I had a difficult time with hitting. But then I got my chance to serve and it felt like I had one of my best service games,” said team captain Wilson Wong. This is the fourth year of boys volleyball at Piedmont. The 2020 season was canceled due to COVID. Last spring, the squad made history by qualifying for the North Coast Section playoffs. As the No. 11 seed, they upset No. 6 Analy 3-2 in the first round, then lost 3-1 to No. 3 Archie Williams in the quarterfinals. Piedmont faces two big deparWilson Wong, the team captain, helped reactivate the sport in 2020. Photo by Erin Callaghan Staff photos Shunji Higashi returns as a team leader for the boys’ volleyball team. tures in the middle with the graduation last year of Mason Kimball and Felix Broach. However, they return several key players from last year’s lineup: Wong, Shunji Higashi, John Champion, Kai Lambert, Owen Kelly, Brayden Day, Eric Olaru-Hagen, and James MaNguyen. “We are definitely an undersized group, but you can tell the boys have played awhile together; they trust one another on the court,” said Cardenas. Wong and MaNguyen played at NorCal volleyball team over the summer and qualified for the club’s Junior National squad.

articles.text: Yosemite National Park is currently open for business and one of the highlights is the annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls. The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracting light from Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 through the end of the month, requiring clear skies around sunset in order for it to be seen, It is also dependent upon sufficient amount of water flowing in Horsetail Falls. In order to manage traffic and crowds drawn to the phenomenon, Yosemite National Park is requiring reservations to enter the park for each weekend in February. Park officials are timing the release of reservations for the last two weekends of February at www.Recreation.gov. Current weather forecast shows mostly cloudy skies throughout the end of the month, meaning Firefall seekers should be paying close attention to developments in the weather. Sunday, February 19, may be the best bet, currently the only day with mostly clear forecast. Snow is expected to enter the area on February 22 and stretch into the first week of March. Those interested in lodging at Yosemite may contact www.travelyosemite.com, but availability at the Curry Village and Yosemite Valley Lodge is limited. For Curry Village, there are currently spots available for Friday, February 17, and February 19-25. Yosemite Valley Lodge has limited availability through the end of the month, with some spots on February 17 and some A photo of Lower Yosemite Falls, an added attraction near the Firefall viewing area. Staff Photos Photo courtesy of Travel & Leisure The annual Firefall usually takes place daily from February 10 to the end of the month.
articles.title: It’s Firefall season at Yosemite National Park

pages.text: Wednesday, February 22, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON It’s Firefall season at Yosemite National Park By Jonathan Comeaux Yosemite National Park is currently open for business and one of the highlights is the annual Firefall at Horsetail Falls. The “Firefall” is a natural phenomenon where the setting sun provides refracting light from Horsetail Falls to create a spectacular orange illusion. The event typically occurs between February 10 through the end of the month, requiring clear skies around sunset in order for it to be seen, It is also dependent upon sufficient amount of water flowing in Horsetail Falls. In order to manage traffic and crowds drawn to the phenomenon, Yosemite National Park is requiring reservations to enter the park for each weekend in February. Park officials are timing the release of reservations for the last two weekends of February at www.Recreation.gov. Current weather forecast shows mostly cloudy skies throughout the end of the month, meaning Firefall seekers should be paying close attention to developments in the weather. Sunday, February 19, may be the best bet, currently the only day with mostly clear forecast. Snow is expected to enter the area on February 22 and stretch into the first week of March. Those interested in lodging at Yosemite may contact www.travelyosemite.com, but availability at the Curry Village and Yosemite Valley Lodge is limited. For Curry Village, there are currently spots available for Friday, February 17, and February 19-25. articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players will present a “Cello Extravaganza” concert on Saturday, March 11, in Lafayette in partnership with the Bay Area Music Consortium. The concert is performed by the Sakura Cello Quintet, which includes Stella Cho, Michael Kaufman, Yoshika Masuda, and Peter Myers, and Nathan Chan as guest cellist. The group explores music that spans eight centuries, and takes inspiration from mentor and artist Ralph Kirshbaum, with whom all five musicians studied. The robust program includes Faure’s Cinq Mélodies “de Venise,” Dvořák’s Silent Woods, Falla’s Ritual Fire Dance, Peter Myers’ Sarabande, and Debussy’s The Girl with Flaxen Hair. The concert will take place at the Don Tatzin Community Hall in the Lafayette Library, 3491 Mount Diablo Blvd, in Lafayette. The concert begins at 7:30 p.m., with a pre-concert discussion at 7 p.m. For tickets, visit www.gccpmusic.com/celloextravaganza. The Sakura Cello Quintet will perform in a Gold Coast Players concert in Lafayette on March 11.

articles.text: The Legion of Honor in San Francisco is currently hosting a major art exhibit, Sargent and Spain, showing the influence of Spain on Sargent’s work, The exhibit is on view through May 14 in the only West Coast show. When we encounter the paintings of John Singer Sargent (1856- 1925), we see a degree of freshness and spontaneity that would lead him to be the most celebrated portrait artist of his era. The demand for his portrait work allowed him to travel the world, with stops in Italy, France, and Spain. Each one of these locales would leave its own unique imprint on the artist. The U.S. provided an incredible commission opportunity. In Paris, Sargent’s aesthetic was greatly shaped in the studio of Emile Carolous Duran, and of course, Italy is Italy. Sargent’s time in Spain was equally impactful. His pilgrimages to the Museo del Prado inspired him with the work of the Baroque master Diego Velazquez. He was mesmerized by some of the Islamic architecture in southern Spain. Meanwhile, his experiences with the Spanish culture provided him with endless inspiration. Join art historian Michael Stehr as he celebrates the work of John Singer Sargent with an illustrated lecture designed to prepare the visitor for the exhibition. The art lecture will be on Friday, March 10, at 6:30 p.m. at the Piedmont Center for the Arts, 801 Magnolia Avenue. Tickets are $20 at the door (cash only). Michael Paul Stehr Founder and Principal Artist … at the Legion of Honor … Discover the effect his time in Spain had on John Singer Sargent, the American painter considered the most celebrated portrait artist of his era, while Michael presents an illustrated lecture preparing you to visit this grand and special exhibit in its only West Coast stop on an extended national tour! articles.text: San Francisco Museum of Modern Art’s exhibit of the work of Bay Area figurative artist Joan Brown will remain open to the public through March 12 with 80 colorful paintings and sculptures from the celebrated artist. Brown is considered one of San Francisco’s most important local artists. She was once dismissed by critics as ‘unserious,’ but was recognized for her influential artistry after her untimely death in 1990. Works on display include The Dancers in a City #2 and Gordon, Joan and Rufus in Front of S.F. Opera House, which both show how much influence the city of San Francisco had on Brown’s art. Her work was included in SFMOMA’s annual exhibits in both 1957 and 1958. She was the youngest artist exhibited as part of Young America 1960 (Thirty American Painters Under Thirty-Six) at the Whitney Museum of American Art. “We are thrilled to present Joan Brown, a reassessment of the unabashedly personal, defiantly independent and enduringly relevant career of one of San Francisco’s most important local heroes,” said Janet Bishop, Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. Visit www.sfmoma.org/exhibition/joan-brown/ to learn more. Museum hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays through Tuesdays and 1 to 8 p.m. on Thursdays. The museum is closed Wednesdays. The Joan Brown exhibit at the SF Museum of Modern Art remains on view through March 12.
articles.title: Joan Brown exhibit on view at SFMOMA

articles.text: Review by Paul Hertelendy Was Béla Bartók his own worst enemy? He composed his fiendishly difficult Piano Concerto No. 2, in which the world-premiere piano soloist was to be Béla Bartók himself. The net result established him not only as prime modernist/technician/theoretician, ahead of his time composing thus in 1930-31, but also as a paragon super keyboard soloist. February 17-19 was a Béla Bartók weekend with the S.F. Symphony in action under EsaPekka Salonen. One block away at Herbst Theatre his chamber music was performed as well. I think the perspiration on the pianist’s forehead carried over to the patrons watching Pierre-Laurent Aimard working fingers to the bone as he read the concerto score and thundered out those harmonies and octaves by the – yes, score. Or, more accurately, by the thousands. Aimard proved to be the right monsieur-professeur for the Herculean task in this sonic tornado of severity. Among other things, composer Bartók was a master at puzzles and palindromes, constructing a symmetric pyramid shape to major sections, allegro-adagio-presto-adagio-allegro. The composer clearly marched to his own drummer, shocking in his audacity and cheeky, unsettling modernism. The orchestra was in the groove February 18, carrying off the adagio even when Esa-Pekka dropped his baton to his side and watched admiringly. This was his production, since the performance was being recorded via a dozen-plus microphones featuring his music, his musicians, his soloist. articles.text: Pianist Yuja Wang will be the guest soloist with San Francisco Symphony in performances of Sergei Rachmaninoff’s Third Piano Concerto Wednesday and Thursday, March 1 and 2. Wang, a Chinese-born classical pianist from Beijing, studied at the Central Conservatory of Music in Beijing and the Curtis Institute of Music in Philadelphia. Wang has performed with orchestras throughout the world, including the Berlin Philharmonic, Oslo Philharmonic, and Toronto Symphony Orchestra. She toured Asia with the San Francisco Symphony and conductor Michael Tilson Thomas in November 2012. The program also includes two contemporary pieces, Bay Area composer Gabriella Smith’s Tumblebird Contrails, an ode to Point Reyes, and Music Director Esa-Pekka Salonen’s tone poem Nyx, which draws from symbols in Greek mythology. articles.text: San Francisco Ballet’s production of Giselle opens this week on Friday, February 24, at the War Memorial Opera House. Performances continue through March 5. Helgi Tomasson’s Giselle is part of the company’s 2023 Repertory Season. Costume and lighting design is by Danish artist Mikael Melbye. Set to a score by Adolphe Adams, the ballet tells the story of a young peasant girl, Giselle, who falls madly in love with nobleman Albrecht. When his true identity is revealed by his rival Hilarion, Giselle goes mad and dies of heartbreak. The two-act ballet is set in Rhineland during the Middle Ages. It is widely hailed as one of the greatest romantic ballets of all time. Giselle premiered at Paris Opera Ballet in 1841. San Francisco Ballet first presented Giselle in 1947, and it was last performed by the company in 2015. “The whole Act II is a work of art like no other – the spirituality of it,” said SF Ballet Artistic Director Tamara Rojo. “Very rarely, as a human body made of flesh, is a performer asked to inhabit the uninhabitable.” To view showtimes and purchase tickets, visit www.sfballet. org/discover/backstage/the-storyof-giselle/. San Francisco Ballet in Tomasson’s Giselle Photo by Erik Tomasson

articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s production of The Headlands is currently being performed at the Toni Rembe Theatre in downtown San Francisco through March 5. The Headlands is Obie Award-winning playwright Christopher Chen’s newest play, described as “a complicated love letter” to San Francisco. The play tells the story of true crime fan Henry Wong, whose father’s unexplained death is the ultimate cold case. Protagonist Wong digs into the San Francisco police department evidence, but he’s haunted by the past of his own family history and upbringing. “I am thrilled beyond measure to be bringing The Headlands to A.C.T., and to be working with Pam MacKinnon to bring it to life. The Headlands is my love letter to San Francisco, the city I spent my entire life in – from birth up to right now. To share this play with my hometown – a place I feel so deeply in my bones – will be one of the most personally meaningful moments of my career,” said Chen. To purchase tickets and for more information, visit www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/the-headlands/. Protagonist Wong digs into the San Francisco police department evidence, but he’s haunted by the past of his own family history and upbringing. “I am thrilled beyond measure to be bringing The Headlands to A.C.T., and to be working with Pam MacKinnon to bring it to life. The Headlands is my love letter to San Francisco, the city I spent my entire life in – from birth up to right now. To share this play with my hometown – a place I feel so deeply in my bones – will be one of the most personally meaningful moments of my career,” said Chen. To purchase tickets and for more information, visit www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/the-headlands/. pages.text: Wednesday, February 22, 2023 19 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Great Cesare By Joseph Gold A few years ago, I was talking to a couple of friends about the news. Maybe you remember Dave McElhatton of KPIX channel 5 and Al Hart of CBS radio. They said that the public loves bad news. I didn’t buy it then and I don’t buy it now. Looking back on history, lots of kids wanted to be President of the United States. Italian kids wanted to be Joe DiMaggio. Lots of black kids aspired to be another Joe Louis, or Marian Anderson. Kids set their sights high. Those have always been my thoughts. Any kid named Caesar had his work cut out for him. And that’s our story for today. Back in 1926, our Caesar was born to Italian parents in North Beach. Being Italian, he spelled his name Cesare, but Americans called him Caesar. At the ripe old age of seven years, he got his first paying concert engagement, his debut as a singer. It was all uphill from there, and that’s a good thing. Cesare had a good local reputation and began to sing with the San Francisco Opera Company. As a very friendly guy, he became acquainted with the famous singers Jussi Bjorling and Mario del Monaco. But it was the great American tenor Jan Peerce, who gave all of them the best advice he ever received: “Get a good education and take it from there.” That sounded like good advice, and he took it. First, came a stint as a paratrooper in World War II. Along the way he attended Stanford and UC Berkeley… and continued his singing. Jan Peerce continued to mentor him. Cesare could have continued to sing with the San Francisco Opera or the Met in New York, but he decided to pursue a career in Europe. That turned out to be a very intelligent decision. His very active career included singing in Munich, Frankfurt, Nürnberg, and Berlin. In addition, he did individual concerts throughout Europe. It helped that he was conversant in five languages and was able to sing the grand operas of Wagner and Verdi, as well as numerous operettas in German and English. Concert and television appearances and teaching were also part of his résumé. He was so busy in Lyric tenor Cesare Curzi was originally from San Francisco’s North Beach. Europe that he didn’t have time to sing at the Met. Can you imagine singing 100-150 concerts a year? I got to know Cesare after he had formally “retired” and returned to California. Even in his later years he had a commanding presence, and a voice that had no limits. He bore a striking resemblance to the famous Italian tenor Giacomo Lauri-Volpi. His voice was a lyric-spinto tenor, notable for its evenness, clear diction and brilliant virtuosity. People like Cesare are inspirations to us. The word indomitable comes to mind. He broke his neck not long ago. For anyone else that would have been a death sentence…but not for Cesare. He was giving voice lessons the day before, and died on February 10, 2023. Cesare Curzi reveled in the joy of making music and living life to its fullest. His rendition of La Danza says everything. articles.text: Judi Dench as Queen Victoria and Ali Fazal as Abdul Karim in Victoria & Abdul My first impression of Victoria & Abdul was of a film that seemed shallow, with very little going on other than the telling of a story about an English monarch who for some 50 years exercised unequivocal power as the titular head of Britain’s vast empire and her jarring relationship with an Indian man. Queen Victoria ruled supreme for over half a century, her colonial reach including India. Two men, Abdul (Ali Fazal) and Mohammed (Adzel Akhtar), are chosen to journey to England to present to her majesty a commemorative coin from her Indian subjects as part of her golden jubilee. The year is 1887. Victoria (Judi Dench) is now an elderly woman grown weary with life and feeling a sense of isolation after the death of her much loved husband, Albert, and two of her nine children. And so, the two Indians arrive and are immediately schooled by the palace staff in the proper way to approach the queen with their coin. They’re told to avoid eye contact no matter the circumstances. Abdul ignores his instructions and it is when he gazes at Victoria and she at him that there is a connection, one that is unexpected and one that surprises all in the royal household. Suddenly, the queen is rejuvenated, her interest in life renewed. She soon wishes only to bask in the company of Abdul. She wants to know all about his language, his culture and his family. And she wishes to learn Urdu. As well, Abdul is transformed from being a mere clerk in India to Victoria’s “Munshi,” meaning teacher and guide, a designation that is unsettling not only to the royal household, but most especially to her son, Bertie (Eddie Izzard), the Prince of Wales and heir to the thrown. Undaunted, Victoria perseveres. When thinking about the narrative, it gradually becomes clear that director Stephen Frears was not simply making a light comedy about the silly reactions by family and staff to the queen’s attachment to this strange man who is, from the point of view of her family, now fastened to the royal ship of state like a barnacle. But there is something more in play in this film. The film is actually a character study of a woman who is not only profoundly lonely, but also free of the entrenched, colonial attitudes of all those who comprise the royal household, to include England’s Prime Minister, Lord Salisbury (Michael Gabon). As a group, led by Bertie, they rebel, their hostility toward both Abdul and Mohammed palpable. They make no effort to know the two men; rather, they reject both outright based on prejudices rooted in the colonial posture of the Brits throughout their empire. Generally, their subjects, so to speak, were brown and were judged as inferior solely because of the color of their skin. Victoria harbored no such assumptions and saw in Abdul another individual who, while different in background and customs and color, was at the very least her equal. When Bertie confronts his mother, he insists that Abdul is nothing more than an opportunist. The queen, taking offense, responds, asking, “How is that any different from the rest of you?” Bertie and household are blind to their own prejudices, hence this becomes a film about racism, a wounding response to a man who could have enriched all of their lives but is instead viewed as a poseur, someone to be discarded. What Frears has done is create a movie that is disguised as a quirky, situational comedy but that is so much more. While the film is a wonderful vehicle for the talent of Judi Dench, who in every way inhabits Victoria, it also asks the audience to look just a bit further for the deeper intent of Frears. Victoria & Abdul. Directed by Stephen Frears, Starring Judi Dench, Michael Gabon, Ali Fazal. 1 hr., 52 min. Rated PG-13. Streaming on Prime/VUDU/Netflix/Apple tv.
articles.title: Victoria & Abdul reprises Victorian England

articles.text: Till opens in Chicago, the year is 1955, and we’re introduced to cheeky 14-year-old Emmett Till (Jaylyn Hall) who is preparing to spend the summer visiting his cousins and his uncle Moses (John Douglas Thompson) for the first time, Moses is a sharecropper and they live in the deep South in the town of Money, Mississippi. Having never been out of Chicago, he is encouraged to make the trip by his grandmother, Alma (Whoopie Goldberg), who thinks it’s time he met his extended family. His single mother, Mamie (Danielle Deadwyler), is not so sure and she tells Emmett that when it comes to being among white people the rules for black people are different and he must “make himself small.” He hears the words but doesn’t understand the message. For reasons unexplained Mamie doesn’t sit her much loved son down and conveys to him the seriousness of what she is saying. Mississippi is not Chicago in ways that Emmett cannot begin to comprehend. It is a state where the Ku Klux Klan is active and part of the culture. And so, Emmett boards the train and for the last time waves goodbye to his mother and grandmother, having no idea, in all his innocence, where he is headed. He will be a stranger in a strange land. It is impossible not to anticipate with a sense of dread what awaits him. On a sunny afternoon his cousins and uncle stop at a mercantile store. Emmett goes inside to buy some candy and without thinking is overly friendly with the cashier, a white woman, Carolyn Bryant (Haley Bennett). Taken by her good looks, he whistles at her as his cousins look on in horror for they, unlike Emmett, realize what he has done, and in that moment the white supremacy of the South, that become evident. Emmett is kidnapped, tortured, and lynched. This is done with a sense of impunity that is unimaginable. His body is found later, floating in the Talahatchie River, beaten and bloated. When Mamie and Alma learn that Emmett has been killed their grief is beyond comprehension, mixed with disbelief and a consuming rage. When she finally manages to get Emmett’s barely recognizable body returned to her she makes a fateful, shocking decision that his funeral casket will be open so all who pass by will be forced to view his unreconstructed remains. His horrible visage will soon become a Black media sensation. When two men are charged (the brother-in-law and husband of Carolyn) with Emmett’s murder, Mamie, against all advice, journeys to Money where she takes the witness stand and gives dramatic testimony to an allwhite male jury. When asked if she is going to stay in town to await the verdict, Mamie bitterly says no, she knows what the outcome will be. And so it is, the men are found not guilty. The performance by Danielle Deadwyler as the grief-stricken mother is Oscar-worthy and yet she was inexplicably passed over. Hopefully, Till will join what has become a pantheon of extraordinary films that touch on America’s history of racism. Till. Directed by Chinonye Chukwu. Starring Danielle Deadwyler, Jaylyn Hall, and Whoopie Goldberg. 2 hrs., 10 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2022. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Till a chilling account of the brief life of Emmett Till

articles.text: Evangeline Lilly and Paul Rudd in Ant-Man and the Wasp Ant-Man (2015) was an unexpected hit and soon joined what is now referred to as the Marvel Cinematic Universe, a galaxy of superhero characters. If you’re a kid, you didn’t have to suspend your disbelief even for a moment, no matter how outlandish the premise for the original Ant-Man movie was. It starred Scott Lang (Paul Rudd) and his mentor, Dr. Hank Pym (Michael Douglas), who design a special suit allowing Scott to shrink himself at will while mind-melding with ants. Having demonstrated its audience chops, meaning the unequivocal appeal to the tween/ teen crowd, a sequel was inevitable, hence Ant-Man and the Wasp. Same crew plus some extras. Only now, Hank’s daughter, Hope (Angeline Lilly), aka the Wasp, takes stage center and demonstrates real athleticism buzzing about, wearing her own designer suit – plus a serious arsenal of stun gun weapons. Using Hank’s device, she, like Scott, can go small and then full-size, as can their cars and buildings. The plot of Wasp is simple. Hank and Hope have picked up a vibe, along with Scott, that Janet (Michelle Pfeiffer), Hank’s wife and Hope’s mom, who 30 years ago vanished into the Quantum Realm (reduction on steroids) is still alive. articles.text: Akeelah and the Bee is a wonderful story that will captivate tweens and newbie teens. Its intention is to empower an 11-year-old African-American girl, Akeelah Anderson (Keke Palmer) who has an extraordinary talent for spelling words. She attends Crenshaw Junior High School (when she’s not skipping class) in Los Angeles, a tough inner-city school, and lives with her mom, Tanya Anderson (Angela Bassett), and her siblings in South L.A. Her father is deceased. When it’s discovered that Akeelah has a remarkable memory and a gift for spelling decidedly esoteric words, she is encouraged by Crenshaw’s principal, Mr. Welch (Curtis Armstrong), to enter the school’s home court spelling bee. Reluctant at first and to her surprise, she wins. And so begins her journey up the spelling bee ladder, moving on to the state competition, followed by the regional bee, which then leads to the National Scripps competition. All of these spelling bees feature abstruse words, each a challenge, and each demonstrating that a stage for a bee can be as exciting as any athletic event. After winning the Crenshaw bee, Principal Welch tells Akeelah that what she needs is a coach. Of course, he has someone in mind. He recruits Professor Joshua Larabee (Laurence Fishburne) who is on leave from a local university. The only glitch is that she will need her mother’s permission. Single mom Tanya (who is often bitter and angry), opposes Akeelah competing. But Dr. Larabee and Principal Welch find a way to convince Tanya that Akeelah’s ability is extraordinary and so they manage to win Tanya over. Before long, as Akeelah practices with Coach Larabee, her siblings volunteer to help, as do some of her classmates. And before long, getting her ready for the national contest becomes a community effort. You can imagine the outcome. In getting to that final moment, when Akeelah nails the last word, it’s impossible not to cheer for this remarkable young girl. Akeelah and the Bee. Written and directed by Doug Atchinson. articles.text: Walking through town, it becomes clear to me that two things stand out as chief characteristics of the architecture in Piedmont. The first is the individuality of the homes — virtually all of the homes are “one-off” designs, built before the advent of seemingly ubiquitous tract homes. Today, even in many expensive new communities, because of economy of scale, developers often build the same home in large groups, robbing the place of the rich character, individuality and texture of the streets and community that we see here. The second observation is the high quality of design and construction throughout the city. Part of the pre-tract home era in which Piedmont was started, also included noted individual architects for each house. We benefited from (and continue to benefit from) the talents and expertise of an era of excellent local architects, including Julia Morgan, Albert Farr, Miller Warneke, and W.H. Weeks. This valuable contribution continues today with top designers and architects such as Mark Becker, Glen Jarvis, and John Malick to name just a few. And with top designers seems to come a higher level of craftsmanship which results in buildings that not only look better, but last for generations. What most people immediately think of when reference is made to architecture, is the exterior appearance of a building. As we will see in this series, although the exterior shape, form or style is only part of what can be considered good architecture, it is of course very important. It is important not only for the owners, but also for the many people experiencing it: guests, neighbors and passers-by. A building and its visual relationship to adjoining buildings and landscapes (its context) necessarily is a part of and helps form the entire community. This is why building height, massing, and lot coverage are so important and written into our zoning codes and design review requirements. There are many other visual considerations that architects work with: the entry, and entry experience; the “fenestration” or window and door sizes, shapes and locations; the materials, the textures of walls, roofs and details, the colors, the relationship to exterior landscape features, not to mention the functional program requirements of the users. How all these elements are proportioned, how they are arranged together, make up the architectural character. Regardless of the style, size, or type of building, successful architectural design needs to form a coherent whole with all parts and pieces of the design in the same family, integrated, to create a visually attractive look and impression. The feeling we get from a building is really what’s important. Often we are able to see and experience a building and like it or not like it, even if we are unable to articulate why. We will be exploring these different elements in future columns. I continue to encourage everyone to walk around, look, reflect, and form opinions of the different principles being discussed. articles.text: It is always a rewarding experience to attend the Zinfandel Advocates and Producers (ZAP) annual trade tasting where the country’s best Zinfandels are showcased. This year the tasting was held in San Francisco at the Palace Hotel on January 27. The large ballroom was packed with producers showing off their new vintages and was a relief to see as attendance the past two years has been low due to the Covid pandemic. Unlike some stuffy, high-end Cabernet tastings, the event has a warm, family-like atmosphere and thankfully Zinfandel prices have not reached to the stratosphere like many Cabernets and Pinot Noirs. For many Americans, Zinfandel really is the perfect wine – quaffable, luscious and affordable. This year there were so many high-quality wines presented it made my job sorting out the best ones very difficult. At the end of the day the following wines really stood out in the crowd: they are 2023’s Best Zinfandels and are worth searching out. new label Once and Future. This is one of California’s oldest vineyards, first planted in 1851, and it contains 16 different varietals of grapes. The wine boasts a dense purple color and has a gorgeous nose of leather, spice box, cherries and blackberries. It is big and full in the mouth but exquisitely balanced. It is built to last for two decades in the cellar. • 2020 Van Ruiten Old Vine Zinfandel, $25 (Great Value) The Van Ruiten Old Vine Zinfandel hails from Lodi and is packed with loads of plum and blueberry, fruit along with pepper, spice, earth and leather. This is a deep, rich full-bodied, spicy zinfandel that is immensely satisfying. A wonderful wine for a very good price. • 2021 Opolo Mountain Zinfandel, $32 Opolo is a perennial ZAP tasting favorite for their huge, opulent, full blown, Zinfandels, and is not for the faint of heart. The 2021 Mountain Zin bursts from the glass with a captivating bouquet in which aromas of roses, cherries and wild berries mingle with nuances of spice and forest floor. Full-bodied, satiny, and expansive on the palate, it’s multi-dimensional, succulent, and juicy, with amazing intensity concluding with a long, perfumed finish. • 2021 Once and Future Zinfandel, Old Hill Ranch, $55 I first encountered this vineyard 20 years ago when Joel Peterson made amazing wine from these grapes for Ravenswood. Now he is doing it again with his At $20, the 2020 St. Amant Old Vine Zinfandel from Mohr-Fry Ranch is the best value of the wines being reviewed. • 2018 Dashe Zinfandel, Todd Brothers Ranch, $44 East Bay favorite Dashe produces and bottles its wines in Alameda. The wine opens with aromas of plum, chocolate, stone fruit preserves, lavender and blackberries. Medium to full-bodied, it explodes with copious juicy fruits and spicy accents, knit by firm tannins and finishing lifted and long.

It will not make old bones but for enjoying over the next 3-4 years it is hard to beat. • 2021 Kokomo Zinfandel, $32 This Dry Creek wine contains a splash of Carignan, Alicante Bouchet and Petite Sirah for added complexity. It has aromas of flowers, sweet briery fruit, raspberries, licorice and cherries that emerge from this attractive, dark ruby-colored, medium bodied Zinfandel. With good sweetness as well as pure fruit, this well-made stylish effort merits attention over the next 3 to 5 years. • 2020 Cast Old Vine Zinfandel, Watson Vineyard, $52 The wines dense purple color is followed by aromas of sweet, jammy black fruits, licorice, pepper, and minerals. Deep, rich and full-bodied, this impressively extracted wine exhibits moderate tannins, adequate acidity, and an impressive finish. Approachable now, it should evolve gracefully for another 7-10 years. • 2018 David Clinton Zinfandel, Teldeschi Vineyard, $34 This Zinfandel from Dry Creek’s Teldeschi Vineyard offers an intensely fragrant nose of spices, pepper, and cassis fruit that shows just how fascinating Zinfandel’s aromatic profile can be. In the mouth, the saturated, dark purple wine exhibits splendid opulence of fruit plenty of grip and structure, wonderful jammy fruit intensity, and a long finish. Would be a great partner to grilled chicken. • 2019 Hendry Primitivo, $40 Napa based Hendry Winery has long been one of the most reliable Zinfandel producers. Here they have used their talents on the charming Primitivo grape a close relative of Zinfandel. The wine reveals ripe raspberry and cherry fruit with notions of spice and leather in its fragrant, expressive bouquet. Medium-bodied, with nicely integrated wood, and no hard edges, it will drink well for 4 to 6 years. • 2020 Peachy Canyon Zinfandel, Nancy’s View, $46 Peachy Canyon is one of the stalwart Zinfandel producers in Paso Robles. The Nancy’s View bottling is a compelling wine graced with expressive dark fruit, flowers, cocoa, and licorice. It shows gorgeous finesse, plenty of mid-palate richness and terrific overall balance. Sweet floral notes and succulent black cherries wrap around the finish. • 2020 Dry Creek Old Vine Zinfandel, $40 Dry Creek is one of California’s pioneers in singling out very old Zinfandel vines for separate bottling and remain one of Sonoma counties flagship wineries. The wine exhibits a sensational nose of blackberry, cherry, and mocha a supple full-bodied, expansive, savory mouthfeel, wonderful purity, and a long satisfying finish The delicious zinfandel can be drunk over the next 7 to 8 years. • 2020 Tres Sabores “Por que no?”, $38 This delightful blend is made up of Zinfandel, Petite Sirah, Cabernet Sauvignon and Petit Verdot. It is a smooth easy to drink red with sweet aromas of cherries, raspberries and currants, with subtle wood and spice in the background. Layered, medium-bodied and savory it shows good structure and balance. Perfect partner to grilled chicken. • 2021 Robert Biale Zinfandel, R.W. Moore Vineyard $65 This wine hails from a historic 100 plus year-old vineyard in the Coombsville district of Napa Valley. The wine opens with scents of tar, earth, and spices over a core of plum, blackberry and currant fruit. The palate is full-bodied, firm and chewy with good concentration and expression and loads of layers finishing long and earthy. • 2019 Saracina Zinfandel Pick and Shovel $32 The town of Hopland in Mendocino County is home to Saracina. The Pick and Shovel Zin is a fleshy, juicy wine loaded with ripe dark red fruit, flower, mint and spices. It possesses excellent mid-palate fleshiness in an open accessible personality best enjoyed over the next few years. • 2020 Wilson Zinfandel Rockpile, Thomas Vineyard, $65 Wilson is a perennial overachiever at the annual ZAP tasing. I have no idea how they do it, but they make an astonishing 35 different Zinfandels and I have never had a bad one. The Thomas Vineyard jumps out of the glass with notes of plum jam, blueberries, chocolate and cherries plus suggestions of baking spices and roses. The full-bodied palate is jam-packed with black and blue fruit, supported by soft tannins and a lively, long finish. • 2020 Perlegos Zinfandel, Stampede Vineyard, $32 This Lodi based wine is powerful and deeply scented showing a touch of oak, luscious berry fruit, glycerin and alcohol, and a generously endowed, velvety textured finish. It is a seductive and opulent, full, broad-shouldered Zinfandel that cries out for grilled burgers. • 2018 Vino Noceto OGP Zinfandel, Grandpere Vineyard, $44 The historic Grandpere Vineyard in the Amador foothills is famous for being one of the oldest in Califonia being planted in the 1860’s. Hard to imagine drinking wine from vines planted during the Civil War! This elegant yet intense wine is medium bodied with cherry and cassis flavors. It’s a balanced, readily drinkable style that carries its alcohol well with ripe velvety tannins and a lingering finish. • 2016 Easton Estate Zinfandel, Shenandoah Valley, $40 Medium garnet-purple colored, the 2016 Easton Zin gives up very spicy notes of pepper, anise, and cloves over prunes and blackberries with hints of currant jelly and soil. It is full, soft and juicy in the mouth with a chewy frame and peppery finish.

Nearly 10 months since the massive fire on April 15, 2019, the cathedral’s condition is fragile amid fierce debate about its survival; its preservation from wind and the natural elements; how to clean and clear toxins; and how best to proceed with rebuilding and restoration. articles.text: The Notre Dame Cathedral, known to hundreds of millions of people worldwide prior to the 2019 fire, was built in the 13th century on the Ile de La Cite, one of the two natural islands on the Seine at the center of Paris. Construction began in 1163 under the tutelage of one of France’s most imminent national heroes, Bishop of Paris Maurice de Sully who is credited with creating a Gothic architectural monument that stunned the medieval world and is universally known and loved. The French king thoroughly approved Sully’s plan for Paris having the grandest cathedral in Europe. Conceived at a height of 107-foot, none was taller; and Sully’s master builders executed methods not yet reliably tested, such as ribbed vault supports and massive flying buttresses. (Saint Denis Basilica with its flying buttresses was constructed about the same time.) The earlier known site for Notre-Dame “to our lady” was built in the late 6th century by the Franks kingdom embracing Christianity. It was destroyed by Vikings in the mid-9th century; and again rebuilt. By the 12th century with Europe in a time of peace and a growing Paris population, the French king and powerful Bishop Sully began to build a Notre Dame cathedral for the ages. Go to Youtube.com to find a new documentary titled “Paris: The Great Saga – How Notre Dame Was Built.”

articles.text: Much loved longtime Piedmont resident Lois Scott Westmont passed away on December 15, 2022, at the age of 91. She had very fond memories of her childhood in Butte, Montana with brothers Don and Owen and parents Clella and Jesse L. Scott. Lois called Piedmont home for over 50 years. She was active in the community including serving on the school board and other civic projects such as support of the Oakland Museum. She and her husband, Dr. Roger Westmont, were long-time patrons of the San Francisco Opera, and her love of music was most dramatically expressed through her exquisite piano playing. Lois is survived by her three children, Karen, Jeff and Clark, and four grandchildren: Taylor, Jessica, Joshua and Zachary. She is also survived by her brother, Don Scott. Lois will be remembered for her kindness, intelligence, her love of elegance, and her quiet stoicism. Friends and family members are invited to a memorial service on Saturday, March 25, at 1 p.m., at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, with a reception to follow. Lois Westmont was a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years.

The fire was in its full fury when help arrived to battle an intense nine-hour blaze. Fortunately, the flames were stopped from reaching the wood timbers in the north belfry, which was heating up. According to the Paris fire service, stopping the fire’s reach to the belfry is believed to have saved the monument from “a chain reaction of collapse.” The destroyed roof also dated to the 12th Century when handcut oak timbers were overlaid with lead panels weighing 210 tons. Atop the roof, the gargantuan 300-foot spire collapsed to the gasps of horror from thousands of Parisians mesmerized by the sight of the out of control blaze. The spire, an architectural feature added 150 years ago, when the monument last had a renovation, was wood coated with 250 tons of protective lead. The cathedral’s rector, Monsignor Patrick Chauvet, said, “A forest of wooden latticework fueled the blaze that consumed the roof whose framework dates back to the 13th century.” About 400 firefighters rushed to save what they could: the towers, façade, the stained glass windows, and walls; and the Paris Fire Brigade tweeted that the cathedral’s stone construction has been “saved.” The “main Fire debris inside Notre Dame Cathedral following the fire. Artifacts saved from the fire are being stored at Paris City Hall or the Louvre for safekeeping. One of the three Rose stained glass windows over the three main portals into the cathedral, which were saved. Notre Dame Cathedral interior prior to the fire in 2019. The precious artifacts Crown of Thorns and the Sacred Blessing were rescued from the fire. works of art” were evacuated while the roof was afire by brigades of officers and ministry personnel. They saved the Crown of Thorns and the Blessed Sacrament; the tunic of sainted Louis IX; and the three 13th Century Rose stained glass windows where the lead rods were melting in the high heat. What couldn’t be removed was affected by varying degrees of smoke, water, and flames, including the very large framed wall paintings, the altar, and two pipe organs, of which the immense one having 8,000 pipes, sustained water damage harming its antiquity possibly beyond reuse. The billowing smoke carried the 460 tons of heavy metal incinerated into lead dust, which settled on every surface. In the months after the fire, concerned parents, laborers, unions, and retailers besieged French officials for rapid response to fears over safety. Lead exposure issues remain, and workers wear protective gear inside the monument. The extraordinary undertaking to rebuild the Gothic masterpiece hasn’t a certain forecast and will likely not be known until June as to whether the cathedral will survive. According to Monsignor Chauvet commenting in December, “there’s a 50% chance the structure might not be saved.” Security guards first heard the fire alarm at 6:20 p.m. and evacuated the cathedral of visitors despite not detecting a fire. A probable unofficial report is that the guard checked the incorrect attic. As early as 6:30 pm smoke was visibly pouring from the roof. At 6:40 pm the alarm sounded again, and this time the guards called in the fire. Firefighters arrived at 6:50 p.m. Invariably, fire officials are being criticized for a response too slow. Early scrutiny of the fire’s origin fell on the firms working to rebuild the spire in a $6.8 million renovation centered in the attic that ignited the roof. One, a major scaffolding company, and the other a specialty firm for art conservancy, provided employees for police questioning. Both firms immediately denied responsibility stating that their workers had left an hour before the fire broke out. Authorities still haven’t yet announced the cause of the fire, although an electrical short circuit is widely considered as the likely cause during the renovation in the attic. It’s rumored that investigators are not admitted to the site due to safety risks. Historical decisions about the cathedral’s severe lack of fire safeguards, like firewalls and sprinkler systems, is viewed as a contributing factor. The Notre Dame cathedral is a developing story. Fire features and updates are available on youtube.com. She and her husband, Dr. Roger Westmont, were long-time patrons of the San Francisco Opera, and her love of music was most dramatically expressed through her exquisite piano playing. Lois is survived by her three children, Karen, Jeff and Clark, and four grandchildren: Taylor, Jessica, Joshua and Zachary. She is also survived by her brother, Don Scott. Lois will be remembered for her kindness, intelligence, her love of elegance, and her quiet stoicism. Friends and family members are invited to a memorial service on Saturday, March 25, at 1 p.m., at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, with a reception to follow. Lois Westmont was a resident of Piedmont for more than 50 years. 4020 Piedmont Avenue Oakland, CA 94611 Hours: Tuesday-Saturday 11am-5:30pm Sunday 1pm-5pm Benefitting Piedmont Education for 40 Years! dressbestforless.org

For example, the city’s definition of a family as applied to zoning use “appears to have potential constraints on persons with disabilities such as requiring families to be ‘traditional,’ ‘sharing household activities’ and requiring a ‘single written lease.’” Furthermore, “while the Element identifies the total number of households overpaying for housing,” reviewers requested that the city quantify “the number of lower-income households overpaying for housing … and add or modify policies and programs as appropriate.” Reviewers asked that the Element demonstrate that the city’s existing and planned water and sewer infrastructure can accommodate the planned housing without any overload. Reviewers also requested that the city clarify, adjust, or shorten the timelines to implement several proposed programs in the Element. If City Council adopts the Element by May 31, the city will have three years to implement a substantial number of these programs. Some of this implementation has already begun. On January 23, the city issued a Request for Proposals for a consulting firm to lead the preparation of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, one of the core parts of the Element. Staff have begun discussions with affordable housing organizations, mainly Bay Area Community Services, about possible future developments. The city also established a new incentive for affordable ADUs, proposed to City Council on November 21, 2022, to make it easier to convert existing spaces into new housing. City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that developing these programs “over the past two years was a tremendous collective effort on the part of Planning staff, consultants, the Housing Advisory Committee, Planning Commission, City Council — and most important, the more than 1,000 community members who participated in this process. While we have some additional technical work to do before final adoption, the state’s letter confirms that we are on the right path and nearing the end of the road.” Planning staff have been in regular communication with state officials since first submitting the city’s Element on November 18, 2022. A list of state requirements and how Piedmont has addressed them is available for download at PiedmontIsHome.org, along with a copy of the official HCD comment letter. Rick Schiller a player and supporter of the sport, said “The Recreation Department has not acted properly. It’s been a bad process, and it’s been a biased process.” Many supporters, like Jeff Trowbridge, appealed for “more recreation for more people in smaller spaces” given that the city’s new Housing Element plans for 587 new units, with likely over 1,000 residents. Many dissenters — particularly those who live near the Beach courts — emphasized the abruptness and bias of the Recreation Department’s pickleball plans. Brando Ibarra voiced his disappointment that “there were no discussions with the residents who live around there. There wasn’t a vote, there was no public hearing for any of us. There was just a letter that was dropped off in my mailbox, giving me six weeks’ notice that everything was going to change.” Mark Katz agreed: “There hasn’t been open discussion, there hasn’t been invitation of views from the tennis players who have … contributed special money to the renovation of the courts.” Katz is one of 238 people who signed a petition opposing the trial. The pickleball trial “is not set up objectively to measure actual demand. The numbers don’t reflect how many [tennis players] wanted to get a reservation for a court but were unable; your system only shows the reservations that are made. And because you’re not asking pickleball people to make reservations, you’re not going to be able to equally judge the demand” for tennis and pickleball reservations,” said Alder Yarrow. Aamir Virani, the Commission member who voted against the trial, said in a closing remark that “Even for the [opposers] of this exclusive trial ... they’re saying it’s both. It’s not really about going back to full-time tennis.” Piedmont’s win over Analy marked their final home game of the season. Wong was a key member of helping the sport return to Binks Rawlings Gym, gathering a team of players from their time together at Piedmont Middle School to restart a high school team the first since 1999. Piedmont looks to continue building on last year’s success. “Coming into the first tryout, it was so great to see where the team is now. We started winning games and I kept the mindset of needing to win at all costs. That’s the mission again. We’re getting way better – but teams in our division are getting better as well,” said Wong. articles.text: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales has confirmed that abatement work has begun on the Piedmont Community Pool project, with demolition to begin next week. The abatement contractor, Anaheim-based AMPCO North, will remove lead and asbestos from the pool site buildings. The Hayward-based firm Forensic Analytical Consulting will manage air monitoring throughout this process, which is expected to last a week. “What we’re dealing with isn’t extensive,” said Gonzales. “It’s very minor and very common for pre-1980 buildings. We’re removing lead paint that’s found in tiles on building walls, and asbestos used for electrical installation and behind the walls of the carriage house — areas the public didn’t go to.” Given that these materials become airborne safety hazards once removal begins, the buildings will be fully contained. “The buildings will all be completely wrapped in plastic,” said Gonzales, “and the contractors will be in full uniform scraping and vacuuming up the materials. It almost looks like they’re walking around in space suits, it’s a pretty interesting process.” The following week starting February 21, demolition will begin. The city issued a demolition permit to the pool contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, at the beginning of the week of January 30. “We’ll start to see buildings coming down,” said Gonzales — “the Carriage House, the existing pool building, the basketball court area. articles.text: On January 17, Piedmont City Council voted to discontinue remote participation for most Commission and all Committee meetings as of March 1. Community members will still be able to comment remotely via Zoom for City Council and Planning Commission meetings. Park Commission and Recreation Commission meetings will continue to be broadcast live on KCOM and streamed on the city website. This format change was prompted by changes to state regulations governing public meetings, which had been relaxed at the beginning of the pandemic to support remote participation for members of legislative bodies. On October 17, 2022, Governor Newsom announced his intention to rescind the COVID- 19 State of Emergency at the end of this month, at which point members of City Councils, Boards, Commissions, and Committees statewide will be required to attend meetings in person, with limited exceptions. At the January 17 council meeting, city staff briefed council members on changes to teleconference regulations and asked the Council to give direction on whether to continue providing remote participation options for community members, After a detailed discussion, the Council chose to continue offering public comment remotely over Zoom for City Council and Planning Commission meetings only, due to low remote participation for other bodies and the strain on staff resources required to support hybrid meetings. Each remote or hybrid meeting requires an additional staff member, working overtime, to manage the logistics and operations of the virtual meeting. More information is available in the staff report for the January 17 City Council meeting, which can be found at bit.ly/3Ywsun8. For questions about remote participation in city government meetings, contact Communications Program Manager Echa Schneider by phone at 420-3039, or by email at eschneider@piedmont.ca.gov. articles.text: Editor: Piedmont Asian American Club and the Lunar New Year planning volunteers were thrilled to welcome over 350 guests and volunteers to the Piedmont Lunar New Year celebration on Friday, February 3, to bring in the Year of the Rabbit. Many families showed up to the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse wearing their traditional cultural outfits. Children gathered joyfully around the craft and food tables. Little hands reached into the air in excitement during the lion dance performance. When we started planning the event, we never imagined the tremendous support we would receive from this community. Cassindy Chao and Catherine Zhang, the co-presidents of PAAC, jumped in to help plan the event. Others pitching in to help included Havens School Principal Anne Dolid, Dr. Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard, School District Director of Diversity, Equity and Inclusion, and Mayor Jen Cavanaugh. This year’s celebration was especially meaningful as many in the Asian American community felt overwhelmed and saddened by the continuous racial incidents and hate crimes that have plagued our community. The affirmation of community support for this event was the most rewarding experience in the planning process. articles.text: Editor: Earlier this year, Piedmont Recreation Department announced a plan to eliminate tennis at the Linda Beach tennis courts, proceeding with a pickleball-only trial in an effort to assess the need for dedicated pickleball courts and a potential goal of establishing it at these courts. However, the current trial design has inherent bias and may be unjustified. Over the past five years, pickleball has gained free access to 4-6 courts seven days per week, the same number as Alameda whose population is eight times that of Piedmont. So how many players on our courts are also tax-paying residents of Piedmont? This question can be answered implementing the same resident-only decal system used for tennis, creating revenue to maintain the courts. With this equitable and accessible solution, PRD can quantify Piedmont residents’ needs, monitor for growth within our community and appropriately allocate resources. The most disconcerting aspect of this trial is the unprecedented way in which it was planned and supported. The pickleball community has targeted these courts due to their upcoming scheduled maintenance, lobbying with PRD for their agenda of dedicated (pickleball-only) space. The fact is that you can play pickleball on a tennis court, but you cannot play tennis on a pickleball court. Every other recreation facility in Piedmont is shared. This is in direct contrast to the extensive outreach that preceded the 2018 introduction of pickleball to Piedmont tennis courts. Since receiving a negative response from tennis players and impacted neighbors, the Recreation Department has developed a dedicated email address to accept commentary. Unfortunately, PRD continues to demonstrate its predetermined position, evident in the biased language in a press release two weeks ago describing the trial as a foregone conclusion. This language has effectively discouraged community input. The Recreation Department and the pickleball community have created a site-specific battleground, and subsequent division within a community where we peacefully shared courts just weeks ago. This result, in which the local community feels marginalized, is in complete opposition of the core mission of a city’s recreation department. All Piedmont residents, please know that your input at the Recreation Commission meeting scheduled for Wednesday, February 15, at 7:30 p.m. at City Hall can impact trial parameters. articles.text: At a Planning Commission meeting on February 13, Senior Planner Pierce MacDonald and Planning Department Director Kevin Jackson provided the Commission with an update on the status of Piedmont’s 6th Cycle Housing Element. The Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the city to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 — a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. This Element drafting cycle is repeated every eight years. On November 15, 2022, said MacDonald, “City Council authorized staff to file the Element with the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD).” This began the 90-day period which HCD has to review the Element and give comments. Jackson confirmed that “the HCD is concluding its review this week.” The state also requires, through the California Environmental Quality Act, that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. On December 9, 2022, the city published an Initial Study-Negative Declaration determining that the Housing Element would not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. On January 12 the Planning Commission recommended during a public hearing that City Council adopt the Element. On January 17 the council unanimously voted to issue a Request for Proposals (RFP) to seek a consultant for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The Plan, which is a major part of the Element, aims to improve existing facilities and incorporate 132 units of housing on 18 acres of city-owned land on both sides of Moraga Canyon, along Moraga Avenue; 60 units of this housing would be available to lower-income households. The land affected by the Moraga Canyon Plan includes Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. MacDonald said that the RFP, which outlines the requirements for a consultant’s analysis of this plan, was issued on January 23. On February 8, “city staff held a pre-bid conference call for prospective proposers. Approximately 11 firms participated in the conference call.” Throughout the process of drafting the Specific Plan and the Housing Element, said Jackson, “the city’s hosted dozens of public engagement events, workshops, surveys, online tools, open houses and town halls, and over 1000 Piedmonters participated in the planning process. We received over 550 comments from residents, school district and city employees, property owners, business leaders, religious leaders and other members of the community. I can’t think of any other city that has been able to engage this a large percentage of its population around the topic of housing.” He said that the comments the city expects to receive from HCD “will probably be mostly technical comments that we can solve fairly quickly,” given that city staff have already met several times with HCD staff, even giving the state reviewer a tour — which Jackson led — of Piedmont Housing Element sites on January 13. After the city does receive comments this week and amend the Element to comply with them, he expects to bring the Housing Element to City Council for adoption in late February or March. “I just want to say that I’m appreciative of the community’s response to the challenges of planning for 587 new housing units,” said Jackson. “I’m proud to say that community members have responded to the state’s call to welcome more people of all backgrounds to live in Piedmont.” More information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For questions about the Housing Element process, contact Kevin Jackson by email kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039.

articles.text: Since March 19, 2018, when City Council adopted Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan 2.0, the city has aimed to reduce GHG emissions 40% by 2030 and be on track to reduce emissions 80% by 2050. A crucial part of this plan is the electrification of homes, buildings, cars, and appliances. On February 13, city Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman spoke with the Piedmont Post about common electrification concerns regarding PG&E power outages and even rate hikes. “As PG&E continues to raise rates,” said Dykman, “I think that cost is always going to be a concern for those considering going electric. However, when you look at the forecast of where electricity rates and natural gas rates are heading, you see a far greater increase in natural gas rates, and a greater proportion [of this increase] going toward maintaining gas infrastructure and service lines.” Gas usage itself remains an issue in light of recent storms and cold spells; PG&E customers have used more natural gas this winter than the five-year historic average, with November usage 20% higher, December 10% higher, and January 10% higher. Despite this, the main concern is the skyrocketing price of these utilities. As of January 2023, the national average of combined utility bills was $328 a month. In the Oakland area, combined utility bills cost households an average of $564 a month. PG&E rates have increased faster than inflation for a decade, with residential rates rising 31% between 2009 and 2019, compared to the consumer price index of 19%. “As of January 25, PG&E projects that [residential energy bills] will be 32% higher from November 2022 through March 2023, compared to the same months last year” said Dykman. Despite these costs, the fact that PG&E shuts off power during periods of high demand and peak fire season is a deterrent to many who consider going electric. Last summer, state regulators fined the company $12 million over poor execution of the widespread power shutoffs that were meant to prevent wildfires in 2020. “To those worried about electric outages, I’d say that their circumstances would be closer [using natural gas] than they think. Many natural gas appliances also have fans, motors, or other ignitions requiring electricity to run. It’s very true that some essential appliances — like stoves — can be lit with matches if using natural gas, but it’s also important to remember that gas can also be cut off during emergencies.” How, then, would Piedmont support residents who have gone Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont.
