articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites the public to a talk via Zoom on Wednesday, March 1 at 4:00 p.m. to hear Dr. Dan Sperling discuss the impact of Electric Vehicles (EVs) on carbon reduction in California. The talk is co-sponsored by Piedmont Connect, the League of Women Voters of Solano County, and the League of Women Voters of Portland, Oregon. Join the discussion to learn what it will take for EVs to make a measurable difference in greenhouse gas reduction. Dr. Sperling is Distinguished Blue Planet Prize Professor of Civil Engineering and Environmental Science and Policy and founding Director of the Institute of Transportation Studies at the University of California in Davis. He holds the transportation seat on the California Air Resources Board and served as Chair of the Transportation Research Board (TRB) of the National Academies in 2015- 16. Among his many prizes and awards are election to the National Academy of Engineering in 2022, the 2018 Roy W. Crum award from TRB, its highest research award; and the 2013 Blue Planet Prize from the Asahi Glass Foundation for being “a pioneer in opening up new fields of study to create more efficient, low-carbon, and environmentally beneficial transportation systems.” He served twice as lead author for the IPCC and shared the 2007 Nobel Peace Prize. He has testiDr. Daniel Sperling, Distinguished Blue Planet Prize Professor of Civil Engineering and Environmental Science and Policy and founding Director of the Institute of Transportation Studies at the University of California, Davis fied eight times before Congress and has provided 20 keynote presentations in the past year. He has authored or co-authored over 250 technical papers and 13 books, including Three Revolutions: Steering Automated, Shared, and Electric Vehicles to a Better Future, and is widely cited in leading media. The talk will be held live on Zoom and YouTube streaming and will include an audience question and answer session. Visit the website lwvpiedmont. org to register for the event and to learn more about the series. Once registered, you will receive the Zoom link by email. The event is free and open to the public.

articles.text: On Monday, February 6 around 4 a.m., a 7.8 magnitude earthquake hit Turkey and Syria. The quake was the most powerful in the country since December 1939, when an earthquake killed 30,000 people in December 1939. As of Tuesday afternoon, February 14, the death toll passed 40,000. The epicenter was 14.2 miles north of Nurdaği, a city in Gaziantep province, where southeastern Turkey borders northwestern Syria. Aftershocks ripped throughout the day and region; the strongest one measured a magnitude of 7.5, 9 hours after and 59 miles north of the original epicenter. Tremors were felt as far away as Israel and Lebanon. Turkish President Recep Erdoğan declared a three-month state of emergency in 10 provinces affected by the earthquake. Turkey reported at least 5,434 deaths and 31,777 injuries. In government-controlled parts of Syria, at least 812 people were killed and 1,449 injured. Civil defense workers in the rebel-held northwest — which already faced a humanitarian crisis nearly 12 years into a bloody civil war — reported at least 1,020 deaths and 2,400 injuries. Thousands of buildings were flattened, leaving inhabitants homeless in near-freezing weather. Governments worldwide are pledging assistance and deploying aid as thousands of rescue workers desperately dig possible survivors from the rubble. The United States announced on Monday that it would deploy two specialized search-and-rescue teams of about 80 members each, one from Los Angeles and another from Virginia. Here are organizations working on rescue and recovery efforts. Donations are greatly needed. UNICEF The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund is in Syria and prioritizing water, sanitation, hygiene and nutrition, and focusing on helping unaccompanied children locate their families. UNICEF is accepting donations at unicefusa.org. Global Giving Global Giving, which helps local nonprofit agencies, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3DSf8JI to help fund emergency medical workers’ ability to provide food, shelter and medicine, among other necessities. As needs in Turkey and Syria change, the organization will focus on longterm assistance. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies The IFRC is requesting donations for its Disaster Response Emergency Fund at bit.ly/3HFJe49 so it can send “immediate cash assistance.” OXFAM OXFAM, an international organization that fights poverty, is working with women’s cooperatives in Turkey to determine an appropriate immediate and longterm response plan. It is accepting donations at bit.ly/3YfjYso. CARE CARE, an organization that works with impoverished communities, is accepting donations that will go toward food, shelter and hygiene kits, among other items. Donate and learn more at bit.ly/3DRU3yO. Doctors Without Borders DWB, which responds to medical emergencies around the world, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3I7Jw5c. The Syrian American Medical Society SAMS is a United Statesbased humanitarian group that supplies medical care in Syria and nearby countries. At least one of its hospitals in northwestern Syria, Al Dana, received major damage. SAMS is collecting donations at bit.ly/3RJdBLz to deliver emergency aid. Save the Children Save the Children is accepting donations at bit.ly/3I6QmIb for its Children’s Emergency Fund, which will help provide children with food, shelter and warm clothing. The Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations UOSSM, which since 2012 has provided medical relief and health care services ins Syria and to Syrian refugees in Turkey, is collecting money at uossm.org/ donate. Empowering the TurkishAmerican Community ETAC, a nonprofit which provides support services and guidance to members of the Turkish community with lack of means or language skills, is collecting donations which will be sent directly and entirely to rescue teams. Learn more and donate at bit.ly/3YeRz5W. Troop 11 Mon 2/27 7:30 pm Troop 1 Tues 2/28 7:30 pm Troop 4 Mon 3/6 7:00 pm Troop 15 Tues 3/7 7:00 pm Troop 6 Wed 3/29 7:30 pm

Turkish, Syrian earthquake relief: how Piedmonters can help By Selen Ozturk On Monday, February 6 around 4 a.m., a 7.8 magnitude earthquake hit Turkey and Syria. The quake was the most powerful in the country since December 1939, when an earthquake killed 30,000 people in December 1939. As of Tuesday afternoon, February 14, the death toll passed 40,000. The epicenter was 14.2 miles north of Nurdaği, a city in Gaziantep province, where southeastern Turkey borders northwestern Syria. Aftershocks ripped throughout the day and region; the strongest one measured a magnitude of 7.5, 9 hours after and 59 miles north of the original epicenter. Tremors were felt as far away as Israel and Lebanon. Turkish President Recep Erdoğan declared a three-month state of emergency in 10 provinces affected by the earthquake. Turkey reported at least 5,434 deaths and 31,777 injuries. In government-controlled parts of Syria, at least 812 people were killed and 1,449 injured. Civil defense workers in the rebel-held northwest — which already faced a humanitarian crisis nearly 12 years into a bloody civil war — reported at least 1,020 deaths and 2,400 injuries. Thousands of buildings were flattened, leaving inhabitants homeless in near-freezing weather. Governments worldwide are pledging assistance and deploying aid as thousands of rescue workers desperately dig possible survivors from the rubble. The United States announced on Monday that it would deploy two specialized search-and-rescue teams of about 80 members each, one from Los Angeles and another from Virginia. Here are organizations working on rescue and recovery efforts. Donations are greatly needed. UNICEF The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund is in Syria and prioritizing water, sanitation, hygiene and nutrition, and focusing on helping unaccompanied children locate their families. UNICEF is accepting donations at unicefusa.org. Global Giving Global Giving, which helps local nonprofit agencies, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3DSf8JI to help fund emergency medical workers’ ability to provide food, shelter and medicine, among other necessities. As needs in Turkey and Syria change, the organization will focus on longterm assistance. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies The IFRC is requesting donations for its Disaster Response Emergency Fund at bit.ly/3HFJe49 so it can send “immediate cash assistance.” OXFAM OXFAM, an international organization that fights poverty, is working with women’s cooperatives in Turkey to determine an appropriate immediate and longterm response plan. It is accepting donations at bit.ly/3YfjYso. CARE CARE, an organization that works with impoverished communities, is accepting donations that will go toward food, shelter and hygiene kits, among other items. Donate and learn more at bit.ly/3DRU3yO. Doctors Without Borders DWB, which responds to medical emergencies around the world, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3I7Jw5c. The Syrian American Medical Society SAMS is a United Statesbased humanitarian group that supplies medical care in Syria and nearby countries. At least one of its hospitals in northwestern Syria, Al Dana, received major damage. SAMS is collecting donations at bit.ly/3RJdBLz to deliver emergency aid. Save the Children Save the Children is accepting donations at bit.ly/3I6QmIb for its Children’s Emergency Fund, which will help provide children with food, shelter and warm clothing. The Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations UOSSM, which since 2012 has provided medical relief and health care services ins Syria and to Syrian refugees in Turkey, is collecting money at uossm.org/ donate. Empowering the TurkishAmerican Community ETAC, a nonprofit which provides support services and guidance to members of the Turkish community with lack of means or language skills, is collecting donations which will be sent directly and entirely to rescue teams. Learn more and donate at bit.ly/3YeRz5W. articles.text: Directly benefiting from its commitment to provide a safe and inclusive educational environment for all students and staff, Piedmont School District will receive a 3-year $200,000 grant as part of the California Department of Education’s Antibias Education Grant. With $20 million to eradicate racism in all California schools, the state has invited school districts to apply for an Antibias Education Grant. In support of the District’s Non-Discrimination board policy, DEI Director Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard applied for a portion of the grant. “This amazing opportunity would not have been possible without the work of Dr. V, who coordinated with PUSD staff and the community to put together an outstanding application detailing the work done so far and how this grant will take Piedmont to the next level,” said Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. “These funds will assist us greatly in achieving our goal of providing everything our students need to succeed.” The grant will be used for training and resources to prevent and address bias or prejudice toward any group of people based on race, ethnicity, religion, gender, gender identity, sexual orientation, disability, immigration status, language, or any actual or perceived characteristic. Emphasis will be on preventing anti-Semitism and bias or prejudice toward groups, including, but not limited to, African Americans, Asian-Pacific Islanders, Latinos, and people who are lesbian, gay, bisexual, transgender, or questioning youth. The school district plans to actively engage with its students, parents, guardians, educators and community leaders to determine the appropriate use of the funds. The Anti Bias Education Grant was authorized under Assembly Bill 130 and provides funding for three years, from January 2023 through March 30, 2026.
articles.title: PUSD awarded $200,000 Anti-Bias Grant from State

articles.text: Piedmont Scouts in Troop One decided to take a trip back in time and explore the former immigration station at Angel Island, now a museum. After taking a short ferry ride to the island on February 11, the Scouts hiked up to the barracks where the immigrants – largely Chinese – were held. We were led on a guided tour through the building. It was heartbreaking to read famous poems on the walls, and to see the cramped living conditions. Immigrants were forced to endure these prison-like conditions for a few months while they were endlessly interrogated, in order to gain access to America. It operated from 1910 to 1940. The beautiful poetry that was carved into the walls was covered up with wood putty and lead paint by the government. Speaking of the government, they were pure devils. The walls were painted jade because of the stereotypical belief that all the Chinese are jade and chop suey. In the beginning, Scoutmaster Bryan Cantrill enjoys the ferry ride with Troop One Scouts. Original beds at Angel Island immigration station Scouts pass the time waiting for their ferry by observing marine life in San Francisco Bay. there were no mattresses because the Chinese sleep on boards on the floor, right? The lights were bare bulbs and the beds were around 18 inches wide, stacked three tall, crammed together with no space or ladders between them. You know how you hate sharing a bathroom? Imagine sharing two bathrooms with 700. What happened at Angel Island was repulsive, patronizing, and should never, ever be repeated. However, by learning about Angel Island, and supporting each other, we can help prevent these dreadful events from repeating. The Scouts found comfort with a quick, uplifting hike to the nearby beach with breathtaking views of San Francisco Bay. The clouds and rain that had greeted us when we arrived had vanished, leaving a baking sun. It felt like the perfect metaphor for the trip: even when things are ugly or miserable, they can aways lift and be better. Samantha Pell is a seventh grade student at Piedmont Middle School and a member of Piedmont Scout Troop One. A breathtaking view of the Bay from Angel Island. PIEDMONT COMMUNITY CHURCH Oakland Museum
articles.title: Troop One Scouts explore the history of Angel Island

articles.text: Final interviews for a permanent Superintendent of Schools in Piedmont were concluded on Friday and Saturday, February 10 and 11, by the five members of the school board. Following the interviews, the job was offered to a candidate, who has accepted. The board is currently engaged in contract negotiations but has stated it won’t announce the name and details of the new superintendent until the March 8 school board meeting. The search firm, Leadership Associates, confirmed it received 39 requests for applications and applications from 22 candidates. The school board settled on interviewing six candidates in the first round on Friday, February 10. At that time each candidate received an one hour interview and responded to a set of 11 questions. “Questions covered a wide range of topics including: budget, board relations, labor negotiations, equity and belonging, educator hiring and retention, communications, and stakeholder engagement,” according to the Piedmont School Board. Three finalists were invited back for a second interview at a breakfast meeting on Saturday, February 11. The second interviews “were in-depth conversations that lasted 45 minutes,” stated the Piedmont School Board. The last time Piedmont hired a permanent Superintendent was eight years ago, a process that resulted in the hiring of Randy Booker. Eric Andrew, a Leadership Associates Consultant who helped lead Piedmont’s search this year, said he was pleased with the quantity and quality of applicants. Andrew explained that the job market has changed since 2015, especially since the pandemic and because of changes in policy and philosophy by school boards. Andrew, a former superintendent, has seen a trend for superintendents to have shorter tenures and retire earlier than in prior times. “Typically the retiring age for superintendents is 61 years of age after 30 years of service. Now, we are starting to see superintendents leave between age 55 and 58,” he said. “In some cases the pandemic took its toll, with masking debates, school reopenings, and some of the cultural wars in-terms of is the district going to implement equity, how far do you take it, how involved is it?” Andrew said. The regularly scheduled board meeting at which the new superintendent will be introduced is scheduled for 7:00 p.m. at City Hall on Wednesday, March 8.
articles.title: New School Supt. picked; announcement set for March 8

articles.text: As we grow up, our dreams evolve and allow us to imagine the endless possibilities of where we can go and who we can become. In September 1992, Dr. Mae C. Jemison made history as the first Black woman to travel into space. Born in 1956 in Alabama, she grew up imagining that one day she would make it into space. As a child, she watched the original Star Trek shows, which inspired her to go into space. In an interview with NOVA’s Secret Life of Scientists & Engineers, Dr. Jemison discusses how the character of Nyota Uhura helped connect her idea of space travel by seeing Uhura in the role as a lieutenant in the show. Nichelle Nichols portrayed Lieutenant Uhura, also noteworthy because she was a Black woman playing an integral role on television. With her drive to reach the stars, Dr. Jemison’s journey began as she attended Stanford University where she received a Bachelor degree in Chemical Engineering and a Bachelor of Arts degree in African American Studies. She then gained a Doctorate in Medicine at Cornell Medical School. Now a physician, Dr. Jemison practiced medicine and joined the Peace Corps. In 1985, she applied to NASA’s astronaut program. According to the National Women’s History Museum, Dr. Dr. Mae C. Jemison was the first Black woman to travel into space. Jemison reapplied in 1987 due to NASA pausing acceptances because of the tragedy of the space shuttle Challenger. However, success came when Dr. Jemison was chosen to be a part of the STS-47 crew as a mission specialist. On September 12, 1992, Dr. Jemison and her crew were launched into space. Chabot Space & Science Center is home to the NASA Ames Visitor Center, which showcases Dr. Jemison’s Autogenic Feedback Training Exercise Suit (AFTE) and a signed replica flight suit. The AFTE suit was used to help astronauts adapt to the environment in space and then to readapt to the environment on Earth upon their return. Dr. Jemison was with NASA for six years. While talking with NOVA’s Secret Life of Scientists and Engineers, Dr. Jemison mentions a full-circle moment she experienced. Star Trek was an inspiration early on in her life and she later became a real-life star on the show. Dr. Jemison is a doctor, engineer, astronaut, and pioneer in the history of women in space. Before her time with NASA, she worked in a Cambodian refugee camp and went with a study group to Cuba. After her time with NASA, she continued her efforts and founded the nonprofit Dorothy Jemison Foundation for Excellence. She also developed an international space camp called The Earth We Share, and founded her own consulting company that focuses on science, technology, and social change. Dr. Jemison is an inspiration
articles.title: The journey of Dr. Mae C. Jemison

Jemison By Isabel Lopez Ramirez As we grow up, our dreams evolve and allow us to imagine the endless possibilities of where we can go and who we can become. In September 1992, Dr. Mae C. Jemison made history as the first Black woman to travel into space. Born in 1956 in Alabama, she grew up imagining that one day she would make it into space. As a child, she watched the original Star Trek shows, which inspired her to go into space. In an interview with NOVA’s Secret Life of Scientists & Engineers, Dr. Jemison discusses how the character of Nyota Uhura helped connect her idea of space travel by seeing Uhura in the role as a lieutenant in the show. Nichelle Nichols portrayed Lieutenant Uhura, also noteworthy because she was a Black woman playing an integral role on television. With her drive to reach the stars, Dr. Jemison’s journey began as she attended Stanford University where she received a Bachelor degree in Chemical Engineering and a Bachelor of Arts degree in African American Studies. She then gained a Doctorate in Medicine at Cornell Medical School. Now a physician, Dr. Jemison practiced medicine and joined the Peace Corps. In 1985, she applied to NASA’s astronaut program. According to the National Women’s History Museum, Dr. Dr. Mae C. Jemison was the first Black woman to travel into space. Jemison reapplied in 1987 due to NASA pausing acceptances because of the tragedy of the space shuttle Challenger. However, success came when Dr. Jemison was chosen to be a part of the STS-47 crew as a mission specialist. On September 12, 1992, Dr. Jemison and her crew were launched into space. Chabot Space & Science Center is home to the NASA Ames Visitor Center, which showcases Dr. Jemison’s Autogenic Feedback Training Exercise Suit (AFTE) and a signed replica flight suit. The AFTE suit was used to help astronauts adapt to the environment in space and then to readapt to the environment on Earth upon their return. Dr. Jemison was with NASA for six years. While talking with NOVA’s Secret Life of Scientists and Engineers, Dr. Jemison mentions a full-circle moment she experienced. Star Trek was an inspiration early on in her life and she later became a real-life star on the show. Dr. Jemison is a doctor, engineer, astronaut, and pioneer in the history of women in space. Before her time with NASA, she worked in a Cambodian refugee camp and went with a study group to Cuba. After her time with NASA, she continued her efforts and founded the nonprofit Dorothy Jemison Foundation for Excellence. She also developed an international space camp called The Earth We Share, and founded her own consulting company that focuses on science, technology, and social change. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. articles.text: Greg Slatoff and Carolyn George in the backyard of their Wildwood Avenue home. Piedmont residents Greg Slatoff and Carolyn George found love in a law school class almost 45 years ago which continues to resonate today. Greg and Carolyn are both lawyers, both enjoy gardening and growing vegetables (think Harvest Festival). Even though he is Piedmont’s Mr. Jazz as the founder and longtime organizer of the annual Piedmont Jazz Festival, it was Carolyn who sparked his love of jazz. “Our law professor credited himself entirely with our happy relationship, because we had Remedies Class together,” she said with a smile. “He would always say ‘Ms. George, how would you respond to what Mr. Slatoff said about that?’ So he got us talking in class and then invited us to dinner a few times.” “Valentine’s Day has always been special,” said Greg. “The nice thing about it is that it’s kind of a moveable feast,” said Greg. “When we were first dating, we had absolutely nothing. We would have a bottle of Franzia champagne and couple of baubles and it was great.” To celebrate their sixth anniversary of dating the couple went to the Ahwahnee Hotel in Yosemite, but Carolyn found that Greg was acting very weird. “He was not communicative and getting dressed in the closet; he was being skittish and I thought, well, that’s it. I’m so frustrated with him; he just can’t even talk anymore,” she said. The next morning Carolyn confronted her boyfriend, asking for an explanation. Greg replied, “Well, last night I had it all planned out. I was going to take you out for a walk in the moonlight and I would ask you to marry me.” Carolyn replied, with “Well, it was about 30 degrees below and there were wolves, why don’t you ask me now?” But Greg stayed with his idea. “I had a tuxedo and a great plan,” he recalled. Finally, Carolyn said, “Just ask me now!” Greg got on one knee and as she nodded yes, an eruption of applause and cheers was heard. Guests at the Ahwahnee behind a glass window had been watching the dynamic unfold and helped celebrate their union. Two weeks later they got married in a small ceremony, at the Unitarian Church on Van Ness in San Francisco. Due to the popularity of the dystopian book and film 1984, they felt the world was on the precipice of change so they decided to get married before 1984 ended – December 31. “It was $100 for the minister and $100 for the church if we had less than 10 people. So some of our family members had to act as photographers so we wouldn’t go over 10,” they said, taking turns narrating the story. Carolyn convinced her dad to use the money they would have spent on an expensive wedding to use as a down payment on a house. They lived in San Francisco for five years, then bought a house right on the Piedmont-Oakland border. After another six years they moved to Wildwood Avenue where their daughters Alexandra and Lara were born in 1990 and 1994. Through their leadership of the Piedmont Jazz Festival and Piedmont Harvest Festival the couple intertwines their interest as they have grown together. Carolyn chooses the judges for the Harvest Festival every year, and Greg not only runs the Jazz Festival, but creates the artwork every year for the flier. Both have been active members of St. John’s Episcopal Church in Montclair for many years. Their home represents their talents, Greg’s instruments (he is now in a stringed instrument phase) are all around the house, and his paintings adorn the walls. Their large backyard was used for subsistence farming by the previous owners. While on a somewhat smaller scale, their garden space is one of the major producers of fresh vegetables and fruits for the Edible Foot Contest at the Harvest Festival. Carolyn and Greg, have different views on what makes their bond so strong. “I think we’ve continued to be friends; it’s very important. I think we really, honestly enjoy each other’s company, and have built a life here that is all our life – not his life and my life,” Carolyn explained. “I think guys approach it differently,” he responded. “You don’t marry your best friend. For me, it was love at first sight; I was just smitten and that hasn’t changed,” Greg said.
articles.title: Greg Slatoff and Carolyn George – 38 years and counting

articles.text: Bob and Kay Cheatham met at Murray High School in St. Paul, Minnesota 67 years ago. Kay, an extroverted cheerleader, made a plan in January of her Senior year of high school to ask Bob to the Senior Prom. It seems that the rest is history. Months ahead of the Prom, she already had her eyes set on him. “I made a calendar. I had to find him somewhere in the school in the halls of school or the lunchroom or somewhere and I had to say something to him. I did that, and the next day I resolved to say more that hi,” she recalled. Two days later, Kay and Bob ran into each other in the hallway, and eventually Bob offered to drive her home after a school basketball game. They stayed in touch through college, but it wasn’t until graduate school, when, separated by the Pacific Ocean, Kay made her final move. While teaching as a graduate student in Japan, Kay placed a long distance call to Bob to ask if she could visit him in Alaska during her spring break. At the time, Bob was a civil engineer and was a little reluctant to have Kay fly out. He was building his own house, which wasn’t yet complete. “I said ‘I’m flying out to visit you in Alaska’,” recalled Kay with a smile, “and he said ‘don’t come.’ So then I said. ‘will you see me if I come? And he said yes.” After one week of skiing and traveling, Bob proposed marriage in a restaurant on a little island outside Juneau, No surprise, Kay said yes. After their wedding in Minnesota in 1964, they took another spring break opportunity. This time it was Bob’s break from law school in order to have a honeymoon, with a destination unknown. “We didn’t know what the Ozarks were, but we decided we would go to the Ozarks,” said Kay. “The design of the trip, since I had five days for spring break, was to drive south for two and half days, stay somewhere and drive back,” said Bob. “We would stop at a gas staBob and Kay Cheatham in their backyard. tion and ask, ‘How far are the Ozarks?” started Kay. “Nobody really knew for sure. We’d ask, ‘Are we in the Ozarks now’?” Bob said finishing Kay’s sentence. Although they never found the Ozarks, Bob returned on time for the next semester and eventually became a lawyer and Kay a school psychologist. Kay and Bob would take many more trips together, including back to Japan where Kay had already made friends. While there, they lived in in a tea house in the backyard of a friend she met on a TV set while playing the role of an American mother in a program about Thanksgiving. Back in the states, Kay gave birth to their first child, Anne in Oakland. Lynn came two years later and their third child, Paul, was born in 1978, 10 years later. All three went to Piedmont school and now Kay and Bob have three granddaughters in Berkeley and three grandsons in Sebastopol. What’s the secret to their longevity? They never stopped dancing and were happy to talk about dancing last weekend in Rossmoor. “Bob’s secret is he is a really good dancer, I was interested in really learning the tango or Waltz, but Bob doesn’t like anyone to tell him how to dance,” Kay said with a grin. “We did take a lesson once, I think, upon your request.” Bob then reminded his wife. Although in their 80s the Cheathams remain remarkably active. “I can still bike. I’m walking with a cane because I can’t walk right, but I can bike just fine,” said Kay. With six decades of marriage and a smiling wife as credentials, Bob offered the following advice on staying together all these years. “Psychologically, when we get upset at the other person, it’s often a projection,” he said. When asked how to handle a situation when your partner appears to be projecting, Bob said, “The best thing would be to just listen and say nothing. I’m just beginning to learn that,” he said with a smile. The Cheathams observe Valentine’s Day every year. This Valentine’s Day Kay will be making her traditional heart-shaped brownies with red frosting to share with Bob, family in Berkeley and friends in Piedmont. > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC Plan for their future and yours. Kay, an extroverted cheerleader, made a plan in January of her Senior year of high school to ask Bob to the Senior Prom. It seems that the rest is history. Months ahead of the Prom, she already had her eyes set on him. “I made a calendar. I had to find him somewhere in the school in the halls of school or the lunchroom or somewhere and I had to say something to him. I did that, and the next day I resolved to say more that hi,” she recalled. Two days later, Kay and Bob ran into each other in the hallway, and eventually Bob offered to drive her home after a school basketball game. They stayed in touch through college, but it wasn’t until graduate school, when, separated by the Pacific Ocean, Kay made her final move. While teaching as a graduate student in Japan, Kay placed a long distance call to Bob to ask if she could visit him in Alaska during her spring break. At the time, Bob was a civil engineer and was a little reluctant to have Kay fly out. He was building his own house, which wasn’t yet complete. “I said ‘I’m flying out to visit you in Alaska’,” recalled Kay with a smile, “and he said ‘don’t come.’ So then I said. ‘will you see me if I come? And he said yes.” After one week of skiing and traveling, Bob proposed marriage in a restaurant on a little island outside Juneau, No surprise, Kay said yes. After their wedding in Minnesota in 1964, they took another spring break opportunity. This time it was Bob’s break from law school in order to have a honeymoon, with a destination unknown. “We didn’t know what the Ozarks were, but we decided we would go to the Ozarks,” said Kay. “The design of the trip, since I had five days for spring break, was to drive south for two and half days, stay somewhere and drive back,” said Bob. “We would stop at a gas staBob and Kay Cheatham in their backyard. tion and ask, ‘How far are the Ozarks?” started Kay. “Nobody really knew for sure. We’d ask, ‘Are we in the Ozarks now’?” Bob said finishing Kay’s sentence. Although they never found the Ozarks, Bob returned on time for the next semester and eventually became a lawyer and Kay a school psychologist. Kay and Bob would take many more trips together, including back to Japan where Kay had already made friends. While there, they lived in in a tea house in the backyard of a friend she met on a TV set while playing the role of an American mother in a program about Thanksgiving. Back in the states, Kay gave birth to their first child, Anne in Oakland. Lynn came two years later and their third child, Paul, was born in 1978, 10 years later. All three went to Piedmont school and now Kay and Bob have three granddaughters in Berkeley and three grandsons in Sebastopol. What’s the secret to their longevity? They never stopped dancing and were happy to talk about dancing last weekend in Rossmoor. “Bob’s secret is he is a really good dancer, I was interested in really learning the tango or Waltz, but Bob doesn’t like anyone to tell him how to dance,” Kay said with a grin. “We did take a lesson once, I think, upon your request.” Bob then reminded his wife. Although in their 80s the Cheathams remain remarkably active. “I can still bike. I’m walking with a cane because I can’t walk right, but I can bike just fine,” said Kay. With six decades of marriage and a smiling wife as credentials, Bob offered the following advice on staying together all these years. “Psychologically, when we get upset at the other person, it’s often a projection,” he said. When asked how to handle a situation when your partner appears to be projecting, Bob said, “The best thing would be to just listen and say nothing. I’m just beginning to learn that,” he said with a smile. The Cheathams observe Valentine’s Day every year. This Valentine’s Day Kay will be making her traditional heart-shaped brownies with red frosting to share with Bob, family in Berkeley and friends in Piedmont. > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC Plan for their future and yours. articles.text: When Dick and Mary Carter got married, it was the first day of 1984, a blistering hot Sunday in Washington, D.C., and the Washington Redskins were playing the Los Angeles Rams. “The priest kept interrupting the ceremony to give updates to people wondering about the score,” Dick said. “The Redskins went on to lose the Super Bowl, so it was a good day for a Mass.” Although Mary’s family lived in D.C., she met Dick — a Piedmont native — in North Carolina two years earlier. Dick lived there for six years, and she for nearly 10. They met while working for the same company. “We both worked for a ‘no-nonsense pantyhose’ company. She was in accounting, I in marketing,” Dick recalled. “We’d go to brunch a lot. That’s what we did before online dating.” After one more year in North Carolina, where Mary had attended college, the two spent nearly three years in St. Louis, where their daughter Katherine, was born in 1985. Now 37, she works for AT&T corporate headquarters in Dallas, Texas. “We’d planned to live in the D.C. area,” said Dick, “but we were both corporate gypsies. We always bonded over our love of traveling, and we’ve instilled the same in our children.” In 1986, the three returned to California to head four Wendy’s hamburger restaurant franchises in Mendocino County, living in Ukiah. Dick working seven days a week and Mary working six — taking one day off to care for Katherine. “Since our marriage survived the Wendy’s experience, it can survive anything,” said Mary wryly. In 1988, the Carters sold their “Wendy’s experience” and moved to Piedmont, Dick’s hometown. They have been here for 35 years this August. Dick returned to marketing, working first for a San Francisco agency and then for his alma mater, UC Berkeley. In 1992, the couple celebrated the birth of twin boys. I remember thinking before the Ultrasound, ‘It’s a good thing the kids will be so many years apart, so no two will be in college at the same time,” Mary said. “Famous last words; they were twins.” Michael and William are now 31. Michael lives in Oakland and works for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s after-school Schoolmates program. William works as the interim General Manager of Merrill Gardens at Rolling Hills Estates, a senior living home outside Torrance in Southern California. All three of the Carter kids grew up much like their father, who attended Havens Elementary School, Piedmont Middle School, and Piedmont High School. The Carter children attended Wildwood Elementary, where Mary began teaching as a paraeducator 20 years ago. “I was born in Seattle, so the kids tell me that they all graduated from Wildwood and I never did,” said Mary with a laugh. “Dick always loved Piedmont. Even when we were in North Carolina, he’d always be looking for Dick and Mary Carter in Torres del Paine National Park, Chile in 2016. a Bay Area-style brown shingle house for us.” Mary’s volunteer experience includes the Piedmont Neighbors & Newcomers Club the Piedmont High School Parent Club; the nonprofit Piedmonters for Resources, Advocacy & Information in Special Education (of which she is a founding member); and Pack 5 and Troop 11 of the Piedmont Scouts. Dick is well-known in Piedmont as a longtime high school football coach, and more recently as a member of the city’s Recreation Commission, He co-founded and frequently leads the Walking on Wednesdays group since 2018,, and recently added a book group and movie group – primarily for seniors – to his arsenal of activities designed for Piedmonters. “Dick got the idea (of weekly walks) from me; I walked every block of Piedmont after work for over a decade, especially the hills. I was training to hike Mount Whitney,” Mary said. “In summer 2009, I finally did so with Mike and Will as part of their Eagle Scout work. I loved the views and the rich history the area held. Dick had the idea of having the Recreation Department sponsor Wednesday group and have it focus on local history,” she said. To celebrate their Valentine’s Day evening before today’s walk, Dick and Mary took a rare break from their outdoor activities and stayed home to share lobster ravioli over champagne. “Wine is one of our love languages,” confirmed Mary. “We’ve been particularly fond of Malbecs since travelling to Argentina and Chile over New Year’s in 2016.” “The holiday is about celebrating love in all its forms, after all,” said Mary. ”I’ve been so fortunate to have Dick in my life throughout the multiple chapters of our family. We hope for many more ahead.” “Yep. Let me add that Mary’s a great cook,” said Dick with a broad grin. 35 years of experience in architectural design www.kaplanarchitects.com (510) 361-0223

articles.text: On their first date, Frank and Michele Helm went to the movies. “He put his arm around my shoulders,” said Michele. “That was it, no creeping. I thought, wow, no moves for a fraternity boy – what’s wrong with this guy?” Afterward, he dropped her off at her sorority house. “We sat in my driveway and talked for three hours straight.” Frank, a man of relatively few words, contemplated this for a moment. “Maybe she talked for three hours and I listened, because I still vividly remember what she looked like — she had on this Brooks Brothers sweater.” “I still have the sweater,” Michele replied. The two met in February 1981 at the Kingfish Pub in North Oakland. Frank, then a senior at UC Berkeley, was bartending; Michele was ending her freshman year. With Frank about to leave for dental school in Boston, Michele decided to leave Berkeley and come with him. “He wanted me to keep him company on the drive (to the East Coast) and then fly back,” she said. “No way. I checked myself into the Y, he stayed with a rugby friend, I said ‘You want to do anything, you know where I am.’ Since I was the only other person he knew in town, he called. I worked as an administrative assistant while studying graphic design [at the Art Institute there.]” For many years Michele has been a highly skilled and in-demand graphic designer. After Frost spent four years at Boston University, the couple moved back to the Bay Area and lived in Chinatown and Pacific Heights in San Francisco. After three years of general practice, Frank returned to school for a two-year orthodontic residency program at the University of the Pacific. After his residency, Frank got a job offer at a practice on Grand Avenue on the Oakland-Piedmont border where he still works. The Helms were married on February 1, 1986, five years after they met. It was a formal ceremony at Grace Cathedral in San Francisco, with 275 people and a swanky reception at the Metropolitan Club. They traveled around Mexico for their honeymoon, eventually stopping in Cancun. “Have you seen the movie ‘10’ by Blake Edwards, with Bo Derek on her honeymoon running around on that beach? It was just like that,” said Frank, “except we both got violently sick and lost our luggage.” “We had no clothes,” added Michele. “We were walking around wearing matching resort clothes — you get red, I get blue. We had a do-over honeymoon with three weeks in Europe later that year; from Amsterdam we took a train to Paris, then a car to the Loire Valley, then Florence and Lake Cuomo, then Munich, and back to Paris. The Helms began their family soon afterward; three out of four children all now grown, remain in the Bay — Alex, 34, is a tech recruiter and Graham, 32, an employment attorney, both in San Francisco; Emilia, 30, works for a lacrosse supply company in Oakland; and Heidi, 19, is a student at Syracuse University in upstate New York studying business finance. “With a 15-year age range across four children, it’s impossible to keep all light switches on all the time and stay sane,” said Michele. “You can only hope to keep up as much as possible, sometimes travel together. The kids are still a huge part of our lives since we’ve been empty nesters.” “Travelling is a great way to connect with each other; you get into a rut if you’re homebound all the time,” added Frank. He and Michele plan to drive down to see his parents in San Diego this month, and plan to show Heidi around New York City in May. “We also volunteer in the community where we can,” said Michele. She has been involved in a number of school parents’ clubs in Piedmont and nonprofits like the Cancer League, Hoe and Hope Garden Club, and the East Bay Agency for Children. Frank has served as a member of the Recreation Commission and as President of the Alameda County Dental Society. The Helms haven’t gone out on their annual couples’ date nights since the pandemic; they will spend this Valentine’s Day at home eating surf ‘n’ turf, courtesy of Frank. “We [regard it] as a day to take pause and show appreciation for the people closest to you,” said Frank. “It does take work in a relationship, making sure you’re accessible timewise and emotionally. Communication is a twoway street. “One of my favorite things about Michele is that her energy always keeps me on track,” he added. And Michele’s favorite thing about Frank? “He’s a decent guy, but a guy has to be a bit of a jerk to be interesting; too much, and it’s creepy. I love Frank because he’s a solidly good person, and just the right percentage of jerk.”

articles.text: Pouyan Assadi has been promoted as head coach of the track and field team. The Piedmont High track and field team will have a new face at the helm this spring. Running coach Jeanine Holmlund was informed in January that after 10 years on the job, her contract was not being renewed. Ironically her track and field team last year set a handful of new school records. The school’s sprint coach Pouyan Assadi is being named as the new track & field head coach. “I loved coaching the team and took a lot of extra time to try to make it fun for our athletes. We had both fun and success over my 10 years,” said Holmlund. “The team welcomed anyone who wanted to put in their best effort. Leaders worked for the team and remained humble despite their success. We have a good group of juniors and sophomores who have already taken on this holistic spirit. I told Bradley [Athletic Director Bradley Smet] in the fall that I thought Pouyan Assadi would make a good head coach some day while I was thinking about who would I trust to eventually take my place,” said Holmlund. Holmlund said the team should be in “good hands” with Assadi. “I’ve brought the track and field program a long way from when I started, and I also contributed time to the WACC league, so I’m happy to leave it in good hands with people I know and trust. I truly expect to see a few [more] school records broken and wish [to see] all our athletes reach their goals,” she added. The decision seemed be a shocking move for the school to after the historic 2022 season. Parker Terrill set the school’s pole vault record several times; Jack Stein became the 1600 and 3200 record holder; Ellie Black accomplished the school’s second and third all-time best times in the 1600 and 3200; and the 4x400 relay team of Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Long broke a 30-year old school record. Holmlund produced five recent Piedmont Post Athlete of the Year winners now competing in college: Reece Proctor in 2018, Sophia Zalewski in 2020, and Terrill, Stein, and Black in 2022. The Post was told that Holmlund faced parent complaints following the spring 2022 track season. Piedmont High athletic Jeanine Holmlund was let go after 10 years leading the track and cross-country teams. Her 2022 track & field team set several school records. director Bradley Smet seemingly confirmed that was the case. “We decided that we want a new direction at the head of the program… We always take input from our families and kids whether it is good or bad. By Jonathan Comeaux The Piedmont High track and field team will have a new face at the helm this spring. Running coach Jeanine Holmlund was informed in January that after 10 years on the job, her contract was not being renewed. Ironically her track and field team last year set a handful of new school records. The school’s sprint coach Pouyan Assadi is being named as the new track & field head coach. “I loved coaching the team and took a lot of extra time to try to make it fun for our athletes. We had both fun and success over my 10 years,” said Holmlund. “The team welcomed anyone who wanted to put in their best effort. Leaders worked for the team and remained humble despite their success. We have a good group of juniors and sophomores who have already taken on this holistic spirit. I told Bradley [Athletic Director Bradley Smet] in the fall that I thought Pouyan Assadi would make a good head coach some day while I was thinking about who would I trust to eventually take my place,” said Holmlund. Holmlund said the team should be in “good hands” with Assadi. “I’ve brought the track and field program a long way from when I started, and I also contributed time to the WACC league, so I’m happy to leave it in good hands with people I know and trust. I truly expect to see a few [more] school records broken and wish [to see] all our athletes reach their goals,” she added. The decision seemed be a shocking move for the school to after the historic 2022 season. Parker Terrill set the school’s pole vault record several times; Jack Stein became the 1600 and 3200 record holder; Ellie Black accomplished the school’s second and third all-time best times in the 1600 and 3200; and the 4x400 relay team of Terrill, Luke Alban, Cooper Downing, and Parker Long broke a 30-year old school record. Holmlund produced five recent Piedmont Post Athlete of the Year winners now competing in college: Reece Proctor in 2018, Sophia Zalewski in 2020, and Terrill, Stein, and Black in 2022. In a successful end to the regular season, Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team won its final three games, capped by a huge 1-nil upset of this year’s Western Alameda County Conference champions, Berkeley, on Wednesday, February 8. The Highlanders finished second in league with a 7-1-4 record (9-1-5 overall), four points shy of the Yellowjackets, who have now won five consecutive league titles. PHS honored its 10 members of the Class of 2023 on Senior Night on Wednesday: Morgan Hunt, Michaela Bini, Ellie DeVan, Kyra Dang, Audrey Harmon, Sophie Hebert, Emily Fitzgerald, Siena Riddel, Audrey Lam, and Cameron Lorin. articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team closed its season in a strong way, defeating Mt. Eden 3-1 on Tuesday, February 7 at Witter Field and upsetting Castro Valley 1-0 on the road on Friday, February 10. Piedmont ends its regular season with an 8-6-4 (W-T-L) overall record and 7-6-3 in league, to finish in 4th place. They closed the season on a three-match winning streak. “We played them (Castro Valley) the week before, so we felt like we knew how to match up against them. It was a tight game and we were able to score on a breakaway. It feels great to get some momentum going into NCS,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. Piedmont enters the Division 4 North Coast Section playoffs as the No. 8 seed and is set to host No. 9 St. Helena tonight, Wednesday, February 15 at Witter Field in the first round of the post-season. “I would have liked a better seed, but that’s how it goes. We just have to accept that and be ready,” said coach Sullivan. ‘We don’t know much about St. Helena, but it should be pretty close. They’ve gotten some good results against the No. 3 seed, Roseland University Prep.” With a victory, Piedmont would likely travel to Santa Rosa to take on the No. 1 seed, Cardinal Newman, this Saturday, February 18. The Highlanders lost to the Cardinals 2-0 on January 6. PHS is the defending Division 4 NCS champions. 3-1 win over Mt. Eden The Highlanders led 1-0 by the end of the first half and the match was tied briefly in the second half before PHS tacked on two more goals. Prior to the game, Piedmont honored its 14 seniors on Senior Night: Brady Hinsch, Andrew Szerdy, Evan Manolis, Soren Dixon, Miles Corcoran, T.J. O’Neil, William Daniel, Myles Gray, Owen Grippando, Jack Nelson, Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai, Max Schleuning, Jordan Miller, and goalie Daniel Malecki. Piedmont’s first goal came in the 20th minute by Evan Manolis following a long throw-in by Jack Nelson. The long toss bounced around the top of the penalty area after Mt. Eden failed to clear the ball. Manolis dashed in front of the Monarchs’ defender for the volley and looped the ball into the net. Mt. Eden tied the game in the 50th minute, but Piedmont regained the lead in the 67th on a corner kick when the ball trickled in front of the net until falling to Woolwine, who finished it off. The Highlanders put the stamp on the game just one minute later when Schleuning rocketed in a low shot from the right side of the penalty area. 1-0 upset win vs. Castro Valley Against the Trojans while on the road in Castro Valley, the two sides went into halftime in a 0-0 deadlock. The Highlanders scored the game-winner in the 55th minute when Woolwine broke down field on a breakaway goal after getting fed by Enzo Bernales to start Piedmont’s counterattack. NEXT UP Piedmont (8-6-4) will host St. Helena tonight, February 14, at 5:00 p.m. in the first game of a double header at Witter Field in the NCS playoffs. articles.text: Piedmont’s Junior Varsity girls’ soccer team wrapped up a successful season with a 6-0 thumping of Encinal on Friday, February 10. The victory vaulted the team to a 10-1-1 final record, on which it outscored its opponents 52-4. The team’s lone loss was a 3-2 defeat to perennial rival Berkeley, a team Piedmont beat 1-0 earlier in the season. Piedmont’s offense was led by striker and co-captain Hannah Sullivan, who led Friday’s win with a hat trick, including scoring the winning goal on a header. She was supported by creative midfielders Elia Kwong, Ryo Woltag, Genevieve Hiller and Reni Suhr. Wing players Samantha Ronen, Ellie Bleharski, Hana Thomas, and Ishaia Goldberg-Berman created and finished numerous chances during the season. The team was anchored all season by box-to-box midfielder and co-captain Malea Hartford, whose communication was like having a coach on the field. The stingy defense was led by co-captain Ava Sauer and Sara Broach and backed by stellar goalkeeper Clio Salzer. Freshmen defenders Kyra Trombi, and Darcy McKee joined Lucy Barton and Samantha Cheunkarndee on the flanks to join the attack. Season highlights included a goal-line slide in stoppage time by Trombi to preserve the 1-0 win over Berkeley; McKee’s 50-yard slalom through O’Dowd defenders to score the winning goal in a 1-0 win against O’Dowd; and a save on a penalty kick by Berkeley. Coach Ben Russell said this was the best JV girls’ soccer team he has coached. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team compiled an impressive 10-1-1 record this season. Pictured are: (front) Hana Thomas (left), Malea Hartford, Samantha Ronen, Ishaia Goldberg-Berman, Kyra Trombi, Elia Kwong, Hannah Sullivan, Sara Broach; (middle row) Clio Salzer, Ava Sauer, Ryo Woltag, Gen Hiller, Ellie Bleharski, Lucy Barton, Darcy McKee, Samantha Cheunkarndee, Reni Suhr; (back) Head Coach Ben Russell, and Assistant Coach Tom Baudendistel
articles.title: Girls’ JV soccer team stands at the top

articles.text: PHS senior Heather Stoneman (right) led a group of over 30 female mountain bike riders for the Girls Riding Together (GRiT) event at Joaquin Miller. A light drizzle on Saturday, February 11, did not deter Girls Riding Together (GRiT) as 35 girls, women coaches, and moms from Piedmont and Oakland joined together to ride their mountain bikes in the dirt, work on skills and have fun. Attendees had a wide range of ages from middle school to high school from several schools in the East Bay. Heather Stoneman, co-captain of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team and a senior at Piedmont High, led the event and gathered girls from all riding levels at Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills. Stoneman was chosen by the NorcCal league as a GRiT Ambassador this year. Her role involves encouraging more girls to try Mountain Biking and host GRiT rides. In addition, she worked to bring in adult coaches from different East Bay mountain bike teams to put on the event. “That was so much fun. I loved seeing all of those girls out on the trails!” said Katrina Rapa, Oakland DEVO coach. FUTURE EVENTS The PHS Mountain Bike team will have its first race of the season this Saturday, February 18, in Modesto. The Piedmont DEVO team will compete the following day, Sunday, February 19. The PHS team is currently running an “Everest Challenge” fundraiser in which riders are challenged to ride 29,000 feet in the month of February. Community members are encouraged to support them by pledging online at: www.pledgeit.org/phs-mtb-everest-challenge. Piedmont DEVO, the team at Piedmont Middle School, is still accepting new riders, both girls and boys. To learn more and sign up, go to: https://piedmontdevo. com/. PHS Mountain Bike Team co-captain Heather Stoneman (left) leads a ride of high school and middle school girls.
articles.title: Mountain Bike Team captain Heather Stoneman leads rides for girls

pages.text: Wednesday, February 15, 2023 15 Girls’ JV soccer team stands at the top Piedmont’s Junior Varsity girls’ soccer team wrapped up a successful season with a 6-0 thumping of Encinal on Friday, February 10. The victory vaulted the team to a 10-1-1 final record, on which it outscored its opponents 52-4. The team’s lone loss was a 3-2 defeat to perennial rival Berkeley, a team Piedmont beat 1-0 earlier in the season. Piedmont’s offense was led by striker and co-captain Hannah Sullivan, who led Friday’s win with a hat trick, including scoring the winning goal on a header. She was supported by creative midfielders Elia Kwong, Ryo Woltag, Genevieve Hiller and Reni Suhr. Wing players Samantha Ronen, Ellie Bleharski, Hana Thomas, and Ishaia Goldberg-Berman created and finished numerous chances during the season. The team was anchored all season by box-to-box midfielder and co-captain Malea Hartford, whose communication was like having a coach on the field. The stingy defense was led by co-captain Ava Sauer and Sara Broach and backed by stellar goalkeeper Clio Salzer. Freshmen defenders Kyra Trombi, and Darcy McKee joined Lucy Barton and Samantha Cheunkarndee on the flanks to join the attack. Season highlights included a goal-line slide in stoppage time by Trombi to preserve the 1-0 win over Berkeley; McKee’s 50-yard slalom through O’Dowd defenders to score the winning goal in a 1-0 win against O’Dowd; and a save on a penalty kick by Berkeley. Coach Ben Russell said this was the best JV girls’ soccer team he has coached. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team compiled an impressive 10-1-1 record this season. A light drizzle on Saturday, February 11, did not deter Girls Riding Together (GRiT) as 35 girls, women coaches, and moms from Piedmont and Oakland joined together to ride their mountain bikes in the dirt, work on skills and have fun. Attendees had a wide range of ages from middle school to high school from several schools in the East Bay. Heather Stoneman, co-captain of the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team and a senior at Piedmont High, led the event and gathered girls from all riding levels at Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland hills. Stoneman was chosen by the NorcCal league as a GRiT Ambassador this year. Her role involves encouraging more girls to try Mountain Biking and host GRiT rides. In addition, she worked to bring in adult coaches from different East Bay mountain bike teams to put on the event. “That was so much fun. I loved seeing all of those girls out on the trails!” said Katrina Rapa, Oakland DEVO coach. FUTURE EVENTS The PHS Mountain Bike team will have its first race of the season this Saturday, February 18, in Modesto. The Piedmont DEVO team will compete the following day, Sunday, February 19. The PHS team is currently running an “Everest Challenge” fundraiser in which riders are challenged to ride 29,000 feet in the month of February. Community members are encouraged to support them by pledging online at: www.pledgeit.org/phs-mtb-everest-challenge. Piedmont DEVO, the team at Piedmont Middle School, is still accepting new riders, both girls and boys. To learn more and sign up, go to: https://piedmontdevo. com/. articles.text: Have you ever seen a group of kids asking for more vegetables? At Fairyland’s Summer Day Camp that actually happened. Campers who joined our Farm to Table session eagerly asked for seconds of carrots and celery after making and tasting Green Goddess dressing. Farm to Table is one of two new camps Fairyland introduced last summer. In Farm to Table campers learn about gardening, animal husbandry, and the journey of how seeds become salads. Our camp area is transformed into an outdoor kitchen with the hustle and bustle of little chefs. Campers make mozzarella cheese, fresh pasta from scratch, and pickle some veggies. From getting their hands dirty, to feeling the joy of cooking, to anticipating that first taste of the fruit of their labor, the children are abuzz with excitement. The Farm to Table camp is two weeks of building practical life skills, making friends, and learning how to collaborate. The other new camp is Fairyland Puppeteer, which involves creating a puppet show from scratch and presenting a beautifully crafted performance to a live audience. Campers collaborate to devise a familiar story, design a puppet stage, make their own sock puppets, and learn how to act out their characters. Campers learn fancy theatre terms like ‘proscenium’ and ‘blocking.’ Campers are engaged in a unique way to tell a story through a traditional art form that has been a part of Fairyland for more than 60 years. Fairyland’s Summer Day Camp has been and continues to be a cherished experience for Oakland and East Bay children. We prioritize connection, cooperation, interaction, attention Kids with puppets make magic at Children’s Fairyland summer camp. and focus, and learning through play, all of which are especially important as children reacclimate after learning in isolation due to the Covid pandemic. Farm to Table, Fairyland Puppeteer, as well as our traditional Theatre Camp and Thematic Camps will be offered this summer. Storytelling, imagination, magic, and play await the arrival of our campers this summer. Vicky Chen is the Senior Director of Education and Community Engagement at Children’s Fairyland, whose mission is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling. You can contact her at vicky.chen@fairyland.org, Storytelling. Imagination. Play. articles.text: Why is interactive storytelling the ticket these days? In a world where social-emotional skills have become a standard in California’s educational curriculum, children need more creative avenues to connect with the world around them. As an arts leader in the Bay Area, I want to create these opportunities and foster environments that are centered around engaging with young people on their terms, inviting them into experiences and offering engagement tools that consider different learning styles. It’s through this approach that the magic truly happens, and children come away excited and inspired by the stories they experience and help create. Bay Area Children’s Theatre has always placed the child’s perspective at the center of our work. Over the last 18 years, we have reached over 1 million children and families through our interactive plays and award-winning educational programs. We want Photo by Melissa Nigro Starting as young as five years old, specially-themed camps allow children to sing songs, play games and use their imagination to tell stories. Photo by Ben Krantz Studios Rigoberto (Mundo Ballejos) and his classmates bond with the audience before the show starts. Everyone creates paper bag puppets and shows them off as the show begins. to celebrate the child and encourage their discoveries throughout our programs. One of our most popular programs, Academy Summer Camps, seeks to build confidence in youth through the exploration of their individual voices. “Storytelling is one of the oldest methods of communicating with one another,” explains teaching artist Katie Sonas. “I love working with youth because you can start fostering that idea of being in community and working as an ensemble to tell stories.” Shows throughout the season lean into inviting children to participate in the story. Our current show, The Day You Begin, based on the #1 New York Times Bestseller by award-winning author Jacqueline Woodson, is a heartwarming musical about finding the courage to make new friends and celebrate one’s differences. Audiences meet characters from different cultural backgrounds – like Rigoberto from Venezuela – and follow these characters on their first day of school. From the interactive puppet-making that opens the show to Rigoberto’s salsa dance lesson with the audience, children and families are invited into the immersive experience. Now more than ever, kids need programs like these to connect with the community around them. So why are interactive storytelling and immersive play the ticket these days? It’s because these methods invest in children, their development, and the future they help create. Khalia Davis is Artistic Director at Bay Area Children’s Theatre, California’s foremost theatre company for young audiences. BACT strives to bring shared experiences to children of all backgrounds, inspiring joy, empathy, and creative thinking. Their award-winning shows and classes have reached more than 1 million children over the past 18 years.

articles.text: The popular annual event Glowfari continues at Oakland Zoo on select dates until March 4. An outdoor illuminated display, Glowfari features hundreds of life-sized glowing animal lanterns throughout the Zoo, with some new displays for the event’s return this year. Previously named “Zoolights,” the reinvented event features larger light displays, longer hours of admission, and more dates for nighttime viewing. This long-standing event tells the story of wildlife through displays of larger than life-sized lanterns. This year’s exhibit features koalas, kangaroos, whales, and otters. The lighted exhibit is on view to the public from 5 p.m. to 9 p.m. on February 15-20, 22-27, and March 1-2, and 4. Visit https://www.oaklandzoo. org/programs-and-events/glowfari to purchase tickets. Note that daytime admission does not include Glowfari. Glowfari illuminated displays are on view at Oakland Zoo through February. articles.text: SF Jazz will host French jazz vocalist Cryille Aimee this weekend, February 18 and 19, at the Miner Auditorium in San Francisco. Aimee’s musical influences come from her French and Dominican background. She was raised in the northern French town of Samois-sur-Seine, the last home of jazz luminary Django Reinhardt. Aimée’s music is heavily influenced by Reinhardt and blends instrumentals from the gypsy lifestyle of Europe. In 2007, she won the Montreux Jazz Festival Competition in Switzerland and was a finalist in the Thelonious Monk International Jazz Competition in 2010. Aimee won the Sarah Vaughan International Jazz Competition in 2012. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.sfjazz.org/tickets/ productions/cyrille-aimee-2223/. Jazz vocalist Cyrille Aimee from France will debut at SF Jazz on February 18 & 19. “The New Black Vanguard” exhibit is now on display at the Museum of African Diaspora in San Francisco.

articles.text: The Museum of the African Diaspora’s (MoAD) exhibition “The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion” is on view until March 5. The exhibit is in its West Coast premiere at MoAD in San Francusci and highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and beyond. Each artist’s work offers a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics. The exhibit has been curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/thenew-black-vanguard.
articles.title: MoAD exhibition “The New Black Vanguard” on view to March 5

articles.text: On February 25, San Francisco’s Legion of Honor museum will host guest lecturer and fashion historian Dr. Minjee Kim, who will discuss eight exhibitions of Korean dress and fashion of the last decade. Kim is a full-time professor at Jeonju Kijeon College and holds adjunct positions at Seoul National University in South Korea, and Academy of Art University in San Francisco. She has served on the board of the Costume Society of America since 2018, and joined Tracing Patterns Foundation as a research associate in 2022. In this one-day lecture and exhibition, Kim will describe the growing international influence of Korean popular trends in fashion in the Western world. The presentation will provide an overview of Korean fashion and its history, both through a classical and modern lens. The event is available both in person and online via Zoom. Registration is required at https:// www.famsf.org/events/fashion-museology-korean-fashion-exhibitions. An exhibit titled Korean Fashion: From Royal Court to Runway is now on view at the Legion of Honor in San Francisco.
articles.title: Fashion historian Dr. Minjee Kim is guest lecturer

articles.text: Opera review by Paul Hertelendy Doubts abounded, with nay-sayers smirking that not even Verdi could set a Shakespearean comedy into a good opera. Those doubting Thomases were silenced when nearing the then-doddering age of 80, Verdi brought off that sparkling operatic masterpiece, Falstaff, which is getting its due and more from a highly animated production at Opera San José. Major companies take note: This smaller troupe with its actor-singers, and only in its 38th season, can run circles around many grand-opera troupes having major funding and backing. The production that opened February 11 struck the delicate balance, with ample buffoonish humor, but without turning the obese, aged knight into a buffoon. However much his earthy desires were thwarted, Falstaff shook off his dunking in the Thames and maintained a measure of self-worth. He walked that tightrope, laughing off the pranks he underwent with the deft final fugue, “All the World Is Mirth.” Baritone Darren Lekeith Drone walks that precarious tightrope, winebelly and all, and sings with sensual ease, however preposterous. Falstaff sings a paean to wine – how appropriate to us Californians! He is surrounded by similar barflies. articles.text: American Conservatory Theatre’s production of The Headlands is currently being performed in the Toni Rembe theatre in San Francisco through March 5. The Headlands is Obie Award-winning playwright Christopher Chen’s newest play, described as “a complicated love letter” to San Francisco. The play tells the story of true crime fan Henry Wong, whose father’s unexplained death is the ultimate cold case. Protagonist Wong digs into the San Francisco police department evidence, but he’s haunted by the past of his own family history and upbringing. “I am thrilled beyond measure to be bringing The Headlands to A.C.T., and to be working with Pam MacKinnon to bring it to life,” said Chen. “The Headlands is my love letter to San Francisco, the city I spent my entire life in, from birth up to right now. To share this play with my hometown, a place I feel so deeply in my bones, will be one of the most personally meaningful moments of my career,” To purchase tickets, visit: https://www.act-sf.org/whatson/202223-season/the-headlands/. He is the center of a great controversy. What follows here is … (Dramatic pause for drumroll) … “The case of Joseph Boulogne”. Joseph Boulogne was born on the French island of Guadalupe in 1745 to a French father and a Senegalese mother. He died in Paris in 1799. His father took him to Paris, where he received an education in music and fencing, among many other things. A touch of history and a lot of fantasy comprise his colorful life. Our readers certainly know that biases are everywhere. There are those who say that StGeorges was simply the greatest; and there are others who think he was a fraud. There was mention that St-Georges was a fine dancer. To them, he was Nijinsky, Nureyev, and Pavlova all in one. He defied gravity. But there is no evidence. There is historical mention that St-George was a competitive fencer. He engaged in a fencing demonstration with a notorious transvestite, and there is an oil painting of this event. articles.text: Alto saxophonist Julian Edwin Adderley was born on September 15, 1928, in Tampa, Florida. In high school, Julian was nicknamed “Cannibal,” because of his large appetite, but through many mispronunciations it became “Cannonball.” He was band director at Dillard High School in Fort Lauderdale until 1950. In 1955, on his way to seek graduate studies at New York conservatories, he was asked to sit in at Café Bohemia with Oscar Pettiford in place of his band’s regular saxophonist, who had forgotten to bring his sax. After Adderley’s performance, Cannonball was acclaimed as an heir to Charlie Parker. Charlie Parker’s death months earlier in March 1955 left a vacuum in the jazz world for a superstar alto saxophonist, and Cannonball was more than prepared to fill that role. There was Benny Carter’s rhythm-and-blues phrasing in his playing; he was fast and he knew his music. Most of all, he was highly disciplined. Although his music was not Cannonball favored a busy style of phrasing that contrasted well with Miles’ understatement. Can nonball and Miles appeared on Cannonball’s 1958 album, Somethin’ Else, with some of Miles’ finest trumpet playing on that album. They’re joined on the album by pianist Hank Jones, bassist Sam Jones, drummer Art Blakey and tenor saxophonist John Coltrane. Cannonball rejuvenated Miles’ group and they created a fresh sound that created a stir in the jazz world. Adderley appeared with Miles on many notable recordings in the late 1950’s, considered benchmarks of hard bop and modal jazz, including Milestones, Kind of Blue and Porgy and Bess. Cannonball also recommended that Miles hire pianist Bill Evans and drummer Jimmy Cobb for the Kind of Blue sessions. Cannonball also played on albums with Bill Evans, Ray Brown, Wes Montgomery, Milt Jackson and Oscar Peterson. Adding to those mentioned above, Cannonball’s Quintet, Alto saxophonist Cannonball Adderley. considered groundbreaking, Cannonball was extremely gifted technically, featuring restless, highly decorated, often florid lines; emphatic blues harmonies and a full, rich tone. As jazz became more atonally obtuse and rhythmically complex during the 1960s, Cannonball’s straightforward approach helped keep jazz popular with mainstream audiences. Miles Davis noticed him and asked Cannonball to play with his group. He joined Miles’ band in October 1957, three months prior to the return of John Coltrane.

articles.text: It was another wonderful weather Wednesday last week for 38 Wednesday Walkers and two K-9 best friends, The prior week the group went to eight locations in Piedmont parks to view the city’s 19 Heritage Trees. Three more would require a walk to the west and southwest sides of town. The morning’s last tree would be near a home where they could also consider Sidney Dearing and his family, the first Black residents of Piedmont. It’s a sad part of the city’s history, but an important one to know, and especially appropriate to remember during February, Black History Month. As the group headed down Magnolia Avenue, they turned on Jerome and saw eight redwoods growing in a circle at the Jerome Triangle at Fairview Avenue. Redwoods often grow this way because they are from the seeds of a mother tree in the center. The walkers continued in a long line down Oakland Avenue. It took two stop light cycles for all the walkers to cross Grand Avenue. They noticed an unusual tree near the curb, with a trunk about five feet in diameter and green, spikey palms 10 to 15 feet above. Rob Smith used a phone app to identify it as a Spineless Yucca, native to Central America. After crossing the Oakland Wednesday Walkers participating on February 8 included Elizabeth Richter, Garrett Clifford, Alan Goldhammer, Karen Palmer, Harriette Louie, Jim Kuo, Larry Olsen, Nancy Olsen, Priscilla Wanerus, Adrienne Hamlin, Pat Keller, Jennifer Peltzer, Brenda Ferrero, Leigh Sorenson, Susan Ode, John Lenahan, Charlene Louie, Mike Henn, Jane Holland with K-9 best friend Sasha, Ian Morgan, Bob Wong, Ann Quinby, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, Phil Witte, Rob Smith, Joanne Larson, Stella Houston, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Sherry Jacobs, Kathy Rolefson, Kat Lang, Tracy Lee, Christine Calliste, Susan Tornlof, Shirley Nakao, Janice Subotnick, and Dick Carter. pages.text: 22 Wednesday, February 15, 2023 Features Walking on Wednesday Wed. Walkers explore more Heritage trees By Dick Carter It was another wonderful weather Wednesday last week for 38 Wednesday Walkers and two K-9 best friends, The prior week the group went to eight locations in Piedmont parks to view the city’s 19 Heritage Trees. Three more would require a walk to the west and southwest sides of town. The morning’s last tree would be near a home where they could also consider Sidney Dearing and his family, the first Black residents of Piedmont. It’s a sad part of the city’s history, but an important one to know, and especially appropriate to remember during February, Black History Month. As the group headed down Magnolia Avenue, they turned on Jerome and saw eight redwoods growing in a circle at the Jerome Triangle at Fairview Avenue. Redwoods often grow this way because they are from the seeds of a mother tree in the center. The walkers continued in a long line down Oakland Avenue. It took two stop light cycles for all the walkers to cross Grand Avenue. They noticed an unusual tree near the curb, with a trunk about five feet in diameter and green, spikey palms 10 to 15 feet above. Rob Smith used a phone app to identify it as a Spineless Yucca, native to Central America. After crossing the Oakland Avenue Bridge to Sunnyside Avenue, they observed at the edge of Linda Beach Park was a grove of four or five more Heritage Tree redwoods. The group went down Sunnyside and enjoyed seeing the distinctive brick home built by Daryl Rush, a Piedmont contractor and builder. It is notable for its long curving brick front wall with a built-in brick bench. Next was a walk to the Wildwood Triangle at the corner of Wildwood and Nova. Before arriving at the mini park that contains another 13 Coast redwoods, the walkers stopped in front of a home owned by Sidney Dearing in the 1920s. He was a successful African-American café owner who was driven from the city in 1924 by other Piedmont citizens. In May of that year, more than 500 people gathered in front of the home and refused to disperse until Dearing agreed to sell the house and leave Piedmont. Later, Dearing and his family moved back to Oakland. (See sidneydearing.com for the full, sad story.) The good news is that the current Piedmont City Council is exploring a tribute to Dearing. Before returning to the Exedra, they took a vote on which tree they liked best. The vote was inconclusive, but the Spineless Yucca seemed to have the edge. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu.
