articles.text: Guests attending a screening of Harold and Maude at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. When a 17-year-old boy’s mother gives him a sports car, he fires up his blowtorch and converts it into a hearse. That’s just one quirky moment in the 1971 movie Harold and Maude, now considered a cult classic. Its screening drew an approving crowd of 20 viewers to the second gathering of Piedmont’s new movie group, the Second Thursday Flix Fest on February 9. Sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, the movie group now takes place in the Center for the Arts at 801 Magnolia Avenue. It meets on the second Thursday of each month. Doors open at 10:15 a.m., with a show time at 10:30. Participants are welcome to bring snacks or lunch. Darby Gragg gave a detailed introduction to the film, which was directed by Hal Ashby. That blowtorch-wielding kid, Harold (Bud Cort) is troubled in a bizarre, charming way – we can’t help liking him. His odd psyche compels him to stage fake suicides, and the movie opens with one of them, in which he pretends to hang himself. His audience of choice is his mother, played by an amusingly arch Vivian Pickles. Wise to his tricks, she’s never alarmed – she just wants to get him married and out of the house. Harold also likes to hang out at funerals, and that’s where Maude, a 79-year old pixie who is as unorthodox as he is, spots him and whisks him away in a stolen car. She lives in an abandoned railway wagon by the side of the road, and that’s where, as their relationship develops, she teaches him the banjo, bolsters him with affection, and, well, seduces him. Talk about May/December! Maude is played by the wonderful Ruth Gordon, and she and Bud Cort work well together in inhabiting a tale that is offbeat in the extreme but also often very funny. It’s a lighthearted black comedy that’s given extra fizz by several Cat Stevens songs. The Piedmont audience gave the film 100% thumbs up. Some comments were: “It’s a refreshing delight,” and, “It has lot of depth.” One viewer wondered “how young people would react to it,” and another liked how it advocated “accepting differences.” “Great music,” said another. The Second Thursday Flix Fest meets again on March 9 to view the Alfred Hitchcock classic thriller, North by Northwest, starring Cary Grant, Eva Marie Saint and James Mason. There is now space for more people to attend. The group is open to anyone over 18 years of age, and there are no fees. Participants may attend on a drop-in basis with no obligations. Registration with the Recreation Department is required at: https:// bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Robert Hall is the longtime theater and dance reviewer in the Piedmont Post.

articles.text: Connie Herrick (front) of Piedmont Connect with the PHS Green Team. Piedmont High School (PHS) is about to become a garden oasis for bees and other pollinators. The PHS Green Club recently launched the “Bee-Friendly Flower Project,” an ambitious plan to install bee-friendly plants in concrete-lined boxes that extend along the walls and walkways of the library and the student center. This landscaping improvement is a much-needed bonus as these boxes are currently occupied by weeds or dead plants. “The planting will start in mid-Spring. We’re getting advice on what to plant from District Facilities Director Pete Palmer, and my mom, Gillian Atchley, who is a native plant gardener. We’ll put in a mix of native flowers that are low maintenance and low-water use,” said Green Club Co-President Max Rivera. The school district is providing the project’s infrastructure. “Possibly starting in the next few weeks, we’ll remove the old landscaping, add new soil amendment and install new irrigation where it’s needed. It’s a great environmental project,” said Palmer. The Green Club currently consists of 45 students and has 20 active members, who meet every week to discuss projects and potential volunteer activities, both within and outside Piedmont. They are supported by PHS history teacher David Keller, who has been the Green Club’s faculty advisor for the past decade. “These students are doing an amazing job for the campus,” he said. “They’re motivated and taking the initiative. I just try to get out of their way.” In addition to the bee-friendly boxes, the club supports the Climate Literacy Resolution, which advocates teaching California students from K-12 about climate change in every classroom. According to Schools for Climate Action, more than 40 California school districts and county education offices have already adopted the resolution. The club is trying to persuade the Piedmont School District to include it in the curriculum. Two years ago, Green Club Co-President Elena Blanco worked on the Club’s fundraising effort to install solar panels on the new high school. “We raised $60,000,” she said. The funds went toward installing solar panels on the mansard roof of the new classroom building, which Palmer noted, was a very difficult job and was greatly benefited with the club’s contribution. Club members also volunteer at city events, including recycling trash at the Harvest Festival and helping load compost at the city’s compost giveaways. Outside of Piedmont, Blanco and other club members volunteer at the Friends of Sausal Creek Nursery and seek out other local organizations to help. Asked what inspired her to get involved, Blanco said, “I wasn’t into hiking and the outdoors until I went backpacking with my aunt in Alaska. That opened my eyes to the beauty and joys of the outdoor world.” Rivera added, “I’ve been surrounded by nature all my life and (now) spend lots of time outdoors – on the mountain biking team, and rafting, rock climbing and hiking in Colorado. I feel like I should give back to nature.” As they walked around the front of the new high school building, Rivera and Blanco noted the scraggly, dying vines attached to vertical posts. “Here’s another opportunity for bee-friendly plants,” they said. The Green Club has a fundraising effort underway with the goal of raising $700 for the new pollinator plants, soil and irrigation. Piedmont Connect has issued a $350 matching grant to the Club to help launch the Bee-Friendly Pollinator Project. Donations may be made at: Gofundme.com/f/help-to-fundphs-green-club. Marjorie Blackwell is a Board Member of Piedmont Connect, a collaborative community organization supporting resident initiatives and city efforts to build a sustainable future. For sustainability and climate action resources, visit Connect’s website: Piedmontconnect.org. Green Club Co-Presidents Max Rivera (left) and Elena Blanco (right), along with Edwin Tang, help identify a plot of land on the high school campus to be planted with pollinator-friendly flowers.
articles.title: Green team to plant bee-friendly flowers on PHS campus

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Department’s First Mondays Reading Group met with a record turnout of 22 readers on February 6 at the Community Hall to discuss Prisoners of Geography, a 2015 non-fiction book about geopolitics by British author and journalist Tim Marshall. The group included Bob and Mady Hall, Mike and Nancy Henn, Melba Yee, Richard Sigel, Carol Warren, Martin Levy, Gerry and Darby Gragg, Ken Young, Lisa Euphrat, Leigh Sorensen, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Lois Price, Laura Goldman, Adrienne Hamlin, Karin Fetherston, Susan Ode, Bella Almanzan, Dick Carter, and discussion leader Priscilla Wanerus. In the book, Marshall uses 10 maps of regions around the world to explain the geopolitical situations and strategies of world powers. Marshall explains that all leaders of nations are constrained by geography. Their choices are limited by mountains, rivers, and seas. Writers often focus on people, ideas, and political movements, but without geography we never fully understand world events. The author explains that Russia lacks its own warm-water ports. Some of its Arctic ports freeze each winter, and Russian ships must contend with the ice packs to the north of the Arctic coastline. Additionally, the flat plain on Russia’s western border provides an easy route for invaders. Marshal contends these needs and conditions made Russia’s annexation of Crimea inevitable. His chapter on Russia, written in 2015, seems prophetic in the light of its 2022 invasion of Ukraine. Prisoners of Geography was another great book for a discussion. Some loved it while others didn’t care for it, so the book provided a catalyst for related topic conversations. Those on the positive side felt they learned a lot, but many readers didn’t understand how geography can affect populations and cultures. They learned how mountains and rivers can keep people from interacting. This was as much a book on history as geography. Readers said Marshall’s detailed information was helpful, and they would now look at maps differently. They said it helped them better understand Putin’s motivations for invading Ukraine. They liked Marshall’s easy writing style and occasion humor too. Those on the negative side they felt the book overpromised and the title was misleading. Ten maps didn’t explain everything about the world, and the book didn’t provide an understanding of different people’s humanity, or how technology will affect the limiting effects of geography. The book generated some side discussions about the relative strengths of the American and Chinese cultural structures. Members of the group also shared experiences in countries where geographic barriers and language dialects can keep people from understanding one another. With their discussion complete the group considered their next books. They had previously selected The Buddha in the Attic, a 2011 novel by American author Julie Otsuka, for March, and Trevor Noah’s memoir, Born a Crime, as the April selection. The group’s next discussion will be on March 6 at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting, they will meet outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, but registration is required at https://bit.ly/3R86PP4.

articles.text: Robert (Bob) Ball, a native Piedmonter and in recent years a resident of Pleasant Hill, passed away of neck cancer at his home on February 6, 2023. He was surrounded his family and died 20 days shy of his 77th birthday. Born on February 26, 1946, in Wisconsin, Bob moved with his family to Piedmont at the age of six. He went through the Piedmont public schools, where he was a star athlete in track and football and earned the coveted Kurkjian Award in football as a junior and senior. The award is given to the athlete who demonstrates the ideals of sportsmanship and team play. While in high school he served as both captain of the football team and student body president. He graduated from Piedmont High in 1964, and then from San Jose State University. He later received his master’s degree in hospital administration from U.C. Berkeley. In his early career, he focused on rural health care in California while working at Woodland Memorial Hospital. After moving back to Piedmont in 1985, he went into hospital administration at the Surgery Center in Oakland and ended his career in 2010 with an anesthesiologist group in Walnut Creek. Bob loved having fun and knew how to have a good time. He loved being outdoors, whether camping, hiking, gardening, or water sports. In the 1980s-1990s, he spent many happy summers on family camping trips to Shaver Lake and Bernie Falls waterskiing, boogie boarding, and playing Bob Ball with his beloved 1970 GTO rounds of Pit, Canasta, and Jenkins Says. He became the stuff of legends in his family. In his retirement, Bob enjoyed traveling, first internationally, and more recently, throughout the Southwest of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico. At home, he spent his leisure time tending his roses and building an impressive world for his Lionel model trains. Throughout his life, Bob was devoted to Piedmont and his close friends from elementary and high school. He played a central role in organizing his class of 1964 reunions and annual gatherings and proudly drove his blue 1970 GTO in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade over the years. Bob is survived by his partner, Lynne Deutscher, and his four children and their spouses: Jeremy Ball and wife Amy, Jeffrey Ball and wife Maggie, Joe Ball, Bob Ball, an avid water skier, in 1984 Bob Ball holds the football team’s coveted Kurkjian Award, which he won as a junior and senior at Piedmont High School. and Jordan Tharp and husband Kevin; his six grandchildren: Charlie, Julia, Emily, Benjamin, Ellie, and Nolan. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations in Bob’s honor be made to the American Cancer Society or the League to Save Lake Tahoe. The family hopes his friends honor Bob by listening to his favorite music, the Beach Boys, and enjoying time outdoors. The family will hold a celebration of Bob’s life at a later date. pages.text: Wednesday, February 15, 2023 25 Obituary Piedmont’s Bob Ball passes away on February 6 Robert (Bob) Ball, a native Piedmonter and in recent years a resident of Pleasant Hill, passed away of neck cancer at his home on February 6, 2023. He was surrounded his family and died 20 days shy of his 77th birthday. Born on February 26, 1946, in Wisconsin, Bob moved with his family to Piedmont at the age of six. He went through the Piedmont public schools, where he was a star athlete in track and football and earned the coveted Kurkjian Award in football as a junior and senior. The award is given to the athlete who demonstrates the ideals of sportsmanship and team play. While in high school he served as both captain of the football team and student body president. He graduated from Piedmont High in 1964, and then from San Jose State University. He later received his master’s degree in hospital administration from U.C. Berkeley. In his early career, he focused on rural health care in California while working at Woodland Memorial Hospital. After moving back to Piedmont in 1985, he went into hospital administration at the Surgery Center in Oakland and ended his career in 2010 with an anesthesiologist group in Walnut Creek. Bob loved having fun and knew how to have a good time. He loved being outdoors, whether camping, hiking, gardening, or water sports. In the 1980s-1990s, he spent many happy summers on family camping trips to Shaver Lake and Bernie Falls waterskiing, boogie boarding, and playing Bob Ball with his beloved 1970 GTO rounds of Pit, Canasta, and Jenkins Says. He became the stuff of legends in his family. In his retirement, Bob enjoyed traveling, first internationally, and more recently, throughout the Southwest of Utah, Colorado, Arizona and New Mexico. At home, he spent his leisure time tending his roses and building an impressive world for his Lionel model trains. Throughout his life, Bob was devoted to Piedmont and his close friends from elementary and high school. He played a central role in organizing his class of 1964 reunions and annual gatherings and proudly drove his blue 1970 GTO in Piedmont’s Fourth of July Parade over the years. Bob is survived by his partner, Lynne Deutscher, and his four children and their spouses: Jeremy Ball and wife Amy, Jeffrey Ball and wife Maggie, Joe Ball, Bob Ball, an avid water skier, in 1984 Bob Ball holds the football team’s coveted Kurkjian Award, which he won as a junior and senior at Piedmont High School. and Jordan Tharp and husband Kevin; his six grandchildren: Charlie, Julia, Emily, Benjamin, Ellie, and Nolan. In lieu of flowers, the family suggests that memorial donations in Bob’s honor be made to the American Cancer Society or the League to Save Lake Tahoe. The family hopes his friends honor Bob by listening to his favorite music, the Beach Boys, and enjoying time outdoors. The family will hold a celebration of Bob’s life at a later date. February #1 Great Read 25 Indie Next Best Reads for February Don’t Fear the Reaper By Stephen Graham Jones, Horror “Not just a worthy sequel to My Heart is a Chainsaw, but one that, after you’ve read it, you can’t imagine the first book without. Jones has a true gift — he can make you shudder in horror and tear up in the same sentence.” —Olivia Morris, Harvard Book Store, Cambridge, MA Secretly Yours By Tessa Bailey, Romance “Get ready to dive into a new favorite book. Secretly Yours is a delight!” — Bridey Morris, R.J. Julia Booksellers, Madison, CT Georgie, All Along By Kate Clayborn, Kensington, Romance “Kate Clayborn always delivers, and Georgie, All Along is no different. This is an excellent winter read to curl up with.” —Preet Singh, Eagle Eye Book Shop, Decatur, GA The Guest Lecture By Martin Riker, Grove Press, Black Cat, Fiction “Riker’s smart and offbeat story takes place over one night, as a newly unemployed economics professor mulls over a lecture she’s about to give. Stretching across five decades and three generations, this powerful novel is for anyone who cares about a woman’s right to decide her future.” —Beth Stroh, Viewpoint Books, Columbus, IN “This is the best mystery I’ve read. The narrator understood that just because he was telling the story, it didn’t make the story about him. Piedmont Real Estate Update February 2023 Two Decades of Data Our residential real estate market has undergone dramatic changes over the past couple of decades. Looking back at 20 years of sales in Piedmont, we found several interesting stories in the data. First, while we saw variation in appreciation rates over time, primarily due to the “Great Recession,” Piedmont still performed well. Homes appreciated 5% per year, on average, over the last two decades. Second, the highest number of sales on the Multiple Listing Service (MLS) for Piedmont was 153 in 2002, likely accompanying the recovery from the “dot-com bust” in 2000. Not surprisingly, the lowest number of total sales was 75 in 2008. The next highest number of sales was 148 in 2021, likely a combination of a low interest rate environment and households electing to make different lifestyle decisions as a result of Covid-19. articles.text: The annual Piedmont Cub Scout Pinewood Derby took over the gym at Piedmont Community Church last Saturday morning, February 4, with more than 100 Cubs racing their homemade cars. In the 56th year of the Piedmont event, the youngest Scouts, the Lions and Tigers, started off the day at 9:00 a.m. and took their best shot on a custom wooden track built in 1967 by James Obando. Next were the Wolves, then the Bears, and then the oldest racers, Junior and Senior Webelos, who had meticulously crafted cars to close out the official races. An anxious silence falls over the crowd of Bear Scouts before their race at the annual Piedmont Cub Scout Pinewood Derby as Webelo Madison Jung aligns the cars. Owners of the fastest cars from the oldest Cub Scout racers, the Webelo division: 1st place Bailey Gregovich (right), 2nd place Ryan Morrison, and 3rd place Colin Hemig-Hance. Girl Scout Troop 31765 had their own Pinewood Derby in the afternoon, but girls in the now coed Scout troops had already stolen the show. Three of the four groups of races were won by girls, including 1st place racers: 3rd grader Winnie Rogan (Bears) and 5th grader Bailey Gregovich (Webelos). Scouts are honored for their hard work in creating race cars beyond a goal of speed. Design, Craftsmanship, and two Judges Awards went to contestants in each group. “The simple block of wood that everyone begins with is turned into an unbelievably diverse range of creations that showcase the kids’ passions, style, humor and eye for design,” said David Cole, co-chair of the Derby this year with Greg Wolff. They were aided trackside by Scout mom Caroline Jung and Webelo scouts Niko Wolff and Madison Jung. The race had some photo finishes, and races so close that the electronic finish line, engineered

articles.text: On January 27, city staff announced that they would bring the Housing Element to City Council for adoption after the state’s 90-day review period, which ends on February 16. Adoption is expected in late February or March. The state deadline for Housing Element adoption was January 31; and cities not meeting the deadline face the “Builder’s Remedy.” This is a clause added to California’s Housing Accountability Act in 1990 by which developers can file an application for a housing development which does not comply with a city’s local zoning laws, if the city has not passed its Housing Element. Any housing development applied for under the Builder’s Remedy must have 20% of its units available to lower-income households, or all its units available to middle-income households or transitional or supportive housing. However, state building limitations still hold — most pertinently the California Environmental Quality Act, a statute passed in 1970 by then-governor Ronald Reagan which limits proposed building projects on the grounds of potentially “significant environmental effects.” “Generally,” said Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson, “[the Builder’s Remedy] is a tool used by developers in cities where there are sites ready to go, where somebody has been working on a project for a while and now they have their opportunity to push it forward. It’s not really that useful for properties that have no developer interests, because it takes time to figure out what kind of project makes sense.” Under the Builder’s Remedy, any noncompliant city is also ineligible for state grants and funding for road repair and infrastructure. articles.text: In preparation for African American History Month this year, I am reading Against The Hounds of Hell: A Life of Howard Thurman by Peter Eisenstadt. I highly recommend the book. It is a definitive biography of one of the great spiritual leaders of our time. (Thurman’s most wellknown book, Jesus and the Disinherited, was, along with the Bible and United States Constitution, one of the three books that Martin Luther King Jr. carried with him when he traveled.) As the story of Thurman’s life unfolds, Eisenstadt describes the then 44-year-old pastor and scholar arriving in San Francisco in July 1944 after a five-day cross country train ride from Washington D.C. where he had been Dean of the Chapel at Howard University. After settling into a home that needed much care (think rodent infestation), Thurman began his work as the Senior Minister of the recently founded Church for the Fellowship of All People. Thurman told the church leaders that he wanted the church’s highest commitment to be to a peace rooted “in the quality of life that emanates from the place rather than from pronouncements of one kind or another.” His words describe my hope for this year’s celebration of AAHM. While it is important, especially in the face of efforts like those being made by Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida to deny the significance of African American history, that we make pronouncements about the significance of this celebration, the lessons we carry with us from the study of African American history are of greater significance than the statements we make about it. That being said, Jemar Tisby, President of the Black Christian Collective, provides five helpful pronouncements about the celebration of Black History Month. • Celebrating honors the historic leaders of the Black Community

Remembrances of Howard Thurman By Pastor Jim Hopkins In preparation for African American History Month this year, I am reading Against The Hounds of Hell: A Life of Howard Thurman by Peter Eisenstadt. I highly recommend the book. It is a definitive biography of one of the great spiritual leaders of our time. (Thurman’s most wellknown book, Jesus and the Disinherited, was, along with the Bible and United States Constitution, one of the three books that Martin Luther King Jr. carried with him when he traveled.) As the story of Thurman’s life unfolds, Eisenstadt describes the then 44-year-old pastor and scholar arriving in San Francisco in July 1944 after a five-day cross country train ride from Washington D.C. where he had been Dean of the Chapel at Howard University. After settling into a home that needed much care (think rodent infestation), Thurman began his work as the Senior Minister of the recently founded Church for the Fellowship of All People. Thurman told the church leaders that he wanted the church’s highest commitment to be to a peace rooted “in the quality of life that emanates from the place rather than from pronouncements of one kind or another.” His words describe my hope for this year’s celebration of AAHM. While it is important, especially in the face of efforts like those being made by Governor Ron DeSantis of Florida to deny the significance of African American history, that we make pronouncements about the significance of this celebration, the lessons we carry with us from the study of African American history are of greater significance than the statements we make about it. That being said, Jemar Tisby, President of the Black Christian Collective, provides five helpful pronouncements about the celebration of Black History Month. • Celebrating honors the historic leaders of the Black Community • Celebrating helps us to be better stewards of the privileges we’ve gained • Celebrating provides an opportunity to highlight the best black history and culture • Celebrating creates an awareness for all people • Celebrating reminds us all the Black History is our history Yet, as important as these pronouncements are, repeating or re-posting them is no substitute for learning from a book like Against the Hounds of Hell, which reminds us in memorable ways of heroes like Howard Thurman. Heroes who faced constant danger, disrespect and disparagement simply because of the color of their skin. Heroes who were still able to teach “Wherever [Jesus’] spirit appears, the oppressed gather fresh courage; for he announced the good news that fear, hypocrisy and hatred, the three hounds of hell that track the trail of the disinherited, need have no dominion over them.” Jim Hopkins is Senior Pastor of Lakeshore Avenue Baptist Church, 3534 Lakeshore Avenue at Mandana Blvd., Oakland. jim@labcoakland.org 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Selen Ozturk Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Sohrab “Seb” Ford (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: On Monday, February 6, around 4 a.m., a 7.8 magnitude earthquake hit Turkey and Syria. The quake was the most powerful in the country since December 1939, when an earthquake of identical magnitude killed 30,000 people in December 1939. As of Tuesday afternoon, February 7, the death toll passed 7,200. The epicenter was 14.2 miles north of Nurdaği, a city in Gaziantep province, where southeastern Turkey borders northwestern Syria. Aftershocks ripped throughout the day and region; the strongest one measured a magnitude of 7.5, nine hours after and 59 miles north of the original epicenter. Tremors were felt as far away as Israel and Lebanon. Turkish President Recep Erdoğan declared a three-month state of emergency in 10 provinces affected by the earthquake. Turkey reported at least 5,434 deaths and 31,777 injuries. In government-controlled parts of Syria, at least 812 people were killed and 1,449 injured. Civil defense workers in the rebel-held northwest — which already faced a humanitarian crisis nearly 12 years into a bloody civil war — reported at least 1,020 deaths and 2,400 injuries. Thousands of buildings were flattened, leaving inhabitants homeless in near-freezing weather. Governments worldwide are pledging assistance and deploying aid as thousands of rescue workers desperately dig possible survivors from the rubble. The United States announced on Monday that it would deploy two specialized search-and-rescue teams of about 80 members each, one from Los Angeles and another from Virginia. Here are organizations working on rescue and recovery efforts. Donations are greatly needed. UNICEF The United Nations International Children’s Emergency Fund is in Syria and prioritizing water, sanitation, hygiene and nutrition, and focusing on helping unaccompanied children locate their families. UNICEF is accepting donations at unicefusa.org. Global Giving Global Giving, which helps local nonprofit agencies, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3DSf8JI to help fund emergency medical workers’ ability to provide food, shelter and medicine, among other necessities. As needs in Turkey and Syria change, the organization will focus on longterm assistance. The International Federation of Red Cross and Red Crescent Societies The IFRC is requesting donations for its Disaster Response Emergency Fund at bit.ly/3HFJe49 so it can send “immediate cash assistance.” OXFAM OXFAM, an international organization that fights poverty, is working with women’s cooperatives in Turkey to determine an appropriate immediate and longterm response plan. It is accepting donations at bit.ly/3YfjYso. CARE CARE, an organization that works with impoverished communities, is accepting donations that will go toward food, shelter and hygiene kits, among other items. Donate and learn more at bit.ly/3DRU3yO. Doctors Without Borders DWB, which responds to medical emergencies around the world, is collecting donations at bit.ly/3I7Jw5c. The Syrian American Medical Society SAMS is a United Statesbased humanitarian group that supplies medical care in Syria and nearby countries. At least one of its hospitals in northwestern Syria, Al Dana, received major damage, and SAMS collecting donations at bit.ly/3RJdBLz to deliver emergency aid. Save the Children Save the Children is accepting donations at bit.ly/3I6QmIb for its Children’s Emergency Fund, which will help provide children with food, shelter and warm clothing. The Union of Medical Care and Relief Organizations UOSSM, which since 2012 has provided medical relief and health care services inside Syria and to Syrian refugees in Turkey, is collecting money at https:// www.uossm.org/donate. Empowering the TurkishAmerican Community ETAC, a nonprofit which provides support services and guidance to members of the Turkish community with lack of means or language skills, is collecting donations which will be sent directly and entirely to rescue teams. Learn more and donate at bit.ly/3YeRz5W.
articles.title: Turkish, Syrian earthquake relief: how Piedmonters can help

articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wealth of opportunities to explore local volunteer work. Here are just a few. Mercy Brown Bag The Mercy Brown Bag program distributes well over one million pounds of food every year, thanks to hundreds of volunteers. The effort was launched in 1982 by residents at the Mercy Retirement & Care Center who saw that seniors in their Oakland neighborhoods were experiencing food insecurity. There are many ways to volunteer, including distributing lunch bags to homebound seniors, helping with special events or administrative tasks, helping at any of the 66 distribution sites throughout Alameda County, and translating written materials. Visit mercybrownbag.org/volunteer to learn more. Piedmont Community Service Crew Piedmont Community Service Crew (PCSC) is a coed youth-led organization under the auspices of the Piedmont Scout Council. It is the largest of the Venturing Crews with approximately 150 members, and actively seeks high school, middle school, and parent volunteers for ongoing programs. PCSC events and programs include meal preparation and cooking for low-income, elderly, and homeless members of the community; home renovation and environmental cleanup; and community engagement work such as youth tutoring. For more information on how to get involved, visit pcservicecrew.org. Asian Health Services Asian Health Services, located in Oakland, provides health, social, and advocacy services for all regardless of income, insurance status, immigration status, language or culture. The organization provides healthcare to more than 50,000 patients in English and over 14 Asian languages. Volunteers are critical to the center and contribute enormously to patients’ experiences. Opportunities are available in both clinical and non-clinical settings, including health education, fundraising, public relations, language access, administration, and midlevel or nurse practitioner positions. You must complete an online application. For more information, call (510) 986-6830, email hr@ ahschc.org, or visit asianhealthservices.org/volunteer-opportunities. Lake Merritt Institute Each month, thousands of pounds of trash accumulate in Lake Merritt. Lake Merritt Institute partners with local citizens and Oakland Unified School District students to help keep the lake’s shoreline and creeks clean on a weekly basis. Volunteers meet at the Institute office, on the shores of Lake Merritt, and usually work for between two and three hours during a shift. Training is provided, as are gloves, trash bags, barrels, nets, directions, and other materials. Cleanups are held five times a week during the school year and 3-4 times a week in the summer. Visit lakemerrittinstitute.org/how-youcan-help to learn more and sign up. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? articles.text: The February 1 edition of the Piedmont Post contained a story with a headline that bears clarification. Details in the story are correct, but the headline, “Fentanyl-laced drugs found in Piedmont,” more accurately would be, “Piedmont teen hospitalization attributed to Fentanyl.” The cursory testing of mushrooms confiscated by Piedmont Police did not show a trace of fentanyl. The confiscated drugs were sent to Alameda County for a full analysis. Results have not yet been received. The confirmation of fentanyl found in the blood of a Piedmont teenager, who was hospitalized and has fully recovered, comes from an article in The Piedmont Highlander, the school newspaper, and Piedmont School District-related emails. There is no evidence to show that fentanyl was purposefully ingested.
articles.title: Clarification on Fentanyl story

articles.text: The California Energy Commission approved Piedmont’s updated reach codes at their January 25 meeting, formalizing this set of local energy efficiency requirements for building projects that reach beyond statewide standards. Piedmont’s reach codes require that all new single-family homes and detached accessory dwelling units (ADUs) be all-electric. Additionally, the reach codes require energy efficiency measures be included in certain renovations to existing properties: • Electric panel replacements or upgrades must have capacity to accommodate future electrification of all appliances • Kitchen or laundry area renovation projects must install outlets that allow for the use of electric appliances in the future • Renovations or additions to existing homes that meet certain project value thresholds must incorporate one or more items from a menu of energy efficiency and electrification measures, such as installing insulation in attics or walls, replacing gas furnaces or water heaters with heat pump alternatives, or swapping incandescent light fixtures with LEDs • Projects that add a new upper level or increase the building’s roof area by 30% or more must install a photovoltaic (solar power) system Improving energy efficiency in existing buildings When Piedmont first adopted reach codes in 2021, it was one of the first cities in California to implement reach codes that apply to renovation projects in existing buildings in addition to new construction. Because the city is largely built out, improving energy efficiency in existing buildings is a critical part of meeting emissions reduction targets set in the city’s Climate Action Plan. Currently, natural gas use in residential buildings comprises about half of Piedmont’s in-territory greenhouse gas emissions. Reach codes, combined with other city initiatives like the recently launched home electrification rebate pilot program, play an important role in reducing the amount of energy used heating and cooling homes across Piedmont. Piedmont’s original reach codes have helped improve energy efficiency in over 150 home renovation projects. Changes in 2023 reach codes The updated reach codes are largely identical to the original set. Because reach codes are local amendments to statewide building codes, Piedmont must re-adopt its reach codes every time the State updates its building standards — which happens every three years. The most recent update to the State code took effect on January 1, 2023. Changes include: • minor terminology changes to align with updated language in the state code • increase in the project value thresholds that trigger reach codes for renovation projects, to accommodate rising construction costs • addition of a new energy efficiency measure (exterior wall insulation) to the menu of options for renovation projects Multifamily reach codes in development Existing reach codes apply only to single-family homes. The city is currently in the process of developing reach codes for multi-family properties. Community members can help inform what electrification and energy efficiency measures will be part of the multi-family reach codes by completing a brief online survey. The survey, found at bit.ly/3wWnegg, is available through March 1. For more information on reach codes, visit the city’s reach code webpage at bit.ly/ 3JA1Chs. For questions about the updated reach codes, contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman by email at sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3058. articles.text: Learn how you can make your home more energy efficient and get help paying for upgrades at a building electrification webinar presented by the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division tomorrow, Thursday, February 9 at 4 p.m. Replacing polluting gas appliances with clean, electric alternatives helps reduce greenhouse gas emissions from your home, improves indoor air quality, and saves money on energy bills. At the webinar, you’ll learn how to get started on electrifying your home, the types of electric appliances you’ll want to consider, and what rebate programs are available to help offset the costs of making these upgrades. Experts from the City of Piedmont, the Bay Area Regional Energy Network (BayREN), and local contractors will be on hand to answer questions. To attend the webinar, register online at: bit.ly/3DMNYng. Home electrification rebates The City of Piedmont launched a pilot rebate program for home electrification projects in January 2023, in hopes of encouraging more residents to make the switch to heat pump water heaters and high-efficiency heat pumps. Although upfront costs for such projects can be high, efficient heat pumps can lower energy bills dramatically, which results in significant savings over the long term. Traditionally, heating, ventilation, and air conditioning systems (HVAC) are the biggest home energy consumers, followed by water heating systems. For the average house, installing electric heat pumps in place of a gas furnace and gas water heater will reduce heating emissions by more than 45% over 10 years. Piedmont’s home electrification rebates help cover installation and labor costs on eligible projects and can be combined with other rebate programs such as those offered through BayREN. Qualified lower-income residents (those earning below $87,00 for a 2-person household) are eligible for double the standard rebate. Rebates are also available for service panel upgrades if they are necessary to support a qualified heat pump appliance. To be eligible for a rebate, upgrade projects must: • Replace an existing gas appliance • Be permanently installed and fixed to an existing single family or multifamily building • Have a City of Piedmont building permit submitted on or after January 3, 2023 • Be installed by a licensed contractor with an active City of Piedmont business license For program details and a full list of requirements, see the City’s Electrification Rebate Program Guide at bit.ly/40wZop6. The City Council has allocated $50,000 in funding for the rebate program pilot. Applications will be considered in the order they are received; the program will continue until funding is exhausted. For more information on the Electrification Rebate Program, see the City’s Rebates and Incentives webpage. With questions, contact Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman by email at sustainability@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3058.

articles.text: Piedmont Wellness Center will screen Like, a social media documentary aimed at pre-teens, teens and their families on Thursday, February 16, at 7 p.m. at the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus. The 50-minute documentary is focused on educating families about the impacts of social media. The screening is being co-hosted by the Wellness Center Support Committee and Piedmont Middle School. The screening was the brainchild of Piedmont Middle School counselor Amy Sharp. “We reached out to the Wellness Center Support Committee because we saw a lot come up with PMS students around social media during the past year. We were seeing instances of unkind and hurtful comments on digital platforms. The primary concern of showing the film was so that our students understand the harm being caused,” she said. The Wellness Center Support Committee responded immediately to the idea. “Counselors have front-row seats to the social-emotional challenges of our kids,” said Laurie Misra, a former Intern Therapist at the Wellness Center The Wellness Center, located at Piedmont High School, provides free mental health services to Piedmont students in middle school, Piedmont High, and Millennium High. So far this school year, students have visited the center well over 1,000 times. Under the supervision of two licensed psychologists, six intern therapists provide mental health support to Piedmont students, meeting once or twice for some or weekly with those who request it. Sharp said that outreach by the Wellness Center Support Committee has been incredibly helpful for the PMS counseling team. “They have been really proactive in reaching out to ask us how they can help,” she said. In the film Max Stossel, Head of Education Content for the Center for Humane Technology, says to the teen viewers, “These devices are not designed for you. You are not the customer; you are the product being sold here. Are you really using technology or is technology using you?”

articles.text: Through love, loss and flamboyant feather headdresses, this year’s high school musical, Hello, Dolly!, hit the stage of the Alan Harvey Theater for four evenings, February 2-5, with a flourish. Directed by PHS dance instructor Amy Moorhead, the show reprised the 1963 musical with brilliant costuming and lively acting and singing. Set in Yonkers, New York, in the early 20th century, the story follows the widowed matchmaker, Dolly Levi, on her own quest for love. Dolly is determined to marry a rich but ill-tempered client, Horace Vandergelder, for his money and money alone. However, in the end, she finds a relationship far more profitable than expected. PHS junior, Breah Bell, displayed exquisite vocal talent in the lead role, accompanied by senior Paden Andrews as Horace Vandergelder. While flashy and outgoing, the Hello, Dolly is very grounded and easy to relate to. “I think what makes Hello, Dolly such a classic and timeless musical, is that it’s so focused on human nature,” said Andrews, “the whole story is all about facing your own fear, and powering through and ‘rejoining the human race’ as Dolly says.” “[Dolly’s] personality matches with mine a lot. We’re both very outgoing and charismatic,” said Bell, “That makes it more enjoyable to play her.” Bell quickly credited the cast as her favorite part of putting on the musical. “Anyone considering going into show business, try out for the musical, any musical, any show, try it. You get to meet so many new people and try so many new things. It is so much fun,” added Bell. The exquisite and bright costumery shined on the new Alan Harvey Theater stage as the performers paid a beautiful homage to Pearl Bailey’s 1967 award winning performance as Dolly. Ensemble members Greta Scheluning (bottom left), Isabelle Myers, Danielle Zaroukian and (top): Amelia Addington, Kaeli Young, and Clare Weiss wearing bright “Sunday clothes” in Piedmont High School’s production of the musical Hello, Dolly Piedmont High School junior, Breah Bell, sang the lead role as Dolly Levi in the musical Hello, Dolly. Tara Kothari (left), as Irene Molloy, and Callan Mitchell, as Corneilus Hackl, dance in Horace’s Hat Shop after another successful match made by Dolly. Senior Callan Mitchell (left) and Junior Ken Sibal, as Barnaby Tucker, head to the big city.

articles.text: Piedmont High School has been awarded the College Board AP Computer Science Female Diversity Award for achieving high female representation in its course, AP Computer Science Principles. Five separate periods of the course are taught by Flint Christensen and Jennifr Newell. More than 1,100 education institutions achieved either 50% or higher female representation in one of the two AP computer science courses, or a percentage of the female computer science exam takers meeting or exceeding that of the school’s female population during the 2021-22 school year. In 2022, PHS was one of 832 schools recognized for female participation in AP Computer Science Principles (CSP). “The single greatest change has been the introduction of AP Computer Science Principles. The College Board actually devised this course in part to address the misperception that girls had around computer science and to provide an experience that would be engaging for a diverse range of students,” said Christensen. “We are honored that Piedmont High School has earned this distinction and will continue our work in and out of the classroom to ensure students of all genders and backgrounds have the resources and opportunities for success,” said PUSD Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. Providing female students with access to computer science courses is critical to ensuring gender parity in the industry’s high-paying jobs and to driving innovation, creativity, and representation. The median annual wage for computer and information technology occupations was $97,430 in May 2021. Women represent 24% of the five million people in computing occupations. College Board research about AP Computer Science is encouraging. According to the data, female students who take the course in high school are more than five times as likely to major in computer science in college. articles.text: The start of a creative journey can happen at any second. It’s just about diving in and starting something new. But sometimes, getting started can feel incredibly daunting. We stop ourselves from trying new creative modalities because of fear of not being “good” or looking silly in front of our kids. Yet, research suggests that trying new things can have great benefits, including: improved memory, increased adaptability and better mood. A new creative activity could fit into a lot of different categories from music to visual art to crafting to baking. Recently, I decided to learn how to paint with gouache. To be clear, I don’t have a huge background in painting, but I have found that every time I play with a new medium I learn something about myself as a creator. It opens up curiosity and respect for artists who work in that medium or discipline. In the case of gouache, I was inspired because I learned that the original Disney animators who hand-painted the movie The Jungle Book used that medium. I have always been drawn into the richness and vibrancy of the colors used in that film. Bottom line: You don’t have to be an expert or a professional to benefit from playing with something new. It’s lovely to say “try something new,” but without inspiration it can feel nearly impossible. So, here are some ideas that might inspire your creative self and/or your creative family. Look at these prompts and just notice if anything comes to mind or sparks your interest. It doesn’t have to be literal, but just something that inspires you to make a connection. And then ask yourself, with this theme or idea, what kind of creative activity would you like to try for the first time? Poetry? Crochet? Oil Pastels? Crayon on Newspaper? • Shadow and Light • Bridge Over Nothingness • What’s at the End of the Rainbow? • Rhythms of Nature • Dragons vs. Unicorns • Your Tropical Island Awaits If none of these strike your fancy, try opening up any book to a random page and see what the first three words are that catch your eye. Then use those words as inspiration to just make something…anything! Have fun and create! Nina Meehan is a Creativity Consultant and speaker and former CEO of Nay Area Children’s Theatre. Find out more information about her work at gocreate. zone.
articles.title: In case you need some creative inspiration

AP Computer Science at PHS receives award for female diversity By Jay Russell Piedmont High School has been awarded the College Board AP Computer Science Female Diversity Award for achieving high female representation in its course, AP Computer Science Principles. Five separate periods of the course are taught by Flint Christensen and Jennifr Newell. More than 1,100 education institutions achieved either 50% or higher female representation in one of the two AP computer science courses, or a percentage of the female computer science exam takers meeting or exceeding that of the school’s female population during the 2021-22 school year. In 2022, PHS was one of 832 schools recognized for female participation in AP Computer Science Principles (CSP). “The single greatest change has been the introduction of AP Computer Science Principles. The College Board actually devised this course in part to address the misperception that girls had around computer science and to provide an experience that would be engaging for a diverse range of students,” said Christensen. “We are honored that Piedmont High School has earned this distinction and will continue our work in and out of the classroom to ensure students of all genders and backgrounds have the resources and opportunities for success,” said PUSD Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. Providing female students with access to computer science courses is critical to ensuring gender parity in the industry’s high-paying jobs and to driving innovation, creativity, and representation. The median annual wage for computer and information technology occupations was $97,430 in May 2021. Women represent 24% of the five million people in computing occupations. College Board research about AP Computer Science is encouraging. According to the data, female students who take the course in high school are more than five times as likely to major in computer science in college. Overall, female students account for 33% of AP Computer Science Principles participants and 25% of AP Computer Science A participants. Currently, 51% of the nation’s high schools teach foundational computer science. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team went into Friday’s match, February 3, against Castro Valley with its eyes on the prize. They knew that a win would mean clinching a berth in the North Coast Section post-season playoffs. Highly motivated, they put in perhaps their best performance of the season, defeating Castro Valley 5-0 at Witter Field before a hometown fan base. The victory improved Piedmont’s record to 7-1-5 overall and 5-1-4 in league (W-T-L) with just two matches left in the regular season. The final league games are tonight, Wednesday February 8 with Berkeley at Witter Field, and Friday at Encinal in Alameda. “I’m happy with how we played,” said veteran PHS coach Dan Chubbock after pinning a shutout on Castro Valley. “We created a lot of chances. We’ve been able to do all season, but we just haven’t been able to convert on a lot of them.. Tonight, we did. We didn’t want to let up,”. With 16 points toward the league table, Piedmont moved into second place (behind Berkeley’s 23 points) in the Western Alameda County Conference. Beating the Trojans was impressive considering Castro Valley entered Witter with a 10-4-5 record. But this time, CV rarely found a scoring opportunity in a game in which Piedmont put in a strong effort for the full 80 minutes. “We haven’t been getting the results we wanted. Tonight it felt like we finished our chances. We’re a really strong team, so it’s been frustrating because we’ve been playing well and just not getting the results we’ve been seeking. It felt good to get one back against a team we lost to earlier this season,” said senior leader Emily Fitzgerald. Piedmont’s goals all came from five different players: Louisa Symkowick, Audrey Lam, Arden Sorensen-Wald, Amy Derr, and Miranda Liu. Game Recap Piedmont came hot out of the gates with Lam firing a hard shot that clanged off of the crossbar around the 10th minute. The ball rebounded to Cameron Lorin whose shot was blocked. In the 19th minute, PHS struck when Symkowick retrieved a loose ball in a scramble in front of the net, slotting it home for the opening goal. Audrey Lam scored against Castro Valley and had three other shots ring off of the crossbar. Sophomore Louisa Symkowick scored the opening goal against Castro Valley in a 5-0 shutout. Piedmont players celebrate a goal against Castro Valley. Staff Photos Nine minutes later, Piedmont scored again when Lam jumped on a ball from a CV defender that was played from the goalkeeper. Lam corralled it and sent a rocket shot over the keeper’s head into the net from the 18-yard box. In first-half stoppage time, Sorensen-Wald scored at the end of some terrific interplay. On a break down the right wing, Liu centered a pass to Fitzgerald for a hard shot on target. It forced a loose ball off of the keeper’s hands, and Sorensen-Wald was positioned well for the rebound, putting it into the net. With a comfortable 3-0 lead, the Highlanders’ first goal in the second half came on free kick by Lorin to Derr who connected for the goal. Piedmont’s scoring ended in the 65th minute when sophomore winger Juliana Thornborrow, with some terrific footwork , worked her way around a defender in the box by the end line. Thornborrow played a pass toward the center of the area, and it took a slight deflection to Liu, who scored on a rightfooted shot. The Highlanders’ offensive onslaught continued in the remaining minutes as they pressed on for another goal. In the 67th minute Lola Beihn had a shot slam off the bottom of the crossbar, and three minutes later Lam hit the cross bar once again. Lam’s final shot on was pushed onto the side post with a diving save by the Castro Valley keeper. NEXT UP Piedmont hosts Berkeley tonight, February 8 for Senior Night at 6:00 p.m. at Witter Field. Ten members of the Class of 2023 will be honored: Morgan Hunt, Michaela Bini, Ellie DeVan, Kyra Dang, Audrey Harmon, Sophie Hebert, Emily Fitzgerald, Siena Riddel, Audrey Lam, and Cameron Lorin. Piedmont plays its final regular season game this Friday, February 10, at Encinal in Alameda at 6:00 p.m. North Coast Section post-season playoffs begin next Wednesday, February 15. The Highlanders will find out what their seeding is later this weekend. Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team saw its hopes of capturing its first Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division banner come to an end last night, Tuesday, February 7, falling to archrivals Bishop O’Dowd 55-49 in Binks Rawlings Gym. Earlier, Piedmont defeated Alameda 73-68 on February 2, and beat Castro Valley 54-30 on Tuesday, January 31. Brit Burden scored 15 points against O’Dowd. It also marked Senior Night for PHS, where the school honored its six seniors: Harris, Evans, Riordan, Teagan Haddawy, and Matteo and Bautista Costa. Final scorers: Harris had 24, Silverberg had eight, Linnane had five, Burden and Riordan had four, Theo Evans had three, and Costa, Holmes, and Bornstein had two. articles.text: PHS will host Berkeley on Friday, February 10 in the season-finale. With the Highlanders’ loss to O’Dowd last night, former Piedmont High head coach Mike Hudson brings his Berkeley Yellowjackets to Piedmont as this year’s league champion. Of last night’s game with O’Dowd, Piedmont coach Ben Spencer said, “The keys to win were to defend, rebound, and outwork them on 50/50 balls. We actually checked off all those boxes, which is usually a win. It didn’t go that way, but we stayed in the game, executed well, and got some really good looks off of running our stuff—we just didn’t knock them down.” “I couldn’t be more proud of this team. It’s a loss in the book, but looking ahead to postseason, I think we match up really well in our division of NCS,” said coach Ben Spencer. It was a productive game for senior forward Brit Burden who led the scoring with 15 points. “We fought hard. We got punked in our first game against them and we came out a lot stronger in this game. Some shots weren’t falling,” said Burden. Piedmont will prepare for the post-season Division 3 North Coast Section playoffs with a first round game scheduled for Tuesday, February 15. 55-49 loss to Bishop O’Dowd Piedmont ended the first quarter holding a 18-12 lead and went into halftime clinging to a threepoint lead, 29-26 after O’Dowd converted a 3-pointer in the final seconds of the half. The Dragons went ahead 34-32 with 3:30 to play in the third quarter and the two sides continued to trade points into the fourth. In the last quarter, Piedmont took a 40-39 lead with 6:45 left in the game when Burden gained an offensive rebound and made a free throw. But O’Dowd hit two free throws to go ahead 41-40. Declan Linnane tied the game at 41-41, but the Dragons hit a 3-pointer to jump ahead 44-41 and never relinquished the lead. PHS was within one point at 48-47 following a nice assist from Matteo Costa to A.J. Harris, but O’Dowd scored the next four points to go up 52-47. Piedmont’s goals all came from five different players: Louisa Symkowick, Audrey Lam, Arden Sorensen-Wald, Amy Derr, and Miranda Liu. Game Recap Piedmont came hot out of the gates with Lam firing a hard shot that clanged off of the crossbar around the 10th minute. The ball rebounded to Cameron Lorin whose shot was blocked. In the 19th minute, PHS struck when Symkowick retrieved a loose ball in a scramble in front of the net, slotting it home for the opening goal. Audrey Lam scored against Castro Valley and had three other shots ring off of the crossbar. Sophomore Louisa Symkowick scored the opening goal against Castro Valley in a 5-0 shutout. Piedmont players celebrate a goal against Castro Valley. Staff Photos Nine minutes later, Piedmont scored again when Lam jumped on a ball from a CV defender that was played from the goalkeeper. Lam corralled it and sent a rocket shot over the keeper’s head into the net from the 18-yard box. In first-half stoppage time, Sorensen-Wald scored at the end of some terrific interplay. On a break down the right wing, Liu centered a pass to Fitzgerald for a hard shot on target. It forced a loose ball off of the keeper’s hands, and Sorensen-Wald was positioned well for the rebound, putting it into the net. With a comfortable 3-0 lead, the Highlanders’ first goal in the second half came on free kick by Lorin to Derr who connected for the goal. Piedmont’s scoring ended in the 65th minute when sophomore winger Juliana Thornborrow, with some terrific footwork , worked her way around a defender in the box by the end line. Thornborrow played a pass toward the center of the area, and it took a slight deflection to Liu, who scored on a rightfooted shot. The Highlanders’ offensive onslaught continued in the remaining minutes as they pressed on for another goal. In the 67th minute Lola Beihn had a shot slam off the bottom of the crossbar, and three minutes later Lam hit the cross bar once again. Lam’s final shot on was pushed onto the side post with a diving save by the Castro Valley keeper. NEXT UP Piedmont hosts Berkeley tonight, February 8 for Senior Night at 6:00 p.m. at Witter Field. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ basketball team saw its hopes of capturing its first Western Alameda County Conference Foothill Division banner come to an end last night, Tuesday, February 7, falling to archrivals Bishop O’Dowd 55-49 in Binks Rawlings Gym. Earlier, Piedmont defeated Alameda 73-68 on February 2, and beat Castro Valley 54-30 on Tuesday, January 31. Brit Burden scored 15 points against O’Dowd. Highlanders fall to Bishop O’Dowd Looking ahead to season-finale and postseason PHS will host Berkeley on Friday, February 10 in the season-finale. With the Highlanders’ loss to O’Dowd last night, former Piedmont High head coach Mike Hudson brings his Berkeley Yellowjackets to Piedmont as this year’s league champion. Of last night’s game with O’Dowd, Piedmont coach Ben Spencer said, “The keys to win were to defend, rebound, and outwork them on 50/50 balls. We actually checked off all those boxes, which is usually a win. It didn’t go that way, but we stayed in the game, executed well, and got some really good looks off of running our stuff—we just didn’t knock them down.” “I couldn’t be more proud of this team. It’s a loss in the book, but looking ahead to postseason, I think we match up really well in our division of NCS,” said coach Ben Spencer. It was a productive game for senior forward Brit Burden who led the scoring with 15 points. “We fought hard. We got punked in our first game against them and we came out a lot stronger in this game. articles.text: With a school enrollment typically around 900 students, it is not uncommon to see student athletes competing on more than one sports team. Here is a feature-piece on three athletes at the school competing in multiple sports. LIAM CAMPBELL Football, Baseball Liam Campbell, a senior, is a two-sport athlete as a receiver and defensive back on the football team in the fall, and on the baseball team in the spring, usually appearing as an outfielder. In football he had two receptions and converted one first down in the season opener with Seaside. The varsity season was shut down after four games due to a lack of players and injuries. It was Campbell’s second season as a varsity starter. Last spring Campbell finished the baseball season with a .304 batting average with seven hits, six RBIs, 10 runs scored, five walks, and two stolen bases. RYAN MCCONATHY Football, Baseball Senior Ryan McConathy is a two-sport athlete in football and baseball. He was a defensive back and receiver on the gridiron, and is an outfielder in baseball. Despite missing last fall’s football season due to a shoulder injury, McConathy was a previous starter on both sides of the ball. In 2021, h scored two touchStaff Photos Liam Campbell was a starting defensive back and receiver for the football team. He is also a varsity baseball player in the spring. down receptions and had two forced fumbles, one of which led to a scoop-and-score touchdown against Bishop O’Dowd. Last spring, the baseball team went 19-9 and 9-1 against Shoreline teams on its way to a 6-5 win over Encinal for the league championship on May 13. In the title game, McConathy went 2-for-2 with a double, RBI, and a run scored. He also went 1-for-2 with one RBI in Piedmont’s 4-3 win over No. 12 Arcata in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs on May 18. In 2022, McConathy hit for a .294 average with 15 hits, five doubles, two home runs, nine RBIs and 13 runs scored. RYLAN NELSON Soccer, Lacrosse Ryan McConathy is a key starter on the baseball team and also was a starter on the football team before an injury ended his 2022 season. Ryan Nelson, a junior, has gotten time on the varsity soccer team this winter and is expected to be a key player on the varsity lacrosse team this spring. This winter, Nelson has spent time on both varsity and JV soccer roster and scored and got an assist in the varsity team’s 5-0 win over Justin-Siena in the season-opener in November. Last spring, Nelson proved to be a major part of coach Al Yu’s lacrosse team, helping Piedmont to win its sixth consecutive Western Alameda County Conference title. He was named to the AllLeague second-team. He scored three goals against Doherty Valley and College Park, scored twice in games with University, O’Dowd and Washington, and had four goals against Moreau. Rylan Nelson is a three-year varsity lacrosse player and is getting time on the soccer team this winter.

articles.text: Following the recent rainstorms, Cataract Falls on the north end of Mt. Tamalpais’ Cataract Creek is the most thriving it’s been in years. Arrive early to this bustling spot to avoid crowds. Throughout this hike, you will enjoy the pleasant sound of running water on a trail bordered by giant trees and shrubbery. The hike has two possible starting points. Beginning at the Cataract Trailhead on Fairfax-Bolinas Road, you will have a 2.8-mile out-and-back day with slightly over 1,000 feet in elevation gain. Beginning off of West Ridgecrest Blvd adds 0.8 miles to your hike, making a 3.6-mile round trip but still around 1,000 in ascent. The trail is lined with stairs that will give your lower body a good workout. Some of the steps require you to bring your knees up past your stomach – which can make it somewhat difficult for small dogs. Each step along the trail reveals some new variation on moss covered boulders and trees standing above you, while many old fallen trees hover above the creek and remain green year-round. The main attraction is the Helen Markt Falls about midway into your hike, where the cascade down Cataract Creek feeds beside a moss-covered boulder and into a pond. Helen Markt Falls is among the highlights of Cataract Falls Trail on Mt. Tamalpais. Staff photos Cataract Falls is a series of cascades that runs along the creek. Cataract Creek is picturesque with water flowing around moss-covered trees and stones.

Tam thrives after recent rains By Jonathan Comeaux Following the recent rainstorms, Cataract Falls on the north end of Mt. Tamalpais’ Cataract Creek is the most thriving it’s been in years. Arrive early to this bustling spot to avoid crowds. Throughout this hike, you will enjoy the pleasant sound of running water on a trail bordered by giant trees and shrubbery. The hike has two possible starting points. Beginning at the Cataract Trailhead on Fairfax-Bolinas Road, you will have a 2.8-mile out-and-back day with slightly over 1,000 feet in elevation gain. Beginning off of West Ridgecrest Blvd adds 0.8 miles to your hike, making a 3.6-mile round trip but still around 1,000 in ascent. The trail is lined with stairs that will give your lower body a good workout. Some of the steps require you to bring your knees up past your stomach – which can make it somewhat difficult for small dogs. Each step along the trail reveals some new variation on moss covered boulders and trees standing above you, while many old fallen trees hover above the creek and remain green year-round. The main attraction is the Helen Markt Falls about midway into your hike, where the cascade down Cataract Creek feeds beside a moss-covered boulder and into a pond. Helen Markt Falls is among the highlights of Cataract Falls Trail on Mt. Tamalpais. Staff photos Cataract Falls is a series of cascades that runs along the creek. Cataract Creek is picturesque with water flowing around moss-covered trees and stones. You can get close to waterfalls on Cataract Creek. Countless wooden and stone stairs line the trail. Some of the steps require you to bring your knees high up, making it a very taxing workout on your lower body. The trees are still green despite being in the winter months. Cataract Falls itself is a series of cascades flowing off a moss-covered rock face down through the creek. The trail is technical with many roots shooting out of the ground. In addition, more of the hike is on a narrow path about three-feet wide. Given it is a popular destination, you’ll frequently have to wait or edge past people on the stairways. The later in the day you start, the more likely you’ll have a difficult day traversing along the creek. Be smart and go early. Look for the Mt. Tamalpais Watershed sign if you intend on beginning your hike off West Ridgecrest Boulevard.

articles.text: A memorial exhibition of the works of August Grahn will open at Piedmont Center for the Arts on Saturday, February 18, at 11 a.m. Born and raised in Piedmont, August Grahn was a student in Piedmont schools and an artist. He died in 2020 at the age of 26. The collection of art on display is representative of the work he did while attending the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) in Santa Clarita from 2018 until his death. This period was one of intense creativity and productivity for him. Starting out in the Photography and Media program, his work transitioned into the canvases at the exhibit. In this brief period, his interests evolved from street photography to studio-based multimedia works, and touched on issues of race, class, masculinity, spirituality and finding one’s place in the world. Augie’s family. mother Robin Ketelle, father Dale Grahn, and sister Emma Grahn, would like members of the Piedmont community to celebrate Augie’s life through viewing and discussing his art. An opening reception at the Center is scheduled for Saturday, February 18, from 5–8 p.m. Gallery hours will be from 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturday and Sunday, February 18-19, and February 25-26. Currently Augie’s art is not offered for sale. Those who are able are encouraged to donate to the August Grahn Memorial Thriving Artist Program, a program in his memory at CalArts. articles.text: The de Young Museum, part of the Fine Arts Museums of San Francisco, presented Lhola Amira: Facing the Future, its newest program of exhibits in December 2022. A series of programs under the exhibition will be launched throughout the year. The solo exhibition interprets the museum’s African art collection as a living and evolving practice through the lens of contemporary art. “Lhola Amira: Facing the Future” centers art from Africa as a site of critical exploration for the evolving nature of African culture. Lhola Amira, a South African artist, is offering visitors ways of becoming more open and more sensitized to the pain of others, and the possibilities of the present,” Natasha Becker, curator of African art for the museum, said. Artworks from de Young’s permanent collection are placed with Amira’s work, exploring the themes of wounding and healing. Selections include African art pieces from the 19th and 20th century art, including sculptures and ceremonial pieces. Also on view is Philisa: Zinza Mphefumlo Wami (2022), an art portal considering sacred spaces for the cleansing of wounds, honoring ancestors, and fostering connection. Guests are invited to enter this interactive art portal with healing in mind. Also included in the exhibition is the single-channel video projection IRMANDADE: The Shape of Water in Pindorama (2018–2020), produced by Amira in Bahia, Brazil. To learn more, visit https:// www.famsf.org/exhibitions/lhola-amira.
articles.title: De Young Museum now exhibiting Lhola Amira: Facing the Future

San Francisco Asian Art Museum is exhibiting Yoshida Hodaka’s Modern Prints and is the first solo exhibition of the celebrated Japanese printmaker’s work in the United States. A native of Tokyo, Hokada was an influential figure of post-World War II Japanese printmaking. Born in 1926, he is known for his abstract and colorful prints. Hodaka included surreal landscapes and abstract forms in his art, which is inspired by photography, poetry, and ancient art. “Hodaka was a rebel in the best sense,” said exhibition organizer Yuki Morishima, associate curator of Japanese art at the Asian Art Museum. “He was someone who imagined a new way of seeing the world. By combining the centuries-old woodblock printing with the modern methods of photo etching and collage and contemporary influences like Pop art and foreign travel, Hodaka opened up a new frontier in Japanese printmaking that was completely original to Yoshida Hodaka’s “Mini Mythology,” a 1966 color woodblock and photo-screenprint is on display at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco.

articles.text: Vitamin Em is back in Piedmont for their Spring concert. The Grammy-nominated classical musicians with strong roots with Berkeley Symphony, bring their exciting range of crossover music to the PCA – from jazz to funk, classical to fiddle, soul to hip-hop. The audience will be treated to fearless improvisations. You’ve never heard music like this played by strings, bassoon and accordion. Featuring new works by Evan Price, Paul Hanson and Emily Onderdonk. Doors open at 3:30 p.m. Tickets $20 available in advance at https://www.vitaminemmusic.com/the-band/. $25 at the door. The program includes 5 arrangements by Emily Onderdonk: Hasse A’s: Arrangement of a Swedish fiddle Polska; very lively and rousing with elements that mimic guitars. Fancy Lady: A hip, soul tune based on the song of the same name by Billy Preston the great gospel and soul keyboardist. Tongue in Cheek: Written in a mixture of styles, including fiddle, rock, R&B and classical, featuring accordionist Dan Cantrel. Shake it Up: A fun, toe-tapping dance tune, in a 60’s pop style. Beautiful Child: Simple and heartfelt, dedicated to the memory of Emily’s brother, Matt, a wonderful musician who was a big influence on her love of the blues, rock, R&B and soul music. Seven Corners Country: An arrangement of the first song Paul Hanson wrote for his first album. This upbeat piece, generally in a jazz fusion style, includes Balkan and Bulgarian influences. It’s a Numbers game: A jazz piece by Evan Price in mixed meter. The piece is driving and rhythmic with a beautiful lyrical section in the middle. Photo by Stephanie Railsback Classical musicians with Vitamin Em include Matthew Szemela and Evan Price, violin; Emily Onderdonk, viola; Michael Graham, cello; Paul Hanson, bassoon; and Dan Cantrell, accordion. going on now!

pages.text: 18 Wednesday, February 8, 2023 MOVIES FOR ADULTS Greta a gripping story with Isabel Huppert By Chris Honoré Greta is a stylish film that quickly finds its sweet spot and remains there. Think of it as malice aforethought. Okay. I agree. The narrative, which has a Grimm’s fairytale quality, can be characterized as a bit pulpy, and the thriller tropes ubiquitous. But still, it’s got nail-biting charm. This is not a B-movie, and director Neil Jordan delivers a tightly wound story with a smiling relish, allowing his two actresses to swing for the cheap seats. I’m going to unabashedly recommend Greta while avoiding disclosing too much of the plot. I saw the trailer and thought it gave away too much. Trailers should tease in a parsimonious way. Many don’t. So, I’ll confine this review to just act one. The film opens with recent Smith graduate Frances McMullen (Chloe Grace Moretz), riding the subway. She’s recently lost her mother, and just moved to New York where she is living with her roommate in an upscale Tribeca apartment. Coming to her stop and moving toward the door, she notices an elegant leather handbag left on a seat. Looking around, she hesitates and then picks it up. And so in that moment the story is set in motion. Frances returns to her apartment, finds her roommate, Erica (Maika Monroe), home and shows Maika Monroe and Chloë Grace Moretz star in Greta. her the bag. Erica, fascinated, and against Frances’ objections, opens it up. Inside are the owner’s address/I.D. card and a wallet with money. Erica thumbs the bills, suggesting they have a spa day, and assumes that it’s finders-keepers. Frances disagrees. In contrast to Erica, Frances is innocent, fresh-faced and unassuming, with a small town quality to her view of the world. And so she decides to return the bag to its owner who, as it turns out, lives in Brooklyn in a downa-wide-alley-to-a-courtyard cottage-like apartment. She rings the bell and when the door opens she meets Greta Hideg (Isabelle Huppert), a middle-aged woman, beautifully dressed, her aristocratic face at first inquisitive then thankful as Frances explains that she found her bag on the subway. Greta, grateful for the bag’s return, invites Frances in for a coffee. And almost immediately, the two women establish a fast rapport. Soon they are meeting for dinner, taking walks, and even making a trip to a dog shelter where they adopt a dog for Greta, who insists she would welcome the companionship. All seems perfectly benign, their connection welcomed by Frances who is drawn to Greta, a mother figure, and ideal for Greta who declares she is alone a great deal of the time, getting few visitors. Her daughter, she explains, is living in Paris. Despite a lengthy getting acquainted montage, there is a subtle sense of menace. All is perfectly normal, their evolving friendship pleasant, almost familial. Until one evening, before dinner, when it isn’t and act two begins. The foreboding that surrounded Greta, the sense that something is not quite right, morphs into a sustained, apprehensive dread for Frances. It’s also at this point that Huppert, a highly regarded French actress, steps forward and flexes her incomparable talent and presence. She conveys warmth and menace simultaneously while looking at Frances the way a lepidopterist might look at a beautiful butterfly, all the while holding a pin. Frances is oblivious; while the audience is saying to the screen, Run. Get on the bike you left unlocked on the street and ride away. This will not end well. She doesn’t. Greta.
