articles.text: Review by Chris Honoré This family-friendly G-rated film opens with a red-haired girl (Francesca Capaldi) moving in across the street from Charlie Brown (Noah Schnapp). Of course, when Charlie gets his first glimpse of her, he is smitten and begins to plan how he can meet her. Naturally, the old gang is still around to offer their opinions to Charlie, and they haven’t changed. Lucy (Hadley Belle Miller) still thinks Chuck is a dufus, and Peppermint Patty (Venus Schulthels) hasn’t given up on hockey. When asked, she tells Charlie to keep his excitement about the red-haired girl to himself. Linus (Alexander Garfin) tells Charlie to simply walk across the street and introduce himself, while little sister Sally (Mariel Sheets) insists that Charlie’s new crush is not all that interesting. Snoopy (Bill Mendez), as always, is ready to support Charlie and he stands solidly at his side. The story is filled with flights of fantasy, especially when it comes to Snoopy’s dreams on top of his doghouse., He dreams of doing battle in the skis above France with his nemesis, The Red Baron. And for good measure, there’s the French poodle Fifi (Kristen Chenoweth), Snoopy’s imagined heartthrob. And not to forget Charlie’s trusty best bud Woodstock (also played by Mendez). There’s even a talent show for good measure, which offers Charlie the opportunity to demonstrate his essential kindness to his friends, despite his unresolved obsession with the red-haired girl. The animation is extraordinary with exceptional colors and background, The simple story is whimsical, warm, and there’s that familiar Chuck Brown selfdoubt, plus his haplessness and the fact that he can be his own worst enemy while always hoping for the best. This is demonstrated at a school pep rally where he wishes only that the red-haired girl will sit next to him. Later, on the school bus, she does sit next to Chuck, sending him into a panic, and causing him to crawl under his seat. The metaphor for all that occurs in a Peanuts’ story is Lucy holding the football for Charlie and pulling it away at the last moment, thus preventing Chuck from ever reaching his goal. He’s always trying, always sincere, and always vulnerable. The Peanuts Movie. Directed by Steve Martino. With voices of Noah Schnapp, Haley Belle Miller, and Mariel Sheets. 1 hr., 29 min. Rated G. articles.text: Lewis MacDougall in A Monster Calls Review by Chris Honoré A Monster Calls is extraordinary and a heartfelt surprise. But take seriously its rating of PG-13. While the trailer seems to promise a child’s tale, involving an enormous monster in the humanoid shape of gnarly yew tree, this British film is so much more. There is not a hint of Disney to be found, and the narrative goes far beyond the familiar “happily ever after”. Palliative. At the film’s center is 12-yearold Conor (Lewis MacDougall) who is in a place in his young life that is almost more than he can bear. He is relentlessly bullied at school, haunted by a traumatic nightmare that causes him to wake in the deep of night. He is coping with life-threatening cancer that is consuming his mother (Felicity Jones). He is unable to turn to his grandmother (Sigourney Weaver), who is rigid and distant. For most of his life his father (Toby Kebbell) has been absent. Though living in America, he arrives briefly due to his ex-wife’s illness, but offers little comfort to Conor. And then one night, as he sits in his room sketching in his notebook, strange things begin to happen, a pencil rolls across his desk, onto the floor. Things begin to move. And then, there, outside his opened window, stands a monster (the voice of Liam Neeson), a giant man-tree, who suddenly crashes into Conor’s room and speaks to him, insisting that he tell him three stories. Conor is both terrified and combative, wanting to suspend his disbelief yet boldly resistant to what is but cannot be. And so, just after midnight the monster returns and shares with Conor a fable that is gorgeously animated in watercolors (which are thematic throughout the film). The stories are puzzling, seemingly unrelated, and at first beyond Conor’s comprehension. And, as the monster points out, each is contradictory and are not what they seem. Meanwhile, Conor goes to school and deals with the bullies and attempts to cope with the reality that his mother is slipping away from him. Together the two of them cling to hope: his that she will live, that each new medical treatment will be a cure. Her hope is to prepare her son for what she knows will be. Deeply conflicted, Conor rages against the arc of his mother’s cancer, his anger uncontrollable, his helplessness ever with him. A Monster Calls is both a children’s allegory and an adult story. It is beautiful in its photography and in its narrative. It never backs away from the issues that young Conor is confronting. Tangentially, the monster demands that Connor tell him a fourth story that must be his own, one that the boy has refused to tell even himself. It is his deepest truth. The film, based on an idea offered by children’s author Siobhan Dowd just before she died, is realized in the 2011 award-winning book written by Patrick Ness. Conor is more a kid than an adult, and yet he stands at an intersection that is asks him to be both. And both is what A Monster Calls is all about. A Monster Calls. Directed by J.A. Bayona. 1 hr., 48 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Netflix.
articles.title: A Monster Calls is a beautiful, thoughtful film

articles.text: Two excellent concerts bookended my week. The first was on Sunday in the Piedmont Center for the arts. Young cellist Melissa Lam played a full recital in masterful fashion. She is young in years, but that belies the level of her artistry. As she played, I could envision the hands of the clock flying backwards. All you had to do was close your eyes, and you could get a hint of the great cellists of the past…including performers like Piatigorsky. Her program was designed to show every aspect of her art. It also helped that she has been coached very well by Sergei Riabtchenko, a teacher who is well-versed in beautiful cello playing. Melissa was also helped by the experienced piano playing of Miles Graber, a favorite at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The audience was very receptive, and I noticed quite a few notable musicians in the audience. All of this encourages the best from performers. The opening number, a sonata by Carl Maria von Weber, showed proof that we were in for a treat. Lam’s interpretation of a Bach solo sonata made the music live. I find this type of playing far superior to the pseudo-baroque stuff that is foisted on a gullible public. Her tone is rich and vibrant, and she has technique to spare when needed. All of this was appreciated by the audience, and they responded with enthusiasm. SF Ballet The second program was presented by the San Francisco Ballet company in the beautiful War Memorial Opera House. San Francisco Ballet company is doing its utmost to create a bigger audience. My wife and I received complimentary tickets, and so did others in the audience. This is sad in a way because the San Francisco Ballet Company is simply fabulous. You’d think that the audience would be breaking down the doors to get in. Some people think that the Super Bowl is where it’s at. Give me the San Ming Luke, a longtime director of Berkeley Symphony’s Music in the Schools program, also assistant conductor of the San Francisco Ballet orchestra Cellist Melissa Lam was impressive in her concert at the Piedmont Center for the Arts.

Saturday, February 18, 11 a.m. – 2 p.m. Augie Grahn Memorial Art Exhibit A memorial exhibition of the art of Piedmont native August Grahn will open at 11 a.m. on Saturday, February 18. Born and raised in Piedmont, he died in 2020 at age 26. The exhibit represents work he did while attending the California Institute of the Arts (CalArts) in Santa Clarita from 2018 until his death. pages.text: 20 Wednesday, February 8, 2023 The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet The Musical Gourmet Bright lights on both sides of the bay By Joseph Gold Two excellent concerts bookended my week. The first was on Sunday in the Piedmont Center for the arts. Young cellist Melissa Lam played a full recital in masterful fashion. She is young in years, but that belies the level of her artistry. As she played, I could envision the hands of the clock flying backwards. All you had to do was close your eyes, and you could get a hint of the great cellists of the past…including performers like Piatigorsky. Her program was designed to show every aspect of her art. It also helped that she has been coached very well by Sergei Riabtchenko, a teacher who is well-versed in beautiful cello playing. Melissa was also helped by the experienced piano playing of Miles Graber, a favorite at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. The audience was very receptive, and I noticed quite a few notable musicians in the audience. All of this encourages the best from performers. The opening number, a sonata by Carl Maria von Weber, showed proof that we were in for a treat. Lam’s interpretation of a Bach solo sonata made the music live. I find this type of playing far superior to the pseudo-baroque stuff that is foisted on a gullible public. Her tone is rich and vibrant, and she has technique to spare when needed. All of this was appreciated by the audience, and they responded with enthusiasm. SF Ballet The second program was presented by the San Francisco Ballet company in the beautiful War Memorial Opera House. San Francisco Ballet company is doing its utmost to create a bigger audience. My wife and I received complimentary tickets, and so did others in the audience. This is sad in a way because the San Francisco Ballet Company is simply fabulous. You’d think that the audience would be breaking down the doors to get in. Some people think that the Super Bowl is where it’s at. Give me the San Cordula Merks, Concertmaster of San Francisco Ballet Orchestra Ming Luke, a longtime director of Berkeley Symphony’s Music in the Schools program, also assistant conductor of the San Francisco Ballet orchestra Cellist Melissa Lam Francisco Ballet any day. From the time the curtain was raised, we knew we were in for a treat. The staging was a feast for the eyes. So was the choreography, but that was not all. The orchestra plays a major role in ballet. They played with elegant precision, brilliance, and virtuosity, as well as inspiration. An orchestral Serenade by Mozart opened the program. My only complaint of SF Ballet is that the printed program does not give complete information. There was no indication who the conductors were. I inquired from some of the musicians and found out that the first conductor was Ming Luke. Likewise, the violin soloist was not named. I inquired, and learned that she is Cordula Merks, the concertmaster of the orchestra. Merkes’ performance was characterized by very expressive violin playing, with a warm tone and refined technique. It certainly was impressive. The two other ballets were equally good. I would be happy to pay any price to see other performances. articles.text: Piedmonter Mary Geong became the first Asian president of Oakland Rotary Club #3 last summer. It is the third oldest in the world at 114 years and has 270 members. In the larger scheme, Oakland Rotary ranks 11th in total donations received out of the 36,000 clubs worldwide. Geong’s path to her presidency began in 2002, when she joined the Rotary Club with the encouragement of friend and fellow CPA Chris Yahng, the first Asian president of the CalCPA society in its 100-year history. Geong’s rise to the top is even more impressive when considering that females were allowed to become members in the Rotary Club only after a 1989 Supreme Court ruling. Geong and friend Mary Liu, the first female Asian president of San Francisco Rotary Club #2 in 2021, refer to their roles as “breaking the bamboo ceiling.” Geong, a leader of the Piedmont Asian American Club for more than 25 years, hosted a Lunar New Year dinner at Peony seafood restaurant in Oakland’s Chinatown, on January 26, and invited Liu’s San Francisco Mary Geong who was born in Guangzhou, China is pictured with new Oakland mayor Sheng Thao. Geong presents a grant of $7,329 to St. Vincent de Paul of Alameda County. Mary Geong, president of Oakland Rotary Club #3, gives a speech at the Rotary Club Lunar New Year dinner on January 26. Rotary Club #2 and the San Francisco Chinatown Rotary Club to attend. The result was a turnout of 114 people The same three Rotary clubs joined forces last summer to hand out over 600 personal safety alarm kits to seniors in Oakland’s Chinatown after anti-Chinese attacks on seniors made national news. Geong’s focus with the Rotary Club continues to be education. Each year the club awards up to 10 scholarships of $10,000 to Oakland students who will be attending college. The Rotary Club follows up with the recipients by providing one-on-one mentorship during their college years. Another large effort taken by the Geong-led club is supporting the expanding Transitional Kindergarten (TK) program for four-year-olds. The club donates three books to every (TK) student in Oakland School District and gives each teacher a $250 gift card to buy supplies for the class. The club also sponsors field trips annually to Fairyland and the Oakland Zoo for TK students. “We feel that education is a way for anybody to move forward and upward. I was one of the first in my family to go to college, and because of college I’ve been able to succeed,” explained Geong. As president, Geong prepares the budget of the Oakland Club for its philanthropy, and allocates funds to all its committees. While much of the work is local, the Oakland Rotary Club is involved internationally and provides funding for projects on five continents. “Most Rotary clubs are in two or three continents, we are in five. That makes us unique and that’s never occurred in our 114 years,” she said. Individual Oakland Rotary Club members donated $15,000 to Ukraine after the war began, and the club matched that amount. Geong’s status as president highlights the start, not the end, of the diversity work that she wants to see happen within the Rotary Club. While female members make up roughly half the membership now, Asians make up only 10%. “We need some more work in that area to encourage more people of different ethnic groups to match the city of Oakland’s demographics,” said Geong. Geong invites all Piedmonters and anyone interested in making a difference to attend Rotary Club’s annual Gala on May 4 at the Sequoia Country Club. To learn more about Rotary Club #3 of Oakland, visit: Oakland-rotary. org . To attend the weekly meetings online, visit Youtube.com/ channel/UCjh-qvFDHqjpHGwFTTssvvg.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California began its popular White Elephant Sale on January 29 with a sold-out crowd of enthusiastic “Preview” shoppers. The sale, which benefits the Museum, will have a series of shopping days in February and culminate with a final “Blow Out Sale” on March 4 and 5. All events require tickets but the final weekend is free of charge. To purchase tickets see: www. whiteelephantsale.org. It takes generous donors, loyal customers, and dedicated volunteers to make the White Elephant Sale a success. One Piedmont resident, Sandra Cook, can claim to have done all three of these “jobs”. A resident of Piedmont for 44 years, she has been shopping at the sale for over 20 years and began working as a volunteer cashier in 2022. When she found out the volunteer commitment was year-round, she offered to help in the Boutique Department which sells fine china, glassware She spends most of her time processing packaging materials for reuse. “We reuse all the packing material. From an environmental standpoint it supports conservation,” she said. Cook is one of over 500 people in Piedmont who have called for the White Elephant van for pickup of a donation in the past four years. “Donors from Piedmont have been very generous over the years”, said Oakland Museum Women’s Board President Renata Dowdakin. “Since its inception, the Oakland Museum Women’s Board has deep roots in this community and that has carried forward as donors look for a responsible place for their belongings”. Cook, for one, is “all in” with her support of the fundraiser. “I admire how the sale takes those things someone might have discarded and gives an opportunity for anyone to purchase them for low prices. People who make the effort to come to the sale really love it,” said Cook. The White Elephant Sale’s donation van will resume pickups at the end of March. To schedule a van appointment, call (510) 839-5919. For more information on items the organization can’t accept, see: www.whiteelephantsale.org/how-to-donate. articles.text: A strong turnout of 44 walkers showed up on February 1 for a walk to the south side of town, to include Prospect and Oakmont Avenue, Oak Road, and Davie Tennis Stadium. But first, a. visit to see the Yulan Magnolia tree in front of the Community Hall that was in full bloom. It is one of the city’s 19 designated Heritage trees. Later they could walk to the other trees and submit their suggestions for Heritage trees this year. own candidate afterwards. A grove of 10 Highland poplars at the Exedra are Heritage trees. They are a hybrid of two North American plain poplars native to the northern hemisphere. On a path to the Community Hall was a second Heritage tree, a large, twisting Coast live oak used frequently for family photos. It’s a Piedmont treasure, and native to California from Mendocino County to northern Baja California. The Yulan Magnolia is native to central and eastern China and produces stunning white flowers this time of year. This tree was planted by arborist and former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel. The walkers thought it was beautiful and took a group photo in front of it. Other Heritage trees in the area include the Coast redwood that serves as Piedmont’s lighted holiday tree, Japanese maples that are native to Japan, Korea, China and eastern Mongolia, and a group of Akebono cherry trees near the Tea House The walkers made their way up the short hill to Guilford Road and found a somewhat hidden 153-foot path and steps down to Hazel Lane. At Hazel and Requa Road, they noted another Heritage tree, a large Coast redwood in the street in front of 71 Hazel Lane, once the entrance to the first school in Piedmont, the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls. Before starting, they took a group photo by the Yulan Magnolia in full bloom in front of the Community Hall. This tree was planted by arborist and former Piedmont Public Works superintendent Dave Frankel. The walkers thought it was beautiful and took a group photo in front of it. Other Heritage trees in the area include the Coast redwood that serves as Piedmont’s lighted holiday tree, Japanese maples that are native to Japan, Korea, China and eastern Mongolia, and a group of Akebono cherry trees near the Tea House The walkers made their way up the short hill to Guilford Road and found a somewhat hidden 153-foot path and steps down to Hazel Lane. At Hazel and Requa Road, they noted another Heritage tree, a large Coast redwood in the street in front of 71 Hazel Lane, once the entrance to the first school in Piedmont, the Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls. It was opened in 1913 by Amy Long, who hired Julia Morgan to design the school building on five acres that is now Hazel Lane. The walkers went down Requa and at Wildwood Avenue, they came to their last Heritage trees, Eastern redbuds that are native to the eastern United States. On the way to Davie Tennis Stadium, they went down Prospect Road to Oakmont Avenue, then took short side trip to Lois Price’s home on Oak Road where she showed them the decorative metalwork on the front gate and entrance to her house that Piedmont designer and builder Daryl Rush had created for her. The aroma of Eucalyptus trees that surround the stadium was present. A quarry was opened at the site in 1878 by the Alameda Macadamizing Company and reopened as the Piedmont Paving Company in about 1892. The land was given to the City of Oakland in 1931 by former Oakland mayor John L. Davie and his family. The facility was built in 1936 as a Depression WPA project. The land is primarily in Piedmont, though the stadium is managed by the Oakland Parks and Recreation Department. There are five tennis courts and a clubhouse, a throwback to the 1930s. The walkers went inside to admire photos of famous tennis players who competed there at national tournaments. Time was passing, and the walkers had to start their return. Their route back to the Exedra went on Park Lane, Lakeshore Avenue, Harvard Road, Prospect, Wildwood Avenues, and then walking through Piedmont Park. It had been about a three-mile walk filled with Heritage trees and history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. articles.text: Did you know that Piedmont is buying 100% California wind and solar power? The city is being served by East Bay Community Energy (EBCE), a not-for-profit public agency providing sustainable power to customers in Alameda County. I spoke with Kelly Birdwell Brezovec, Director of Account Services at EBCE and a Piedmont resident, about how EBCE serves customers and the environment. EBCE is what’s called a Community Choice Aggregation (CCA). “CCAs have been around for more than ten years in the state of California, enabled by a piece of legislation that allowed the development of these programs within communities to provide local control and an energy mix that more closely matches the demands or the requests of the population,” said Brezovec. With EBCE, residents have the option to power their homes sustainably. “We offer our customers a really easy way to be served by 100% renewable energy,” said Brezovec. Piedmont was the first city in Alameda County to default municipal and residential customers to the Renewable 100 plan — 100% California solar and wind energy — which aligns with Piedmont’s Climate Action Plan goals. In addition to benefiting the environment, EBCE can also save customers money if they choose to enroll in the Bright Choice plan, priced 3% below PG&E rates. EBCE estimates that its Bright Choice customers save $19 million each year compared to what they would have paid PG&E. EBCE’s Board of Directors comprises local elected officials and Piedmont’s mayor has a seat on the board. Starting March 1, Councilmember Betsy Anderson will represent Piedmont. “You can be in touch with a local city council member and voice your opinion. You can also join our public board meetings and make a public comment,” Brezovec said. Because EBCE is not-forprofit, they reinvest earnings back into the community. “We offer community sponsorships of up to $2500 to local organizations like youth sports teams, social services, and stem programs,” said Brezovec. In 2020, the Piedmont Makers Robotics Team received a sponsorship. In addition to community groups and businesses, EBCE supports local governments with technical and financial assistance. Last year, EBCE assisted Piedmont in conducting a municipal fleet electrification study and provided gap funding to replace all remaining gas water heaters in municipal buildings with energy-efficient heat pump water heaters. The city is also working with EBCE to install the city’s first publicly accessible electric vehicle DC fast chargers near the Exedra.

articles.text: Joe Cross Creason III, known as Cross, passed away suddenly on the morning of January 27, 2023 at his family home in Piedmont. He was 52 years old. While the glow of his brilliance and caring heart faded far too soon from this world, he lived a life of passions, achievements and dedication that we will always remember. Born in San Francisco on June 22, 1970, he lived the first years of his life with his mother and father before moving to Piedmont where he was soon joined by a sister, Winnie. Cross attended Piedmont schools from preschool through Middle School. He graduated from high school at College Preparatory School in Oakland. Furthering his education, Cross attended the University of California, Santa Barbara, then graduated from the University of California, Davis. He gained a law degree from the McGeorge School of Law, in Sacramento, where he was a staff writer for the Law Review and earned numerous scholastic honors, including three American Jurisprudence Awards, as well as being a member of the Roger J. Traynor Honor Society and the Order of the Coif. For over 20 years, Cross practiced law in San Francisco at the law firm of Dillingham and Murphy, where he was a partner. Cross was a true Renaissance man with an expansive intellect and curiosity. He immersed himself in each of his interests in order to obtain a level of ability and knowledge that would have been impressive for the focus of just a single subject. There was hardly a string instrument that Cross didn’t know how to play. His musical passions started as a child with the bass and guitar, before expanding his abilities to the ukulele, banjo, mandolin and others later in life. Cross’s language skills were as impressive as his musical talents. He was a fluent Spanish speaker and read a range of books from novels to non-fiction in the language. Cross had expanded his repertoire to include parts of Mandarin and French as well. He was a gifted writer and lover of literature. Cross enjoyed an eclectic group of authors including Faulkner and Asimov. He was deeply informed on history and politics. He closely followed debates regarding public policy and played a limited but Alice Creason with son Cross Creason, grandson Joe Creason, and daughter Winnie Creason in 2002. Cross Creason with son Joe Creason on Joe’s 1st Birthday in 1999. Cross Creason engaged role in local politics in Alameda County where he had resided for over 10 years. A life-long sports enthusiast and excellent athlete, Cross was a talented tennis player and former member of the Berkeley Tennis Club. More recently he had taken up the sport of pickleball, displaying his advanced skills and superior strokes, as well as returning to golf. He was a longtime basketball player, following in the footsteps of his father and winning a CIF title for College Prep during his senior year in 1988. Piedmont basketball courts were a favorite of his, where he frequently shot baskets and played pickup games. On weekends Cross enjoyed cooking using various techniques, cooking methods, and cookbooks as he carefully learned new recipes. Cross also had a green thumb and was able to produce beautiful vegetables and seasonings for his dishes. Cross loved his son, Joe Cross Creason IV, very much. They played guitar, hiked in the Oakland hills, and kayaked in the Bay. Cross leaves behind many family members, his mother Alice Creason, sister Winnie Creason, Son Joe Creason, wife Tiffany Sun, stepson Joshua Gu, aunt Estelle Hood, uncle William Creason, aunt Louise Creason, and cousins Hunt Cochrane and Harriet, Herbert Cochrane and Posey, Philippe Patat, Scott Creason and Mollie, Lyman Creason and Sharon, and many more. A memorial celebrating the life of Cross Creason will be held at the Claremont Country Club this Saturday, February 11, at 3:00 pm. In lieu of flowers the family requests that memorial contributions be made to the Bay Area Music Project or the charity of your choice. articles.text: The Piedmont Park entrance at the corner of Highland and Guilford Road is fenced off during construction. Renovation of the steps at the corner of Highland and Guilford at the eastern edge of Piedmont Park began on January 27. Despite a three-week delay due to winter rainstorms, the Oakland contractor Bay Construction is on track to finish in midMarch. The $155,000 renovation project is a collaboration between the City and the Piedmont Beautification Foundation. The fundraising was initiated by generous donations from the family of Denny and Ruthie McLeod in December 2020 and was approved by City Council on September 6, 2021. Piedmont Beautification Foundation donated $82,000 toward the project. The Public Works Department issued a notice to proceed with the project in early December 2022. The first priority was to clear out existing vegetation and concrete. An excavator removes concrete and an old wooden walkway. Construction of the Highland-Guilford Steps is currently underway. “After that,” said Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales, “they’ll be establishing grades — putting in foundations in order to get a level base and establish a rough outline of where things will be constructed. The main priority of this project is safety,” he said. The city will replace the current walkway of wooden railroad ties of varying sizes with colored concrete steps and landings and add metal handrails on both sides of the steps and landings. Further additions will include benches, trees, and a small plaza with a permeable-pavement floor to accommodate for groundwater runoff. Parking has not been impacted and the contractor is not using parking spaces in the Community Hall lot. The park entrance at the corner of Highland and Guilford Road is fenced off. Caution for pedestrians and drivers is advised during construction hours of 8 a.m. to 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. The Highland Steps project plans are available online at bit. ly/3jlK65z. For more information, contact Gonzales by email at dgonzales@ piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3061. comments. articles.text: Vandals invaded the nativeplant nursery, Friends of Sausal Creek, in Joaquin Miller Park on Friday, January 24, throwing thousands of plants to the ground, smashing pots and overturning tables and benches. The preliminary damage estimates ranged from $4,500 to $7,000. The event mirrored a few of the experiences that Piedmont Scouts have experienced with their service projects. Scouts with Troop 6 have performed many service projects at Sausal Creek. Piedmont Scout Council President Lisa Gros, also a longtime leader with Troop 6, said, “The vandalism was indicative of one of the things we try to counteract in Scouts. We try to foster the ‘we’ instead of the ‘me.’ I hope that this was an isolated incident and not a bigger issue where people are caring more about whatever they want than what’s good for the broader community.” Gros’ son Jack encountered vandalism only a few days after the construction of his Eagle Scout project in May 2019, a Graffiti on the fence at the El Centro Trailhead of the Dimond Canyon Trail by Sausal Creek 160-foot fence at the El Centro Trailhead of the Dimond Canyon Trail, protecting the genetically pure trout native to Sausal Creek. The fence was damaged with graffiti and completely torn down in some sections. Gros speculated that a few homeless people were living up the hill on the other side of the canyon and possibly broke the Two Scouts from Troop 6 repair the broken fence. fence. “The Scouts do things like this to better their community, and it’s a shame that not everyone appreciates that intent,” said Gros. Since then, parts of the fence were washed out in the recent winter storms. The fence, and other Troop 6 projects, are intended to protect the parklands of the Oakland Hills from erosion. Toward that end, many Troop 6 projects involve replanting the hillsides with native-plant life, in collaboration with Wendy Tokuda, a former Piedmont resident and TV news anchor, who now leads many environmental restoration efforts under Friends of Sausal Creek. Throughout Gros’ seven-year involvement with Friends of Sausal Creek, Troop 6 Scouts have been working with Tokuda to stabilize native plant life, clear potentially flammable redwood debris, and clear the trail. “If the Sausal Creek damages were really only $7,000,” said Gros, “someone could open their wallet. But what’s irreplaceable are the plants, the decades of commitment it took to grow natives from the seedlings. Money alone can never replace that; time doesn’t work that way.” But Gros emphasized how rarely Troop 6 Scouts and Friends of Sausal Creek have encountered vandalism. “In our work, the Scouts are encouraging to exhibit the power of the community to overcome the behavior of the few. Incidents like this certainly shouldn’t have us lose hope for the power that our projects have to better our community.” The fence at Sausal Creek was an Eagle Scout project of Jack Gros of Piedmont Troop 6.
articles.title: Scout projects vandalized at Sausal Creek nursery

Many guests and volunteers, like Janet Cheng, and sons James Chew and Connor Chew (front right), wore traditional clothing and wished for health, luck and prosperity. included a ballet solo and a violin and piano performance. The lion dancers wowed the crowd on stage, and especially as they walked through the crowd. “After the devastating shootings (in Half Moon Bay) at the start of Lunar New Year, it was important to continue this program to show that Lunar New Year is a time to celebrate togetherness and not let tragedy define this moment. We’re all doing this for our children for their futures as citizens in a diverse community that welcomes them,” said Bierhaus. articles.text: At a closed meeting tonight, the Piedmont School Board will begin reviewing applications received for a permanent School Superintendent, a position posted last summer. Only the five board members and the two representatives from the search firm Leadership Associates will be involved in the discussion, which begins at 4:00 p.m. The board plans to hold the first round of interviews on February 10 and 11 for the candidates they select today. “We actually present the good, the bad, and the ugly – what we know about them, [and] all of the things our reference-checking has shown. Then the board is going to decide which of the top applicants they are going to interview,” explained Jacqueline Horejs of Leadership Associates. In the December 14 board meeting, Leadership Associates gave an update on their community outreach. At the time they announced they had received 22 requests for applications, including one from Hong Kong. The application deadline was January 16, and the search firm advised Piedmont’s board to not give an update on the number of applicants until at least after candidates for interviews are selected. In the December 14 meeting, Amal Smith asked what Leadership’s research had uncovered which made Piedmont’s Superintendent job description unique. “Someone who can work collaboratively with an active and engaged community, and board, that’s what makes Piedmont unique. The collaboration you have with the city, with other organizations, with colleges, that is unique,” said Search Consultant Eric Andrew. A total of 417 online survey responses were received during their outreach. Consultants Andrew and Horejs highlighted that the community wants a leader with communication and collaboration skills and someone to continue the DEI work. “All of the stakeholders want someone who really values that give and take, two-way communication and has a collaboration leadership style, making sure that it isn’t just within the district itself. They really want a broad base of communication,” said Andrew. To view the job description created by Leadership Associates for the Superintendent position visit: Leadershipassociates.org/ wp-content/uploads/2022/12/ P i e d m o n t - U S D - S u p e r i nt e n d e nt- Po sit io n - D e s c r iption-12-9-22.pdf.
articles.title: School Board begins reviewing superintendent applications today

articles.text: Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed on January 27 that the city is moving forward with parking, traffic, and access changes proposed to City Council on January 17. The changes will be in effect for the duration of the Piedmont Community Pool construction project, starting January 19 and for 335 working days, including adjustments for weather. Originally slated for opening in Spring 2024, the actual completion may not be accomplished until summer next year. Parking, traffic, and access impacts • All parking on Bonita Avenue between Magnolia and Vista Avenues will be removed. • Parking on Magnolia Avenue in front of the pool site will be removed. • Portions of the sidewalk will be closed on Bonita Avenue between Magnolia and Vista Avenues. Bonita Avenue will support one-way traffic towards Oakland Avenue. • The bus stops in each direction on Highland Avenue between Sierra and Sheridan Avenues will be eliminated. 13 diag- • • • onal and 4 parallel parking spaces will be added on the eastern “Highland Strip” side for Permit A holders and twohour parking. 13 parking spaces will be designated for Permit A holders and city employees in the Community Hall parking lot. 9 parallel parking spaces will be designated for Permit A holders and city employees around the intersection of Hillside and Magnolia Avenues. The Recreation Department basketball courts will be closed. Staff photo Construction will soon begin on the Piedmont Community Pool, with changes in traffic and parking in the vicinity of Magnolia and Bonita Avenues.
articles.title: Parking, traffic, access changes begin for pool construction

articles.text: Piedmont police officers and firefighters were called to a home on Greenbank Avenue at 11:28 p.m. on Friday, January 20, for a person suffering from the effects of drug consumption. Officers arrived at a house party of a Piedmont teen who, with two friends, had ingested psilocybin in the form of mushrooms. The juvenile in distress was transported to the hospital, where fentanyl was found in the blood stream. The teen has been released from the hospital and has fully recovered. The other two juveniles interviewed by the police stated they were not feeling effects the same. During the initial investigation, officers discovered the mushrooms possibly came from another Piedmont student. Officers confiscated the remaining mushrooms and sent them to the toxicology lab for testing to identify the complete narcotic makeup. The testing is still in process. Superintendent Donald Evans has sent out communications to the Piedmont school district alerting the community and the school newspaper The Piedmont Highlander also notified students through its social media account. “Because fentanyl is so strong (100x stronger than morphine), it takes only a small amount to cause an overdose, and overdose can happen quickly. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont invites the community to a discussion on February 8 at 4 p.m. for a compelling talk by Dr. Rupa Basu. A free livestreamed Zoom and YouTube event titled “Health Impacts from Heat: What to Know and What You Can Do,” Basu will discuss the known negative healthcare impacts of climate pollution. She will also discuss achievable, current solutions for reducing and avoiding heat-related health risks. Dr. Basu identifies heat increases and their resulting health impacts as a global problem. Heat deaths are reported worldwide and are currently significantly underreported. She will present the scientific consensus on the health impacts of rising temperatures, such as the known cardiovascular impacts and adverse birth and mental health outcomes, providing examples from California epidemiologic studies. Basu’s own research quantifies heat-related health disparities, primarily by race and ethnicity, and identifies reasons for these disparities. Dr. Basu will discuss risk perceptions of climate change-induced health risks, and offer guidelines developed for prevention. Most importantly, she vulnerable populations. Prior to joining OEHHA, she worked at the U.S. Environmental Protection Agency, after obtaining her PhD in epidemiology from Johns Hopkins University and her MPH from UCLA. She serves on several national and state climate change committees and has been a frequent guest speaker in academic settings, including UC Berkeley, and for governmental leaders including California Governor Gavin Newsom. Basu was featured in the “Mercury Rising” episode of the Emmy award-winning climate change documentary, “Years of Living Dangerously.” Her work is widely cited in the new media, including the New York Times, the New Yorker, Loa Angeles Times, SF Chronicle, National Public Radio, and BBC World News. She collaborates with external agencies such as the Scripps Institute of Oceanography and the Kaiser Division of Research. articles.text: The City of Piedmont took the first step towards implementing its updated Housing Element when it issued a Request for Proposals (RFP) for the development of a Moraga Canyon Specific Plan on January 23. Responses are due March 13, 2023. The city expects to select a consultant and begin the Specific Plan process in late Spring 2023. Once a consultant has been selected, the Specific Plan process is expected to take 18-24 months to complete. The final product of this process will be a detailed plan for how to maintain and improve existing city facilities, open space, and recreational amenities in the Moraga Canyon area while also: • incorporating 132 units of new housing, including 60 units designated for lower income households • improving wildfire safety • improving pedestrian, bicycle, and traffic safety The initiative will study all city-owned land in Moraga Canyon, including Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. Public engagement Robust involvement from the community will be critical for a successful Specific Plan process. Firms submitting proposals to lead this project will need to provide a detailed plan for how they intend to engage community members in the process. Community members are encouraged to stay informed throughout the process by subscribing to the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan email list at bit. ly/3wySeTk. Affordable housing Once the Specific Plan process is underway, the city’s priority will be to identify a site within the plan area for the potential development of affordable housing. The City hopes to pinpoint an appropriate site by late 2023, with the intention of using Piedmont’s allocation of $2.2 million from the Alameda County Measure A1 low-interest loan program to support this development. The city would then need to identify an affordable housing developer to build the new homes. Specific Plan implementation The final Specific Plan will include how land use in this area could be reconfigured, and could include specific implementation measures, including: • standards and criteria for new development • infrastructure projects needed to support the Plan’s goals • financing measures to support the construction of new facilities and housing • an evaluation of the economic feasibility of the plan • fiscal analysis of potential revenues and expenses related to new development
articles.title: RFP issued for Moraga Canyon Specific Plan

articles.text: City staff will bring the 6th Cycle Housing Element to City Council for adoption after the conclusion of the State’s 90-day review period, which ends on February 16. Currently, the city expects that adoption will happen in late February or March 2023. The Planning Commission reviewed the proposed Housing Element at a special meeting on January 12 and unanimously voted to recommend that the City Council adopt the proposed Housing Element. Planning staff meeting with State reviewers Since the city submitted the Draft Housing Element to the State Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review on November 18, 2022, Planning staff have been in communication with Piedmont’s HCD reviewer, holding multiple meetings to discuss the City’s plan, answer questions, and provide a personal tour of the city sites listed in the sites inventory. Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson provided a verbal update on the status of the Housing Element at the January 17, 2023, City Council meeting. Next steps: adoption, implementation HCD will provide written comments to city staff regarding the Draft Housing Element at the end of the 90-day review period. If reviewers determine that changes are needed, Planning staff will work with HCD to develop amendments, then bring the proposed updates to City Council for approval. After City Council adopts the Housing Element, the city will have three years to implement a substantial number of the proposed programs and regulatory changes outlined in the document. Some of this work has already begun: the City issued an RFP this week seeking a consultant to lead the preparation of a Moraga Canyon Specific Plan, one of the key elements of the city’s plan to accommodate 587 new homes by 2031. Implementation of the Housing Element involves additional environmental review, which is already underway; the city is currently preparing an Environmental Impact Report that studies the impacts of the homes and residents which could come to Piedmont once implementation is complete. More information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontisHome. org. For questions about the Housing Element process, contact Kevin Jackson by email kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. articles.text: Uppsala University, Scandinavia’s oldest institution of higher learning, has awarded a prestigious Honorary Doctorate to long-time Piedmont resident, and UC Berkeley Distinguished Professor Emeritus Ralph Catalano. Catalano won the award on January 27, 2023, for his five decades of research into the health effects of population stressors including contracting economies, natural disasters, and terrorist attacks. In conferring the award, the faculty at Uppsala noted that much of Catalano’s scholarship uses Swedish data and has influenced doctoral training and faculty research at Scandinavian universities. Catalano earned his PhD from the Maxwell School of Syracuse University in 1972 and has since served on the faculty of the University of California at both Irvine and Berkeley. He and his wife June, City Manager of Pleasant Hill, have lived in Piedmont for 32 years. Their daughter Liz, a graduate of Piedmont schools, Ralph Catalano has received an Honorary Doctorate degree from Uppsala University in Sweden UC Berkeley, and UCLA, lives in San Francisco and serves as Director of Corporate and Foundation Relations at UC San Francisco. The University’s announcement, in English, of the Honorary Doctorate awards is at: htt ps://w w w.uu.se/en /news/ article/?id=19760&typ=artikel&lang=en

articles.text: Russian scholar Anastasia Edel will be teaching a 6-week course online through Healdsburg American Association of University Women on the topic of Russia’s Invasion of neighboring Ukraine. The classes will be held on Thursdays from 10:00 to 11:45 a.m. from February 2 to March 9. Starting on the day when Russian missiles first struck cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine, Edel will tackle the key questions: Why did Russia become an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common heritage? How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call the war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And how does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? The cost for the 6-week course is $95. Online registration is available at healdsburg-ca.aauw. net or by mail to AAUW Forum, P.O. Box 1603, Healdsburg CA 95448. Be sure to provide your e-mail address. Classes will be presented online via Zoom. Once registered, each student will be emailed a Zoom link before each class, which will allow them to access the live class and a recording of the live classes. In 2019 Edel gave the Healdsburg audience a fascinating and well received lecture on Russian politics, history and culture. Her course will also examine the heroism of the Ukrainian resistance. Writer and social historian Anastasia Edel will lead a 6-week online class on Russia’s War on Ukraine through the Healdsburg American Association of University Women, starting February 2. Audience members will be given a brief overview of Russian-Ukrainian history to help understand why Ukraine’s rebirth is matched by Russia’s civilizational and moral collapse. The origins of Russian fascism will be explored. We will consider how the dark side of Russian culture (chauvinism, cruelty, conformism) masks and justifies the suffering in Ukraine. Anastasia will select works of Russian art that present this “dark side” and will discuss and consider whether they still belong in the world’s cultural canon. Anastasia Edel A Piedmont resident, Edel is an acclaimed Russian-American writer, social historian, and New York Times contributor. She’s the author of Russia: Putin’s Playground, a concise guide to Russian history, politics and culture. Her prose is forthcoming in the Cream City Review and World Literature Today. Since the invasion of Ukraine, she has been a frequent guest commentator on national networks, including CNN and NBC News. Of mixed Russian and Ukrainian heritage, she grew up in a small town in the south of Russia near the Ukrainian border. During the last years of the Soviet Union, she graduated with a degree in English and German studies from Kubansky State University and worked as a translator in Austria. After receiving the Chevening Award, she moved to England for postgraduate studies, and then to the U.S, where she earned her MFA in writing from Pacific University. She is on the Literary Council of the Oakland Book Festival and teaches Russian Culture and history for UC Berkeley Osher Livelong Learning Institute. Her prose has appeared in the New York Times, The New York Review of Books, Foreign Policy, Project Syndicate, and World Literature Today. To read some of her articles go to: https://www. nybooks.com/contributors/anastasia-edel/ The course uses a multimedia format, where the latest political, economic, and cultural events are illustrated with movie clips, music, art, and literature.
articles.title: Edel course on Russia’s War on Ukraine starts tomorrow

articles.text: Piedmont adults and youth have a wide range of opportunities for volunteer work. Here are just a few. Piedmont Center for the Arts Throughout the year, the all-volunteer nonprofit Piedmont Center for the Arts hosts music performances, art exhibits, literary events, and public speakers. Volunteers do everything — from production, carpentry, and painting to hosting receptions for events, handling box office duties – even set design, and costuming for theater productions. The PCA particularly needs volunteers to help staff art exhibits and to assist at other events. To learn more and get involved, email the PCA at info@piedmontcenterforthearts.org. Oakland Zoo There are several volunteer opportunities at the Oakland Zoo for people who love working with animals. You can work alongside a zookeeper assisting with daily animal care as a conservation volunteer interpreting the Zoo’s conservation initiatives to guests, or as a docent sharing your passion for wildlife and conservation with Zoo visitors. There are also a variety of internships available to teens and adults in fall, winter, and summer sessions. To learn more about volunteer programs at the Zoo, visit oaklandzoo.org/volunteer-and-internship-opportunities. Alameda County Food Bank The Alameda County Community Food Bank needs volunteers to prepare food in the ACCFB Oakland warehouse, and to help distribute food at neighborhood distribution sites throughout the county. For a full list of volunteer needs at local pantries and other organizations, email volunteer@accfd.org, or visit accfb.org/ get-involved/volunteer. A calendar of all volunteer opportunities for adults and youth 10 years old and up is available at accfb.org/ get-involved/volunteer-calendar. Donations are also welcome. Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland Wardrobe for Opportunity Oakland provides access to transformational career support services for low-income individuals seeking employment. The organization was founded in 1995 to help low-income women look professional in workplace settings, and has since evolved to provide a complete suite of career development services to men, women, and youth. There are various ways you can volunteer with the organization, which is seeking volunteers to conduct mock interviewers, style clients, facilitate workshops, and process donations. Wardrobe for Opportunity also accepts gently-used and new clothing donations. Visit wardrobe.org/donate to learn more. Is there a volunteer effort or organization that you would like to highlight? Interested in expanding this list? Please send your suggestions to Selen Ozturk at ozturkselen@gmail.com.
articles.title: Volunteer opportunities for Piedmonters

articles.text: Dr. Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard, Piedmont School District Director of Diversity Equality and Integrity, will lead an online informational session tonight, Wednesday, February 1, at 6:00 p.m. to discuss the district’s LCAP goals. The Local Control Accountability Plan sets goals for three years to set the foundation for education standards, focus and objectives in schools. This meeting is a chance for parents and community members to learn more and comment about the district’s goals for Piedmont kids. This community engagement addresses administrative changes that can affect the schools in future years. In tonight’s meeting, Goal 2, Student Support, will be a featured talking point along with associated actions from Goal 3. Goal 3 is: Teachers and staff, with district partners, will ensure an outstanding educational experience for every student through collaboration, innovation and professional growth. The next forum date will be Thursday, March 9 in which Goal 1, Student Academics, will be discussed “We will be reviewing the existing plan’s goals, progress toward those goals thus far, and any refinements needed as we head into our last year of this 3-year plan,” said Vanden Wyngaard. articles.text: Piedmont’s School Board finalized changes to the school district core philosophical ideologies during their January 25 board meeting. This redrafting updates policy aims that were initially adopted in 1999 and most recently updated in 2011. “Setting a districtwide vision, mission, and strategic direction is one of the most important responsibilities for a school board. In advance of our superintendent search, we decided to update ours to reflect current needs and contexts,” said School Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen. The path leading to the changes began with board workshops in July and September last year. Two public workshops were held in October, including one with a large turnout on October 19 at the Student Center at PHS. Subsequent discussions occurred during the first reading at the January 11 board meeting. At that time two possible Mission Statements were discussed, and one was selected. The school board made changes with the intent that the following philosophies represent “accurate reflections of what this community wants to see our schools focus on.” The school district “Strategic Philosophy Plan” now read as follows: Our students are compassionate leaders and courageous problem-solvers, ready to take on challenges and make a difference in a complex and interconnected world. Piedmont Unified School District provides all students with an excellent education and opportunities for personal growth, delivered by skilled, diverse, and well-supported staff, in a school community that is inclusive and inspiring.
articles.title: School district rewrites its core philosophies

articles.text: Piedmont High School’s men’s basketball coach received a surprise at a game on Friday night, January 27. Students from his fourth grade class at Beach School – his day job – showed up to surprise him with appropriate signs of support. Parents Bonnie Forbes and Beth McNeill came up with the idea and coordinated the surprise that the kids kept secret from Spencer for months. The students met before the game for burgers and shakes at Park Burger, where they made signs of support for their favorite teacher, who moonlights as Coach Spencer. “Tonight was the best surprise ever! I can’t believe the kids kept it a secret from me all day. Thank you to everyone who showed up to cheer us on at our game. You have no idea how much it meant to our players and to me. It was the loudest and the best crowd we’ve ever had at a home game,” Spencer told his class. The Spencer-led Highlander basketball team defeated longtime rival league foe St. Joseph of Alameda by a whopping 67-43. “My daughter has never had a teacher that she talks about more or is more excited to see every day,” said parent Heidianne Pillsbury. “Mr. Spencer is truly a special guy. We need more Mr. Spencers in Piedmont.” Spencer is one of only two teachers in Piedmont School District to also coach a varsity sport. Coach Ben Spencer with some surprise guests at a Piedmont High basketball game – students from his 4th grade class at Beach School.
articles.title: Coach Ben Spencer surprised by his 4th grade students at PHS basketball game

articles.text: Our district embraces these core values in educational practice and operational strategy: Integrity: We elevate honesty and ethics as the centerpiece of all that we do. Equity: We foster a welcoming, inclusive and safe environment where individuals are nurtured, where barriers to success are eliminated, and where everyone has the opportunity to collaborate with others and reach their potential free from racism and other forms of inherent bias. We model compassion and respect for other perspectives. Academic Excellence: We provide outstanding academic content that paves the way for students to achieve mastery of core academic subjects, literacy in media and technology, and cultural competency in preparation for college, careers and a future of their own design. Curiosity: We create opportunities for students to ask questions, identify current and future problems, explore their interests and talents, innovate, and find joy in life-long learning. Courage: We promote resilience and diligence and taking action with purpose and resolve, even when doing so may be difficult. We model compassion and respect for other perspectives. Academic Excellence: We provide outstanding academic content that paves the way for students to achieve mastery of core academic subjects, literacy in media and technology, and cultural competency in preparation for college, careers and a future of their own design. Curiosity: We create opportunities for students to ask questions, identify current and future problems, explore their interests and talents, innovate, and find joy in life-long learning. Courage: We promote resilience and diligence and taking action with purpose and resolve, even when doing so may be difficult. articles.text: No two childhoods are exactly the same, yet there are a handful of experiences that so many adults remember from growing up. • Being a first grader and thinking the fourth graders were huge • Coveting a trinket that wasn’t yours • Checking for monsters in shadows and dark spaces • Feeling amazed when an adult took the time to actually talk with you That last one in particular is one worth exploring. When we are young there is something mystical about the adult world – from their dumb rules to the choices that seem beyond reason and prudence. As we grow up, the fog clears and the boons and burdens of adulthood become ours to share. But that doesn’t mean those childhood memories dissipate. We remember, often very clearly, how people made us feel when we were children. • An uncle who looked at your drawings and scribbles with an artist’s perspective, recognizing your use of shape, line and color • A neighbor who gave you the time to fully explain your thoughts and feelings, asking follow-up questions that showed you were really being heard • A teacher who pulled you aside to share that the assignment you turned in was more than good. It left her awed and she wanted to know how you felt while working on it These adults made us feel like we were more than ‘just a kid’. Their attention wasn’t just a nicety like a gold star or pat on the head, but affirming, encouraging, and inspiring to our growing identities. How do you get more of these patient and magical adults into the path of our children? Perhaps unsurprising and coming from a camp director, I recommend sending them to camp. The adult world moves quickly, with few adults stopping to bend down to notice the smaller of the humans. Camp Augusta changes that formula. We don’t have children being swept along the waves of the adult world, but a world for children that we hire adults to run. Wonderful, magical, kind, kidsat-heart counselors and staff who we hired for their innate ability to see children for the wonders they are. Not perfect angels or naive brats, but smallish humans who have their own unique interests, attributes and lenses through which they see the world. keeping our ratios tight (camper to staff 1:2 overall and 1:5 in cabins), we create opportunities every day for a camper to experience the magic of being seen and heard. I am proud to report that we see those special moments all the time: an adult turning on their listening ears, seeing not ‘just a kid’, but a person they are happy to give their full heartfelt attention to. Affirmed. Interesting. Valuable. Creative. Loved. Special. Whatever wonderful feeling was felt, it was felt because someone took the time to help them feel the goodness that was already in themself. At Camp Augusta, we believe there is something awesome in every child, we need only to take the time to notice. Randall Grayson, Ph.D. (psychology) has been Camp Augusta’s director for over twenty years. The camp, nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills outside Nevada City, has been beloved by many Piedmont families since 1931. Information about our summer program, family camps, and program philosophies can be found at www.campaugusta.org. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Sunday, January 22nd, marked the first day of the Lunar New Year, a special holiday celebrated by many Asian communities to usher in the first day of the lunar calendar. It is a festive time where friends and family gather to eat, play games, and do other activities to welcome health, good fortune, and happiness in the new year. The Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging Committee at Beach Elementary School hosted a Lunar New Year party on Saturday, January 28, on the Beach School blacktop. More than 140 people came together for the festive event, which featured an amazing spread of food – homemade zongzi, noodles, japchae, turnip cake, tteokbokki, and sticky buns. Kids made Korean crafts, played a Vietnamese dice game and a mahjong matching game, and read books about the Lunar New Year. While most Asian cultures are celebrating the Year of the Rabbit, some, including the Vietnamese, are celebrating the Year of the Cat. Organizers of the event were Doan Nguyen and Tam Bui, co-chairs of the Beach Parents Organization’s Diversity, Equity, Inclusion and Belonging ComBPO members Helen Kang Shin, Doan Nguyen, Tam Bui, and Stephanie Tietbohl celebrate Lunar New Year at Beach School. Kids play Lunar New Year games. Beach Parents Organization Co-President Helen Kang Shin wearing a hanbok, a traditional Korean dress, leads a crafts activity at Beach School’s Lunar New Year event. Tam Bui plays “bầu cua tôm cá” a traditional Vietnamese new year game, with kids. Doan Nguyen, John Le, and Oliver Sun Le in front of a large spread mittee. Lunar New Year (Tết in Vietnamese) is one of our favorite holidays and we have fond memories celebrating with our friends and family. articles.text: Miranda Liu scored twice against San Leandro. Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team continues its quest for the WACC Foothill Division title with a 5-0 win over San Leandro at Witter Field on Wednesday, January 25. Two days later they drew 1-1 with Alameda, also a home game. The pair of games brings their record to 6-1-4 (W-T-L), 4-1-3 in league. Although PHS has three league losses, it is still in the thick of the race. It sits in third place behind Berkeley (5-2-1, 17 points) and Castro Valley (4-4-1, 16 points). Piedmont has matches against Castro Valley this Friday, February 3, and with Berkeley on Wednesday, February 8 to determine the fate of league standings. “This league is so tight and every game is so close. Every game is like one goal apart. It’s crazy how close it is still,” noted PHS coach Dan Chubbock. “Someone is going to have to go out and win the rest of their games to win the league.” 5-0 win over San Leandro Miranda Liu scored the first of her two goals in the 12th minute of action after twice rebounding her own shot attempts in close distance. She converted a third effort after receiving a pass down the right side and running it towards goal for the shot attempt. After that, Emily Fitzgerald scored in the 25th minute on a shot from around 20 yards. She scored once again in the 38th minute after rebounding a shot on target that was saved by the Pirates’ keeper. Staff Photos Emily Fitzgerald also had two goals in a game with San Leandro. Liu scored her second goal in the 53rd minute on a through-ball by Audrey Lam. 10 minutes later, Lam scored the game’s final goal on a run down the right side and into the box. 1-1 tie with Alameda On January 27 Alameda opened the game with a goal in the second minute of action after Piedmont’s defense committed a giveaway when trying to clear the ball. It was the Hornets’ only serious threat in the game. Piedmont nearly tied the game in the 18th minute when Liu fed Lam on a nice pass on a counterattack, but Lam’s shot went straight to the keeper. Fitzgerald also had a shot go high in the 35th minute and Hailey Marshburn had a shot go wide two minutes later. In the second half, Marshburn had shots on target in the 45th and 51st minutes, but couldn’t convert. The equalizer came in Amy Derr scored on a 35-yard free kick against Alameda.

articles.text: With three games left in the regular league season, Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team is on the final leg to capture its first Western Alameda County Conference championship in the league’s 11 year history. This past week on Wednesday, January 25, the Highlanders defeated last year’s WACC winners, San Leandro, by a one-sided score of 70-28 at Binks Rawlings Gym. “Overall, we like the effort day-in and day-out. Now it’s just a matter of staying focused and staying humble,” explained PHS coach Bryan Gardere. “We’re trying to make sure everyone is on the same page offensively and defensively. We want to execute well, make sure our rotations are on point defensively, and talking a little more on the floor.” The Highlanders are set to close out their regular season with three home games in the next nine days. They’ll face Alameda on February 2, Bishop O’Dowd on February 7, and a season-finale with Berkeley on February 10. If all goes well, Piedmont will win its first WACC banner. Piedmont has defeated all three schools, a 7-point squeaker, 69-62, over O’Dowd on January 18, and two lopsided wins, 73-14 over Alameda on January 12, and 57-20 over Berkeley on January 20. Natalia Martinez scored 14 points against the Pirates. Staff Photos Eva Levingston led Piedmont with 15 points against San Leandro. O’Dowd has won nine of the last 10 WACC titles. “Closing out the season strong is definitely our focus. We want to make sure our energy and effort is channeled in the right direction. We have a lot to clean up but things are obviously going well too. We’re just trying to stay sharp. We’ve talked about not peaking too early, and now is the time,” said Gardere. Game Recap It was never a close game against the San Leandro Pirates. Piedmont led 13-4 by the end of the first quarter and 30-15 by halftime. From there, Piedmont extended the gap with 22 points in the third quarter, 52-22, and added 18 more points in the fourth and just allowed six points, 70-28. Notably, the Highlanders were still without senior forward and team captain Trinity Zamora, who suffered a leg injury against O’Dowd on January 18. Eva Levingston, Natalia Martinez, Perseas Gioukaris, and Maddie Hill picked up the scoring and rebounding load, each finishing with double-digit scoring. PHS was electric from beyond the arc, knocking down 10 three-pointers. Hill and Adrienne Blackwell each sank three baskets from beyond the arc and Martinez and Gioukaris had two each. Final scoring: Levingston had 15 points, Martinez and Gioukaris had 14 points, Hill had 13 points, Blackwell had nine points, Katarina Melian scored five. Tuesday vs. Castro Valley The Highlanders traveled to Castro Valley last night, Tuesday, January 31. See next week’s Post for game results. NEXT UP Piedmont (20-0 overall, 6-0 league) hosts Alameda in Binks Rawlings Gym tomorrow, Thursday, February 2 at 6:30 p.m. They will host Bishop O’Dowd on Tuesday, February 7 at 5:30 p.m. Perseas Gioukaris tied Natalia Martinez with 14 points.

articles.text: Staff Photos Piedmont coach Todd Sullivan looks ahead to the final four games of the regular season. The Highlander boys’ soccer team played two of the top teams in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division over the past week, tying Berkeley 1-1 on Friday, January 27, but losing to Castro Valley 2-0 at Witter Field on Monday, January 30. “We were in the game in the first half and were arguably stronger than them. We looked really good in the first 20 minutes and then CV got back into the game. My message at halftime was to be careful of the second balls and try to win the initial ball. That was kind of where Castro Valley started to take over,” said coach Todd Sullivan. Piedmont entered the game with no losses in six games – albeit only two of which were wins. With four games left in league season, the Highlanders are looking to sharpen things up. Playoffs are coming up and Piedmont is the defending North Coast Section champion, 2-0 loss to Castro Valley The Highlanders struggled to break down the Trojans to create clear scoring opportunities and had their best chances early in the first half. Piedmont finished with five shots in the game with just three on target, all coming in the second half. The two sides went into halftime in a 0-0 tie. In the 17th minute, T.J. O’Neil had a shot from a few yards above the penalty area sail high over the net. In the 31st Gianluca Bini nearly received a pass in front of the net but he was called offside. Myles Gray also had a shot attempt from distance go high in the 35th. In the second half, Piedmont had three shots on target t no avail. In the meantime Castro Valley did well to create counterattacks and scoring chances. Piedmont goalkeeper Daniel Malecki made a diving save for Piedmont in the 51st minute. Jack Nelson was credited with PHS’ first shot on target in the 55th minute, but it was deflected. CV drew a free kick in the 60th minute and scored the go-ahead goal on a long ball into the penalty area. Castro Valley scored again nine minutes later on a counterattack on the left wing with PHS pushing its attack higher up the field. Piedmont’s Jacques Saldanha had a shot on target from the right wing in the 70th minute, Aiden Woolwine had a goal against Berkeley and a scoring opportunity late in the game against Castro Valley. articles.text: There is no better time for viewing bodies of water than after rains. Just nine miles from Piedmont is a trail that will make you forget that you’re in the hustle and bustle of the Bay Area. It’s the Kings Canyon Loop off of Canyon Road on the way to Moraga. Parking at East Bay MUD’s Valle Vista Staging Area, the Kings Canyon Loop is a moderately challenging trail that walks alongside the Upper San Leandro Reservoir. Hiking the loop requires 6.4 miles of walking and around 950 feet in elevation gain. The reservoir is near capacity right now, providing fantastic views for the majority of the hike. Walking along the northern portion of the reservoir, there’s a continuous view of the rolling East Bay hills. It’s a great location for birding or catching sight of little critters. On multiple occasions, California newts were spotted passing by on the trail. As for the difficulty of the trail, about 75 percent of the trail was manageably flat. Once you hit the 4.5-mile mark, the trail begins an elevation gain of 460 feet in a half mile, so roughly half of the day’s elevation gain is in one portion of the trail. But beware: at least 10 portions of the trail were saturated with mud, making it difficult to walk through without slipping. A close view of the San Leandro Reservoir is available on the Kings Canyon Loop Trail. Staff Photos The San Leandro Reservoir is at its highest level in years after the storms in December and January. A view of the reservoir from a road on the ridgeline.
articles.title: HIKING WITH JON Hiking the Kings Canyon Loop
