Hiking the loop requires 6.4 miles of walking and around 950 feet in elevation gain. The reservoir is near capacity right now, providing fantastic views for the majority of the hike. Walking along the northern portion of the reservoir, there’s a continuous view of the rolling East Bay hills. It’s a great location for birding or catching sight of little critters. On multiple occasions, California newts were spotted passing by on the trail. As for the difficulty of the trail, about 75 percent of the trail was manageably flat. Once you hit the 4.5-mile mark, the trail begins an elevation gain of 460 feet in a half mile, so roughly half of the day’s elevation gain is in one portion of the trail. But beware: at least 10 portions of the trail were saturated with mud, making it difficult to walk through without slipping. A close view of the San Leandro Reservoir is available on the Kings Canyon Loop Trail. Staff Photos The San Leandro Reservoir is at its highest level in years after the storms in December and January. A view of the reservoir from a road on the ridgeline. California newts are seen on the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Electric power lines are seen overhead on the Kings Canyon Loop trail. Hikers are cautioned to watch for several muddy areas which are slippery. The Kings Canyon Loop brings hikers under groves of oak trees. Caution and patience are advised. After walking alongside the reservoir for 4.5 miles, the trail goes into the hills and narrows from over 10 feet wide to just a few feet in some sections. It traverses underneath groves of oak trees and eventually provides an overhead view of the reservoir. At the 6-mile mark, you come to an intersection to continue on the Kings County Loop Trail to your left or to an added trail, Rimer Creek Trail to the right. The Post’s suggestion is to take the trail on the left which leads back to the reservoir. The trail on the right adds one mile to your afternoon of hiking and has some of the muddiest parts. This magnificent trail is severely underrated and little known to many. In 7.5 miles of hiking at noontime on a Saturday, we came across only 21 other hikers.

articles.text: A lion dance will be performed this Sunday at the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco. San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum welcomes the public this Sunday, February 5, for its Lunar New Year celebration with art, dance and music. Lunar New Year, sometimes called Chinese New Year, is celebrated widely in China but also in Tibet, Japan, Korea, Thailand, and in the Bay Area. Festivities involve honoring ancestors and making preparations for a prosperous and joyous new year. On the zodiac calendar this is the Year of the Rabbit, the fourth in the 12-year cycle of animals. Online activities Families can visit the Asian Art Museum’s website for printable coloring sheets related to the Year of the Rabbit, as well as an instructional page on how to create their own Lunar New Year red envelopes. You can also watch youth dancers from dance company LionDanceME perform a lion dance, a traditional way to ring in the new year. Online, you can also view “At the Table Dumpling Adventure’’ with Kristina Cho. Cho is a food stylist and blogger who shows her technique for making traditional Chinese pork and shrimp dumplings, a common dish for any time of the year. Cho is the author of the cookbook Mooncakes and Milk Bread, which includes the recipe for these dumplings and other traditional dishes. Family fun day Visit the Asian Art Museum in San Francisco on Sunday, February 5, for storytelling and family-friendly Lunar New Year activities. Art activities will begin at 11 a.m., where children and adults will learn about traditional Chinese art. Storyteller Fred Sheng will read “Why the Rat Comes First,” Miriam Mills reads “The Tet Pole,” and Leta Bushyhead reads “Nian, the Beast.” Visit https://asianart.org/cultural-celebrations/celebrate-lunar-new-year/ for a full schedule and to purchase tickets. San Francisco public art statues The city of San Francisco is celebrating the Year of the Rabbit with five large, colorful rabbit statues placed at the Chase Center, Chinatown-Rose Pak Station, Union Square, Lucky Supermarket on Sloat Boulevard, and the Asian Art Museum. The project is sponsored by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce.
articles.title: Asian Art Museum celebrates Year of the Rabbit this Sunday

articles.text: San Francisco Playhouse currently is performing Cashed Out by Native American playwright Claude Jackson, Jr. The story takes place on the Gila River Indian Community reservation in Arizona. The main character, Rocky, and her family try to hold themselves together after she develops a gambling addiction. SF Playhouse commissioned the theater work, which includes a cast of acclaimed actors of Native American and indigenous descent. The production features reallife father and daughter Matt and Louisa Kizer, playing the characters of Buddy and his granddaughter Maya. The play was the 2019 winner of the Native Voices at the Autry short play festival. The play will run through February 25. The San Francisco Playhouse is located at 450 Post Street near Union Square. For tickets and more information, visit www.sfplayhouse.org or call the box office at 415-677-9596. Photo by Roberto A. Jackson Claude Jackson, Jr., playwright of Cashed Out, now in performance at San Francisco Playhouse
articles.title: SF Playhouse presents Cashed Out now through Feb. 25

articles.text: Photo by Kevin Berne Louis Reyes McWilliams (left) and Cyndii Johnson in Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s current production of Clyde’s Berkeley Repertory Theatre’s current production, Clyde’s, written by Lynn Nottage, will be performed through February 26. Nottage’s newest play has been nominated for the 2022 Tony Award for Best Play. The two-time Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright describes it as a “feel-good comedic drama,” which follows formerly incarcerated kitchen staff workers at a truck-stop sandwich shop as they attempt to rebuild their lives. Their demanding boss aims to sidetrack their dreams, however. Each staff member is asked by a mysterious chef to imagine and then create the perfect sandwich. The play opened on Broadway in November, 2021 to favorable reviews. It is directed by Taylor Reynolds in a co-production with Huntington Theatre Company of Boston. Post-show discussions at Berkeley Rep will be held on February 3, 9, and 14, led by members of the Berkeley Rep staff. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/clyde-s/.
articles.title: Berkeley Rep production of Clyde’s on stage through February 26

articles.text: Treasure Island Museum, a nonprofit that preserves the island’s little-known, Pacific-themed heritage, has opened a new, free exhibition entitled Little Island, Big Ideas. The museum is also currently exhibiting Portal to the Pacific in War and Peace Monday through Friday, 8:30 a.m. to 5 p.m. Little Island, Big Ideas details the first 70 years of the island’s history. Guests may visit the gallery in Room 111 and view artifacts, photographs, and other items of historical relevance. The ongoing exhibition, Portal to the Pacific, presents Treasure Island’s dynamic and unique history in a series of banners and panels on display throughout the lobby in Building One. The panels feature many previously unpublished color photographs of the island. A permanent exhibition is on view during the island’s monthly lecture series, but it is temporarily removed when events are held in the lobby. Before visiting, view the museum’s calendar at: https://www.treasureislandmuseum.org/exhibitions. Both exhibitions are free and open to the public, Monday through Friday, from 9:00 a.m. to 5 p.m. The museum is located at 1 Avenue of the Palms on Treasure Island. Treasure Island Museum also offers several online exhibitions throughout the month. A permanent exhibition, Portal to the Pacific, is located in the lobby of the Treasure Island Museum.
articles.title: Treasure Island Museum opens new exhibit, Little Island, Big Ideas

Nottage’s newest play has been nominated for the 2022 Tony Award for Best Play. The two-time Pulitzer Prize-winning playwright describes it as a “feel-good comedic drama,” which follows formerly incarcerated kitchen staff workers at a truck-stop sandwich shop as they attempt to rebuild their lives. Their demanding boss aims to sidetrack their dreams, however. Each staff member is asked by a mysterious chef to imagine and then create the perfect sandwich. The play opened on Broadway in November, 2021 to favorable reviews. It is directed by Taylor Reynolds in a co-production with Huntington Theatre Company of Boston. Post-show discussions at Berkeley Rep will be held on February 3, 9, and 14, led by members of the Berkeley Rep staff. To purchase tickets, visit https://www.berkeleyrep.org/ shows/clyde-s/.

articles.text: Artist and art historian Michael Stehr is resenting an illustrated lecture celebrating one of the world’s great museums. “A Stroll Through the Musée d’Orsay: An Evening with the Impressionists” will be presented at the Piedmont Center for the Arts this Friday, February 3 at 6:30 p.m. Doors open at 6:00 p.m., and admission is $20 per person at the door, Cash only. Some regard the Impressionist movement that began in Paris in the second half of the 1800’s to be the most important movement in art history since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Impressionists marked the departure from the oppressive constraints of traditional painting while serving as a stepping stone in the evolution towards becoming “modern.” The broken brush strokes and vaporous colors associated with the movement have these pictures being some of the most widely appreciated in Western art. For those cherishing the art of the Impressionists, there is one ultimate destination to enjoy these remarkable paintings: the Musée d’Orsay in Paris. Join art historian Michael Stehr as he makes a return visit to Piedmont Center for the Arts to guide visitors on a virtual stroll through this brilliant museum.

articles.text: There’s hope for us all when a lead dancer here moves on to choreography and finds his inspiration with 13th century Persian poets. The Frenchman Nicolas Blanc, a principal here shortly after the Millennium, turned to the poet Rumi in creating his new Gateway to the Sun for the San Francisco Ballet. The main character is the lonely, reflective Poet, presumably Rumi himself, separate but connected with the community around him. Max Cauthorn played that lead barefoot in a breakthrough dancing interpretation. His solemnity contrasts beautifully with the animated crowds all about, then lightened by joining in a pas de trois with two women. Blanc’s unusual holds and lifts in his choreography make this a work crying out to be revived long after the festival of nine premieres is packed way. Not the least of the attractions has been one of the memorable scores by Anna Clyne, today ranking in the front lines of female composers. Her work is episodic and consistently expressive, underlining the action withPoured into this drama without headlines were the eminent interpreters Sasha de Sola and The lead in Yuri Possokhov’s new Violin Concerto was Sasha Mukhamedov decked out in pink and with hip-wiggles to prove that she never takes herself too seriously. All but stealing the show was the electric dynamism of Joseph Walsh’s solos, enough to overshadow his black pompadour rivaling in height JFK’s (that president was shorter than most, and the extra topside hair helped raise him above the dais at speeches). What I like best about Possokhov’s work is a certain strain of whimsy—never easily arrived at. Feet and Feats Yes, Violin Concerto offered us daring feet. In addition, daring feats as well, most notably a strong dancer with arms aloft supporting a knotted-up partner for a good five seconds. Which was more arresting: The stratospheric lift, or the complex knot of a woman? Program Three opened with yet another world premiere, Claudia Schreier’s Kin. Dores André who is tapped for one lead role after another, is the salient figure emerging from a melee of dancers running about to a forgettable but portentous score. She is drawn into a community by WanTing Zhao, offering a welcome kinship, even though penetrating the group fully proves daunting. articles.text: Piedmont cartoonist Philip Witte, creator of the Flip cartoons that appear weekly in the Piedmont Post, nationally in the New Yorker and Wall Street Journal, and internationally throughout the UK including Dublin, Ireland, is having an exhibit of selected works at Piedmont CenThe exhibit ends on Sunday, February 5. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Since leaving his legal career seven years ago, Piedmonter Phil Witte has sold more than 1,000 cartoons to dozens of publications in the U.S., U.K., and Ireland. A cartoonist from an early age, once he began his studies at Princeton he abandoned cartooning. Following some time working in Bangkok, he entered law school at the University of Chicago. Although life as a litigation attorney was all-consuming, Phil tried to find time for creative activities. He wrote a few humor pieces, which attracted the attention of a book publisher and which led to a joke book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and a sequel on turning 60. Sales to date are approaching 175,000 copies. “I knew I could write jokes, so I figured if I could combine that with drawing, I could become a cartoonist,” he said. “I was decent in art, but I needed to get a lot better, plus I had to develop a style… I’m still working on that.” He showed his early work to Phil Frank, the late cartoonist at The San Francisco Chronicle, who encouraged him. While working on his art, Witte collaborated as a gag writer for syndicated cartoonists, including Dan Piraro, creator of “What took you so long?” “Uh-oh” “That’s a mammoth. I told you to bring home a mastodon.” Photo by Rob Yelland Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte will have an exhibit of his work at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from January 21 to February 5. the cartoon feature “Bizarro.” Phil has 25 original ink drawings by Piraro that resulted from their collaboration. He began selling his cartoons to major markets, including The Wall Street Journal, which encouraged him to put more time into cartooning. When he felt he had developed enough professional relationships with editors, he made the decision to leave his law practice. “The firm threw a blow-out farewell party at a restaurant, and even closed the office for the afternoon. It was the best day in my former career,” he recalled. He has licensed his cartoons to greeting card companies with great success. Textbooks and professional groups started leasing his cartoons as well. He has also written a few dozen humor pieces for magazines and online sites. Six years ago Phil and former Piedmont resident Rex Hesner began a blog critiquing the cartoons in The New Yorker magazine. That effort caught the eye of Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. Witte was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. His cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. He has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. There is even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of his cartoons in their permanent collection. Private collectors, including the documentary filmmaker Ken Burns, have bought Witte’s original artwork. “We actually swapped work – my cartoon for dozens of his DVDs. He wrote a wonderful thank-you note and sent me a photo of him posing with the cartoon in his office,” he said. Upon reflection, Witte added, “The cartooning career has gone far better than I even imagined it would, I’m content that I made the right career move.” “Not too short, or people won’t know I’m God.” “Not moonshine—small batch, artisanal grain alcohol.”

And therein began a beautiful Bravo, maestro A Salute to Stockton Symphony and conductor Peter Jaffe cat and mouse game between the conductor and snare drum virtuoso Tennison Watts. You know the scene… each one imitates the By Joseph Gold A cynic once said: “In the world of music, the charlatan has the greatest chance of success by being a conductor.” That is not the case in Stockton. The conductor indicated every variety of dynamics. Watts was able to do everything, seemingly with telepathic communication. And that was only the beginning…It got better. The first piece on the program was a world premiere by Alex Orfaly entitled “sol Invictus.” When I looked at the music, it looked like one of those boring and repetitive modern compositions, but it was nothing like that. It retained both the interest of the audience, and of all the musicians. The concert continued with the ever popular Rachmaninov Second Piano Concerto. The soloist was a young Venezuelan-American pianist, Gabriela Martinez, who proved to be a master of dynamics, tone color, and an abundant technique. There is hardly any piece in the entire orchestra repertoire so brilliant as this one. To say that the performance was memorable, is putting it mildly. Conductor Jaffe re-created tonal pictures that were vivid, and he inspired the orchestra to play with real inspiration. Things like this are a way of life with the Stockton Symphony. pages.text: Wednesday, February 1, 2023 21 MOVIES FOR KIDS A fresh look at Cinderella by Disney Review by Chris Honoré If you see the title Cinderella and shrug, feeling the story is all too familiar, wondering what could possibly be new in this narrative. Know that you have not seen the story presented in this surprising and beautiful way. And once again done by Disney. This is a contemporary version of what is an iconic fairytale, fresh and engaging (with a tweak here and a change there by the writers), but not surprising given that it’s directed by the talented Kenneth Branagh. The story, in essence, is simple and direct, and unlike those that have come before (the most memorable being the animated version by Disney some 65 years ago), relies very little on special effects or CGI. Of course, there is the scene when Ella’s Fairy Godmother (Helena Bonham Carter) appears and turns a simple pumpkin into a startlingly beautiful, ornate coach, and the house mice slowly morph into six white steeds and two lizards become the coachmen. In the main, and to its credit, this film is character driven, and the wonder of Cinderella can be found in watching each individual revealed – from the very kind and enchanting Ella (Lilly James), to the cruel and sadistic Lady Tremaine (Cate Blanchett). The set up for the movie takes almost all of act one to Lily James and Richard Madden in Disney’s latest retelling of Cinderella. construct. Ella is living an idyllic life with her mother (Hayley Atwell) and father (Ben Chaplin) in a gorgeous, English countryside mansion. She is embraced by her loving family and secure in her place as a much cared for daughter. Unexpectedly, sadly, Ella’s mother falls suddenly ill and dies, leaving Ella with just her father. Time passes, years slip by, and he decides to remarry, choosing a benign widow (or so he believes), Lady Tremaine, who has two daughters Ella’s age, Drisella and Anastasia (Sophia McShera and Holliday Granger). With their arrival, Ella’s life changes as act two unfolds. At first she is tolerated by her stepmother, and mocked by the sisters. But when her father dies on a business trip, Ella, now orphaned, finds her position in the household one in which she is ostracized and turned into a servant, relegated to the attic, always at the beck and call of the three women. And it is they who name her Cinderella, for she sleeps by the den fireplace because the attic is too cold in winter. And so the story blossoms in a most compelling and captivating manner. The king (Derek Jacobi) announces that he will give a magnificent royal ball. His young son (Richard Madden), the heir and prince, insists that all of the single maidens of the kingdom must be invited. As it turns out, the prince is about to choose a bride at the ball, whether a commoner or titled. Naturally, Tremaine forbids Cinderella from going. That is until there is a magical moment when the fable soars. It is both glorious to watch and touching in its emotions, none of which are disguised behind computer trickery. The visuals – and they are stunning – create a magnetism that transcends and surprises, even though the outcome is solidly based on the Disneyesque idea of “happily ever after.” It is in getting to that moment that separates this Cinderella from all its precursors (and there have been many, to include a TV special starring Julie Andrews). As an aside, just before Ella’s mother dies, she takes her daughter’s hand and asks her to always have courage and above all else, be kind, a moral principle that Ella tries to live by, and one that is woven with sensitivity, never pedantically, into the story. Ella is, indeed, courageous and reflexively kind no matter the abuse heaped upon her by the mean-spirited Tremaine. She is also by nature innocent; but also tenacious and someone who, in every frame, is believable as she demonstrates how deeply her decency frames her life. It’s a wonderfully resonant message, brought to you once again by Disney, who has always chosen to see the world not as it is but as it should be (the last line of the film). Cinderella. Directed by Kenneth Branagh. Starring Cate Blanchet, Lily James, Richard Madden. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released 2015. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv/Disney+.

articles.text: Part 60 in a biweekly series Our increasing accommodation of the automobile takes more and more resources, and more and more space, not only with roads of all kinds, but also with parking. Homes started out years ago often with only a carriage house as a garage. Over the years the market need has grown for larger 2, 3, and even 4 car garages. Unfortunately, aside from the financial and environmental costs, there are aesthetic limitations that result from so much garage space as a part of the average sized home. On typical medium or small sized home lots the popular 2-car garage must most often be located close to the street, jutting out in front of the rest of the house. A large garage door necessarily then assumes an upfront, dominant position in the building massing. As a result the front door and main entry is limited With smaller houses on narrow lots, a single car garage is the reasonable proportion, allowing the subordination of the garage to the mass of the house. Wonderful detailing and landscape treatment turns these Piedmont garages into real amenities. Even a 3-car garage can enhance the aesthetic as shown in this Piedmont property. Using the larger lot to set back the garage subordinates it to the house and the front door. Nicely designed garage doors with attached landscaped trellis add to the success. This is as it should be: a house with a garage instead of a garage with a house. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs

articles.text: A recipe for an olive oil cake always catches my eye and piques my curiosity. I love them because they bake with a moist and tender crumb and keep for a day or so with little diminution of these ideal traits. It is still citrus season here, and by my casual observations this year is delivering bumper crops. I’m seeing front yard gardens with tons of ripening fruits, notably lemons, oranges, limes and some other varieties I cannot identify without trespassing onto private property. This recipe is from Bake from Scratch, September-October 2020. I knew I would bake this as soon as I saw it, and can confirm it has been in regular rotation ever since. Pear Almond Olive Oil Cake Adapted from Baking from Scratch, Laura Crandall INGREDIENTS • 2 extra-large eggs, room temperature • 3/4 cup granulated sugar • 1/2 cup extra-virgin olive oil • 2/3 cup blanched almond flour • 1/3 cup whole milk • 1 tablespoon lemon zest, lightly packed. (Zest the lemon before squeezing the juice.) • 1 teaspoon vanilla extract • 1/4 teaspoon almond extract • 1-1/3 cups all-purpose flour • 1-1/2 teaspoons baking powder • 1/2 teaspoon sea salt • 1 large or 2 small Anjou or Bosc pear(s), firm-ripe • 2 teaspoons lemon juice • 1/2 cup sliced almonds • Confectioners’ sugar, optional INSTRUCTIONS Position an oven rack to the mid-oven position and preheat the oven to 350°F. Oil the sides of a 9-inch round springform pan, lightly dust with flour. Line the removable bottom with parchment and fasten the sides back accordingly. Whisk flour, baking powder, and salt together in a medium bowl. Set aside. Using a handheld electric mixer, beat the eggs on medium speed until foamy, about 1 minute. Add sugar in a slow, steady stream. Increase to high speed until the mixture is fluffy and pale yellow, about 2 minutes. Reduce speed to low speed, and while mixer is running, pour the olive oil in a slow, steady stream. Mix until oil is fully incorporated. Add almond flour, milk, lemon zest, and extracts. Beat on medium speed until combined. On low speed, add the flour mixture and mix until barely incorporated. Stop to scrape the sides and bottom of the bowl if needed. Folding in the flour with a spatula toward the end as necessary, Be careful to not over mix. Pour the batter into the prepared springform pan. Cut the pear(s) in half lengthwise, core and destem. Slice the pear halves into 1/8-inch- thick slices. Divide the slices into groups of 4–5 and arrange into a fan-shape and gently arrange on top of the batter in a decorative pattern, leaving a 1-inch boarder around the outside edge of the pan. Brush the slices with lemon juice. Sprinkle almonds between the arranged groups of pears and around the edge of the pan. Bake about 50-55 minutes. Test for doneness by inserting a toothpick in the center of the cake. It should come out with only a few crumbs clinging. Transfer the pan to a wire rack and cool for 15 minutes. Remove the sides of the springform pan and cool completely before serving. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: Pear Almond Olive Oil Cake is a Winter treat

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Oakland Zoo Construction crews have been working on repairing the road at the entrance of Oakland Zoo since the new year. Having the Zoo closed caused an estimated loss of $500,000 per week. Oakland Zoo will reopen to the public this Friday, February 3, one month after being forced to close due to a 40-foot sinkhole resulting from storm damage that collapsed a culvert under the vehicle entrance to the Zoo at Golf Links Road. Since the Zoo’s closure on January 1, the Zoo staff have continued to care for the animals and maintain Zoo grounds in addition to working to recover from the damage caused by rainstorms in December. The volume and velocity of the water flowing across the Zoo grounds caused eucalyptus trees to fall, flooding in various buildings, major soil erosion, and the drainage system to be overwhelmed. “We are excited to welcome guests back to the Zoo after the month-long closure. We’ll finally be able to start the year off the way we intended and open our doors to the many visitors who have been waiting to enjoy the Zoo,” said Nik Dehejia, CEO of Oakland Zoo. Starting this Friday, February 3, at 10:00 a.m., guests with reservations will be able to visit the Zoo, as well as attend the Zoo’s popular nighttime lantern event, Glowfari in the evening. Glowfari, originally scheduled to conclude on January 29, has been extended through March 4. Ticket reservations for Glowfari are on sale now at Oaklandzoo.org/ tickets. Tickets and member reservations for regular daytime admission are also available for reservation online. Daytime admission tickets are available four weeks in advance on a rolling basis.
articles.title: Oakland Zoo set to reopen this Friday, Feb. 3

pages.text: 24 Wednesday, February 1, 2023 Walking on Wednesday Walking on Wednesday group visits Dracena Park By Dick Carter Spring was in the air last Wednesday, and a near record turnout for a stroll with the Walking on Wednesdays group – 50 walkers and five K-9 best friends. Charlene Louie and Priscilla Wanerus had agreed to lead the group to Dracena Park. Before the walk an announcement was made that 15 of the walkers had gone to Phil Witte’s cartoon art exhibition at the Piedmont Center for the Arts and had a great time. Charlene led the walkers on Hillside Avenue, across Oakland Avenue and down Blair Avenue to the corner of El Cerrito Avenues where Walter Blair once had a dairy farm. This was also the edge of a quarry he created – now Dracena Park. The group entered at the bottom of the park where there is a bench in memory of Ralston Louie who died tragically in 2021. The group went up a path to the Tot Lot, where Charlene told more of the park’s history. Originally, this land was a part of the 8,000 acres that Blair bought. The property was quarried in 1852 for stone that was used to pave Oakland and Piedmont’s early streets and railways. In 1873, a quarry crew, which consisted mainly of Chinese laborers, struck water from a subterranean creek. It turned the bottom of the quarry into a lake, some 60 feet deep. Attempts to pump out the water failed, and the lake remained. It turned into a swimming hole for Piedmont boys, and sadly there were at least 12 drownings in 20 years. Finally, the quarry was fenced and locked for more than 40 years. There was a lake, called “Blair’s Pond,” complete with ducks, until at least 1977. Around 2000 the tot lot play area was renovated. Kids wanted a climbing wall and swings, while the adults wanted restrooms. Funds were raised for both, and the project was completed in 2006. Charlene then took the walkers the park’s lower entrance, and the K-9 best friends were let loose to run on the path and through the beautiful grove of redwood trees. The walkers stopped at a plaque at Storyteller Bridge, which looms above the path. Charlene also told its history. It was built in 2013 as Cole Becker’s Eagle Scout project. It replaced a bridge built in the 1920’s which crossed a ravine and creek bed. This bridge was demolished in the early 1960’s after falling into disrepair. The creek is long gone. The walkers continued up the path past huge eucalyptus trees and circled back to walk over Storyteller Bridge. At the top of the park on Dracena Avenue Priscilla Wanerus took over for Charlene and led the group on Dracena to Blair Avenue where they retraced their steps to Hillside and Magnolia Avenues and to the Exedra. The temperature started to rise and the walkers experienced something new: being warm on a Wednesday walk. At the conclusion of the walk, a little over an hour the group expressed their thanks to Charlene and Priscilla for taking them on an enjoyable tour of one of Piedmont’s most beautiful parks and sharing its history. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. articles.text: The two small tennis courts at Beach School will be used for pickleball on a trial basis. A five-month trial for pickleball play at Beach School tennis courts will begin on February 27. The Recreation Commission will receive an update and vote to confirm or modify trial parameters at their February 15 meeting. The trial is designed to help the city evaluate options for the demand for pickleball play. During the trial period, the Beach courts will be converted to pickleball play as follows: • Court hours will be 9 a.m. to 9 p.m. (dusk) • Courts will be locked in the evenings • Organized drop-in pickleball play will be available Monday through Friday, 10 a.m.-1 p.m. • Courts will be open for informal drop-in play during remaining hours The Recreation Department will offer additional pickleball programming, including youth classes after school and free evening lessons for families and beginners. The Piedmont Pickleball Group plans to host a potluck event on March 4 to welcome new players. Meeting a growing interest Currently, kids, families and working adults have no place to play pickleball in Piedmont during the week. Pickleball is available only during limited designated hours, spread across Hampton, Beach, and the middle school courts on different days. Nets must be switched out at the beginning and end of every pickleball session. During the trial period, pickleball hours at the Hampton courts will be suspended, making 8 of Piedmont’s 10 tennis courts available full-time for tennis play. The Beach courts were selected for the trial because they are the City’s least used tennis facility, and because they cannot be used for competitive tennis play due to their small size. This trial will help the Recreation Commission and city staff better understand the full scope of pickleball demand among our community. The February to July trial period was chosen in part because it allows staff to monitor court usage across two seasons, providing a more complete picture of how dedicated pickleball courts would be used in the longterm. Community feedback will be critical in evaluating the success of the trial. The Recreation Commission invites public comments at its meetings on April 19 and June 21. The city will invite feedback through a community survey this spring, after the trial has begun.

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors group recently received a tutorial from two Piedmont High AP Computer Science students. The 30-minute session at the Community Hall was the first of what hopes to be a monthly occurrence for help with cell phones and tech troubleshooting. Sophomores Ishaia Goldberg-Berman and Bruno Banuelos forfeited their lunch times to answer tech questions from the group of seniors organized by Janet Epstein. How do I get rid of all these notifications on my phone? When I delete a photo, why does my storage still say full? What is a personal hotspot? Members of the Piedmont Seniors were able to open up their phones and get answers to their questions. Topics included: cloud storage, how to change passwords, and how to connect to printers. “It’s a wonderful kind of community service and is really needed. This is starting with our Seniors Group, but I’m hoping for it to expand to more people wanting tech help and to get more tutors from the high school,” said Epstein. Participants were shown how to connect to the internet through another cell phone, a cellular hot spot turned on by Goldberg-Berman. “We are going to use her phone as the internet right now,” Epstein clarified for the group. The Piedmont Senior group meets once a month on the last Wednesday of the month. They routinely go on excursions around the Bay Area to see museums and areas of historical importance. The Tech Tutorials will be held every fourth Wednesday in the Community Hall from 12:45-1:15 p.m. More student volunteers are welcome and there is plenty of room for participants. For more information, contact Janet Epstein at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. 3820 Broadway, Oakland Owners: Leah and Benjamin Bloom Piedmont High Class of ‘03

articles.text: Gary Rinehart, a resident of Piedmont for 55 years, passed away at home in the early morning hours of January 4, 2023. He was 87. Born Gary Ray Rinehart on December 15, 1935 in Oakland, he was the son of Raymond and Patricia Rinehart of Piedmont. He graduated from St. Joseph High School in Alameda. He attended the Navy School of Music in Washington, DC. and served on the USS Salem, the flagship of the 6th Fleet, from 1954 to 1958. He relished this time of his life and music, particularly the opportunity to play with Dizzy Gillespie in Istanbul, Turkey. Upon his honorable discharge from the U.S. Navy, Gary met the love of his life, Sharon Duffy. They were married on January 30, 1960, after which he attained an undergraduate degree in Business Administration from the University of California, Berkeley, and a Juris Doctor degree from Boalt Hall (Berkeley School of Law). A prominent eminent domain attorney, Gary helped establish legal precedent on business goodwill and relocation assistance rights. Gary also argued before both the Supreme Court of California and the United States Supreme Court. He prevailed as the attorney for the defendant in California v. Muller which estabGary and Sharon Rinehart were married on January 30, 1960. Piedmont attorney and pianist Gary Rinehart died on January 4 at age 87. lished compensation for business owners impacted by public improvement projects. He was Counsel to the City of Oakland, the City of Walnut Creek, Port of Oakland, and East Bay Regional Park District among many municipal and regional organizations. Gary touched the lives of thousands with his beautiful piano playing, whether classical, jazz, or music from the Great American Songbook. He loved pianos, and proudly owned several impressive grand pianos. The practice of law was a necessity, but piano was his passion. “I was born to be a performer,” he once said. He could play any song from the Great American Songbook in most any key. He studied under Frank Denke of Piedmont, the pianist for the NBC Radio Orchestra. He performed numerous times at the initial Piedmont Jazz Festival and was a patron and performer at the Piedmont Center of the Arts. His greatest gift was to share his appreciation of music. Those lucky enough to walk by his Wildwood Avenue home early on a weekend morning could enjoy his proficient offerings of Chopin waltzes, Nocturnes, Polonaises, or a Joplin Rag. He loved noticing young people carrying forward musical traditions, and was an ardent supporter of the Summer Musicals at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland Hills. Following in his father’s footsteps, he served on the Woodminster Board of Directors for many years. Several CDs of his music are available on Spotify: h t t p s: //o p e n . s p o t i f y. c o m / artist/6kMbongjXMBYv1MAisQFkP?si=wYILhl9pT2yDMLQIpIfvPQ Gary is survived by his wife, Sharon Rinehart, brother Jim Rinehart of El Dorado Hills, son and daughter-in-law Greg and Melina Rinehart of Piedmont, and son and daughter-in-law Geoff and Kristi Rinehart of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho. He is also survived by grandchildren Kelsey and Michael Kennelly of Diablo, California, Hannah Rinehart of Brooklyn, New York, Maddi Rinehart of Seattle, Washington, and Carrington Rinehart of Spokane Valley, Washington. Additionally, he is survived by a great-granddaughter, Kailey Kennelly. Pianist Gary Rinehart plays at an early Piedmont Jazz Festival in Piedmont Park.

articles.text: John Constantine — a largerthan-life personality to friends everywhere — was born in Flushing, Queens, in New York on March 10, 1951. He was the eldest child of Constantine “Gus” Constantine and Sophie Klarides Constantine, shared his name with a famous Hellblazer comic and many other Greek men, and was one of a kind. He genuinely loved people and always saw the best in them. He was a great conversationalist, networker/connector, and enjoyed talking with anyone and everyone. He could “work a room” with ease. The Constantine family moved all around the East Coast during John’s childhood, including stops in Port Washington and Smithtown in Long Island, New York as well as Great Barrington, Massachusetts. There, John made great, life-long friends and learned about business and hard work thanks to time spent in the family’s delicatessen and bowling alley/restaurant endeavors. John’s interest in business led him to Villanova University to get his degree from the Villanova School of Business, where he became a loyal Wildcat and member of both the school band — playing clarinet — and Lambda Chi Alpha fraternity. Everyone he spent time with at Villanova remained a cherished friend throughout his life. March became John’s favorite month to show his admiration and support for his alma mater — clad in blue and white to cheer on his “Cats” during basketball’s March Madness. John began his career in finance at Hertz on the East Coast. When his family moved to San Diego, he decided to also move West and continued working in finance at Warner. When Warner acquired Atari, it paved the way for the “golden days” of his career. At Atari, he helped globalize operations for the iconic video game brand while living abroad in Hong Kong and London. His time in China led him to take on roles as president of the Americas at Bondwell, General Electronics, and Elite Industrial Group and drove him to share his knowledge and expertise while on the board of the Hong Kong Association of Northern California. John fell madly in love with his wife — Debra Anne Cardella Constantine — when they were both living in San Francisco and met at a Bay Club party in 1984. They were engaged and married in 1985. Family and friends who came from near and far for their wedding now note that it was the beginning of their tradition of hosting visitors in the Bay Area. Many more memories were made as John and Debra moved to Piedmont and joined various organizations together — including Piedmont Newcomers and Neighbors and Claremont Country Club — that helped start and foster their loving community of friends. John and Debra welcomed twin girls — Alexandra Patrina Constantine and Jonna Michelle Constantine — in January 1987. John Constantine died on January 28, 2023. He was 71. John was an active cheerleader in the early extracurricular activities of “The Girls” and grew into their trusted confidant in financial, business, and life advice. John enjoyed being a fellow Wildcat with Alexandra. He was endlessly proud of his daughters’ professional and personal accomplishments — big and small. They inherited his laughter — even in life’s most challenging moments — as well as keeping in touch with friends all over the country and world. While John always had an appreciation for the finer things in life, he was deemed a “poster child” for retirement and enjoyed dedicating time to the things he already loved as well as trying out new activities. As a long-time member of the East Bay Wine Group, he also did wine tastings with the Friends of the Grape (FOG) in San Francisco. He learned new games — especially bridge and golf — that kept him challenged and social. Serving the community allowed him to spend time with wonderful friends, new and old. He held many committee positions at Claremont Country Club and as a volunteer with the Ascension Cathedral’s annual Golf Tournament and Greek Festival. John also continued his love of playing the clarinet in Urquhart Concert Band and in the Piedmont Community Band in the 4th of July Parade. He was committed to Mended Hearts — an organization that gives hope to heart disease patients, their families, and caregivers. John also continued his college-era connections in the Bay Area with the Villanova NorCal Alumni community, where he served as president for many years, as well as advising the Lambda Chi Alpha chapter at UC Berkeley. For an endlessly optimistic and easy-going guy, John encountered many difficult health issues recently that he could not overcome. He left this life on January 28, 2023, which was way too soon. John is survived by his heartbroken wife, Debra, and daughters Alexandra and Jonna. A celebration of his life will be held at a later date. The family suggests memorial donations in the name of John Constantine be made to Mended Hearts, Chapter 188, 1500 Dawson Road, Albany, GA. 31707 (https://mendedhearts.org/), or the Rheumatoid Arthritis Foundation (https:// www.rheumatoidarthritis.org/).

pages.text: 26 Wednesday, February 1, 2023 Obituary Piedmont pianist Gary Rinehart dies on January 4 Gary Rinehart, a resident of Piedmont for 55 years, passed away at home in the early morning hours of January 4, 2023. He was 87. Born Gary Ray Rinehart on December 15, 1935 in Oakland, he was the son of Raymond and Patricia Rinehart of Piedmont. He graduated from St. Joseph High School in Alameda. He attended the Navy School of Music in Washington, DC. and served on the USS Salem, the flagship of the 6th Fleet, from 1954 to 1958. He relished this time of his life and music, particularly the opportunity to play with Dizzy Gillespie in Istanbul, Turkey. Upon his honorable discharge from the U.S. Navy, Gary met the love of his life, Sharon Duffy. They were married on January 30, 1960, after which he attained an undergraduate degree in Business Administration from the University of California, Berkeley, and a Juris Doctor degree from Boalt Hall (Berkeley School of Law). A prominent eminent domain attorney, Gary helped establish legal precedent on business goodwill and relocation assistance rights. Gary also argued before both the Supreme Court of California and the United States Supreme Court. He prevailed as the attorney for the defendant in California v. Muller which estabGary and Sharon Rinehart were married on January 30, 1960. Piedmont attorney and pianist Gary Rinehart died on January 4 at age 87. lished compensation for business owners impacted by public improvement projects. He was Counsel to the City of Oakland, the City of Walnut Creek, Port of Oakland, and East Bay Regional Park District among many municipal and regional organizations. Gary touched the lives of thousands with his beautiful piano playing, whether classical, jazz, or music from the Great American Songbook. He loved pianos, and proudly owned several impressive grand pianos. The practice of law was a necessity, but piano was his passion. “I was born to be a performer,” he once said. He could play any song from the Great American Songbook in most any key. He studied under Frank Denke of Piedmont, the pianist for the NBC Radio Orchestra. He performed numerous times at the initial Piedmont Jazz Festival and was a patron and performer at the Piedmont Center of the Arts. His greatest gift was to share his appreciation of music. Those lucky enough to walk by his Wildwood Avenue home early on a weekend morning could enjoy his proficient offerings of Chopin waltzes, Nocturnes, Polonaises, or a Joplin Rag. He loved noticing young people carrying forward musical traditions, and was an ardent supporter of the Summer Musicals at Woodminster Amphitheater in Joaquin Miller Park in the Oakland Hills. Following in his father’s footsteps, he served on the Woodminster Board of Directors for many years. Several CDs of his music are available on Spotify: h t t p s: //o p e n . s p o t i f y. c o m / artist/6kMbongjXMBYv1MAisQFkP?si=wYILhl9pT2yDMLQIpIfvPQ Gary is survived by his wife, Sharon Rinehart, brother Jim Rinehart of El Dorado Hills, son and daughter-in-law Greg and Melina Rinehart of Piedmont, and son and daughter-in-law Geoff and Kristi Rinehart of Coeur d’Alene, Idaho. He is also survived by grandchildren Kelsey and Michael Kennelly of Diablo, California, Hannah Rinehart of Brooklyn, New York, Maddi Rinehart of Seattle, Washington, and Carrington Rinehart of Spokane Valley, Washington. Additionally, he is survived by a great-granddaughter, Kailey Kennelly. Pianist Gary Rinehart plays at an early Piedmont Jazz Festival in Piedmont Park. Piedmont’s John Constantine dies on January 28 John Constantine — a largerthan-life personality to friends everywhere — was born in Flushing, Queens, in New York on March 10, 1951. He was the eldest child of Constantine “Gus” Constantine and Sophie Klarides Constantine, shared his name with a famous Hellblazer comic and many other Greek men, and was one of a kind. He genuinely loved people and always saw the best in them. He was a great conversationalist, networker/connector, and enjoyed talking with anyone and everyone. He could “work a room” with ease. The Constantine family moved all around the East Coast during John’s childhood, including stops in Port Washington and Smithtown in Long Island, New York as well as Great Barrington, Massachusetts. There, John made great, life-long friends and learned about business and hard work thanks to time spent in the family’s delicatessen and bowling alley/restaurant endeavors. John’s interest in business led him to Villanova University to get his degree from the Villanova School of Business, where he became a loyal Wildcat and member of both the school band — playing clarinet — and Lambda Chi Alpha fraternity. Everyone he spent time with at Villanova remained a cherished friend throughout his life. March became John’s favorite month to show his admiration and support for his alma mater — clad in blue and white to cheer on his “Cats” during basketball’s March Madness. John began his career in finance at Hertz on the East Coast. When his family moved to San Diego, he decided to also move West and continued working in finance at Warner. When Warner acquired Atari, it paved the way for the “golden days” of his career. At Atari, he helped globalize operations for the iconic video game brand while living abroad in Hong Kong and London. His time in China led him to take on roles as president of the Americas at Bondwell, General Electronics, and Elite Industrial Group and drove him to share his knowledge and expertise while on the board of the Hong Kong Association of Northern California. John fell madly in love with his wife — Debra Anne Cardella Constantine — when they were both living in San Francisco and met at a Bay Club party in 1984. They were engaged and married in 1985. Family and friends who came from near and far for their wedding now note that it was the beginning of their tradition of hosting visitors in the Bay Area. Many more memories were made as John and Debra moved to Piedmont and joined various organizations together — including Piedmont Newcomers and Neighbors and Claremont Country Club — that helped start and foster their loving community of friends. John and Debra welcomed twin girls — Alexandra Patrina Constantine and Jonna Michelle Constantine — in January 1987. John Constantine died on January 28, 2023. He was 71. John was an active cheerleader in the early extracurricular activities of “The Girls” and grew into their trusted confidant in financial, business, and life advice. John enjoyed being a fellow Wildcat with Alexandra. He was endlessly proud of his daughters’ professional and personal accomplishments — big and small. They inherited his laughter — even in life’s most challenging moments — as well as keeping in touch with friends all over the country and world. While John always had an appreciation for the finer things in life, he was deemed a “poster child” for retirement and enjoyed dedicating time to the things he already loved as well as trying out new activities. As a long-time member of the East Bay Wine Group, he also did wine tastings with the Friends of the Grape (FOG) in San Francisco. He learned new games — especially bridge and golf — that kept him challenged and social. Serving the community allowed him to spend time with wonderful friends, new and old. He held many committee positions at Claremont Country Club and as a volunteer with the Ascension Cathedral’s annual Golf Tournament and Greek Festival. John also continued his love of playing the clarinet in Urquhart Concert Band and in the Piedmont Community Band in the 4th of July Parade. He was committed to Mended Hearts — an organization that gives hope to heart disease patients, their families, and caregivers. John also continued his college-era connections in the Bay Area with the Villanova NorCal Alumni community, where he served as president for many years, as well as advising the Lambda Chi Alpha chapter at UC Berkeley. For an endlessly optimistic and easy-going guy, John encountered many difficult health issues recently that he could not overcome. He left this life on January 28, 2023, which was way too soon. John is survived by his heartbroken wife, Debra, and daughters Alexandra and Jonna. A celebration of his life will be held at a later date. The family suggests memorial donations in the name of John Constantine be made to Mended Hearts, Chapter 188, 1500 Dawson Road, Albany, GA. 31707 (https://mendedhearts.org/), or the Rheumatoid Arthritis Foundation (https:// www.rheumatoidarthritis.org/).

pages.text: 28 Wednesday, February 1, 2023 History of Piedmont By Gail G. Lombardi To attract more riders on their cable car line to Piedmont, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company built a Bandstand for concerts, a Tea House, Maze, Venetian Canal and small amusements for children. As the Cable Company failed to make a profit and was going into receivership in 1893, they added balloon ascensions to attract more riders on their cable cars. Hot Air Balloon Ascensions There was always an element of excitement and danger with the hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park, and they drew many visitors. By 1896, there were balloon ascensions every Sunday and on the 4th of July. Balloonists were considered daredevils, and for 25 cents visitors could ride up with the balloonist. Most of the balloon ascensions at Blair Park were aerial gymnasts, “dressed in spangles and tights” and doing “hair raising” stunts on a trapeze suspended from a captive balloon. It was exciting to watch the balloon fill with hot air. Young boys were allowed to hold the anchor lines as the balloon filled. As the aerialist climbed into the balloon basket, the balloon handler ordered the boys to “Let Go!” Visitors watched in awe as the balloon rose over their heads. One particularly daring aerialist hung upside down from the trapeze bar as it ascended. After several acrobatic stunts on the bar, the aerialist finished with a parachute drop from a height of 1000 feet. The balloon was on a long tether, and the balloon manager pulled it back to earth at the end of the show. One Sunday a balloon ascension ended fatally. Little Bertram Hills was visiting Blair Park with his aunt in July 1897. He had been holding onto one of the The end of Blair Park sand bag anchor lines when the balloon began to rise. He failed to let go of the line and rose with the balloon - 300, 600, 900 feet up in the air. The tether failed. It was a terrible sight to see little Bertram dangling from the line and holding on for his life while balloonist Charles Conlon attempted to return the balloon to earth. Unfortunately, Bertram’s strength gave out before the balloon could descend, and he fell to his death. His body was found a half mile away on farmland in the Montclair hills. Mountain View Cemetery bought 1-1/2 acres on the northern edge of the park. In 1901, the Cable Company announced that it was abandoning the park and that it would not reopen that spring. By 1902, Frank C. Havens and the Realty Syndicate owned the park land. The park was set for development. Throughout these last years, Blair Park continued to operate. By 1903 it was called Oakland Park, because the Blair family no longer owned the land. Charles Vosmer, one of the park’s balloonists, managed the park up to 1905 when its listing disappeared from city directories. The Blair Park land was still vacant in 1913 when the City of Piedmont, then six years old, voted to acquire land for parks. The balloon shaped sign is a reminder of the ascensions in the 1890s. The Oakland Tribune printed this sketch in 1967 with an article on the historic hot air balloon ascensions in Blair Park. aga Avenue. Today, the former grove of eucalyptus is just a narrow row of trees along the cemetery border. There were cascading waterfalls in Blair Park in the 1880s. The stream that ran down Moraga Canyon is now in a conduit under Moraga Avenue. The canyon was filled for decades ultimately creating Coaches Field. You may wonder, as I did, how all the Blair Park attractions could fit in the narrow strip of land between Moraga Avenue and Mountain View Cemetery. For one thing, the lots along Moraga Avenue are very deep, up to 300 feet deep. They slope steeply from the street and are relatively level out to the cemetery land. They form a large, relatively flat area for the Bandstand, Venetian Canal, Japanese Tea House and all of Blair Park’s amusements. Fragments of the paved paths still exist in some of the backyards on Moraga. The name “Blair Park” continues to live on current maps of Piedmont. Today the City calls the land opposite Maxwelton Road, “Blair Park.” This is a portion of Walter Blair’s greater 235 acres, but the Blair Park of history was at the end of Highland Avenue. Continuing the Tradition Blair Park began as an amusement park where visitors came to enjoy being outdoors. It is fitting that today the tradition has come full circle with Coaches Play Field and the William F Kennelly Skate Park. articles.text: A profound and moving interfaith gathering took place in Guild Hall at Piedmont Community Church on Friday, January 27. Initiated by Amy Kelly, representing the Jewish Affinity Group of Piedmont, and enthusiastically embraced by Senior Pastor Steve Schibsted, this Shabbat (Sabbath) dinner of Jews and Christians honored International Holocaust Remembrance Day. In 2005, the United Nations General Assembly designated January 27 as a day to honor the six million Jewish victims of the Holocaust. It was the date in 1945 that the monstrous Nazi Concentration and Extermination Camp of Auschwitz-Birkenau was liberated. This joint interfaith event was a lively one, attended by more than 75 participants, consisting of approximately equal numbers of people of Jewish and Christian faith. The meal was served potluck, along with a hearty soup prepared by members of the church. The room was filled with conversations while guitarist and singer Isaac Zones provided beautiful music, playing classic songs such as Leonard Cohen’s Hallelujah. The Friday meal ushering in the Jewish Day of Rest after sunset began with the lighting of the candles, a prayer beautifully chanted in Hebrew by 13-yearold Aaron Bennett. and a prayer over the braided bread known as challah. The evening was an emoPhotos by Michael Barber Amy Kelly, representing the Jewish Affinity Group of Piedmont, chats with Piedmont Community Church members Suzie Skugstad and Lisa Fuller ahead of the event. Aaron Bennett, 13, chants a prayer in Hebrew before Shabbat. Children gather around a table filled with coloring pages depicting Jewish language and culture. Singer Isaac Zones entertains guests as they line up for dinner. Dressed in a princess costume, four-year-old Olivia Castro waits with her mom, Sharon Petrowsky, for the event to begin. Ilana Bennett reads a reflection of the Holocaust written by her son, Aaron. The Piedmont Church Courtyard offers a place for children to play after dinner. Rachel Leonard shares a story revealing a Jewish tradition, naming her children after relatives who survived the Holocaust. tional one as speakers shared the pain of losing relatives and their fear that the unspeakable horrors of the Nazi Holocaust are fading with the passage of time. It was also an evening of hope as many of the Jewish participants thanked the church for making them feel “welcomed and not othered”. Among the City of Piedmont dignitaries in attendance were Mayor Jen Cavanaugh and recently elected Board of Education member Ruchi Medhekar. “This joint interfaith event demonstrates that we are stronger together,” said Cavenaugh. Sharon Petrowsky spoke about her grandmother Eva Libitzky, an Auschwitz survivor, and generously provided copies of her grandmother’s book Out on a Ledge at each table. Ilana Bennett shared a portion of her son Aaron’s Bar Mitzvah speech which was inspired by his visit to the Holocaust Remembrance Museum in Jerusalem. There he learned of a 13-year-old Czech boy also named Aaron who was killed by the Nazis in 1942. In a touching gesture, Aaron’s speech said he was sharing his Bar Mitzvah with the deceased Aaron, “a boy just like me who could not have his own Bar Mitzvah” honoring his “Bar Mitzvah twin” as a hero. “I’m pretty sure that what happened here tonight made God smile,” said Pastor Schibsted.

articles.text: and Chinese, to name a few. Beach parent Anna Kneitel even made zongzi from scratch, which is hard to make. Zongzi is a traditional Chinese rice dish made of glutinous rice stuffed with different fillings and wrapped with bamboo leaves. Anna looked up the recipe and went to the grocery store to buy the ingredients just for this event. Tammy Choi, another Beach parent, made Tteokbokki, a Korean spicy rice cake. People also shared oranges, dumplings, and noodles, foods that traditionally bring good luck and fortune. It was beautiful how it all came together, and we are so appreciative of the outpouring and support from the community. Bầu cua tôm cá – which translates to “Gourd, Crab, Shrimp, Fish” – is a Vietnamese game traditionally played during Tết. There are three dice and a board with six objects on them: a deer, gourd, chicken, fish, crab, and shrimp. We played with candy, and players tried to guess which animal would appear on the dice. The kids were taught to be generous if they won and gracious if they lost, as well as to give to others during the rest of the year. Guests feast at a huge spread of food. Kids enjoy the games and activities at the Lunar New Year party.

Zongzi is a traditional Chinese rice dish made of glutinous rice stuffed with different fillings and wrapped with bamboo leaves. Anna looked up the recipe and went to the grocery store to buy the ingredients just for this event. Tammy Choi, another Beach parent, made Tteokbokki, a Korean spicy rice cake. People also shared oranges, dumplings, and noodles, foods that traditionally bring good luck and fortune. It was beautiful how it all came together, and we are so appreciative of the outpouring and support from the community. Bầu cua tôm cá – which translates to “Gourd, Crab, Shrimp, Fish” – is a Vietnamese game traditionally played during Tết. There are three dice and a board with six objects on them: a deer, gourd, chicken, fish, crab, and shrimp. We played with candy, and players tried to guess which animal would appear on the dice. The kids were taught to be generous if they won and gracious if they lost, as well as to give to others during the rest of the year. He made his most appearances in the 400 and 800, recording respective personal records of 54.28 and 2:05.50. Jack Zirkelbach-Ngai is a forward in soccer and also runs track. articles.text: Piedmont City Council agreed on January 17, to continue to allow members of the public to attend Council, Planning Commission, and Committee meetings remotely through Zoom. However, Zoom will no longer be used for Park and Recreation meetings, which are attended and viewed less frequently. Virtual participation for members of legislative bodies was first introduced on March 4, 2020, when Governor Newsom announced a COVID-19 State of Emergency. This executive order relaxed the state’s public meetings laws to allow for use of teleconferencing by members of legislative bodies without the strict public access requirements contained in the Brown Act. However, on October 17, 2022, Newsom announced his intention to rescind the State of Emergency as of February 28, 2023. This means that the teleconference requirements of the Brown Act which were in place prior to the pandemic will come back into effect on March 1, 2023. Accordingly, Council, Commission, and Committee (e.g. Budget Advisory, Bond Oversight, Pool Advisory) members will have to attend meetings in person. The Brown Act, a 70-year-old California law, guarantees the public’s right to attend and participate in local government meetings. However, as Piedmont City Clerk John Tulloch explained, “Public participation is not covered under the Brown Act,” nor does the Act restrict city staff or consultants from participating remotely if the legislative body chooses to continue hybrid meetings after the State of Emergency is revoked. articles.text: On January 17 Piedmont City Council approved offering naming rights at the Piedmont Community Pool to donors of $250,000 or greater. The Council also discussed the announcement, released by the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization the previous week, that all donations to the PRFO would be matched dollar for dollar up to $500,000, thanks to an anonymous donor. PRFO has already raised over $1.25 million of their $2.1 fundraising goal to bridge the gap presented by construction costs which have inflated since Piedmonters approved Measure UU in November 2020; this Measure allocated $19.5 million in bonds toward pool construction. PRFO General Counsel Eric Havian affirmed that the anonymous donor had not placed a deadline on the fund-matching; however, “as a practical matter, we want to try and get … the great bulk of the money in the next two or three months.” As of January 21, Havian also affirmed that the $1.25 which PRFO raised does not include donations matched by the anonymous donor. “We have not taken count of how much we have matched so far,” he said, “but the donations are certainly coming in.” While the facility will be named the Piedmont Community Pool, City Administrator Sara Lillevand identified four sites for Naming rights for the new pool is offered to donors of $250,000 or greater.

articles.text: This application deadline for candidates for Piedmont School District’s next superintendent was January 16, and the school board now begins reviewing the applications. The school board will have a closed meeting on February 1 to begin a review with their hired search firm, Leadership Associates. The school district has stated it does not intend to announce how many applications have been received. “Typically districts do not share the number of applications until after a candidate is selected. Our search firm advises we follow the same protocol,” said Board President Veronica Anderson Thigpen. The superintendent search in 2015, which resulted in an internal selection of Randy Booker was facilitated by Bill Levinson and Barbara Young of the firm Hazard, Young, Attea and Associates. In that search 45 applications came in from eight different states. In the January 11 school board meeting Anderson Thigpen said, “A handful of applications have been received.” She confirmed that if the board is not pleased with the applicants, the application period could be reopened. The school board anticipates making a hiring decision in March. “The board will look through those applications on February 1. We will determine candidates to interview and once those interviews are complete, we will make a decision.” said Anderson Thigpen. Only school board members will participate in the interviews and selection. The Superintendent is their one and only employee. Community engagement by the search firm concluded in November, with one meeting open to the public, 52 meetings offered to targeted groups and an online survey which received 417 responses. articles.text: Starting January 27, the city will make a number of changes to parking and traffic flow on Bonita Avenue between Magnolia and Vista Avenues in advance of construction of a new community pool. • All parking on this block will be removed for the duration of pool construction. • Portions of the sidewalk will be closed. • Construction site fencing will be placed in the middle of the street. This block of Bonita Avenue will continue to have one lane of traffic. • There will be no access to the tennis courts on Bonita Avenue. During pool construction, the tennis courts will be accessible through the main entry on Vista Avenue. Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales confirmed that the first working day assigned to pool construction contractor Wickman Development & Construction was January 19, with 335 working days thereafter, including adjustments for weather; thus, the project could finish as soon as summer 2024. On-site construction work will take place from January 27 onward, between 8 a.m. and 5 p.m., Monday through Friday. There will be occasional weekend work during the project, which will be approved by the city on a case-by-case basis. Contractors will provide street and sidewalk directional signage and flaggers while construction vehicles are entering and leaving the site and during deliveries. articles.title: Pool parking, traffic changes to begin Jan. 27

articles.text: Russian scholar Anastasia Edel returns to the Forum this winter presented by Healdsburg American Association of University Women for an in-depth look into Russia’s war on Ukraine. She will lead a six-part class on Thursdays from February 2 to March 9. Starting on the day when Russian missiles first struck cities across the sovereign nation of Ukraine, Edel will tackle the key questions: Why did Russia become an aggressor bent on destroying a neighboring nation with whom it shares centuries of common heritage? How did it happen? Why does Putin’s regime refuse to call the war “war”? What’s behind Ukrainians’ resilience and Russians’ acquiescence? And how does this all end for Russia, Ukraine, and the world? Online registration is available at healdsburg-ca.aauw.net or register by mail to AAUW Forum, PO Box 1603, Healdsburg CA 95448. Be sure to provide your e-mail address. In 2019 Edel gave the Healdsburg audience a fascinating and well received course on Russian politics, history and culture. Her course will also examine the heroism of the Ukrainian resistance. Audience members will be given a brief overview of Russian-Ukrainian history to help understand why Ukraine’s rebirth is matched by Russia’s civilizational and moral collapse. The origins of Russian fascism will be explored. We will consider in a small town in the south of Russia near the Ukrainian border. During the last years of the Soviet Union, she graduated with a degree in English and German studies from Kubansky State University and worked as a translator in Austria. After receiving the Chevening Award, she moved to England for postgraduate studies, and then to the U.S, where she earned her MFA in writing from Pacific University. She is on the Literary Council of the Oakland Book Festival and teaches Russian Culture and history for UC Berkeley Osher Lifelong Learning Institute. Her prose has appeared in the New York Times, The New York Review of Books, Foreign Policy, Project Syndicate, and World Literature Today. To read some of her articles go to: https://www.nybooks. com/contributors/anastasia-edel/ The course uses a multimedia format, where the latest political, economic, and cultural events are illustrated with movie clips, music, art, and literature. The following letter was sent to Brian Killgore, the school district’s Communications Director, and the Piedmont School Board. Editor: I read that this Wednesday’s PUSD Board of Education meeting would include a discussion on “whether to continue holding meetings on Zoom.” But the published agenda for January 25th does not list this topic as an agenda item. Is this an oversight? I’m hoping it is because your published remarks may have resulted in some interested stakeholders from corresponding with the school board members on this matter. That doesn’t seem appropriate, especially given how much community support PUSD receives. Would you clarify? –Dai Meagher hood as evidence of our decency. I was, therefore, surprised and concerned that the Council failed to make clear that the plan should not segregate low-income, possibly minority, families from the remainder of the new neighborhood and from Piedmont at large. My concern stems from the fact that Council members and others have suggested that the 60 units of low and very low income housing be assigned to Blair Park. As earlier EIR’s and studies prepared for proposed projects in Moraga Canyon have documented, putting any housing in Blair Park would be a mistake because impassable topography and a treacherous speedway would endanger residents and separate them physically as well as socially from the remainder of our community. Housing low-income minority families in Blair would make such a mistake even worse because it would smack of racist segregation. The fact that the Council could have directed planners to preclude housing in Blair would make the inference of segregationist intent even more compelling. The corporation yard, which must be rebuilt under any plan, could be moved to Blair to make more room for a safe, integrated neighborhood centered around the old corporation yard site and recreation facilities including Coaches Field. Time remains for the Council to direct staff to keep housing out of Blair Park. But if those of us concerned by the prospect of a segregated neighborhood in Piedmont remain silent, the Council may fail to act. Therefore, I urge Piedmonters who want the new Moraga Canyon neighborhood to reflect the best rather than worst of our values to make your wishes known to Council. We will otherwise invite our children and future Piedmonters to rightfully doubt our decency and to call our values into question. –Ralph Catalano, Ph.D. It’s time for decent Piedmonters to speak out The Piedmont City Council has begun the process of planning a whole new neighborhood in Moraga Canyon. articles.text: The League of Women Voters of Piedmont hosted a Zoom event on January 18 entitled “Sustainable Groundwater in California: The Challenges Ahead”. The discussion featured Tim Godwin, Technical Policy Advisor for Sustainable Groundwater, who filled in for the scheduled speaker, Paul Gosselin, Deputy Director of Sustainable Groundwater for the State Department of Water Resources, who had a last-minute Godwin spoke in detail about the requirements and mechanics of the Sustainable Groundwater Act (SGMA), the first California law to regulate groundwater. SGMA became law in 2014. In times of drought, groundwater supplies up to 60% of the State’s total water needs. Even in wetter years, groundwater can account for 40% of total state usage. Some basins are 100% dependent on groundwater. SGMA implementation is envisaged over a 20-year period. It enables the formation of local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs), which oversee basins in their areas. Of more than 500 alluvial basins, SGMA has identified 21 that are critically overdrafted. An additional 94, representing 90% of total groundwater pumping in California, are considered high and medium priority. Currently, plans for eight of the 21 critical overdraft basins have been approved. SGMA defines sustainability in terms of six conditions to be avoided: 1) lowering groundwater levels 2) reduction of groundwater storage 3) seawater intrusion 4) degraded water quality 5) land subsidence 6) depletion of interconnected streams As an example of land subsidence, Godwin told of the Friant-Kern Canal, which has had a 60% reduction in its ability to convey water, due to the partial collapse of land subsidence. He noted that when land above an aquifer starts to collapse, it threatens bridges, railways, pipelines and water pipes. Godwin explained that determining the appropriate metrics for groundwater pumping, water levels and recharge is a complex process. Each local agency needs to evaluate the level of demand for water, sources of supply, risk of contamination, performance of local wells, and many other factors. To learn more about this talk and see the presentation, visit the League’s website at www. lwvpiedmont.org. articles.text: Is your New Year’s resolution to read more? Maybe you want to learn more about climate science. Here is a list of engaging books about climate change. Some will leave you hopeful for the future while others are a stark reminder of what’s at stake if we don’t address the climate crisis. The list also includes a novel that tackles environmental issues. 1. All We Can Save: Truth, Courage, and Solutions for the Climate Crisis, Edited by Ayana Elizabeth Johnson and Katharine K. Wilkinson “All We Can Save illuminates the insights of dozens of diverse women leading on climate in the United States . The list includes scientists, journalists, farmers, lawyers, teachers, activists, innovators, wonks, and designers across generations, geographies, and race. It aims to advance a more representative, nuanced, and solution-oriented public conversation on the climate crisis. These women offer a spectrum of ideas and insights for how we can rapidly, radically reshape society.” 2. Braiding Sweetgrass by Robin Wall Kimmerer “Drawing on her life as an indigenous scientist, a mother, and a woman, Kimmerer shows how other living beings – asters and goldenrod, strawberries and squash, salamanders, algae, and sweetgrass – offer us gifts and lessons, even if we’ve forgotten how to hear their voices. In a rich braid of reflections that range from the creation of Turtle Island to the forces that threaten its flourishing today, she circles toward a central argument: that the awakening of a wider ecological consciousness requires the acknowledgment and celebration of our reciprocal relationship with the rest of the living world.” 3. The Day the World Stops Shopping: How Ending Consumerism Saves the Environment and Ourselves by J.B. MacKinnon “Consuming less is our best strategy for saving the planet — but can we do it? In this thoughtful and surprisingly optimistic book, journalist J. B. MacKinnon investigates how we may achieve a world without shopping. Drawing from experts in fields ranging from climate change to economics, MacKinnon investigates how living with less would change our planet, our society, and ourselves. Along the way, he reveals just how much we stand to gain: an investment in our physical and emotional wellness. The pleasure of caring for our possessions. Closer relationships with our natural world and one another. Imaginative and inspiring, The Day the World Stops Shopping will embolden you to envision another way.” 4. Climate Change is Racist: Race Privilege and the Struggle for Climate Justice by Jeremy Williams “In this eye-opening book, writer and environmental activist Jeremy Williams takes us on a short, urgent journey across the globe – from Kenya to India, the USA to Australia – to understand how White privilege and climate change overlap. We’ll look at the environmental facts, hear the experiences of the people most affected on our planet and learn from the activists leading the change.” “That bridge you said we would cross when we came to it? Well, we’ve come to it.”
