pages.text: Wednesday, January 25, 2023 3 LWV hosts discussion on Sustainable Groundwater By Jennifer Trainor The League of Women Voters of Piedmont hosted a Zoom event on January 18 entitled “Sustainable Groundwater in California: The Challenges Ahead”. The discussion featured Tim Godwin, Technical Policy Advisor for Sustainable Groundwater, who filled in for the scheduled speaker, Paul Gosselin, Deputy Director of Sustainable Groundwater for the State Department of Water Resources, who had a last-minute emergency. Godwin spoke in detail about the requirements and mechanics of the Sustainable Groundwater Act (SGMA), the first California law to regulate groundwater. SGMA became law in 2014. In times of drought, groundwater supplies up to 60% of the State’s total water needs. Even in wetter years, groundwater can account for 40% of total state usage. Some basins are 100% dependent on groundwater. SGMA implementation is envisaged over a 20-year period. It enables the formation of local Groundwater Sustainability Agencies (GSAs), which oversee basins in their areas. Of more than 500 alluvial basins, SGMA has identified 21 that are critically overdrafted. An additional 94, representing 90% of total groundwater pumping in California, are considered high and medium priority. Currently, plans for eight of the 21 critical overdraft basins have been approved. SGMA defines sustainability in terms of six conditions to be avoided: 1) lowering groundwater levels 2) reduction of groundwater storage 3) seawater intrusion 4) degraded water quality 5) land subsidence 6) depletion of interconnected streams As an example of land subsidence, Godwin told of the Friant-Kern Canal, which has had a 60% reduction in its ability to convey water, due to the partial collapse of land subsidence. He noted that when land above an aquifer starts to collapse, it threatens bridges, railways, pipelines and water pipes. Godwin explained that determining the appropriate metrics for groundwater pumping, water levels and recharge is a complex process. Each local agency needs to evaluate the level of demand for water, sources of supply, risk of contamination, performance of local wells, and many other factors. To learn more about this talk and see the presentation, visit the League’s website at www. lwvpiedmont.org. To view a recording, visit the League’s YouTube channel at https://www.youtube.com/channel/UC3v60XGmr13V_9WaYj6qUJg. articles.text: On January 17, City Council unanimously voted to issue a request for proposals (RFP) to seek a consultant for the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan. The Plan, which is part of Piedmont’s draft 6th Cycle Housing Element, aims to improve existing facilities and incorporate 132 units of housing on 18 acres of city-owned land on both sides of Moraga Canyon, along Moraga Avenue; 60 units of this housing would be available to lower-income households. The land affected by the Moraga Canyon Plan includes Blair Park, Coaches Field, Kennelly Skate Park, and the Corporation Yard. The RFP outlines the requirements for a prospective consultant’s analysis of this plan. Planning Director Kevin Jackson said that the city will “engage professional services … and begin the planning process” by April. Jackson emphasized the three most significant requirements of the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan as identified by the RFP: “a robust public engagement program … [the determination of] a site for the development of at least one affordable housing project … [and] a fiscal analysis of potential revenues and expenses.” City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that she expected these public engagement methods — ranging from “online activities, mapping tools … to scoping meetings with neighbors and experts, to … meetings with City Council [and] Commissions” — to be “a lot more fun than our Housing Element,” because Piedmonters “know Moraga Canyon. They drive it, or live there … it’s much more tangible. And people understand what they think should happen there. I think it’s going to be much easier to get people engaged here.” Due largely to the fact that much Housing Element public engagement was remote during the pandemic, Jackson said that Moraga Canyon outreach will be more hands-on and more similar to community meeting about the new Piedmont Community Pool. “People will get to think about the space in a geometric way,” he said. The identification of a possible affordable housing site will take priority in these discussions, said Jackson, as this site must qualify for the $2.2 million allocated to Piedmont by Alameda County through its Measure A1 low-interest loan program for affordable housing development. Piedmont will seek the County’s approval for this loan funding by 2024. While the RFP does not set a price for the Moraga Canyon plan altogether, Lillevand said that, per a study published by the Association of Bay Area Governments in 2019, “the preparation of a specific plan cost an average of $544,237,” and that the city expects a similar price. The Moraga Plan will be funded by the General Plan Maintenance Fee collected from building permit applications and instituted in Piedmont on July 1, 2019. Last year, this fee generated $427,000. Although similar revenue is expected this year, Jackson said that the city has already spent much of the fee on expenses incurred through the Housing Element drafting process. Given that the Moraga Plan is what councilmember Tom Ramsey called “a non-funded state mandate,” the city is investigating state grants to recoup costs not covered by the Maintenance Fee. The RFP city staff report states that “the most promising [funding source] may be a Priority Development Area Planning Grant from MTC [Metropolitan Transportation Commission]. However Piedmont has no Priority Development Areas – which are “generally tied to major transit facilities like a BART station or ferry stop or the intersection of several bus lines,” explained Jackson. Nevertheless, the state is seeking to create new Priority Development Area categories which increase transportation mobility. Jackson told Council that the city has already begun working to identify Moraga Canyon as such an area, and possibly apply for the grant this way. The RFP staff report is available at bit.ly/3ZR5RLn. Those with questions about the Moraga Canyon Specific Plan can contact Planning and Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039.
articles.title: City Council seeks consultant, funding for Moraga Canyon Specific Plan

articles.text: Planning Director Kevin Jackson told City Council that the city expects to adopt the Element before the state deadline, January 31, and before it receives a letter of compliance from the state. City Council will hold a special meeting on January 30 to consider adopting the 2023-2031 6th Cycle Housing Element. In a special meeting on January 12, the Planning Commission voted unanimously to recommend to the Council that it adopt the Element. Because cities which do not adopt an Element by the deadline face penalties from the state, Piedmont is expected to adopt the plan even if it does not receive comments by then from the California Department of Housing and Community Development, confirming that the Element complies with state standards. Piedmont submitted its Housing Element to the state on November 15. Because the HCD sets a 90-day review period before releasing comments regarding Housing Element compliance, the city expects to receive a letter from the state by February 16. Jackson stated that Piedmont would not be unique in adopting the Element before it is confirmed by the state: While “there are communities in southern California who are ahead of us in the phases of Housing Element adoption,” he said, “here in the Bay Area, particularly in Alameda County, most jurisdictions are planning to adopt prior to getting a letter of substantial compliance from HCD.” Furthermore, emphasized Jackson, city staff has already been communicating with the HCD to clarify the standards which Piedmont must meet and to ensure that the city does meet them. “In December and the first part of January,” he said, “city staff and our consultant have had a handful of virtual meetings with the HCD staff member assigned to review Piedmont’s Housing Element.” These meetings “enabled the reviewer to ask questions and make comments and for us to respond with answers and clarify how the Element complies with state law.” Jackson gave the HCD staff member assigned to Piedmont a tour of the city on January 13. “I didn’t get a lot of feedback; it was mostly me presenting the sites that we have [in the Element],” Jackson said that the tour nevertheless allowed the reviewer to confirm Piedmont’s compliance, site-by-site, against “a checklist of items of state law which we need to comply with.” Given that Housing Element compliance is a “much more cumbersome process than in prior cycles” due to “additional requirements of state law that the legislature has adopted in recent years,” Jackson told the Council that many cities in the Bay Area like Piedmont are finding it more efficient to adopt the Element and direct staff to “make changes that would bring our element into compliance” after comments are received, rather than withholding adoption before the state deadline and facing subsequent penalties. Information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontIsHome. org. Those with questions about the Element can contact Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont. ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039.
articles.title: City expects to adopt Housing Element by Jan. 31

articles.text: As of January 20, the pedestrian footbridge at the base of Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park, has reopened for public use. On December 25, the handrail on one side of the bridge collapsed, rendering it unsafe and forcing pedestrian detours. “While we did get a contractor to repair the bridge,” said Gonzales, “it’s a temporary measure. It doesn’t change the fact that we still feel we have to replace the bridge, but our priority since late December has been making sure that it’s safe and that access can The pedestrian bridge in Piedmont Park at the base of Bushy Dell Creek. A footbridge in Piedmont Park was temporarily closed in December. be restored.” When the city first identified the bridge as deficient in 2015, the wood decking was temporarily patched with plywood. In 2019, the Public Works department consulted several contractors and determined that, due to site conditions, a replacement bridge could not be prefabricated; it would have to be a custom design. The bridge is scheduled for replacement this summer using funds from California Proposition 68, a $4 billion bond measure including a $395 million competitive grant program for local park expansions and upgrades. Piedmont’s total grant allocation is $184,932.

Piedmont submitted its Housing Element to the state on November 15. Because the HCD sets a 90-day review period before releasing comments regarding Housing Element compliance, the city expects to receive a letter from the state by February 16. Jackson stated that Piedmont would not be unique in adopting the Element before it is confirmed by the state: While “there are communities in southern California who are ahead of us in the phases of Housing Element adoption,” he said, “here in the Bay Area, particularly in Alameda County, most jurisdictions are planning to adopt prior to getting a letter of substantial compliance from HCD.” Furthermore, emphasized Jackson, city staff has already been communicating with the HCD to clarify the standards which Piedmont must meet and to ensure that the city does meet them. “In December and the first part of January,” he said, “city staff and our consultant have had a handful of virtual meetings with the HCD staff member assigned to review Piedmont’s Housing Element.” These meetings “enabled the reviewer to ask questions and make comments and for us to respond with answers and clarify how the Element complies with state law.” Jackson gave the HCD staff member assigned to Piedmont a tour of the city on January 13. “I didn’t get a lot of feedback; it was mostly me presenting the sites that we have [in the Element],” Jackson said that the tour nevertheless allowed the reviewer to confirm Piedmont’s compliance, site-by-site, against “a checklist of items of state law which we need to comply with.” Given that Housing Element compliance is a “much more cumbersome process than in prior cycles” due to “additional requirements of state law that the legislature has adopted in recent years,” Jackson told the Council that many cities in the Bay Area like Piedmont are finding it more efficient to adopt the Element and direct staff to “make changes that would bring our element into compliance” after comments are received, rather than withholding adoption before the state deadline and facing subsequent penalties. Information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontIsHome. org. Those with questions about the Element can contact Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont. ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039. articles.text: The new header of the website which has school board meeting archives, Simbli.eboardsolutions.com/Index.aspx?S=36030373, states that Zoom will be available “until further notice.” The Piedmont School Board will convene for a regularly scheduled meeting tonight, January 25 at 7:00 p.m. in City Hall. At its meeting on January 11 the school district announced a plan to quickly phase out Zoom for school board meetings after the January 25 meeting, however it appears the school board is rethinking the decision due to community feedback. According to the school district, financial factors are largely at play after the normal staffer running the meetings, Assistant to the Superintendent Sylvia Eggert, became unable to run the Zoom meetings. The January 11 meeting’s hybrid features of the meeting, which allow for public comment from parents, teachers, students, or any viewer remotely, had to be facilitated by Communications Director Brian Killgore. “Unfortunately, the staff that has been supporting the Zoom option is no longer available. The decision to phase out Zoom meetings was initially guided by considerations of cost, as well as the low number of attendees using this option,” stated the PUSD Board of Education on January 24. In the January 11 meeting the intent to discontinue Zoom was stated but was not discussed because it was not on the agenda. The future of Zoom is again not on the agenda of the January 25 meeting, but the school board is showing an interest in reconsidering the decision “Community feedback has demonstrated continued interest in allowing the public to comment on Zoom, so we are in the process of working with the Interim Superintendent to explore other solutions,” the School Board stated jointly. On the Simbli website, which holds the archived school board meetings, the header now states “Regular Board Meetings will be on Zoom until further notice.” This is a change from earlier in the week when the district announced that Zoom would only be available “until the end of the January 2023.” Agenda for tonight’s meeting • Progress Update on the LCAP Goal 2: Academics. • Second Reading to approve the newly updated District Philosophy, Goals, Objectives and Comprehensive Plans • Approve Facilities Steering Committee Recommended 2023 Summer Projects • First Reading to adopt a new Piedmont Middle School Health Class • Approve 2022 School Accountability Report Cards • Update on Governor’s 2023-24 Budget To participate in the meeting via public comment, individuals may attend in person at City Hall or view the meeting on Zoom at Zoom.us/j/86833908908 . School board meetings may be watched, without the option of participation, via KCOM’s website, and local TV channel 27. Comments and questions may be emailed to schoolboard@piedmont.k12.ca.us.
articles.title: Preview of School Board meeting tonight; future of Zoom

articles.text: Raiyaan Shah (left), Jasper Tripp, Jasper Zietlow, Chelsea Yi, Gabi Kong, Zain Shah, Rahimeen Shah, and Derek Chan On Friday, January 20, a group of students from Piedmont High’s Asian Student Union (ASU) stayed after school to decorate the campus halls with handmade lanterns and gold streamers in preparation for the Lunar New Year for the Year of the Hare. It was only the fourth year of the decorating tradition. ASU is one of the high school’s many identity-oriented clubs, which gives students who lack representation within the student population a place to connect and build community. ASU spreads knowledge about different Asian cultures to the entire school, with decorations being one of the ways ASU can represent identities. With Kaeli Huh and Zoe Saldanha having graduated in 2022, senior Gabi Kong has picked up the reins this year as club president. Kong joined ASU as a freshman and immediately found value the club provides. “I think especially in Piedmont, where we’re a majority white community, it’s important to have these types of clubs like ASU and BSU (Black Student Union), the social justice clubs, and all the cultural clubs because it’s another doorway for representation,” said Kong. “It creates a safe space for these students who are a minority. They can feel like they are seen and heard through these communities.” Many students are grateful for the community the club has created. “I joined ASU just to celebrate Asian heritage and to hang out with other people that also have similar cultures and backgrounds,” said junior Derek Chan, who joined as a sophomore. While ASU is currently highSenior Jasper Zietlow hard at work lighting the Lunar New Year, a holiday most celebrated in East Asia, the club represents South Asians as well. “I joined ASU because I think that South Asians are quite underrepresented in our school,” explained Senior Rahimeen Shah. “I want to bring more attention to different things such as Eid, a Muslim holiday, which is not necessarily South Asian, but I feel like many people don’t know about it.” ASU has given many students a space to build bonds and celebrate their diverse backgrounds. At the beginning of the new year ASU hopped into action by working on a new student social justice project to create systemic change, started by PUSD DEI director Dr. Marguerite Vanden Wyngaard. Faculty Advisor Shelley Seto (left), with members of Piedmont’s Asian Student Union Gabi Kong, Madelyn Hill, and Chelsea Yi. Derek Chan hangs up a string of lanterns in the background. ASU President Gabi Kong with a string of handmade lanterns
articles.title: Piedmont High Asian Student Union celebrates Lunar New Year

articles.text: NASA built a test to measure “creative genius” by looking for high levels of divergent thinking, a thought process that tackles problems using innovative approaches. It’s pretty important when your line of work is hurtling rockets into space. This test was simple enough that a child could take it, and so, NASA administered the test to 1600 five-yearolds. The result? Ninety-eight percent tested within the bounds of “creative genius”. NASA decided to test the same children again five years later. Only 30% of the now 10--yearolds were considered to have creative-genius-level thinking. Fast forward five more years and the number dropped to 12%. The final test, conducted after another five years, resulted in only 2% of adults testing within genius level divergent thinking. What happened to those children’s creativity over the years? The general consensus is that school happened. Instead of favoring open-ended divergent thinking, evaluative and judgment-oriented convergent thinking was rewarded and prioritized. “Two plus two is four” and “W-O-R-D spells word” are examples of convergent thinking, which favors facts with right and wrong answers. Unfortunately, most schools do not offer spaces and Children utilize divergent thinking throughout their time at summer camp. lessons for divergent thinking to thrive alongside analytical thinking, which may explain how we lost 96% of our creative geniuses. The good news is that we don’t need to sit around twiddling our thumbs waiting for schools to change. Creative thinking can be nurtured and strengthened with a little practice. Expanding our divergent minds can be as simple as coming up with as many uses for a paperclip as possible, or considering all the ways a common fork could be improved. For children, summer camp can be an extremely liberating experience after spending all year in a classroom. Free from outside influence and expectations, campers can pursue a week that is entirely their own. Part of the magic of summer camp lies in the truth: there is no right or wrong way to be. Summer camp staff can attest to having seen time and time again children expand in front of their eyes as they take on new activities, challenges, and identities. In truth, divergent thinking doesn’t make us rocket scientists, but it does help us imagine a better world. If children are the future, then right now a good many of them are still full-fledged creative geniuses. Let’s give them every shot at staying that way. Randall Grayson, PhD, is the Director of Camp Augusta, which sits nestled in the Sierra Nevada foothills near Nevada City and is beloved by Piedmont families since its founding by Edwin and Charlotte Ehmann in 1931. Information about the camp’s summer programs and family camps can be found at www.campaugusta.org.
articles.title: Thinking Outside the Classroom Nurture reinvigorate creative thinking at summer camp

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. articles.text: Havens Dad Jimmy Lee won the 15th annual Havens Dads Club Poker Night tournament, on Friday, January 20, an event which raised an all-time record $48,328. Lee outlasted every other player in a field of 150 to take home the ultimate poker bragging rights and the championship bracelet. Dueling Lee at the final table after four hours of play were the top three runners-up, Brandon Bercovich, Stephanie Ho, and Barron Hong. The event, hosted by Dads Club President Roger Tsai and a team of 21 volunteer parents, was held at the Veterans Hall, and generated a crowd of 185 people for Havens School’s single largest fundraiser. Havens Principal Anne Dolid along with school board members and Havens staff Havens Parents Club President Katie Castles Shaffer (left) and Havens Principal Anne Dolid welcome the crowd to the annual Havens Dads Club Poker Night on January 20. The first card was dealt at 6:30 p.m. Friday night until the large field of 150 hopeful players dwindled down to one winner, Jimmy Lee. Piedmont Veterans Hall was filled with high rollers Friday night. cheered on the bettors. “We want our event to be representative of our community and everyone showed up in full support,” noted parent T.J. Won. “We also had many more women [as contestants] than before, a major goal for the event organizers.” The evening was a Texas Hold’em tournament costing $100 to join, with dozens of professional tables and dealers. Since all the proceeds go to the schools, when a player was knocked out, they had the option to get more chips for another $100, as many times as desired. “I usually have a pretty good strategy when playing small cash games for fun with friends; I play pretty conservative. You have to throw that all out the window with this fundraising event and the unlimited buy back. A guy at my table spent $4,000 a few years ago by constantly buying back in,” said Havens dad Jon Essner. Proceeds from the event will be used for Havens School projects, such as supplemental funding for the Becker Field replacement turf, Ellen Driscoll Playhouse mural repairs, lunch tables and awnings, and playground blocks. The event received sponsorship from Lisa Chan-Carnazzo of The Grubb Company, and Chris Kwei of Oakland Kia. Photos by Babak Sanii and Jay Russell 3rd place finisher Stephanie Ho (left) makes a bet as champion James Lee awaits his turn. A large crowd was on hand for Havens Poker Night at the Veterans Hall.

articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series returned to the Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on Thursday, January 19, for the screening of an engaging, powerful documentary, Through the Night. The film was followed by a remarkable and informative talk and Q & A. The film, a New York Times Critics Pick in 2020, showcases the multiplicity of “women’s work” – paid, underpaid, and unpaid – through a tender portrait of strength, love, and selflessness. This film is an intimate cinema verite portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift as an essential worker at a pediatric hospital, another holding three jobs to support her family, and an inspirational woman delivering exemplary 24-hour care and education for over two decades. Support for working mothers remains very limited across the country. The costs of daycare for a three-year-old rivals the cost of rent in most U.S. cities. Childcare providers themselves are often struggling in a mountain of expensive bureaucracy and minimum wages. The audience warmly received three speakers who followed the screening: Kym Johnson, Director of the acclaimed East Bay childcare referral and family resources center Bananas, and Nancy Harvey and Tasha Jordan, childcare providers. Johnson summarized local childcare needs and new state bills bringing some increased and sorely needed funding to Oakland. Harvey and Jordan of Oakland were able to explain the hardworking, caring network of childcare/early education first line workers who support families, especially when no other support exists. They announced that AB 378: Building a Better Early Care & Education Act, was signed by Governor Newsom and gives providers the right to form a union. Subsequently CCPU (Child Care Providers United: childcareprovidersunited.org) was formed and currently represents over 30,000 child care providers in California. Visit the Appreciating Diversity Film Series website (diversityfilmseries.org) to read its mission, its documentary film archive, and an opportunity to subscribe to its e-mail list to receive notices of all films scheduled this year.

articles.text: The Highlanders took a hit to their league record over the past week, taking a 69-49 loss at Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, January 18, and losing 58-54 at Berkeley on Friday, January 20. They rebounded with a comfortable 65-41 win against nonleague opponent El Cerrito at the Gauchos home gym on Monday, January 23. “I thought our boys played really hard. That’s one thing I can always say about our team is that they always compete from start to finish. It doesn’t matter who our opponents are. The effort was there, but we just couldn’t hit some open looks,” said coach Ben Spencer. Their batch of results brings Piedmont’s record to 13-6 overall. The games with O’Dowd and Berkeley were their first league defeats in the Western Alameda County Conference’s Foothill Division. They entered Wednesday’s game at O’Dowd in first place in the WACC, but are now a game behind Berkeley and Alameda. “When we lost to Oakland High, I thought we played scared. I don’t think we played scared against O’Dowd or Berkeley, so it had nothing to do with nerves. We gave up a lot of fouls against Bishop O’Dowd; we just weren’t sharp or crisp. Against good teams, you can’t expect to win if you don’t make shots,” said Spencer. 65-41 over El Cerrito Piedmont led 9-6 in a low-scoring first quarter, but went up 23-15 by halftime. The Highlanders scored 20 points in the third quarter to extend the gap to 43-25, and added another 22 points in the fourth for the 65-41 final. Final scorers: A.J. Harris led with 34 points, Brit Burden had 15, Declan Linnane had six, Alex Anderson had four, Arjun Bornstein scored three, and Matthew Riordan had two. 58-54 loss to Berkeley Berkeley jumped out to a 19-10 lead and held a 37-25 lead by halftime. Piedmont cut the deficit to 47-39 to start the fourth quarter and outscored the Yellowjackets 15-11 in the fourth quarter, but couldn’t take the lead in the closing minutes. Final scorers: Harris led with 25 points, Ravi Silverberg scored Staff Photos A.J. Harris scored 34 points against El Cerrito, 25 in a game with Berkeley, and 16 points against O’Dowd. 15, Burden had 10, and Linnane had four. 69-49 loss to Bishop O’Dowd O’Dowd led 15-9 to open the game and led 28-19 at halftime. The Dragons extended their lead to 49-33 to start the fourth quarter and finished with 20 points in the fourth for a 20-point margin of victory, 69-49. Harris fouled out with 5:27 left in the game. Final scorers: Harris had 16 points, Silverberg had 10, Linnane had six, Matteo Costa, Teagan Haddawy and Theo Holmes had three, Anderson had two, and Burden had one. NEXT UP Piedmont (13-6 overall, 3-2 league) hosts San Leandro tonight at Binks Rawlings Gym at 7:00 p.m. They have a busy week ahead, hosting St. Joseph on Friday, January 27, playing a game in an Leandro the following day, Saturday, January 28. articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team continues to be regarded as one of the best in Northern California, and possibly in the state. During the past week they won four games all on the road, significantly including a 69-62 win against rival Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, January 18. They beat last year’s nemesis, San Leandro, 79-57 on Monday, January 23, bashed Berkeley 52-20, and outscored North Coast Section power Acalanes 66-51 at the Sabrina Ionescu 20 Showcase on Saturday, January 21. The result? The Highlanders remain on top of many lists with a sterling 19-0 record. Piedmont dinged by O’Dowd, Berkeley By Jonathan Comeaux The Highlanders took a hit to their league record over the past week, taking a 69-49 loss at Bishop O’Dowd on Wednesday, January 18, and losing 58-54 at Berkeley on Friday, January 20. articles.text: Piedmont High’s JV boys’ soccer team overwhelmed the Tennyson Lancers 4-1 on Friday, January 20 at Witter Field. The win continues the team’s hot streak, improving their record to 7-0-1 (W-T-L). The Highlanders went up 2-0 in the first half but conceded a goal with just a minute to play in the first half. Piedmont coach Andrea Salvadei, a native of Italy, recounted his message to the team at halftime. “Focus. Focus and Concentration. I’m not sure why we were so unfocused,” he said. “My bet is because last year they beat this team 15-0 and were thinking, ‘Oh, we’ll come and destroy’. I told them we need to treat every team the same way, with focus and concentration. Just the simple passes, the simple dribbling, the shot,” said Salvadei. Piedmont dominated the early play with sophomore Logan Faucher scoring four minutes into the first half after receiving a ball over the top of the defense to set up the goal. Piedmont scored again in the 21st minute after a pass from sophomore Gianluca Bini caused a scramble in the center of the penalty area, resulting in a goal for junior Rylan Nelson. Tennyson had almost no offensive chances in the first half until its goal in the 34th minute, when a shot rocketed off the crossbar and into the goal. There was an immediate shift in the tempo going into the second half after Piedmont narrowly Staff Photos Gianluca Bini scored twice in Piedmont’s 4-1 win over Tennyson. missed a header by Bini that bounced off the crossbar in the early minutes, among other close calls. Tennyson had very few offensive chances, with only one shot in the half which went wide of the goal. Piedmont scored two more goals by Bini. The tall forward scored in the 53rd minute after Riley Stratman headed a pass over the defense to Bini standing free in the box. Then in the 66th minute, Bini scored on a beautiful long shot from 30 yards after dribbling through the Tennyson defenders, to reel off a hard rightfooted shot. NEXT UP Piedmont (7-0-1) travels to Berkeley on Friday, January 27 for a 4:00 p.m. game. Rylan Nelson scored a goal against Tennyson. Logan Faucher scored the opening goal against Tennyson.

articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team improved its record to 5-4-2 (W-T-L) last week, defeating Tennyson 3-2 on Friday, January 20 at Witter Field and tying Alameda 1-1 on Wednesday, January 18 on the road. Both matches were with non-league Shoreline Division teams of the Western Alameda County Conference. Piedmont competes in the Foothill Division. PHS is unbeaten in its last five matches. Against Tennyson, the Highlanders controlled possession and were up 2-0 before relinquishing a goal minutes before halftime. Piedmont made it 3-1 in the early minutes of the second half and had several opportunities to extend the lead. However, the Lancers closed the final score to 3-2 with a penalty kick in second half stoppage time. “It was a bit of a disjointed start. Tennyson showed up 10 minutes before the game and I knew things would carry over into the game,” said coach Todd Sullivan. “We created chances but we never got going in terms of possession and quality. I think it’s very rare to see us play like that.” Sophomore forward Enzo Bernales currently leads the team in goals through 10 matches with four to his credit. He scored on a free kick from around 25 yards against Tennyson. He’s a firstyear starter this year and closed his freshman season with a few appearances on varsity. “It’s hard to step up after players like Andre Stankiewicz, Conner Curtis, and Ian Work leave from last year’s team. They were a huge part of this team. Practically everyone has to step up to fill their roles,” said Bernales. 3-2 win over Tennyson The Highlanders were on the offensive against Tennyson, recording three shots on target through the first 20 minutes but had a goal wiped out due to an offside call in the 16th minute. Piedmont’s first goal came in the 21st minute at the end of a corner lick when Evan Manolis’ connected with Sam Shelby for the goal. Bernales scored the next goal in the 34th minute after the Highlanders drew a foul about 25 yards out. Bernales rocketed in a low-bending shot for a 2-0 lead. Tennyson scored in the closing minute of the first half when playing a long ball to their striker, resulting in the athletic forward chipping the ball over Piedmont goalkeeper Brady Hinsch. Staff Photos Enzo Bernales scored on a nice free kick against Tennyson, his fourth goal of the season. Myles Gray scored against Tennyson and Alameda. He’s pictured here scoring a penalty kick as the Lancers’ players watch. In the second half, Piedmont was awarded a penalty kick when Jacques Saldanha drew contact in the area. Myles Gray stepped to the ball, slotting it home to put his team ahead 3-1. The Highlanders stayed on the attack, recording shots on target by Shelby, Bernales, and two by Jack Nelson. Int in the closing minutes of stoppage time, the Lancers were awarded a penalty after a long ball was played into the box—making it a 3-2 final. 1-1 draw with Alameda The Hornets took the lead moments before halftime after drawing a foul just inside Piedmont’s half. Alameda played their free kick into the area, leading to a header goal by the Hornets’ striker. Piedmont came out in its usual pressing style in the second half to close down passing lanes for Alameda and forcing them to run. It took a toll on the opposition, forcing a few players to the ground with leg cramps. Sullivan then subbed Andrew Szerdy into the attacking midfield role. Szerdy sent a pass into the area toward Gray, using his speed to beat a defender and score the 1-1 equalizer. From there, Piedmont had several opportunities to take the lead but were unable to find the finishing touch. They had at least three shots ring off of the post, while forcing multiple saves by the Alameda keeper. Tuesday vs. Hayward Piedmont hosted Hayward for another non-league match on Tuesday, January 24. See next week’s Post for match details. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-4-2 overall, 4-4-1 league) heads to Berkeley on Friday, January 27 for a 6:00 p.m. game. They will host Castro Valley on Monday, January 30 at Witter Field at 6 p.m. Both matches are against Foothill Division opponents. Sam Shelby scored against Tennyson and nearly bagged a brace in the late minutes.

articles.text: Photo courtesy of Barstool Sports Mackie McDonald (right) exited the Australian Open in the third round, but only after pulling off the biggest win of his career over Rafael Nadal last week. Mackie McDonald put up a battle but lost in the third round of the Australian Open to No. 31 seed Yoshihito Nishioka on Thursday, January 19 in three sets, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3, 6-2. Regardless of the exit for McDonald, he walked out of the Grand Slam after pulling off the biggest win of his professional career when defeating Rafael Nadal in three sets a week ago on January 17. McDonald reflected on his win over Nadal and how the Spanish legend dealt with a nagging hip injury late in the match. “I’m really happy with how I started that match, I thought I was playing really well, serving great, and returning well too. I was really taking it to him. But I hated to see him (injured) in the third set. It was pretty tough to stay mentally engaged, but I just found a way to pull it out,” said McDonald. McDonald admitted that he got out of rhythm after Nadal suffered his injury. “He’s an incredible champion, he’s never going to give up regardless of the situation, so even closing it out against a top guy like that is always tough. I was trying to stay focused on what I was doing and he got me out of rhythm with that. I’m happy that I just kept focusing on myself in the end and got through,” said McDonald. Regardless of Nadal’s injury, McDonald played steady throughout the match and he’s aware just how on top of his game he was on that Wednesday morning in Melbourne. McDonald has always been best on the hard courts and feels he had the “guns” to keep up with the former champion. “I think I have the guns to do it. I was blasting the ball, hitting really flat. Last time I played him, he kicked my butt. On clay courts, it’s tough to hit through, but here I like my chances on hard courts. I really wanted to take it to him on a hard court, I happy I got that opportunity and got away with it,” said McDonald. Former Piedmont coach Neil Rothenberg, who coached McDonald when he was a student at Piedmont High School, made an appearance on ABC7 News to talk about Mackie. “It was awesome to watch it. You’re always on pins and needles, especially when you’re playing one of the greatest players of all time. After the first set, you always get nervous and ask ‘Can he win the second set?’ and then it became, ‘Well, can he actually win the match?’ He has a lot of fans in Piedmont, we were all communicating with each other,” said Rothenberg. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen him play as well as he did and I’ve known him since he was seven years old. He would go to some of the clinics that pros would hold and he was always involved as one of the participants. You could tell even at seven- and eight-years old that he had an unbelievable amount of presence. We were just hoping that when he got to high school that he would play for Piedmont because it’s very unusual to have a world class player play high school tennis,” said Rothenberg. We’ll cover McDonald once again in the coming months with the next Grand Slam tournament the French Open from late May to early June.
articles.title: Mackie McDonald exits Australian Open after stunning upset of Nadal

articles.text: Hikers and mountain bikers often love the same trails. But sometimes that love can lead to tension, such as when a biker approaches without warning and a collision is narrowly avoided. As a Scout in Piedmont Troop 15, Schuyler Sawicki knew he wanted to do his Eagle service project at nearby Joaquin Miller Park where he loves to ride his bike and train for the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team. He approached a conservation group, The Friends of Joaquin Miller Park, for ideas. It led to an initiative suggested by the Bicycle Trails Council of the East Bay – building a bike bell kiosk. On Saturday, January 21, Sawicki led a crew of Scouts and mountain bike team members in constructing two bike bell kiosks at the park, encouraging mountain bikers to borrow a ball for their rides. The bike bells provide hikers with an early warning of oncoming bikers and are a common trait for several local trails. opportunity to borrow a bell, the goal of the kiosk is to increase bell usage and educate mountain bikers about their benefits. “I love it when I can hear people on bikes racing down the hill. Sharing the road is not a concept for many bikers. Thank you for providing bells for riders,” marveled local hiker, Margaret Charnas. Sawicki first gained approval for the project by presenting it to the City of Oakland’s Parks and Recreation Commission, which eventually approved it. He then set up a GoFundMe page and raised enough to pay for building materials, signs, and attachable bike bells. Many of his donors are from the mountain bike community. In addition, Economy Lumber agreed to donate material for the kiosk. Bikers are asked to return the bell to the kiosk or make a donation to the BTCEB to support replacement bells. The bike bell kiosks that Sawicki and friends installed at Joaquin Miller are in two locations, one near the meadow on the approach to Sunset Trail, and the other just off Skyline Road at the start of the Palos Colorados and Sequoia-Bayview trails. “I just want bikers to realize how much of an impact they can have in bettering the community through riding with a bell and being friendly to other trail users. I want everyone to have a good experience in the park,” said Sawicki. Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is very proud of Sawicki’s work and is excited to see how his project is received by the community. Schuyler Sawicki (left) and Piedmont MTB team captain Heather Stoneman assemble a bell kiosk. Enzo Choi puts the very first mountain biker bell to use at Joaquin Miller. pages.text: 14 Wednesday, January 25, 2023 Piedmont Mountain Bike team members stands next to their recent installation of bells to be used by mountain bikers at Joaquin Miller Park in Oakland. Pictured are John Roberts of Bicycle Trails Council of the East Bay (left), Heidi Sawicki, Eagle Scout Project coach Bill Bocheff, Heather Stoneman, Schuyler Sawicki, Max Rivera, Trenton Downing, Aleksi Valkonen, and Corbin Breeden. Piedmont Mountain Bike team donates bells for bikes at Joaquin Miller Park Hikers and mountain bikers often love the same trails. But sometimes that love can lead to tension, such as when a biker approaches without warning and a collision is narrowly avoided. As a Scout in Piedmont Troop 15, Schuyler Sawicki knew he wanted to do his Eagle service project at nearby Joaquin Miller Park where he loves to ride his bike and train for the Piedmont Mountain Bike Team. He approached a conservation group, The Friends of Joaquin Miller Park, for ideas. It led to an initiative suggested by the Bicycle Trails Council of the East Bay – building a bike bell kiosk. On Saturday, January 21, Sawicki led a crew of Scouts and mountain bike team members in constructing two bike bell kiosks at the park, encouraging mountain bikers to borrow a ball for their rides. The bike bells provide hikers with an early warning of oncoming bikers and are a common trait for several local trails. By providing cyclists with the opportunity to borrow a bell, the goal of the kiosk is to increase bell usage and educate mountain bikers about their benefits. “I love it when I can hear people on bikes racing down the hill. Sharing the road is not a concept for many bikers. Thank you for providing bells for riders,” marveled local hiker, Margaret Charnas. Sawicki first gained approval for the project by presenting it to the City of Oakland’s Parks and Recreation Commission, which eventually approved it. He then set up a GoFundMe page and raised enough to pay for building materials, signs, and attachable bike bells. Many of his donors are from the mountain bike community. In addition, Economy Lumber agreed to donate material for the kiosk. Bikers are asked to return the bell to the kiosk or make a donation to the BTCEB to support replacement bells. The bike bell kiosks that Sawicki and friends installed at Joaquin Miller are in two locations, one near the meadow on the approach to Sunset Trail, and the other just off Skyline Road at the start of the Palos Colorados and Sequoia-Bayview trails. “I just want bikers to realize how much of an impact they can have in bettering the community through riding with a bell and being friendly to other trail users. I want everyone to have a good experience in the park,” said Sawicki. Piedmont Mountain Bike Team is very proud of Sawicki’s work and is excited to see how his project is received by the community. Schuyler Sawicki (left) and Piedmont MTB team captain Heather Stoneman assemble a bell kiosk. Enzo Choi puts the very first mountain biker bell to use at Joaquin Miller. By Jonathan Comeaux Mackie McDonald put up a battle but lost in the third round of the Australian Open to No. 31 seed Yoshihito Nishioka on Thursday, January 19 in three sets, 7-6 (8-6), 6-3, 6-2. Regardless of the exit for McDonald, he walked out of the Grand Slam after pulling off the biggest win of his professional career when defeating Rafael Nadal in three sets a week ago on January 17. McDonald reflected on his win over Nadal and how the Spanish legend dealt with a nagging hip injury late in the match. “I’m really happy with how I started that match, I thought I was playing really well, serving great, and returning well too. I was really taking it to him. But I hated to see him (injured) in the third set. It was pretty tough to stay mentally engaged, but I just found a way to pull it out,” said McDonald. McDonald admitted that he got out of rhythm after Nadal suffered his injury. “He’s an incredible champion, he’s never going to give up regardless of the situation, so even closing it out against a top guy like that is always tough. I was trying to stay focused on what I was doing and he got me out of rhythm with that. I’m happy that I just kept focusing on myself in the end and got through,” said McDonald. Regardless of Nadal’s injury, McDonald played steady throughout the match and he’s aware just how on top of his game he was on that Wednesday morning in Melbourne. McDonald has always been best on the hard courts and feels he had the “guns” to keep up with the former champion. “I think I have the guns to do it. I was blasting the ball, hitting really flat. Last time I played him, he kicked my butt. On clay courts, it’s tough to hit through, but here I like my chances on hard courts. I really wanted to take it to him on a hard court, I happy I got that opportunity and got away with it,” said McDonald. Former Piedmont coach Neil Rothenberg, who coached McDonald when he was a student at Piedmont High School, made an appearance on ABC7 News to talk about Mackie. “It was awesome to watch it. You’re always on pins and needles, especially when you’re playing one of the greatest players of all time. After the first set, you always get nervous and ask ‘Can he win the second set?’ and then it became, ‘Well, can he actually win the match?’ He has a lot of fans in Piedmont, we were all communicating with each other,” said Rothenberg. “I don’t think I’ve ever seen him play as well as he did and I’ve known him since he was seven years old. He would go to some of the clinics that pros would hold and he was always involved as one of the participants. You could tell even at seven- and eight-years old that he had an unbelievable amount of presence. We were just hoping that when he got to high school that he would play for Piedmont because it’s very unusual to have a world class player play high school tennis,” said Rothenberg. We’ll cover McDonald once again in the coming months with the next Grand Slam tournament the French Open from late May to early June.

pages.text: Wednesday, January 25, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Oakland creeks bustling following rains By Jonathan Comeaux With parks being re-opened following the storms in recent weeks, it is the perfect time to visit local creeks, streams, and waterfalls. Staying in the Oakland hills, you can find several cascading creeks with just a little hiking. Here are some parks and trails to consider. Joaquin Miller Park The Palo Seco Creek is flowing at nearby Joaquin Miller Park. Taking the Sunset Trail from the Sequoia Bayview Trailhead puts you beside a good portion of the creek, while it also intersects with the Fern Ravine Creek in less than a half mile and Cinderella Creek at just around a mile. Redwood Regional Park Redwood Regional’s Redwood Creek along the Stream Trail is the most active it’s been in a long time with some sections of cascades down the hillsides. It’s also The Stream Trail at Redwood Regional finally has some running water. However, entry is only at the Skyline Gate on Skyline Boulevard. Leona Heights has a magnificent cascade down Horseshoe Creek. Leona Canyon’s Rifle Range Creek is flowing after the rains. Leona Canyon has a 1940s era car lodged inside the creek. Joaquin Miller’s small Palo Seco Creek is the most active it’s been in years. still a great time to get a look at the ladybugs as they swarm along the trail. However, the usual trailhead at the Canyon Meadow Staging Area off of Redwood Road is closed due a massive sink hole. Currently, the only way to access the Stream Trail is at the Skyline Gate Staging Area. The entire Stream Trail is 2.8 miles from the Skyline Gate to Canyon Meadows. Leona Heights Leona Heights’ 2.3 mile outand-back York Trail has remained open and has a magnificent cascade of Horseshoe Creek. It’s easy to forget you’re in Oakland and not in a forest more akin to Yosemite with the gushing flow of water and tall redwood trees. The park is also the home of the only old growth redwood tree in the East Bay, 600-year-old giant Old Survivor. Staff Photos Leona Canyon About half of Leona Heights is closed due to the rain, but you can still experience an up-close look at the thriving Rifle Range Creek when parking off of Campus Drive. The creek is flowing higher than its been in considerable time after usually being bone-dry. The water zooming past the abandoned 1940s vehicle in the creek makes for a unique sight. articles.text: Filoli House and Garden is celebrating women in the field of floristry by inviting local shop owners and florists to share their craft onstage. “Stories in Bloom” began this year, honoring the many creative women who have shaped Filoli’s story over the years, from its residents to historic staff. The speaker event showcases women’s storytelling in poetry, music, and the art of flower arranging. All speaker events are free with Filoli admission; however, a reservation is required to attend due to limited space. On February 5, Diosa Blooms, a Filipina-owned and family-run floral boutique, will demonstrate how they create floral arrangements that convey their own cultural stories and traditions. The owners of Diosa Blooms, located in San Francisco’s Mission District, have been invited to Filoli previously for a “flower takeover” event. To learn more about the new program and to purchase tickets, visit https://filoli.org/events/stories-in-bloom/. Spencer Look (left), Katie Militante, Kaylene Militante, Krisha Militante, Jas Beltran, and Kurt Militante of Diosa Blooms at Filoli House and Garden for its Stories in Bloom.
articles.title: Stories in Bloom at Filoli highlights local florists

articles.text: San Francisco Ballet is celebrating its 90th anniversary with “Next@90,” a festival beginning Friday, January 20, with performances at the War Memorial Opera House through February 11. Next@90 is curated by the ballet’s former long-standing artistic director Helgi Tomasson. The festival follows 2018’s “Unbound: A Festival of New Works” with nine world premieres by choreographers, including Robert Garland, Jamar Roberts, Danielle Rowe, Val Caniparoli, Bridget Breiner, Yuka Oishi, Claudia Schreier, Nicolas Blanc, and Yuri Possokhov. HAFFNER SERENADE: Choreography by Robert Garland; music of Wolfgang Amadeus Mozart RESURRECTION: Choreography and Scenic Design by Jamar Roberts; Music of Gustav Mahler MADCAP: Choreography by Danielle Rowe; music by Pär Hagström; music arranged by Philip Feeney. The Grammy-Award winning San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under Music Director Martin West will accompany dancers for all performances. Visit https://www.sfballet.org/ productions/festival-a/ to learn more and to purchase tickets for performances. $19 tickets may be available for weekday performances. Use promotional code LETSGO from noon to 6:30 p.m. on the day of the show. Limited seating. San Francisco Ballet is currently celebrating its 90th year.

articles.text: Dominique Morisseau’s Paradise Blue premieres at Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre on January 27. Morisseau, known for her onstage hit Detroit ‘67 continues her “Detroit Trilogy” with Paradise Blue, a jazz-infused drama that follows central character Blue, a skilled trumpeter who owns a nightclub in Detroit’s Blackbottom neighborhood. The play takes a turn when Silver, a mysterious woman, comes to town. Cast includes Michael J. Asberry, Rolanda D. Bell, Kenny Scott, Anna Marie Sharpe, and Titus VanHook. The play is directed by Aurora Theatre’s Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. A post-show discussion with the director and cast takes place February 3, 7, 15 and Michael J. Asberry is a major cast member in Paradise Blue. 23. The play will stream online February 21 through 26. articles.text: Earl Lee will lead San Francisco Symphony as visiting conductor in a special Lunar New Year performance on Sunday, February 5, at 5 p.m. This performance draws upon Asian traditional music and established composers to celebrate the Year of the Rabbit. Soprano Sumi Jo is the guest vocalist. Lee is a Korean-Canadian conductor currently serving as Assistant Conductor of the Boston Symphony Orchestra. He was a guest conductor with San Francisco Symphony in its 2021-2022 season, and led the Seoul Philharmonic and Ann Arbor Symphony in subscription series concerts. Lee also guest conducts the New York Philharmonic in its annual Lunar New Year Gala. The San Francisco program includes the Saibei Dance from Saibei Suite No. 2 by An-lun Huang; Three Wishes of a Rose by Huang Tzu; As the Spring Approaches Across the River by Geung-Su Lim; “Selections from Folk Songs for Orchestra” by Huang Ruo; Se Chỉ Luồn Kim (The Spinning Song) by Trần Mạnh Hung; Pioneer by Du-nam Cho; In the Flower Clouds by Hong-ryeol Lee and selections from Transcend by Zhou Tian. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2022-23/LNYYear-of-the-Rabbit to purchase tickets. Guest conductor Earl Lee will lead San Francisco Symphony in a special Lunar New Year concert on February 5. Open Wednesday to Sunday • 8:30 a.m. to 5:00 p.m.
articles.title: SF Symphony presents Lunar New Year concert on Feb. 5

articles.text: Berkley Symphony & Friends, the 10-year-old chamber music series at Piedmont Center for the Arts, returns on Sunday, February 5, for a concert titled “Winter of Love” “Winter of Love is inspired by the season of romance and love that February represents,” said René Mandel, Artistic Director at Berkeley Symphony. “The program stems from Elvis Costello’s The Juliet Letters, an extraordinary work for baritone and string quartet, that takes the audience on a rich and passionate journey through the human condition.” The concert features baritone Bruce Rameker making his Berkeley Symphony debut, and chamber musicians Rene Mandel (violin), Stephanie Bibbo (violin), Joy Fellows (viola), Evan Kahn (cello), and Britt Day (piano). A reception with treats and drinks will follow the performance. Advance tickets are $35 and may be purchased online at https://bit.ly/3iz8qAV.
articles.title: Berkeley Symphony & Friends concert at PCA on Feb. 5

articles.text: Michelle Williams and Ryan Gosling in Blue Valentine It’s not uncommon to hear a film praised for being unflinchingly honest, even stark. But embedded in that praise is the question: how close to life do audiences really want their movies to be? That is the dilemma inherent in Blue Valentine. Essentially, it takes what might be called a romance and juxtaposes it with life six years later. The film opens in real time with Dean (Ryan Gosling) and Cindy (Michelle Williams) and their little girl, Frankie (Faith Wladyka), living in a modest house in Scranton, PA. Dean paints houses and Cindy is a nurse. Life has intruded, leeching the joy out of their relationship, and burnishing all the spontaneity from their marriage. Cindy is bone tired and deeply discontent. Dean seems oblivious to her personal struggle. Dean has a ukulele and begins singing, “You Always Hurt the One You Love,” as Cindy does a soft shoe tap dance. articles.text: This may sound a bit hyperbolic, and Sam Elliott would likely reject the praise out of hand, using some purple language that would seem completely in character, but the fact is, as an actor, Elliott is a national treasure. He possesses not only that easily recognizable, sonorous voice, but he is also the last of a type, that cowboy who rode across a red dirt plain, stacked Colorado pillars in the distance, the sun at his back, ever alone. Elliott, after decades wearing worn western garb has merged with that mythic image that we carry with us when we think of the West. Granted that may never have been, but there it is. This is Sam Elliott: lean as a weathered fence post long ago abandoned on the prairie, his 70 some years etched in the crevasses of his leathery, tanned face, his frame all angles, his persona to a fault laconic, often sardonic, and ever conveying a sense of isolation that can overwhelm. Elliott portrays the character, Lee Hayden, in The Hero. A man holding his regrets at bay with alcohol and weed, still able to scratch out a living making voice-over commercials for the likes of Lone Star Barbecue Sauce, his one great western film, The Hero, now lost somewhere in his history but not in his dreams. This film finds a sweet spot and manages to stay there because of Elliott’s ability to never let his character slip in the Sam Elliott and Laura Prepon star in The Hero. realm of the maudlin, even when he gets some medical news that gives him bridled pause. Suddenly his life is derailed, and his estrangement from his daughter, Lucy (Krysten Ritter) and ex-wife, Val (Katherine Ross), give his very brief contact list (kept on his phone) new urgency. He also meets a far younger woman, Charlotte (Laura Prepon), who makes him realize that his self-centered halcyon days are gone and he now finds himself standing alone on a beach gazing at the horizon. Though the story is as spare as Elliott’s grin, this is never a vanity film; rather, it’s Elliott at his best, and as Lee, he refuses to turn away from who he has become. And now is. Filled with life still, a life constantly tempered by a sense of loss. Some of the moments in The Hero are sublime. Others are filled with an abiding melancholy. But perhaps melancholy is how you ultimately define growing old, each day slipping through your grasp like so many grains of sand, each night given over to restless sleep, always confronting what was and will never be again. The Hero. Directed by Brett Haley. Starring Sam Elliott, Laura Prepon and Katherine Ross. 1hr., 33 min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Apple tv. Paris in the Spring-time …

articles.text: Amandla Stenberg and Nick Robinson star in Everything, Everything. Everything, Everything is a sweet teen movie that will have special appeal to young girls. It’s reminiscent of countless stories of forbidden love, which makes it familiar, universal, and, of course, hugely sentimental. The basic set up: A girl, Maddy (Amandla Stenberg), on the cusp of her 18th birthday, looks out at the world through walls of glass. Since infancy she has grown up trapped in her hermetically sealed home, unable to venture outside lest she become lethally ill. Her diagnosis: severe combined immunodeficiency (SCID). Maddy, standing in front of the countess windows, dreams of running along beaches, floating in the ocean or walking along a residential street. Her mother is a doctor and treats her illness while the two of them live in a beautiful, modern upscale house designed to protect Maddy. One spring day, new people move in next door, to include an 18-year-old boy, Olly (Nick Robinson), a skateboarder who, standing by the moving truck, looks up and sees Maddy looking down at him from her wide window. He is intrigued; she is captivated. They tentatively wave hello. As it turns out their bedroom windows are across a narrow walkway and gradually they watch each other, then begin to text, talk and grow close, all within the parameters of what she can and cannot do, meaning for any reason she can’t go past the front door. Of course, this is a love story, so Maddy and Olly find a way. And finally, given permission by Maddy’s nurse, Carla (Ana De La Reguera), Olly is allowed inside the house, as long as he keeps his distance and definitely no touching. To tell any more about the plot would be unfair. Suffice it to say that Stenberg and Robinson are perfectly matched and exude chemistry. There is a deep innocence about their connection and the fact that Maddy has been sheltered from the world only contributes to what will be an overwhelming sense of awe once she risks everything to be with Olly. Teenagers, the target audience, will love this movie. Everything, Everything. Directed by Stella Meghie. Starring Amandla Stenberg, Nick Robinson and Ana De La Reguera. 1 hr., 36 min. Rated PG-13. Released 2017. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Everything, Everything a sweet story of teens

articles.text: One of Disney’s favorite tropes has been the adorable princess and the wicked stepmother. Recall Snow White and the spiked apple; Cinderella, forced to scrub and clean; or Rapunzel, locked away in a high tower. Pixar’s contribution, Brave, does feature a strong-willed teenage princess, Merida (Kelly MacDonald), who rebels not against an unkind stepmother, but against her imperious mother, queen Elinor (Emma Thompson). The period is medieval Scotland, filled with crags and castles and rolling highlands. And there is, of course, Merida, with her massive ginger-colored tresses, a young royal who happens to identify with her father, onelegged, big lug King Fergus (Bill Connoly). She can ride like the wind and is an expert archer (not unlike Katniss Everdeen of The Hunger Games). She would rather be racing horseback through the surrounding forests than spending time with the staid ladies of the court. Elinor, of course, has her own ideas of how a young princess should behave. But Merida, as wild as her red mane, snorts when she laughs, scoops up food from the pantry, and is a tomboyish, headstrong teenager who has her own ideas regarding gender equality. Queen Elinor is not to be deterred in her efforts to civilize Merida in the image of a proper princess, marriage being at the fore. She therefore invites three suitors to the yearly Highland Games, deciding that the best of the three will win her daughter’s hand. Merida, of course, has other plans. She finds all three definitely unsuitable as prospective husbands, and declares to her mother that she’ll not marry, period, followed by an age-appropriate tantrum to make her point. To further drive home wishes to be her own person, she dominates the archery contest with extraordinary skill and accuracy. But when her mother insists that she will accept the best suitor, Merida runs away into the forest. To her surprise she comes upon a cottage inhabited by an old witch, a crone with magical powers who tells the princess that she can, indeed, cast a spell on Elinor. Merida rashly, rebelliously, agrees. She realizes, too late, however, that her decision has some unintended consequences. In other words, be careful what you wish for when you say, “I want my freedom!” Brave, has more than a few Disneyesque life lessons that result in some tender moments between daughter and mother. This is a wonderfully animated tale that is easy to like. And it’s Pixar’s first female lead out of 13 feature films. Brave. Pixar animation. Directed by Mark Andrews and Brenda Chapman. With voices of Kelly MacDonald, Bill Connoly, Emma Thompson. 1 hr., 33 min. Rated PG. Released 2012. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+.

articles.text: Piedmont cartoonist Philip Witte, creator of the Flip cartoons that appear weekly in the Piedmont Post, nationally in the New Yorker and Wall Street Journal, and internationally throughout the UK including Galway, Ireland, is having an exhibit of selected works at Piedmont Center for the Arts from now through February 5. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. A bit of background Since leaving his legal career seven years ago, Piedmonter Phil Witte has sold more than 1,000 cartoons to dozens of publications in the U.S., U.K., and Galway, Ireland. A cartoonist from an early age, once he began his studies at Princeton he abandoned cartooning. Following some time working in Bangkok, he entered law school at the University of Chicago. Although life as a litigation attorney was all-consuming, Phil tried to find time for creative activities. He wrote a few humor pieces, which attracted the attention of a book publisher. That led to a joke book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and a sequel on turning 60. Sales to date are approaching 175,000 copies. “I knew I could write jokes, so I figured if I could combine that with drawing, I could become a cartoonist,” he said. “I was decent in art, but I needed to get a lot better, plus I had to develop a style… I’m still working on that.” He showed his early work to Phil Frank, the late cartoonist at The San Francisco Chronicle, who encouraged him. While work on his art, Witte collaborated as a gag writer for syndicated cartoonists, including Dan Piraro, creator of the cartoon feature “Bizarro.” Phil has 25 original ink drawings by Piraro Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. Even most of the “regular” cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time, Phil noted. Witte was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. His cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. He has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. There is even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of his cartoons in their permanent collection. Private collectors, including the documentary filmmaker Ken Burns, have bought Witte’s original artwork. “We actually swapped work,” said Phil, “my cartoon for dozens of his DVDs. He wrote a wonderful thank-you note and sent me a photo of him posing with the cartoon in his office.” “The cartooning career has gone far better than I even imagined it would,” Witte noted. “I’m content that I made the right career move.” Photo by Rob Yelland Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte currently has an exhibit of his work at the Piedmont Center for the Arts through February 5. that resulted from their collaboration. All this time, Phil was working at least 50 hours a week as a lawyer while “trying to be a good father and husband,” he added. He began selling his cartoons to major markets, including The Wall Street Journal, which encouraged him to put more time into cartooning. When he felt he had developed enough professional relationships with editors, he made the decision to leave the law. “The firm threw a blow-out farewell party at a restaurant, and even closed the office for the afternoon. It was the best day in my former career.” He has licensed his cartoons to greeting card companies with great success. Textbooks and professional groups started leasing his cartoons as well. He has also written a few dozen humor pieces for magazines and online sites. About six years ago, Phil and former Piedmont resident Rex Hesner began a blog critiquing the cartoons in The New Yorker magazine. Burr will present their first joint CD release concert in celebration of their new CD, Ramblin’. Winner of two Grammy Awards and a veteran of both the Turtle Island Quartet and bassist Stanley Clarke’s band, Tolling frequently performs at SF Jazz and other major venues in the Bay Area and all throughout the world. articles.text: Cassoulet is a classic French dish which is especially enjoyable during cold winter months. It has a reputation for being very difficult to make, but here is a version that is easy as can be. I have provided a number of variations to make it even simpler. The classic cassoulet is made with white beans and a variety of flavorful meats. The usual recipe uses duck, bacon, and sausage for the meats. This is combined with white beans, leeks, herbs, and some white wine. This recipe will serve two. Preheat the oven to 275°. It is best to use a cast-iron skillet. Put a tablespoon of olive oil in the pan. Mince one carrot, one stalk of celery, one shallot or half an onion, a leek, and some garlic. Put into the skillet to brown and add about a tablespoon of whole peppercorns, some French herbs, a healthy squeeze of tomato paste and anchovy paste. If you want the classic, use one can of white beans. Spaniards would use a can of garbanzos. Put these on top of your browned, vegetables, and top with some breadcrumbs. For the meats my first choice is duck confit, one duck leg per person. Add any of your favorite sausage. Other meats that could be used are fresh chicken legs, or turkey. Put the meat on top of your vegetables and pop in the oven for at least one hour. Add white wine to taste.

pages.text: 20 Wednesday, January 25, 2023 Witte cartoon exhibit continues through February 5 Piedmont cartoonist Philip Witte, creator of the Flip cartoons that appear weekly in the Piedmont Post, nationally in the New Yorker and Wall Street Journal, and internationally throughout the UK including Galway, Ireland, is having an exhibit of selected works at Piedmont Center for the Arts from now through February 5. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. A bit of background Since leaving his legal career seven years ago, Piedmonter Phil Witte has sold more than 1,000 cartoons to dozens of publications in the U.S., U.K., and Galway, Ireland. A cartoonist from an early age, once he began his studies at Princeton he abandoned cartooning. Following some time working in Bangkok, he entered law school at the University of Chicago. Although life as a litigation attorney was all-consuming, Phil tried to find time for creative activities. He wrote a few humor pieces, which attracted the attention of a book publisher. That led to a joke book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and a sequel on turning 60. Sales to date are approaching 175,000 copies. “I knew I could write jokes, so I figured if I could combine that with drawing, I could become a cartoonist,” he said. “I was decent in art, but I needed to get a lot better, plus I had to develop a style… I’m still working on that.” He showed his early work to Phil Frank, the late cartoonist at The San Francisco Chronicle, who encouraged him. While work on his art, Witte collaborated as a gag writer for syndicated cartoonists, including Dan Piraro, creator of the cartoon feature “Bizarro.” Phil has 25 original ink drawings by Piraro Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. Even most of the “regular” cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time, Phil noted. Witte was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. His cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. He has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. There is even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of his cartoons in their permanent collection. Private collectors, including the documentary filmmaker Ken Burns, have bought Witte’s original artwork. “We actually swapped work,” said Phil, “my cartoon for dozens of his DVDs. He wrote a wonderful thank-you note and sent me a photo of him posing with the cartoon in his office.” “The cartooning career has gone far better than I even imagined it would,” Witte noted. “I’m content that I made the right career move.” Photo by Rob Yelland Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte currently has an exhibit of his work at the Piedmont Center for the Arts through February 5. that resulted from their collaboration. All this time, Phil was working at least 50 hours a week as a lawyer while “trying to be a good father and husband,” he added. He began selling his cartoons to major markets, including The Wall Street Journal, which encouraged him to put more time into cartooning. When he felt he had developed enough professional relationships with editors, he made the decision to leave the law. “The firm threw a blow-out farewell party at a restaurant, and even closed the office for the afternoon. It was the best day in my former career.” He has licensed his cartoons to greeting card companies with great success. Textbooks and professional groups started leasing his cartoons as well. He has also written a few dozen humor pieces for magazines and online sites. About six years ago, Phil and former Piedmont resident Rex Hesner began a blog critiquing the cartoons in The New Yorker magazine. articles.text: Many of us have personal New Year’s resolutions, but have you thought of making some for your home? Give your home a comfort and safety refresh to start the year right. You can avoid expensive repairs by warding off problems before they begin and put yourself in a joyful mood for 2023. 1. Clear clutter, one step at a time Most of us vow to dispense with things we don’t use–but that can be much easier said than done. Find a system for yourself that reduces mental hurdles. Our advice? Start with a big box and take one room at a time. Put away anything you don’t absolutely use on a regular basis and move it into a closet first. Once you’ve had time to absorb living in your clutter-free space, you can decide on what to donate and give away. 2. Safety checks for the start of the year There are a couple of potential “silent dangers” in the home that are both harmful and also, thankfully, easy to ward off. One in fifteen homes has elevated radon levels, an odorless, radioactive gas that can be toxic, so we recommend a quick test at the top of every year. Also, give your carbon monoxide detectors a once over - gas can build up when furnaces and vents get obstructed. We’d be remiss if we didn’t include inspecting for blockages: the vents behind your clothes dryer, your chimney flue, furnace vents, and the supply and return vents in each room. 3. Deep clean the kitchen after the holidays Kitchens see a lot of use during festivities, so give them a fresh start in January. Check the temperature of your fridge and freezer and clean the condenser coils to be sure you’re not using unnecessary energy. Also check grout lines and tiles for surface damage and repair any issues. A thorough cleaning in the pantry, around the fridge, and behind appliances will help keep your kitchen hygienic and pest-free. 4. Don’t forget your storm damage check-up Heavy rains have been the theme of January, and so it’s a good idea to keep an eye on a few key parts of your home that may be affected. Look along the walls on the inside and outside of the house (including windows) for any signs of damage such as cracks or bulges. Be sure to replace any loose siding or trim on the exterior, as leaks can develop here. In the basement, look for any debris or dirt that may have washed out from the foundation walls – standing water can move soil out from the base which may not show up right away, so add a reminder to check again in a couple weeks.
