articles.text: I am periodically asked how I knew I wanted to become an architect. My journey to becoming an architect is grounded both in certain proclivities that I had in my nature as well as other interests that were developed through my early interactions with my family. Serendipity also played a large role in my choosing this professional path. I grew up in a family that had some creative talent (my mother and older brother had artistic skills), but everyone in the family had little interest in fix-it repairs. If something was broken and needed fixing, I became the go-to guy at any early age. I had no fear about taking apart something that was broken, and was fascinated by how things worked, how they were put together. Many times, I couldn’t get things back together, but there were many successes when I found the root of the problem and reconstructed things in a working order. My parents empowered me to develop those skills. I also enjoyed watching my mother and brother doing their artwork, which mostly consisted of sketching and oil painting. I would steal my brother’s paint and make my own paintings. In high school I was a decent art student, but I gravitated to the wood shop, metal shop, and automotive repair classes. When it came time to apply for colleges I decided that engineering would be right for me. Just before dropping the application into the mailbox, I had a second thought, I was also interested in making art, so at the last minute I changed my application to the architectural program. That last-minute decision was fortuitous, as I have never regretted it. It hasn’t always been an easy path, but it has definitely been a fulfilling one. Edward Kaplan AIA, NCARB, is principal of Kaplan Architects in Oakland and San Francisco since 1985. Kaplan Architects believes that excellent design solutions emerge through a thoughtful iteration of ideas, challenging preconceptions, and rethinking the solutions we develop. For information contact info@kaplanarchitects.com. Clock and table built from rough sawn lumber, milled and sized in a high school woodshop. articles.text: The Piedmont Senior group, organized through the Recreation Department, will begin to receive technology help. Starting today, Wednesday, January 25, after their monthly meeting at the Community Hall, they will receive tips on troubleshooting with computers from 12:45-1:15 p.m. Students in the in Advanced Placement Computer Science course at the high school will assist with the use of cell phones and computers. The first two students to provide assistance are sophomores Ishaia Goldberg-Berman and Bruno Banuelos. “We are hoping [to have] up to 20 seniors. I think Ishaia and I will be able to handle all the questions, but it would be really nice to have more students helping so seniors can have more personalized attention,” said Banuelos. The impetus for the Tech Help session came from the Senior Group’s leader Janet Epstein, who has wanted do improve seniors’ tech savvy ability for years now. “A lot of older people don’t know how to ask for help. I’m hoping that this will bring them out, to be comfortable to try new technology in a very informal manner,” said Epstein. The Tech Help session will be an open forum for seniors to bring their own computers and phones and ask questions. Topics include but are not limited to phone apps, QR codes, and opening digital menus at restaurants. Phones, tablets, smart watches, laptops or any other technological device can be brought in. For more information contact Epstein at: archie3333@aol.com.

articles.text: Dear Jim: I need your help. My basement flooded with 6 inches of water this year after it has been dry for the 30 years we have lived here. I’m assuming multiple atmospheric rivers got this started. We had an old sump pump in place and had plumbers come and install 2 more during this recent series of storms, but they don’t help at all. What should I do? The sump pump can be a lifesaver in the correct application. Unfortunately, it is not an effective tool for most of the drainage problems we experience in the Bay Area, which are accelerating with climate change and are demanding a more comprehensive approach. What a Sump Pump is good for A sump pump is primarily useful for removing localized surface water inside your home in the location it is placed, or at the exterior as part of a drainage system to pump water to the street. If you have water on the floor in a furnace room the sump pump will remove the bulk of the standing water. If you have a crawlspace or basement where water is being channeled to a specific location, the sump pump may help. A sump pump will generally only remove underground water in relationship to its depth- i.e. a sump well which is 2’ deep will normally remove water that gets within 2 feet of it. Why Sump Pumps are generally ineffective Unfortunately, our clay soils do not allow water to flow very well laterally. Translated this means the water that is migrating under our foundations will not be able to find the sump pump unless it is directed there. Subterranean water is frequently traveling under our foundations and popping up downstream in our crawlspaces or basements at various locations, and these locations can change as soils expand and contract in relationship to wet and dry conditions and vary with storms coming from different directions. A sump pump may seem like it is working because it sits in a hole below the water table causing it to fill up with water, but that may not be the water you need to get rid of. What is the Answer? The answer is to install a proper drainage system, sometimes expensive, never fun, always time consuming, but very effective (if done correctly). A well-designed combination of French Drains and downspout drainage will protect the perimeter of your home and never allow water to get to those locations that are getting flooded, channeling water away from your house. In effect, we would be putting a moat around your home to protect it. Water does not belong under your house and can lead to settlement, foundation damage and structural issues that can lead to costly repairs. Now may be the time to consider how to best protect what is likely your most valuable financial investment. Foundations exposed to significant long-term moisture eventually fail. This column is a regular feature by Jim Gardner of Jim Gardner Construction Inc. Jim is a longtime Piedmont resident and has been doing structural repair and basement renovation in your neighborhood since 1983. articles.text: Mary Rickard was a Piedmont resident from 2009 to 2020. Former Piedmont resident Mary Kathryn Rickard passed away unexpectedly on January 9, 2023, near her home in Fall City, Washington. Born in Waterloo, Iowa on July 22, 1962, she graduated from the University of Northern Iowa and moved to the Bay Area, where she met her husband Graham Rickard. After a courtship that spanned a few years and several cities, they wed in London in January, 1998. After living in London, Detroit, and Alameda, they moved to Piedmont in 2009. Their family included two beautiful children, Alex and Zoë, who both graduated from Piedmont High School. Two years ago, as empty nesters, Mary and Graham moved to Fall City to begin their next adventure. Mary loved the beauty, space, verdant landscape, and warm community there. She took great joy in mowing the lawn, planning for her summer garden, cultivating fruit trees, keeping an eye on the local bear, and helping Graham with his beekeeping. She kept in close contact with her family and friends around the world, checking in often and visiting regularly. Mary loved hiking, biking, knitting/sewing, Scrabble, the New York Times crossword puzzle, Bruce Springsteen, Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods, the Giants, and the Warriors. She was a wonderful wife, mother, daughter, sister, and friend, with a tremendous sense of loyalty and a delightful sense of humor. Her family and friends are grateful that she passed with a heart overflowing with love and a soul filled with life’s greatest experiences. While we will miss her forever, she will live on in all of us. Mary was a great believer in the power of public service and community. In lieu of flowers, please make donations to Habitat for Humanity, one of Mary’s favorite organizations. “If I had a flower for every time I thought of you . . . I could walk in my garden forever.” –Alfred Lord Tennyson
articles.title: Mary Rickard dies unexpectedly on January 9

articles.text: A strong turnout of 18 readers showed up at Piedmont Community Hall for the First Monday reading group in January for a discussion of Afterparties. On hand were Bob and Madeline Hall, Adrienne Hamlin, Ken Young, Darby and Gerry Gragg, Mike Bandrowski, Phil Witte, Martin Levy, Dick Carter, Bella Almanzan, Albert Chen, Melba Yee, Mike Henn, Sarah Johnson, and discussion leaders Priscilla Wanerus and Carol Long. Afterparties is the highly acclaimed debut collection of short stories by Anthony Veasna So, who died in 2020 at age 28 from a drug overdose. He was a young, queer, Cambodian American who wrote about issues associated with his ethnic Khmer identity and sexuality. The book was named a “Best Book of the Year” by the New York Times, National Public Radio, the Washington Post, the Loa Angeles Times, and others. Reader Darby Gragg shared that the book is required reading for her grandson’s college gender studies course. Afterparties is a set of stories about Cambodian-American life in America. The book is comic, but intense, and sexually graphic, providing insight into the life of queer and immigrant communities. The primary characters are often the children of refugees who suffered terrible trauma during the Cambodian Genocide, where 25% of the population was killed. These parents later created lives for themselves and their children in the Central Valley of California. In Afterparties these young people grapple with race, sexuality, friendship, and family in a place where their vocational options often came down to fixing cars, selling donuts, or going on welfare. So’s stories include two drunken brothers who attend a wedding afterparty and decide to expose their shady uncle’s snubbing of the bride and groom, and a high school badminton coach who tries to relive his glory days by beating a rising teenage star. There’s also a love affair between an older tech entrepreneur and a disillusioned, young teacher. In the final story, a nine-year-old child learns that his mother survived a racist school shooter. The book generated strong positive responses from most of the group. They felt So was an extremely talented writer, who wrote powerfully, creatively, and beautifully. His writing style was also crisp, fast, direct, raw, and impactful. He wrote as if he was talking directly with his readers, but tragically died at a very young age, and thus deprived them of his future works. So’s characters are rich in detail, and they reflect their immigrant families’ stressful experiences; which some readers could personally relate to. The generational effect of the genocide on the survivors and especially the children is evident and important to realize. Some members of the group had read nothing before about Cambodian refugees in the Central Valley, so the book provided this understanding too. It was noted that So was bipolar and could have periods of creative brilliance, but also falling-off-the-cliff depression. The cause behind So’s overdose death is unknown. However, there were readers who were less enthusiastic about the book. Some liked some of the stories, but not all of them. Some didn’t like his treatment of the Cambodian American culture, and questions were raised about how So’s community feels about the book. Still others found his detailed descriptions of gay sex more than they wanted to know. The situations of the characters were also depressing for some, and this led to an interesting discussion of the responsibilities of the writer and the reader. It was asked if a writer has an obligation to provide something positive for the readers, or is it the reader’s responsibility to make the effort to understand what the writer is trying to share? It was accepted that each reader bring her/his own baggage to a book that can determine if the book is enjoyed, but it was also said that well-written works are always exhilarating. Afterparties provided an understanding of experiences and a culture previously unknown to most of the readers, and this was appreciated. Additionally, readers agreed this was a book they would not have read if not for the First Mondays Reading Group, and they benefited from it. With their discussion complete the group considered their next books. They try to alternate fiction and non-fiction. They had previously selected Prisoners of Geography: Ten Maps that Explain Everything About the World, by Tim Marshall for February, and The Buddha in the Attic, a 2011 novel by American author Julie Otsuka, for March. For April the group selected Trevor Noah’s memoir Born a Crime. The group’s next discussion will be on February 6 and will start at 1:30 p.m. Weather permitting, they will meet outside the Japanese Tea House in Piedmont Park, otherwise inside the Community Hall. New readers are welcome to join the group. There is no fee to participate, Registration is required with the Recreation Department at 510- 420-3070. > edwardjones.com | Member SIPC We’re excited to hear from you. Former Piedmont resident Mary Kathryn Rickard passed away unexpectedly on January 9, 2023, near her home in Fall City, Washington. Born in Waterloo, Iowa on July 22, 1962, she graduated from the University of Northern Iowa and moved to the Bay Area, where she met her husband Graham Rickard. After a courtship that spanned a few years and several cities, they wed in London in January, 1998. After living in London, Detroit, and Alameda, they moved to Piedmont in 2009. Their family included two beautiful children, Alex and Zoë, who both graduated from Piedmont High School. Two years ago, as empty nesters, Mary and Graham moved to Fall City to begin their next adventure. Mary loved the beauty, space, verdant landscape, and warm community there. She took great joy in mowing the lawn, planning for her summer garden, cultivating fruit trees, keeping an eye on the local bear, and helping Graham with his beekeeping. She kept in close contact with her family and friends around the world, checking in often and visiting regularly. Mary loved hiking, biking, knitting/sewing, Scrabble, the New York Times crossword puzzle, Bruce Springsteen, Jack Nicklaus, Tiger Woods, the Giants, and the Warriors. She was a wonderful wife, mother, daughter, sister, and friend, with a tremendous sense of loyalty and a delightful sense of humor. Her family and friends are grateful that she passed with a heart overflowing with love and a soul filled with life’s greatest experiences. While we will miss her forever, she will live on in all of us. Mary was a great believer in the power of public service and community. In lieu of flowers, please make donations to Habitat for Humanity, one of Mary’s favorite organizations. “If I had a flower for every time I thought of you . . . I could walk in my garden forever.” –Alfred Lord Tennyson

articles.text: Members of Walking on Wednedays turned up in big numbers on January 18, a day with no rain in sight. The participants included Christine Calliste, Siow Fang Tan, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Bob Wong, Noemi Alvarado, Lisa Euphrat, Garrett Clifford, Martin Levy, Sarah Johnson, Melba Yee, Jim Kellogg, Elizabeth Richter, Jennifer Peltzer, Karen Palmer, Lois Price, Charlene Louie, Mark Davis, Kat Lang, Gloria DaSilva, Kathy Rolefson, Harriette Louie, Brenda Ferrero, Will Adams, Adrienne Hamlin, Phil Witte, Mike Gallant, Stella Houston, Matt Gerhardt, Edith Lee, Lilly Guardia-Labar, Sherry Jacobs, Leigh Sorensen with K-9 best friend McDuff, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, Mary Hedley, Allan Goldhammer, Pat Keller, Mike Henn with K-9 best friend Roger, and Dick Carter. The good walking weather returned last Wednesday, January 18, for the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays group. It was cool and a little cloudy, but no precipitation, and a great morning to get outside and walk after the many recent days of rains. A strong showing of 44 walkers and three K-9 best friends were at the Exedra to enjoy it. An announcement was made, reminding the group that Piedmont Post Phil Witte, a regular walker with the group, was going to have an exhibition of his work for three weekends, starting on January 21st, at the Piedmont Center for the Arts. Phil invited all the walkers to come to an opening reception on Friday night. Dick Carter, back after missing several weeks due to a medical procedure, was warmly greeted by the walkers. He offered his thanks to Will Adams, Melba Yee, Mike and Nancy Henn, Charlene Louie, and Priscilla Wanerus for leading the walks in his absence. Dick proposed that this day’s walk leaders come from the group. He showed a red baton (actually about 12 inches from the top of an old broom stick) and asked for a volunteer to start the day’s walk. They could go in any direction, and in about seven minutes Dick would toot a whistle and the baton would be handed to another walker. There was only mild trepidation and hesitation before Matt Gerhardt raised his hand and took the baton in it. Matt is especially qualified to lead a walk in Piedmont because a little over a year ago he created a walking route around Piedmont’s entire perimeter. He took the group down the west side of Highland Avenue where they passed a home in the 200 block that is way back off the street. This home was built in 1890 on the other side of Vernal (now Highland) Avenue. However, someone determined the street needed to be widened and the house’s front garden had to be taken for the expansion. The owner was determined this would never happen again, and had the home put on log rollers and moved across the street and far back of it. Matt handed off the baton to Pat Keller at the corner with Blair Avenue, where she took the group down to Waldo Avenue, street was once the backside of the home of Walker Blair, the first European settler in what was to become Piedmont. Pat took the group up Waldo to Park Way, and then passed the baton to Christine Calliste. Christine led the group down Park Way past Dracena Park, which was once Walter Blair’s quarry next to his dairy farm. She then passed the baton to Sherry Jacobs, who led the group down the Park Way hill. They passed many beautiful cedar shake homes built around 1908 after the San Francisco Earthquake. Architects Will Adams, Bob Wong, and Jim Kellogg all provided insights into this architectural style and type of construction. At the bottom of Park Way the street takes a hard right and on the left is a hidden path that goes down to Artuna Avenue and the panhandle part of Dracena Park. Sherry led the group down the path to Artuna and then to another path on Ricardo Avenue that connects with York Avenue. There Sherry handed the baton to Phil Witte who took the group up York. On York Charlene Louie pointed out a home that she had seen in an old photo and was the only house in open fields. City Administrator Sara Lillevand said that, since Council, Commission, and Committee meetings were televised through the cable station KCOM for 13 years prior to the pandemic, “we already have the staff and audiovisual capability for Zoom. From a resource allocation perspective, it would be reasonable to continue to offer hybrid opportunities … not everyone can come into the Chambers, and we have public meetings to allow the public to participate,” she said. To have meeting covered by Zoom technology costs the city of between $55 and $80 per hour for a member of city staff to work overtime and facilitate the meetings, including setup and takedown time. “I don’t think the cost is the biggest driver. The Overstory: A Novel by Richard Powers The Overstory, winner of the 2019 Pulitzer Prize in Fiction, is a sweeping, impassioned work of activism and resistance that is also a stunning evocation of the natural world. From the roots to the crown and back to the seeds, Richard Powers’ twelfth novel unfolds in concentric rings of interlocking fables that range from antebellum New York to the late twentieth-century Timber Wars of the Pacific Northwest and beyond. There is a world alongside ours ― vast, slow, interconnected, resourceful, magnificently inventive, and almost invisible to us. This is the story of a handful of people who learn how to see that world and who are drawn up into its unfolding catastrophe.” Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking. 5. Merchants of Doubt: How a Handful of Scientists Obscured the Truth on Issues from Tobacco Smoke to Global Warming by Naomi Oreskes and Erik M. Conway “Merchants of Doubt has been praised and attacked around the world for reasons easy to understand. This book tells the disquieting story of how a loose-knit group of high-level scientists and scientific advisers, with deep connections in politics and industry, ran effective campaigns to mislead the public and deny well-established scientific knowledge for more than four decades. The same individuals who claim the science of global warming is ‘not settled’ have also denied the truth about studies linking smoking to lung cancer, coal smoke to acid rain, and CFCs to the ozone hole. ‘Doubt is our product,’ wrote one tobacco executive. These ‘experts’ supplied it. Merchants of Doubt rolls back the rug on this dark corner of American science.” The portrayals are superb. Michele Williams is stunning as Cindy. And Ryan Gosling captures Dean perfectly. These are fine actors who bring to bear all of their talent. Director Derek Cianfrance, with cinematographer Andrij Parekh, shot the flashbacks in 16-mm, creating a softness to their courtship. Real time scenes are shot in digital, giving them a crisp, almost flat look, with less depth and color. Though the audience may not be aware of the difference, most filmmakers will insist that the message is the medium, so to speak. This is a film that is provocative, engaging, and is far from the happy meal being served up by Hollywood. Hopefully, it will find an audience Blue Valentine. Directed by Derek Cianfrance. Starring Ryan Gosling, Michelle Williams, John Donan and Faith Wladyka. 2 hrs. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Apple tv.

They see what they want to see and so remain, essentially, strangers to one another. They easily succumb to the romantic dream. Cindy compromises her hopes of being a doctor while Dean (who never graduated from high school) incrementally makes clear that he has no real ambitions other than coming home to his family. His job as a laborer is unimportant, a means to an end. What was easy and emotive and sensually loving, eventually morphs into something else, their interactions laced with tension, and therein resides potential tragedy. This contrast is revealed unsparingly, absent any glow that comprises so many relationship films (call them rom-coms). Think of Blue Valentine as the antidote. Shown with Witte are: (front) Nancy DeRoche (left), Siow Fang Tan, Sherry Jacobs, Swee Ling Chen; (back) Priscilla Wanerus, Dave DeRoche, Mary Carter, Will Adams, Adrienne Hamlin, Alicia Rivera, Melba Yee, Phil Witte, Charlene Louie, Dick Carter, Harriette Louie, and Brenda Ferrero. articles.text: Automatic license plate readers at Moraga and Ramona Avenues were triggered by a stolen black 2020 Hyundai Elantra on January 16 shortly after 11 a.m. The vehicle was stolen in Oakland on December 31. A Piedmont police officer located the vehicle parked on the second story of the Rockridge Safeway parking lot at 5100 Broadway. After activating his emergency lights the officer observed a woman in the front passenger seat. As the officer went to the vehicle, the woman reached over and locked the vehicle. She then moved over to the driver’s seat and used pliers to start the vehicle. The officer broke out the driver side window with a baton in attempt to detain the occupant before she fled. The occupant then quickly reversed the vehicle into the patrol vehicle with the officer nearby and proceeded to flee at high speed. Piedmont Police Sgt. Wright authorized a pursuit of the vehicle. The suspect collided with a pole and a red 2018 Lexus ES300 in the area of Broadway and Coronado Avenue in Oakland. The driver got out of the vehicle and fled on foot on Broadway towards Pleasant Valley Avenue. Officers were able to detain the driver and place her under arrest. The driver provided a false name which had no warrants. The suspect driver was transported to Santa Rita Jail and booked for fleeing, possession of a stolen vehicle, and hit and run. Santa Rita records revealed that the suspect’s real name was Tiffany Washington, 33, of Oakland. Washington was on parole for robbery and had an outstanding no bail warrant. There were no injuries to officers, citizens, or suspects. Oakland PD arrived on scene and completed an accident report. The stolen vehicle was returned to the owner.

articles.text: A city staff report from City Administrator Sara Lillevand confirmed that Bonita Avenue between Vista and Oakland Avenues will be used for Piedmont Community Pool construction staging. A Notice-to-Proceed to the pool contractor, Wickman Development & Construction, confirms that work may begin as early as tomorrow, Thursday, January 19, with plans for 335 working days so the pool may be completed by early spring in 2024. The pool construction will involve the loss of 57 parking spaces around a block that includes the Recreation Department and tennis courts. Specifically, all parking on Bonita Avenue between Magnolia and Vista Avenues; Magnolia Avenue between the Recreation Department building and Bonita Avenue; and the Carriage House parking lot will be eliminated. articles.text: More than 400 people spent Monday morning at Piedmont’s 26th annual Martin Luther King Jr. Day in the Alan Harvey Theater. The annual event is co-sponsored each year by the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) and the City, and features speakers, meaningful song and dance and a common theme. PADC Co-Presidents Ellen Lee and David Gard offered opening remarks for the event titled “Beyond Race, Reyond Class, Beyond Nation.” Moving words about Native Land were spoken by Corrina Gould, spokeswoman and Tribal Chair of the Confederated Villages of Lisjan/Ohlone. The event founder, Piedmont resident Lois Corrin, provided a welcome and introductions of the mont event; it was presented on a projection screen. “It’s time to usher in a moment of change. We must continue to beat the drum for justice and create a world where all people, regardless of their race, gender, sexual orientation, sexual identity or any other identity, are treated with respect and dignity,” said Lee. Dr. Martin Luther King Jr.’s life was taken from him almost 55 years ago on April 29, 1968. In his 39 years Dr. King delivered over 2,500 speeches, addressing topics not only about race and equality, but also about militarism, poverty, extreme materialism and ending the war in Vietnam. –Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. speakers and event hosts. articles.text: At the most recent school board meeting, Wednesday, January 11, new board president Veronica Thigpen announced the hybrid option, via Zoom teleconferencing, would be phased out by the end of January. This would eliminate the option for public comment from meetings from anyone not at City Hall, including parents, teachers, and PHS alumni. “A little housekeeping, not withstanding the problems we have had tonight with Zoom, but we will be phasing out Hybrid board meetings. Beginning next month the community can view our meetings in-person at the City Chambers or see it streamed on KCOM online or on cable TV,” said Thigpen. The announcement came at the 21-minute mark in the Communications/ Announcements section of the meeting. It was not on the agenda, voted on, and no rationale was given during the meeting. Cause for concern came from parents participating in the meeting remotely via Zoom at the next opportunity for comment 15 minutes later. “I was a little surprised to hear Veronica say you were going to stop doing hybrid board meetings,” said parent Laura Maestrelli via Zoom. “I would at least like to have a discussion about it.” Another parent cited similar concern shortly after. articles.text: Editor: Last Wednesday new school board members took their seats behind the dais and the board elected a new president. I want to offer congratulations to Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar in their new roles. And to Veronica Andersen Thigpen who now, as board president, is well poised to lead the school board in its selection of a new superintendent and as it ushers in an updated mission and vision for the Piedmont School District. The foundation for this time of transition was thoughtfully laid due, in large part, to the leadership, skill, and hard work of the previous board president Cory Smegal (who will continue on the school board for another two years). She has ably guided the school district these last two eventful years. Those who attended meetings no doubt observed her keen ability to zero in on issues and ask hard questions, and witnessed her compassion for our entire school community when she provided reports to calm, challenge, unite, and inspire us all. There is also much more that Cory did behind the scenes. She asked questions, verified facts, and sought to gain an understanding of issues through research and countless conversations with parents, administrators, educators, staff, students, other board members, as well as educational leaders outside of Piedmont. Cory encouraged board members to share thoughts and ideas and engage in authentic dialogue during meetings. She set a positive tone for these conversations by her ability to be direct while respectful, to disagree and also take time to listen and consider other perspectives. Because of this, Cory can take a great deal of credit for the way we were able to operate as a governance team with civility and transparency at a time when many boards of neighboring school districts were splintered. Always at the heart of Cory’s work on the board has been her deep care for and commitment to our students. We all witnessed her emotion when we heard heartbreaking stories of their mental health issues, her passion for girls’ equality in sports, or her desire to support all students in our schools. She has been no less of a driving force when advocating within the board to support our teachers and staff, or when meeting with state officials to lobby for an increase in funding for public schools. Her strong beliefs drove her perseverance to help the district honestly face district challenges and strive to make changes to meet the changing needs of our students. I am so grateful to have had the privilege to work with Cory, especially while I was vice president and she as president. I know that the board is, once again, in capable hands to help the district to progress and thrive with Veronica Andersen Thigpen at the helm as president. -Megan Pillsbury, for School Board member 1139 Oakland Avenue, Piedmont, CA 94611 Phone: 652-2051 • email: news@piedmont-post.com Publisher & Editor: Gray Cathrall City Editor: Jay Russell PRODUCTION MANAGER Victor Cheng REPORTERS Selen Ozturk Ed Gilligan Will Becker (intern) Sohrab “Seb” Ford (intern) SCHOOLS Ada Cliff SPORTS Jonathan Comeaux B. articles.text: A legend of his time and a highly charismatic leader, Martin Luther King Jr. came to Oakland to headline a civil rights rally at the Coliseum Arena, complete with music and lead entertainers Harry Belafonte and Joan Baez. It was early fall of 1967 and was the kickoff event of a nationwide tour. Having a political stance quite apart from MLK, the Oakland Tribune, for which I worked, chose to not send one of its political analysts to cover it. I volunteered, and our city editor was delighted. It was the only time in a 35-year career as music critic that I was pressed into service on social issues at the heart of the political scene. The highlight of the rousing evening before a meager crowd was the MLK speech discussing civil rights. His most memorable quote was the importance of total harmony through integration and interaction. Play only the black notes on a piano, he explained, you can produce beautiful themes. Play only the more numerous white keys, you can harmonize as well. But to reach the full potential of the keyboard and of your music, you need both, blending, harmonizing, adding great depth to your creativity. As long as the whites and blacks remained totally separate, you were stymied. He was warmly received. Afterward, as apparently the only reporter of the Northern California media in attendance, I was invited backstage to interview him. He appeared very tired, with bloodshot eyes, and I lacked a bundle of questions to activate
articles.title: Encountering the unforgettable M.L.K.

articles.text: Over the past three weeks, mudslides, flooding, and falling trees have become a frequent sight in Piedmont as the city has had to deal with repeated storms – most recently, last weekend’s heavy rain. Speaking on his experience mitigating the damage, Public Works Director Daniel Gonzales said that “Storms are like a test: It’s how we see where the things we do to address these events proactively are working and where they’re not.” The creek cleanup crews included eight Public Works staff working around the clock, along with three on-call contractors, to clear Piedmont’s waterways during the heavy rains from December 30 to January 2. With the more intermittent recent rains, however – like the storm bringing one to two inches of rain to the Bay last weekend, January 13 and 14 – Gonzales said, “we typically only have two staff members out monitoring creeks and clearing inlets at any given time, though there are always more crew on call if something significant occurs — when they can’t remove a large tree from the trash racks.” “If debris like branches and trees are flushed down waterways and not removed,” he emphasized, “the water will flood houses and roadways rather than flowing downhill.” While storm drain inlets throughout Piedmont are regularly being cleared, they’re operating at full capacity. This owes to the fact that the debris catch basins of the drains “were installed 50 to 70 years ago — not up to today’s standards.” Either the grates are too small, whereby any branch washed into the drain could obstruct it entirely, or else the drain itself is too small. Trash rack at foot of Bushy Dell Creek in Piedmont Park Photo by Public Works Dept. Bushy Dell Creek runs full during recent rainstorms. While Gonzales affirmed that the city’s storm system experienced no significant issues over the past three weeks, “they have identified the portions of the system we could proactively change — mainly height, size, and knowing where the drain system’s pressure points are and where we need staffing the most when branches and trees do fall.” “Four fairly significantly sized trees fell as a result of the storm,” he added. One was an 80-foot pine knocked down in Piedmont Park on December 30; another was a Sequoia Redwood split by lightning on Crocker Avenue near Crocker Park on January 10; and a third was a Eucalyptus tree which fell onto communication wires by the Wallace, Winsor and Wildwood Avenue intersection. As a result of the latter incident, Comcast and AT&T lines were out for a day and a half, and the road was not fully cleared until a Comcast crew arrived the next evening. “Nevertheless,” said Gonzales, “our city has 8,000 to 9,000 trees. The fact that we have lost 12 in this storm at our last count” — January 11 — “is a good rate, all things considered.” Public Works has since identified a tree leaning in Piedmont Park which, “while not fallen, is not safe. We plan to bring it down proactively, and continue identifying other potential dangers as the storms continue.” “In Public Works, if you’re doing your job, the damage you face isn’t nearly as involving as maintenance and cleanup,” said Gonzales. “While these storms have really been testing Piedmont’s storm systems, that’s certainly been the case here.” Those with questions about the storm damage and mitigation in Piedmont can email Daniel Gonzales at dgonzales@piedmont.ca.gov, or call him at (510) 420-3061. articles.text: Please join the League of Women Voters of Piedmont today, January 18, at 4 p.m. to hear Paul Gosselin from the California Department of Water Resources talk about sustainable groundwater management in California. In this free livestreamed Zoom and YouTube event, “Sustainable Groundwater in California: The Challenges Ahead,” Gosselin will discuss how California is implementing the Sustainable Groundwater Management Act (SGMA) and adjusting to climate change, while trying to balance agriculture’s pressing water needs. The talk is co-sponsored by the League of Women Voters and Piedmont Connect. The talk will include an audience question and answer session. California depends on groundwater for up to 60% of its annual supply in times of drought. The SGMA was enacted in 2014 to halt overdraft and bring groundwater basins into balanced levels of pumping and recharge. Under SGMA, basins must reach sustainability within 20 years of implementing their plans. Gosselin oversees the Sustainable Groundwater Management Office, which includes statewide groundwater management activities and the implementation of SGMA. He joined the Department after serving 13 years as Butte County’s Director of Water and Resource Conservation, where he managed the county’s State Water Project Table A alloFor 24 years, Piedmont residents have made sure their travels are well documented, with photos of family members reading the Piedmont Post in far-off places throughout the world, and some nearby. articles.text: The American Red Cross will host a blood donation drive on Saturday, January 21, from 9 a.m. to 3 p.m., in the Main Hall of the Veterans Memorial Building, 401 Highland Avenue. Blood donations typically drop during the winter due to travel, illness, and weather, but the need for blood is constant. Volunteer donors are the only source of blood for trauma and cancer patients, accident and burn victims, people with blood disorders, and more. Blood donors in the state of California must be 18 years old (or 16-17 with parental consent), weigh at least 110 pounds, and wait a minimum of eight weeks between whole blood donations. To make an appointment, visit redcrossblood.org/give.html/finddrive and use the sponsor code “PIEDMONT”. To learn more about who can and cannot donate blood, visit donateblood.org/faqs/#who-candonate. Parental consent forms can be found at bit.ly/3HF715S.
articles.title: Blood Drive in Piedmont this Saturday, Jan. 21

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s highly-anticipated White Elephant Sale will return this month with a preview sale on January 29. The sale, touted as Northern California’s “biggest rummage sale,” is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 yearround members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The preview sale begins at 12 p.m. To purchase tickets and learn how to donate items to the sale, visit https://museumca.org/event/ white-elephant-preview-sale/. The ongoing sale will be from, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. daily from February 1-25. The sale will be limited to 1500 people per day. Tickets are $5. The warehouse is located at 333 Lancaster Street in the Fruitvale district of Oakland.
articles.title: Oakland Museum White Elephant Preview Sale on January 29

articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series continues tomorrow, Thursday, January 19, with a free screening of the documentary Through the Night. Childcare, who needs it? Everyone. If you are a parent, grandparent and/or community member, you know that society can’t function without it. High quality, dependable and affordable childcare is the essential service necessary to every family and to the American workforce and yet it is always a struggle to find. If you are a doctor, nurse, police officer or in a myriad of other work sectors such as transportation or hospitality, you know the additional challenge in finding night care. This important topic is brought to life in a powerful, uplifting documentary film, Through the Night, directed by Loira Limbal. The film is an intimate cinema verite portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift as an essential worker at a pediatric hospital, another holding 3 jobs to support her family and an amazing woman (Nunu) who, for over 2 decades, has cared for the children whose parents have nowhere else to turn. A tender portrait of strength, love, and selflessness, Through the Night showcases the multiplicity of “women’s work”-paid, underpaid, and unpaid--all while negotiating the terms of a dignified existence under the 3 arrows of racism, sexism, and capitalism in America. The screening is at 7 p.m., followed by a short talk and Q & A with Kym Johnson, Executive Director of Bananas, Inc., an early care and education organization that provides resources for families and child care providers to support and educate our youngest Ellen Driscoll Playhouse is at Havens School, 325 Highland Avenue.
articles.title: Diversity Film at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse tomorrow

articles.text: Max Rivera “Climate anxiety” refers to persistent fear, worry or distress linked to uncertainty about the future in a changing climate. The term has also been defined as a chronic fear of environmental doom. Given that teens and young adults are more likely to witness the worsening effects of climate change in their lifetime, it’s not surprising that many young people are affected by climate anxiety. A 10-country survey of 10,000 young people ages 16 to 25 published in the medical journal The Lancet showed that climate change and inadequate responses by governments and previous generations are associated with climate anxiety in young people globally. Of those surveyed, 83% believed that people have failed to care for the planet and 75% believed that the future is frightening. Hana Thomas, a junior at Piedmont High School, said that climate change “sparks a lot of anxiety for my generation.” She also feels climate anxiety personally: “In all my visions for the future,” she said, “there’s this voice in the back of my head saying this could all be impossible if we don’t stop climate change. It definitely affects big life choices, like do I want to have children, do I want to bring children into a world like this? These are conversations I have with my friends, even at age 16, because it feels like there is so little action on such a big issue.” Piedmont High classmate Max Rivera first learned about the severity of climate change as a fifth grader in science class. “I’m still looking forward to possible changes people can make towards helping the environment and limiting climate change,” he said, “but I know that my life is going to be impacted by this pressing [issue]. If we don’t act now, it’s going to be impacting more people later on in life.” Young people who are concerned about climate change often feel powerless. Of those surveyed in the study published in The Lancet, 65% believed furthermore that we are failing young people and 58% believed that people in power are betraying youth and future generations. “I’m putting all the hope I have of fixing climate change into people of power, like the government, and I don’t know if I necessarily trust that their actions will really be reflected as beneficial to everyone including the environment,” Rivera said. Along those lines, Thomas expressed her wish that older generations felt climate anxiety as deeply as young people do, because it would inspire action. “It’s my generation’s problem now, even though we have done very little to worsen the effects of Hana Thomas it,” she said. Nevertheless, many young people are turning their climate anxiety into action. According to a partnership survey between the Washington Post and the Kaiser Family Foundation, about 1 in 4 American teens have participated in a walkout, attended a rally, or written to a public official about climate change. Thomas herself began interning for Youth vs Apocalypse when she was in middle school. She has since helped to organize climate marches in San Francisco and she currently interns with Undaunted K-12, an organization whose mission is to support public schools in transitioning to zero emissions. She plans on majoring in environmental studies in college. Rivera is the co-president of Piedmont High School’s Green Club whose goal is to “spread awareness about climate change and other environmental issues. “By spreading awareness and acting on these issues that are present, we can make Piedmont and surrounding areas and our community a better place overall,” he said. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. Contact her at sroberts@ piedmont.ca.gov with questions on electrification, plant-based eating, or hiking.
articles.title: Climate anxiety: how young Piedmonters are addressing climate change

articles.text: The Havens Dads Club will host its 15th Annual Havens Poker Night this Friday, January 20, at the Veterans Hall. A beginner tutorial starts at 6:00 p.m., the first cards will be dealt at 6:30 p.m. and the night will continue until the sold-out field of 150 bluffers and betters are whittled down to one champion. Proceeds from the event will go to supporting Havens Elementary School projects. Previous projects included partial funding for the Becker Field replacement, Ellen Driscoll mural, lunch tables and awnings, and playground blocks. The tournament, whose motto is “All in the for Kids,” will feature professional card dealers and poker tables. The unlimited re-buy-in format should allow for players on full-tilt to utilize their gambling skills. The most recent champions of the Texas Hold ‘Em Tournament were Ted Kinch (14th annual), Jason Harris (13th), Alex Seiden (12th), and Dustin Frazier (11th). Hors-d’oeuvres will be provided by Piedmont chef Robert Dorsey, and Top Dog. Adult beverages will include cocktails, beer, and wine with Havens Dad mixologist Peter Day in charge. Max Rivera Climate anxiety: how young Piedmonters are addressing climate change By Sophie Roberts “Climate anxiety” refers to persistent fear, worry or distress linked to uncertainty about the future in a changing climate. The term has also been defined as a chronic fear of environmental doom. Given that teens and young adults are more likely to witness the worsening effects of climate change in their lifetime, it’s not surprising that many young people are affected by climate anxiety. A 10-country survey of 10,000 young people ages 16 to 25 published in the medical journal The Lancet showed that climate change and inadequate responses by governments and previous generations are associated with climate anxiety in young people globally. Of those surveyed, 83% believed that people have failed to care for the planet and 75% believed that the future is frightening. Hana Thomas, a junior at Piedmont High School, said that climate change “sparks a lot of anxiety for my generation.” She also feels climate anxiety personally: “In all my visions for the future,” she said, “there’s this voice in the back of my head saying this could all be impossible if we don’t stop climate change. It definitely affects big life choices, like do I want to have children, do I want to bring children into a world like this? These are conversations I have with my friends, even at age 16, because it feels like there is so little action on such a big issue.” Piedmont High classmate Max Rivera first learned about the severity of climate change as a fifth grader in science class. “I’m still looking forward to possible changes people can make towards helping the environment and limiting climate change,” he said, “but I know that my life is going to be impacted by this pressing [issue]. If we don’t act now, it’s going to be impacting more people later on in life.” Young people who are concerned about climate change often feel powerless. Of those surveyed in the study published in The Lancet, 65% believed furthermore that we are failing young people and 58% believed that people in power are betraying youth and future generations. “I’m putting all the hope I have of fixing climate change into people of power, like the government, and I don’t know if I necessarily trust that their actions will really be reflected as beneficial to everyone including the environment,” Rivera said. Along those lines, Thomas expressed her wish that older generations felt climate anxiety as deeply as young people do, because it would inspire action. “It’s my generation’s problem now, even though we have done very little to worsen the effects of Hana Thomas it,” she said. Nevertheless, many young people are turning their climate anxiety into action. According to a partnership survey between the Washington Post and the Kaiser Family Foundation, about 1 in 4 American teens have participated in a walkout, attended a rally, or written to a public official about climate change. Thomas herself began interning for Youth vs Apocalypse when she was in middle school. She has since helped to organize climate marches in San Francisco and she currently interns with Undaunted K-12, an organization whose mission is to support public schools in transitioning to zero emissions. She plans on majoring in environmental studies in college. Rivera is the co-president of Piedmont High School’s Green Club whose goal is to “spread awareness about climate change and other environmental issues. “By spreading awareness and acting on these issues that are present, we can make Piedmont and surrounding areas and our community a better place overall,” he said. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division. articles.text: Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford Millennium High School senior Samiya Jones (left) and freshman Tobias Del Bono walk to class Millennium High School (MHS) was given its name in 2000. It had existed earlier under the name Piedmont Independent High School. Under the new name and leadership of Principal Ken Yale, it became a school designed to serve students within Piedmont and the broader Bay Area who would benefit from a non-competitive, personalized education that traditional high schools don’t provide. After 22 years of fostering a wonderful space for its students to grow, it is time to acknowledge and appreciate Millennium High school. The small high school with roughly 70 students actively works to ensure that its class structure and grading systems promote a democratic and safe environment for students to flourish. Inside MHS classrooms, teachers and administrators encourage students to share their unique voices and participate in constructive group activities. Under the school’s motto “Respect, Impact, Skills, and Engage” (R.I.S.E.), students are asked to take responsibility for their personal lives and in the school community. Students are expected to be actively working towards goals and benefitting the whole, whether in monthly “Falcon Meetings,” which brings the entire student body together for a conversation, the school’s leadership class, or seeking and engaging in extracurricular opportunities. Students are also asked to take ownership of their schedules. Just like Piedmont High School (PHS) students, MHS students must fulfill the “University of California A-G” requirements to graduate. Unlike PHS, Millennium creates a space for students to customize how they meet these requirements. Students can gain credit through college courses, community service, electives at PHS, internships, and work experience. This allows students to work as fast as they want in order to achieve their full potential. Due to the school’s encouragement of community participation, MHS has formed a safe space for students to engage with one another. Outside of the standards of traditional high schools, students can truly enjoy learning and companionship without the stress of competition. “I love just feeling welcome and safe and just happy to be at school,” said Shybrea Ottaviano a sophomore at MHS, “I’ve never really been excited to go to school before. In middle school and elementary school, I did not like the people there and I just Staff photo MHS senior Dariush Kashani, pictured as a freshman in 2020, points out student portraits taken in conjunction with The American Teenager Project, the telling of each MHS senior’s personal tale through interview and portrait photography. didn’t feel safe.” Ottaviano is not the only student who expressed feeling safe and welcome since coming to Millenium. Fifty percent of Millenium students came into the school as freshmen through interdistrict transfers. The other 50% are Piedmont residents, the majority of whom came to MHS after struggling in PHS’s exceptionally competitive atmosphere. It turns out that the school’s small size is one of its advantages. “We leverage our size, to Photo by Sohrab “Seb” Ford The entrance to Millennium High School at 760 Magnolia Avenue is connected to the west side of the Piedmont High School campus. be able to create spaces where everyone is 100% seen and heard. And our teachers do a good job of lifting up and validating our students’ experiences and giving them space to shine,” said MHS Principal Shannon Fierro. MHS definitely has a lead with community, ensuring that all members of this community are fully validated, to be fully heard, and are aware that everyone’s on their own path. There’s room enough in the world for all of us to win, for everyone to be successful, for everyone to go crush it and do their thing,” Fierro added. Whether you are looking for the appropriate high school for your eighth grader or have seen your high schooler struggle in the competitive atmosphere of a traditional high school, MHS is a wonderful option in Piedmont that may provide your child with the appropriate space to learn and grow. To learn more about Millennium High School visit their website at Piedmont.k12.ca.us/mhs or contact MHS Principal Shannon Fierro at sfierro@piedmont.k12. ca.us. Sohrab “Seb” Ford is a senior at Piedmont High School.

The Girl Scout Pinewood Derby Race Day is Saturday, February 4 from 3:00-6:00 p.m. in the chapel at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue. Advance registration for Derby Race day is needed. Registration and Car kits are available at the Car Making Workshop at Piedmont Middle School on January 22 or by contacting Beth Wiesbrock, ewiesbrock@gmail.com.

articles.text: While checking the weather again and again this week, we wondered: what’s the biggest storm in the Solar System? Jupiter’s Great Red Spot is 10,000 miles across in the planet’s Southern Hemisphere. That makes it 1.3 times bigger than the diameter of Earth. This great storm has been raging for more than 150 years with winds peaking at 400 mph. In comparison, the strongest hurricane to hit the U.S. mainland featured winds of 185 mph during the Labor Day Hurricane of 1935 in Florida. Since Jupiter’s weather functions under the same physics as Earth, learning more about the planet’s storms could help us better understand weather on our planet. Astronomers have been observing this storm for centuries, watching it shrink and become more circular over time. Additionally, scientists observe storms across the Solar System. Like Jupiter’s Great Red Spot, Neptune’s Dark Spots are formed in areas with high atmospheric pressure. Winds have clocked as high as 1,500 mph in these swirling storms. Closer to home, Mars has massive dust This illustration combines an image of Jupiter from the JunoCam instrument aboard NASA’s Juno spacecraft with a composite image of Earth to depict the size and depth of Jupiter’s Great Red Spot. storms around 60 mph. articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

They were loud and relentless, as if someone was constantly blow-drying a giant’s head. At the same time our fridge decided to take a vacation. It suddenly stopped working, and all the workers we asked to help couldn’t fix it. They told us it would be a ridiculous amount of money to fix, and never got back to us. Luckily, we had a backup fridge in the garage. Then came time for a decision: what type of new floors did we want? To repair the water damage, workers tore up 75 years’ worth of layers of linoleum. One of the layers, a geometrical linoleum, I actually quite liked and lobbied to keep that throughout the laundry room and kitchen, but nobody shared my retro design vision. My mother was set on tile and convinced my father, who wasn’t particularly excited to spend his Christmas break listening to the sound of tile being cut, but she told him it would look stunning. So. of course he agreed. The problem with tile is that it’s fragile. If my mother bangs pots and pans on it, like one can do on a wooden floor, she would crack that tile in no time. My mother dismissed my concern, but I could see that her determination for tile was someone dented (pardon the pun). Two stores and several hours later, with no floor type found and low morale, it seemed like there was no hope. pages.text: 10 Wednesday, January 18, 2023 CRYSTAL’S REFLECTIONS By Crystal Vacker This adventure actually started the week before winter break. I was being driven home from an end-of-season tennis banquet at my school, when my father told me that something had happened – but I shouldn’t worry about it. I guess he wanted me to not get too panicked before I even got home. The faded streetlights by highway 24 led us home as the world around us descended into darkness. Finally home, it was revealed that after decades of functioning, our washer and dryer unit had passed on. As a parting gift, half of the house and our basement were flooded. At our house it’s not entirely uncommon for something to suddenly stop working and wreak havoc – but this was on a completely new level. My mother had wanted a new laundry room for quite some time, though never under these circumstances. She had turned on the machine, something she had done countless time before, and left the house to run some errands. Four hours later, as she sat in the kitchen making a cup of coffee she noticed a stream of water making its way out of the utility room with the washer and dryer and into the kitchen. The machine was still cycling, Winter Break from Hell and the sound was a bit unusual. When she ran to the basement, she encountered a mini Niagara Falls, with water roaring down from the ceiling and into the basement. Apparently, the machine had become stuck on the “extra rinse” cycle, and had been pumping water into the basement for hours. And in a twist of cruel fate, the storm drain had been clogged by leaves that fell during the previous night’s windstorm. Water was up to her knees, and one can only imagine the effort it took to unclog the drain and then deal with the flood inside the house. A handyman was called. He was able to turn the washer off…but the chaos continued. First, several huge industrial-size dryers had to be brought into the house and left on for 24 hours for several days. They were loud and relentless, as if someone was constantly blow-drying a giant’s head. At the same time our fridge decided to take a vacation. It suddenly stopped working, and all the workers we asked to help couldn’t fix it. They told us it would be a ridiculous amount of money to fix, and never got back to us. Luckily, we had a backup fridge in the garage. Then came time for a decision: what type of new floors did we want? To repair the water damage, workers tore up 75 years’ worth of layers of linoleum. One of the layers, a geometrical linoleum, I actually quite liked and lobbied to keep that throughout the laundry room and kitchen, but nobody shared my retro design vision. My mother was set on tile and convinced my father, who wasn’t particularly excited to spend his Christmas break listening to the sound of tile being cut, but she told him it would look stunning. So. of course he agreed. The problem with tile is that it’s fragile. If my mother bangs pots and pans on it, like one can do on a wooden floor, she would crack that tile in no time. My mother dismissed my concern, but I could see that her determination for tile was someone dented (pardon the pun). Two stores and several hours later, with no floor type found and low morale, it seemed like there was no hope. But as we drove home in despair, I jokingly pointed out a store which we passed hundreds of times on our way to and from Piedmont Ballet, aptly named Simple Floors. Simple Floors saved us. It had a perfect floor – waterproof wood that looked like tile. The material could be picked up and installed within the next few days. Our kitchen had never looked so good. Oddly, around the same time the refrigerator which had gone on a vacation started working again. At first we didn’t believe it, so we only moved a couple things from the other fridge, but the fridge in the kitchen kept cold. One could only wonder what it was up to. Then came what should have been an exciting part: buying a new washer and dryer. But in our household, one never knows. First, my mother insisted that we drive all the way to Pleasant Hill, because she didn’t want to go to Best Buy in Emeryville. Once we arrived in Pleasant Hill we were greeted by a torrential downpour. My mother and sister proceeded to inspect every machine in the store and listen to lengthy explanations of the salesperson, which only seemed to confuse them further. Meanwhile my dad and I walked around aimlessly figuring that our opinion didn’t really matter. Finally, the choice was made and the installation arranged for the day before the New Year. Then my father jokingly asked my mother how she would reach the bottom of the tall washing machine. She’s only 5-4, but the question sent her into a panic attack. For the next 10 minutes we all demonstrated how she would get the clothes from below. It was quite the show to other parking lot visitors. Not until the machines arrived and were installed on the promised day did my mother calm down. So now, with the f loor redone, the walls repainted, the machines put in their rightful place, the reborn fridge washed, the house fixed, one could kick back and relax, right? Wrong. That same day, our car decided on its own to continuously run the fan – even after the engine was turned off. What followed was an expensive trip on New Year’s Eve, the 31st of December. But we got it fixed and finally there was peace and quiet in our household. And then the rain came and our basement flooded, this time with rainwater. It was unclogged right away with a broom. A few days later my sister went back to college, and I have been on flood watch ever since. On January 3rd, I went back to school, hoping that all these incidents weren’t going to become a trend for the new year. And despite the revenge of the appliances, I had a great break. I got to spend time with my sister, I hung out with friends, and enjoyed an amazing Christmas. Crystal Vacker is a Piedmont resident and a sophomore at Bentley School in Lafayette. articles.text: An art piece submitted for the event called “Equality is Justice” by Meena Duzak-Forestier, PMS 8th grade. The cadence of the event was spiced up at this point by young musicians of the Oaktown Jazz Workshops, playing “What Do You Say Dr. J” by James Williams and “For Children of all Ages,” by Bobby Watson. The keynote speaker, Kate Schatz, author of “Do the Work!” and the “Rad Women” book series, read a passage from Dr. King’s 1963 Letter from a Birmingham Jail. “In that letter, he wrote about the grave danger of ‘the white moderate,’ which he called the biggest stumbling block for racial justice. [Someone who is] more devoted to ‘order’ than to justice. That is so relevant today,” said Schatz. Schatz and Lee both highlighted a poignant term useful on the day, “Intersectionality, is pretty much the opposite of pretending that we’re just all the same. pages.text: Wednesday, January 18, 2023 11 MLK Celebration Continued from page 1 An art piece submitted for the event called “Equality is Justice” by Meena Duzak-Forestier, PMS 8th grade. The cadence of the event was spiced up at this point by young musicians of the Oaktown Jazz Workshops, playing “What Do You Say Dr. J” by James Williams and “For Children of all Ages,” by Bobby Watson. The keynote speaker, Kate Schatz, author of “Do the Work!” and the “Rad Women” book series, read a passage from Dr. King’s 1963 Letter from a Birmingham Jail. “In that letter, he wrote about the grave danger of ‘the white moderate,’ which he called the biggest stumbling block for racial justice. [Someone who is] more devoted to ‘order’ than to justice. That is so relevant today,” said Schatz. Schatz and Lee both highlighted a poignant term useful on the day, “Intersectionality, is pretty much the opposite of pretending that we’re just all the same. It’s a framework for understanding how aspects of a person’s social and political idenKeynote speaker Kate Schatz, an activist and author of “Do the Work!” Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. By Lanea Patty, 3rd grade A star in the sky and a bright moon in the dead of night. A tiger as confident as an eagle flying through the sky. A voice as gentle as angels singing soft tunes in the clear sky. As strong and calm as the deep blue sea lifting a small sailboat as it drifts through. As strong as a lion sprinting after its prey in the dead of night. As kind as a flower blossoming in the spring. He is Dr Martin Luther King Jr. The New Style Motherlode dance troupe. The Oakland Dynamites Cheer team performed a high-energy dance routine to conclude the MLK Day ceremony. The new Alan Harvey Theater was nearly full on MLK Jr. Day with approximately 400 people. tities combine to create different modes of discrimination and privilege.” Schatz said. “Intersectionality is a way of understanding our differences, and also our connection points,” Schatz summarized the theory which she accredited to Black feminist scholar Kimberlé Crenshaw. Images were then projected with recorded recitations by young poets, a tradition of the event in Piedmont. Ellen Lee worked with teachers and students to gather finished pieces and produce the presentation. 26 students submitted art pieces or poetry, which were also displayed in the lobby of the theater. The event saved the best for last. Corey Action, Artistic Director of the dance and entertainment troupe, New Style Motherlode Entertainment, introduced himself and the performers. “This was my dream when I was a little guy. I was always doing performances and dancing,” he said. Action’s crew performed playful interpretative dance and choreography in sparkling disco ball outfits with style to spare. The Oakland Dynamites, a youth cheerleading troop, followed with a crowd-captivating dance routine to hip-hop classics. The day’s festivities, lessons, and challenges ended with PHS senior Morgan Hunt delivering a Call to Action. PADC members who helped organize the event included Veronica Andersen Thigpen, Richard Turner, Anna Weber Kneital, Sachin Adarkar, Sheila Leunig, and Co-President David Gard. For more on PADC visit Padc. info. Oaktown Jazz Workshop performs, directed by Ravi Abcarian. CHAPEL OF THE CHIMES - OAKLAND DOCENT GUIDED TOUR TRULY A PLACE LIKE NO OTHER ! Originally designed in 1909, this Oakland Historical Landmark Building has long been considered one of the most beautiful historic buildings in all of California with designs from noted architects Julia Morgan and Aaron Green. articles.text: Staff Photos Eva Levingston led with 21 points against Salesian, but PHS had to adjust after she fouled out 4:24 left in the game. Make no mistake about it; Piedmont High’s girls’ basketball team is well on its way as being recognized as of the best squads in the state. Currently holding SportsStar Magazine’s No. 1 ranking in NorCal, the Highlanders toppled No. 5 ranked Salesian by six points, 69-63, on Monday, January 16, at Bishop O’Dowd’s MLK Day Showcase. Over the past week, Piedmont also defeated Cathedral Catholic of San Diego 80-37 on Saturday, January 14, at St. Mary’s of Stockton in its MLK Showcase. Earlier, on Thursday, January 12, they overwhelmed league opponent Alameda 73-14. Facing Salesian, the Highlanders had to overcome a lot after three starters had to leave the game early. Guard Adrienne Blackwell suffered an injury in the first quarter, and two players fouled out. Guard Perseas Gioukaris fouled out in the third quarter, and with a 13-point lead midway through the fourth quarter, forward Eva Levingston, its leading scorer, fouled out. It required big contributions from role players Shakila Zuberi and Katarina Melian. “I definitely think it wasn’t our best game and we could’ve played more aggressively. But, we pulled it out and it was a fun game,” said team captain, senior Trinity Zamora, who finished with 18 points. “Close games like this show us who we really are. We changed up our defense coming out of the first half and were just being more patient and smart with the ball.” Piedmont’s win moved its record to 15-0, the best start since the era of the celebrity Paris twins in _____. The team has set its sights on winning the WACC for the first time in the league’s 11-year history. 69-63 over Salesian The two sides traded points in the first quarter to make it a 12-12 deadlock at the end of the first quarter. By halftime the Pride held a narrow 33-30 advantage. But Piedmont responded strongly to outscore Salesian 23-10 in the Trinity Zamora scored 18 points against Salesian. third quarter to go ahead 53-43 to start the fourth. Salesian chipped away at the lead and narrowed the score to 65-61, but the Highlanders closed out productively at the free throw line. In the third quarter, Piedmont took an 8-point lead, 44-36, after going on a 12-0 scoring run at the start of the quarter. When Levingston fouled out with 4:24 left in the game, Piedmont had increased its lead to 61-48. The Highlanders persevered through the Pride’s aggressive press from then on. Final scorers: Levingston led with 21 points, Zamora had 18, Natalia Martinez and Maddie Hill each scored 13, and Gioukaris and Melian had two points. 80-37 win vs. Cathedral Catholic Piedmont led 12-8 by the end of the first quarter and extended the lead to 29-18 by halftime. PHS made it 47-28 in the third quarter and closed out with a mighty 33-point final quarter. Final scorers: Levingston had 25 points, Zamora had 18, Martinez and Hill had 15, Blackwell scored five, and Gioukaris had two. 73-14 over Alameda In something of a non-contest, Piedmont opened at 25-3 and pushed the lead to 41-8 at halftime. PHS extended the lead to 60-9 to start the fourth and closed out with 13 points in the final going, 73-14. Final scorers: Martinez led with 26 points, Zamora had 14, Levingston had 13, Hill scored eight, Blackwell had five, Gioukaris had four, and Zuberi three. NEXT UP Piedmont (15-0 overall, 2-0 league) has a critical league match at Bishop O’Dowd today, Wednesday, January 18, at 5:30 p.m. They have three more game during the next week. PHS is at Berkeley on Friday, January 20, at 5:30 p.m.; a game with North Coast Section foe Acalanes at Carondelet in Concord for the Sabrina Ionescu Showcase on Saturday, January 21, at 5:30 p.m.; and a critical game on the road with league opponent San Leandro on Monday, January 23, at 6:30 p.m. Maddie Hill knocks down a 3-pointer against Salesian.

articles.text: Piedmont High’s boys’ basketball team wrapped up a strong week of action, defeating Alameda 59-57 at home on Thursday, January 12, beating St. Mary’s 65-38 at an MLK Showcase at Berkeley High on Saturday, January 14, and losing to top-ranked Oakland High 73-57 at the MLK Day Classic at Merritt College on Monday, January 16. The wins over Alameda and St. Mary’s extended Piedmont’s winning streak to four games before playing the highly touted Oakland High squad, which came in as SportStar Magazine’s No. 20 ranked team in NorCal. Piedmont’s win over Alameda was the highlight of the week, with sophomore Ravi Silverberg scoring the game winner on a 3-pointer in the closing seconds for a 59-57 win. “The wins over Alameda and St. Mary’s were awesome, I think our defense in the second quarter against St. Mary’s was the best we’ve played all season. The Alameda buzzer-beater was another great win; our guys were ready for the critical moment. Playing Oakland High is great for us. Playing teams like this gets you ready for late in the season,” said coach Ben Spencer. The victory over the Hornets put Piedmont in first place in the Western Alameda County Conference (WACC) with a 3-0 record ahead of Berkeley (3-1), San Leandro (2-1), Alameda (2-1), and O’Dowd (2-2). With nine of the 10 remaining games against league opponents, the focus is now to become the WACC’s first champion other than Bishop O’Dowd since the league’s inception. The Dragons have won all 10 league titles of the WACC’s existence, sharing first-place honors with San Leandro in 2016 and 2019. Piedmont plays at O’Dowd today, Wednesday, January 18, and at Berkeley on Friday, January 20. “Wednesday will be a great test for us. They (O’Dowd) will play a similar style to Oakland High. Our guards now know what to expect,” said Spencer. 59-57 thriller over Alameda In a heated win over Alameda, Piedmont led 12-8 to end the Staff Photos Ravi Silverberg scored the game-winning 3-pointer against Alameda, putting Piedmont on top of the WACC. first quarter and 27-21 by halftime. The Hornets cut the deficit to 39-38 by the end of the third quarter, and the two sides traded points back and forth down to the wire. With Alameda clinging to a 57-56 lead in the waning seconds, Silverberg moved the ball up court. He kicked the ball inside to Harris, who passed to Matteo Costa after a couple of dribbles. Costa then drove inside, stopped, and turned to pass outside to Silverberg. The sophomore guard instinctively put up the 3-pointer, draining it as time expired. Final scorers: Harris scored 18 points, Silverberg scored 14, Brit Burden had 10, Declan Linnane scored eight, while Costa and Thorin Holmes had four. 65-38 victory over St. Mary’s The game was the first time Piedmont and St. Mary’s have faced each other since the North Coast Section championship won by Piedmont in 2020. The Highlanders trailed 10-5 at the end of the first quarter and then exploded for 28 points in the second to lead 33-20 at the half. PHS extended its lead to 51-31 in the third period and closed out with 14 points in the fourth for the 65-38 victory. Final scorers: Harris led with 17 points, Theo Evans had 10, Burden and Silverberg scored nine, Holmes had eight, while Cairo Osman, Teagan Haddawy, Costa and Linnane had three. A.J. Harris scored 37 points against Oakland High, 18 in a game with Alameda, and 17 points against St. Mary’s.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team had a tough week with two consecutive league losses on the road. They lost 3-2 at Castro Valley on Wednesday, January 11 and 1-0 at Berkeley on Friday, January 13. “We looked rusty, to be honest,” said coach Dan Chubbock following the loss to Berkeley. “We worked hard and tried hard, but we lacked quality. There’s no shame to losing to these teams. Today, we just couldn’t break them down.” The pair of games brings the Highlanders’ record to 5-0-3 overall and 3-0-2 in league (W-TL), placing them third. Berkeley’s win jolted them to first-place at 4-0-1, while Castro Valley is in second at 3-1-1. Despite the losses the matches revealed how close the WACC’s Foothill Division is. Castro Valley recently tied San Leandro 1-1, a team which PHS beat 6-1 one week earlier. Berkeley, meanwhile, lost to Bishop O’Dowd 2-1 on January 6, and Piedmont beat the Dragons 1-0 on December 7. “We’re looking to bounce back. It’s tough after taking any loss, especially when these girls believe they can win the league. Now we have to beat Berkeley, Castro Valley, and pretty much go undefeated the rest of the season. Everyone has beaten everyone,” explained Chubbock. 1-0 loss to Berkeley Berkeley did well against Piedmont to sit defensively and not allow clear looks on the middle of the pitch. They pressured the Highlanders when they entered the zone to force loose balls up field. The Jackets’ goal in the 28th minute came after the referee called a handball outside of the box on Piedmont. The Berkeley goalie Polzin took the free kick a foot above the penalty area, arching her ball to the far post for the eventual game-winner in the 28th minute. Piedmont had only one goal Staff Photos Emily Fitzgerald was narrowly short of the equalizer against Berkeley. Audrey Lam scored against Castro Valley.
