articles.text: Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team came out of an unusual double-header undefeated on Thursday, January 12 at Witter Field. It tied Encinal 3-3 earlier in the day before defeating Arroyo 1-0 in the evening. PHS was originally set to face Arroyo on January 10, but the match was moved due to rain. Encinal, meanwhile, was suffering from its own flooded field and moved the game to Piedmont. Both matches were with nonleague Shoreline Division opponents. “It’s obviously tough to play two matches in one day, but it was a way to get the games played. We felt that we have enough depth to still be successful,” explained coach Todd Sullivan. The pair of games brings Piedmont’s record 4-3-2 overall and undefeated in league at 2-1-0 (W-T-L). PHS now has nine matches left in the regular season with six of those against Foothill Division teams. 1-0 over Arroyo Piedmont’s game-winning goal came in the 56th minute when Bosco Lorin slotted home a shot on a counterattack. It came moments after Arroyo had a shot from close distance clang off of the crossbar and fall to Soren Dixon. The defender sent a pass to junior striker Aiden Woolwine, who showed tremendous hold-up play by retrieving possession between two defenders, and flicking a pass out wide to Sam Shelby. From the right wing, Shelby sent a ball across the face of goal to Lorin steaming down the left Photos by Scott Stratman Aiden Woolwine (left) and Bosco Lorin celebrate after Lorin’s goal against Arroyo, while a Dons defender lays dejected on the floor. side unmarked. He scored on a left-footed shot past the keeper. Lorin, notably, was called up from the junior varsity squad for Thursday’s games. 3-3 tie with Encinal Piedmont trailed 1-0 to end the first half and fell behind 2-0 at the start of the second half when Encinal caught the Highlanders’ keeper off his line, launching a shot from the midfield mark and into the net. However, the Highlanders rallied for three consecutive goals by Gianluca Bini, Evan Manolis, and Enzo Bernales to save the day. In the 47th minute, a buildup to Bini’s goal started with Rylan Nelson racing down the right side and sending a cross to Bini in front of the net. The ball skipped off his foot and back to Bernales on the left side. With no delay, Bernales sent a pass on the volley to Bini, who scored by redirecting the ball into the net. Piedmont scored again two minutes later on a beautiful, bending shot by Manolis. His goal came after Bernales stormed into the area. A ball hit off a defender led to Manolis jumping on possession. The Highlanders didn’t take any time to get their next goal when Woolwine drew a penalty kick in the 51st minute after a Enzo Bernales had a goal and assist against Encinal. Evan Manolis scored on a beautiful, bending shot against Encinal.

Describing a sports team as a sum greater than its parts has become a cliché for good reason: seeing a group of individuals band together to accomplish something they couldn’t individually is always rewarding. Those who watched the Piedmont Middle School girls’ basketball team this season got that reward. The Scots finished their season with a sterling 10-2 record, capitalized by winning a four-team end-of-season tournament hosted by King Middle School in Berkeley. The season was marked by incredible individual and team improvement overseen by head coach Maddie Mills and assistant coach Michael Love. The team demonstrated a season-long commitment to playing with effort and intensity. The Scots were overflowing with team camaraderie, and no play occurred without cheers or words of encouragement from the players on the bench. The Scots won their first game of the season against Walnut Creek Intermediate, and followed a tough loss to Joaquin Moraga with a narrow 20-17 road win against Stanley Intermediate of Lafayette. Point guard Olivia Stevens showed her talent and poise during this pre-Thanksgiving stretch. The 16-player team showed their strength by dividing and conquering in two separate games scheduled at the same time. The team of the hard-charging Elly Mak and Lauren Udovch defeated Willard, while a second team of fierce rebounder Hannah Joerger held MLK to only four points in a win. Sharpshooter Olivia Humphries sank threes all season and scored 14 points in Piedmont’s 15-10 win over Stanley. Improvement became apparent at this point in the season; Lucy Dorsey’s hustle, Edie Elmquist’s ferocity, and Ella Thomasson’s defense and rebounding started to shine. Nicole Li’s all-around game and Maggie Eidt’s screening and passing were highlights all season as well. The Scots earned another victory over Walnut Creek Intermediate before losing to Joaquin Moraga before beating Head Royce in a preview of the tournament to come at MLK. Izara Dando and Sophia Puckett and their fantastic attitudes made them valued members of the team. The Scots had already beaten MLK and Head Royce, still nothing was easy. Starting slowly in their first game against Head Royce, they were spurred on by the defense and energy of Madeline Lee and Cory Minor in the win. articles.text: SOREN DIXON Soccer & Lacrosse With an enrollment of roughly 900 students, you will often see athletes at Piedmont High playing more than one sport. Here is a feature on some influential athletes competing in multiple sports. Soren Dixon, a senior, is a key starter on Piedmont’s soccer and lacrosse teams. On the soccer pitch, Dixon is a defender in Todd Sullivan’s system and is a leading scorer on the lacrosse team. As a junior in 2022, Dixon was a captain of the lacrosse team’s sixth-consecutive WACC Championship. In the championship game against Bishop O’Dowd, Dixon scored four goals in a 10-9 win and earned first-team AllLeague honors. Dixon also helped Piedmont’s soccer team win last year’s Shoreline title with an undefeated league record of 10-0-0. He helped their defense keep a clean sheet in a 1-0 shutout of University and led lead the team to the school’s first-ever Div. 4 North Coast Section NCS Championship. Staff Photos Peter Krumins is a two-sport athlete on water polo and baseball. He was The Posts’ 2022 Sophomore of the Year. PETER KRUMINS Water Polo & Baseball Peter Krumins, a junior, is a leading player on the water polo team in the fall and baseball team in the spring. He’s already won three WACC championships, with two consecutive titles in water polo and as a member of the defending Shoreline champion baseball team. This past fall Krumins helped lead the Highlanders to its second WACC title by scoring six goals in the 13-4 win over Alameda on October 29. He was also a key player in Piedmont’s 2021 WACC title, the first in school history, in which he where he scored twice in a 12-8 win over Berkeley. On the baseball diamond last spring, Krumins started at third base and hit for a stellar .324 average, with 22 hits, three doubles, three triples, and a home run. In the league championship 6-5 win over Encinal, he was 2-for-4 with two runs scored, while also having one hit and one run scored in Piedmont’s 4-3 NCS opening round win over St. Patrick, and adding another hit and run scored in the NCS 6-5 loss to St. Joseph. The Post named Krumins the Sophomore of the Year in 2022. Friedie Schickedanz is a two-sport athlete on water polo and lacrosse. FRIEDIE SCHICKEDANZ Water Polo & Lacrosse Friedie Schickedanz is a senior and a two-sport athlete in water polo and lacrosse. She is a two-year starter as the water polo goalie and played on the varsity lacrosse team last spring. In water polo, Schickedanz led Piedmont to a fifth-place finish in the league tournament by recording 11 saves in a 13-12 sudden-death overtime win over Berkeley, including three clutch saves in overtime. In the spring, Schickedanz scored in a 14-9 game with Tamalpais in lacrosse. Piedmont finished went 4-1 against league opponents, and lost in the first round of the North Coast Section playoffs. Soren Dixon is a key player on both the soccer and lacrosse teams.
articles.title: More multi-sport athletes at Piedmont High

articles.text: We’re in January now, meaning it’s the start of the ATP Tennis Tour’s Grand Slam lineup and the Australian Open underway. Former Piedmont High player Mackie McDonald made his sixth appearance in the main draw of the Aussie Open, making his way to the second round after defeating 21-year-old American Brandon Nakashima and then pulling off a stunning upset of one of the world’s greatest players, Rafael Nadal. Against Nakashima, McDonald won a heated match in five sets, which included three sets going to 7-point tiebreakers, 7-6 (7-5), 7-6 (7-1), 1-6, 7-6 (12-10), 6-4. In the match with Nadal, McDonald led 6-4, 5-3 before the No. 1 ranked player exited the match. Nadal re-entered the match to make it 5-4, but McDonald won with set-point, 6-4. McDonald, 27, is currently No. 64 overall on the ATP Tennis Tour and should improve after defeating No. 46 Nakashima and going stride-for-stride with Nadal. Mackie won the first set 6-4 after taking set-point when forcing deuce and gaining advantage, leading 4-1 at one point in the set. You could see what it meant to him, beaming a smile during a successful first set victory against when of the best players of all time. McDonald stole the first game of the second set as the returner with three break-point opportunities and then went up 2-0 as the server. He nearly took the third game of the second set as the returner by forcing deuce and briefly having advantage, but Nadal powered through. Nadal tied 2-2 as the returner and then went ahead 3-2. McDonald tied 3-3 and then went ahead 4-3 as the returner forcing deuce and taking advantage, once again. McDonald then went up 5-3, and Nadal wound up hampered by a nagging hip injury. Mackie smashed two straight aces and Nadal went to the bench with an injury. Nadal returned after a medical timeout to make it 5-4 but McDonald won as the Photos courtesy of Australian Open Twitter Mackie McDonald is set to play in the third round of the Australian Open after a shocking upset of No. 1 Rafael Nadal. returner, 6-4, closing out the second set. In the third set, Nadal regained some form. The two players traded games as server until the set was at 5-5. From there, McDonald went ahead 6-5 as the returner up with two break point opportunities up 40-15. With match point, Mackie closed out the biggest match of his life
articles.title: Former PHS player advances to 3rd round of Australian Ope

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA) has celebrated Lunar New Year for over two decades with a day of festivities, art, music and dance. This year’s event, honoring the Year of the Rabbit on Sunday, January 29, is the museum’s 22nd annual Lunar New Year celebration. Festivities begin at 11 a.m. At noon at the outdoor garden stage, a lucky lion dance will be performed by Developing Virtue Secondary School students and kick off a series of events. Events at the outdoor garden stage include: 12:30–1:00 p.m. – Nanta Drum Play and Pan-Gut by Hansamo’s Nanta, Pungmulnori & Dance Teams 1:15–1:45 p.m. – Vietnamese 16-string đàn tranh (zither) performance by Vân-Ánh Võ 2:00–2:30 p.m. – Filipino Singkil dance performance and lesson by Earlene Escobal and the Pilipinx American Student Association at CSU East Bay 2:45–3:00 p.m. – Malaysian 24 Seasons Drumming by Developing Virtue Secondary School 3:15–3:35 p.m. – Street style dance performance and lesson by Str8jacket, as seen on America’s Got Talent The celebration concludes at 3:45 p.m. with a dragon dance performed by Developing Virtue Secondary School students. Throughout the day in various locations in the museum, children will have the opportunity to participate in arts activities, including creating paper lanterns, cut-out colorings of rabbits, and creating care cards for elders in the Oakland community. Ticket prices vary. To learn more, and to purchase tickets, visit https://museumca.org/event/ lunar-new-year-at-omca-year-ofthe-rabbit/. Oakland Museum will conclude its Lunar New Year celebration with a dragon dance performed by Developing Virtue Secondary School students.
articles.title: Oakland Museum celebrates 22nd annual Lunar New Year on Jan. 29

articles.text: San Francisco’s Asian Art Museum invites everyone to celebrate the Year of the Rabbit in this year’s Lunar New Year event on Sunday, February 5, when the museum will host an array of family-friendly activities. Lunar New Year, sometimes called Chinese New Year, is celebrated widely in China but also in Tibet, Japan, Korea, Thailand, and here in the Bay Area. Festivities involve honoring ancestors and making preparations for a prosperous and joyous new year. The rabbit is the fourth in the 12-year cycle of animals that appear in the Chinese zodiac. Online activities Families can visit the Asian Art Museum’s website for printable coloring sheets related to the Year of the Rabbit, as well as an instructional page on how to create your own Lunar New Year red envelope. You can also watch youth dancers from dance company LionDanceMe perform a New Year Lion dance, a traditional way to ring in the new year. You can also view “At the Table Dumpling Adventure’’ with Kristina Cho. Cho is a food stylist and blogger who shows her technique for making traditional Chinese pork and shrimp dumplings, a common dish for any time of the year. Cho is the author of the cookbook “Mooncakes and Milk Bread,” which includes the recipe for these dumplings and other traditional dishes. Family fun day The Asian Art Museum will have storytelling and family-friendly Lunar New Year activities. Art activities will begin at 11 a.m., in which children and adults will learn about traditional Chinese art. Storytellers include Fred Sheng (“Why the Rat Comes First”), Miriam Mills (“The Tet Pole”), and Leta Bushyhead (“Nian, the Beast”). Visit https://asianart.org/cultural-celebrations/celebrate-lunar-new-year/ for a full schedule and to purchase tickets. SF marks Lunar New Year with public display of large statues The city of San Francisco is celebrating the Year of the Rabbit with large, colorful rabbit statues placed in five locations: the Chase Center, Chinatown-Rose Pak Station, Union Square, Lucky Supermarket on Sloat Boulevard, and the Asian Art Museum. The project is sponsored by the Chinese Chamber of Commerce.
articles.title: Year of the Rabbit family fun day is February 5

articles.text: A photo exhibit, The New Black Vanguard: Photography between Art and Fashion, is now on view at The Museum of the African Diaspora (MoAD) in San Francisco through March 5. The exhibition is having its West Coast premiere at MoAD and highlights the work of 15 contemporary fashion photographers from London, Lagos, New York, Johannesburg, and more. Each artist’s work showcases a fresh perspective on fashion, beauty, race, gender, and aesthetics. The New Black Vanguard is curated by Antwaun Sargent and organized by Aperture, New York. Visitors will see over 100 select works from international artists and photographers, including Tyler Mitchell, the first Black photographer hired to shoot a cover story for American Vogue. To learn more and to purchase tickets to MoAD, visit https:// www.moadsf.org/exhibitions/thenew-black-vanguard. ®
articles.title: The New Black Vanguard exhibit at MoAD through March

articles.text: Ruth Bancroft Garden in Walnut Creek will host a “Sip and Paint” evening class on Friday, January 27 at 5 p.m. The garden and nursery will be closed for this special event, which is hosted by Super Paint Party, a collective of local artists who will guide guests through an art class geared toward Ruth Bancroft’s famous dry weather foliage. All guests will paint a design on a 16×20″ canvas. Adult beverages will be provided. Artists of all levels are encouraged to join, socialize, and learn more about the gardens through this art collective. Everyone from art beginners to art experts are invited to participate. To learn more and to purchase tickets, visit https://www.ruthbancroftgarden.org/event/sipand-paint/. Artists of all levels are invited to participate in a Sip and Paint event at Bancroft Gardens in Walnut Creek.
articles.title: Bancroft Garden hosts “Sip and Paint” party January 27

articles.text: Earl Lee leads the San Francisco Symphony in a special Lunar New Year performance on Sunday, February 5, at 5 p.m. This performance draws upon Asian traditional music and established composers to celebrate the Year of the Rabbit. articles.text: Local artist and art historian Michael Stehr will offer an illustrated lecture at the Piedmont Center for the Arts on Friday, February 3, titled “A Stroll Through the Musée’ d’Orsay: An Evening with the Impressionists.” Doors open at 6 p.m. and the lecture will begin at 6:30 p.m. The lecture celebrates one of the great museums of the world. Some regard the Impressionist movement that began in Paris in the second half of the 1800’s to be the most important movement in art history since the Renaissance. Indeed, the Impressionists marked the departure from the oppressive constraints of traditional painting while serving as a stepping stone in the evolution towards becoming “modern.” The broken brush strokes and vaporous colors associated with the movement have these pictures being some of the most widely appreciated in Western art. For those cherishing the art of the Impressionists, there is one ultimate destination to enjoy these remarkable paintings: the Musée d’Orsay in Paris. articles.text: Wild Tales is a complete surprise – creative, dark, comedic, over-the-top and a Oscar nominee for Best Foreign Language Film. The film is an anthology of six completely unrelated vignettes, each outrageous, unruly (or not), but all, in some way, touching on the idea that revenge is best served cold, Each episode is stylish, many encapsulating how difficult it can be to live in the 21st century (no matter which city), while delineating what can occur when ordinary people reach their An example: A demolition engineer parks in front of a bakery. He’s picking up a cake for his daughter’s birthday. His wife has called and told him to be home on time. When he comes out of the bakery, he finds his car gone, towed. He didn’t park in a red or yellow zone; nevertheless, a notice is taped to the curb informing him where his car is. He merely has to pay a ransom (also known as a fine) to get it liberated from the city lot, which means standing in line until it’s his turn in front of a window manned by a by a bored individual. He’s now late, has had a long day, and feels violated, his temperature rising. What he does next, well, it’s dramatic. One story focuses on road rage as a not uncommon occurrence as people rush from home to work and back, all a bit harried, many wound just a tad too tight. In this tale, we encounter two men on a remote road, one A scene from the Argentinian film, Wild Tales. driving a trashed pickup, the other in a new Audi. The Audi guy is in a hurry. The pickup guy, not so much. They get into a road duel that takes unintended consequences to a whole new level and definitely does not end well. It is breathtaking how quickly the patina of civility, which we all rely on to get us through the day, can drop away, exposing a side to human nature that is seriously devolved. Each of these carefully crafted vignettes begins in a benign way. But like the handle of a jack-inthe-box being turned, with each slow revolution the awareness builds (you only have to see the first story to know this is not your usual movie) that something is going to pop up and be, in some way, beyond startling. Wild Tales – a perfect title – is from Argentina and the actors are likely unknown to an American audience. Actually, this fact enhances the comedic authenticity of the desperation shown by some of the characters. The final story takes place at a wedding where a happy, joyous occasion drops off a cliff and becomes an event that escalates to a point where you want to watch the last part with one hand covering your eyes… almost. If you love movies and appreciate when a writer-director like Damian Szifron attempts something that is unabashedly creative, riveting and ghoulish while making you smile, sometimes unwillingly, then you will find Wild Tales hits the sweet spot. But be prepared. It does possess a certain twisted, satirical quality. Wild Tales. Directed by Damien David Szifron of Argentina in a co-production of Argentine and Spain. English subtitles. 2 hrs., 2 min. Rated R. Released in 2014. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv.
articles.title: Wild Tales – hold onto your hat

articles.text: Hustlers could easily be called Band of Sisters, for at its center is a group of women who, while pole and lap dancing in a Manhattan strip club called Moves, form a cohort akin to family. The story is based on a piece of 2015 investigative journalism by Jessica Pressler, which appeared in New York Magazine. The narrative focuses, at least initially, on two women, one the veteran Ramona (Jennifer Lopez), and the newbie, Dorothy, aka Destiny (Constance Wu). At first, Ramona agrees to teach Destiny the club workarounds. And in one long scene, she demonstrates the art of delivering a very hot, seductive pole dance that will, she insists, cause the raucous clients to shower the stage with money. It’s actually a moment of stunning athleticism by Lopez that defies her age of 50. After a few weeks working together, and Destiny proving her chops, Ramona suggests that the Wall Street hustlers who show up with pockets of cash, and credit cards to match, can be scammed. The rationale is that they scam their marks all day (this is early 2000s) and now it’s their turn. All they have to do, with the aid of a drug, dropped into the men’s drinks, lift from their pockets their plastic credit cards, max them out, and while they’re sleeping it off, the women cash in. Bottom line is that the lascivious wolves from The Street are themselves run to financial ground. When they later find out they’ve been had, well, they’re afraid to admit they’ve been taken, considering wedding rings and humiliation are in play. The scheme is called “fishing.” And it takes proves hugely successful, so much so that Ramona and Destiny recruit some sisters to assist and that’s when some serious money begins to roll in. Think of it as transactional economics where the mark is played and reeled in. Meanwhile, Ramona and Destiny, who both have children, and the regulars, and Destiny’s grandmother, celebrate as an extended family. When not in the club, or hanging out with each other, they’re shopping, meaning serious shopping with matching Chinchilla coats and over the knee boots. And that’s the hustle. Ridiculously successful – until it isn’t when the stock market crash of 2008-09 causes the wolves of Wall Street to vanish. The sisters, now short on cash, are forced to get regular jobs. And when the cops show up things really got dicey. There was a lot of Oscar buzz around J-Lo’s performance, considered to be her best. And she is good, really good in a role that runs the table: soft, caring, maternal and hard-edged. It’s a multi-dimensional role that stretches her performing ability. Hustlers. Directed by Lorene Scarafina. Starring Jennifer Lopez, Constance Wu and Julia Stiles. 1 hr., 47 min. Rated R. Streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. Two-time GRAMMY award-winner

articles.text: Buck Brannaman in Buck Perhaps part of the appeal of Buck is that from the first frame of this fine documentary we are looking at Buck Brannaman, the quintessential cowboy, an iconic image that has resonated for generations. Buck travels the U.S., conducting horse clinics for owners who have young colts who need breaking in, or horses that are a bit dysfunctional. Buck shares his approach, one that is firm and gentle and always respectful of the horse. He guides, cajoles and reassures, taking a skittish animal and transforming it. Think of his methods as Zen and the art of horse handling. The film also includes Buck’s tragic backstory. As youngsters, he and his brother were taken from state to state as trick ropers. When they weren’t performing at rodeos and fairgrounds, their father physically abused them until they were scarred. Buck is testimony to how one man, with grace and will and discipline, altered every aspect of his life. When young, he was simply looking to find a peaceful place where he didn’t feel threatened. What he found instead was his life’s work. To bear witness, to come, even briefly, to know this man is to understand how elusive it is to do what you love and thereby feel complete. To know that your insights, your knowledge, created out of years of experience, are significant and offer a certain wisdom regarding the human condition. Buck tells people firmly that horses mirror their owners, and how people treat their horses is how they treat others – family, friends and strangers. Buck is a remarkable film. Buck, Directed by Cindy Meehi. Documentary, with Buck Brannaman, Gary Meyers, Bib Frazier. 1 hr., 28 min. Released in 2011. Now streaming on Prime/ Apple tv
articles.title: Buck a remarkable film for young and old

articles.text: First, I should disclose that I have never been a fan of the X-Men franchise, hence have missed all of its incarnations, dating back to 2000 when Logan/ Wolverine was first introduced. But when I saw the trailer for Logan I immediately sensed that this movie would be different. And indeed it is. The year is 2029 and most of the mutants are gone, hence Logan (Hugh Jackman) is essentially alone with the exception of Charles Xavier (Patrick Stewart) and Caliban (Stephen Merchant). They are hiding somewhere on the southern border, living in a converted metal-framed warehouse and converted, fallen water tower. The surrounding land is desert, the tones rust and sepia. Like Logan, Charles and Caliban, all is aged, worse for wear, and hard used. Meanwhile, Logan is lost in his personal rage constantly sipping from a bottle while working as a limo driver. It’s quickly evident that Logan is broken down, and his once superhero powers are slowly diminishing. What is also evident is that director James Mangold has adopted a western trope with Logan as the quintessential antihero. He is cynical, angry, foulmouthed, and insists that he only cares about getting Professor X, whose mind is fast eroding and prone to seizures, away to a boat where they can live out their days on the ocean. However, a young girl, Laura (Dafine Keen), is literally dropped on their doorstep and Logan finds himself, against his will, being her caretaker. She is, like him, a mutant, created in a lab, and as Logan learns, the feds and their Mad Max crew are out to find her and at all cost return her to the scientists. And so Logan morphs into a chase film with, admittedly, a high body count. But it’s not gratuitous. Nicely fitted into one scene, Charles and Laura are watching television and the movie is Shane. Of course, the similarities between Logan and Shane are irrefutable and the ending of Shane telegraphs the final scenes of Logan. This story is essentially a western, which makes it far more interesting than having to suspend one’s disbelief as 14 mutants/ superheroes confront all that CGI can create and then some. You don’t have to be a fan to enjoy or understand Logan. You just have to like movies in all of their forms. Logan. Directed by James Mangold. Starring Hugh Jackman, Patrick Stewart and Dafine Keen. 2 hrs., 15 min. Rated R. Hugh Jackman as Logan (Wolverine)
articles.title: Logan a different kind of Western

articles.text: Piedmont cartoonist Philip Witte, creator of the Flip cartoons that appear weekly in the Piedmont Post, nationally in the New Yorker and Wall Street Journal, and internationally throughout the UK including Galway, Ireland, will have an exhibit of selected works at Piedmont Center for the Arts from Saturday, January 21, through February 5. Gallery hours are 11 a.m. to 2 p.m. on Saturdays and Sundays. An opening reception on Friday night is available by e-mailing philwitte1@gmail.com. A bit of background Since leaving his legal career seven years ago, Piedmonter Phil Witte has sold more than 1,000 cartoons to dozens of publications in the U.S., U.K., and Galway, Ireland. A cartoonist from an early age, once he began his studies at Princeton he abandoned cartooning. Following some time working in Bangkok, he entered law school at the University of Chicago. Although life as a litigation attorney was all-consuming, Phil tried to find time for creative activities. He wrote a few humor pieces, which attracted the attention of a book publisher. That led to a joke book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and a sequel on turning 60. Sales to date are approaching 175,000 copies. “I knew I could write jokes, so I figured if I could combine that with drawing, I could become a cartoonist,” he said. “I was decent in art, but I needed to get a lot better, plus I had to develop a style… I’m still working on that.” He showed his early work to Phil Frank, the late cartoonist at The San Francisco Chronicle, who encouraged him. While work on his art, Witte collaborated as a gag writer for syndicated cartoonists, including Dan Piraro, creator of the the eye of Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. Even most of the “regular” cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time, Phil noted. Witte was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. His cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. He has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. There is even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of his cartoons in their permanent collection. Private collectors, including the documentary filmmaker Ken Burns, have bought Witte’s original artwork. “We actually swapped work,” said Phil, “my cartoon for dozens of his DVDs. He wrote a wonderful thank-you note, and sent me a photo of him posing with the cartoon in his office.” “The cartooning career has gone far better than I even imagined it would,” he noted. “I’m content that I made the right career move.” Photo by Rob Yelland Piedmont cartoonist Phil Witte will have an exhibit of his work at the Piedmont Center for the Arts from January 21 to February 5. cartoon feature “Bizarro.” Phil has 25 original ink drawings by Piraro that resulted from their collaboration. It was the best day in my former career.” He has licensed his cartoons to greeting card companies with great success. Textbooks and professional groups started leasing his cartoons as well. He has also written a few dozen humor pieces for magazines and online sites. Truth be told, many orchestra conductors don’t even know how to hold a baton. Sometimes the critic needs to be honest and admit culpability. Many years ago, I went to hear a famous cellist. Hearing him was a revelation. His command of the instrument was overwhelming, as was his emotional impact. articles.text: park, Blair Park now sold refreshments and boasted a restaurant. Venetian Canal The Venetian Canal was popular for old and young visitors alike. Opening in March of 1891, flat-bottomed boats floated in a meandering circular water flume, propelled by a large water wheel driven by an engine. The flume was 1000’ long, elevated to a “considerable height,” and ran over babbling brooks and across small ravines before returning to its start. Riders were given a small pole to ease the boats along when they became stuck. Dancing Pavilion Open on all sides with just a roof above, the Dancing Pavilion was designed as a cooler, more pleasant alternative to the stuffy indoor dancing clubs in downtown Oakland. It was open to the public during the day and could be leased for private parties in the evening. On those occasions the refreshment stand remained open. The 1891 Tribune claimed “…a large electric light in the center of the pavilion abundantly illuminates the structure.” The pavilion was close to the bandstand so visitors could dance to the bandstand music. The French Maze Sometimes called the French Puzzle or the Mystic Maze, the French Maze challenged visitors in Blair Park. Designed after a maze in Paris, it was built with 6-foot tall lattice panels planted with Chinese honeysuckle vines. These panels formed 64 intersecting paths creating a bewildering journey to the center (and back). This maze was only 1600 feet long, but it could be as long as 7000 feet given the wrong turns that one could take. As late as 1954, there was a miniature Japanese pagoda in one of the backyards on Moraga Avenue that reportedly had been in the middle of the French Maze in Blair Park. The Photo Gallery No amusement park would be complete without a photo gallery. The gallery in Blair Park offered mementos by sketch artists in just 10 minutes of one’s visit to the park. Visitors could also buy photographic souvenirs of Blair Park, such as this photo showing the lake in the park and the cemetery monuments beyond. Japanese Tea House Blair Park also had its own Japanese Tea House, an exact replica of an ancient tea house in Japan. It was constructed in Yokohama, then shipped in sections to Piedmont. Rebuilt on the site in the Japanese style, its fitted joints were tightly secured with ropes. Nails were used only to hold the roof tiles. It was This souvenir photo from Blair Park shows Blair’s lake and the cemetery beyond. Japanese Tea House open on three sides with a circular Japanese window. Although the sketch shows ladies seated on chairs, operators originally planned to serve tea in the traditional Japanese manner – to guests sitting on straw mats or standing. There were also plans to bring in two Japanese maidens and their chaperone to serve tea in Oriental gowns. An adjacent Japanese garden was planted with 1000 Japanese lily bulbs. A Family Park Blair Park was planned as a family park. Park operators widely advertised that they maintained a comfortable park where ladies and children could attend without fear of encountering any “objectionable persons.” No wine or liquor was sold in the park, and a deputy constable was present to keep any “toughs” out of the park. In addition to the Venetian Canal for children, there were swings and see-saws scattered throughout the park and a horse-driven merry-goround. articles.text: The bandstand and fountain at the Blair Park entrance. In a previous column, we described the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company, its cable cars and famous gravity loop in Piedmont. The cable car line was expensive to build and expensive to maintain. To encourage more riders on the cable cars, the company leased the Blair Park land and built several popular amusements to draw more riders on their cable cars. The Oakland Daily Evening Tribune described the new “Attractions of Blair Park” on June 20, 1891. (Most of the illustrations here are from that article.) Today it’s difficult to image that so many exciting attractions were squeezed into that narrow strip of land on Moraga Avenue. The cable company thinned more trees and shrubs in the 75-acre park, paved the paths throughout the park and planted purple and white wisteria to grow The Venetian Canal Beautiful Bronze Fountain A large 28-foot bronze fountain stood adjacent to the bandstand. The fountain represented the ascending orders of the animal kingdom. Water lilies filled the basin of the fountain. Four dolphins formed the fountain base, each spouting a stream of water into the basin below. Four swans formed the middle tier, Dancing Pavilion. over the large arched entrance. More purple and white wisteria grew near the bandstand. (Could this be the beginning of Piedmont’s purple and white tradition?) As visitors entered the park under this arch, they passed through lawns with benches in a semi-circle and came to a large bandstand, the first attraction the cable company built. Blair Park now offered free concerts each Saturday and Sunday afternoon performed by the 21-piece 5th Infantry Regiment Band and Ritzau’s “Orchestra of Soloists.” The concerts were free, but the cable company now charged an admission to the park. Small boys often tried to save the 10-cent admission charge by climbing over the cemetery fence. with each swan spraying water from its beak. At the top of the fountain a small child held a fish, which also spouted a stream of water 60 feet into the air. Benches were scattered around Blair’s small lake for rest and reflection. Following the path easterly from Blair’s lake, visitors could climb to Inspiration Point. More benches were added for the weary, and the cool mountain spring continued to provide refreshment for these adventurers. The spectacular view of the Golden Gate always rewarded these hardy hikers. The Oakland Tribune reported that the cable company cleaned out the spring, increasing its flow to 80,000 gallons per day. This greater water supply kept the park green and ran its waterworks. Our friend the internet gives us confusing statistics, but it seems that about half of dog owners walk their best friends on a regular basis. From what I observe, it is easy to believe that the number of dog owners in Piedmont raises the average. This is good news for both species, human and canine, for a number of reasons. The vast majority of American humans, and about half of American canines are overweight or obese. This of course leads to heart problems, joint limitations, and digestive issues. Studies have shown that adults who regularly walk their dogs and benefit from the associated exercise are less likely than non-dog owners to Unclear On the Concept (actually witnessed outside Dracena Park) be afflicted with many physical problems from diabetes to cancer. Just like humans, obese dogs do not live as long as lean dogs. Plus, they suffer more heart problems and joint ailments that affect their quality of life. Dog walking has a positive impact on both canine and human mental and emotional health as well, as walking exercises the mind as well as the body. Neither dogs nor people like to be bored. Given something non-electronic and constructive to do like watching wildlife, exploring new paths, seeing other people with their pets provide great mental stimulation. Walking also releases excess energy and helps you sleep better at night. But what I find especially valuable is the enhanced sense of community fostered by this popular activity. People I have seen who respect and love another species, like most dog walkers, go out of their way to say hello and interact with other walkers on the streets, getting to know neighbors and strengthening the community we live in. Will Adams is a Planner, Urban Designer and Architect, who has lived in Piedmont for 30 years. He can be reached through Will@MakingDesignSense.com. articles.text: I was impressed with their great value. The Bousquet family hail from the city of Carcassonne in the South of France and have 4 generations of history in the winemaking tradition. Their goal is to produce wines of superior quality, leading them to Argentina to begin a new chapter. A 1990 vacation in Argentina was all it took. For third-generation winemaker Jean Bousquet, it was love at first sight. The object of the Frenchman’s desire: the Gualtallary Valley, a scenic, remote, arid terrain high in the Tupungato district of the Uco Valley in Argentina’s Mendoza region, close to the border with Chile. Here, with condors flying overhead and not a vine in sight, Bousquet discovered his dream terroir – an ideal location in which to nurture organically-grown wines. With altitudes ranging up to 5,249 feet, Gualtallary occupies the highest extremes of Mendoza’s viticultural limits. Fast-forward to the present: wine cognoscenti recognize it now as the source of some of Mendoza’s finest wines. Back then, it was virgin territory: tracts of semi-desert, nothing planted, no water above ground, no electricity and a single dirt track by way of access. Locals dismissed the area as too cold for growing grapes. Bousquet, on the other hand, reckoned he’d found the perfect blend between his French homeland and the New World (sunny, with high natural acidity and a potential for relatively fruit-forward wines). Nowadays, Domaine Bousquet produces 4 million liters a year and export 95% of its volume to more than 50 countries. Domaine Bousquet currently ranks in the top 20 Argentine wineries in terms of exports and is the leader in organic wine. I recently had the opportunity to taste three of the Domaine Bousquet wines. In addition to their high quality, • 2021 Domaine Bousquet Chardonnay, $18 Golden in color, the Bousquet Chardonnay has a nose that is robust with aromas of apple pears and oak as well as essence of citrus blossom and spices. Medium to full-bodied, the wine has a thoughtful complexity ending with lingering flavors of oak and a mineral flush. • 2021 Domaine Bousquet Cabernet Sauvignon, $18 Deep garnet-purple in color, the 2021 Caberrnet Sauvignon gives up notes of blackberries, cassis and chocolate with a waft of tobacco. Medium to full-bodied the palate is full of bright black fruit flavors with a solid foundation of fine-grained tannins, finishing long and juicy. • 2021 Domaine Bousquet Malbec, $18 The purple-colored 2021 Malbec is sensational for an entry level wine. It gives up an alluring nose of weed smoke, Asian spices, floral notes and raspberry. Layered smooth-textured, and plush, this is a mouth-coating effort that is ready to drink but that will continue to deliver satisfaction for another 5 or 6 years.
articles.title: Domaine Bousquet – where France meets Argentina

articles.text: Oakland Zoo took guardianship over two more rescued mountain lion cubs recently. Hazel, a 4-5 month old cub, emaciated and abandoned in Soquel near Santa Cruz, was rescued on Sunday, January 8. A resident reported seeing the cat, but the California Department of Fish and Wildlife was unable to locate the mother. Fish and Wildlife official transferred the cat, suffering from anemia and hypoglycemia, to the vet staff at the Oakland Zoo. “Three days after being rescued [the] orphaned mountain lion [was] learning to eat on her own,” stated the Zoo. Hazel initially received an IV and since has progressed in vigor to be hand fed solid food from zookeepers. In December, the zoo received another kitten puma of similar age from the same region and gave her a new home for rehabilitation and treatment. That cub, Holly, named for the winter season, was found under an abandoned house, underweight and in need of care. Both cubs have been putting on weight and recovering since treatment at the Oakland Zoo’s Veterinary Hospital. Both are still kittens, the official designation of mountain lions until they are 8-10 months old and weigh about 60 pounds. Hazel, a 4-5 month old mountain lion cub, is the most recently adopted animal by the Oakland Zoo after being rescued from Soquel near Santa Cruz. Captain Cal, the media-star mountain lion, captivated the hearts of Bay Area residents when he was found burned from a wildfire in Redding during the Zogg Fire in September 2020. Captain Cal was the 12th mountain lion the Oakland Zoo’s Vet Hospital had rehabilitated. He now resides as a healthy and fully grown mountain lion at the Columbus Zoo in Ohio. Zoo Weather Report The Oakland Zoo remains closed to guests due to an enormous sinkhole at the entrance to the park. Reopening is not expected until the beginning of February. Holly, a mountain lion cub seen at 3-4 months, was rescued in December.
articles.title: Rescued mountain lion kittens receiving TLC at Oakland Zoo

articles.text: Rain proved to be little deterrent to the Walking on Wednesdays group last week, January 11. On hand at the Exedra with umbrellas in hand, were Glen Tripp, Jim Kuo, Lois Price, Pat Keller, Tom Reese, Garrett Clifford, Meghan Bennett, Mark Davis, Sherry Jacobs, Claudia Lopez, Alicia Rivera, Priscilla Wanerus, and Dick Carter. Piedmont Post columnist Will Adams was also there to talk with the group about the architecture of Piedmont houses. A little atmospheric river last Wednesday morning didn’t deter an intrepid band of 14 members of the Walking on Wednesdays group from enjoying their weekly walk. The group has a mantra of “we walk rain or shine,” but not in thunder and lightning. Readers of the Piedmont Post saw photos the recent storms have caused around the city. They learned that the prior lightning had blown off the top half of a sequoia tree in the backyard of a home that borders Crocker Park. The Post article also told of flooding that had turned Witter Field into Witter Lake and other water damage around the city. Off they went, first to see the strong water flow in Bushy Dell Creek at the top of the Piedmont Park, then off to Crocker Park. The top half of the tree was gone, and its trunk had been torn open, exposing about 10 feet of the tree’s core. The remaining branches looked like they were part of a very large Charlie Brown Christmas tree. On the ground were tree chunks of splintered wood that could have filled a large fireplace. A light rain was falling, but the group was not ready to call it quits for the morning. They continued to King Avenue, where they noted a home that had been remodeled in a contemporary design. Will Adams offered some design comments and appreciated the use of wood and different levels of depth in the home’s exterior that provides visual interest. The group crossed Hampton and went to Farragut Avenue, admiring more beautiful homes along the way. At Crocker, the walkers stopped to talk about a Julia Morgan designed home on the corner and noted the owner has built a new home next door in a similar design that matches Morgan’s concept. They retraced their steps back to town center and the Community Hall parking lot. It had been about an hour, and almost two miles. The walkers saw some effects of the strong, recent rains and had a renewed respect for Mother Nature’s power. The group will continue to walk, rain or shine, but for sure not in lightning storms. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Bushy Dell Creek was flowing at capacity through Piedmont Park during the rain on Wednesday.
articles.title: What’s a little rain among friends?

articles.text: The newly launched movie group, Second Friday Flix, opened with a screening on January 13 of Wait Until Dark, a thriller with Audrey Hepburn and Alan Arkin. More than 30 eager Piedmonters braved a driving rain last Friday to crowd into the Piedmont Recreation Department’s big front room to watch Audrey Hepburn face off against a trio of baddies. The occasion was the kickoff of the town’s newest attraction, Second Friday Flix, a movie-and-discussion event sponsored by the Recreation Department, where local film fans are invited to watch a movie together and chat about it afterward. Second Friday Flix is a monthly affair on the second Friday of the month from 12:30 to 3:30 p.m. at the Recreation Department, 358 Hillside Avenue. The group is open to anyone over age 18. There are no fees, and participants may attend on a drop-in basis by registering at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP, or by contacting the Recreation Department at (510) 420-3070. Snacks and bag lunches are welcome. Attendees on opening day were treated to chewy squares of fudge, provided by movie-goer Pat Keller. The first showing was the 1967 suspense/thriller Wait Until Dark, starring Audrey Hepburn as recently blinded Susy Hendrix, whose husband, Sam (Efrem Zimbalist Jr.) has come into possession of a doll with packets of drugs sewn inside. The stash is a means to smuggle drugs into the United States. Neither Susy nor Sam know the truth about the doll, but three desperate criminals (Alan Arkin, Richard Crenna and Jack Weston) know all about the cache. They know who has it, too, and when Sam is away, they set their sights on innocent but resourceful Susy in her basement apartment. In order to discover the whereabouts of the doll, they try trickery, but when trickery fails, terror takes over, though Susy proves that a lone blind woman can be more than a match for a trio of toughs. Movie group member Darby Gragg capably introduced the film and led the discussion afterward. The audience largely approved, giving the movie many thumbs ups, especially for its performances, though there were some dissenters who pointed out plot weaknesses. The most notable objection was to Sam’s behavior at the climax, which some called “reprehensible” and “laughable” – it elicited groans. Nonetheless almost everyone thought Wait Until Dark provided an auspicious new offering. Second Friday Flix was organized and assembled by Dick Carter and volunteers Darby Gragg, Mike Gallant, Jasmine Cai, Gerry Gragg, and Bob Hall, with the assistance of Eva Phalen. Future screenings will be oriented to a different genre each month, such as comedy, romance, western, musical, drama. The next film, in the romance category, is 1971’s offbeat Harold and Maude, which will be screened on February 10 and presented by Mike Gallant. Attendees at Second Friday Flix’s premiere included: Alicia Bacon, Dick Carter, Helene Farber, Brenda Ferrero, Karin Fetherston, Darby and Gerry Gragg, Mike Gallant, Greg and Pat Keller, Bob and Madeline Hall, Jim and Kim Kellogg, Edith Lee, Claudia Lopez, Elene Manolis, Karen Murphy, Sarah Pearson, Karin Rawlins, Barbara Reding, Lisa Reynolds, Harriette Louie, Dorothy Shipp, Margaret Phillips, Noemi Alvarado and Mark Davis, Anne Alper, Swee Ling Chen, Albert Chen, Mike Henn, Alicia Rivera, and Melba Yee. articles.text: One of the best things about Piedmont is having interesting neighbors. In the Palm Drive enclave alone, to which my family had moved some 16 years ago, I have met CEOs whose companies disrupted their industries, academics from top universities, civil activists, musicians, and architects of renown. Still, I couldn’t help being surprised when I learned that a diminutive woman with bright blue eyes and a down-to-earth manner, with whom I occasionally discussed politics, held one of the toughest jobs in town. Meet Kim Hunter, Senior Deputy District Attorney for Alameda County. A native of Carmel, Kim attended Hastings College of the Law and served as an Alameda country DA for 37 years. In addition to working at the Family Justice Center, a collection of agencies and programs that provide services and support to victims of domestic violence, sexual exploitation, child abuse, and stalking, Kim also serves on the Bay Area Judicial Selection Advisory Committee and is a member of the Earl Warren American Inn of Courts. An avid reader of the Piedmont Post, Kim agreed to sit down with me over Christmas break and talk about her work, her community involvement, and her experience of living in Piedmont. A district attorney’s office is a tough place. You get to see the ugly side of life concealed from most people. How does one end up in the DA’s office? I was always interested in politics. When I started to analyze how people who ran for public office got there, I learned that most of them were lawyers. I went to law school, and though I spent the summer between my Kim Hunter with younger son Holden in front of the US Supreme Court building while attending American Inns of Court Celebration of Excellence in 2022. – Kim Hunter Alameda County Senior Deputy District Attorney first and second year at a boutique law firm, I saw myself more as a public defender. I wanted to defend people who were wrongfully accused. When I got an offer to join the Alameda County District Attorney office, I wasn’t sure: my leanings were against putting people in jail for no reason. During my first day in court, when I saw that 90 percent of defendants were black, I left the room and called my [African American] father. He told me, “Go back in there and make sure that the system is just and fair.” That’s what I’ve doing. Are there any specific qualities one must have to pursue a district attorney career? What’s the hardest part of your job? Kim Hunter with a photograph of her father, Robert Hunter, who taught PE for 39 years at Joaquin Miller Junior High School after retiring from the Army. You must be competitive to do this job. The mental game, the combination of tactical and strategic is what attracts me most. I’ve always played sports. At Cal I played field hockey–and though I was neither the tallest nor fastest, I was the most determined. So, of course I loved going to trial, loved the court room, loved public speaking. Being a DA really suited who I was. As for the toughest part. As a DA you have so much power, you must wield it very carefully, with great integrity and fairness. It’s a humbling task. If you’re going to charge someone over a serious crime, you don’t take that lightly. On the other hand, there are lots of people who lie, on both sides. Our job is to make sure that it’s not our side. To get to that point, you must do a lot of work with victims and the witnesses, and lots of follow-up. You also have to be able to present the case from the perspective of the victim. What is the best way for a child to explain what happened to them? How to you get them to trust you? How do you create a safe space for them, empower them? What is your career highlight? It’s not the cases that I won, it’s the relationships I developed with the victims. Working at the Family Justice and seeing that the victims get the help they need has been truly rewarding. We’re trying to match our victim’s courage of speaking out and to assist them in doing whatever they need while remaining safe. Being a mentor is also very important to me. I love watching people grow, love seeing them navigate themselves through the office or doing the cases they’re most passionate about. articles.text: Larry Hu (left), Tanya Hu, Sandra Curach, Mona Jamieson, Elizabeth Wierzbianska, Gregory Jurin, Larry Singer, Janet Epstein; Martin Rossom in the space capsule at Chabot Space & Science Center. Not pictured: Patti Singer, Fred Pemberton, Jim Ayotte, and Irene Westler. The Piedmont Seniors plowed through rough weather conditions on their recent visit to the Chabot Space & Science Center located in the Oakland hills. The Center allows visitors to step into the role of a NASA scientist by getting a close-up look at cutting–edge technology of historic and future NASA missions. The NASA experience features some of the most fascinating items in space research and exploration, including space suits from the Mercury and Gemini missions, experimental heat shield technology, and even a fan blade from the world’s largest wind tunnel. Many of these items have never been on display to the public. On their visit the Seniors were able to explore pieces of NASA’s groundbreaking technology that make discovery possible, as well as embarking on hands-on challenges. At the NASA Ames Visitor Center the Seniors experienced an exhibition that brings to life the thrilling, challenging and inspiring process of scientific discovery by showcasing the real stories and people at NASA’s Ames Research Center. Visitors step into the role of a NASA scientist through an exhibit with more than 30 objects that show Ames’ past and future. One of the highlights of the trip was a visit to Chabot’s 70-foot dome-shaped Planetarium, where the show, “Lunaverse,” allowed thems to explore the nature of Earth’s Moon: its motion and phases, lunar and solar eclipses, tides, and the Moon’s origin. The story unfolds Piedmont Seniors enjoy lunch at the Paradiso restaurant after their visit to the Chabot Space & Science Center. as a conversation between a curious young child and the Moon — Luna — over the course of a night, from moonrise to moonset, all from the comfort of relaxing seats and a climate- controlled theater. Every Friday and Saturday night, weather permitting, the Chabot Observatory Deck is open to the public for free telescope viewing from 7:30 p.m. to 10:30 p.m. This is an opportunity to explore stars, planets, and various heavenly bodies through Chabot’s historic three large telescopes. During their excursion, the Piedmont Seniors were able to get close to spacecraft and explore how humans are expanding our boundaries by moving farther into the universe than ever before. With inspiration and content provided by NASA’s Ames Research Center, Cal Tech’s Jet Propulsion Laboratory, Planet, and SpaceX, the exhibit traces a journey through the cosmos ad what lies ahead. The seniors were also able to see out-of-this world objects, from the space program workhorse, an authentic 7K-OK Russian Soyuz Descent Module, to a Dove Cube Satellite Model, an example of the next generation of Nano satellites used to gather Earth imagery from space. After exploring the Center, the Seniors headed to Paradiso, a wonderful Italian restaurant located nearby in San Leandro. The camaraderie and delicious food more than made up for having endured the inclement weather. To learn more about the Piedmont Seniors, including future excursions, contact Janet Epstein, Seniors Coordinator, at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. Meetings are held on the fourth Wednesday of each month at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. The Seniors go on monthly excursions throughout the greater Bay Area.

articles.text: It’s your superpower. You’ve used it your entire life as a parent: Trouble shoot, problem solve, come up with the answers. As a grandparent, these skills may be more acutely honed than ever before. But now, with adult children who’ve become parents themselves, you need to develop a brand-new talent: become a listener. Remember when your name was called a million times a day? You were asked to find lost items, explain complex information, recommend how to do a new task, remember other family members’ birthdays, and in general explain to your children the way the world works. More often than not, these requests persisted until they were no longer little kids, but young adults. Now your child is a parent. You probably remember that you managed with Dr. Spock’s book, your mom (maybe), your pediatrician, and a couple of friends who had babies, too. Today, caring for a newborn or young child hasn’t really become more complex, but the input is much greater. It can feel like everyone is watching. You may hear your child struggling with all kinds of dilemmas during those first few years. Perhaps breast-feeding is a huge challenge as she returns to work and needs to pump regularly. Maybe the exhausted parents are torn between recommendations for sleep-training and attachment parenting. They may wonder if they should be promoting their child’s independence or making them feel super secure. And figuring out how to manage working from home when your child is sick can be a lot harder than it sounds. Other questions many new parents ask themselves are: • How do I know if I have picked a good daycare? • Is my baby sick or is it allergies? • Did I introduce peanuts early enough? • Should I read one book per night or three? • Did my baby have the right amount of tummy time? • When is it normal for toddlers to get out of diapers? • Does my child have to eat vegetables? • How can I help my child make friends? Every stage of parenthood has unique challenges and some may be tougher than others. When you see your child grappling with an issue, even when expressing true distress, it still may be the best choice to simply be a listener. Psychologists call this bearing witness, and it has been identified as being a tremendously healing action for those who are under stress or who have undergone a serious trauma. Is new parenthood traumatic? For some people the answer is yes. The drive to be successful at the raising of another human, the fear of making errors that may have lifelong consequences, and the terror of feeling judged to be inadequate in the role are enough to cause trauma in some cases. The next time your adult child shares with you how upset they are about something, listen and try to identify the message underlying the distress. Most likely it will be I’m scared, I’m tired, I’m confused. Sit quietly with them to bear witness to their experience without trying to solve the problem. What can you say instead? That sounds exhausting. I bet that was hard for you. You’re on the right track. I like the way you’re thinking about this. When you bear witness, you may find that your child comes to you more often with their life experiences (both positive and negative). People grow in strength and competence when they are provided with an empathetic listener instead of a problem solver, and we all want that for our children. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. Cynthia can be reached at cynthia@itstheirturn.com

Other questions many new parents ask themselves are: • How do I know if I have picked a good daycare? • Is my baby sick or is it allergies? • Did I introduce peanuts early enough? • Should I read one book per night or three? • Did my baby have the right amount of tummy time? • When is it normal for toddlers to get out of diapers? • Does my child have to eat vegetables? • How can I help my child make friends? Every stage of parenthood has unique challenges and some may be tougher than others. When you see your child grappling with an issue, even when expressing true distress, it still may be the best choice to simply be a listener. Psychologists call this bearing witness, and it has been identified as being a tremendously healing action for those who are under stress or who have undergone a serious trauma. Is new parenthood traumatic? For some people the answer is yes. The drive to be successful at the raising of another human, the fear of making errors that may have lifelong consequences, and the terror of feeling judged to be inadequate in the role are enough to cause trauma in some cases. The next time your adult child shares with you how upset they are about something, listen and try to identify the message underlying the distress. Most likely it will be I’m scared, I’m tired, I’m confused. Sit quietly with them to bear witness to their experience without trying to solve the problem. What can you say instead? That sounds exhausting. I bet that was hard for you. You’re on the right track. I like the way you’re thinking about this. When you bear witness, you may find that your child comes to you more often with their life experiences (both positive and negative). People grow in strength and competence when they are provided with an empathetic listener instead of a problem solver, and we all want that for our children. Cynthia Kane is a board-certified, licensed genetic counselor with 25 years of clinical experience. A grandmother, Cynthia has a certificate in Grandfamily Leadership and is the founder of It’s Their Turn, which provides counseling, support, and education for grandparents. Online Grandparent Groups are forming now. Her website, https://itstheirturn.com/, provides a wealth of information and resources for grandparents. pages.text: Wednesday, January 18, 2023 29 By Cookie Segelsein Computer tips and helpful suggestions, especially for people who are not entirely comfortable using their computers. Dear MacMama: I just brought home a new MacBook Air, and the salesperson at the Apple store told me I can use iCloud to sync my items from my older computer to my new one. How does that work exactly? I don’t actually understand how iCloud works. – Oliver D., Piedmont Dear Oliver: Simply said, Apple’s iCloud is a storage service that can both store your files and sync them across all your devices. But there is much more to iCloud. We use it to sync contacts, reminders, calendars, and photos. We use it to store documents, folders, and passwords. If your computer has OS Catalina or later, when you turn on location services, you can use it to find misplaced iPhones, air pods, and Apple watches. If we use Air Tags, we can keep track of almost any item like wallets, keys, and anything to which we can attach an Air Tag. If your older Mac had OSX Yosemite or later, you can turn on iCloud Drive, enable “Desktop and Documents” and then all items on your desktop and in your “documents” folder will be stored in iCloud. They will still exist on your computer, and any other device in which you were signed in with the same Apple ID and have enabled iCloud Drive. This is great for people who have more than one device and need to keep their files in sync. So, for example, since I have iCloud enabled, if I work on a file in one computer, as soon as my other computer connects to the Internet, that file will be updated. And all my files are on both machines. If the operating system on your old computer is current enough and iCloud is enabled, you can set up the new computer, sign into iCloud, and these files will be downloaded onto your new computer. The same goes for photos, contacts and calendars. But this is not a complete solution for moving all your data over. For examMackie McDonald Continued from page 14 up 40-15 thanks to a ball out by Nadal, two winners, and a ball into the net by Nadal to close it, 7-5 for McDonald. ple, if you purchased Microsoft applications, Adobe applications, any non-Apple applications that don’t come on your machine from the factory, these will not transfer over with iCloud. And if you organize your mail into local folders, meaning the folders that exist in Apple Mail under the heading “On My Mac”, these will also not transfer over. So, in some cases, using Time Machine (assuming you have been backing up your old machine with Time Machine to an external drive) is a better way to transfer your data from an old machine to a new one. There are so many features in iCloud that it would take much more than this column to explain them all. Even if you use Time Machine on an external drive from your previous computer, in many cases, it is still prudent to enable iCloud to store and sync your desktop and documents. This acts as a cloud back up and makes these files accessible on your iPhone and iPad on the “Files” app, assuming the operating system on your device is current enough. There have been so many times that I have been without my computer, and somebody needs a file very quickly, and I have been able to email it by accessing my computer files right from my iPhone. Of course, keeping all personal data as well as sensitive data in a cloud storage system has its risks. Although Apple takes privacy seriously and protects your information by encrypting it when it’s in transit, and storing it in an encrypted format, there are always security risks. It’s really important to use a secure password for your Apple/iCloud ID. It’s not just Apple that has security risks. Dropbox, Google Drive, any cloud storage is vulnerable to security breaches. But used wisely, with a good secure password, iCloud can be a real timesaver. articles.text: On January 11, the city published a survey asking for Piedmonters’ input on electrification and energy policies for new and existing multifamily buildings. The survey will remain open through March 1, and the results will inform the development of Piedmont’s new reach codes. The survey is available at bit. ly/3wbaWAk. It concerns: • the impacts of climate change as it relates to public health, safety, and multifamily buildings • measures to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in multifamily buildings • electrification and energy efficiency measures for multifamily buildings, including both market rate and affordable housing • electric vehicle charging infrastructure. Those who complete the survey and provide an email will be eligible to win a free home energy savings toolkit and PG&E bill credit. A reach code is a local government ordinance that requires something in addition to the requirements of the state’s building code, and which can address all types of buildings: new buildings, existing buildings, single family buildings, multifamily dwellings, commercial buildings, and industrial buildings. Reach codes are used to achieve policy aims like greenhouse gas emission reduction and other climate-efficiency goals, saving energy and money, increasing the resilience of existing buildings. On October 17, 2022, Piedmont City Council adopted a new Reach Code Ordinance for single-family buildings, to be effective with the new California Building Code on January 1, 2023 and through December 31, 2025. The Reach Codes are specifically regulated under Title 24, Part 6 of the California Building Code, which is known as the “Energy Code.” The previous Piedmont Reach Codes, in effect from June 2021 to December 2022, regarded both single-family and multifamily buildings under the requirements of the state’s 2019 Energy Code, which expired on December 31, 2022. However, the new Energy Code requires that separate Reach Codes be developed for these buildings. To learn more about the single-family and multifamily Reach Code adoption process in Piedmont, visit bit.ly/3Xz1tyw. articles.text: In a special meeting tomorrow, January 12, the Piedmont Planning Commission will consider a recommendation to City Council to adopt the 2023-2031 6th Cycle Housing Element, and to adopt the Initial Study-Negative Declaration (IS-ND) for the Element which the City released on December 9, 2022. This is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. Part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require these homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support this growth. City Council will hold a special meeting on January 30 to consider adopting the Housing Element. The State deadline for cities to adopt a Housing Element or face penalties is January 31. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s 26th annual Martin Luther King, Jr. Day celebration will take place on Monday, January 16. Martin Luther King, Jr. Day – a national holiday. The event, sponsored by the Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee, will be held for the first time in the Alan Harvey Theater on the high school campus, 800 Magnolia Avenue, from 11 a.m. to 12:30 p.m. The event is free and open to the public. Speakers will include Congresswoman Barbara Lee; Corrina Gould of the Sogorea Te’ Land Trust; Dr. Clayborne Carson, founding director of the MLK Research and Education Institute; radical history author Kate Schatz; and Piedmont mayor Jen Cavenaugh. The event will also include performances by Oaktown Jazz Workshops and New Style Motherlode Entertainment. To register for the event and learn more, visit padc.info/mlkday.

articles.text: The “Lights Down” event at Piedmont Community Hall will be delayed until Thursday, January 12, due to weather. The public is invited to come at 9 a.m. on Thursday and help take down the lights on all the trees by the Community Hall, by the Exedra and in Piedmont Park. For more information, contact Barbara Love at blovegustke@ gmail.com. articles.text: In late November 2022 New York Times columnist Michelle Goldberg wrote, For most of my adult life, antisemites – with exceptions like Pat Buchanan and Mel Gibson – have lacked status in America. The most virulent antisemites tended to hate Jews from below, blaming them for their own failures and disappointments. Now, however, anti-Jewish bigotry, or at least tacit approval of anti-Jewish bigotry, is coming from people with serious power: the leader of a major political party, a famous pop star, and the world’s richest man. Goldberg is not wrong and is not alone in sounding this alarm. Antisemitism is on the rise. Locally, nationally, and globally it threatens the lives of many, and threatens the very well-being of our society. This reality must call the church to action. It is important to recognize that antisemitism is antithetical to both the central message of Christianity and to the meaning of the church’s celebration of the Day of Epiphany on January 6. The central message of Christianity is that God, in Christ, is always and forever demonstrating a boundaryless love for the entire cosmos. Antisemitism collides with this truth. Epiphany celebrates the journey, recorded by the writer of the Gospel of Matthew, of the magi, the astrologers from the east, who, bearing gifts of gold, frankincense and myrrh, followed the star to worship the newborn king. The message of Epiphany is that the good news of God’s love is for gentile star-gazers as well as for Jewish families living in an often hostile empire. The message of Epiphany is one of inclusion. The message of the Apostle Paul is essentially an Epiphany message. While he does not reference the journey of the magi, Paul, in many of his writings, emphasizes his belief that there is a place for Jew and Gentile alike in the expansive love of God. He makes it clear that in the eternal love of the Christ, Jew and Gentile are on level ground. This message that God is helping Jew and Gentile to find common ground receives very clear expression in Paul’s letter

articles.text: A fire department truck (left) is stuck in a sinkhole caused by rainstorms at the entrance to Oakland Zoo on December 31. Since January 1, Oakland Zoo has been closed due to a large sinkhole at the entrance to the zoo. Zoo officials estimate they may not be able to complete repairs until January 17. A culvert by the vehicle entrance to the Zoo at Golf Links Road collapsed due to heavy rain and rushing water. The culvert, overburdened by the historic amount of rainfall throughout the region over the new year, serves as a connect for Arroyo Viejo Creek and runs beneath the entry road to the Zoo. The sinkhole is approximately A sinkhole caused by excessive rain and flooding at the entrance to Oakland Zoo. 10 feet wide and approximately 10 feet deep and is impassable to vehicles, prohibiting guests from entering the Zoo. “As a 100-year-old organization, we are reminded that basic infrastructure must continue to be upgraded at the Zoo while disaster preparedness is vital for everyone across the State,” said Oakland Zoo CEO Nik Dehejia. “Unfortunately, the Zoo is now losing nearly $500,000 per week in revenue while needing to keep up our expenses to ensure animals and staff are cared for.” Zoo officials are working with a local engineering company to repair the damage. They have been advised that it may take until the third week of the year or longer for materials to arrive and the work to be completed. In other areas of the Zoo on December 31 the volume and velocity of the water flowing across the Zoo grounds caused extensive soil erosion, with eucalyptus trees falling and flooding in some buildings. All animals and staff are fine and have remained safe during the extreme weather. While closed, Zoo staff will continue to be onsite to take care of the animals, provide maintenance needs, and conduct clean-ups from damage caused by the rain. Guests with reservations to visit the Zoo or attend Glowfari will receive an email about a refund or rescheduling their visit. Once reopened, the Zoo may extend the popular Glowfari event into February. Piedmont, by Piedmont, for Piedmont. Subscribe to the Post and we’ll deliver You may now subscribe online at:

articles.text: Many people are becoming more aware that their daily choices impact the environment and marketers have taken notice. In a survey of people from over 60 countries, Nielsen’s Global Corporate Sustainability Report found that 66% of consumers would spend more on a product if it is marketed as sustainable. As a result, companies have a financial incentive to market their products as environmentally friendly – regardless of whether they are taking steps to be more sustainable. What is greenwashing? Greenwashing is a marketing tactic that involves using unsubstantiated claims to present a product as eco-friendly. Greenwashing undermines companies that are engaged in sustainable business practices and, by extension, the consumer’s ability to vote with their dollar. Look further into a company’s claims If you see a claim that you’re dubious about, go to the company’s website to investigate further. If you can’t find any record of it or if the information is vague, it’s likely an example of greenwashing. Watch out for terms with no clear meaning These include terms such as “eco-friendly,” “green,” “all-natural,” “earth-friendly,” “nontoxic,” “plant-based,” “plant-derived,” “pure,” “raw,” “healthy,” “biodegradable,” and “organic” (without certification). These words don’t have any legal or technical definition, and therefore don’t say anything concrete about whether a product is truly environmentally friendly. Look for well-known certifications Certifications such as “Fair Trade Cer tif ied,” “USDA Organic,” “Non-GMO Project Verified,” “Rainforest Alliance Certified,” and “Certified B Corporation” are all trustworthy labels. Don’t fall for the “lesser of two evils” concept For example, a fashion label creating a sustainable collection is better than the brand ignoring the subject of sustainability entirely, but it doesn’t change the fact that the fast-fashion business model is inherently unsustainable. Beware of irrelevant claims An example of an irrelevant claim is a company that claims their product is “CFC Free”. Since chlorofluorocarbons (CFCs) are banned by law, they wouldn’t be found in the product regardless. The marketing tactic is to imply a choice that does not exist. Buy fewer things According to data from the University of California, Berkeley and its consumption emission analysis firm EcoDataLab, Piedmonters have among the highest consumption emission rates in the country. Even if the products you’re buying are more eco-friendly than alternatives, the best thing for the environment is to buy less. Sophie Roberts is a Climate Corps Fellow with the City of Piedmont’s Sustainability Division.
