articles.text: “2nd Friday Flix,” a new movie-viewing and discussion group sponsored by the Piedmont Recreation Department, has been created for adults over age 18. The informal group will meet once a month with optional brown bag lunches to see a movie and discuss it afterwards. A group of volunteers with PRD staff support has developed the group. Program leaders are: Darby and Gerry Gragg, Jasmine Cai, Mike Gallant, Bob Hall, and Dick Carter, with staff support from Eva Phalen. The group’s first screening will be on Friday, January 13 at 12:30 p.m. on the ground floor of the Recreation Department, 358 Hillside Avenue. The plan is to meet on the second Friday of every month from 12:30 to 3:30 PM with doors opening at 12:15 PM. There are no fees. Register at https://bit.ly/3PJyxkP. Each month a group volunteer will pick a movie of a defined genre and lead a discussion after the movie has been shown. The January movie will be Wait Until Dark, a thrilling 1967 American produced crime mystery directed by Terence Young and produced by Mel Ferrer, starring Audrey Hepburn as a young blind woman and Alan Arkin as a violent criminal searching for drugs. Darby Gragg will lead the discussion. The planned genres for 2023 are: • January: Crime, Mystery • February: Romance, ROMCOM, Wedding • March: Action, Sports, Adventure • April: Drama, Social Issues • May: Fantasy, Animation, Musical • June: War, Conflict, Story Placed During War-Time • July: Science Fiction, Dystopian, Space • August: Western, Big Horizons, Spectacular Cinematography • September: Historical, Biographical, Documentary • October: Thriller, Horror, Noir • November: Foreign, Foreign Setting, Cultural • December: Comedy, Spoof, Satire For more information contact Darby Gragg at cdarbygragg@ yahoo.com or Mike Gallant at mikeyg@gmail.com.

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California’s highly-anticipated White Elephant Sale will return this month with a preview sale on January 29. The sale, touted as Northern California’s “biggest rummage sale,” is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 yearround members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The preview sale begins at 12 p.m. To purchase tickets and learn how to donate items to the sale, visit https://museumca.org/event/ white-elephant-preview-sale/. The ongoing sale will be from, 10 a.m. to 2 p.m. daily from February 1-25. The sale will be limited to 1500 people per day. Tickets are $5. The warehouse is located at 333 Lancaster Street in the Fruitvale district of Oakland.

articles.text: On October 17, 2022, the Piedmont City Council adopted a new Reach Code Ordinance to be effective with the new California Building Code on January 1, 2023. A reach code is a local government ordinance that requires something in addition to the requirements of the state’s building code, and which can address all types of buildings: new buildings, existing buildings, single family buildings, multi-family dwellings, commercial buildings, and industrial buildings. Reach codes are used to achieve policy aims like greenhouse gas emission reduction and other climate-efficiency goals, saving energy and money, increasing the resilience of existing buildings.

articles.text: Staff photos Staff photos Nicholas Christ recently was hired as a new member of the Piedmont Fire Department. Nicholas “Niko” Christ and Nadder Shehadeh have joined the Piedmont Fire Department as firefighter-paramedics. Nicholas Christ Christ began his career in mid- 2016 as an EMT in Napa County, where he was raised. After three years he moved to Santa Rosa and worked as an EMT for a private ambulance service. Wanting to expand his career to include firefighting, he moved to Winters, west of Sacramento, and attended its fire academy. After graduating in February, he began working in Piedmont. “I’ve never been part of a city that regards their public services and public servants so well,” said Christ. “I feel spoiled by the way the community here treats us, and I really take pride in giving back to that community.” Christ knew that he wanted to be a firefighter as soon as he began EMT school in Napa seven years ago. “I wanted to make sure I was a good paramedic before I took on any more responsibility. After all, more than 70% of the calls we take here are medical.” Much of Christ’s family still lives in Napa, and he still resides with his girlfriend in Winters. Nevertheless, he has every intenNadder Shehadeh is a new firefighter-paramedic with the Piedmont Fire Department. tion of continuing to work in Piedmont over the years to come. “This is my first full experience as a firefighter, and there’s been such a change and increase of responsibility on the job compared to my experience of training for it,” he said. “Regardless, Piedmont has been a great place to start this new part of my career. I really feel accepted by everyone here.” Nadder Shehadeh Although Shehadeh was born in northern California, he was raised in Palestine. In 2006, when he was 10, his parents moved back to California to an eightacre property in Placer County that they had purchased in the 1980s. With his father and four brothers, Shehadeh built stables and arenas and began a horse ranch business which continues to this day under the name Boarding on the Lake. The ranch, located in Granite Bay, borders Folsom Lake and currently has over 50 horses. After high school, Shehadeh earned his EMT certification. In 2019, he attended the fire academy at Sierra College in Rocklin. He worked for one year with the South Placer Fire District; and after that, three seasons with Cal Fire. “While that work wasn’t particularly stressful, there was a lot on my plate for those years,” said Shehadeh. “Honestly, I initially stuck with it because I’d been working at the horse ranch since I was 10, and I wanted something different.” Nevertheless, Shehadeh is “still definitely very hands-on at the ranch.” He still helps with everyday tasks. This week he will be helping his brothers repair fences and clear fallen trees in the wake of damage caused by the recent rainstorms. “Where I grew up in Placer County,” Shehadeh said, “Folsom, Roseville, and Granite Bay were similar to Piedmont in that they were all small, tight-knit communities.” He concurs with Christ that “the community is a lot more family-oriented here, compared to other departments nearby, like Oakland. I’m very lucky to have started this job in Piedmont, and I’d like to see out my career here.” HEATING AND AIR CONDITIONING COMPANY

articles.text: Piedmont students ranked first amongst all K-12 California public school districts in Science, with 75% “meeting or exceeding” the state standards on the 2022 California Assessments of Student Performance and Progress (CAASPP) standardized test. The CAASPP is a collection of computer-based assessments in English Language Arts/Literacy, Mathematics and now, Science. The CAASPP replaced the paperbased Standardized Testing and Reporting (STAR) program in 2014. In addition, PUSD’s percentage of 5th- and 8th-graders who “met or exceeded” state standards was the highest in the state of all K-12 and K-8 school districts. In comparison, 40% of students in Alameda County and 29.45% of students in California met or exceeded state science standards. Piedmont students also ranked among the top three K-12 school districts in California in English Language Arts and Math. Last spring, Piedmont students in grades 3–8, and 11, participated in the 2021-22 CAASPP for English Language Arts and Math, while students in grades 5, 8, and 12, participated in the California Science Test (CAST). The school district showed an improvement of more than six percentage points from the previous year and is higher than its pre-pandemic performance in 2018-19. Met or Exceeded’ Science Percentages: 2018-19 70.11% 2019-20 No Data due to COVID 2020-21 68.86% 2021-22 74.95% To view full results, visit Tinyurl.com/pusdcast2022. “We congratulate our students for their outstanding performance on the California Science Test and setting the standard among school districts in the state,” said PUSD Interim Superintendent, Dr. Donald Evans. “In addition, much appreciation to our educators for their dedication in finding innovative methods to teach this important subject and help our students succeed.” Like class assignments and report cards, the CAASPP assessments are one gauge of measuring student progress, providing information to schools, teachers, and parents about how students perform relative to California’s goals for both learning and college and career readiness. Individual student score reports were made available in the fall and can be accessed at anytime by families on the Infinite Campus Parent Portal. Piedmont students ranked first in science in California based upon results of (CAASPP) state tests.
articles.title: Piedmont students rank 1st in state on science tests

articles.text: January is a time for New Year’s resolutions and taking action to meet your goals. If you have been intending to improve your English, you can now take advantage of a free, local, and convenient option. Piedmont Adult School is offering free English as a Second Language (ESL) classes. These classes are designed to help non-native English speakers increase their skills in reading, writing, listening, speaking, grammar and pronunciation. All levels are welcome, and lessons are tailored to individual needs. “We are excited to offer these state-funded English classes to the community, to help students achieve their academic, professional or personal goals,” said Shannon Fierro, director of Piedmont Adult School. “By offering both morning and late afternoon classes, we hope to serve as many students as possible.” Classes will be taught by Michelle Mazzeo, a credentialed Piedmont teacher who holds a California bilingual authorization. Prior to teaching for Piedmont, Mazzeo taught English learners and adult refugees in Washington D.C. for two years. She has also worked abroad in Costa Rica and Uganda. “I love seeing the camaraderie among the students in my classes, as well as the increased confidence they get from improving their command of English,” said Mazzeo. ESL classes started the week of January 10, and registration is available during the first class session. For more information, please email mmazzeo@piedmont.k12.ca.us. To register for other Piedmont Adult School classes, visit piedmontadultschool.org, or call (510) 594-2655.

articles.text: Happy 2023! Here we are at the start of a new year, full of endless possibilities. Arriving at the top of another year is an exciting opportunity for renewal and reflection. 2022 was to be the big comeback from COVID-19 and related setbacks, but it came with its fair share of complications for families – COVID-19, RSV, and inflation to name a few. All of that was a setup for 2023 to be the break we need between crises (big and small). Whether the year ahead will be the respite we need or not, I’d like to suggest ways we can create joy for ourselves and our families. Activating and prioritizing joy has many benefits. including reducing anxiety, boosting learning and curiosity, and navigating difficult situations. Regardless of what scenarios 2023 brings, let us control how we feel and manage it all. Show Gratitude - Gratitude is widely believed to be linked to overall happiness. and, at an early age, can be helpful in building a joyful life. Noticing and recognizing when something has been given (time or things) is a first step in building a grateful routine. Practice Compassion - Being helpful to others strengthens relationships and makes us feel good. Additionally, self-compassion is also incredibly useful in the pursuit of joy. We don’t often turn our care and understanding inward to support ourselves. When we are compassionate, it There is much joy and activity to be found at Children’s Fairyland improves our ability to cope and boosts our well-being. Find Contentment - Creating satisfaction with what we already have in life (rather than being motivated by desire) is an essential skill. In our consumer-driven society we can be prone to always wanting more. Additionally, with social media it is way too easy for youth (and adults) to compare themselves to others. Appreciating what we have is a key component in cultivating joy. Live Actively - There are numerous studies about the connection of well-being and physical activity. Unstructured outdoor play, especially as a family unit, is the best kind of activity. It checks many boxes: exercise, appreciation of nature, working with others, and it’s largely free. We are done with 2022, but the ripple effects caused by the events of 2020 are not over. Although we cannot control the external forces, we can manage how we navigate them and how we feel — 2023 is a new year of possibility and I am rooting for all of us to find our joy. Kymberly Miller is the Executive Director of Children’s Fairyland, whose mission is to spark imagination, learning, and development through the power of storytelling
articles.title: Happy New Year from Children’s Fairyland

articles.text: The Piedmont Appreciating Diversity Film Series continues on Thursday, January 19, with a free screening of the documentary Through the Night. Childcare, who needs it? Everyone. If you are a parent, grandparent and/or community member, you know that society can’t function without it. High quality, dependable and affordable childcare is the essential service necessary to every family and to the American workforce and yet it is always a struggle to find. If you are a doctor, nurse, police officer or in a myriad of other work sectors such as transportation or hospitality, you know the additional challenge in finding night care. This important topic is brought to life in a powerful, uplifting documentary film, Through the Night, directed by Loira Limbal. The film is an intimate cinema verite portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift as an essential worker at a pediatric hospital, another holding three jobs to support her family and an amazing woman (Nunu) who, for over two decades, has cared for the children whose parents have nowhere else to turn. A tender portrait of strength, love, and selflessness, Through the Night showcases the multiplicity of “women’s work”-paid, underpaid, and unpaid--all while negotiating the terms of a dignified existence under the three arrows of racism, sexism, and capitalism in America. The screening is at 7 p.m., followed by a short talk and Q & A with Kym Johnson, Executive Director of Bananas, Inc., an early care and education organization that provides resources for families and child care providers to support and educate our youngest Ellen Driscoll Playhouse is at Havens School, 325 Highland Avenue. Through the Night will be screened on Thursday, January 9, at the Ellen Dirscoll Playhouse.
articles.title: Diversity Film at Ellen Driscoll Playhouse on Jan. 19

articles.text: James Clear, author of Atomic Habits, in one of my absolute favorite quotes about goals says, “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.” As we enter the season of new year’s resolutions, which are basically goals in bunny ear disguises, I often think of Clear’s concise description of why resolutions don’t work. We can resolve all we want, but if we don’t create the systems to scaffold those resolutions, there is no way that those resolutions will get past January 17th. If your goals are around exercise and eating healthy, there are millions of “systems” that appear this time of year: “30 days to a Healthy You,” advertises your gym, “Yoga Fit in 45 Days,” screams a new app, “Clean Eating One Day at a Time.” a new diet program calls out. But what happens if your goals are less concrete? What if you desire a life that has more creativity? A worldview that is less binary and more open? What if joy and connection with others is the resolution? Daily creative expression can help move us towards all of those things, but using Clear’s guidance, it requires systems, not just goals. Here are some ideas for how to give structure and scaffolding to your creative goals: • Choose something small that you can add into your daily routine and tag it on to something you are already doing. For instance, if you already spend five minutes reviewing and updating your to-do list every morning, add 10 minutes to start a color journal where you just explore one color each day with watercolor. • Find something that you enjoy, like a dance class or zumba and mark it on your calendar weekly. Make it sacred. The same way that you would never schedule over Thanksgiving dinner, this weekly appointment cannot be moved. Make sure everyone at work and in your family understands that this is a non-negotiable. • Calendar in creative breaks, the same way you might give yourself a 5 minute stretch break in between zooms, change half of those stretch times to creative times. Put on a song you enjoy listening to and sing along, doodle a fun little cartoon for your kids, dance between your desk and the bathroom…whatever feels fun and easy. I hope your new year’s resolutions turn into systems and structures that last a lifetime. And, if they don’t…you can always declare a new month’s resolution, a new week’s resolution or even a new day’s resolution. Nina Meehan is a Creativity and Communication Coach and Speaker. You can view her latest Tedx Talk at https://youtu.be/ ITM2oD2mhR0. New Year’s resolutions require systems, not just goals.
articles.title: Turning your New Year’s resolutions into systems

Childcare, who needs it? Everyone. If you are a parent, grandparent and/or community member, you know that society can’t function without it. High quality, dependable and affordable childcare is the essential service necessary to every family and to the American workforce and yet it is always a struggle to find. If you are a doctor, nurse, police officer or in a myriad of other work sectors such as transportation or hospitality, you know the additional challenge in finding night care. This important topic is brought to life in a powerful, uplifting documentary film, Through the Night, directed by Loira Limbal. The film is an intimate cinema verite portrait of working mothers whose lives intersect at a 24-hour daycare center: a mother working the overnight shift as an essential worker at a pediatric hospital, another holding three jobs to support her family and an amazing woman (Nunu) who, for over two decades, has cared for the children whose parents have nowhere else to turn. A tender portrait of strength, love, and selflessness, Through the Night showcases the multiplicity of “women’s work”-paid, underpaid, and unpaid--all while negotiating the terms of a dignified existence under the three arrows of racism, sexism, and capitalism in America. The screening is at 7 p.m., followed by a short talk and Q & A with Kym Johnson, Executive Director of Bananas, Inc., an early care and education organization that provides resources for families and child care providers to support and educate our youngest Ellen Driscoll Playhouse is at Havens School, 325 Highland Avenue. Turning your New Year’s resolutions into systems By Nina Meehan James Clear, author of Atomic Habits, in one of my absolute favorite quotes about goals says, “You do not rise to the level of your goals. You fall to the level of your systems.” As we enter the season of new year’s resolutions, which are basically goals in bunny ear disguises, I often think of Clear’s concise description of why resolutions don’t work. We can resolve all we want, but if we don’t create the systems to scaffold those resolutions, there is no way that those resolutions will get past January 17th. If your goals are around exercise and eating healthy, there are millions of “systems” that appear this time of year: “30 days to a Healthy You,” advertises your gym, “Yoga Fit in 45 Days,” screams a new app, “Clean Eating One Day at a Time.” a new diet program calls out. But what happens if your goals are less concrete? What if you desire a life that has more creativity? A worldview that is less binary and more open? What if joy and connection with others is the resolution? Daily creative expression can help move us towards all of those things, but using Clear’s guidance, it requires systems, not just goals. Here are some ideas for how to give structure and scaffolding to your creative goals: • Choose something small that you can add into your daily routine and tag it on to something you are already doing. For instance, if you already spend five minutes reviewing and updating your to-do list every morning, add 10 minutes to start a color journal where you just explore one color each day with watercolor. • Find something that you enjoy, like a dance class or zumba and mark it on your calendar weekly. Make it sacred. The same way that you would never schedule over Thanksgiving dinner, this weekly appointment cannot be moved. Make sure everyone at work and in your family understands that this is a non-negotiable. • Calendar in creative breaks, the same way you might give yourself a 5 minute stretch break in between zooms, change half of those stretch times to creative times. Put on a song you enjoy listening to and sing along, doodle a fun little cartoon for your kids, dance between your desk and the bathroom…whatever feels Through the Night will be screened on Thursday, January 9, at the Ellen Dirscoll Playhouse. fun and easy. I hope your new year’s resolutions turn into systems and structures that last a lifetime. And, Advertise Here! if they don’t…you can always declare a new month’s resolution, a new week’s resolution or even a With the... Piedmont Post new day’s resolution. articles.text: At a moving reception and concert dedication filled with song, words, and love for the recipient, longtime board member Sue Malick was presented with the Founder’s Award by the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir at its Candlelight Concert on December 10 at First Congregational Church in Berkeley. The award was created to honor and acknowledge individuals who have shown exceptional commitment and extraordinary service in the choral community. Past recipients include founder Suzie Rahl, founding artistic Directors Bob Geary and Sue Bohlin, as well as standout volunteers including Paul & Andrea Swenson, Ray Perman, Terry Amgott-Kwan, and the Munich family. “At the heart of our work are the connections and the loving community we create through music, as many voices sound as one. Sue Malick’s warmth, advocacy, and dedication to the Choirs on behalf of children and youth from Richmond to Oakland to Piedmont and beyond exemplify our values. Whether championing homestays for entire tours, opening her heart and home to staff and board, for decades she has authentically and earnestly cared for everyone within our community. Honoring her with this award is a delight and rare privilege,” said current Executive Director Keri Butkevich. A reception was held across the street at First Presbyterian Church of Berkeley prior to the evening concert. Many well wishes sent prior to the event reflected on Sue’s contributions to both Choir and community, including the Malick family hosting large groups of Piedmont Sue Malick was presented with the Founder’s Award honored in December for her long support of the Piedmont East Bay Children’s Choir. choristers at their home in Hochhausen, Germany since 2018. “Sue is an amazing contributor to so much of our local culture. She is smart, energetic, and very talented”,” said Carol Brown. During the concert and reception, Malick was gifted a quilt of homes, honoring her commitment to securing homestays for the triennial international Golden Gate Festival hosted in the East Bay for many years. She was also presented with an engraved stein connecting to her deep roots in Hochhausen and the local community. Prior to the Choirs and community singing the traditional Estonian song “Ta Elagu” (Long Life), Artistic Director Eric Tuan thanked Malick for her decades-long devotion to PEBCC. “Over the past four decades, Sue has dedicated herself to building the Choir community through her generous hospitality, inclusive welcome, and gracious spirit. She has been one of the longest-serving members of the Board of Directors; she has hosted countless receptions for members of the Choir community and for our visiting guests from abroad; and she has volunteered whenever and wherever her help was needed,” said Tuan. “Thank you for all you have done for our community over the past four decades,” he added. In her time on the board, Malick has seen the organization grow from a local Piedmont group in its earliest years, to an internationally acclaimed K-12 youth Choral music organization serving close to 300 singers from 90 schools and 23 Bay Area communities. To learn more about how your family can become part of the Choirs, visit www.piedmontchoirs.org/.
articles.title: Sue Malick honored with Piedmont Choirs Founder’s Award

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. articles.text: Steve Schibsted was formally installed as Senior Pastor of Piedmont Community Church on Sunday, January 8, with a service, the traditional laying on of hands, and a courtyard reception. He began as the church’s Transitional Pastor in January 2021. Sunday marked the return to town of former Piedmont resident, Dr. Mark Labberton, the guest preacher, who recently retired as head of Fuller Theological Seminary in Pasadena. During the installation, covenants were made between Schibsted and the congregation, as well as a prayers for and blessing on the new Senior Pastor as he undertakes this important work. “In many ways it was like a marriage ceremony,” said Patricia Leicher, President of PCC. “The congregation, lay leadership and staff found the installation to be truly inspiring,” “Remarkably Steve has made incredible progress despite beginning his time during the worst pandemic in a century. Longtime members are coming back and new people, including families with children are coming to see what PCC offers. Attendance figures are up 56% from the pre-pandemic years,” confirmed Leicher. Steve Schibsted is the new Senior Pastor at Piedmont Community Church. Photographs by Michael Barber Piedmont Community Church Senior Pastor Dr. Steve Schibsted, left, listens as Dr. Mark Labberton delivers the sermon during the installation service Sunday, January 8. More than 260 people attended the service in person, with more than 100 watching online. Steve was called by the congregation in March of 2022. Board of Trustees member Rich Thompson, center, delivers Questions to the Pastor. Church President Pat Leicher delivers Questions to the Congregation. Church board members gather with clergy to begin the ceremony.

articles.text: Coach Ben Spencer’s talented basketball team returned from winter break and immediately posted a satisfactory 62-46 win against St. Joseph in Alameda on Friday, January 6. It marked the team’s first game against a Western Alameda County Conference opponent and improved its record to 9-3. It was a close game through the first one-and-a-half quarters with the game deadlocked 18-18 in the second quarter. But Piedmont began taking over the game to lead 30-23 by halftime, including a strong defensive fourth quarter to allow just four points. “What is great about our program is that every team is going to give us their best. I think people circle Piedmont on their calendars now, which wasn’t always the case. Tonight, I thought we were really good defensively. St. Joe made a lot of tough shots and we nearly held them under 40 points – that’s a goal of ours (this season) to hold teams under 40,” said Spencer. Good ball movement resulted in finding Brit Burden at the top of the key and A.J. Harris working his way around the court. Harris finished with 30 points and Burden had 19. “We knew this was going to be a battle, St. Joseph is such a renowned program. We knew not to get worried if it was a close game early and to just continue to play our brand of basketball,” said Harris. “They were having two guys extend out and left the middle open, so Brit would get the ball in the middle and drew a lot of contact.” “I think their zone defense rattled us at the beginning, but we just stayed with the game plan. Shots started to fall, we started working well with each other. They ran a 2-3 zone but the middle guy wasn’t staying close to me at the free throw line, so we were able to run our offense through the middle,” said Burden. Game Recap The two sides were tied at 14-14 to end the first quarter, but Piedmont jumped ahead 30-23 by halftime. St. Joseph narrowed the gap to 45-41 to start the fourth quarter, but PHS dominated defensively in the final going, allowing the Pilots just four points while the Highlanders scored 17. With the game tied 18-18 through the early portion of the second quarter, Piedmont went on a 9-2 scoring run to go ahead 27-20. The Pilots added a 3-pointer to make it 27-23, but Harris tacked on three more points via free throws, 30-23. In the third quarter, St. Joes came out hot to score seven of the next nine points to put themselves within one possession at 32-30, but that is at close as things would get. From there, Piedmont put up eight of the next nine of the next 12 points to lead 41-33. However, the quarter ended with PHS holding a narrow 45-41 lead. A.J. Harris finished with 30 points against St. Joseph. Staff Photos Brit Burden scored 19 points in Piedmont’s return.

articles.text: Piedmont’s girls’ basketball team finished 2022 in style by winning the SoCal Holiday Prep Classic’s premier division December 27-30 at San Diego’s Canyon Hills HS. They won four games, including 60-42 over ‘Iolani of Hawaii, 82-69 over Rancho Christian of Temecula, had a narrow 55-54 win over Westview of San Diego in the semifinals, and won their division with a 83-67 victory over Centennial of Corona. Piedmont’s Natalia Martinez and Eva Levingston named to the All-Tournament team. Piedmont is off to one of its strongest seasons since winning the State championship with the Paris twins in 2004 and 2005, The team currently is undefeated at 11-0. “This is a great team,” exuded coach Bryan Gardere, “We have a lot of eyes on us and strong teams always get a lot of invitations to high-level tournaments. It’s been a great start to the season and now we go into our league schedule.” PHS beats Centennial 83-67 for tourney title Piedmont jumped out to a 21-11 lead after the first quarter and 41-31 by halftime. They extended the gap to 60-48 in the third quarter and closed out the game with 23 points in the fourth quarter, conceding just 19 to finish 83-67. All of Piedmont’s eight players finished with points. Final scorers include: Trinity Zamora led the way with 28 points, Martinez finished with 22, Levingston had 18, Maddie Hill scored five, Shakila Zuberi and Adrienne Blackwell had three, Perseas Gioukaris had four, and Samantha Smith had two. One-point barnburner vs. Westview In a razor-thin close semifinal, Piedmont trailed 16-13 at the end of the first quarter but went ahead 34-33 by halftime. The Highlanders struggled in the third quarter and were outscored 17-6 to allow Westview a 10-point advantage, 50-40. But with a strong rally in the last quarter, Piedmont’s defense limited Westview to four points, wnd its offense did the job with 15 points. Zamora led with 13 points, Martinez had 12, Levingston had nine, Gioukaris and Hill had eight points, while Blackwell scored five. 82-69 over Rancho Christian Piedmont trailed 19-15 to end the first quarter but stormed ahead for a 38-34 lead at the half. PHS then exploded for 29 points in the third quarter to put the game away. They entered the fourth quarter leading 67-49 and added 15 points to close out the victory. Staff Photo Trinity Zamora scored 28 points in the championship game with Centennial. Eva Levingston (left) and Natalia Martinez were named to the AllTournament team in San Diego. Final scorers include: Martinez had 22 points, Levingston scored 16, Hill had 13, Zamora had 15, Zuberi had eight, and Gioukaris had seven. 60-42 over ‘Iolani Piedmont built a 22-10 lead in the first quarter and made it 36-23 by halftime. PHS only scored 10 in the third but held Iolani to seven points to make it 46-30 to start the fourth. They added 14 points in the final going for the 60-42 win. Final scorers include: Levingston had 17 points, Martinez scored 15, Zamora had nine, Blackwell scored seven, Hill and Zuberi each had six. Tuesday vs. Castro Valley Piedmont started the league portion of its schedule last night, Tuesday, January 10, against Castro Valley. See next week’s Post for game details. NEXT UP Piedmont (11-0) heads to Alameda tomorrow, Thursday, January 12 for a 6:30 p.m. game. In a historic first, they will play in MLK Showcases at two locations, facing San Joaquin Memorial at St. Mary’s of Stockton on Saturday, January 14 at 9:00 p.m. and Salesian at Bishop O’Dowd in Oakland on Monday, January 16 at 2:00 p.m.

articles.text: In an impressive return from winter break, Piedmont’s girls’ soccer team buried San Leandro 6-1 at Burrell Field on Friday, January 6. Despite the one-sided score, the Highlanders trailed 1-0l midway through the first half and went into halftime tied 1-1. “We were very sluggish and didn’t start the game too well,” confirmed coach Dan Chubbock. “They were able to score 20 minutes into the game and we tied it with a penalty. I told the team at halftime that if we wanted to win our league, this was a game that we needed to handle. They responded really well,” Piedmont was led by Cameron Lorin, who scored three goals, with two by Emily Fitzgerald, and one by Audrey Lam. San Leandro scored the game’s opening goal on a ball over the top where goal keeper Morgan Hunt rushed out of the net to defend. However, the Pirates’ attacker was able to nick the ball away and score on the open goal. In the closing minutes of the first half, Piedmont was awarded a penalty kick after Lam was Staff Photos Cameron Lorin scored a 3-goal hat trick against San Leandro. pulled down in the box. Lorin stepped to the spot and buried her kick to knot it up at 1-1. “This wasn’t a game we could afford to lose. We need to make sure every opportunity to win, we take. I think it was a case of coming back from winter break; we know there’s going to be some mistakes after a long break. We were missing some players, so we knew it’d be a challenge. Everyone responded well,” said ChubEmily Fitzgerald scored two goals in Piedmont’s win against San Leandro. Audrey Lam scored once on the Pirates and drew a penalty kick to tie the game in the first half. bock. Lorin scored once again in the early minutes of the second half, followed by Fitzgerald launching in a longshot from around 25-yards out—all in the first five minutes of the action. At the 52nd minute, Piedmont showed some slick passing when Fitzgerald scored after some nice combination play from the attack. From there, Lorin landed her hat trick after Ellie DeVan sent a cross into the area to find the goal scorer. “Ellie had a great game. She held off a defender and sent a ball into the box to find Cam [Lorin]. It was a great performance from Ellie,” said Chubbock. Lam finished the game with a goal in the closing minutes on an open shot inside the area. The victory improves Piedmont’s record to 5-0-1, and undefeated at 3-0 in league. They look ahead to two of the Foothill’s stronger teams, Castro Valley tonight (January 11) and Berkeley on Friday, January 13. The Trojans of CV is currently 6-0-4 overall while the Yellowjackets are 6-1-2. Berkeley has finished on top in the Foothill Division the past four years, “Castro Valley and Berkeley are on a good run, they’ve been doing well and I know some of their players. Both usually compete for the division, I think the difference will be if our goal-scorers show up that night and we’re able to keep in our formation,” said Chubbock. NEXT UP Piedmont (5-0-1 overall, 3-0-0 league) head to Castro Valley tonight, January 11, at 7:00 p.m. They’ll travel to Berkeley on Friday, January 13 for a 6:30 p.m. game.

articles.text: Junior striker Aiden Woolwine calls out directions. Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team lost a 2-0 decision to North Coast Section foe Cardinal Newman in Santa Rosa on Friday, January 6. It was the first time Piedmont faced Cardinal Newman since the season-opener last season, a scoreless draw. “The score line might not reflect that it was a close game. I think we deserved a result. We’re hoping to get them again in NCS,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. In the early minutes the Cardinals scored on a set piece, and was similar to their game-winning goal in the second round of the NCS playoffs in 2020. From there, Piedmont pressed forward for the goal but were unable to find the finishing touch—including one attempt that rang hard off of the crossbar. “We played it tight after that point. We hit the crossbar and really pushed for the equalizer, but we were just unable to get it,” said Sullivan. In the closing minutes of action, Piedmont pressed forward to try and tie the match. But with players on the attack, the Highlanders were left vulnerable on defense—allowing Cardinal Newman’s finishing goal by way of a counter attack. “Towards the end of the game, they were able to catch us on a counterattack and converted,” explained Sullivan of the second goal. Piedmont was scheduled to play yesterday, January 10, against Arroyo, but Witter Field once again due to heavy rain. In some quick rescheduling, the Highlanders are scheduled for a double-header this week on Thursday, January 12, a 4 p.m. game with Encinal at 4:00 p.m., Staff Photo and a 7 p.m. match with Arroyo. Sullivan is confident that they have enough depth to play two matches on the same day. “Encinal was originally set to be an away game but their field in Alameda is flooded as well. Instead we’ll play both teams on Thursday. It’s rough to play twice in one day, but it’s the option to get the games played. We feel like we have the depth to play the games and do well,” said Sullivan. Piedmont looks ahead to Alameda on Wednesday, January 18 for a Foothill Division game. The Hornets are currently 5-1-4 overall and are leading the Foothill Division with a 3-1-1 record. “Alameda looks strong, they are always a tough opponent. Their field might not be available due to the rain, so this week is really just watching the weather,” explained Sullivan. NEXT UP Piedmont (3-2-2 overall, 2-2-1 league) are set to host Encinal and Arroyo on Thursday, January 12. Matches start at 4:00 p.m. and 7:00 p.m. William Daniel is a key player in Piedmont’s midfield.

They responded really well,” Piedmont was led by Cameron Lorin, who scored three goals, with two by Emily Fitzgerald, and one by Audrey Lam. San Leandro scored the game’s opening goal on a ball over the top where goal keeper Morgan Hunt rushed out of the net to defend. However, the Pirates’ attacker was able to nick the ball away and score on the open goal. In the closing minutes of the first half, Piedmont was awarded a penalty kick after Lam was Staff Photos Cameron Lorin scored a 3-goal hat trick against San Leandro. pulled down in the box. Lorin stepped to the spot and buried her kick to knot it up at 1-1. “This wasn’t a game we could afford to lose. We need to make sure every opportunity to win, we take. I think it was a case of coming back from winter break; we know there’s going to be some mistakes after a long break. We were missing some players, so we knew it’d be a challenge. Everyone responded well,” said ChubEmily Fitzgerald scored two goals in Piedmont’s win against San Leandro. Audrey Lam scored once on the Pirates and drew a penalty kick to tie the game in the first half. bock. Lorin scored once again in the early minutes of the second half, followed by Fitzgerald launching in a longshot from around 25-yards out—all in the first five minutes of the action. At the 52nd minute, Piedmont showed some slick passing when Fitzgerald scored after some nice combination play from the attack. From there, Lorin landed her hat trick after Ellie DeVan sent a cross into the area to find the goal scorer. “Ellie had a great game. She held off a defender and sent a ball into the box to find Cam [Lorin]. It was a great performance from Ellie,” said Chubbock. Lam finished the game with a goal in the closing minutes on an open shot inside the area. The victory improves Piedmont’s record to 5-0-1, and undefeated at 3-0 in league. They look ahead to two of the Foothill’s stronger teams, Castro Valley tonight (January 11) and Berkeley on Friday, January 13. The Trojans of CV is currently 6-0-4 overall while the Yellowjackets are 6-1-2. Berkeley has finished on top in the Foothill Division the past four years, “Castro Valley and Berkeley are on a good run, they’ve been doing well and I know some of their players. Both usually compete for the division, I think the difference will be if our goal-scorers show up that night and we’re able to keep in our formation,” said Chubbock. By Jonathan Comeaux Piedmont’s boys’ soccer team lost a 2-0 decision to North Coast Section foe Cardinal Newman in Santa Rosa on Friday, January 6. It was the first time Piedmont faced Cardinal Newman since the season-opener last season, a scoreless draw. “The score line might not reflect that it was a close game. I think we deserved a result. We’re hoping to get them again in NCS,” said PHS coach Todd Sullivan. In the early minutes the Cardinals scored on a set piece, and was similar to their game-winning goal in the second round of the NCS playoffs in 2020. From there, Piedmont pressed forward for the goal but were unable to find the finishing touch—including one attempt that rang hard off of the crossbar. “We played it tight after that point. We hit the crossbar and really pushed for the equalizer, but we were just unable to get it,” said Sullivan. In the closing minutes of action, Piedmont pressed forward to try and tie the match. But with players on the attack, the Highlanders were left vulnerable on defense—allowing Cardinal Newman’s finishing goal by way of a counter attack. “Towards the end of the game, they were able to catch us on a counterattack and converted,” explained Sullivan of the second goal. Piedmont was scheduled to play yesterday, January 10, against Arroyo, but Witter Field once again due to heavy rain. In some quick rescheduling, the Highlanders are scheduled for a double-header this week on Thursday, January 12, a 4 p.m. game with Encinal at 4:00 p.m., Staff Photo and a 7 p.m. match with Arroyo. Sullivan is confident that they have enough depth to play two matches on the same day. “Encinal was originally set to be an away game but their field in Alameda is flooded as well. Instead we’ll play both teams on Thursday. It’s rough to play twice in one day, but it’s the option to get the games played. We feel like we have the depth to play the games and do well,” said Sullivan. Piedmont looks ahead to Alameda on Wednesday, January 18 for a Foothill Division game. The Hornets are currently 5-1-4 overall and are leading the Foothill Division with a 3-1-1 record. “Alameda looks strong, they are always a tough opponent. Their field might not be available due to the rain, so this week is really just watching the weather,” explained Sullivan. articles.text: With an enrollment typically around 850 students, many Piedmont High athletes play more than one varsity sport. Descried below are three influential athletes at the school competing in two sports. MORGAN HUNT Soccer & Softball Senior Morgan Hunt is a key member of both the soccer and softball teams. She’s a four-year starter on both teams – as a goalkeeper in soccer, and outfielder and first baseman in softball. On the soccer pitch, Hunt earned a first-team All-League selection in 2022 and is helping lead the team, now with a 5-0-1 record. PHS is currently on a fivematch winning streak and Hunt has allowed just one goal during that span. Last spring’ Hunt was a power hitter on Gene Denard’s softball team with six home runs, 18 RBIs on 17 hits with 17 runs scored, carrying a .279 batting average. She helped the team post a 18-7 record and win the Shoreline title with a perfect 10-0 record in league. She was named to AllLeague first team. Notably she hit two home runs in a 4-0 win over Mt. Eden on April 27. Staff Photos Morgan Hunt is an All-League recipient in both soccer and softball. Last spring, she led softball with six home runs. MARKOS LAGIOS Football & Baseball Sophomore Markos Lagios is the football team’s quarterback and center fielder on the baseball team He was named Freshman of the Year by the Post after helping the baseball team win the WACC’s Shoreline Division championship. Last spring he batted .324, had 22 hits, six doubles, 19 RBIs, and scored 18 runs in baseball. He put together his best performance in the critical final three games of the year, which included four RBIs in Piedmont’s 6-5 win over Encinal for the WACC title, and two RBIs in their NCS opening round 4-3 win over St. Patrick., Last fall, Lagios was the starting quarterback for the varsity football team before the season was canceled due to injuries and lack of enough varsity players. He threw a touchdown pass on September 16 against Pierce, and had two touchdown passes against St. Mary’s on September 23. Hailey Marshburn is a threeyear starter on the soccer team and is an All-League recipient in lacrosse. She wears the captain’s armband this winter on Dan Chubbock’s soccer team, and is considered a versatile player, appearing as a midfielder, fullback, and as a winger bombing down the flank. In lacrosse, she is a key defender for coach Carlton Chan and was often tasked with defending the opposing team’s best players. She earned first-team All-League honors in 2022, and helped Piedmont reach the first round of the North Coast Section post-season playoffs. articles.text: Margo Donahue (left), PHS Class of 2019, has earned a spot on the United States’ Under-24 Ultimate Frisbee team. In the growing sport of Ultimate Frisbee, there is no greater honor than representing your country. Competing in the 2023 World Flying Disc Federation from July 1-8 in England will be Piedmont native and current U.C. Davis senior Margo Donahue as a member of the U.S. Women’s Under-24 team. The tournament is essentially the World Cup of Ultimate Frisbee. “The U-24 level tends to be the best college players competing in the whole world. The United States historically does really well because we’re the leading country in the Ultimate Frisbee world. For U-24, the United States has won 11 out of 12 opportunities in all divisions of men’s, women’s, and mixed Ultimate. The U.S. team is always the team to beat,” said Donahue. She plays on multiple teams, including U.C. Davis’ women’s club team, a mixed team called the San Francisco Polar Bears, and another mixed club team in Davis called the Davis Heatwave. Of those, the Polar Bears are a nationally ranked team. Getting noticed from the United States required her to attend a tryout in November in San Diego where she impressed the coaches enough to get a spot. “After you apply and get accepted, there is a West coast and East coast tryout, and then it’s a matter of being selected by the coaches. There’s a pool of around 200 people who tryout and maybe around 1,000 who apply. Donahue, 1 2018 graduated of Piedmont High, has been competing in the sport competitively for the past seven years but feels like she was destined to play since before her birth given her parents met playing while playing. “I’ve been playing seven years competitively, but my parents actually met playing Ultimate, so it’s been in my life a long time. I played on a youth club team during high school and then once I got to college, I started on the women’s team. The rest is hisMargo Donahue (left) will compete in the 2023 World Flying Disc Federation in England, the sport’s equivalent of the World Cup. tory. Ultimate has been kind of my whole life after that,” said Donahue. Making the United States team has been a long sought-after accomplishment for Donahue since she picked up a Frisbee to play competitively back in high school. “Competing on the U.S. team on the world stage means a lot to me. It’s something I’ve been dreaming about since I began playing competitively in high school. I would see people on ESPN and think, ‘Wow, these people are just 21 years old and getting Gold.’ It’s something I’ve been thinking about since I was 15 and now that I’m on the team, it’s kind of insane to me,” said Donahue. Ultimate Frisbee, known simply as Ultimate, is a fast-growing sport all over the world. As Donahue describes, the culture of the sport is nothing like anything she’s experienced after being a varsity runner at Piedmont High’s track and cross country teams. “Ultimate is special in that it’s such a positive and supportive community. One of the biggest aspects that drew me to Ultimate is something we call, ‘The Spirit of the Game.’ When you play the game, you compete with respect, integrity, and honesty. Ultimate Frisbee began as a self-refereed sport and in many cases still is. Our referees are called Observers, who don’t usually make call but are just there to clarify rules. A lot is on the players to make calls themselves with integrity and honesty. Everyone treats everyone with respect. The idea behind Ultimate is we’re playing the most competitively we can be while being the most respectful people we can, that culture is really held up around the world,” said Donahue. Margo Donahue leaps to grab the Frisbee. She is a senior at U.C. Davis and previously ran track and cross country at Piedmont High.
articles.title: Margo Donahue, PHS Class of 2019, named to U.S. U-24 Ultimate Frisbee team

pages.text: Wednesday, January 11, 2023 15 HIKING WITH JON Storm conditions closing East Bay Regional Parks Bring your waders for a look at Leona Canyon after the rain By Jonathan Comeaux The list of re-opened parks As of Tuesday, January 10, East Bay Regional Parks announced that only a select number of parks along the bay’s shoreline and Delta area have re-opened amidst storm conditions. All other parks remain closed until further notice. includes: • Antioch / Oakley Shoreline • Bay Point • Big Break (Oakley) • Carquinez Strait (Martinez) • Coyote Hills (Union City) • Crown Beach (Alameda) • Hayward Shoreline • Judge John Sutter (Oakland) Staff Photos During the first storm system, Leona Canyon’s pond was overflowing when it is typically dry. A whirlpool emerged at the Leona Canyon pond. Downed trees are common hazard at nearby parks. This trees is hanging over the trail at Leona Heights. Another fallen tree over the trail at Leona Heights. Photo courtesy of EBParks.org Nearly all of East Bay Regional Parks are closed due to the ongoing storm system. • Martin Luther King Jr. (Oakland) • Martinez Shoreline • McLaughlin East Shore State Park (Berkeley) • Miller/Knox (Richmond) • Oyster Bay (San Leandro) • Point Isabel (Richmond) • Pt. Pinole (Richmond) “We need the public to heed all park closure signs and not enter or park in any closed parks. Your safety is paramount. Rescues in closed parks can also put first responders at risk. Help keep yourself and first responders safe by staying out of closed parks. It may not seem unsafe, but the dangers and the potential for injury or loss of life are real,” said East Bay Regional Park District Fire Chief Aileen Theile. Here in the Oakland hills, hazards include downed trees, fallen branches, potential mudslides, trail erosion and flooding from nearby creeks. During the initial day of the passing atmospheric river, this writer ventured to Leona Canyon and Leona Heights to get a look at how the storm was impacting the region. For Leona Canyon, the usual drained pond at the trailhead off of Camps Drive was abnormally large—causing a whirlpool to appear on top of one of the storm drains. As the trail began, there was seemingly a river pouring from down the hill into Rifle Range Creek. A few days following the first storm, the cascading creek down Leona Heights Park was magnificent and should continue thriving once trails are safe enough to visit again. There were several downed trees that draped over the narrow trail, while there was some visible erosion on other sections. A shot of the cascading creek at Leona Heights Park. The rain should provide a magnificent sight through the winter. Leona Heights has the largest natural waterfall in Oakland at about 5 feet tall. A river seemingly passing over the trail at Leona Canyon.

articles.text: Gold Coast Chamber Players will present the in-demand Horzowski Trio this Saturday, January 14, at 7:30 p.m. in a concert at the Lafayette Library, 3491 Mt. Diablo Blvd., Lafayette. Cellist Chris Costanza from the St. Lawrence Quartet will provide a pre-concert talk at 7 p.m. The Quartet includes Jesse Mills on violin, Ole Akahoshi on cello, pianist Rieko Aizawa, and with Gold Coast founder Pamela Freund-Striplen as guest violist. The program includes Louise Violist Pamela Freund-Striplen, founder of Gold Coast Players in Lafayette Farrenc’s Piano Trio No. 1 in E-flat Major, Dmitri Shostakovich’s Trio No. 1, and Gabriel Fauré’s Piano Quartet No. 1 in C minor. The Gold Coast Chamber Players are one of the nation’s first chamber music collectives and have been performing in the Bay Area since 1987. Gold Coast was founded by Freund-Striplen, who has performed with San Francisco Symphony and on their chamber music series, Chamber Music Sundaes. Tickets are $45 general, $40 for seniors, and $15 for students and are available at https://www. gccpmusic.com/connectionsintime. Kongkee: Warring States Cyberpunk is on view through January 23 at the San Francisco Asian Art Museum.
articles.title: Gold Coast Chamber Players concert this Saturday

articles.text: Guest conductor Elim Chan Guest conductor Elim Chan will lead the San Francisco Symphony January 12 through 14. Chan is a Hong Kong-born conductor who has served as the chief conductor of the Antwerp Symphony Orchestra since 2019, and became the permanent guest conductor of the Royal Scottish National Orchestra in 2018. Beginning this week on Thursday, January 12, Chan will lead the San Francisco Symphony in a series of performances highlighting the work of Tchaikovsky. The program will include Moondog, a San Francisco Symphony world premiere, Elizabeth Ogonek’s Violin Concerto No. 2, Sergei Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 2, James Ehnes is the guest violinist. To purchase tickets and for performance times, see https:// www.sfsymphony.org/Buy-Tickets/2022-23/Elim-Chan-Conducts-Tchaikovsky.
articles.title: Elim Chan to conduct SF Symphony Thursday through Saturday

articles.text: Join the San Francisco Ballet as the company celebrates its 90th anniversary with “Next@90,” a festival beginning Friday, January 20, with performances through February 11 at the War Memorial Opera House in San Francisco. Next@90 is curated by the ballet’s former artistic director Helgi Tomasson. The festival follows 2018’s “Unbound: A Festival of New Works” with nine world premieres by choreographers Robert Garland, Jamar Roberts, Danielle Rowe, Val Caniparoli, Bridget Breiner, Yuka Oishi, Claudia Schreier, Nicolas Blanc, and Yuri Possokhov. The Grammy-Award winning San Francisco Ballet Orchestra under Music Director Martin West will accompany dancers for all performances. To purchase tickets and learn more, visit https://www.sfballet. org/productions/festival-a/. All performances will take place at San Francisco’s War Memorial Opera House. ®
articles.title: SF Ballet celebrates 90th anniversary with festival Jan. 20-Feb. 11

articles.text: Kongkee: Warring States Cyberpunk is now on view at the San Francisco Asian Art Museum through Monday, January 23. London-based artist Kongkee is known for his animation direction and visual artistry. He co-founded Penguin Lab studio in 2008 and created the graphic comic book “Travel to Hong Kong with Blur” for a British pop music band. Kongkee is well-known for his graphic novel “Detournements: La littérature de Hong Kong en bande dessinée,” published in 2012. The museum describes the exhibition as immersive, animated, futuristic fantasy, and “part comic book, part motion picture.” Visit https://exhibitions.asian art.org/exhibitions/kongkee-warring-states-cyberpunk/ to learn more.
articles.title: Kongkee exhibit, Warring States Cyberpunk, at SF Asian Art Museum through Jan. 23

articles.text: Dominique Morisseau’s Paradise Blue premieres at Berkeley’s Aurora Theatre on January 27. Morisseau, known for her onstage hit Detroit ’67, continues her “Detroit Trilogy” with Paradise Blue, a jazz-infused drama that follows central character Blue, a skilled trumpeter who owns a nightclub in Detroit’s Blackbottom neighborhood. The play takes a turn when a mysterious woman, Silver, comes to town. The cast is led by veteran Bay Area actor Michael J. Asberry. Cast members include Rolanda D. Bell, Kenny Scott, Anna Marie Sharpe, and Titus VanHook. The play is directed by Aurora Theatre’s Artistic Director Dawn Monique Williams. Post-show discussions with the director and cast are scheduled for February 3, 7, 15 and 23. The play will stream online February 21 through 26. Visit https://www.aurorathea t r e.o r g /i n d ex .ph p /s how s - events/20222023-season/paradise-blue to learn more and purchase tickets. Michael J. Asberry stars in Aurora Theater’s upcoming production of Paradise Blue. “WE PAY YOUR SALES TAX”* *On all installed jobs
articles.title: Paradise Blue premieres at Aurora Theatre January 27

articles.text: Dunkirk is a stretching expanse of sandy beach on the northernmost tip of France. There is a shallow-water harbor with a long breakwater pier called “the mole.” If you look toward the horizon, just 28 miles across the Strait of Dover, you can almost see England and its iconic white Between May 26 and June 4, 1940, before the Battle for Britain, before America entered the war, some 400,000 allied troops – Brits, Canadians, French and Belgians – were gathered on that immense Dunkirk beach, waiting. Most stood in long, ragged lines, others sat at the water’s edge, in the foamy white water. Countless soldiers crowded shoulder to shoulder on the mole, desperately hoping to be ferried out to ships that had yet to arrive. Behind them, advancing ever closer, was the full might of the German army which had already invaded Poland, Denmark, Norway, Belgium and now France. Its objective was to capture or annihilate these men now in full And in the grey-blue sky above, often obscured by a hazy sun, were the German Luftwaffe, remorselessly bombing and strafing the exposed soldiers. This moment in British history is now the stuff of myth. While it was, indisputably a retreat, a A scene from Christopher Nolan’s Dunkirk. graphic statement of defeat, it was also viewed in its totality as heroic, a prelude to events that will never be forgotten. Written and directed by Christopher Nolan, Dunkirk is shot in large format film (not digital), it conveys the feel and the texture of the men, as well as the urgency of their dilemma. The terrifying problem for them, for the officers standing on the mole, for those in England (to include Churchill) was: is rescue possible? To simply leave them there was unimaginable and would likely change the course of the war. Nolan approaches his narrative from three points of view: the beach, the sea, and the air. On the beach are the soldiers, their isolation total; in the air are the British Spitfires, especially two whose mission it was to provide defense against the German bombers and Messerschmidts; and on the sea were the ships. What is remarkable is that a call went out by the English command for help, of any kind. An ad hoc flotilla was quickly assembled – tugs, trawlers, merchant ships, fishing boats, weekender yachts, small motor boats – all leaving England without hesitation, headed for Dunkirk and the stranded troops. Their mission was to ferry the troops to those few waiting ships. Other small craft would return to England directly, laden with desperate, oil- soaked, traumatized soldiers. Of course, we as Americans know the story of D-Day. Many have seen Steven Spielberg’s astonishingly good Saving Private Ryan. And what we know is that the allied troops that landed on those harrowing beaches of France, on that early June, 1944, day, were advancing, headed onto shore and beyond. It was an army of liberation, prepared to fight a long, deadly battle against fascism. There was dread, every day of the war, shrouded by a carnage that we cannot imagine. But the direction was clear. Dunkirk involved a different quality of dread, which the film graphically conveys with its minimalist dialogue, its ensemble of actors that are all but indistinguishable, with the exception of naval Commander Bolton, portrayed by Kenneth Branagh, or the two Spitfire pilots who gaze down on the beaches and know that their mission possesses an overwhelming urgency. What is remarkable about Nolan’s film is that while we are witnessing a stark retreat, we are also bearing witness to astonishing heroism; the two never feel contradictory. Dunkirk is beautifully photographed by cinematographer Hoyte Van Hoytema, its narrative balanced between one hour in the air, one day on the sea and one week on that excruciatingly memorable beach at Dunkirk. Dunkirk . Written and Directed by Christopher Nolan. Starring Fionn Whitehead, Tom Glynn-Carney, and Jack Lowden, 1 hr., 47 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2017, Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/Apple tv. articles.text: Caleb McLaughlin, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, and Gaten Matarazzo in the first seasons of Stranger Things. Stranger Things is a compelling investigative drama with supernatural elements (sci-fi and horror) that will appeal to tween/ teen sensibilities. According to its creators, Matt and Ross Duffer, this series was, from the outset, influenced by the works of Steven Spielberg, Stephen King, Wes Craven, and H.P. Lovecraft and has attracted a record-setting Netflix viewership/fanbase. It’s earned high praise for its creepy, chilling atmosphere, superb acting, excellent directing and exceptional writing. It has also received a bevy of awards and nominations, to include the Golden Globes, the Directors Guild of America Awards, The British Academy Television Awards, and the People’s Choice Awards. Stranger Things is set in a small mid-western town called Hawkins. The time is the 1980s, and the narrative opens with quasi-supernatural forces, all of which are connected to the nondescript Hawkins National Laboratory. The lab is known to carry out not just government research, but is rumored to conduct under the radar experiments into the paranormal using human subjects. The lab inadvertently creates a portal to another dimension referred to as the “Upside Down” that has an unanticipated effect on the residents of Hawkins in calamitous ways. Season 1, episode one, begins with the abduction of tween Will Byer (Noah Schnapp) by a creature from the Upside Down. And it’s his mother, Joyce (Winona Ryder), and the Chief of Police Hopper (David Harbour) who set out to find him. And thus begins what proves to be a remarkable adventure that has captured audiences’ imaginations, season after season. Stranger Things. Written and produced by Matt and Ross Duffer, aka the Duffer Bros. Starring Winona Ryder, David Harbour, Millie Bobby Brown, Finn Wolfhard, Gaten Matarazzo, Caleb McLaughlin, Natalie Dyer, and Charlie Heaton, Released as a T.V. series in 2016 and now streaming on Netflix. Season 1 (8 episodes) 2016. Season 2 (9 episodes) 2017. Season 3 (8 episodes) 2019, Season 4 (9 episodes) 2022.

articles.text: Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2, released in 2011, is the eighth and last film in a series that began the same year that the twin towers fell in New York. It’s been a remarkable ride, these movies and books, in the aggregate a stunning achievement, unequaled in sheer breadth and depth. It was J.K. Rowling who wrote seven volumes totaling some 4200 pages, each book resonating with her fans, all those young Potterheads. From the depths of her imagination, she created a cultural phenomenon that remains thus far unrivaled. Youngsters sat outside of bookstores at midnight, wearing peepers and pointed hats, carrying wands, waiting for the next book, often a tome the size of the New York phone book. Each was quickly devoured and discussed. The eight films, waited for with delicious anticipation, comprise 20 hours of screen time and have generated some $7 billion in box office receipts. All of this begs the question: Why? What is there about an orphaned boy, Harry Potter, sent off to wizard school by his disgruntled Muggle relatives, to a place named, improbably, Hogwarts? Perhaps it’s as simple as Harry possessing a magical power and an abiding fearlessness, something that every young person would delight in having. As the series progresses, as multiple narrative strands are gradually brought together, Harry prepares to confront his nemesis, Lord Voldermot. And so we arrive at part two of the final film. For all those Potterheads who have passed the last fourteen years immersed in the labyrinthine adventures of Harry (Daniel Radcliffe) and Hermione (Emma Watson) and Ron (Rupert Grint), this last film will be bittersweet. The long, rambling narrative could easily have been brought to the screen as a series of B-movies. Instead, each film has been lavishly crafted and richly produced and adapted. Part two of Deathly Hallows may be the best of the eight. It is intense and astonishingly good. As are the English actors who have, at the insistence of Rowling, peopled the franchise from the outset. Of course, when walking in to the theater, it helps to have been immersed in Potter lore. Which is no small thing. You need more than a program to get current; you need a wizard dictionary. For some filmgoers, part two will merely amaze. As for the already initiated, and even the recently ordained, this last installment will be captivating. It dazzles as the climax draws near and as Harry moves ever closer to that moment when he may, indeed, die at the hands (or wand) of He Who Shall Not Be Named. Of course, the outcome is known to those who have read the seventh book; but no matter. It is all wonderful and again wonderful and an appropriately soaring finale. As an aside: In a scene from act three, Dumbledore says to Harry, “Words are our most inexhaustible source of magic.” Indeed. Harry Potter and the Deathly Hallows – Part 2. Directed by David Yates. Starring Daniel Radcliffe, Emma Watson, Rupert Grint. 2 hrs., 11 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2011. Now sStreaming on VUDU/Prime/ peacock/ HBO max.

articles.text: A contrafact is a new melody written on an existing chord progression. The tradition is based on contrafactum (from Medieval Latin contrafacere, to counterfeit). Religious vocal works in Europe were modified by changing the lyric text from sacred to secular. For example, What Child Is This was changed to Greensleeves. Contrafacta was used in hymns in fourth-century Syria, seventh-eleventh century Palestine and Constantinople, tenth century Byzantium, and in twelfth and thirteenth century West European secular song (troubadours, trouvères and Minnesinger). A parody mass, from the 16th century, uses multiple voices of pre-existing piece of music, such as a fragment of a motet or a secular chanson. The U.S. Copyright Law of 1909 protects a composer’s rights to lyrics and melody, but not chord progression, unless the chord progression is very unique. The 1909 law said that the publication of a sound recording did not publish the musical work. To get rights to the song, you had to submit a notated copy of the music. In the decades that followed, record companies would hire people to make those manuscripts, allowing them to pay the musicians per recording and claim all rights to the songs themselves. Louis Armstrong said: “They used to either buy the tune outright, or ask us if we cared to collect the royalties… Of course you don’t have to make any guesses as to our decisions… Aye?… Sure… Our slogan was ‘A bird in hand gathers no moss.’” Publishing houses would sometimes purchase songs from songwriters in exchange for exposure of their songs to producers, musical directors, and commercial radio networks. In the 1940s, beboppers came up with a solution to the problem of having to pay the composers and to be able to get their own royalties: they wrote new melodies on chord progressions of standards, which we call “contrafacts.” Here’s a list of jazz contrafacts: https://en.wikipedia.org/ wiki/List_of_ jazz_contrafacts. He was sincere, and always kept his word. I was also impressed by his musicianship. Under Braun’s leadership, the San Francisco Chamber Orchestra was immensely successful. The concerts were always well attended, and the quality of the music making was always very high. Upon Edgar Braun’s retirement and death, leadership passed to Ben Simon. articles.text: A hardy group of 14 members of the Piedmont Recreation Department’s Walking on Wednesdays got lucky last Wednesday and beat the incoming rain by several hours. Nancy and Mike Henn led the walk for Dick Carter who had missed several weeks due to a medical procedure. The plan was to stay in central Piedmont, but if there was no serious rain the route could be extended – exactly what happened. The group went up Highland Avenue to Guilford Road and onto Requa Road and Hazel Lane. It was recalled this was once the entrance to a historical spot. At the start of the twentieth century, Amy Requa Long wanted her daughters to have good educations, so she got Isaac Requa to build a one-room schoolhouse on his property at what is now the Requa Place cul-de-sac. Amy Long hired a teacher for her daughters and a few neighborhood children for the first school in Piedmont. Interest in the private school grew and in 1905 Amy leased a house at the corner of Highland Avenue and Hazel Lane and hired Marion Ransom and Edith Bridges from the Anna Head School in Berkeley to be the new school’s teachers. The school attracted the daughters from many prominent Piedmont and California families and soon outgrew its space. In 1908 Amy Long hired Julia Morgan to design a new school building with classroom and dormitory rooms on five acres of land that is now Hazel Lane. The new Miss Ransom and Miss Bridges School for Girls opened in 1913. However, the Stock Market crashed in 1929 and the Depression created financial difficulties for many parents. Piedmont High, which opened in 1921, was less expensive and the Ransom Bridges’ enrollment declined dramatically. In 1932 there were only 12 graduating seniors and it closed in June that year. In 1936 the school building was demolished and the land was developed by architect Albert Farr as Ransom Gardens. The group walked to the tall redwood tree at 71 Hazel Lane, where the entrance to the Ransom Bridges School once was. The walkers went through the Hazel Lane loop to the school’s former site at 141 Hazel Lane. Walker Jim Kellogg, an architect, expressed admiration for the Albert Farr craftsman design of the home, including the beauty of the stone wall in front and the house’s copper gutters. The walkers continued to Piedmont Court, walking on the sidewalk behind the wide strip of grass that was once a Key System train track. At Piedmont Court they noted a birdhouse in a front yard that is a miniature of the actual house. A path at the end of the Piedmont Court cul-de-sac took the walkers to Mountain Avenue. The rain had not yet begun so the group went to Piedmont Park to see how much water was flowing in Bushy Dell Creek. There was a good flow, but the group knew more was going to come soon. Taking the park path behind Piedmont High School, they went through the high school campus, past the library and student center where they could see San Francisco and the clouds and rain on their way. The walkers had a dry, almost two-mile leisurely walk in about an hour. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no charge. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Registration with the Piedmont Recreation Department is required at https://tinyurl. com/3ethkehu. Wednesday Walkers showed up at the Exedra on Wednesday, January 4, prepared for a stroll in the rain. The walkers included Jim Kuo, Jim Kellogg, Sherry Jacobs, Jane Holland with K-9 best friend Sasha, Rob Smith, Karen Palmer, Melba Yee, Alicia Rivera, Priscilla Wanerus, Albert Chen, Joyce Bailey with K-9 best friend Lucy, and Nancy and Mike Henn with their K-9 best friend Roger. articles.text: Bruce Leslie Wolfe, Piedmont’s most famous artist and sculptor, passed away on December 27, 2022 at age 81. A resident of the city for more than 50 years, he was a loving husband and the father of two daughters. Born on March 29, 1941 in Santa Monica, California, he was the son of Elsie June and Vance Wolfe. He grew up in Redwood City where he attended Sequoia High School. In 1957 Bruce and his wife-to-be, Linda, met at First Christian Church camp in Redwood City and began their life-long love. They married on September 2, 1962 and gave birth to their first daughter, Heather in 1966. They moved to Piedmont, in 1967 and welcomed their second child, Hilary, in 1968. Bruce studied art at San Jose State University and the Art Institute of San Francisco. Additionally, he studied with renowned artists Bettina Steinke and Bruno Lucchesi. Adept in both oils and Portrait of the family home in Elk. outside Consol Energy Center. Bruce had just turned 20 years old when he was employed by one of the largest advertising agencies, Foote, Cone & Belding, as an art director. He had intended on finishing his last year to earn his degree, but the job was too good to pass up, and he began to make a name for himself in the advertising world doing design, layout and television. In his downtime and nights – including many all-nighters – he painted and sculpted portraits of people. He was commissioned to do the memorial bronze of San Francisco Opera’s revered director Kurt Herbert Adler in the San Francisco War Memorial Opera House. At the time, he had never sculpted anything larger than a head, but completed the project to much acclaim. At age 30, he left the ad agency business to focus on a career as a commercial artist. He could frequently be seen doing daily walks on the town’s many steep hills or around the high school track. He often stopped for lively chats with people he would meet along the way. Vacations and weekends were spent with his family in Elk in Mendocino County, where he painted, walked the beach and hiked. Bruce was a tall man with a larger-than-life presence and vibrant personality. He was an artist through and through, always striving for better. He was a lovable, personable guy – someone who made you want to be around him, and feel special. He will be missed by many. Two of Bruce’s favorite quotes ring true to those who know and love him: “We’re not here for a long time, we’re here for a good time.” “It’s a beautiful world.
