pages.text: 28 Wednesday, January 11, 2023 The History of Piedmont Cable Cars in Piedmont By Gail G. Lombardi Part 8 in an ongoing series A cable car ride to the country was the perfect way to spend a Sunday afternoon in the 1890s. From 1890 to 1893, riding the cable car to the Piedmont hills was a favorite pastime. Cable cars provided convenient transportation for residents in the Piedmont hills to downtown Oakland and San Francisco, and almost more importantly, they brought visitors and future residents into the hills. In 1873, Andrew Hallidie built the first cable car line in San Francisco, and by 1889, there were eight cable car lines in the city. The first cable car in Oakland was running in 1886 along San Pablo Avenue. A cable car stops at the passenger shelter at Oakland and Vernal Avenues before turning north on the turntable towards Blair Park. Note the vacant “8,000 passengers rode the cable cars [into Piedmont on the opening day of the cable car company in 1890].” In 1890, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company began operating a cable car line into the Piedmont hills. The company built a large brick powerhouse to run two cables. One cable ran from the powerhouse up Oakland Avenue to Vernal Avenue (now Highland). The other cable ran to 8th and Clay Streets in downtown Oakland. Steam from the powerful engines heated the water for the popular Piedmont Baths next door. The opening day for the cable car to Piedmont was August 1, 1890. The cable company reported that 8,000 passengers rode their cable cars that day. While some cars were open, new green cable cars were designed with large windows and roofs “six to eight inches higher than those of other cars, so as to give passengers a better view of the scenery on route.” This was quite an improvement from the old land in 1890. horse cars. Dressed in their Sunday best, passengers enjoyed the picturesque ride up the hill to Piedmont. From the powerhouse, cable cars traveled at a swift eight miles per hour up Oakland Avenue through grassy fields and down, up more hills and across the wood trestle over the Linda Avenue ravine. As the cars ascended the final hill, passengers enjoyed views of downtown Oakland, Lake Merritt, and then the Bay and Golden Gate. Many rode the cable cars for the view alone. The cable car reached its apex at the turntable at Oakland and Vernal Avenues, an elevation of 341 feet. The cable car stopped at the turntable, and passengers bound for the Piedmont Springs Hotel disembarked and took the short walk south to the hotel. Five dining rooms, a wide veranda, a main salon and saloon offered pleasant places to enjoy an afternoon. Two years later, 1892, Piedmont Springs Hotel burned down. After arriving at the end of the line, the cable car conductor would rotate the car on the turntable to the north and release the cable, allowing the car to coast gently down Vernal Avenue to Moraga Road and Blair Park. Here, the remaining passengers enjoyed a larger, more improved Blair Park. To encourage ridership, the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company added more attractions to the park, transforming it from Blair’s small picnic haven to a popular amusement park. (These new attractions will be explored in a future column.) The Piedmont cable car line was famous for its gravity loop, and some passengers rode the cable car for its exciting return ride. From Blair Park, the cable car coasted diagonally toward Oakland Avenue, gaining speed, sometimes reaching roller coaster speeds, on a winding course across Blair’s wheat fields. The conductor recaptured the cable near what is now Carmel Avenue, and the car proceeded at a more sedate speed to downtown Oakland. In her memoir, Evelyn Craig Pattiani remembers the famous “gravity loop” as “that most thrilling ride through the grain fields.” The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company was financially unsuccessful. It went into receivership in 1893 and was sold at auction in 1895. It was The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Company built the powerhouse (right) and cable car barn (left) on Harrison Street near Lake Merritt in 1890. The engines that drove the cable ran on coal creating the black plume of smoke from its 136-foot smokestacks. The building was remodeled as a Cadillac showroom by architect Clay Burrell in 1925. It has been the Whole Foods building since 2007. An open air cable car in front of Blair Park on Moraga Road. Passengers wore their Sunday best outfits, complete with hats for this trip in the country. The Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company ran five cable cars on Oakland Avenue every day and seven cars on Sunday. expensive to build and expensive to run. The tracks were set in solid concrete with a trench for the cable. To encourage more riders, the cable car company leased Blair Park and added many attractions including a bandstand for concerts on Saturdays and Sundays. Later, balloon ascensions with daring aerialists drew visitors to the park by cable car. These attractions also were expensive, and the Consolidated Piedmont Cable Car Company failed to make a profit each year it ran. Though the cable car company did not prosper, it was a boon to early Piedmont real estate. Cable cars brought efficient public transportation to Piedmont. Many weekend visitors enjoyed the views and the climate and decided to build their homes here. A good number of Piedmont’s early 20th century houses were built near the cable car line on Oakland Avenue. It’s not surprising that the early horse cars, cable cars and electric streetcars were built by real estate investors. If you enjoy reading these biweekly columns on the history of Piedmont, consider becoming a member of the Piedmont Historical Society and receiving its annual newsletter. More information on Piedmont’s history and membership is on the website, Piedmonthistorical.org. For additional information, contact Gail Lombardi at lombardg@ pacbell.net. Nevertheless, physical changes that would result from the implementation of policies proposed in the Housing Element are currently being studied as part of an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) covering updates to the City’s General Plan and changes to the City Code that would happen after the Housing Element is adopted. After City Council adopts the Housing Element, the City will have three years to implement a substantial number of the proposed programs and regulatory changes outlined in the document. This process involves additional environmental review. Accordingly, the Planning Commission has affirmed that, even after their review and prospective recommendation of the Housing Element and IS-ND, Piedmont staff will continue to develop an EIR for future housing and land-related amendments to City policy. The IS-ND document is available for download and review on the City’s website at the following link: bit.ly/3FDqFhg. Physical copies of the IS-ND and the Housing Element are available at City Hall. While the IS-ND public comment period closed on January 8, those with questions can contact Planning & Building Director Kevin Jackson by email at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3039. articles.text: Although December and January have brought several storms to the Bay Area, the state’s largest reservoirs remain depleted. As of last week, California’s status is currently at 0% exceptional drought, 27% extreme drought and 71% severe drought. To protect California’s water reserves, the City of Piedmont encourages residents to take advantage of the water conservation rebates available to all EBMUD customers. Free water-saving devices E B M U D of f e r s f r e e water-conserving items like faucets, aerators, showerheads, and hose nozzles. To request them, order and fill out a free Home Survey Kit at bit.ly/3GzyFyP. Graywater rebates Put laundry water to good use on your landscape and get a rebate for a graywater system 3-way diverter valve. Submit a Graywater Rebate Application, found at bit.ly/3X0hJIN, within 90 days of purchase. Flowmeter rebates Flowmeter devices monitor water use and identify leaks in near real-time, compared to the use information provided every one or two months from EBMUD water bills. Learn about eligibility and application requirements at bit.ly/3QwWk7F. Lawn Conversion Convert your lawn through sheet mulching to improve soil and plant health, reduce yard waste, and achieve long-term drought resilience. EBMUD offers three lawn conversion rebate types at bit.ly/3k6ez87. Those who are approved for a lawn conversion rebate also qualify for a fully compensated $200 Landscape Design Assistance session; information about this program is available at bit.ly/3vVe0k8. Irrigation upgrades To save water and money, EBMUD offers rebates for irrigation-efficiency upgrades like drip irrigation, self-adjusting “smart” controllers, and high-efficiency nozzles. Apply at bit.ly/3QCMFwE. Mulch and Compost Coupons EBMUD offers coupons for mulch and compost, redeemable at local nurseries. Find coupons and locations at bit.ly/3Xdd8mu. To learn more about water conservation rebates available to Piedmonters, visit ebmud.com/ water/conservation-and-rebates/ rebates. For questions and comments about Piedmont’s sustainability policies, contact the City’s Sustainability Program Manager Alyssa Dykman by email at adykman@piedmont.ca.gov, or by phone at 420-3058.

Some lawyers are reluctant to retire because they haven’t cultivated other interests. Phil counts himself lucky because he knew exactly what he was going to do, starting the day after he stopped practicing law: continue to cartoon, but doing it more or less full-time. Phil has also licensed his cartoons to greeting card companies with great success. Textbooks and professional groups started leasing his cartoons as well. He has also written a few dozen humor pieces for magazines and online sites. About six years ago, Phil and former Piedmont resident Rex “You’re not going anywhere until we finalize our estate plan.” “He’s part-terrier, part-Triceratops.” Hesner began a blog critiquing the cartoons in The New Yorker magazine. That effort caught the eye of Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker, who hired them to write a bi-monthly blog called “Anatomy of a Cartoon” for the CartoonStock site (cartoonstock.com), resulting in almost 100 posts and counting. Over the years, Phil has developed relationships with major cartoonists familiar with The New Yorker readers, such as Roz Chast. Last year Phil met Garry Trudeau, creator of “Doonesbury,” and reminded him that Garry was one of the judges in a cartoon contest that named Phil as one of the winners when he was just starting out as a cartoonist. After trying for years to place his cartoons in The New Yorker, he decided to collaborate with one of the magazine’s veteran cartoonists, Kaamran Hafeez. “I sent him hundreds of gags over the past couple of years. He drew 50 or so of them and submitted them with his own cartoons.” Last year, two of them were published in The New Yorker. “Even most of the ‘regular’ cartoonists at the magazine get their work rejected over 95 percent of the time,” Phil noted. Phil was recently elected by his peers to the National Cartoonist Society. “I’ve met very talented people at the annual meetings, including people working in TV animation like ‘The Simpsons,’ graphic novelists, and editorial cartoonists.” Phil’s cartoons have been exhibited in San Francisco, Oakland, Minneapolis, London, Galway, Ireland, and most recently at Dominican University in San Rafael. His show at the Piedmont Center for the Arts will include cartoons from the Dominican show, plus a few new cartoons. Phil has been a guest cartoonist at the Cartoon Art Museum in San Francisco and the Charles Schulz Museum in Santa Rosa. “There’s even a museum of cartoon art in Bulgaria that has one of my cartoons in their permanent collection,” he added with a laugh. Piedmont’s unsung heroes, Millosovich’s crew of eight maintenance workers have been working around the clock to keep the waterways clear and to clean up the debris. Their daily checklist included 31 hotspots around the city which they check hourly, including catch basins in a half dozen creeks. Keeping these key locations unclogged is crucial for water to flow safely downhill and not onto properties and into homes. On December 30, six members of the of the team worked through the night, and then worked all day on New Year’s Eve. Millosovich said a couple of his crew, worked from the from the 30th all the way to the 2nd, four-days of shifts, spanning two years. With rain now forecast to continue intermittently through the month, the hardest working people on town are the men with responsibility for helping prevent flooding. “Stay home if you don’t have to go out,” cautioned Millosovich. “It was amazing when we were out on Moraga Avenue checking catch basins to see people are driving in the pouring rain going 40 miles an hour,” said Millosovich. articles.text: 2022 was a year of change for Piedmont schools. Most visible was the unexpected announcement by Superintendent Randy Booker who in May suddenly called it quits after seven years. Three of the six school principals went elsewhere during 2022. With ample notice Piedmont Middle School Principal Ryan announced his family would be moving to Colorado, and High School Principal Adam Littlefield announced his plans to retire in June. Nine days before the start of the new school year, Beach Principal Michael Corritone took a job as principal of an elementary school in Walnut Creek. The change in guard brought in new blood, new faces, and new ideas as Piedmont School Board hired Dr. Donald Evans of Berkeley as Interim Superintendent for one year. Evans came out of retirement to steady the ship in the wake of Booker’s untimely announcement. Internal hires vaulted Karyn Shipp as new principal at Piedmont Middle School, and Anne Valva as the new principal at Beach School. Piedmont High selected Sukanya Goswami from Miramonte to be its new Principal. 2022 was a year of conflict, of change, and also renewal. School shootings rocked the nation, yet again, and students rose up to say enough is enough. New School Board President Veronica Thigpen and Vice President Hilary Cooper have been on the board for just two years. New members Lindsay Thomasson and Ruchi Medhekar were elected in November, both with children in elementary school. One year ago, COVID dominated the headlines, but now learning loss can be addressed. Piedmont is first and foremost, a school-centered community.
articles.title: 2022 – a year of rebirth for Piedmont schools

articles.text: Piedmont’s most distinctive and well-known artist, Bruce Wolfe, passed away on December 27. He was 81. A California native, he lived most of his life in Piedmont. Bruce was a gifted artist and from the time he was a little child illustrating pictures that astonished his friends and family. He began to make a name for himself during his time in advertising doing design, layout and television. His career spanned five decades doing paintings and sculptures that include many notable pieces. Bruce is survived by his wife Linda, his two children, Heather Wolfe and Hilary Wolfe, and brother Steve Wolfe. He is also survived by grandchildren, Walker, Audrey and Blair, his son-in-law Brian Mahany, and Dave Conlan. A memorial service will be held on Saturday, January 14 at 11 a.m. at Piedmont Community Church, 400 Highland Avenue, with a reception to follow.

articles.text: When I think of life as it was before the unexpected arrival of the COVID pandemic and all that entailed, what comes to mind is the year 2019. My inclination is to refer to it as our last “normal” year, but of course that word doesn’t quite offer a meaningful contrast as we attempt to understand the changes that have taken place since, to include 2022. Over the last three years, the mood of the country feels darker. Though masks and social distancing have fallen away, there still seems to be a psychological quarantine that prevails. For some it’s an unsettling, fog-like dis-ease, and for others it can slip into an inexplicable rage. This was made manifest by the riotous mob that invaded the U.S. Capitol last January 6, an insurrection that continued to graphically linger as the Congressional Committee spent a year researching and taking testimony, much of it in granular detail, while attempting to understand what provoked this unprecedented event. It resulted finally in an 845-page report and analysis. We seem to be unable to find reservoirs of good will. School board meetings echo with discontent and criticism, including book banning in some pockets of the U.S. Threats and vitriol that stun are directed at poll workers, politicians and public servants, from Nancy Pelosi to the extraordinary Dr. Anthony Fauci. Extremism, disinformation/alternative facts, and toxic social media continue to saturate our national discourse while dividing us as a democracy. And should we not ask ourselves if platforms such as Tik Tok and Meta-Facebook, et al., have not contributed to the increase in adolescent depression and anxiety? To be generous, perhaps we should keep in mind that our nation continues to be in the midst of a prevailing grief due to the tragic deaths of 1.1 million people caused by the ever-changing malevolent pandemic (now a trifecta). But how do we comprehend 640 mass shootings in 2022 alone, to include the heart-rending and still inexplicable killing of 19 elementary school children and two teachers in Uvalde, Texas? Anti-Semitism increased in 2022, as have unprovoked attacks against Asians as well as those who identify as LBQT. And, as anticipated, our Supreme Court rejected precedent and overturned Roe v. articles.text: The City of Piedmont’s proposed submission for 6th Cycle Housing Element is available for public review and comment through January 8, 2023. It is available on the following link: bit.ly/3FDqFhg. Physical copies of the documents are available for review at Piedmont City Hall, 120 Vista Avenue. Community members who wish to provide feedback may send comments in writing to Planning Director Kevin Jackson at kjackson@piedmont.ca.gov, or by mail to City Hall. This study is the next step in the City’s Housing Element update, a process that has been underway since Spring 2021. Part of Piedmont’s General Plan, the Housing Element outlines a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. Adopting a Housing Element does not require that the homes be built. The purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support this growth. The California Environmental Quality Act (CEQA) requires that public agencies study and disclose the potential impacts of proposed projects before making a decision. A review of the City’s Draft Housing Element based on these guidelines determined that, as a policy document, the Housing Element alone will not have adverse physical impacts on the environment. Physical changes that would result from the implementation of policies and programs proposed in the Housing Element are currently being studied as part of an Environmental Impact Report (EIR) covering updates to the City’s General Plan and changes to the City Code that would happen after the Housing Element is adopted. The City submitted its proposed Draft Housing Element to the California Department of Housing and Community Development (HCD) for review on November 18, 2022. HCD will review the City’s Draft Housing Element for compliance with State law. If reviewers determine that changes are needed, Planning staff will work with HCD to develop any necessary amendments, then bring the proposed updates to City Council for approval. After the City Council adopts the Housing Element, the City will have three years to implement a substantial number of the proposed programs and regulatory changes outlined in the document. This process involves additional environmental review. This review is already underway. The City is currently in the process of preparing a programmatic EIR that studies the impacts of the new homes and residents that could come to Piedmont once implementation is complete. Information about the Housing Element update process is available at PiedmontIsHome.org. For questions about the Housing Element process, write to PiedmontIsHome@piedmont.ca.gov.

articles.text: Because holiday trees can quickly dry out and become a fire hazard, they should not be left in homes or garages. Here’s how to dispose of natural and flocked or artificial trees. Natural trees The waste disposal company Republic Services will collect natural, unflocked Christmas trees curbside until Friday, January 6. The trees will be turned into compost and mulch. For pickup place the trees out on the curb on your regular service day. Remove all decorations and the tree stand. If the tree is more than 6 feet tall, cut it in half. Flocked or artificial trees Flocked or “snow-covered” trees are not compostable or recyclable. To dispose of a flocked or artificial tree, cut it up so that it fits in black waste bins with the lid closed. Alternatively, Republic Services will collect non-compostable trees curbside by request at a cost of $30.82. To schedule a pickup, call 800-320-8077.

articles.text: The City of Piedmont is offering rebates for the removal of existing gas appliances and replacement with certain electric appliances. Rebates are available for single family and multi-family properties. Eligible low-income applicants may qualify for additional funding. Rebates will only be issued for existing buildings; new construction is not eligible for this program. Rebates can also be applied to equipment and installation labor for projects applying for a Building Permit. Why is the City of Piedmont offering this program? The City is offering this rebate program to incentivize homeowners to electrify their homes. Building electrification has the potential to reduce greenhouse gas emissions in Piedmont and help meet the City’s goal of reducing greenhouse gas emissions 40% by 2030, as set by the Piedmont Climate Action Plan 2.0, which is available at bit.ly/3FI54mE. Will installing electric appliances increase my monthly utility bills? The exact costs and savings will vary depending on your individual situation. Switching from a gas to electric-powered appliance may increase your electricity bill, while decrease your gas bill. Nonetheless, using an efficient heat pump can lower your heating bills dramatically, especially in Piedmont where winters do not get too cold. If I can only afford to make one change, which appliance would be best for me to swap out first? As with many things, it depends on your home and your energy use. Traditionally, heating, ventilation and air conditioning systems (HVAC) are often the biggest energy consumers, followed by water heating systems. It also may be best to swap out the oldest appliance that is most in need of being replaced. Are there any additional or hidden costs to electrification? Besides the labor and appliance cost there may be costs to upgrade your home’s electrical system, depending on its age and condition. Fortunately, California has introduced a number of rebates and incentives that make electrifying your home more affordable than ever. Visit switchison.org/ incentives to learn more. What happens to my old gas appliances when I make the switch to electric? Consider donation or resale before recycling. Appliances may be recycled with Republic Services. Call Republic Services at 800-320-8077 to schedule a special bulky item pickup. In order to be hauled away, all doors must be sealed with duct tape and appliances must be empty. Appliances may also be recycled through the retailer. Confirmation will have to be documented on the receipt as recycled. Funding for the program is limited and applications will be accepted until funding is exhausted. To learn more about qualification for the program, rebate amounts, and eligible electric appliances, please visit the following link: bit.ly/3WPHpIo. Find the answers to more frequently asked questions about the rebate program at bit.ly/3YCKZXg. If questions or for more information, contact Piedmont Planning Director Kevin Jackson at 420-3039 or kjackson@piedmont. ca.gov.
articles.title: City electrification rebate program underway

articles.text: Oakland Museum of California (OMCA)’s highly-anticipated White Elephant Sale will return this year, beginning with a preview sale on January 29. The sale, touted as Northern California’s “biggest rummage sale,” is run exclusively by the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The sole purpose of the board, a group of over 100 yearround members, has been to raise proceeds to support OMCA in art acquisitions, exhibitions, educational programs, capital improvements, and more. Since the Board’s inception in 1959, it has contributed over $23 million to the Museum. The White Elephant Sale garners a significant amount of funding for the museum. The Sale also boasts many volunteers from Piedmont, most of whom are members of the Oakland Museum Women’s Board. The preview sale begins at 12 p.m. To purchase tickets and learn how to donate items to the sale, visit https://museumca.org/event/ white-elephant-preview-sale/.

articles.text: Piedmont Anti-Racism and Diversity Committee (PADC) is calling for students to contribute to the second annual Art and Writing Showcase. All submissions will be featured in Piedmont’s 26th annual Dr. Martin Luther King Celebration, which will be held on Martin Luther King, Jr. Day, Monday, January 16, at the Alan Harvey Theater. All contributors will also be entered in a raffle to win prizes, including $25 gift cards. This year’s theme is based upon a quote from Dr. King: “This call for a worldwide fellowship that lifts neighborly concern beyond one’s tribe, race, class and nation. It is in reality a call for an all-embracing and unconditional love for all men.” Last year Piedmont students produced a powerful collection of illustrations, collages, poetry and essays. They were compiled for a slide show now available on PADC’s website, padc.info. The deadline for submissions is January 10. See the website for rules and directions.
articles.title: PADC art, writing showcase on MLK Day

articles.text: Piedmont Middle School 8th grade students will have an opportunity to join a WorldStrides program to Washington, D.C. this coming summer from June 3-June 7. Students will be able to explore the nation’s most important historical sites and experience incomparable learning moments. WorldStrides has 50 years of experience leading educational tours that ensure learning occurs in a safe and fun environment. The Piedmont group will be led by a WorldStrides-certified Course Leader. The trip cost of $2400 includes transportation, meals, accommodations, and experienced guides. This is not a school sponsored trip. Parents are invited to attend a meeting via Zoom on Wednesday, January 11 at 7 p.m.. During this session, a representative from WorldStrides will be presenting detailed information about the trip and will hold a Q&A session. The final day to register for the trip is January 20. The link to the Zoom meeting is: https://worldstrides.zoom.us/ j/82081299087?pwd=UkxrZ2dLbU9jWE9UR1UwZy9UeXpIdz09 Meeting ID: 820 8129 9087 Passcode: 902339 For more information, contact Stacy Morgan at smcgihon@ yahoo.com.

articles.text: Each week the Piedmont Post prints excerpts from the Piedmont Police Department’s daily log, highlighting the crime items of greatest interest to residents. Some items, especially those that sound quirky, even humorous, end up being selected as the Post’s PPD Pick of the Week. The list below is a collection of our favorite PPD Picks from the year 2021. articles.text: French classes at all levels start the week of January 9 at Piedmont Adult School. Classes will be taught by Jean Monnier, an instructor at Piedmont Adult School since 2007. A native French speaker, Monnier grew up in the Brittany region of France and later moved to the U.S. where he received a bachelor’s degree in English and a master’s degree in Comparative Literature from UC Berkeley. After teaching French at UC Berkeley for five years, Monnier moved to Tours, France, where he taught French and earned a Ph.D Jean Monnier will be teaching the French classes. degree in French literature. On moving back to the U.S. he settled in Oakland, since then has taught at Head Royce and Campolindo High School. Monnier’s fascinating career has included stints as a journalist for French National TV, and as an interpreter during the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics Games. He has written multiple papers and books on French involvement in the California Gold Rush and other topics. “I love teaching at the Adult School because my students are so motivated and excited to learn,” said Monnier. “Often I can provide them with useful information and travel advice, in addition to language skills. We have great conversations about culture, politics, government and the like. The atmosphere is very friendly and social.” Register for Piedmont Adult School at www.piedmontadultschool.org, or by calling (510) 594- 2717. All classes will be taught at Piedmont High School. A $10 discount is offered to seniors.

articles.text: To help Piedmont’s Department of Public Works keep the streets free of leaves during the fall and winter months, residents are asked to observe four rules: 1. Do not put branches in the street, even small branches! They damage the street sweeping equipment. 2. Do not sweep debris from your yard into the gutter – sweep only leaves that fall naturally into the street. 3. Sweep leaves into narrow rows outside the flow line of the gutter. Do not put them in piles. The street sweepers cannot pick up piles of leaves effectively. 4. If you want to rake your leaves, you can now add them to your weekly unlimited green waste cart. If you don’t have enough room in your cart, call Republic Services (1-800- 320-8077) and request free compostable bags to place with your green cart on garbage day. Do not bag them and then empty the bags on the street on sweeping day. The Post will publish the weekly street sweeping schedule from now through February, 2023. You can now make your cemetery and mortuary arrangements in the same location. From traditional ground burial and services, to cremation and more progressive services, whatever your needs are, we are here to help you. Piedmont Funeral Services is now open to serve the funerary needs of our community.

pages.text: 10 Wednesday, January 4, 2023 Year in Review Continued from page 1 Many Piedmonters showed solidarity with Ukraine after it was invaded by Russia on February 24, 2022. from houses citywide. On March 21, faced with cost estimates for the Piedmont Community Pool Project soaring well above budget due to inflation, the City Council approved a trimmed pool design which met its $19 million budget. Eliminations included most of a planned second-story pool building, a family-changing areas; and a multi-purpose, poolside room at deck level. April Plans to electrify the pool remained uncer tain, with estimated additional cost of $500,000. With plans for private fund-raising and a commitment from the non-profit Piedmont Recreation Facilities Organization, the City Council voted on April 4 to move forward with full electrification plans. That week, on April 8, the City published its Draft Housing Element for the 6th Housing Cycle and opened the document Art-lovers view works on display at the annual Piedmont Art Walk. 4th of July Parade Former Piedmont Mayor Teddy King. for public comment. The Housing Element update, a mandatory process that had been underway since Spring 2021, outlined a series of proposed policies and programs that would allow the City to accommodate the development of 587 new homes by 2031 – a number assigned to Piedmont by regional authorities. Mayor Teddy King’s State of the City Address, delivered in City Hall on April 17, addressed both the fatigue and optimism that many Piedmonters felt after more than two years of pandemic related isolation. Piedmont’s first annual Food Festival drew 1,500 people on April 24 and offered some needed cheer. May May rendered Piedmont and the Bay Area a COVID hotspot once again, although high vaccination numbers divorced transmission rates from hospitalizations, which remained low. A total of 55 COVID cases were reported at Piedmont schools over the week of May 2-6 alone. Meanwhile, the third annual Art Walk on May 7 raised money for visual and performing arts programs at Piedmont schools struggling under the pandemic. June As Piedmonters flocked to Veterans Hall to cast their ballots for the California Primary Election in early June, they did so with faces covered, as the County indoor mask mandate was reinstated in the face of case numbers surging nearly to the level of COVID cases in the Winter. As cases eventually reduced, the mask mandate was lifted again on June 25. Annual Piedmont Turkey Trot. The site of the former Piedmont community pool. On June 20, the City Council voted to delay submitting its Draft Housing Element to the State for review. Its responses to public criticism emphasized that the adoption of a Housing Element does not require that homes be built. Rather, the purpose of the document is to demonstrate that the City has a plan for how it could support this growth. July On July 4, these public criticisms took the form of an online petition titled “Protect Central Piedmont from Overdevelopment”. It garnered over 600 signatures within two weeks. Piedmont’s largest annual public event, the 4th of July Parade, was back in full force after two years without a real parade. The 55th annual parade on Highland Avenue drew a crowd of nearly 3,000 people. With immunologist and Piedmont resident Dr. George Rutherford serving as the parade grand marshal. August In August, six individuals took out papers as candidates for the City Council election in November. The candidates included incumbents Jennifer Long and Betsy Andersen, Planning Commissioner Tom Ramsey, Bridget Harris, Jeanne Solnordal, and Nancy Bostrom. On August 10, City Administrator Sara Lillevand announced her intention to retire – but not until Spring of 2023. On August 15, City Council approved plans to raise money for the $2.1 Community Pool construction budget gap. These efforts were reflected by the Piedmont Recreational Facilities Organization’s own grassroots Capital Campaign fundraising effort, launched on August 25. See Year in Review on page 11

September October As the sweltering triple-digit heat wave of September 6 and 7 subsided, election signs sprouted up on lawns throughout the city. The city’s annual Harvest Festival scheduled for September 18 was cancelled due to the possibility of rain, but no alternative plan was in place. Piedmont Police Department hosted its 3rd annual Classic Car Show in the middle of town on a sunny day on September 24, with several hundred people attending. The City Council rejected both of the bids it received for pool construction on October 17. The lowest of the two was for $24.6 million, roughly 15% higher than the city engineer’s cost estimate. November On November 8, Piedmont voters re-elected Betsy Andersen and Jennifer Long to city council, to be joined by veteran Planning Commission member Tom Ramsey. Pool architect Clarence Mamuyac (left), City Council member Betsy Andersen and former Mayor Teddy King, PRFO board member Eric Havian, and City Administrator Sara Lillevand. The City staff received the City Council’s authorization to prepare a Draft Housing Element for submission to the State. On Thanksgiving morning more than 2,300 people converged on Highland Avenue for the City’s 21st annual Turkey Trot, a 3-mile run on city streets. Piedmont’s 55th annual Scout Tree Lot enjoyed record sales of Christmas trees, wreaths and mistletoe during its opening weekend of November 26,, and sold out its entire stock in two weeks. December Hall in Piedmont Park on December 7. The event included new overhead lighting by the Japanese teahouse, lights on many trees in Piedmont Park, a menorah, and an interactive activity hosted by Piedmont’s Girl Scouts. By December it became apparent that Community Pool fundraising efforts had paid off, as PRFO confirmed during a December 5 City Council meeting that it had raised $1 million toward construction. In that meeting, the Council unanimously voted to award a construction contract for $21.7 million to Wickman Development & Construction. A groundbreaking ceremony for the new pool was held on December 17. The three elected City Council members were sworn into office two days later. Outgoing mayor Teddy King reflected many Piedmonters’ experiences of the prior year when she said, in her farewell remarks before the Council during that December 19 meeting, that “With the help of my colleagues, I have always tried to hold closely to my ideals of optimism and service to the public good.” Despite the tumult of 2022, Piedmont emerged close to its ideals of service to the public good, with strong support from residents who continue to volunteer wherever and whenever needed. articles.text: Staff Photo It’s difficult to recall that 2022 marked the full return to sports following two years of COVID- 19 interruptions. During 2022, Piedmont High won a total of 15 league, two section titles and had 11 students win League Athlete of the Year honors. Here are our top moments from 2022: Boys’ Soccer wins League & NCS titles The Highlanders’ boys soccer team finished last winter with a 15-2-4 overall record on its way to the WACC Shoreline title by going undefeated 10-0-0. They won the Division 4 North Coast Section title as the No. 1 seed in a 1-0 win over No. 2 University on February 26 and reached the Division 4 CIF State Tournament for the first time ever as the No. 6 seed before losing 2-0 to No. 3 Sacred Heart Prep in the first round on March 1. It was coach Todd Sullivan’s second league title and third time as the No. 1 ranked team in league. No banners were awarded in 2021. It was the second consecutive season that Piedmont was undefeated against league opponents teams. They were moved into the more competitive Foothill Division this winter. To reach the North Coast Section finals, Piedmont won 11 straight shutouts prior to the CIF tournament. They defeated No. 8 Justin-Siena 5-0 in the NCS quarterfinals on February 19 and No. 5 Branson 2-0 in the semifinals on February 23. On February 26 at Witter Field, PHS defeated No. 2 University 1-nil for the Div. 4 North Coast Section title. A jubilant, emotional, Sullivan shot his hands in the air and had his emotions on high during our postgame interview, talking with a rattling voice, said after the game he could break into tears he was so happy. articles.text: Piedmont resident Phil Witte, a former attorney, is the cartoonist whose FLIP has appeared in the Piedmont Post since 2008. His cartoons have been published in dozens of publications in the U.S. and U.K., including The Wall Street Journal, Reader’s Digest, San Francisco Chronicle, New Statesman, and Private Eye, as well as in books, calendars, and greeting cards. His humor book, What You Don’t Know About Turning 50, and the sequel on turning 60 have sold over 170,000 copies. Phil also co-writes the Anatomy of a Cartoon blog for CartoonStock, founded by Bob Mankoff, the former cartoon editor at The New Yorker. Phil’s cartoons have been exhibited in group shows in San Francisco, Minneapolis, London, and Galway, Ireland. He has been a cartoonist-in-residence at the Charles Schulz Museum and the San Francisco Cartoon Art Museum. Phil is a member of the National Cartoonists Society. See www.philwitte.com. The cartoons shown below represent our favorite picks from 2022. Self-drawn sketch of cartoonist Phil Witte. “It’s an Eisenhower jacket. It says I’m a traditional Republican.” “I will speak truth to power and, when circumstances permit, to voters.” “We’re intestinal parasites— we don’t need to thank the host.” “Your printing press will spread knowledge throughout the world for 500 years. After that--pffft .” Farm-raised salmon visit the big city. “Actually, the effects and side effects are pretty much the same.”

articles.text: Guest conductor Elim Chan will lead San Francisco Symphony January 12-14. Guest conductor Elim Chan will lead the San Francisco Symphony January 12 through 14. Chan is a Hong Kong-born conductor who has served as the chief conductor of the Antwerp Symphony Orchestra in Belgium since 2019 and is a permanent guest conductor of the Royal Scottish National Orchestra in Glasgow. Beginning Thursday, January 12, Chan will lead the symphony in a series of performances that highlight the works of Tchaikovsky. The program includes the San Francisco Symphony world premiere of Moondog,,Elizabeth Ogonek’s Violin Concerto No. 2, Sergei Prokofiev’s Symphony No. 2, and music by Piotr Ilyich Tchaikovsky. James Ehnes is the violin soloist. Visit https://www.sfsymphony. org/Buy-Tickets/2022-23/ElimChan-Conducts-Tchaikovsky to see performance times and purchase tickets.

articles.text: Dominique Morisseau’s Paradise Blue premieres at Aurora Theatre in Berkeley on January 27. Known for her stage hit Detroit ’67, Morisseau continues her “Detroit Trilogy” with Paradise Blue, a jazz-infused drama that follows central character Blue, a skilled trumpeter who owns a nightclub in Detroit’s Blackbottom neighborhood. articles.text: There is a stillness in the air and the streets are almost devoid of traffic. The cold winter sun casts long shadows. The Christmas rush is over as the old year raced towards its inevitable close. Observations like this cause us to reflect on the year past. Generally speaking, our thoughts depend on our outlook on life. A certain overindulgence causes most of us to make New Year’s resolutions. 2023…Quo vadis? Maybe we should ask the plural version of this famous question. Quo vadimus – Where are we going? While some of the world has gone into artistic hibernation, others have found ways to be productive. A talented musical friend of mine has written five books on violin technique. He claims that these books are his musical autobiography. There is no doubt that he has lived a full life and the books are proof of that. For some musical organizations, Spring has come early. Both San Francisco Symphony and San Francisco Opera have a new Music Director. Oakland Symphony continues its search for a luminary to illuminate the podium. On the home front, the Piedmont Chamber Orchestra is planning some exciting concerts. The Piedmont Center for the Arts continues on its successful course despite some roadblocks instigated by politicians and petty bureaucrats. On a personal note, my wife and I enjoyed a New Year’s Eve feast at one of our favorite restaurants, Italian Colors. The festive spirit was everywhere despite the storm… um, I mean… The atmospheric river. We enjoyed superb prawns stuffed with Dungeness crab on the first official day of San Francisco’s crab season. A unique pizza topped with fragrant black truffles was not exactly Neapolitan, but it was memorable nevertheless. Adding to the evening’s enjoyment was a visit to the table by owner Alan Carlson and his son Dylan who stopped by to give us extra slices of both black and white truffles. A lively couple at the neighboring table brought over some of their prize-winning wine and aged brandy. As the Germans say. “Das leben ist Lebenswert (literally, “life is beautiful”). And the atmospheric river continues on its way to the sea. So… Whether you ask the question in singular “Quo vadis” or you make it more general… “Quo vadimus” Have a great year.
articles.title: Winter thoughts

articles.text: The new Joan Brown exhibit at San Francisco Museum of Modern Art comprises 80 colorful paintings and sculptures from the celebrated artist. The exhibit is on display now through March 12. A Bay Area figurative artist, she is considered one of San Francisco’s most important local artists. She was once dismissed by critics as ‘unserious,’ but was recognized for her influential artistry after her death in 1990. Works on display include The Dancers in a City #2 and Gordon, Joan and Rufus in Front of S.F. Opera House, which both show how much influence the city of San Francisco had on Brown’s art. the youngest artist exhibited as part of Young America 1960 (30 American Painters Under Thirty-Six) at the Whitney Museum of American Art. “We are thrilled to present Joan Brown, a reassessment of the unabashedly personal, defiantly independent and enduringly relevant career of one of San Francisco’s most important local heroes,” said Janet Bishop, Curator of Painting and Sculpture at SFMOMA. Visit https://www.sfmoma. org/exhibition/joan-brown/ to learn more. Museum hours are 10 a.m. to 5 p.m. on Fridays through Tuesdays and 1 to 8 p.m. on Thursdays. The museum is closed Wednesdays. articles.text: Golden Gate Park’s public art installation. Entwined, is back at Peacock Meadow for the third year. It will be on display through March. Entwined was created by San Francisco industrial artist Charles Gadeken in 2020 at the height of the COVID pandemic as a way to encourage park-going activities. The installation creates a whimsical, illuminated wonderland where visitors can explore paths and sit under a grove of three entwined sculptural trees. Gadeken’s public artworks reimagine the world “post-nature.” His artwork commissions include Black Rock Arts Foundation, City of San Francisco, Coachella Festival, City of Palo Alto, City of Calabasas, City of Los Altos, and Stanford University, Many of Gadeken’s works have been exhibited internationally. Entwined will remain in Golden Gate Park through March and will remain lit until 10 p.m. each night. The project is sponsored by the San Francisco Parks Alliance. To learn more about the installation and its history, visit https:// sanfranciscoparksalliance.org/ projects/entwined/.
articles.title: Entwined public art installation returns to Golden Gate Park

articles.text: Buried is a high risk/high gain movie. The risk is this: Paul Conroy (Ryan Reynolds), a private contractor working for a trucking company, wakes to find himself buried in a pine box somewhere beneath the Iraqi desert. In the opening moments of the movie the screen is dark and all that’s heard is someone breathing, and the creaking of boards. Then there’s a clicking sound and a dim, wavering light comes on from a Zippo lighter, and for the first time we see Conroy, sweaty, bloody, trying to remain calm while assessing his situation. He’s in a pine box, a coffin of sorts, with only inches between the tip of his nose and the rough wood above. Taking inventory, he finds he has a small flask, a knife, and a pencil. A cell phone rings, the florescent glow of the screen lighting up the other end of the box. The caller is his kidnapper, demanding $5 million in ransom. Conroy pleads with him that he is only a truck driver, ferrying supplies to an American outpost, and not a soldier. He is told that he has only 90 minutes of oxygen and ninety minutes to get the money. And so the ordeal begins. Using the cell phone, trying to control his rising panic, he begins calling for help. The gamble for the filmmakers is that taken at face value audiences will not willingly spend Ryan Reynolds stars in Buried. 90 minutes with Conroy beneath the ground. The movie never cuts away to the surface. There are no backstory shots. There are no other actors, just the disembodied voices on the cell phone: the FBI, the State Department, an executive from his trucking company, and the kidnapper. His waning hope is that he can reach someone, anyone, who will set a rescue in motion, perhaps using his phone signal as a GPS locator. Buried represents a huge gamble for director Rodrigo Cortes. And yet, push comes to shove, the film possesses an intensity that is undeniable. Conroy’s situation is a crisis on steroids and it’s objective, clearly, is to tap into those atavistic, claustrophobic fears we all possess of being trapped – in a room, a vault, a crypt, a basement, or in a place where all is impenetrably black. Countless Hollywood films use the idea of no exit to rev up what can be palpable tension. Call them container movies. One example is the riveting Jodie Foster film, Panic Room. She and her daughter are trapped in a small room on the third floor of a New York mansion while burglars prowl through the house. Parodied Snakes on a Plane comes to mind. Buried is clearly looking for a niche audience. This is extreme filmmaking, taking a thin premise and attempting to turn it into a movie experience, one that, albeit, will be very unsettling for most. Buried. Directed by Rodrigo Cortes. articles.text: I often find myself still trying to sort out what has changed in the film industry over the past three years due to the pandemic. I recall a time in late 2019 when I walked into a darkened movie theater to spend some two hours with strangers, watching a breaking film, eager to be entertained by one of a spectrum of genres from thrillers to romances to tragedies, starring actors (some referred to in worshipful terms as “movie stars”) who possessed the ability to portray a character in a story that captured my imagination. And there was, of course, the Academy Awards ceremony, a red carpeted evening that defined the word glamour, replete with gold statues that acknowledged stellar performances in a variety of categories. But that was then and this is now. It’s not that we don’t relish still being told a good story; what has changed is how. This tenacious virus, aka COVID-19 and its variants, may have changed forever the movie-going experience. Audiences have thinned, countless theaters have closed, and movies that were intended to be box office hits (last year’s Licorice Pizza, Nightmare Alley, Power of the Dog for example) flat-lined. Even dedicated moviegoers who usually seek out prestige films (those released in the fall with the Academy Awards in mind) stayed home. With few exceptions (this year’s Top Gun: Maverick grossed roughly $1.5 billion, and Avatar: The Way of Water earned $1.4 billion worldwide), audiences found themselves forsaking the big screen for the small screen, content to stream movies from the comfort and safety of their sofas. As COVID evolved, and the country struggled with overwhelmed hospitals, mask-wearing, social distancing, vaccines, school and business closures, weeks of quarantining, movie studios remained ever hopeful that films, to include summer blockbusters, could still be made that would find large enough theater audiences to justify their cost. Gradually the impact of the virus began to be felt. Consider films that opened “exclusively” in theaters. Armageddon, as example, was made at a cost of $30 million, and earned only 6 million at the box office. Tar was produced for $35 million and has earned less than $6 million. And the much-anticipated movie Devotion, which had a price tag of just under $100 million, grossed less than $20 million. Even the autobiographical Steven Spielberg film, The Fablemans, which cost $40 million to make and market has thus far earned less than $6 million after four weeks in theaters. What Hollywood has come to realize, reluctantly, is that it’s not that films are mediocre but that those once dependable audiences are now reluctant to sit in enclosed movie theaters knowing that even today there is a trifecta of viruses still present. In the alternative there are the increasingly ubiquitous large televisions available with remarkable technology and clarity. Combine that with countless platforms, from Netflix, Disney+ to HBO Max and Amazon Prime, which stream current films as well as countless movies that were perhaps missed when released years ago. In other words, the walk-in, big screen venues, once iconic, have taken on far less importance – and not to forget the cost of popcorn and drinks. The question now begged is will the Oscars follow? What we are experiencing, it would seem, is an extraordinary change in an industry that was, for the better part of a century, part of our entertainment culture. It is an industry that is now in the midst of being redefined. Will we ever return to those days of yesteryear?
articles.title: That was then; this is now

articles.text: I admit that I have always possessed a bias against Hollywood musicals. When dialogue abruptly shifts to singing and music from the background to the foreground, I have found it difficult to suspend my disbelief. And so it was with some reluctance that I sat in a darkened theater and waited for La La Land to begin. I admit that even the title gave me pause. When it started, the opening scene, while energetic, seemed a bit retro (I flashed on Grease). I was already growing restless. Young, beautiful people, stuck on an L.A. freeway in bumper to bumper traffic, suddenly leave their cars and start singing while standing on the hoods and roofs of their cars, the song, Another Day of Sunshine. Palm trees dot the horizon, the colors lift off the screen. A perfect day in L.A… But singing? Dancing? And then something completely unexpected and surprising happens. La La Land becomes almost magical, quickly morphing into a creative and seamless story that is incredibly winning. At the risk of sounding hyperbolic, it is magnificent and wonderful, crafted by writer/director Damien Chazelle, with music composed by Justin Hurwitz, and lyrics by Benji Pasek and Justin Paul. And what lyrics they are. Together they have created an astonishing collaboration that is transformative and delightful, most especially the theme song, a wistful ballad called City of Stars. So I sit here, with my computer, looking at the screen, asking myself how to write sentences that will encourage moviegoers to discover this film and allow themselves to be swept away by the music and the superb performances of Emma Stone as Mia and Ryan Gosling as Sebastian. Both are denizens of L.A., and both possess dreams yet to be fulfilled. His is to use his talent on the piano to play jazz in a club of his own. Hers is to audition (which she does time after time, to heartbreaking effect) for a part that will allow her to not only display her deep reservoir of talent but to truly unleash it. Sebastian and Mia meet briefly, then meet again, and, inevitably, they begin a journey that is heartfelt and sad and wonderful, their moments together enriched by songs and thematic music that will echo for days after you leave the theater. There are moments in this film that are breathtaking. They are so original and filled with artistic risk-taking. At its core La La Land is a simple story: boy meets girl, fall in love, and finally sing and dance as the early evening lights of L.A. appear like so many thousands of surreal stars, the horizon still a gauzy red-purple glow as the sun reluctantly sets. Sensational. Don’t hold back. Trust me. This film is far more than an attempt to pay homage to old-time Hollywood musicals that were once ubiquitous. Chazelle has crafted something glorious, and has elicited from Stone and Gosling startlingly good performances – I mean they are really good. Sit back and open your heart and let La La Land charm you and make you smile, sadly, especially at the end. If given a chance, you will be enchanted, I promise. La La Land. Directed by Damien Chazelle. Starring Emma Stone, Ryan Gosling, John Legend. 2 hrs., 8 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2016. Now streaming on Prime/VUDU/Apple. Emma Stone and Ryan Gosling star in La La Land.
articles.title: La La Land a magical film with memorable music, outstanding acting

articles.text: Robert Downey Jr. reprises his role as Tony Stark in Iron Man 2. “Jump the shark” and “Nuke the fridge” are Hollywood terms which come to mind when a sequel is released following a successful debut movie. The first Iron Man movie was released in 2008. It had a high “wow factor” to be sure. It was fresh and interesting, a shiny adaptation of the Marvel Comics’ character, Iron Man, brought to life by the talented actor Robert Downey. Iron Man 1 delivered the necessary backstory regarding how Iron Man came to be, along with the astonishing technology that turned industrialist Tony Stark into a high flying weapons system. The Iron Man suit defines cool. Plus, it’s always a thrill watching a superhero’s history unfold, watching as he or she begins to take control of newly discovered and unexpected abilities. Recall Superman, arriving on earth in the center of a meteor; or Spider Man, bitten by a spider, grappling with his metamorphosis. It’s a rush. That first Iron Man movie, now in franchise mode, was superb entertainment. The challenge was how to craft a sequel that would be equally gripping. Comic book adaptations have become an entertainment staple using familiar characters: Batman, Hulk, X-Men, Superman, Spider Man, Hellboy, to name a few. Which brings us to the Iron Man 2. For writer Justin Theroux and director Jon Favreau, the trick was to find a story that presented a now established Tony Stark aka Iron Man in a new and interesting way. Plus, a new antagonist had to be introduced, an opponent worthy of Stark’s incomparable strength, wealth and intelligence. The term “jump the shark” is most often used to describe the moment when a TV series or movie franchise begins its downturn and things spin off into absurdity. The intensity and crispness of the first movie has been dulled, and the story has lost its edge and the originality. The film has devolved into the formulaic. It happens. In an effort to make Stark extraordinary and more complex, the writers make him decidedly un-heroic. He’s arrogant, hubristic, and seemingly consumed with his new-found fame and power. He’s not very appealing. In one scene he arrives before a government oversight committee with studied insouciance, flashing the peace sign, declaring world peace has been privatized, while displaying an ego that is in need of deflating. Downey is a consummate actor as is Gwyneth Paltrow as Pepper Potts, his unacknowledged love interest and solidly competent girl Friday. Mickey Rourke, in all his grungy splendor, is passable as a Russian named Ivan Vanko, wingnut scientist, and Stark’s bad dude nemesis. Samuel L. Jackson makes an appearance briefly as Nick Fury, as does Scarlett Johansson in the role of Natalie, aka Black Widow. Does Iron Man 2 have the right stuff? The answer is no. The hardware is wonderful. The suit is still a treat to watch. But the rest – the loud climactic battle, the flights at supersonic speeds – all are familiar. Fallback position: craft a great screenplay. Otherwise, the thrill is gone. Iron Man 2. Directed by Jon Favreau. Starring Robert Downey, Don Cheadle, Gwyneth Paltrow, Scarlett Johansson and Mickey Rourke.. 2 hrs., 4 min. Rated PG-13. Released in 2010. Now streaming on VUDU/Prime/ Disney+.
articles.title: Iron Man 2 – the thrill is gone

Starring Neel Sethi, Bill Murray and Ben Kingsley. 1 hr., 45 min. Rated PG. Released 2016. Now streaming on VUDU/ Prime/Disney+. The Jungle Book is a dazzling, vibrant film that will draw kids in and easily keep them in their seats. Starring Neel Sethi as Mowgli (the only human, also known as the “man cub”), the film is a marvel of CGI (computer graphics). A thought that keeps coming to mind as the film evolves is that kids today may take for granted the seamless creation of animals, such as the bear Baloo (Bill Murray), or the panther, Bagheera (Ben Kingsley). For those of us who have watched movies over the years, the technical accomplishments of this film are nothing short of astonishing. Using the work of Rudyard Kipling as the source material, Mowgli is confronted with a difficult choice. If he is to survive, he must leave his family of wolves and all that he has known and escape the lethal wrath of Shere Khan (Idris Elba), a tiger that hates men so much that he is intent on killing Mowgli. His journey takes him deep into the Indian jungle where he is confronted with one adventure after the next. It is there that he meets the lazy Baloo, who asks Mowgli to climb a steep cliff to get at the honey hives hanging from the rocks. He also falls under the spell of an enormous snake Kaa (Scarlett Johansson), and meets to his peril King Louie, a Gigantopithecus (Christopher Walken), from whom he barely escapes. Mowgli’s goal – the purpose of his adventure – is to find a place A scene from the 2016 live-action remake of The Jungle Book.

articles.text: Brian Kelly, the Piedmont Post’s popular and well-respected editorial cartoonist and a mainstay of the paper since its founding in 1998, brings clear images of civic matters each week to readers of the Post. articles.text: The recent cold snap, followed by days of rains, have landed me back to the pantry for meal inspiration. Fortunately, I keep a cache of pulses (the edible seed from a legume plant) for just these situations. Channa dal is a type of chickpea, which closely resembles a dried, yellow split pea. We are fortunate here in the Bay Area for the availability of Indian groceries, and I highly recommend you seek these out if possible. The warming spices, fresh ginger, and bit of chile heat make this soup a welcome antidote to the wet, chilly days of late. Don’t be put off by the long list of ingredients. I store peeled ginger and turmeric in the freezer since I use so much, but powdered or dried works too. Similarly, if the individual spices seem too much effort, a curry powder blend will work in their place, about one tablespoon total or to your taste preference. I hope this idea provides inspiration for your own improvisation. Any pulse can be substituted, and canned garbanzo or other beans are fair territory. Add any vegetables that suit your fancy – cauliflower, green beans and a squash are a few ideas, along with pieces of cooked chicken if you desire additional protein. Chana Dal Vegetable Soup Makes about 2 quarts INGREDIENTS • 1 tablespoon ghee • 1 tablespoon olive oil, extra virgin • 1 medium white or yellow onion, cut into 1/4ʺ dice, about 1 cup • 2 stalks celery, cut into 1/4ʺ dice, about 1 cup • 2 medium carrots, cut into 1/4ʺ dice, about 3/4 cup • 3 medium cloves garlic, minced, about 1 tablespoon • 1-inch knob of fresh ginger, minced, about 1 tablespoon • • • • • • • • • • • (substitute 1 teaspoon ground ginger powder) 1-inch knob of fresh turmeric, minced, about 1 tablespoon (substitute 1 teaspoon ground turmeric powder) 2 medium bay leaves 1 cup chana dal 1 quart chicken broth, low-sodium or homemade (substitute vegetable broth if desired) 1 14.5 ounce can diced tomatoes, with the juices (substitute fire-roasted diced tomatoes) 1 teaspoon garam masala 1/2 teaspoon ground cumin 1/2 teaspoon ground coriander 1/2 teaspoon black pepper, freshly ground 1/4 – 1/2 teaspoon chile flakes, or to taste 1/4 teaspoon sea salt, or to taste INSTRUCTIONS Place the chana dal in a medium mixing bowl. Rinse a few times, then drain. Cover with freshly boiled water to cover and set aside while you prepare the vegetables. Drain before adding to the soup. In a 3-to 4-quart saucepan or soup pot, melt ghee and add olive oil over medium heat. Add the prepared onion, celery, carrot, garlic, ginger, turmeric and bay leaves. Stir to combine, then add the garam masala, cumin, coriander, black pepper, chile flakes, and salt. Stir frequently until the onions turn translucent. Add the soaked and drained chana dal. Add the chicken stock and canned, diced tomatoes, along with the juices in the can. Bring to a full boil, then reduce to a simmer and cook until the dal are tender, about 45 minutes to one hour. To serve, add coarsely chopped, fresh cilantro and a squeeze of lemon juice. A warm piece of naan or roti is an ideal accompaniment. For more information and to suggest a food to be reviewed, see the blog of Piedmont resident and cook Deborah Quok: PiedmontPantry.com.
articles.title: An Improvisation from the Pantry

articles.text: The Piedmont Seniors recently met for a holiday party at the beautiful Claremont Country Club which did an outstanding job decorating for the holidays. The private room for the group was artfully draped with greenery all along the ceiling, with two Christmas trees framing a view of the golf course. Approximately 40 Piedmont Seniors were on hand to celebrate the holidays. The group feasted on a gourmet lunch consisting of butternut squash soup, grilled chicken breast, vegetarian crepes and dessert. A cupful of Jelly Bellies, acquired during the Seniors’ last excursion, was placed at each person’s place setting. The December holiday gathering has been an annual tradition since the group’s inception in 1996. The Seniors were treated to the music of pianist David Miotke who played a variety of holiday tunes that got everybody into the spirit of the season. The group also had a gift exchange, where they each selected a colorfully wrapped package to take home. After another grueling year of COVID, it was very comforting to get together to enjoy each other’s company in such a beautiful setting. To learn more about the Piedmont Seniors and their activities, contact Janet Epstein, Seniors’ Coordinator at jepstein@piedmont.ca.gov. If you would prefer to stop by for a meeting, the group meets on the fourth Wednesday of each month at 10 a.m. at the Piedmont Community Hall, 711 Highland Avenue. Members of the Piedmont Seniors group enjoy their annual festive holiday luncheon at Claremont Country Club.
articles.title: Piedmont Seniors celebrate holiday season with annual luncheon

pages.text: Wednesday, January 4, 2023 21 Features Time for New Year’s financial resolutions It’s that time of year when many of us promise ourselves we’ll go to the gym more, or learn a new language, or take up a musical instrument, or any number of other worthy goals. But this year, when making New Year’s resolutions, why not also consider some financial ones? Here are a few to consider: • Don’t let inflation derail your investment strategy. As you know, inflation was the big financial story of 2022, hitting a 40-year high. And while it may moderate somewhat this year, it will likely still be higher than what we experienced the past decade or so. Even so, it’s a good idea to try not to let today’s inflation harm your investment strategy for the future. That happened last year: More than half of American workers either reduced their contributions to their 401(k) s and other retirement plans or stopped contributing completely during the third quarter of 2022, according to a survey by Allianz Life Insurance of North America. Of course, focusing on your cash flow needs today is certainly understandable, but are there other ways you can free up some money, such as possibly lowering your spending, so you can continue contributing to your retirement accounts? It’s worth the effort because you could spend two or three decades as a retiree. • Control your debts. Inflation can also be a factor in debt management. For example, your credit card debt could rise due to rising prices and variable credit card interest rate increases. By paying your bill each month, you can avoid the effects of rising interest rates. If you do carry a balance, you might be able to transfer it to a lower-rate card, depending on your credit score. And if you’re carrying multiple credit cards, you might benefit by getting a fixed-rate debt consolidation loan. In any case, the lower your debt payments, the more you can invest for your long-term goals. • Review your investment portfolio. At least once a year, you should review your investment portfolio to determine if it’s still appropriate for your goals, risk tolerance and time horizon. But be careful not to make changes just because you feel your recent performance is not what it should have been. When the financial markets are down, as was the case for most of 2022, even quality investments, such as stocks of companies with solid business fundamentals and strong prospects, can see declines in value. But if these investments are still suitable for your portfolio, you may want to keep them. • Prepare for the unexpected. If you encountered a large unexpected expense, such as the need for a major home repair, how would you pay for it? If you didn’t have the money readily available, you might be forced to dip into your long-term investments or retirement accounts. To prevent this, you should build an emergency fund containing three to six months’ worth of living expenses – or a year’s worth, if you’re retired – with the money kept in a low-risk, liquid account. These resolutions can be useful, so try to put them to work in 2023. This article was written by Edward Jones for use by your local Edward Jones Financial Advisor. articles.text: This column appeared in the Post originally on August 3, 2022. It was the 49th column by Will Adams in his biweekly observations and comments on the architecture of Piedmont with examples from around the world. All good designs have at their source a strong, clear vision, or concept. This can be defined as the overall main idea – a view into the future of what the project should look like, feel like and how it will function. The built environment around us – the places we work, live, play and interact with each other – is in reality an ongoing design process that has an important effect on all of our lives, often much more than we realize. As we must continually upgrade, accommodate, and adapt to the new, this process especially requires a strong vision. Walking around Piedmont and looking at the various finished buildings, landscapes, urban designs and planning decisions at various different scales, it is instructive to judge how clear the initial visions were, and how well they were adhered to during the often lengthy design and construction processes. It makes us ask how strong will be our evolving city vision(s) going forward in the next months, years and decades? Inspiration for concept direction in the built environment can be derived from many sources, such as the local architectural history of a place, the logical transportation connections, the solar orientation, a response to a dramatic view, or surrounding existing geographical features. Vision can also be inspired by a need for change, an opportunity to accommodate current needs by adjusting existing patterns to enhance function, aesthetics and/ or to build and strengthen the community. In most cases there are a number of considerations, sometimes competing, that make up a vision. For effective implementation, the best concepts and resulting designs will have a clear hierarchy of importance assigned to each of their parts. It is a way to prevent small or unimportant aspects from controlling the big picture and compromising the vision. Communicating a vision is essential for success. It should be clear enough to be stated, drawn or written. Resorts. He astutely insisted that with any project, the concept and goal should be able to be stated in one concise sentence. He was absolutely right! articles.text: One year ago the Post announced the closure of Children’s Support League, a revered non-profit based principally in Piedmont. The League’s announcement, which appeared in the December 29, 2021 edition of the Post, is reprinted as a reminder of what the community has lost. After almost forty years of serving East Bay children in need, the non-profit Children’s Support League is closing its doors. CSL grew out of a small, dedicated group of local women who originally raised funds exclusively to benefit the Junior Center of Art and Science in Oakland The members soon decided they wanted to expand the range of children they could help with the money they raised and, because they were having fun, they wanted to keep working together. CSL was incorporated as a stand-alone, nonprofit organization in June 1987. To this day, CSL remains an all-volunteer organization that operates with a 3% overhead. As the group learned about local agencies that help at-risk children, they began to see how much need there was in the surrounding community. The fundraising strengths this small organization exhibited were evident from the very beginning. CSL tried various types of fundraisers – a fashion show, a casino night – then settled on an annual kitchen tour. The proceeds from the first tour allowed the group to donate $6,000 to three children’s charities. Eventually, the tour grew beyond the kitchen to become the Heart of the Home Tour each Spring, raising over $4.1 million and supporting programs that serve at-risk children and their families at more than 100 non-profit agencies in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. The last Friday and Saturday in April each year were ‘reserved’ for the CSL Heart of the Home Tour. It soon became an annual tradition for many Bay Area residents. As CSL life member and Piedmont resident Nancy DeRoche explained, “It was a rite of spring – an opportunity for people to do something fun, with friends, spouses, or parents, to walk around beautiful homes and gardens when flowers were in full bloom. Having lunch al fresco at the Community Center and shopping at the boutique added to the feel of a mini-vacation for some of us.” “Our membership never grew much larger than 40 but support from the surrounding community was enormous,” said Mary Jean Haley, who held several CSL board positions before settling in to edit the annual tour book. In the 31 years of the house tour, more than 150 owners graciously opened their homes in Piedmont and Oakland. More than140 local businesses donated as underwriters, and an additional 400 bought ads in the tour book. Many local residents generously contributed funds as individual donors, and volunteers gave endless amounts of time on tour days. Local publications, including the Piedmont Post, helped put out the word about the tour each year. For Miriam Mangini, who joined CSL in 1989, the most important thing about the organization was “helping children other than my own.” She and her husband John have three children, and Miriam was very involved in the Piedmont schools throughout her children’s years there. Reaching out beyond her own community to help children was important to her. Like many other members she took on a wide variety of CSL jobs, among them President, VP, Tour Chair, and Treasurer. Miriam is one of many long-time CSL members who mention how much they still value and enjoy the friendships that developed as members worked together each year to bring all the facets of the tour together. Lillis Stern, who also had three children in the Piedmont schools, one a senior this year, says she first attended the tour in 2001. By the following year she was already on the grants committee, which researched agencies that serve children and determined where the CSL grants should go. “I was excited to learn about the various agencies in the area and what they were doing for kids,” she says. “I was impressed by the ability of such a small group to raise so much money.” Donna Somerville, Executive Director of Grateful Gatherings, a charity that helps homeless families as they transition into housing, recently said, “CSL is one of those rare organizations where their heart and their resources went straight to those who needed their help. They had a clear mission to help children and that is what they did in so many ways. “The families we help are mostly sleeping on the floor. CSL contributed funds for us to buy beds for children. The reaction of a child when they see their very own warm and cozy bed for the first time is pric^S eless; it is something you will never forget. CSL provided that moment for many of the children we have helped over the years. Thank you CSL for caring enough to make such a huge difference in the lives of children in the Bay Area,” Somerville said. Even as CSL is reluctantly closing its doors, long-time members recognize that the needs of at-risk children are ongoing and, in this post-pandemic era, even greater than before. “We are so sorry to close up,” said long-term CSL member and former president and tour chair Jan Howland, “Our funding model just doesn’t work right now. We don’t have the members and volunteers we used to have, and it’s much harder to find homeowners willing to open their homes for the tour. We are hoping to find another way to continue to help, and I think I speak for all of our members.

articles.text: The Piedmont Recreation Depar tment’s Walking on Wednesdays group finished off their 2022 walks last Wednesday with an almost unblemished record of walks without rain. Only one time in October on a visit to Hampton Park, the group was caught in a brief shower. The walk on December 28 was a continuation of their good fortune. It had rained the day before, and was forecast to rain again on Thursday, but Wednesday was clear, cool, and beautiful. There was a great turnout of 40 walkers and two K-9 best for the walk organized by Harriette Louie in the temporary absence of Dick Carter. She took the group on an uphill hike with gradual elevation beginning on Highland Avenue, going to Sheridan Avenue, and then continuing to climb steadily up Caperton Avenue to Mountain Avenue. Before ascending Bellevue Avenue, the walkers stopped to greet an old friend, the giant redwood tree at the intersection of Mountain and Bellevue. The group continued their walk and explored Pacific, Hagar, Mountain, Blair, Alta and Scenic Avenues, enjoying the views of Oakland, San Francisco, and the Bay as they did. At 37 Bellevue, the walkers admired the home’s expansive grounds. Sherry Jacobs recounted the past glory of Piedmont High’s bird-calling contests and a reunion at the home where the contest winners reprised their winning birdcalls. Later, the group could not walk past 575 Blair and without taking a photo and recalling that this was the house where Jack London lived while he wrote his famous novel Call of the Wild. The group then descended to Highland and back to the Exedra, concluding a satisfying 2.3-mile hike on another beautiful morning with friends. It was a great way to end their 2022 Wednesday walks. The Walking on Wednesdays group meets every Wednesday at the Exedra (Highland & Magnolia Avenues) at 10:30 a.m. Everyone is invited to join the group and there is no cost. New walkers and their friendly K-9 best friends are especially welcome. Register with the Piedmont Recreation Department at https:// tinyurl.com/3ethkehu. Members of the Walking on Wednesdays group stop for a photo in front of the house on Blair Avenue in which Jack London wrote Call of the Wild. Participants on the December 28 walk included Albert Chen, Brenda Ferrero, Jim Kuo, Elane Rehr, Laura Goldman, Nancy Henn, Mike Henn, Jim Kellogg, Martin Levy, Marion Lim Yankowitz, Claudia Lopez, Mary Hedley, Sherry Jacobs, Kathy Rolefson, Rob Smith, Kat Lang, Charlene Louie, Phil Witte, Judith Lee, Edith Lee, Helene Farber, Elizabeth Richter, Bill Ahern, Pat Keller, Melba Yee, Helen Dong, Quincy Dong, Wenny Young, Lisa Euphrat, Ian Morgan, Ann Quinby, and Harriette Louie.
