Courteous, Reliable Service Eric (510) 841-2891 (510) 982-9757 cell City Milestones One year ago the Post announced the closure of Children’s Support League, a revered non-profit based principally in Piedmont. The League’s announcement, which appeared in the December 29, 2021 edition of the Post, is reprinted as a reminder of what the community has lost. After almost forty years of serving East Bay children in need, the non-profit Children’s Support League is closing its doors. CSL grew out of a small, dedicated group of local women who originally raised funds exclusively to benefit the Junior Center of Art and Science in Oakland The members soon decided they wanted to expand the range of children they could help with the money they raised and, because they were having fun, they wanted to keep working together. CSL was incorporated as a stand-alone, nonprofit organization in June 1987. To this day, CSL remains an all-volunteer organization that operates with a 3% overhead. As the group learned about local agencies that help at-risk children, they began to see how much need there was in the surrounding community. The fundraising strengths this small organization exhibited were evident from the very beginning. CSL tried various types of fundraisers – a fashion show, a casino night – then settled on an annual kitchen tour. The proceeds from the first tour allowed the group to donate $6,000 to three children’s charities. Eventually, the tour grew beyond the kitchen to become the Heart of the Home Tour each Spring, raising over $4.1 million and supporting programs that serve at-risk children and their families at more than 100 non-profit agencies in Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. The last Friday and Saturday in April each year were ‘reserved’ for the CSL Heart of the Home Tour. It soon became an annual tradition for many Bay Area residents. As CSL life member and Piedmont resident Nancy DeRoche explained, “It was a rite of spring – an opportunity for people to do something fun, with friends, spouses, or parents, to walk around beautiful homes and gardens when flowers were in full bloom. Having lunch al fresco at the Community Center and shopping at the boutique added to the feel of a mini-vacation for some of us.” “Our membership never grew much larger than 40 but support from the surrounding community was enormous,” said Mary Jean Haley, who held several CSL board positions before settling in to edit the annual tour book. In the 31 years of the house tour, more than 150 owners graciously opened their homes in Piedmont and Oakland. More than140 local businesses donated as underwriters, and an additional 400 bought ads in the tour book. Many local residents generously contributed funds as individual donors, and volunteers gave endless amounts of time on tour days. Local publications, including the Piedmont Post, helped put out the word about the tour each year. For Miriam Mangini, who joined CSL in 1989, the most important thing about the organization was “helping children other than my own.” She and her husband John have three children, and Miriam was very involved in the Piedmont schools throughout her children’s years there. Reaching out beyond her own community to help children was important to her. Like many other members she took on a wide variety of CSL jobs, among them President, VP, Tour Chair, and Treasurer. Miriam is one of many long-time CSL members who mention how much they still value and enjoy the friendships that developed as members worked together each year to bring all the facets of the tour together. Lillis Stern, who also had three children in the Piedmont schools, one a senior this year, says she first attended the tour in 2001. By the following year she was already on the grants committee, which researched agencies that serve children and determined where the CSL grants should go. “I was excited to learn about the various agencies in the area and what they were doing for kids,” she says. “I was impressed by the ability of such a small group to raise so much money.” Donna Somerville, Executive Director of Grateful Gatherings, a charity that helps homeless families as they transition into housing, recently said, “CSL is one of those rare organizations where their heart and their resources went straight to those who needed their help. They had a clear mission to help children and that is what they did in so many ways. “The families we help are mostly sleeping on the floor. CSL contributed funds for us to buy beds for children. The reaction of a child when they see their very own warm and cozy bed for the first time is pric^S eless; it is something you will never forget. CSL provided that moment for many of the children we have helped over the years. Thank you CSL for caring enough to make such a huge difference in the lives of children in the Bay Area,” Somerville said. Even as CSL is reluctantly closing its doors, long-time members recognize that the needs of at-risk children are ongoing and, in this post-pandemic era, even greater than before. “We are so sorry to close up,” said long-term CSL member and former president and tour chair Jan Howland, “Our funding model just doesn’t work right now. We don’t have the members and volunteers we used to have, and it’s much harder to find homeowners willing to open their homes for the tour. We are hoping to find another way to continue to help, and I think I speak for all of our members.

articles.text: Ambrose Bierce was one of the most original writers in American history. His magnum opus, The Devil’s Dictionary, reveals his pugnacious sarcasm to best effect. While there is no information about Bierce’s interest in music, I obtained a document purportedly by Bierce. This “lexicon of musical terms“ has all the earmarks of Bierce’s sharply-pointed humor. Here are a few examples: Piccolo: noun, A small instrument which causes considerable bodily injury. The bane of audiologists. Trombone: noun, the comedian of the orchestra. Given to scatological humor and flatulence. Usually played by mischievous boys who want to annoy girls. Percussion instruments: plural, tone-deaf musicians released on early parole. Some of them become conductors. Violin: noun, when played well, you think you are in heaven. When played badly you think you are in hell. Violin bow: a club made of wood resembling a slender baseball bat and strung with horse hair from the rear end of a horse. Generally used to beat a Violin black and blue. Practice: noun or a verb, an unpleasant hour devoted to repeating your mistakes ad nauseam. Concert: noun, practicing in public. See above. Conductor: noun of questionable progeny. Literally the prince of fools. Usually an egotist from highest Valhalla who thinks he knows everything. Despised by members of the orchestra even though they aspire to the position. Please note: It is not a violation of Section 1771.1 for an unregistered contractor to submit a bid that is authorized by Section 7029.1 of the Business and Professions Code or by Section 10164 or 20103.5 of the Public Contract Code, provided the contractor is registered to perform public work pursuant to Section 1725.5 at the time the contract is awarded. Any bids submitted without proof that Bidder and any listed subcontractor(s) are currently registered and qualified to perform public work, pursuant to Labor Code Section 1725.5, shall not be accepted by the City. In accordance with California Civil Code Section 1771.4, the project is subject to compliance monitoring and enforcement by the Department of Industrial Relations. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 3300, a valid class A or class C32 California contractor’s license is required to bid on the project. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to postpone the date and time for the opening of proposals at any time prior to the date and time announced in the advertisement in accordance with applicable law. The City of Piedmont reserves the right to reject any and all bids or to waive any defects or irregularity in bidding in accordance with applicable law. In accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20103.8, if the City elects to award a contract for performance of the project, the contract will be awarded in accordance with California Public Contract Code Section 20162 and other applicable law to the responsible bidder submitting a responsive bid with the lowest total bid price for the base bid without consideration of the bid price for any additive or deductive items. All bids will remain valid for 90 days after the bid opening. Except as permitted by law and subject to all applicable remedies, including forfeiture of bidder’s security, bidders may not withdraw their bid during the 90- day period after the bid opening. articles.text: Two juveniles broke into a classroom at Piedmont Middle School on Saturday, December 17 at 3:25 p.m. hours and graffitied an anti-Asian slur on a wall. The two juvenile suspects entered room 306 on the top floor of the school by prying open a window. Damage was estimated at $100. The graffiti was reported to police three days later on Tuesday, December 20 at 10:04 a.m., and the students were identified as Piedmont Middle School Students following an investigation. A school administrator met with the students involved and their parents. On December 22, School Superintendent Donald Evans provided the following information on the incident: Dear PUSD Community: I’m providing you with an update involving the break-in, vandalism and anti-Asian graffiti at Piedmont Middle School last weekend. After conducting an investigation, the school has identified the students responsible for the damage. The individuals are PMS students and their parents have been notified of the situation. PMS administration believes the students’ actions were not targeting the Asian community with any malicious intent. However, there was a school break-in resulted in damage to school property. Therefore, consequences must be given in accordance with District policy. While the students took responsibility for their actions, it’s important to use this opportunity as a “teachable moment.” We’ve outlined several actions for each student to complete. My goal is to not only ensure this never happens again, but to educate these students in a way where they can grow from this experience and contribute to the community in a positive way. Following Winter Break, we will also be working to bring our community together to understand the harm that came from this incident. PMS has a plan in place to provide learning opportunities for its students and respond to those directly impacted. The PMS Parents Club, in partnership with the Piedmont Racial Equity Campaign (PREC), will be planning an evening event in January. We will provide additional details after Winter Break. The school has also reached out to the Asian-American Pacific Islander community to organize efforts on a District-wide level. My thanks to PMS staff, the Piedmont Police Department, and to all who came forward with information ensuring an efficient and thorough investigation. Our goal is to use this unfortunate event as an opportunity to learn and grow together. We will continue working toward providing an environment where everyone feels safe and has the opportunity to succeed without fear of hate or bias. I welcome your suggestions and feedback. Thank you for your time and I wish you a fun and safe Winter Break. Happy Holidays. –Donald Evans Interim Superintendent

articles.text: • • • • • • Have insurance policies handy and take photos of each room in your home. Clean on and around your property as needed: gutters, rain downspouts, driveways, culverts, trash and debris around fences and gardens. Clear basement drains. Have sandbags on hand in case of flooding. Residents can get free sandbags at the City’s Corporation Yard (898 Red Rock Road) 7:00 a.m.-3:30 p.m., Monday-Friday. Check submersible pumps and sump pumps to make sure they are operating properly. Keep flashlights and spare batteries on hand in case of power failure. Stock up on food, water, necessary medications, pet needs, and other essential supplies in case of road closures or power outages that last for several days. Avoid flooded areas It is never safe to drive or walk into flood waters. During an intense storm, water levels and the rate at which water is flowing can change rapidly. A mere 6 inches of fast-moving flood water can knock over an adult, and 12 inches of rushing water is enough to carry away most cars. • Do not walk through or allow children to play in flood waters. • Do not drive through pooled water that you cannot see the depth of. • Do not drive around the barriers blocking a flooded road. The road may have collapsed under that water. Prepare for power outages Storm damage to power lines may cause outages. Stay informed by signing up to get outage alerts from PG&E for your address by text, email, or phone. PG&E also has an online Pge.com/outagecenter which is updated every 15 minutes.
